sections.en: Torah as Companionship in a World of Toil

items.h: In a world of movement and distraction, Torah joins a person to the whole creation and provides the truest companionship; Shabbat reveals the rest beyond worldly toil.

Seif 1 — Torah as the Companion of Creation
Torah connects a person to all creation and sustains him through the toil and distraction of this world.

p: הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה צָרִיךְ לְצַוְותָא,
Man in this world needs companionship,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת1 Berakhot 6b — “The sum of the matter, when all has been heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole man.” What is meant by “for this is the whole man”? R. Elazar said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said — the entire world was created only for the sake of this one. R. Abba bar Kahana said: This one is worth as much as the entire world. R. Shimon ben Azzai says — and some report it in the name of R. Shimon ben Zoma — the entire world was created only to be a companion to this one. Rashi: "Only for the sake of this one" — that is, in order that this one be created; and "to be a companion" he renders by the Old French for keeping a man company. Maharsha: By its plain sense the verse should have said "hear it all" in the imperative, as it goes on "fear God"; but since it says "all having been heard," the verse is speaking in praise of the God-fearing man, and so the close of the verse, "for this is the whole man," must be his praise as well. The three Sages therefore do not disagree — each took up one of the three worlds. "The entire world was created only for this one" takes in even the world of the angels, which was created for the sake of man, who has free choice, so that he might earn merit; "he is worth as much as the entire world" is said of the middle world; and "the entire world was created only to be a companion to him" of the lower world, created only to attend upon him and do his service, as Ben Zoma said, "Blessed is He who created all these to serve me." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 1): R. Elazar's "the entire world was created only for this one" means, as was said above, that the world was created for the sake of the fear of Heaven. He is "worth as much as the entire world" because creation is due to the world on one ground, that it is the totality of the world, and due to the God-fearing man on a second, that he makes himself an effect subordinate to his Cause; the two grounds are equal, and so the two are equal. Ben Azzai held that neither may be said, for the Holy One, blessed be He, surely willed to create the world in its own right; rather the God-fearing man is the essence of the creation, being the effect for whom creation is fitting, and the rest of the world was created for his sake. (ו:):
just as they stated in Berakhot (6b):
"כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ לֹא נִבְרָא אֶלָּא לְצַוֵּת לָזֶה",
"The entire world was created solely to accompany this one,"
שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ דְּהוּא צָרִיךְ לְצַוְותָא דִּנְבְרָאִים.
inferring from this that he requires the company of created beings.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֵירוּבִין נד2 Eruvin 54a — R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: One who walks along the road and has no escort with him should occupy himself with Torah, as it is stated: "For they shall be a graceful wreath [livyat chen] for your head" (Proverbs 1:9). Maharsha: "For they shall be a graceful wreath [livyat chen]" — occupation with Torah gives him grace upon the road in the eyes of all who see him, as we say in the Wayfarer's Prayer, "and grant us grace and kindness … in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see us." Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 62): One who walks the road needs an escort because he departs from settled habitation, which is the very substance of existence, for "He did not create it a waste, He formed it to be inhabited"; where existence is not, he has cause to fear that he will come to non-existence, and this is why they said that all roads are presumed dangerous. Now the Torah is the order of existence, so that when a man occupies himself with it he is joined and attached to that order, and it is this that guards him from all evil, that nothing outside the order should befall him. Therefore they said that if he has no escort he should occupy himself with Torah, for then he will certainly not be in danger..):
And our Sages of blessed memory taught (Eruvin 54a):
"הַמְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְאֵין לוֹ לְוָיָה יַעֲסֹק בַּתּוֹרָה",
"One who travels on the road without an escort should engage in Torah,"
וְהָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כֻּלּוֹ נִקְרָא הִילוּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ,
and this entire world is termed 'walking on the road,'

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה כא.)3 Sotah 21a — And [Scripture compared] the Torah to light, to tell you: just as light protects forever, so the Torah protects forever. And it says: "When you walk it shall lead you; when you lie down it shall watch over you; and when you awake it shall talk with you" (Proverbs 6:22). "When you walk it shall lead you" — this is in this world. "When you lie down it shall watch over you" — this is death. "And when you awake it shall talk with you" — this is in the time to come. Rashi: "It shall talk with you" — it will plead your merit on your behalf. Maharsha: This verse, which immediately precedes "For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light," also speaks of the Torah and teaches that it protects forever: in this world "it shall lead you" — in the sense of giving you rest from all troubles; when you lie in the grave "it shall watch over you" against the beating of the grave; and in the World to Come "it shall talk with you," pleading on your behalf against the judgment of Gehinnom. As for Tosafot's difficulty — that by the Gemara's conclusion a mitzva too protects forever — a mitzva protects forever only in this world, whereas the Torah protects even in the World to Come from the judgment of Gehinnom, as the verse "and when you awake it shall talk with you" shows. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 21a): The Torah is intellectual, and whatever is intellectual does not fall under time; therefore it protects forever, as befits that which is beyond time and has no change, whereas the mitzva, like everything physical, falls under time and comes to an end, and so protects only for the moment. And since light signifies complete existence — without light nothing has existence, which is why a blind man is considered as though dead — one who holds fast to the Torah, which is complete light, cannot be abandoned by it to nonexistence: in this world, where a man is a "walker" who has no rest and may do something that brings him to ruin, it leads him; after death, the time of dissolution, it guards him from loss and gives him existence; and in the time to come, when he returns to life, it gives him speech, which is life — "it shall talk with you." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 10): Death stems from the first corruption of Adam, and its repair is through occupation with words of Torah, of which it is said: "When you walk it shall lead you" — this is this world; "when you lie down it shall watch over you" — this is death; "and when you awake it shall talk with you" — in the time to come. For then, at the resurrection of the dead, the clarification will be complete, [showing] that death was only like sleep in this world, as the Sages called death "when he lay down to sleep," and the dew of Torah revives him. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): The world is full of turmoil and has no rest; therefore they said, "When you walk it shall lead you" — in this world, for this world is the time of walking, since "man is born to toil." But there are those whose toil is with knowledge and skill in deed, and whose walking is in holiness. The angels are called "standing," for they remain on the one level at which they were created, but man walks constantly from level to level and has no rest, like the righteous mentioned above — and this is truly the ultimate rest. Beis Yaakov (Vayeishev 5): One who has no words of Torah has none of the good itself, for through words of Torah a person is awakened to all good things, as they expounded: "When you walk it shall lead you" — in this world; "when you lie down it shall watch over you" — this is death; "and when you awake it shall talk with you" — in the time to come. In the time to come the Blessed One will fill the treasuries of Israel and reveal to their eyes the light hidden in the performance of the mitzvos, and then they will see that all the knowledge, intentions and lights Israel had in this world were like a dream compared to its interpretation. עַל פָּסוּק "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ תַּנְחֶה וְגוֹמֵר" – בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sotah 21a) on the verse 'When you walk, it will lead you, etc.' – in this world.
וּכְשֶׁאֵין לוֹ צַוְותָא יַעֲסֹק בַּתּוֹרָה,
So when one lacks companionship, he should immerse himself in Torah,
שֶׁהוּא דְּפוּס מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית וְשֶׁל כָּל הַנִּבְרָאִים,
for it is the blueprint of Creation and of all created beings,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א,
as they said in Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 1),
וְנִמְצָא יֵשׁ לוֹ צַוְותָא שֶׁל כָּל הַבְּרִיאָה וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ.
and it turns out that he has the companionship of all Creation and the entire world.
וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא עוֹלָם הַזֶּה "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ",
For this reason this world is called 'when you walk,'
דְּהִילוּךְ רָצָה לוֹמַר טִרְדָּא,
since walking signifies preoccupation,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (יא4 Berakhot 11a — As it was taught: “When you sit in your house” — this excludes one who is engaged in a commandment; “and when you walk on the way” — this excludes a bridegroom. From here they said: One who marries a virgin is exempt, and one who marries a widow is obligated. … If so, even one who marries a widow [should be exempt]! — This one is preoccupied, and that one is not. If the exemption is on account of preoccupation, then even one whose ship sank at sea [should be exempt]! And should you say that is indeed so, why then did R. Abba bar Zavda say in the name of Rav: A mourner is obligated in all the commandments stated in the Torah except tefillin, since “splendor” is said of them, as it is said: “Bind your splendor upon you” (Ezekiel 24:17)? — There [the bridegroom] is preoccupied with the preoccupation of a commandment; here [the mourner] is preoccupied with the preoccupation of an optional matter. Rashi: Rashi explains that the bridegroom needed a verse of his own because the exclusion drawn from "in your house" removes only one busy with the actual work of a commandment, while the bridegroom's is an occupation of the mind alone — he is thinking about the consummation of the marriage. On the resolution at the end: since all we are deriving here is an exclusion — "excluding a bridegroom" — it is enough that what the verse excludes be a preoccupation belonging to a commandment [and not preoccupation of every kind]. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 13): One kind of sinking into forgetfulness of the Blessed One comes through the power of action — zeal and excessive effort in worldly affairs, the rich man with his money and trade, the ruler with his rule — until a man has not a moment's rest to take time to remember the Blessed One, for he is preoccupied and confused by his affairs. This is called Ashur, for Ashur denotes strength and power and also way and walking, which is preoccupation, as the Sages said on the verse "and when you walk on the way" that he is preoccupied..):
as they stated in Berakhot (11a):
"בְּלֶכְתְּךָ וְגוֹמֵר" – הָא טִרְדָּא דְּמִצְוָה.
'When you walk, etc.' – this refers to preoccupation with a mitzvah.
וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כֻּלּוֹ טִרְדָּא,
And this world is entirely preoccupation,
דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא יוֹם הַמִּיתָה בַּתַּלְמוּד "נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ", שֶׁנָּח מִטִּרְדָּתוֹ,
which is why the day of death is called in the Talmud 'his soul rested,' meaning he rested from his toil,
כִּי אָדָם לְעָמָל יוּלָּד.
for 'man is born to toil.'

וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ב דִּבְרָכוֹת הֲלָכָה ד, יז5 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 — R. Yirmiah said in the name of R. Elazar: One who prayed and did not direct his heart — if he knows that he can go back and direct his heart, let him pray; and if not, let him not pray. R. Chiya the Great said: I have never in my days had proper intention. Once I sought to concentrate, and my mind wandered and I said: Who enters before the king first, the arkafta [a Persian official] or the Exilarch? Shmuel said: I counted chicks. R. Bun bar Chiya said: I counted courses of masonry. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "I have never in my days had proper intention"): It was because he was preoccupied with meditating upon Torah — and so with all those that follow. The "arkafta" is the alkafta, an official who ranks above the Exilarch, and his musing was whether those admitted before the king are presented from the lower rank upward or from the higher downward, since the alkafta precedes the Exilarch. "Courses of masonry" are courses of a building.:):
And therefore they said in the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 2:4, 17b):
"אֲנָא מִן יוֹמַי לָא כִּוַּוֹנִית",
'In all my days, I never achieved full concentration,'
כִּי טִרְדָּא הוּא הֵיפֶךְ הַכַּוָּנָה כִּדְאִיתָא בִּבְרָכוֹת שָׁם,
because preoccupation is the antithesis of focused intention, as brought in Berakhot there,
וּלְכָךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר כַּוָּנָה שְׁלֵימָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּלָל.
and hence complete intention is wholly impossible in this world.
וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא שַׁבָּת "מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא" שֶׁהוּא יוֹם מְנוּחָה,
Therefore Shabbat is called 'a semblance of the World to Come,' being a day of rest,
וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה זְמַן הַטָּרְחָא,
whereas this world is the era of labor,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.)6 Avodah Zarah 3a — They said before Him: Master of the Universe, give it to us anew and we will perform it. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: Fools of the world! One who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat; one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat — from where will he eat on Shabbat? Rashi: "On the eve of Shabbat" means in this world. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a, s.v. "and sukkah is its name"): Since the nations claim to be fit for the Torah, which is intellectual and beyond nature, He gave them the commandment that shows a person going out of his nature: leaving his fixed, natural dwelling to sit in the shade of the sukkah. The nations, whose whole conduct is natural, cannot bear this and kick at it; Israel too are somewhat natural, for man is not an angel, and are exempt from the sukkah when it causes them suffering, yet they do not kick, for they desire and love to go beyond nature, only that at such times it is impossible for them. This shows that the Torah, the whole of which is beyond nature, is not fit for the nations at all. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a, s.v. "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat"): That is, this world is the physical world, which is always in potential, and therefore commandments and good deeds belong to it, for in it things go out from potential into actuality. But in the World to Come a person is already in actuality, and going out into actuality has no place there, since it is not physical; the World to Come is therefore cessation and rest. Hence he said that one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat, the day of action, will eat on Shabbat, the day of rest, on which nothing goes out into actuality — and so the commandments pertain to this world alone. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 25): Shabbat is [the day on which God Himself is one's light, needing no fire of fear]; nevertheless one must toil to cook the food on the eve of Shabbat, for "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, what will he eat on Shabbat?" and "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward": this light does not come to a person by itself. So too the Shabbat lamp must be lit from the eve of Shabbat, for on Shabbat there is no longer time to arouse fear, the day being entirely love and cleaving to God. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): This world is the world of toil, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat" refers to the world to come, the day that is entirely Shabbat, where there is no doing even of Torah and mitzvot, as they said, "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; and Shabbat is a semblance of the world to come, the time of the Blessed One's rest. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Sukkah): Shabbat alludes to the future, when there will be no labor, but only what a person acquired in this world through his deeds will then be fixed in his heart, according to how much he toiled in this world. Therefore all labors are forbidden on Shabbat in this world, and only what one toiled for on the eve of Shabbat does one eat on Shabbat. Beis Yaakov (Vayeishev 3): All the possession a person acquires for himself in the world of action comes only from performing the mitzvot, and clarity [of understanding] alone does not suffice; by this he acquires the life of the world to come, for this world is like the eve of Shabbat and the world to come like Shabbat, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will have what to eat on Shabbat." Tiferes Yosef (Shemini Atzeres 4): A person calls his labor "toil" only where he does not see its purpose; on Shabbat he attains the light of the Blessed One and recognizes that he attained it through the work of the six days. This is "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat": through the toil and labor he expended he attains this light, and so he recognizes retroactively that all the activity of the six weekdays was not futile toil for him either. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 18): In the future the nations will want to begin from the start, without first entering the gate of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Blessed One answers that this is impossible: "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat" means that had they first refined themselves to be included in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, within "every citizen in Israel" [which includes converts], they too could have kept the mitzvah of sukkah. But to begin now without that prior inclusion is impossible, for one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat has nothing to eat on Shabbat, and from where would he gain a share in the mitzvah of sukkah?: "מִי שֶׁטָּרַח בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת וְכוּלֵי".
as they taught (Avodah Zarah 3a): 'He who toiled on the eve of Shabbat, etc.'

sections.en: Intellect, Will, and the Gathering of the Soul

items.h: The mind and heart shape one another; sin fragments their powers, while divine help gathers the scattered faculties of the soul into integrated righteousness.

Seif 1 — Intellect, Will, and Inner Integration
Mind and desire shape one another, while divine help gathers the soul's scattered powers into wholeness.

p: הַשֵּׂכֶל וְהָרָצוֹן הֵם שְׁנֵי מַנְהִיגֵי הָאָדָם,
The intellect and the will are the two governors of man,

דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי סוֹף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דִּבְרָכוֹת (ט7 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 1:5 — "You shall not commit adultery" corresponds to "You shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes" (Numbers 15:39). R. Levi said: The heart and the eye are the two agents of sin. It is written, "My son, give Me your heart, and let your eyes observe My ways" (Proverbs 23:26). The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you give Me your heart and your eye, I know that you are Mine. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "It is written, 'My son, give Me your heart'"): He expounds "and your eyes" as belonging to what precedes it: if you give Me your heart and your eyes, then "they will observe My ways" — as he concludes, "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you give Me your heart and your eye, I know that you are Mine." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 35): Because of the Yerushalmi's "if you give Me your eye and your heart, I know that you are Mine," they expounded "you shall guard yourself [from every evil thing]" as a warning against [impure] thoughts: even where such a thought incurs no punishment, the mitzvah of guarding one's heart rests upon him. For the essence of Jewishness is in the heart, and fear [of Heaven], the essence of what God asks of you, is only in the heart. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): In the Yerushalmi's "if you give Me your eye and your heart," the eye is wisdom ("the wise man's eyes are in his head"; "who is wise? one who sees what will be born") and the heart is the understanding of the heart, the two powers by which a person overcomes his inclination and gives birth to a good deed; [the Yerushalmi] reverses the order of the verse "after your hearts and after your eyes." A person need give the Blessed One only these, while the completion comes from the Blessed One's help. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 10): Of the righteous man whose nature is not evil Ezekiel speaks in the future tense, yet "his eyes he did not lift" and "his neighbor's wife he did not defile" are in the past tense, for these are the two agents of which the Sages said, "if you give Me your eye and your heart, I know that you are Mine." Once he has handed these two over to the Blessed One in actual deed, through the effort of turning from evil when a transgression came his way and he was saved, he no longer needs effort in deed, only that his heart be ready to turn from evil and do good when the occasion comes. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 6): David, praised as "beautiful of eyes", was truly pure of all the filth of this world's desires, and this showed in the eyes, for the eye and the heart are the two agents of sin, and "if you give Me your eye and your heart, I know that you are Mine." The heart is hidden from all ("man sees with the eyes, but God sees into the heart"), whereas the eyes are in the open. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 190): The eye and the heart are the agents of sin, as the Yerushalmi says, and likewise agents for good, as it says there, "if you give Me your eye and your heart"; they are the two levels of seeing and knowing, of which it is said "Send Your light and Your truth," the essence of seeing being light. They are the levels of Jacob and Joseph: "truth to Jacob" and "light is sown for the righteous.":):
which is why they said in the Yerushalmi at the end of the first chapter of Berakhot (9b):
"אִי אַתְּ יָהֵיב עֵינָא וְלִבָּא לִי, אֲנָא יָדַע דְּאַתְּ דִּילִי".
'If you give your eye and your heart to Me, I know that you are Mine.'
"עַיִן" רָצָה לוֹמַר עֵינֵי הַשֵּׂכֶל,
'Eye' denotes the eyes of intellect,

וְאָמְרוּ (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כח:)8 Avodah Zarah 28b — There was a certain maidservant in the house of Mar Shmuel whose eye became inflamed on Shabbat. She cried out, and there was none who attended to her, and her eye burst. The next day Mar Shmuel went out and expounded: An eye that has rebelled — it is permitted to apply eye salve to it on Shabbat. What is the reason? Because the tendons of the eye are bound up with the understanding of the heart. Rashi: "An eye that has rebelled" — it seeks to come out [of its socket], like a man who rebels and goes out; and its being "bound up with the heart" means that the light of the eye is intertwined with and held fast in the membranes of the heart [so that the danger is to life itself]. Tosafos (s.v. "the tendons of the eye are bound up with the heart"): Rashi explains that the light of the eye depends on the membranes of the heart, but it seems rather that the reading is "upon the understanding of the heart" — that is, the eye's seeing depends upon the heart's understanding. Accordingly the word for "tendons" is spelled with a shin, from "I behold him," or with a samekh, from the expression "he surveys his property"; and "understanding" is with a bet, from the word for comprehension, as is said of the Chariot, "he would see with the understanding of the heart." Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 190): Joseph [whose level is the eye] reported that his brothers "cast their eyes" [on the daughters of the land], for he held that "the tendons of the eye are bound up with the heart," as they also said, "a bride whose eyes are beautiful [needs no examination of her whole body]." But in truth the essence is the heart, "for from it are the issues of life," since in it lies the essence of vitality and of cleaving to the living God.: "שׁוּרְיָינָא דְּעֵינָא בְּלִבָּא תַּלְיָא",
yet they stated (Avodah Zarah 28b): 'The sinews of the eye are dependent on the heart,'
כִּי הָעִיקָּר הַלֵּב כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים.
for the heart is primary, as 'from it flow the springs of life.'
וְהַשֵּׂכֶל נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר הָרָצוֹן,
And intellect is drawn after desire,

כְּעִנְיַן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שְׁמוֹת כג, ח)9 Exodus 23:8 — And you shall take no bribe, for the bribe blinds the clear-sighted and perverts the words of the righteous. Rashi: "You shall take no bribe" — even in order to judge truthfully, and all the more so in order to pervert judgment, for the perverting of judgment is already forbidden elsewhere: "you shall not pervert justice." "It blinds the clear-sighted" — even one learned in Torah who takes a bribe will in the end have his mind confounded, forget his learning and lose the light of his eyes; and "the words of the righteous" means words that are just, true judgments.: "כִּי הַשֹּׁחַד יְעַוֵּר וְגוֹמֵר",
as it is written (Exodus 23:8): 'For bribery blinds, etc.,'
כִּי הָרָצוֹן מַטֶּה הַשֵּׂכֶל.
because the will bends the intellect.

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב:)10 Yoma 72b — R. Shmuel bar Nachmani said that R. Yonatan said: What is meant by "Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, seeing he has no heart?" Woe to them, the enemies of the Torah scholars [that is, the scholars themselves], who occupy themselves with Torah and have no fear of Heaven in them. R. Yannai would proclaim: A pity for him who has no courtyard, yet makes a gate for his courtyard. Rashi: "Courtyard": a court. "And makes a gate for his courtyard": for the Torah is only a gate through which to enter into the fear of Heaven; therefore he must acquire the fear of Heaven first. Maharsha (s.v. "seeing he has no heart"): Taken plainly [the verse is difficult], for even one who has no heart to understand should study Torah, which "makes wise the simple"; therefore they said that a fool can certainly come to wisdom through study, but "he has no heart" means that it is not in his heart to fulfill it, only to acquire a name, as Rashi explains on the verse, that is, he has no fear of Heaven. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 4): Casting off the yoke of the fear of Heaven is graver in Torah scholars than in other men, since such a one knows his Maker and leads others to cast it off as well; hence "woe," for they were fit for a great and supreme level, and now that level is turned for them to evil, more so than for others. R. Yannai speaks of a scholar who is not careful in his deeds, though he does not sin outright, of whom one would not say "woe," yet it is "a pity": for Torah and wisdom are the gate by which one enters, while through the fear of Heaven a man has his dwelling with the Blessed One, as it is written, "The fear of the Lord is His treasure," so that the fear of Heaven is the house. One who has Torah without the fear of Heaven has made a gate where there is no house; his Torah is in vain, and he is further from the Blessed One than another man. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on completing the Talmud 5): "Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to acquire wisdom, seeing he has no heart" speaks of one who has Torah [without fear of Heaven]: lacking fear of Heaven, the fencing of the heart from evil desires, he wants to put his effort into wisdom alone, and of him they said, "whoever says he has only Torah does not have [even Torah]," for effort applies only below wisdom, not to wisdom itself. Through this he comes to deny the Oral Torah and believe only in the Written Torah.: "לָמָּה זֶה מְחִיר וְגוֹמֵר וְלֵב אָיִן".
Regarding this they said (Yoma 72b): ''Why is there a purchase price... when there is no heart?'

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ גַּם כֵּן (בְּמִדְבַּר רַבָּה י, ב11 Bamidbar Rabbah 10:2 — "My son, give Me your heart, and let your eyes observe My ways" (Proverbs 23:26). What did the Holy One, blessed be He, see, that He asked of Israel the heart and the eyes, that they should follow after Him? Because transgression depends upon them, as it is written: "You shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes" (Numbers 15:39). The eye and the heart are the two agents of sin. "For a harlot is a deep pit" (Proverbs 23:27) — as Moses said, "after which you stray" (Numbers 15:39), to say that harlotry depends upon them: the eyes see the harlot, and the heart contemplates her. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 16): The Sages' words "the eye sees, the heart desires, and the organs of action complete [the deed]" describe three levels. Wisdom is the stage still at "the eye sees" alone, momentary and not yet spread through to the end, unlike prophecy, which has passed through all the levels and is fully possessed; yet wisdom is superior, in the manner of "better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul" (Ecclesiastes 6:9). Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 1): A thought that reaches the root of wisdom in the brain is joined to the understanding in the heart, so that it is at once felt in the heart and gives birth to the powers of action, as in "the eye sees, the heart desires, and the organs of action complete [the deed]"; for we find seeing associated with wisdom, as it is written, "my heart has seen much wisdom" (Ecclesiastes 1:16). Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Tetzaveh): The kapores corresponds to the heart and the menorah to the eyes, and these alone were of pure gold [without a core of acacia wood], because in them a person must be clean of any self-interest in this world, since "the eye and the heart are the two agents of sin: the eye sees and the heart desires." The eye should be stripped of all worldly desire and serve only as an instrument for the soul, like clear glass through which the soul looks at each thing and judges whether to accept it; but when the eye itself craves the delights of this world, it is no longer the soul's instrument but acts on its own and covets, and the soul cannot sort the good from the bad.):
Nevertheless, they also said (Bemidbar Rabbah 10:2):
"עַיִן רוֹאָה וְלֵב חוֹמֵד",
'The eye sees and the heart covets,'
שֶׁהַשֵּׂכֶל מוֹלִיד הָרָצוֹן.
showing that intellect generates desire.

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז12 Pirkei Avot 3:17 — R. Elazar ben Azariah said: Where there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; where there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. Where there is no wisdom, there is no fear [of Heaven]; where there is no fear, there is no wisdom. Where there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; where there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. Where there is no flour, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no flour.):
And concerning this they taught (Avot 3:17):
"אִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה, אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה",
'If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom,'
שְׁנֵיהֶם קְשׁוּרִים יַחַד זֶה בָּזֶה וְהָא בְּלֹא הָא לָא סַגִּי.
the two being bound together such that neither can function without the other.
וְאִיתָא "אָבִי וְאִמִּי עֲזָבוּנִי וְגוֹמֵר",
And it is written: 'My father and my mother have forsaken me, etc.,'
כַּיָּדוּעַ אַבָּא וְאִמָּא הוּא מוֹחָא וְלִבָּא,
for as is known, 'father and mother' represent brain and heart,
וּשְׁנֵיהֶם עֲזָבוּנִי בַּעֲווֹנוֹת:
and both abandon a person through sin:
אֵין חָכְמָה וְאֵין בִּינָה בְּעִידָּן דְּיֵצֶר הָרָע,
there is neither wisdom nor understanding in the hour of the evil inclination,

לֵית דְּמִדְכַּר לְיֵצֶר טוֹב (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ נְדָרִים לב13 Nedarim 32b — Rami bar Abba said: What is meant by that which is written, "There was a little city, and few men within it"? "A little city" — this is the body; "and few men within it" — these are the limbs; "and there came a great king against it and besieged it" — this is the evil inclination; "and built great bulwarks against it" — these are the sins. "And there was found in it a poor wise man" — this is the good inclination; "and he by his wisdom delivered the city" — this is repentance and good deeds. "Yet no man remembered that same poor man" — for at the hour of the evil inclination there is none who calls the good inclination to mind. Maharsha (s.v. "a little city"): On the plain sense the verse should have said that the great king came against it with many men and his armies, for there is no king without a people — as it did say of the city itself, "and few men within it"; and "besieged it and built great bulwarks against it" implies that he did so by himself, without a people, which is not the way of a king. But according to the interpretation, the "great king" is the evil inclination, which itself surrounds the city — that is, the body — and itself builds against it; and "the men" Rashi explains in Ecclesiastes, following the interpretation, as a man's limbs, and so it is in the Midrash Rabbah. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTochachah 2): The body is called a city, as they said of the verse "a little city and few men within it"; and the intellect within the body rules over the body and directs [its limbs] in what they are to do. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 220): As long as a person remembers the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, of Torah and of the commandments upon him, he can easily rebuke the inclination and push away every alien thought; the inclination's work is to make him forget this, as they said, "at the hour of the evil inclination no one remembers the good inclination," as it says, "yet no man remembered" (Ecclesiastes 9:15), for then the good thoughts of the unity of the Creator are forgotten from the heart and none of them is recalled. For this is the commandment of tzitzis: to remind him. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Vayeishev): "At the hour of the evil inclination no one remembers the good inclination": when the Blessed One wishes to test a person, He makes him forget the whole gravity of the prohibition in the matter in which He tests him. So it was with the brothers when they wished to kill Joseph: the prohibition was hidden from them, and he was saved only by counsel outside the law, Judah's worldly reasoning "What profit is it?"; as soon as they agreed not to kill him, they saw the gravity of the prohibition. Beis Yaakov (Vayechi 23): Joseph the righteous is the "trace of life" that stays awake within the community of Israel, rousing their souls through his service so that they do not fall asleep in the darkness and concealment of this world. Thus, although the Gemara says, "at the hour of the evil inclination no one remembers the good inclination," Joseph does not let it be forgotten entirely, God forbid, but constantly reminds Israel. Tiferes Yosef (Ki Savo 2): Going out "on the way" alludes to distraction, and one fears that amid the distraction he will forget the Blessed One, as "at the hour of the evil inclination no one remembers the good inclination." The counsel for this is "take counsel with your Maker and then go out": to accept the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven before entering the distraction, so that even in its midst he will not forget the Blessed One.:),
and none remembers the good inclination (as noted in Nedarim 32b),
וְאֵין לָנוּ שֵׂכֶל וְלֹא רָצוֹן.
leaving us devoid of intellect and worthy will.
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם "ה' יַאַסְפֵנִי",
Yet nonetheless, 'the Lord will gather me,'
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְיָכוֹל לוֹ גַּם בַּדּוֹרוֹת אַחֲרוֹנִים,
for the Holy One, blessed be He, assists man and prevails for him even in the final generations,

כְּעִנְיַן "אֱמוֹר לָאוּמָּן שֶׁעֲשָׂאַנִי כַּמָּה מְכוֹעָר וְכוּלֵי14 Taanit 20a–20b — Our Rabbis taught: A person should always be soft as a reed and not hard as a cedar. It once happened that R. Elazar son of R. Shimon was returning from Migdal Gedor, from the house of his teacher, riding on a donkey and making his way along the riverbank, and he was rejoicing greatly, and he felt himself lofty because he had learned much Torah. There chanced upon him a man who was exceedingly ugly, who said to him: “Peace be upon you, my master.” He did not return his greeting. He said to him: “Empty one! How ugly is that man! Is everyone in your town as ugly as you?” He answered: “I do not know. But go and say to the Craftsman who made me — how ugly is this vessel You have made.” When he realized that he had sinned, he dismounted from the donkey, prostrated himself before him and said: “I have wronged you; forgive me.” He said: “I will not forgive you until you go to the Craftsman who made me and say to Him: how ugly is this vessel You have made.” He walked behind him until he reached his city. The people of his city came out to greet him, saying: “Peace be upon you, my master, my master, my teacher, my teacher.” He said to them: “Whom are you calling ‘my master, my master’?” They said: “The one walking behind you.” He said to them: “If this is a master, may there not be many like him in Israel.” They said: “Why?” He told them what he had done to him. They said to him: “Even so, forgive him, for he is a great man in Torah.” He said: “For your sakes I forgive him — provided he does not make a habit of acting this way.” Immediately R. Elazar son of R. Shimon went in and expounded: A person should always be soft as a reed and not hard as a cedar; and it is for this reason that the reed merited that a quill be taken from it with which to write a Torah scroll, tefillin and mezuzot. Rashi: "Making his way": [strolling] for enjoyment. "There chanced upon him a man": some texts read, "Elijah, of blessed memory"; and he meant to rebuke him, so that he would not make a habit of the matter. Tosafos (s.v. "there chanced upon him a man who was exceedingly ugly"): In Tractate Derekh Eretz it is explained that this man was Elijah, and he meant it for good, so that [R. Elazar] would not make a habit of the matter. Maharsha: He called him "empty one" perhaps because, being exceedingly ugly and black, the man looked to him like a foreigner from Cush — hence "is everyone in your town [that is, in the land of Cush] as ugly as you?"; and he answered, "I do not know" — I cannot tell you that they are ugly, for Scripture did not speak disparagingly even of an unclean animal, since that imputes a defect to the creation; but you, in saying of me "how ugly," impute a defect to the creation, and to the Craftsman as well, who made an ugly vessel. "I have wronged you; forgive me" means: I confess that I did not speak well. "Provided he does not make a habit of acting this way" cannot mean that he may do so now and then; rather: provided he does not do what habituates him to it — that his mind not be haughty, for that is what habituated him to speak disparagingly of people as he did. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAnavah 7): The name Migdal Gedor — "tower" and "fence" — found nowhere else, teaches that this was no sin of real pride in the righteous man: the Torah is high above all like a tower and set apart from the world like a fence set apart from the public domain, so its master naturally has a little pride, seeing himself as high and set apart from other creatures. But because R. Elazar was not sufficiently on guard against pride, he came to say "how ugly is this man," disparaging the creation, which is from the Blessed Name — unfitting for one great in Torah; had the man been born lacking an eye, which is not the way of the world, one could not say "go to the Craftsman who made me," but this man had no blemish, so his form was indeed the Craftsman's work. Knowing that he had sinned, he expounded that the scholar who has risen to the eminence of the Torah must be soft as a reed, which the higher it grows the more it bows its head, for it is soft; whereas the cedar, being hard, grows ever more erect the higher it rises. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Savo 10): Elijah, the angel of the covenant, came upon R. Elazar b. R. Shimon in the guise of an "ugly" man, one flawed in the covenant, to rebuke him for disparaging such a person as though he were beyond hope. If such a person only sets his heart to improve his ways, he can repair all that has passed with this very plea, "go to the Craftsman who made me": after repentance it becomes clear that all that befell him was also from the will of the Blessed One, who created man with the evil inclination, which "overpowers him every day, and were it not for the Holy One, blessed be He, helping him, he could not withstand it." Not everyone may make this plea, God forbid, as license to do as his heart desires; only one who knows that all his attainments come from the Blessed One and not from his own strength may strengthen his heart with it after a stumbling. Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Ta'anis 16): As his father explained: no creature may claim to be refined of himself, so a person must ascribe his own failing to himself even when he believes himself clean; but a failing he sees in his fellow he may not ascribe to him, and must judge him favorably, that he is surely clean of the bad traits that appear in him and the sin was "like an error that proceeds from the ruler." R. Elazar judged the man as unrefined, and the man answered: though I must lay the deficiency on myself, you have no right to lay it on me but must judge me favorably, so "go to the Craftsman who made me and say, How ugly is this vessel that You have made."" (תַּעֲנִית כ:),
similar to: 'Tell the artisan who made me, how ugly is, etc.' (Ta'anit 20b);
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הוּא אוּמָּן שֶׁעֲשָׂאָנוּ כָּךְ,
and the Holy One, blessed be He, is the artisan Who made us thus,
בְּלֹא שֵׂכֶל וּבְלֹא בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב וְרָצוֹן.
without intellect, without understanding in the heart, and without holy desire.
"הוּא יַאַסְפֵנוּ" – פֵּירוּשׁ אֲסִיפָה הוּא קִבּוּץ הַנִּדָּחִים,
'He will gather us' – meaning gathering is the assembly of the dispersed,
וְזֶהוּ כָּל עִיקַּר הַיְשׁוּעָה "וְקַבֵּץ נִדָּחֵינוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
and that is the essence of salvation: 'and gather our dispersed, etc.,'
שֶׁל כָּל פְּרָט נֶפֶשׁ –
concerning each individual soul –
אִם יְקוּבְּצוּ נִדָּחָיו, כָּל חֶלְקֵי נַפְשׁוֹ לְמָקוֹם אֶחָד,
if its scattered parts and all facets of its soul are reunited into one place,
הוּא צַדִּיק וְנוֹשָׁע.
it becomes righteous and redeemed.

sections.en: Sleep, Soul, and Spiritual Exchange

items.h: Sleep resembles death and exposes the soul to spiritual exchange; entrusting oneself to Hashem through Bedtime Shema preserves and redirects these forces toward good.

Seif 1 — The Soul during Sleep
Sleep opens the soul to spiritual exchange, and Bedtime Shema entrusts it safely to Hashem.

p: בַּשֵּׁינָה אֶפְשָׁר לַנְּשָׁמָה לְהִתְחַלֵּף,
During sleep, it is possible for the soul to be exchanged,
שֶׁהֲרֵי דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר כ"ה עַל פָּסוּק "חֲדָשִׁים לַבְּקָרִים וְגוֹמֵר",
for our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded in Shocher Tov (Psalm 25) on the verse 'They are new every morning, etc.,'
שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַחֲלִיף הַנְּפָשׁוֹת,
that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not exchange souls,
שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ דְּאֶפְשָׁר לְהַחֲלִיף,
inferring from this that an exchange is indeed possible,
רַק שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נֶאֱמָן וְאֵין מַחֲלִיף פִּקְדוֹנוֹתָיו.
only that the Holy One, blessed be He, is trustworthy and does not switch deposits entrusted to Him.
וְזֶהוּ מִי שֶׁמַּפְקִיד בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁאוֹמֵר "בְּיָדְךָ אַפְקִיד וְגוֹמֵר",
This applies to one who commits his soul into the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, saying 'Into Your hand I commit, etc.,'
אֲבָל מִי שֶׁחוֹשֵׁב הַכֹּל מִקְרֶה וְעוֹלָם כְּמִנְהָגוֹ יוּכַל לְהַחֲלִיף.
but for one who regards everything as chance and nature running its course, it can be exchanged.

וְאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת נז:)15 Berakhot 57b — Five things are each a sixtieth part, and these are they: fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep and a dream. Fire is a sixtieth of Gehinnom; honey, a sixtieth of the manna; Shabbat, a sixtieth of the World to Come; sleep, a sixtieth of death; a dream, a sixtieth of prophecy. Maharsha: "One-sixtieth" is not meant precisely, as Tosafot write in several places. One may also explain it from the law of nullification, where one part in sixty is not nullified but retains something of substance — as we learn from the boiled foreleg [of the nazirite's ram]; so too here he speaks by way of resemblance, that in each of the things enumerated there is some small measure of the substance of that which it resembles. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Gemilus Chasadim 3): Precisely a sixtieth, since [one who shares another's illness] does not receive the essence of the illness; and anything that is not the essence of a thing is one part in sixty of it — as the Sages said, "a dream is a sixtieth of prophecy." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 18): The first stage of the falling is sleep, "and [the Lord God] cast a deep sleep" [upon Adam], as Bereishis Rabbah expounds on that verse; it is "one-sixtieth of death," for in it wisdom and understanding depart, as do all the attributes man possessed at the start of creation, when "God made man upright" and fit to dwell in the Garden of Eden.: "שֵׁינָה אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בְּמִיתָה",
And they taught (Berakhot 57b): 'Sleep is one-sixtieth of death,'

כְּמוֹ אַחַר הַמָּוֶת אָמְרִינַן (חֲגִיגָה טו16 Chagigah 15a — Acher said to R. Meir: R. Akiva your teacher did not say so, but rather: He created the righteous and He created the wicked; He created the Garden of Eden and He created Gehenna. Each and every man has two portions, one in the Garden of Eden and one in Gehenna. If he is worthy, being righteous, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden; if he is found guilty, being wicked, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in Gehenna. Maharsha: The word "corresponding" cannot govern the righteous and the wicked, for these are not equals but a thing and its opposite; the correspondence here is only partial — He created the righteous and He created the Garden of Eden, He created the wicked and He created Gehinnom, creating for each what belongs to it. And since the choice to be righteous or wicked is given to man, for all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, and the Holy One, blessed be He, withholds from no creature its reward or its punishment, He created the Garden of Eden for all, should they all merit it, and Gehinnom for all, should they not. He also reads it from the end of the verse, "so that man should find nothing after him": when the wicked man dies he finds nothing of his portion in the Garden of Eden, for the righteous man has taken it — and conversely. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 19): At the giving of the Torah Israel merited to separate the portion of good from the portion of evil, as is known from the secret of "if worthy, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion." A gentile too is called "fellow": as long as the nations exist in this world there is some life-giving holy spark in them which Israel must absorb, each the one belonging to him, while he hands over to the gentile the portion of evil in himself that belongs to him; in this respect they are called "fellows" in this dictum. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:17): Every person has a portion of good and of evil, that is, a good inclination and an evil inclination, as in the Arizal's words on "if worthy, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden"; and Moses' "fellow's portion" was the Midianites among whom he grew up. Since a person departs the world once he has completed all he can, Moses' final completion was the vengeance against Midian, when Balaam, his exact opposite, "the one corresponding to the other," was killed. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on the Book of Joshua 23): Even stumblings are of the Blessed One's ordering and a preparation for words of Torah, which is why through repentance intentional sins become merits; but if one did not merit to repent in his lifetime, another stands upon the words of Torah that he prepared through his stumbling. This is "if not worthy, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in Gehinnom," that is, in the stumblings that were his fellow's due, while his fellow, who is worthy, takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 5): R. Akiva, though descended from converts, was in his essential soul of the stock of Israel, that small root of Israelite holiness that was in Esau; and that portion truly belongs to Jacob, as in "if worthy, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden": Jacob was worthy and took it from Esau, and therefore R. Akiva cleaved to the house of Jacob. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 4): All of man's service in this world is to sort the good from the evil and set each apart, as they said, "each and every one has two portions... if worthy, being righteous, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion": although He created righteous and wicked, in each there is also a portion of the opposite, and "God has made the one corresponding to the other," so that opposite every righteous person stands a wicked one in the portion of evil. The righteous must refine himself and separate the evil from himself so that it remains wholly in the wicked one's portion, and absorb the portion of good in that wicked one which belongs to him; thus he is completed wholly in holiness, and the evil, left wholly evil, goes to perdition. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 15): Among human beings good and evil are mixed: though there is complete evil, there is also complete good, one corresponding to the other, and through man's dominion over man they are intermingled. About this they said, "if worthy, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden, and the other takes both portions in Gehinnom," for the good is separated from the evil; and this is the seventy souls of Israel corresponding to the seventy nations. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 250): Esau had the greater force of desire, and Jacob acquired his birthright with a "pottage," his own boiling for the delights of this world: he gave Esau that boiling and absorbed the good boiling, the boiling of Torah. This is in the manner of "if worthy, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion... if guilty, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion": Jacob exchanged with Esau, giving him his share of boiling in its animal form and receiving the good from him [such as the souls of R. Akiva and R. Meir, absorbed into the seed of Jacob through this acquisition], for each person necessarily has two portions, the good inclination and the [evil] inclination. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): "God has made the one corresponding to the other" was the whole matter of creation, and man's task in this world is to recognize and separate good from evil: there is no righteous person without a wicked "fellow" opposite him, joined to him through this correspondence that God made. About this they said, "each one has [two portions]... if worthy, being righteous, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in the Garden of Eden; if guilty, being wicked, he takes his own portion and his fellow's portion in Gehinnom"; and not for nothing did they call him "his fellow," for there is necessarily a bond between them through which one can take his fellow's portion, the one for good and the other for the opposite..):
just as after death we maintain (Chagigah 15a):
"זָכָה צַדִּיק – נוֹטֵל חֶלְקוֹ וְחֵלֶק חֲבֵירוֹ בְּגַן עֵדֶן, נִתְחַיֵּיב רָשָׁע וְכוּלֵי",
'If a righteous person merits, he receives his portion and the portion of his peer in Gan Eden; if a wicked person is found guilty, etc.,'
כָּךְ יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת בַּשֵּׁינָה
so too can it happen during sleep
שֶׁיִּתְחַלֵּף חֵלֶק הַטּוֹב שֶׁבְּנֶפֶשׁ רָשָׁע יַגִּיעַ לְאַחֵר הַזּוֹכֶה,
that an exchange occurs where the spark of goodness in the soul of the wicked is transferred to another who merits it,
וְהוּא יִקְלוֹט הָרַע שֶׁבַּחֲבֵירוֹ.
while he absorbs the evil in his counterpart.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה רְשָׁעִים שֶׁהָיוּ מַשְׁכִּימֵי בַּבֹּקֶר וְגוֹמֵר,
Concerning this they described the ways of the wicked who would arise early in the morning to pursue evil, etc.,

וּבְהֵיפֶךְ אִיתָא (בִּבְרָכוֹת טז:)17 Berakhot 16b — R. Elazar, after he had finished his prayer, would say thus: May it be Your will, Lord our God, that You cause to dwell in our lot love and brotherhood and peace and companionship; that You broaden our borders with disciples; that You prosper our end with a future and a hope; that You set our portion in the Garden of Eden; that You furnish us with a good companion and a good inclination in Your world. And may we rise early and find our heart's yearning to fear Your name, and may the contentment of our soul come before You for good. Rashi: Rashi glosses "in our lot [pureinu]" as "in our portion," and "a future and a hope" as: that our end be good and that we see what we have hoped for. On "may we rise early and find our heart's yearning to fear Your name": that the evil inclination not overcome us through the thoughts of the night and so turn us from You by day; rather, when we rise each morning may we find our heart yearning toward You. "May the contentment of our soul come before You" means the supplying of our needs and our peace of mind. Maharsha: Beside Rashi's rendering of "pureinu" as "our lot," Maharsha offers a second reading: it is our marriage bed, that our household be whole in love — and it is for this reason that the same words, love and brotherhood and peace and companionship, were fixed in the seven wedding blessings. On "and may we find the yearning [yichul] of our heart" he prefers to read the word with a yod, from trembling and dread, as in "my heart trembles within me," and he hears in "the contentment [korat] of our soul" an allusion to "as cold water [mayim karim] to a faint soul." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3): Kerias Shema is the constant acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, in which one must be so bound up in thought that even lying on his bed he knows before Whom he lies, so that it will be as in "may we rise early and find our heart's yearning": as soon as he rises he finds himself in the place where he lay down, in that same thought. So it was with Jacob, "and behold, the Lord stood over him," for all day the Lord was before him and even at night his heart did not lie down in another thought. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim Katan 2): The Shulchan Aruch opens with "one should strengthen himself like a lion," for the main thing is to overcome the evil inclination and rise in the morning to the service of one's Creator; this is akin to "may we rise early and find our heart's yearning to fear Your name," meaning that without any preparation or deeds our heart's longing should be for the fear of Heaven and His service. Only afterward can the evil inclination gain strength, and for this the Rema opened with "I have set the Lord before me always.": "וְנַשְׁכִּים וְנִמְצָא יִחוּל לִבָּנוּ וְכוּלֵי".
whereas conversely it is stated (Berakhot 16b): 'May we awaken and find the yearning of our heart directed toward You, etc.'

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין עא:)18 Sanhedrin 71b — Wine and sleep for the wicked are a benefit to them and a benefit to the world; and for the righteous they are an evil to them and an evil to the world. Rashi: As long as they are drinking and sleeping they do not sin and do no harm to people. For the righteous it is an evil to them, for [then] they are not occupied with Torah; and an evil to the world, for the Torah with which they occupy themselves protects the generation, and when they are idle from it, punishment comes to the world. Maharsha: From the pleasure of the wine on which he becomes drunk he comes to the pleasure of sleep in the morning until the fourth hour, as is said of the gentile kings. So it is with the rebellious son: wine and sleep are a benefit to him and a benefit to the world, for as long as he has the means to buy wine and is asleep he does not rob people, until he has used up his property. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): "Wine and sleep for the wicked are a benefit to them, etc., but for the righteous an evil, etc." — for wine "was created only to comfort mourners and to give reward to the wicked," who through it are sunk in lust as they please, which is their whole desire and their benefit; and it is also a benefit to the world that they are sunk in lust and do no harm to others. For the righteous, however, it is the beginning of a fall: even when wine causes no outright evil, it brings on sleep and a slackening of the hands from the service of the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 238): Sleep too is good for re-awakening after the mind has fallen into a confusion of alien thoughts: in sleep the mind departs and afterwards a new soul returns, so that one can strengthen himself anew and forget all that was the day before. This is the reason for "sleep for the wicked, etc." and the reverse for the righteous: the mind and holy thoughts they held all day depart, and the next day they need a fresh strengthening and a new beginning, and all beginnings are hard, whereas within the day the thought remains bound and continues. With the wicked it is the reverse: their scheming thought continues all day, so that it can hardly cleave to words of Torah except with great difficulty, so strongly is it bound to the alien things he thinks of.: "שֵׁינָה לִרְשָׁעִים הֲנָאָה לָהֶם לְפִי דַּרְכָּם וַהֲנָאָה לָעוֹלָם".
And this explains what they stated (Sanhedrin 71b): 'Sleep for the wicked is beneficial for them in their way, and beneficial for the world.'
וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בַּצַּדִּיקִים,
The reverse is true for the righteous,
שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁיִּקְלוֹט הַטּוֹב הַהוּא, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מְעוֹרָב בְּרַע הַרְבֵּה שֶׁבְּשָׁרְשָׁם מִמְּקוֹר מוֹצָאָם וְצָרִיךְ מֵירוּק וְתִיקּוּן,
for even though he absorbs that good, it is nonetheless deeply entwined with much evil from its original source and requires refinement and rectification;
וּלְכָךְ רַע לָהֶם וְרַע לָעוֹלָם שֶׁקּוֹלֵט הַטּוֹב מִנִּבְרָאֵי הָעוֹלָם בְּעֵת הַשֵּׁינָה.
hence it is detrimental for them and detrimental for the world, since he absorbs that good from the creatures of the world during sleep.

וְהָעֵצָה לִשְׁנֵיהֶם הוּא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע שֶׁעַל הַמִּטָּה וְחַד פְּסוּקָא דְּרַחֲמֵי "בְּיָדְךָ אַפְקִיד וְגוֹמֵר" (בִּבְרָכוֹת ה19 Berakhot 5a — If he is a Torah scholar, he need not [recite the Shema upon his bed]. Abaye said: Even a Torah scholar must recite one verse of supplication, such as "Into Your hand I entrust my spirit; You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth." And R. Yitzchak said: Whoever recites the Shema upon his bed — the demons keep away from him. Rashi: "If he is a Torah scholar" — one who is regular in his learning and constantly reviews it; that is sufficient for him. Maharsha: His Torah certainly protects him, as the passage of the Shema does; nevertheless he must also say one verse of supplication in place of the evening prayer, namely "Into Your hand I entrust my spirit." This accords with the Midrash: a mortal deposits an article with his fellow and receives it back worn and spoiled, but a man deposits his soul each evening in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, weary, and He returns it to him rested. That is "You have redeemed me, Lord, God of truth" — not like a mortal, who lays a hand upon the deposit entrusted to him and ruins it. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 19): The power of the demons lies in duality — which is why the Sages forbade eating and drinking in pairs — for they were not created at the first and in essence as the rest of creation was, but follow after this world and are not the essence of creation; they were made at twilight on the eve of the Sabbath, and having no unity with the world, they harm it. Therefore one who recites the Shema, declaring "the Lord is One," cleaves to unity and is delivered from the duality that is the demons; and since the recitation at night exempts him for the whole night, that Torah shields him all night long. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 243): The Shema upon the bed, through which "the demons keep away," is the acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven "with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might," which nullifies every kind of alien thought; though it lasts but a brief moment, it helps when close to sleep. "If he is a Torah scholar he need not," for his thoughts are in any case always immersed in words of Torah; yet he still needs "one verse of mercy," because being a Torah scholar means not that he has wholly escaped the inclination in the left chamber of the heart, only that he draws it toward words of Torah, and in sleep, when the mind departs from words of Torah, the inclination can burn with the fire of its lust and bring about a nocturnal emission, Heaven forfend. Therefore he must say "Into Your hand I entrust my spirit," handing over his spirit — the will of the heart with which he longed for words of Torah — as a deposit in the hand of the Blessed One..),
The remedy for both is the Bedtime Shema and one verse of divine mercy, 'Into Your hand I commit, etc.' (Berakhot 5a),
וְאֵין רַע יוֹצֵא מִלְּפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ לְשׁוּם בְּרִיָּה בָּעוֹלָם וְעַל כֵּן הַכֹּל יִהְיֶה לְטוֹבָה.
for no evil emanates from Before Him, blessed be He, to any creature in the world, and therefore all will be for the good.

sections.en: Torah and Prayer: Humility and Elevation

items.h: Torah descends to the lowly, while prayer rises to the heights; both meet in genuine humility, where divine greatness and descent are revealed together.

Seif 1 — Sinai, Moriah, Torah, and Prayer
Torah descends to genuine humility, while prayer rises through the same lowliness toward divine greatness.

p: שְׁנֵי יְסוֹדוֹת הֵם תּוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה,
Two foundational pillars are Torah and prayer,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב20 Midrash Tehillim 87:2 — “Its foundation is in the holy mountains.” The foundation of the world stands in the merit of two mountains of holiness — Mount Sinai and Mount Moriah. R. Pinchas said in the name of R. Reuven: In time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will bring Sinai, Tabor and Carmel, and set Jerusalem at their head, as it is said, “The mountain of the Lord’s house shall be established at the head of the mountains.” (מִזְמוֹר פז) עַל פָּסוּק "יְסוּדָתוֹ בְּהַרְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ":
as they stated in Shocher Tov (Midrash Tehillim, Psalm 87) on the verse "Its foundation is in the holy mountains":
הַר סִינַי וְהַר הַמּוֹרִיָּה.
Mount Sinai and Mount Moriah.
הַר סִינַי נִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַסְּנֶה כַּיָּדוּעַ,
Mount Sinai is named after the bush (seneh) as is well known,

וְאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת21 Shabbat 67a — “Thornbush, thornbush! Not because you are the tallest of all the trees did the Holy One, blessed be He, rest His Presence upon you, but because you are the lowliest of all the trees did the Holy One, blessed be He, rest His Presence upon you.” Maharsha: Since these verses of the thornbush allude to the healing of the soul, they were taken for healing the body; and the thornbush is addressed thus because the essence of the healing of the soul is that a man lower himself and so be healed — as is expounded of the leper, that of "flesh" it is written "and it is healed" (Leviticus 13:18): if a man makes himself as flesh, [he is healed]. (סז.):
and they said in Shabbat (67a):
"הַסְּנֶה וְכוּלֵי מִשּׁוּם דְּמַיֵּיכַת וְכוּלֵי",
"the bush, etc., because it is low, etc.,"
הוּא מוֹרֶה עַל שִׁפְלוּת,
which signifies humbleness and lowliness,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית22 Taanit 7a — The daughter of the Emperor said to R. Yehoshua ben Chananya: “Such splendid wisdom, in so ugly a vessel!” — for R. Yehoshua was of unattractive appearance. He said to her: “Your father keeps his wine in earthenware vessels.” She said: “In what else should he keep it?” He said: “You, who are people of importance, should store it in vessels of gold and silver.” She went and told her father, and the wine was put into gold and silver vessels — and it turned sour. They came and told him. He said to his daughter: “Who told you to do this?” She said: “R. Yehoshua ben Chananya.” They summoned him and he said: “Just as she said to me, so I said to her.” — “But there are handsome men who are learned!” — Had they been ugly, they would have been more learned still. Rashi: "Your father keeps his wine in earthenware vessels": he said it in jest, hinting: What are you saying to me — does not your father put wine in ugly earthenware vessels? "Just as she said to me": she said, "Alas for glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel," and so I said to her that wine is preserved in an ugly vessel — so too the Torah endures in me more than if I were handsome. "Had they been ugly" — those handsome men who are learned — "they would have been more learned still," for a handsome man cannot humble his mind, and so he comes to forgetfulness. Tosafos (s.v. "were they ugly"): That is: had they hated beauty, they would have been greater Torah scholars still. Maharsha (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 50b): The root of this matter is set out in the first chapter of Taanit: words of Torah endure only in one whose mind is lowly, and a handsome, good-looking man is apt to grow haughty, as in the episode of the Nazirite [Nedarim 9b]. Tosafot there, who explain "had they been ugly" as "had they hated beauty," meant this too: it surely does not depend on one's natural make-up, as though an ugly man learns and reasons better than a handsome one; rather, had they hated their beauty and not grown haughty because of it, they would be more learned than they are now. So the wording implies, for the word he uses is from the language of hatred — he did not say "had they been ugly." Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 50b): [R. Yehoshua's reply, "so too the Torah,"] is explained by what they said (Taanit 7a) of the Torah, which is likened to water: just as water leaves a high place and goes down to a low place, so words of Torah are not found in one who is haughty, only in one who humbles himself. For pride pertains to the physical, and the Torah, a divine and separate wisdom, is not fitting for one whose soul has an affinity with the physical; therefore he said that beauty, which belongs to the body, is a physical excellence and not fitting for the Torah. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTorah 2): An earthenware vessel, on account of its simplicity, does not act upon the liquid, whereas silver and gold, which are not simple as the humblest of vessels is simple, change it; so too the Torah endures only in one whose mind is lowly, for then he has the quality of simplicity. And so with what is said right after [R. Oshaya's teaching], "Alas for glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel": this whole matter is because the more a person has of the quality of simplicity, the more fit he is to receive the simple intellect. (ז.):
just as they taught in Ta'anit (7a):
דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוֹלְכִים לְמָקוֹם נָמוּךְ,
that words of Torah flow to a lowly place,
וְאֵין רְצוֹנָם לוֹמַר נְמִיכוּת בְּדַעַת שֶׁלֹּא בֶּאֱמֶת,
and they did not mean false modesty or ungrounded lowliness of mind,
רַק לְנָמוּךְ בֶּאֱמֶת,
rather to one who is genuinely lowly,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם23 Taanit 7a-7b — [R. Oshaya had likened words of Torah to water, wine and milk, which keep only in the meanest of vessels; and the emperor's daughter had said to R. Yehoshua ben Chananya, who was ugly: Alas for glorious wisdom in so ugly a vessel!] The emperor said to him: But there are handsome men who are learned! [He answered:] Were they ugly, they would be more learned still. Rashi: "Were they ugly": those handsome men who are learned. "They would be more learned still": for a handsome man cannot humble his mind, and so he comes to forgetfulness. Tosafos (s.v. "were they ugly"): That is: had they hated beauty, they would have been greater Torah scholars still. Maharsha (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 50b): Tosafot's explanation, "had they hated beauty," means this: it surely does not depend on one's natural make-up, as though an ugly man learns and reasons better than a handsome one; rather, had they hated their beauty and not grown haughty because of it, they would be more learned than they are now — for words of Torah endure only in one whose mind is lowly, and a handsome, good-looking man is apt to grow haughty. So the wording implies, for the word he uses is from the language of hatred: he did not say "had they been ugly." Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 50b): He said that beauty, which belongs to the body, is a physical excellence and not fitting for the Torah, [a divine and separate wisdom]. Nor is this contradicted by "A man's wisdom makes his face shine" (Ecclesiastes 8:1), [cited just before, Nedarim 49b,] from which it would seem that beauty befits the man of intellect: that is as it was with Moses, of whom it is said, "the skin of his face shone" (Exodus 34:29) — not a physical beauty but a separate light, befitting a master of intellect, for wisdom is surely light; but the beauty spoken of here is physical beauty, and that is not fitting for wisdom. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 6): Wisdom does not bring about a shedding of corporeality to the same degree [as prophecy], and of this it was said, "Glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel," and he answered, "Were they ugly, they would be more learned still" — for so the Blessed One established, that it be specifically in an ugly vessel. The beauty and ugliness of which the Sages spoke are all in terms of bodily deeds, as in "Are you not as the children of the Kushites to Me" and "Do not look upon me, that I am swarthy"; for through the ugliness of the body his heart is broken and anxious within him, and thereby he becomes a vessel to receive words of Torah, which descend only to a low place.):
as they said (there):
"אִי הֲווֹ סָנוּ הֲווֹ גְּמִירֵי טְפֵי",
"Had they been plain/unattractive, they would have learned even more,"
וְכִיעוּר בִּלְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא הַיְינוּ בְּמַעֲשִׂים,
and 'ugliness' in the language of the Gemara refers to deeds,
וְלֹא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּמַעֲשִׂים מִצַּד רִשְׁעוּתוֹ,
yet Heaven forbid it should mean deeds rooted in wickedness,
רַק מִצַּד עֶצֶם שׁוֹרְשׁוֹ,
rather from the very humble station of one's origin,

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים פא24 Nedarim 81a — They sent from there [the Land of Israel]: Be careful with grime; be careful to study in company; and be careful with the sons of the poor, for from them the Torah goes forth, as it is stated: "Water shall flow from his branches [midalyav]" — from the poor [midalim] among them the Torah goes forth. And for what reason is it not common for Torah scholars to have sons who are Torah scholars? Rav Yosef said: So that they should not say the Torah is their inheritance. Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi said: So that they should not lord themselves over the community. Mar Zutra said: Because they domineer over the community. Rav Ashi said: Because they call ordinary people donkeys. Rashi: "Be careful to study in company" — for a man only sharpens his reasoning through his fellow's learning; "be careful with the sons of the poor" — that they should not be light in your eyes, so that you teach them Torah. "So that they should not say" — so that people should not say that the Torah is an inheritance for them and that we need not trouble ourselves to learn it; "so that they should not lord themselves" — that they should not assume authority when they see that they and their fathers and their sons are Torah scholars. "Because they call ordinary people donkeys" — because they do not treat them with respect but despise them on account of the Torah they possess. Tosafos: "Be careful with grime" means be careful about laundering, and "be careful in a group" means that you should learn Torah in company. "The Torah is an inheritance" — for the Torah scholars, and [people say] we need not trouble ourselves to learn it. Maharsha: In the chapter Chelek they expounded "water shall flow from his branches" of kingship, but here they expound it of Torah, which is called water, as it is said, "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water"; the sense is that the water which is Torah flows from the poor, so that the offspring of the poor shall be "in many waters," that is, Torah scholars. "Because they call ordinary people donkeys" — as though by the very nature of their creation they were unfit for wisdom, like this donkey; and on their own premise that one begets his like, the objection follows: since they themselves are scholars, why are their sons not scholars? Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 81a): "Water shall flow from his branches" means that the Torah is more readily brought forth into actuality through the poor, who do not possess wealth, which is the rank of this world; for when a man is removed from the rank of this world it is fitting that the intellectual Torah, which is separate from this world, should come forth through him. As for "so that they should not say that the Torah is an inheritance for them": intellectual wisdom is separate from man, and inheritance does not apply to it, for a man bequeaths to his son only what is bodily, since his kinship to his son is on the side of the body alone — he bequeaths stature and beauty and the like, but not a thing entirely separate from bodily man, as the Torah is. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:145): Hence the difference between "Torah scholars' sons are not Torah scholars" and what they said in Eduyos, "a father confers merit on his son in wisdom": "confers merit" means by virtue of his righteousness, not by virtue of his wisdom. For the Torah scholar and the righteous man who serves God, the pillars of Torah and of service, correspond to mind and heart; from the heart "are the issues of life," the extension of the seven lower [attributes] into the body, and these are the seven things in which a father confers merit on his son, whereas from the side of the mind there is no such extension. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): From the standpoint of Torah, inheritance by one's offspring does not apply, for it is ownerless to all; on the contrary, the Blessed One is particular that people should not say the Torah is an inheritance, as they said, "Why is it not common for Torah scholars [to have sons who are Torah scholars]..." Therefore Moses our teacher did not bequeath his crown to his sons — not on his own account, although a father confers merit on his son in wisdom, but because the Blessed One did not wish it on account of the generation, which was not worthy and could have erred [into thinking] that Torah is an inheritance. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, Thirteen Principles of Conduct 10): One who is righteous, his offspring too is not forsaken, and is a Torah scholar; and though "Torah scholars are not commonly succeeded by sons who are Torah scholars," that refers to [sons who are] likewise exceedingly great. And it returns to the seed of their seed: whoever is a Torah scholar, and his son and his grandson, is assured that it will not cease..):
and along the lines of what they taught (Nedarim 81a):
"בְּנֵי עֲנִיִּים מֵהֶם תֵּצֵא תוֹרָה",
"Be heedful of the children of the poor, for from them Torah emerges,"
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין מָצוּי לִהְיוֹת בְּנֵיהֶם וְכוּלֵי,
whereas with Torah scholars, it is uncommon that their children become scholars, etc.,
כִּי תוֹרָה מַנַּחַת מָקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ בֶּאֱמֶת
because the Torah leaves a place of intrinsic loftiness
וְיוֹרֶדֶת לְכָל מָקוֹם הַיּוֹתֵר נָמוּךְ.
and descends to whatever place is lowest.
וּלְכָךְ כָּל שֶׁהַדּוֹרוֹת הוֹלְכִים וּמִתְקַטְּנִים,
And therefore, as the generations decline and diminish,
רָזֵי הַתּוֹרָה הוֹלְכִים וּמִתְגַּבְּרִים וּמִתְפַּשְּׁטִים וּמִתְרַחֲבִים בְּלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם,
the mysteries of the Torah intensify, expand, and broaden within human hearts,

וְכֶתֶר תּוֹרָה מוּנָּח לַכֹּל (יוֹמָא עב25 Yoma 72b — R. Yochanan said: There are three crowns — that of the altar, that of the Ark, and that of the table. That of the altar — Aaron was worthy of it and took it. That of the table — David was worthy of it and took it. That of the Ark still lies unclaimed: whoever wishes to take it, let him come and take it. Lest you say it is the lesser of them, Scripture states, "Through me kings reign." Rashi: "Three crowns": they were made on the holy vessels: that of the altar a sign of the crown of priesthood, that of the Ark a sign of the crown of Torah, and that of the table a sign of the crown of kingship, for the table is a sign of the wealth of kings. "That of the altar, Aaron was worthy of it and took it; that of the table, David was worthy of it and took it": for the priesthood was given to Aaron as "a covenant of salt" (Numbers 18:19), and likewise the kingship to David and his seed. "Through me kings reign": and he who makes kings is greater than the king, and it is the Torah that speaks this verse. Maharsha (s.v. "there are three crowns"): These are precisely the three crowns taught in Avos, "There are three crowns: the crown of priesthood, the crown of kingship and the crown of Torah": the crown of kingship is meant literally, David's crown, which fitted him; the crown of priesthood is the tzitz upon the High Priest; and the crown of Torah is the tefillin upon the head of every man, for whoever wishes to take it may take it. "Lest you say it is the lesser," since every man can merit it, Scripture states, "Through me kings reign," as Rashi explains; and in regard to the priesthood too it is said [of the Torah], "She is more precious than pearls," [more precious] than the High Priest, who wears pearls upon the tzitz. Maharal (Derech Chaim 4:13): The crown of priesthood requires a special preparation, and therefore Aaron and his seed in particular merited it, for they are prepared for it; so too the crown of kingship requires a special preparation, and David and his seed merited it; and one who is prepared for the one is not prepared for the other, for they are divided. But the crown of Torah, since this crown is the intellect, which is separate from man, requires no preparation, and therefore it lies before all. The Torah alludes to this: of the crowns of the table and of the altar it is written, "you shall make for it," a word of possession, but of the Ark, "you shall make upon it," which implies that it is separate. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 2): The golden crown of the incense altar alludes to the crown of priesthood, which Aaron merited and took for himself and his descendants, and the crown of the table to the crown of kingship, which David merited and took for himself and his descendants; Moses merited the crown of Torah, the source and root of them all. Therefore he too served as priest and was "king in Jeshurun," but only by virtue of the crown of Torah, in which everything is included, not in their own right, and so they did not pass to his descendants.
