Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 62): The great ones of the generations each merited a particular level and took it for their descendants after them (Jacob the name "Israel", Joseph "righteous", David "pious", Levi "pure", Aaron "holy"), but Moses, who merited the level of Torah and wisdom, did not merit it for his descendants, for the sons of Torah scholars are not usually Torah scholars. That is why they said, "the crown of Torah lies ready for all," and why Moses is called "father in Torah": he is the father of all the Torah scholars in Israel.:).
and the crown of Torah lies open to all (Yoma 72b).
אֲבָל כֶּתֶר כְּהֻנָּה זָכָה אַהֲרֹן וּנְטָלוֹ,
However, regarding the crown of priesthood, Aaron merited and took it,
וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב וְגוֹמֵר,
and 'the commoner who draws near shall die,' etc.,
רַק כֹּהֲנִים מְיוּחָסִים.
belonging exclusively to priests of designated lineage.

וְהוּא נִקְרָא הַר הַמּוֹרִיָּה עַל שֵׁם הַמּוֹר כַּיָּדוּעַ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נה26 Bereshit Rabbah 55:7 — "And go to the land of Moriah." R. Chiya the Great and R. Yannai: one said, to the place from which instruction went out to the world; the other said, to the place from which awe went out to the world. R. Shimon ben Yochai said: to the place that corresponds to the Temple above. The Rabbis said: to the place where the incense is offered, as you say, "I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense."),
And that mountain is called Mount Moriah after myrrh (mor), as is known (Bereishit Rabbah 55),

שֶׁהוּא רֹאשׁ לְכָל הַבְּשָׂמִים (מְגִילָּה י:)27 Megillah 10b — R. Shmuel bar Nachmani opened his exposition of this passage from here: "Instead of the thorn shall come up the cypress, and instead of the nettle shall come up the myrtle" (Isaiah 55:13). "Shall come up the cypress" — this is Mordecai, who is called the chief of all the spices, as it is stated: "And you, take for yourself choice spices: flowing myrrh" (Exodus 30:23), which we render [in Aramaic] as "pure myrrh." Maharsha: As is set out at the end of tractate Chullin, Mordecai had other names, Petachiah and Bilshan, yet in the Megillah he is called Mordecai on account of his eminence and greatness — that he was chief in greatness, like "flowing myrrh," which is rendered "pure myrrh" and is the chief of the spices. That is the meaning of "shall come up the cypress": that he should rise to greatness, after the pattern of the chief of the spices, which is itself so named for its excellence. Maharal (Ohr Chadash, Pesichah): Among the excellences of this Megillah is that from it one learns a very great thing about the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He: that He cuts off the wicked and sets the righteous in their place, and this is to His renown and praise. If His Name is sanctified when He takes vengeance on His enemies, as He did with Pharaoh and Sennacherib, all the more so is it sanctified when He takes vengeance on His enemies and puts those who love His Name in their place. Moreover, when He takes vengeance on His enemies one might suppose that the blow came upon the enemy by chance; but when the righteous one comes in his place — as here, where Esther came in place of Vashti and Mordecai in place of Haman — it cannot be ascribed to chance. וְדָבָר חָשׁוּב וְאֵינוֹ הֶפְקֵר לַכֹּל.
which is the foremost of all spices (Megillah 10b), a matter of distinction and not ownerless for all to take.
וְכֵן עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב זוֹ תְּפִלָּה,
So too is service of the heart, which is prayer,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת (סד28 Yevamot 64a — R. Yitzchak said: Isaac our father was barren, as it is said, "And Isaac entreated the Lord opposite his wife." It does not say "for his wife" but "opposite" — teaching that both of them were barren. If so, why does it say "and the Lord let Himself be entreated by him"? It should say "by them"! Because the prayer of a righteous man who is the son of a righteous man is not like the prayer of a righteous man who is the son of a wicked man. Rashi: "It should say 'by them'": Granted, if you say that Isaac's prayer was on behalf of his wife, that is why it is written "and [the Lord] let Himself be entreated by him," since he was praying for her, "and Rebecca his wife conceived"; but if you say he was praying for himself, and "opposite his wife" implies that both of them were crying out, facing one another, it should say "by them." "Because it is not alike": his prayer, for he was a righteous man son of a righteous man, is not like her prayer, for she was a righteous woman daughter of a wicked man; therefore Scripture ascribed it to him. Maharsha: On the initial assumption that only Rebecca was barren, Isaac prayed on her behalf rather than she for herself, because the prayer of another on a person's behalf is more readily accepted than his own — "a prisoner cannot free himself from prison" — and so "He let Himself be entreated by him" was fitting. But now that R. Yitzchak explains "opposite" as "equal to her," he too being barren as she was, both of them prayed, each for the other, and so it should have said "by them." And although in Berakhot (7a) the suggestion that the righteous man who prospers is a righteous man son of a righteous man, and the righteous man who suffers a righteous man son of a wicked man, is rejected, this reasoning stands with regard to prayer being more readily accepted to annul the decree of barrenness. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Yevamos 64a): [The Gemara] explains that the forefathers were barren because the Blessed Name longs for the prayer of the righteous: the forefathers are the fathers and the foundation of the world, and prayer is the binding of the caused to its Cause, so that when they are bound to Him the whole world is bound to Him, blessed be He, as is fitting — for the Blessed Name wishes and desires that the caused be attached to its Cause and not separated from Him. Jacob, however, was not barren, for Jacob cleaved to the source of life from which children come — Jacob our father did not die; but Isaac was barren, and Abraham and Sarah even more so..):
as they taught in Yevamot (64a):
"אֵין דּוֹמֶה תְּפִלַּת צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק לִתְפִלַּת צַדִּיק בֶּן רָשָׁע",
"The prayer of a righteous person born of a righteous person does not compare to the prayer of a righteous person born of a wicked person,"
וְאֵין רְצוֹנָם לוֹמַר מִצַּד קִבּוּל הַתְּפִלָּה בִּזְכוּת אֲבוֹתָיו,
and they did not mean regarding the reception of the prayer through ancestral merit,
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹמֵעַ תְּפִלַּת כָּל פֶּה וְקָרוֹב לְכָל קוֹרְאָיו,
for Hashem, blessed be He, hears the prayer of every mouth and is close to all who call upon Him,
רַק אַתְּפִלָּה עַצְמָהּ שֶׁאֵין דּוֹמֶה תְּפִלַּת זֶה לְשֶׁל זֶה.
rather regarding the intrinsic nature of the prayer itself, wherein one's prayer does not resemble the other's.

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה29 Rosh Hashanah 18a — It was taught: R. Meir used to say — two men took to their sickbeds with the same illness, and likewise two men went up to the scaffold to be judged on the same charge; one came down and one did not, one was saved and one was not. Why did this one come down and that one not, this one escape and that one not? This one prayed and was answered, and that one prayed and was not answered. And why was this one answered and that one not? This one prayed a complete prayer — with full concentration, as Rashi explains — and was answered; and that one did not pray a complete prayer, and was not answered. Rashi: "To the scaffold" — a house of assembly where capital cases are tried for execution. "And their judgment was the same" — both had been seized on the same charge. "This one came down" — from the bed; "this one was saved" — from the tribunal. "A complete prayer" — he directed his intent. Maharsha (s.v. "two who went up to bed"): They are compared in the same way in chapter Bameh Madlikin [Shabbat 32a], where it is said that one who went up to his bed and fell ill should regard himself as though he had been brought up to the scaffold, and it concludes there, "These are a man's advocates: repentance and good deeds"; the same holds for prayer, as we say here, "this one prayed and was answered, and that one prayed and was not answered." [The baraita] could just as well have said "and that one did not pray at all," but it teaches that even if he prayed, if [his prayer] was not complete he was not answered. (יח.):
And along the lines of what they stated in Rosh Hashanah (18a):

"מִפְּנֵי מָה זֶה הִתְפַּלֵּל וְנַעֲנָה וְכוּלֵי – זֶה כִּיוֵּון לִבּוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (כְּפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י30 Rashi on Rosh Hashanah 18a:3:1 — On the teaching "Why was this one answered and this one not answered? This one prayed a complete prayer and was answered, and this one did not pray a complete prayer and was not answered" — Rashi: "A complete prayer" — he directed his intent.),
"Why was this one answered when he prayed while the other was not? This one focused his heart, etc." (as Rashi explains),
כִּי בִּתְפִלָּה הַכֹּל לְפִי כַּוָּנַת הַלֵּב הֵן הַדְּבָרִים.
for in prayer, the essence of the matter depends entirely on the intention of the heart.
וְהַכֹּל הוּא לְפִי זֹךְ הַלֵּב,
And everything corresponds to the purity of the heart,
וְאֵין דּוֹמֶה צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ לְבָבוֹ זַךְ.
and a righteous person born of righteous parentage is incomparable, as the root of his heart is pristine.

וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא תְּפִלָּה בִּבְרָכוֹת (ו31 Berakhot 6b — One of the Sages said to Rav Bibi bar Abaye, and some say Rav Bibi said to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: What is the meaning of "when vileness is exalted among the sons of men"? He said to him: These are the things that stand at the very height of the world, and people treat them lightly. Rashi: "When vileness is exalted" is the latter half of the verse quoted just above, "The wicked walk round about." And "matters that stand at the very height of the world" — such as prayer, which ascends on high. Maharsha: This plainly refers back to the opening of the verse: one who prays round about the synagogue, that is, outside it, is called wicked precisely because he treats prayer lightly, prayer being one of those "matters that stand at the very height of the world." Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Tehillim 34): Although in human eyes the deed seems to be the main thing, the chief guarding is truly of the mouth and tongue, for everything is clarified through the tongue — as the Baal Shem Tov explained the Gemara's "things that stand at the height of the world": it is words [spoken words] that stand at the height of the world. As the holy Zohar says, "once he has brought a word out of his mouth, that word becomes a voice, splits the airs and firmaments, and rises on high.":):
Therefore prayer is described in Berakhot (6b) as:
"כְּרוּם זֻלֻּת" – דְּבָרִים שֶׁעוֹמְדִים בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם,
"when vileness is exalted" – matters that stand at the highest pinnacle of the world,
כִּי הֵם הוֹלְכִים לְמָקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ דַּוְוקָא.
because they ascend specifically to an exalted place.

אֶלָּא מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ32 Zevachim 54b — They had thought to build the Temple at Ein Eitam, which is higher ground; but they said, let us set it somewhat lower, as it is written, “and He dwells between his shoulders.” Rashi: We shall make it a little lower and build it in Jerusalem, which lies below — for Scripture writes “his shoulders” and does not write “his head.” Rashi (s.v. "they had thought to build it at Ein Eitam"): It seems to me that this is the spring of the waters of Nephtoah mentioned there [in Joshua], after the ascent of the mountain that faces the valley of Ben Hinnom, with no descent written in between. Maharsha: Although Ein Eitam is then higher than the Temple, "Then you shall arise and go up to the place" is still rightly said of the Temple relative to all "your gates," for Ein Eitam did not count as a city with a gate, since it was removed from the Temple by only twenty-three cubits, as Rashi explains in his commentary on the Torah. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Zevachim 54b): We have already said that Benjamin in particular is prepared to receive the glory of the Divine Presence, and therefore it is written "and He dwells between his shoulders": for the shoulders are designated to receive a burden — the head is not designated to receive, only the shoulders. Therefore it is fitting to build only at a place resembling that which receives, namely the shoulders. (זְבָחִים נד:):
Nevertheless, they stated (Zevachim 54b):
"נֵיחוּת בֵּיהּ פּוּרְתָּא מִשּׁוּם דִּכְתִיב 'בֵּין כְּתֵפָיו' וְכוּלֵי",
"Let us descend a little lower, because it is written: 'between his shoulders, etc.',"
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ "תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי" דִּמְעַטְּפָא כָּל צְלוֹתִין
for in truth there is 'the prayer of the afflicted' which envelops all prayers

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, כג33 Zohar 1:23b — “A prayer of the poor man, when he is faint.” The poor man’s prayer wraps itself about all the other prayers and holds them back, so that none of them enters before it — until the prayer of the poor man has entered. “When he is faint” means that he delays them.34 Zohar, Bereshit 17:187 — And David, because of the exile, said, "hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness," for he saw the Shekhinah laid waste and parched, and he bore suffering on her account. Afterward, when he saw that Israel were returning in joy, he composed ten kinds of song, and at the end of them all he said, "A prayer of the poor man, when he is faint." This is the prayer that wraps up all the prayers that precede it, [holding them back] until his own prayer enters. For this reason the poor man precedes them all.:):
(as stated in Zohar Part I, 23b):
"אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא וְגוֹמֵר".
"I dwell with him that is of a contrite spirit, etc."
כִּי בִּמְקוֹם גְּדוּלָּתוֹ – הַתְּפִלָּה הוּא מְקוֹם גְּדוּלָּתוֹ,
For in the place of His greatness—and prayer represents the place of His greatness,

כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר בִּמְגִילָּה (כז.)35 Megillah 27a — Bar Kappara expounded: What is meant by “And he burned the house of the Lord, and the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great house he burned with fire”? “The house of the Lord” — this is the Temple. “The king’s house” — these are the king’s palaces. “And all the houses of Jerusalem” — as they are plainly meant. “And every great house he burned with fire” — R. Yochanan and R. Yehoshua ben Levi: one said, a place where Torah is made great; and the other said, a place where prayer is made great. The one who said prayer — as it is written, “Tell me, I pray, the great things that Elisha has done,” and what Elisha did, he did through prayer. Rashi: “And he burned the house of the Lord … and every great house” — this is written of Nebuzaradan. Maharsha: “And every great house” is superfluous, since such houses are already included in “all the houses of Jerusalem”; they therefore expounded it of a place where Torah is made great, for through a study hall, where many gather to learn, Torah is increased and made great, as they said, “the more study, the more wisdom.” And the one who said “a place where prayer is made great” means that the prayer of the many, gathered together in a synagogue, is the more readily accepted, as it is said, “for they were with me in multitudes”; and the proof from Elisha is that in his prayer he was answered as though many were praying with him.: "הַגְּדוֹלוֹת – מָקוֹם שֶׁמְּגַדְּלִין בּוֹ תְּפִלָּה",
as the authority states in Megillah (27a): "'Great houses' refers to places where they magnify prayer,"
שָׁם עַנְוְותָנוּתוֹ לִהְיוֹת יוֹרֵד גַּם כֵּן לִמְקוֹמוֹת נְמוּכִים.
there His humility manifests to descend into the lowliest places as well.

וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ח36 Berakhot 8a — R. Chiyya bar Ami said in the name of Ulla: Since the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His world but the four cubits of halakhah alone. And Abaye said: At first I would study in my house and pray in the synagogue; but once I heard this teaching of R. Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla, I would pray only where I study. R. Ami and R. Asi, although they had thirteen synagogues in Tiberias, would pray only between the pillars, where they studied. Rashi: "Between the pillars" — for the study house was built upon them, above. Maharsha: While the Temple stood there was the Chamber of Hewn Stone, from which decided halakhah went forth by the Sanhedrin, and with them the Divine Presence surely dwelt. Now that the Temple is destroyed, those four cubits of halakhah which every Torah scholar fixes as the place of his study in the Talmud stand in its stead, so that the Divine Presence is with him there. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael 70): The Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in the corporeal world, for the corporeal is removed from Him; what is His is the four cubits of halakhah. It is called halakhah because, as one who walks a road does not swerve to right or left, so a ruling of halakhah does not swerve from the point of truth. Just as He chose the Temple, which is fit for holiness because it stands at the centre — and the centre has no distance about it, distance belonging to the corporeal — so halakhah is wholly simple intellect, with no relation to the corporeal, and therefore the place where halakhah is belongs to Him. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 11): Torah is "voice", the male, and prayer, said in a whisper, is "speech", the female; and just as "a woman who seeds first bears a male" and the females are made dependent on the males, so it says "they would pray only where they studied", and in Megillah the reverse, "they would study only where they prayed": for through the voice of Torah one merits prayer, and through prayer one begets the voice of Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): The word "voice" is joined to Jacob because the voice of the Oral Torah is the essential root of Jacob, and the voice of prayer is drawn from it, as with R. Ami and R. Asi, who would pray only between the pillars where they studied. For [the Sages] instituted that one first say "O Lord, open my lips", since one can pray only when the Blessed One opens his lips, and this opening comes through the Oral Torah..):
Therefore they said (Berakhot 8a):
"בִּמְקוֹם תּוֹרָה שָׁם תְּהֵא תְּפִלָּה",
"In the place of Torah, there prayer should be,"
וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ יוֹתֵר.
and this is not the place to elaborate further.

sections.en: Faith in the Darkness of This World

items.h: Faith sustains a person amid bodily darkness, transforming physical pleasure through blessing and Shabbat into recognition that all delight comes from Hashem.

Seif 1 — Faith in Night and the Holiness of Shabbat
Simple faith transforms bodily darkness and pleasure into recognition of Hashem and prepares for Shabbat's higher delight.

p: עִיקַּר עֵסֶק אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא הָאֱמוּנָה,
Man's primary occupation in this world is faith,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מְנָחוֹת כט37 Menachot 29b — As R. Yehuda bar R. Ilai expounded: These are the two worlds that the Holy One, blessed be He, created — one with the letter heh and one with the letter yod. And I do not know whether the World to Come was created with the yod and this world with the heh, or this world with the yod and the World to Come with the heh. When Scripture says "These are the generations of the heaven and the earth when they were created [behibare'am]" (Genesis 2:4), do not read it behibare'am but beheh bera'am — He created them with the letter heh. Rashi: "One with a heh and one with a yod" — He divided His Name and let three drops fall from each of the letters, and from those drops were made water and fire and air and the whole world; so it is written in Sefer Yetzirah. Maharsha (s.v. "they hook the roof of the ḥet"): The letters yod and heh themselves allude to this, that with them the Holy One, blessed be He, formed the two worlds; and the uncertainty is only which of them takes precedence — this world, which is prior in time, or the World to Come, which is prior in rank. Maharal (Derech Chaim 5:1): The World to Come was created with the yod because the numerical value of the yod is ten, and the number ten belongs to everything that has a sacred elevation. This world was created with the heh because the heh has two parts, to hint that this world contains two things: it is a physical world, and yet a higher, sacred rank cleaves to it as well — for the heh is a dalet, and within the dalet there is a yod.:):
and as they stated (Menachot 29b):
"בְּהֵ"א נִבְרָא עוֹלָם הַזֶּה",
"With the letter Hei this world was created,"
וְהִיא הֵ"א אַחֲרוֹנָה
which corresponds to the final Hei of the Tetragrammaton,

(וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, צג38 Zohar, Lech Lecha 34:383 — And this is what is written, "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created" — and we have learned: with the letter heh He created them; and we have learned: for the sake of Abraham. What do they mean? Rather, this one is Chesed and this one is the Shekhinah, and all descends as one; there is no difficulty — it is both this and that..):
(and as they stated in Zohar Part I, 93a):
מִדַּת אֱמוּנָה,
the attribute of faith,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב39 Psalms 92:3 — To declare Your kindness in the morning, and Your faithfulness in the nights. Rashi: “To declare Your loving-kindness in the morning” — at the time of the redemption; “and Your faithfulness in the nights” — and while the distress of the exile still lasts, to believe in You that You will keep Your promise: all this is comely and good. Radak: By day and by night it is for us to declare the loving-kindness You have done with us in giving us the Sabbath day for rest, and the faithfulness by which You will fulfil Your loving-kindness to us at all times. He says “in the morning” because on all the days of the week a man rises in the morning and goes out to his labor, whereas on this morning he rises to rest and to the delight of body and soul, and then I recall the loving-kindness of God; and he says “in the nights” in the plural because the nights are freer than the days for declaring the Lord’s loving-kindness and His faithfulness. Metzudas Dovid: “In the morning” — every morning; “and Your faithfulness” — the fulfilment of Your promise we shall declare in every night. Malbim: The natural governance is called “faithfulness,” for at the creation of the world He promised to keep the statutes of nature as a law that does not pass away, while the wondrous governance is called “loving-kindness,” since to that He did not obligate Himself. The poet marks these two by the morning and the night: the morning, when the creatures are roused to fresh activity and God renews the work of creation, signifies the time when God performs new deeds through His providential governance — “to declare Your loving-kindness in the morning”; and the night, when the living rest from their labors and God lets nature run its course, signifies “and Your faithfulness in the nights,” that all the works of creation keep their statutes and stand in their nature as He implanted it in them in the six days of creation. (תְּהִלִּים צב, ג):
and as it is written (Psalms 92:3):
"וֶאֱמוּנָתְךָ בַּלֵּילוֹת" –
"'And Your faithfulness in the nights' –"
עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה
this world, which is compared to night,

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פְּסָחִים ב40 Pesachim 2b — They raised an objection: “And I said: Surely darkness shall envelop me, and the night shall be light about me” (Psalms 139:11) — evidently “light” means day! There, this is what David said: I had said, surely darkness will envelop me in the World to Come, which resembles day; [but] now this world, which resembles night, is light about me. Rashi: [On the objection:] David had thought in his affliction, when he was pursued, that he would surely die in this darkness, which would "envelop" him — darken over him continually (from the word for twilight) — and instead the night and darkness in which he dwelt became "light about me"; since it is set against "night," "light" means day: the night became day for me. [On the answer:] "I said" that because of my sin I would be driven even from the World to Come; and now that He has forgiven me that sin, even this world, in which I had dwelt in darkness and disgrace, has shone about me — for in Solomon's days, when he sought to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies and the gates cleaved to one another, the Holy One, blessed be He, made known to David's enemies that He had forgiven David (Moed Katan 9a). Maharsha: At first sight, on the Gemara's present assumption that "night" is said figuratively of his being in distress and darkness, as Rashi explains, one could equally say that "light" comes from "to shine" [and does not mean day] — just as the Gemara takes it at the end, where "night" is a figure for this world and "light" is from "to shine," as Rashi explains; and this can be resolved. Maharal (Derashas Shabbos HaGadol): This world, being a physical world, is called "night" because of matter, which does not exist in complete actuality; and what does not [fully] exist is called "night" and "darkness." For whatever stands within turbid matter is said to be in darkness, and what is in darkness is reckoned as though it does not exist at all. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 19): [On "to declare Your kindness in the morning and Your faithfulness in the nights":] "Morning" is the World to Come, which is entirely light, as in the first chapter of Pesachim, where the World to Come is called "morning" and this world "night." In the World to Come the kindness and good that the Holy One, blessed be He, does with the righteous will be seen; but in this world, which is like night and in which the righteous do not dwell in good, one declares His faithfulness — for though he is in distress, he believes in Him that the good will be his in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): Truth is what is clarified and revealed in the heart and needs no faith, but in concealment truth is clothed in faith (the secret of "True and firm" in the morning and "True and faithful" in the evening), so that even in concealment one believes in the Life of the worlds by way of faith. This is the state of all of man in this world, which is likened to night, and all the more so in the time of exile, the full darkness of night; and since this world is full of deceptions and the darkness of the evil inclination, one must at least strengthen himself in faith.:).
(as they stated in Pesachim 2b).
וְטַעַם חֶשְׁכָּתוֹ הוּא מִשּׁוּם יֵצֶר הָרָע דְּמַחְשִׁיךְ וְכוּלֵי,
The reason for its darkness is on account of the evil inclination which darkens, etc.,

וְהַיְינוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין ל41 Kiddushin 30b — The Sages taught: "And you shall place [vesamtem] these words of Mine upon your heart" — read it as sam tam, a perfect remedy; the Torah is likened to an elixir of life. A parable: a man struck his son a great blow and laid a bandage upon the wound, and said to him, My son, so long as this bandage is on your wound, eat what you please and drink what you please and bathe as you please, and have no fear; but if you remove it, the wound will fester. So the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: My children, I created the evil inclination, and I created the Torah as its antidote; if you occupy yourselves with Torah you will not be delivered into its hand. Rashi (s.v. "a perfect remedy"): "A perfect remedy" means a complete one, lacking nothing needed for the cure. "What you please" — whatever your mind is drawn to, even honey and every kind of sweet thing, which are bad for a wound. Maharsha: In a homiletic vein the baraita speaks of an elixir of life in place of sam tam, for the opposite of tam, "whole", is met, "dead" — that the drug upon his wound would otherwise be a deadly one, since the evil inclination is the angel of death. In the analogue: so long as you occupy yourselves with Torah, which is the bandage over the wound that is the evil inclination, you may take pleasure in this world and will not come to sin, for the Torah shields a man as the bandage shields the wound from festering; but to leave off Torah is to remove the bandage, and then it is impossible not to come to sin, as in "an ignoramus cannot be pious" — he does not know wherein he will stumble. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 30b): The Torah is likened to an elixir of life and prevails over the inclination because nothing of privation pertains to the Torah: the intellect is complete in actuality, and the Torah above all is a rank over which privation has no dominion. Therefore the Torah does not let the evil inclination gain the upper hand, for the evil inclination is privation, and privation cleaves to matter; once a man follows the intellect of the Torah, the evil inclination that is the privation cleaving to matter does not overcome him, and in this sense the Torah is the antidote to the inclination. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:19): As the Midrash HaNe'lam says, even in the future the evil inclination will not be nullified, for without it there would be no delight in Torah; and on this they said, "I created the evil inclination, I created Torah as its spice", literally like a spice that seasons a food until it becomes "very good", as the Sages said of "very good": this is the evil inclination. For one places all his longing and desire and the natural passion of his body into desire for words of Torah, in which there is truly great desire to know the depth of its wisdom; and then the evil inclination becomes a good inclination, "inclination" meaning desire in one's mind and heart. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 11): Prayer, "the service of the heart", requires toil to direct one's heart, like a servant before the king; whereas Torah, like a minister, requires no toil to direct the heart, for through delving deeply into words of Torah the heart straightens of itself, in the sense of "I created Torah as its spice", since mind and heart are inseparable companions, and through the wisdom in the heart the heart too is aroused. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 9): The creation of evil is not written explicitly in the account of creation because in truth the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing evil in the world: even the evil inclination was not created for evil, as it says, "I created the evil inclination, I created Torah as a spice against it"; it is only you who make it evil. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 97): The rectification of mazal is occupation with Torah, as it says, "I created the evil inclination, I created Torah as its spice." A spice is to sweeten the food, that is, to turn the evil into "very good", as the Sages said that ["very good"] is the evil inclination, which is sweetened through words of Torah.:):
which aligns with (Kiddushin 30b):
"בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע וְכוּלֵי",
"I created the evil inclination, etc.,"
שֶׁכֵּן נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא,
for the world was created with darkness first,
וְהַחֹשֶׁךְ הוּא מִכְּלַל הַבְּרִיאָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
and darkness is an intrinsic part of creation in this world,
וְהוּא יִצְרָא דַּעֲרָיוֹת בְּתַאֲוָה,
namely the inclination toward forbidden sexual unions through lust,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִנְיַן עוֹלָם הַזֶּה בַּגּוּף –
which is the nature of this world in bodily existence –
כְּשֶׁנִּמְשָׁךְ אַחַר תַּאֲוַת גּוּף הוּא חֹשֶׁךְ.
when one is drawn after bodily desire, it constitutes darkness.
"וּבַבֹּקֶר חַסְדֶּךָ" –
"'And Your lovingkindness in the morning' –"
חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם,
which is the attribute of lovingkindness associated with Abraham,
הַיְינוּ כָּל תַּאֲווֹתָיו לַשָּׁמַיִם,
meaning when all of a person's desires are solely directed toward Heaven;
אָז מַשִּׂיג הַבֹּקֶר דְּאַבְרָהָם
then one attains the morning of Abraham,
לְהַשִּׂיג אוֹר בָּהִיר הַנּוֹכָחַ דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
attaining the radiant, immediate Presence of Hashem, blessed be He.
אֲבָל מִצַּד הַשִּׁיקּוּעַ בַּתַּאֲווֹת
However, from the vantage point of immersion in bodily desires,
אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג הַנּוֹכָחַ דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
it is impossible to perceive the direct Presence of Hashem, blessed be He.
וְעַל זֶה תִּקְּנוּ חֲכָמִים בִּרְכַּת הַנֶּהֱנִין,
And regarding this, the Sages instituted the blessing over physical pleasures,
קוֹדֶם הַשִּׁיקּוּעַ בַּהֲנָאָה
such that prior to sinking into sensory pleasure,
אָז יֹאמַר הַבְּרָכָה "בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה וְגוֹמֵר" בְּנוֹכָח
one recites the blessing 'Blessed are You, etc.' in direct second-person address,
וּמַכִּיר שֶׁכָּל הֲנָאוֹתָיו מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
recognizing that all of his pleasures stem from Hashem, blessed be He.

וְזֶהוּ (שַׁבָּת לא42 Shabbat 31a — Reish Lakish said: What is meant by "And the faithfulness of your times shall be a store of salvation, wisdom and knowledge"? "Faithfulness" — this is the Order of Zeraim; "your times" — this is the Order of Moed; "a store" — this is the Order of Nashim; "salvation" — this is the Order of Nezikin; "wisdom" — this is the Order of Kodashim; "and knowledge" — this is the Order of Taharot. And even so, "the fear of the Lord is his treasure." Rashi: "Faithfulness" is the Order of Zeraim, for one relies on a person's faithfulness to set aside his tithes properly. "A store" [חוסן] is an expression for heirs, and heirs are born through a woman; "salvation" is the Order of Nezikin, for it saves them by warning them to keep away from causing damage and from incurring monetary liability; and "knowledge" surpasses wisdom. "Is his treasure": it is the chief thing, esteemed in his eyes, to store away and make a treasured possession for remembrance. Tosafos (s.v. "'faithfulness' — this is the Order of Zeraim"): The Yerushalmi explains: because he trusts in the Life of the worlds and sows. Maharsha: "Faithfulness" may also refer to Berakhot, the first tractate of Zeraim, on account of the hundred blessings mentioned in it, for greater is the one who answers "Amen" to them; and "salvation" is Nezikin because the four primary categories of damage on earth allude to four heavenly damages, from which we need mercy to save and rescue us. Although, as Rashi says, knowledge surpasses wisdom — knowledge being the holy spirit — so that "knowledge" should properly have been Kodashim, since holiness surpasses purity, [Reish Lakish] took the orders in their sequence, Kodashim before Taharot. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 31a): "Faithfulness — this is the Order of Zeraim": since the Blessed Name sustains man, man should have faith in Him in all things; and the Yerushalmi's explanation, that one trusts in the Life of the worlds and sows, means that sowing is itself faith in Him, for it shows that the Blessed Name sustains man. "Even so, 'the fear of the Lord is his treasure'": eternal permanence comes only through the fear of the Blessed Name — hence it is called a treasury, where things are put to be preserved — so that even the whole Torah has permanence only through it, for what is caused has no permanence of its own, only from its Cause. Love, being between two parties, leaves each a thing of its own; but one who fears Heaven nullifies himself entirely before the Blessed Name, as though he were nothing and all were from Him, and so, wholly given over to Him, he receives eternity. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 10): In the six orders the Sages divided all of existence, ascending from the material to the separate: Zeraim, the growth of the earth, is "faithfulness" because the earth does not alter what was deposited in it, like a faithful man who returns a deposit; Moed belongs to the heavens, whose sun and moon fix the festivals; Nashim and Nezikin correspond to woman, the more material, and to man in general; Kodashim, treating of holiness, is "wisdom," and Taharot "knowledge," for purity is separate from matter and cleaves wholly to the Blessed Name. "Even so, the fear of the Lord is his treasure": all the wisdoms are only a preparation for a higher level, not eternal permanence itself, which comes from the Blessed Name alone through cleaving to Him — and that is through fear rather than love, for one who fears counts himself as nothing and nullifies his existence before Him, whereas the lover is joined to Him as two lovers are joined. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 1): "Faithfulness is the Order of Zera'im": faith is the goal toward which all the commandments of the Torah are directed, as "Habakkuk came and based them on one", and all of man's essential needs in this world lie in seeds, which sustain his life. Therefore the positive and negative commandments of Zera'im came to root in his heart that the sustenance of his life is from the Blessed One, and he was commanded to give the first of his harvest, grain and dough to the kohen, so that his thought at the beginning of his deeds is for the sake of God. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis 2): "Faithfulness" is the Order of Zera'im, for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows, as Tosafos explain. Seemingly the gentiles also sow although they have no faith; but this is precisely the novelty of Israel's faith: though he acts as the way of nature requires, as with sowing, which makes things grow because the world follows its natural course, he nevertheless knows with certainty that everything comes from the Creator's providence, even what is left to human action. Beis Yaakov (Noach 37): Sowing is a garment for prayer and faith in the Blessed One, as in "Faithfulness is the Order of Zera'im", which the Yerushalmi and the Midrash on Psalms explain, "for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows." Harvest is the opposite, for at harvest time one may err and say "my strength and the might of my hand made me this wealth"; and the connecting vav [in "seedtime and harvest"] teaches that even at harvest there must be something of sowing, standing in faith and prayer to the Blessed One. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 72): Sowing is in truth a matter of prayer, as in "Faithfulness is the Order of Zera'im", explained in the Midrash, "for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows": for without faith how could one sow? Perhaps his sowing would be lost and nothing would grow; rather, the very fact that a person sows proves that he believes in the Life of the worlds, that his sowing will surely not be lost but will grow. Sha'ar HaEmunah (Entrance to the Gate 1): The fear of the Lord is the vessel for receiving the Torah, as it says, "the fear of the Lord is his treasure"; so in Shabbat, "Faithfulness" is the Order of Zera'im (as Tosafos explain, for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows), and the Gemara concludes, "even so, if the fear of the Lord is his treasure, yes; if not, no." The matter is that the beginning of judgment is about faith, for faith is the root of fear and fear is the vessel that holds the faith: a person believes in the Blessed One, and through faith in His surpassing power and exaltedness [comes to fear Him]..):
And this corresponds to (Shabbat 31a):
"'אֱמוּנַת' – זֶה סֵדֶר זְרָעִים",
"'Faith' refers to the Order of Zera'im (Seeds),"
שֶׁמַּאֲמִין בְּחֵי עוֹלָמִים וְזוֹרֵעַ
for he believes in the Life of the Worlds and sows

(תּוֹסָפוֹת מִיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וְהִיא בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים מִזְמוֹר יט43 Midrash Tehillim 19:11 — R. Tanchuma expounded it of the six orders of the Mishnah: "The Torah of the Lord is perfect" — this is the order Nashim; "the testimony of the Lord is faithful" — this is the order Zera'im, for he has faith in the Life of the worlds and sows; "the fear of the Lord is pure" — this is the order Tohorot, for it separates between impurity and purity. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 1): Knowing this [that the earth and its fullness are the Lord's] is called faith, and the Yerushalmi explains, "for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows": the very beginning of sowing comes from believing in the Life of the worlds and recognizing that the Blessed One (who gives life to every living being and to all the worlds, and from whom grow the seeds that sustain our life and the life of the seeds themselves, which is the title "Life of the worlds") is the One who makes it grow; not nature alone, but He gives nature its power. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 14): R. Chanina ben Dosa recognized explicitly that everything is from the Blessed One, and that oil burning is also a miracle; and this is the meaning of "Faithfulness is the Order of Zera'im", which Tosafos explain from the Yerushalmi, "for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows": the nations sow and think that it grows by nature, while Israel believe in the Life of the worlds, that it is He who makes it grow. Beis Yaakov (Mikeitz 3): Joseph's attribute of restraining oneself in every action draws down all good influence, like a king who wished to give a man a maneh and he accepted only half, so that the king must give anew. This is also why there is no growth except through sowing: the Blessed One gave man grain, which is his to eat, but man restrains himself, gives it back, and "believes in the Life of the worlds and sows"; therefore the Blessed One makes a great increase grow for him anew. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 10): Sowing is a garment in this world for faith, as the Sages said, "Faithfulness is the Order of Zera'im, for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows"; but one who stole a se'ah of wheat and sows it certainly has no faith, so what sowing is this, and if it is no sowing, how could anything grow from it? What appears outwardly as sowing and growth is mere imagination, born of the concealment by which the world seems to follow its natural course, while in truth the Blessed One never relinquished His governance.),
(Tosafot from the Yerushalmi, found in Shocher Tov, Psalms 19),
וּמְקַבֵּל הֲנָאוֹתָיו מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
and receives his sustenance and pleasures from Hashem, blessed be He,
הֲגַם שֶׁהוּא בְּמַחְשָׁךְ מַעֲשֵׂהוּ,
even while his labor is engaged down in earthly obscurity;
עַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "צַדִּיק בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ יִחְיֶה" (חֲבַקּוּק ב, ד),
concerning this Scripture declared: 'The righteous shall live by his faith' (Habakkuk 2:4),
וְדָבָר זֶה חֲבַקּוּק אֲמָרוֹ
and this principle was articulated specifically by Habakkuk
שֶׁהוּא מִסִּטְרָא דִּילֵיהּ דְּנוּקְבָא
because he stems from the feminine aspect (Nukva),

כַּיָּדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, מד44 Zohar, Beshalach 1:12 — "And Gehazi said: But she has no son." Elisha said to her: Surely the hour has come, for the day brings it about. "And he said: At this season, when the time comes round, you shall embrace a son." Afterward he died. Why did he die? Because he was given to her and not to her husband, and he was bound from the place of the female; and whoever is bound to the female — death is made ready before him. How do we know that he was given to her? Because it is written, "you shall embrace a son." Come and see: of Abraham it is written, "I will surely return to you" — to you and not to her; in you he was bound, and not in the female. Whoever comes from the side of the female — death runs before his feet.:).
as is known in the Zohar (Part II, 44b).
וְזֶהוּ הָעֵצָה
And this is the vital counsel:
בְּעֵת שִׁיקּוּעַ הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
during the moments of man's necessary immersion in this world,
אַל יָזוּז מִמֶּנּוּ עַל כָּל פָּנִים אֱמוּנָה הַפְּשׁוּטָה
let him at the very least never abandon the simple faith
דְּהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ.
that everything originates from Hashem, blessed be He, and there is none besides Him.
וְהַמִּזְמוֹר שֶׁל יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת מוֹדִיעַ זֶה:
The psalm for the Sabbath day proclaims this:
"לְהַגִּיד וְגוֹמֵר",
"'To declare in the morning Your lovingkindness...,' etc.,"

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת45 Shabbat 118a — R. Shimon ben Pazi said in the name of R. Yehoshua ben Levi, citing Bar Kappara: Whoever fulfils the obligation of three meals on Shabbat is saved from three calamities — from the birth-pangs of Mashiach, from the judgment of Gehinnom, and from the war of Gog and Magog. Rashi: "The birth-pangs of Mashiach" — as we say in Ketubot (112b): the generation in which the son of David comes will see accusation against Torah scholars, as it is said, "And if there be yet a tenth in it" etc.; "pangs" [chevlei] is an expression for the pangs of a woman in childbirth (Hosea 13). Maharsha: The birth-pangs of Mashiach precede his coming, and the meaning is that one will be saved from them and merit the day of his coming. He is saved from these three days of distress because after them will come the days of cessation and rest for the righteous, which Shabbat signifies; therefore one who keeps Shabbat and delights in it properly with the three meals deserves that these days of distress, too, be for him days of rest and peace, with no distress after them. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 118a): One who keeps the three meals, corresponding to the three parts of the day, fulfills the true essence of the Shabbat day, whose three parts are delight and good; he is therefore saved from the three calamities that exist in the world by the nature of existence — for these, unlike most calamities, which come incidentally on account of sin, stem from man's deficiency and are ordained by the Blessed One from the very essence of creation. Shabbat is the completion of creation, and its three meals signify the good in the Blessed One's creation; therefore, by virtue of the good and completeness in creation, those who keep them are saved from the three calamities that arise from creation's deficiency. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shemini 9): The birth-pangs of Mashiach and the war of Gog and Magog will come only in that generation — and Bar Kappara lived some two centuries before Mashiach could come — yet every individual soul is saved from them, for just as "whoever has knowledge, it is as if the Temple was built in his days," every Jewish soul can build the Temple inwardly, and so the rectifications of the birth-pangs of Mashiach and of the wars of Gog and Magog also exist spiritually in each soul. These three calamities rectify the three evil traits from which the damage grew since creation — envy, lust and honor — and their remedy is the three Shabbat meals, which draw on the holiness of the three Patriarchs. The Friday-night meal corresponds to Isaac's holiness, the fear of the Lord, and saves from the birth-pangs of Mashiach — the "accusation against Torah scholars" — which correspond to the blemish of envy and baseless hatred. (קיח.):
just as they stated in Shabbat (118a):
"הָאוֹכֵל שָׁלֹשׁ סְעוּדוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת נִיצּוֹל מִשָּׁלֹשׁ פּוּרְעָנֻיּוֹת וְכוּלֵי",
"Whoever eats three meals on Shabbat is saved from three tribulations, etc.,"
וְדִינוֹ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם הוּא הַשִּׁיקּוּעַ בַּתַּאֲווֹת,
and the punishment of Gehenna is itself the unrestrained sinking into base desires,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין (יט46 Eruvin 19a — But is there not also "Gehinnom"? — A valley so deep that all go down into it for the sake of worthless things. But is there not also "Tophteh," as it is written, "For Tophteh is ordered from of old"? — That is the place where everyone who is enticed by his impulse falls. Rashi: "For worthless things [hinnam]" means forbidden relations. "Tophteh" is Gehinnom, for in that very verse it is written, "its pile is fire and much wood" (Isaiah 30:33). Tosafos (s.v. "but is there not also Tophteh"): It is puzzling that "the leech" (Proverbs 30:15) was not counted among the names of Gehinnom. Rabbeinu Tam explains that "leech" is the name of a sage, like "to Ithiel," and that the reason it is applied to Gehinnom in Avodah Zarah [17a] is only that the verse goes on, "the grave, and the barren womb." Maharsha: It appears that two things are being said at once: it is called Gehinnom after the Valley of ben Hinnom named at the beginning of the verse, because that valley is seen to be exceedingly deep; and further, because all go down into this valley for the sake of "nothing [hinnam]," that is, forbidden relations, as it is expounded, "which we ate in Egypt for nothing" — this refers to forbidden relations. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): The fire of Gehinnom has no dominion over Torah scholars, whose whole body is fire, because the fire of Gehinnom is the fire of lust — as written in Eruvin that all go down "for the sake of worthless things," and as it is said, "Your spirit is a fire that shall consume you," so that the fire of Gehinnom is made from the sin itself — and the fire of the Torah is a fire that consumes the fire of Gehinnom. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): Our father Abraham, head of the circumcised, brings all Israel up from Gehinnom, for all go down there "for the sake of worthless things," and whoever is enticed by his impulse falls there — that is, through lust — and the seal of the covenant testifies to save them, [showing] that their lust came only from the thorns surrounding the myrtle, while at their root they are circumcised and fenced off from lust. The exception is one who has relations with a gentile woman: through his desire to cleave to the nations she becomes for him a foreskin enveloping the circumcision; yet since one whose foreskin is drawn forward is still circumcised by Torah law, "Abraham does not recognize him" means that to the human eye he looks uncircumcised, and only the Blessed One Himself, who sees into the heart, saves him, for in the depths of his heart he too is circumcised. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 15): The Gemara in Eruvin goes on to say that all go down into Gehinnom "for the sake of worthless things," which Rashi explains as forbidden relations — implying that this is because it is a commonly found transgression, and also that the main dominion of Gehinnom's fire is to consume the fire of the impulse for forbidden relations, which is itself a fire, as it is said, "They are all adulterers, like an oven heated … burning like a flaming fire." Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 194): When one reaches such fear of Heaven that he sweats, the river of fire of his fear burns away the whole root of the evil lusts in his heart, which is what is called "the heads of the wicked in Gehinnom" — for Gehinnom is essentially lust, as stated in Eruvin, that all go down "for the sake of worthless things." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Through circumcision Israel are saved from Gehinnom, and our father Abraham, who by his own effort attained circumcision and left the ranks of the uncircumcised, is the one who saves them; for all of Gehinnom is over evil lusts, as they said that all go down "for the sake of worthless things" and forbidden relations, and circumcision testifies that the organ of lust of the children of Israel is holy to God. Even one who has relations with a gentile woman, whose foreskin is drawn forward, is truly circumcised by Torah law and needs re-circumcision only for appearance's sake; so "Abraham does not recognize him" refers to outward appearance, for man — even the greatest of giants, like our father Abraham — "sees what is before the eyes," while "the Lord sees into the heart" and will save them too..):
and as they noted in Eruvin (19a):
שֶׁהַכֹּל יוֹרְדִין עַל עִסְקֵי הִנָּם
that all descend thither on account of empty, vain pursuits,
וְכָל הַמִּתְפַּתֶּה בְּיִצְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי,
and anyone seduced by his base inclination, etc.,

וְשָׁם (יח47 Eruvin 18b — Our Rabbis taught: One who counts out coins to a woman from his hand to hers or from her hand to his in order to gaze at her — even if he is like Moses our teacher, who received the Torah at Mount Sinai — will not be cleared of the judgment of Gehinnom. Of him Scripture says, "Hand to hand, the evil man shall not be cleared" — he shall not be cleared of the judgment of Gehinnom. Rashi: "Counts out" means that he counts them. "Hand to hand" refers to one who passes the coins from his hand to hers — even if he is like Moses, who received the Torah from the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, into his own hand. Tosafos (s.v. "hand to hand, the evil man shall not be cleared"): This is not the verse expounded in Sotah [4b] with regard to arrogance; there the exposition is from "Everyone that is proud in heart is an abomination to the Lord; though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished" (Proverbs 16:5), whereas the verse here is "Hand to hand, the evil man shall not be cleared, but the seed of the righteous shall escape" (Proverbs 11:21). Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaPerishus 2): The eyes are instruments that serve licentiousness, and the hands too are instruments by which a man — who is himself an intellectual being — carries out the deeds he ought to do; this man presses those instruments into the service of a licentious act, and therefore he is not delivered from the judgment of Gehinnom, even if he received the Torah from the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, and those very hands served to receive it. There is no evil like this, for these limbs were not created that a man should use them for so degraded an act, and that is why it is evil. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 2): When the Sages say of Gehazi that he "was not holy, for he grabbed her," it cannot mean that he grabbed her intentionally for his pleasure, for of that one would not say merely that he is not holy — he would even be called wicked, as follows from "one who counts out coins …" in Eruvin. Rather, as he came to push her away it happened that he grabbed her, and such a thing does not happen to one who is holy.:):
and there (18b):
"הַמַּרְצֶה מָעוֹת וְכוּלֵי אֲפִילּוּ וְכוּלֵי אֵין נִיצּוֹל מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם",
"One who counts out coins into a woman's hand, etc., even if he possesses Torah like Moses, is not saved from the judgment of Gehenna,"
הֲרֵי שֶׁעִיקַּר דִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם הוּא עַל יְדֵי תַּאֲוָה.
proving that the essential retribution of Gehenna arises specifically through bodily lust.
וְכֵן הַגַּן עֵדֶן שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ גֵּיהִנָּם,
Likewise Gan Eden, which is the antithesis of Gehenna,

רַק צַדִּיקִים יוֹשְׁבִים וְכוּלֵי וְנֶהֱנִים מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה (בִּבְרָכוֹת יז48 Berakhot 17a — Rav was wont to say: The World to Come is not like this world. In the World to Come there is no eating and no drinking, no procreation and no commerce, no envy and no hatred and no rivalry. Rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads and take delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence, as it is stated: “And they beheld God, and they ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11). Rashi: "And they ate and drank" — they were sated by the radiance of the Divine Presence as though they had eaten and drunk. Maharsha: He derives the point from the redundancy and the change of wording in the verse: Scripture had already said "and they saw the God of Israel," and then says again "and they beheld God" — and "beholding" generally denotes an intellectual vision, a prophecy. They beheld and took delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence as though they had eaten and drunk; for at the giving of the Torah they were in the likeness of the World to Come, their crowns upon their heads, as it is said [in Shabbat 88a] that every Israelite received two crowns, and they were removed from bodily things, as it is said of Moses that he did not eat for forty days. Maharal (Derech Chaim on Avot 3:16): The meaning is that in the World to Come a man needs no completing, unlike this world, in which a man must receive his completion; there he will be complete on a higher level. He will therefore need no eating and drinking to complete himself, nor procreation — for offspring are a man's completion — nor commerce, by which a man supplies what he lacks; and there will be no envy or hatred, since these are themselves a defect. And "the righteous sit": the World to Come is not a thing of motion as this world is, and sitting signifies that a man is already complete in actuality and no longer moving toward his completion. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 4): Seeking to be a son of the World to Come purely for one's own sake is no different from seeking a reward in this world; but the essence of the World to Come, that "they delight in the radiance of the Shechinah," is not self-benefit. One can merit this even in this world — the "one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world" that is better than all the World to Come — when the reward of a mitzvah brings one to repentance, love and cleaving; for such a reward one may hope, and serving for it is wholly for its own sake, out of love. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 7): Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World to Come, and the World to Come is the absence of the action of "today to do them" — only "the righteous [sit] … and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah" — and Shabbat holds a semblance of this, which is why, though there is no reward for mitzvos in this world, Shabbat is called "a good gift." In this world one employs the powers of action, whereas the World to Come is the heart alone. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): From within this world, which is likened to night, they will merit the light of the World to Come, which is wholly day with no darkness or evil — the light of the world of Atzilus, the light of the seven days of creation hidden away for the righteous — when they sit "with their crowns on their heads," that is, their attachment to their root in the Blessed One, "and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah," that is, the upper Shechinah. This is the first heh of the Name, alluding to the understanding in the heart, the secret of the World to Come, where the attachment of the hearts of Israel to their source is revealed. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 1): With the creation of man "tohu and bohu" were set aside, for a person can raise his actions without limit and reach a lofty place, as stated: "In the World to Come there is no eating and no drinking … rather the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah." Through the act of the mitzvah of shofar one arouses the "great shofar," which shows that Israel raise all their actions up to the "upper sun," to the place where the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah, and through the shofar one can reach with one's actions and service to the light of the Infinite..),
where righteous souls sit crowned and delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence (Berakhot 17a),
וְעַל יְדֵי שִׁיקּוּעַ בַּתַּאֲווֹת גֹּורְשׁוּ מִשָּׁם;
whereas through immersion in illicit desires mankind was originally expelled from there;
וְעוֹנֶג שַׁבָּת הוּא מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
yet Sabbath delight is a positive commandment of Hashem, blessed be He,
לְעַנֵּג עַצְמוֹ בְּכָל חֲמוּדוֹת וְתַאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה לִכְבוֹד שָׁמַיִם.
to take pleasure in all bodily delicacies and worldly delights solely for the honor of Heaven.
וְעוֹנֶג זֶה מַמְשִׁיךְ עוֹנֶג דְּכָל יְמֵי הַשָּׁבוּעַ עִמּוֹ,
And this sacred delight elevates and draws the physical enjoyment of all weekdays along with it,

כְּמוֹ בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת: "מָצָא מִין אֶת מִינוֹ וְנִיעוֹר" (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה עג49 Avodah Zarah 73a — When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came [from the Land of Israel] he said that R. Yochanan said: They taught this only where the pitcher of water fell in first; but if the pitcher of water did not fall in first, [the forbidden wine] has found its own kind and is roused. Rashi: "First" means before the libation wine, for when the libation wine fell in the water was already there and nullified it. "It has found its own kind" — at the end — "and is roused," that is, it gathered strength and its prohibition grew, and the wine outweighed the water; "roused" is like a man who wakes [ye'or] from his sleep, as in "one who is awake [ha-ni'or] at night.".),
as established in multiple contexts: 'Like finds like and is reawakened' (Avodah Zarah 73a),

"טְחִינָה גּוֹרֶרֶת טְחִינָה וְכוּלֵי" (שַׁבָּת עא50 Shabbat 71a — Reaping draws in reaping, and grinding draws in grinding [so that the atonement for one act extends to the other]. But if he became aware of the reaping done knowing it was the Sabbath but unaware that the labors were forbidden, the reaping draws in the reaping and the grinding done with it, and the grinding opposite it stays in its place. Abaye said: Grinding, too, draws in grinding, for it is all one category of grinding. Rashi: "Reaping draws in reaping": [it draws] the second into its atonement, and grinding draws in the second grinding, and all are atoned. For we hold that one who ate two olive-measures of forbidden fat in one lapse of awareness is liable only once; and although the lapse in the second reaping differs somewhat from that in the first [the one forgetting that it was Shabbat, the other that the labors were forbidden], it is still one lapse, since he did not learn of his sin in between, and it is awareness of the sin that divides — so the sin-offering brought for the first reaping and grinding stands for both the reaping and the grinding, and with the reaping all his reapings of that lapse are atoned, and with the grinding all his grindings. "It is one category of grinding": even though the first grinding itself is atoned only by being drawn in, [Abaye holds that] what is drawn in draws in further. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos, on Rashi s.v. "reaping draws in reaping"): Some object to Rashi: if a lapse that differs in this way still counts as one lapse, what was the Talmud's difficulty above in finding a case of "if he did them all in one lapse he is liable for each one"? It could be found where he did thirty-eight labors knowing it was Shabbat but not that they were forbidden, and one labor forgetting that it was Shabbat. One may answer that such a case is certainly not called "one lapse" without qualification; Rashi means only that two reapings in such a situation have the law of one lapse, so that he is liable only once..),
'Grinding draws further grinding, etc.' (Shabbat 71a),
וְכַיּוֹצֵא טוּבָא –
and many similar principles –
כָּל דָּבָר גּוֹרֵר וּמוֹשֵׁךְ עִמּוֹ דָּבָר אַחֵר הַדּוֹמֶה לוֹ,
every entity draws and aligns with itself whatever resembles it,
אִם גַּם בְּכָל יְמֵי הַשָּׁבוּעַ הָיָה לוֹ עַל כָּל פָּנִים אֱמוּנָה דְּכָל הֲנָאוֹתָיו מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
provided that throughout the weekdays he maintained at least the basic faith that all his pleasures originate from Hashem, blessed be He.
עַל יְדֵי הֲנָאוֹת הַשַּׁבָּת נִמְשָׁךְ הַכֹּל לִקְדוּשָּׁה
Through the sanctified pleasures of Shabbat, all weekday enjoyment is drawn upward into holiness

(וְעַיֵּין זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קנד51 Zohar, Terumah 47:517 — And the priests would gather the fruit of the Table from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve, to show that supernal sustenance issues from within that Table. And because of that bread which the priests gathered, all the food and drink that they ate and drank was blessed, so that the evil inclination should not accuse them over it — for the evil inclination is found only through eating and drinking. This is what is written, "lest I be sated and deny" — for through eating and drinking the evil inclination grows in a man's innards.:).
(and see Zohar Part II, 154b).
וְחֶבְלוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ וּמִלְחֲמוֹת גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג
The birth pangs of the Messiah and the apocalyptic wars of Gog and Magog
הֵם הַהֲכָנוֹת לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא בְּיִסּוּרִין מְצָרְפִין
are the final preparations for the World to Come via purifying afflictions,
מִשְּׁנֵי הַכֹּחוֹת דְּ"קוּם וַעֲשֵׂה" וְ"שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה",
working through both active service ('arise and do') and restraint ('sit and do not do'),
לִהְיוֹת בִּלְתִּי לַה' לְבַדּוֹ,
so that man becomes consecrated exclusively unto Hashem alone;
וְזֶה יוּכַל לִזְכּוֹת גַּם כֵּן לְהִצְטָרֵף בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת
and through this, one can merit to become refined through the holiness of Shabbat,
שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
which itself is a foretaste of the World to Come,
וְיִזְכֶּה לְהַגִּיד וְגוֹמֵר.
and thereby merit 'to declare in the morning Your lovingkindness...,' etc.

sections.en: Prayer, Intention, and the Power of Opposites

items.h: Prayer emerges from lack and reaches fulfillment through sincere intention; mitzvot can reverse natural outcomes when performed for Heaven's sake.

Seif 1 — Accepted Prayer and the Reversal of Nature
Joy signals accepted prayer, and a mitzvah performed with pure intent can reverse its apparent natural effect.

p: סִימָן לִתְפִלָּה הַמְקוּבֶּלֶת הוּא הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁלְּאַחֲרֶיהָ,
A sign of an accepted prayer is the joy that follows it,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר מח)52 Midrash Tehillim 48:2 — "The joy of all the earth" — and in what way was it a joy? That it gladdened all the earth. If a man committed a transgression, he would be anxious in his heart and his heart was bowed down within him; as Solomon said, "Anxiety in a man's heart bows it down, but a good word gladdens it." He would go up to Jerusalem and bring an offering and be atoned for, and his heart was glad within him, and he would leave there rejoicing. Therefore, "the joy of all the earth." עַל פָּסוּק "מְשׂוֹשׂ כָּל הָאָרֶץ"
and as it is written in Shocher Tov (Midrash Tehillim, Psalm 48) on the verse "The joy of the whole earth,"
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַקָּרְבָּן הָיָה בְּשִׂמְחָה.
that through the sacrificial offering one experienced joy.
וְכֵן הַתְּפִלָּה שֶׁהִיא בִּמְקוֹמָהּ,
So too is prayer, which stands in its stead,
וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי".
and thus Scripture states: "And I will make them joyful in My house of prayer."
וְכָל דָּבָר הַבֵּירוּר הוּא בְּהֶפְכּוֹ,
Now, the clarification of every matter is manifested through its opposite,
כִּי הַמִּצְוֹת נוֹתְנִים הֵיפֶךְ מַה שֶּׁהֵם כִּפְשָׁטָן,
for the commandments produce the opposite outcome of what they appear to yield on the surface,
כְּעִנְיַן "עַשֵּׂר שֶׁתִּתְעַשֵּׁר"
as in the teaching: "Tithe (asser) so that you may become rich (titasher)"

(תַּעֲנִית ט53 Taanit 9a — R. Yochanan met the young son of Reish Lakish. He said to him: Recite for me your verse. He said to him: “You shall surely tithe.” He said to him: And what is “you shall surely tithe”? He said to him: Tithe so that you may become rich. He said to him: How do you know this? He said to him: Go and test it. He said to him: And is it permitted to test the Holy One, blessed be He? Is it not written, “You shall not test the Lord”? He said to him: Thus said R. Hoshaya — except in this case, as it is said, “Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house, and test Me now in this, says the Lord of Hosts, if I will not open for you the windows of heaven and pour out for you blessing until there is no sufficiency.” Rashi: "The young son of Reish Lakish": the son of R. Yochanan's sister, and [this was] after Reish Lakish's death, as is evident below. "He said": [that is,] the child [said] to R. Yochanan, "What is 'you shall surely tithe'?" "He said to him": the child [said], "But is it not written, 'You shall not test'?" Tosafos (s.v. "you shall surely tithe"): So the Sifrei expounds "all the produce of your seed" to include interest, commerce and every other profit; and the Aggadah reads "that which comes forth from the field year by year" to mean that if you do not tithe your field properly, it will yield only what you used to set aside from it as tithe. So it happened with a rich man whose field yielded a thousand kor, of which he set aside a hundred; when his son withheld the tithe, the field yielded only a hundred, and his kinsmen told him: at first you were the householder and the Holy One, blessed be He, the priest; now that you did not set aside His portion, He is the householder and you are the priest. Maharsha: "Tithe so that you may become rich": the second verb [of "you shall surely tithe"] would then denote wealth; alternatively it too denotes tithing, and it means: give a tithe of what is yours, and by this you will merit to tithe of your own yet again. "And test Me now in this": because in this a person is especially prone to put [God] to the test — how can it be that by diminishing his money to give a tithe his wealth will be increased? So He says: do not wonder at this, "test Me now in this" great matter, "if I will not open for you the windows of heaven," from which the curse came upon the world in the Flood, as it is written, "and the windows of heaven were opened" — and from them, through the tithe you give, "I will pour out for you blessing until there is no sufficiency." Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:13): When a person gives of his money to the Blessed Name, blessing comes from the Blessed Name upon his money, for he has brought of his wealth near to Him; therefore He commanded that one of every ten be given to Him, and thereby one brings his money into His domain. The particulars [up to nine] are mere parts, and every part is deficient, but the tenth, which completes the ten, is no particular and has no deficiency; so one who gives the tithe to the Blessed Name cleaves to Him in that He encompasses all, and then he has blessing and increase, for the whole is blessing — in the whole there is no deficiency, only wealth. For this reason the tenth is called by the term "wealth.".),
(Ta'anit 9a),
דִּלְפִי טֶבַע מַעֲשֵׂר הוּא מַעֲנִי אָדָם שֶׁנּוֹתֵן מֶכֶס שְׁנֵי מַעַשְׂרוֹת וּתְרוּמָה,
for naturally a tithe would impoverish a person who gives the tax of two tithes and the priestly gift,
אֲבָל בְּמִצְוָה בְּהֵיפֶךְ זֶה מַעֲשִׁיר.
yet in a mitzvah, on the contrary, it enriches.

וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּשַׁבָּת (קיט54 Shabbat 119a — R. Yehuda HaNasi asked R. Yishmael son of R. Yosei: The wealthy of the Land of Israel, by what do they merit it? He said to him: Because they tithe, as it is said, "You shall surely tithe" — tithe so that you may become wealthy. And those of Babylonia, by what do they merit it? He said to him: Because they honor the Torah. And those of the other lands, by what do they merit it? He said to him: Because they honor the Sabbath. Rashi: "By what do they merit it": [by what do they merit] such great wealth. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 119a): One who honors the Shabbat or the Torah is fit for wealth, for both are holy — the Shabbat is holy of itself, unlike the festivals, which Israel sanctify — and what is holy, being separate from the physical, has no deficiency, so one who honors it is full and complete and lacks nothing; moreover, whoever gives honor is himself honored ("for those who honor Me I will honor"), and wealth is honor. "Honoring the Torah" means honoring its scholars, since that is done for the Torah's sake. The tithe works the same way: the tenth is everywhere set apart and belongs to the Holy One, blessed be He, and when one's wealth contains the tenth that is His, the supernal blessing, which lacks nothing, cleaves to his wealth — hence "wealth" (עושר) and "tenth" (עשירי) are one word, and the tithe, the honor of the Torah and the honor of the Shabbat are all one matter..):
And so it is stated in Shabbat (119a):
"עֲשִׁירִים שֶׁבְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ בִּשְׁבִיל שַׁבָּת".
"The wealthy outside the Land of Israel merit riches on account of honoring Shabbat."

וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ אֵיכָה (פְּתִיחָה יז55 Eikhah Rabbah, Petichta 17 — R. Abbahu opened: "They that sit in the gate talk of me" — these are the nations of the world, who sit in theatres and circuses; once they have sat and eaten and drunk and grown drunk, they sit and talk of me and mock me, saying, "May we never be reduced to carobs like the Jews." They bring the dead into their theatre with his head shaved, and say to one another, "Why is this one's head shaved?" And he answers: "These Jews are Sabbath-keepers, and whatever they toil for all the days of the week they eat on the Sabbath. They have no wood to cook with, so they break their beds and cook with them; and they sleep on the ground and are covered with dust and anoint themselves with oil — and therefore oil is dear.")
And in Midrash Eichah (Introduction 17)
דְּהָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת מְגַנִּים יְהוּדִים שֶׁהֵם עֲנִיִּים בִּשְׁבִיל הַשַּׁבָּתוֹת,
that idolaters disparage the Jews, claiming they are impoverished because of the Sabbaths,
שֶׁהֵם בְּטֵלִים שְׁבִיעִית יְמֵיהֶם וְעוֹד צְרִיכִים לְעַנְּגָם,
since they remain idle a seventh of their days and must furthermore indulge them,
וּבֶאֱמֶת מִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ עֲשִׁירוּת.
whereas in truth, wealth is directly drawn down from this.
וְכֵן בַּמִּדּוֹת
And similarly concerning internal character traits:
הַמְעַנֵּג הַשַּׁבָּת נִיצּוֹל מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם,
one who delights in Shabbat is spared from the judgment of Gehenna;
רָצָה לוֹמַר כִּי מֵהַתַּעֲנוּג נוֹלָד בַּלֵּב חֵשֶׁק לְתַאֲווֹת לְתַעֲנוּגִים,
which means to say: because physical delight naturally breeds in the heart a lust for worldly pleasures,
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ דְּאַדְּרַבָּה נִיצּוֹל מִדִּינָהּ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שֶׁהוּא הַשִּׁיקּוּעַ בַּתַּאֲווֹת.
and on this they taught that, on the contrary, he is spared from the judgment of Gehenna, which consists of sinking into base desires.
וְאָמַר בְּפָרָשַׁת רְאֵה בְּמִצְוַת עִיר הַנִּדַּחַת:
And Scripture states in Parashat Re'eh regarding the commandment of the wayward city:
"הַכֵּה תַכֶּה וְגוֹמֵר",
"You shall surely strike, etc.,"
שֶׁמּוֹלִיד אַכְזָרִיּוּת גָּדוֹל לְהַכּוֹת עִיר שְׁלֵימָה וּמְלוֹאָהּ וּלְאַבְּדָהּ מִכֹּל וָכֹל,
which naturally induces tremendous cruelty—to smite an entire populated city and utterly destroy it.
סִיֵּים עַל זֶה: "וְנָתַן לְךָ רַחֲמִים וְרִחַמְךָ",
Yet Scripture concludes upon this: "And He will grant you mercy, and have compassion on you,"

וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשִׁילְהֵי שַׁבָּת (קנא:)56 Shabbat 151b — It was taught: R. Gamliel son of Rabbi says: "And He will give you mercy, and have mercy upon you, and multiply you" — whoever has mercy upon [God's] creatures is shown mercy from Heaven, and whoever has no mercy upon creatures is not shown mercy from Heaven. Rashi: "And He will give you mercy" — that you will have mercy upon creatures. Maharsha: It is brought here in connection with charity: whoever has mercy upon creatures by giving charity is shown mercy [from Heaven], as is found in Tractate Beitzah. In this light one may explain "Let Your mercies speedily come to meet us, for we are brought very low" (Psalms 79:8): although the order is that one is shown mercy from Heaven only after he has mercy upon creatures — as in the verse cited here, first "He will give you mercy," that you have mercy upon creatures, and afterward "and have mercy upon you" — we ask that His mercies come first, before we show mercy, "for we are brought very low" and have not the means to give charity and have mercy upon creatures beforehand. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 151b): The quality of mercy comes from one's being bound and united with the one upon whom he has mercy — which is why a man has mercy upon his son, for his mind is bound up with his son. One who holds fast to this quality cleaves to the level at which divided things are united and bound together, and it is not a thing by halves: just as he binds himself to the one who needs mercy, [namely] the poor man, so too the Blessed Name binds Himself to him, and so he too is shown mercy on account of this unity. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Nisan 3): Anger has no good in it at all, [serving] only against Amalek; and likewise being cruel to the wicked, as with the condemned city, which is complete mercy, as is said in the passage of the condemned city, "And He will give you mercy and have mercy upon you." Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Re'eh): "And He will give you mercy and have mercy upon you": since the passage of the condemned city, which commands killing the whole city, appears to human eyes as cruel wrath, it says of this, "and He will give you mercy and have mercy upon you" — that through fulfilling the Lord's command the trait of compassion will come into you, so that you will be merciful where mercy is called for. Beis Yaakov (Vayeira 25): As is written, "And He will give you mercy and have mercy upon you": there are things for which the Holy One, blessed be He, sends a person mercy, so that he will have mercy on them and pray for them that they may endure; for though they are forbidden in themselves they do have being, and if they rise by stages from level to level they will become fit to be included in the form of man and be refined for their good within Israel. Sod Yesharim (Parashas Zachor 16): This cruelty [toward Amalek] was rightly reckoned as compassion, for the essence of compassion is to remove a destroyer from the world — as we find with the condemned city, that after judgment was executed upon them it says at once, "And He will give you mercy and have mercy upon you," for eliminating evil is truly the essence of compassion. מִזֶּה:
and our Rabbis of blessed memory expounded at the end of Shabbat (151b) from this:
"הַמְרַחֵם עַל הַבְּרִיּוֹת מְרַחֲמִין וְכוּלֵי",
"Whoever has mercy on created beings is granted mercy from Heaven, etc.,"
מְבוֹאָר דִּמְפָרֵשׁ "לְךָ רַחֲמִים" – שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְךָ רַחֲמִים עַל אֲחֵרִים.
which clearly explains 'grant you mercy' to mean that you will possess a merciful disposition toward others.
וְאָמַר "וְנָתַן" בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
And it says 'He will grant' without independent effort,
רַק עַל יְדֵי מִצְוָה זוֹ שֶׁתִּהְיֶה אַכְזָר עַל הָרְשָׁעִים כְּפִי רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
rather solely through this mitzvah—by acting ruthlessly against the wicked in accordance with the will of Hashem, blessed be He—
עַל יְדֵי זֶה תִּזְכֶּה לְמִדַּת רַחֲמָנוּת עַל הַצַּדִּיקִים כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
you will thereby merit the trait of genuine compassion toward the righteous according to the will of Hashem, blessed be He.

וְאָמְרוּ בְּסוֹטָה57 Sotah 46b — Our Rabbis taught: “And all the elders of that city, who are nearest to the slain man, shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley, and they shall say: Our hands did not shed this blood, neither did our eyes see it.” — Would it enter our minds that the court are shedders of blood? Rather: he did not come into our hands and we dismissed him without food, and we did not see him and let him go without escort. Rashi (on the Mishna, 45b): "He did not come into our hands and we dismissed him" — the Gemara explains: without food; and this is "our hands did not shed": he was not killed through us, in that we dismissed him without food so that he was forced to rob people and was killed on that account. "We did not see him and let him go" — alone, without company; and this is "neither did our eyes see." Maharsha (on the Mishna, 45b): The Yefeh Mar'eh objected to Rashi's "alone, without company" that a court is hardly obliged to provide company for everyone who travels alone, and took it as escort at his leaving the city; but the teachings about one who walks alone on the road and about escort in Chullin show that Rashi is right — this is escort on the road, so that he not be alone in a place of danger, for all roads are presumed dangerous. Yet escort applies even in the city, even for four cubits and even when he is not alone, as a special virtue by which the escorted man is saved from harm: since the escort means to protect him on his way, his thought and will benefit his fellow along the whole road — either as "He will fulfill the desire of those who fear Him" or because the escort's angels carry out his intention and go with the traveler in his stead.
