Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 46b): A man's strength is greater when he is within the community of mankind, for then he has the strength of the many, whereas one who is alone and separate has only individual strength, and then harms befall him; escorting a departing man shows that the many are joined to him, and then he is joined above as well, so that the higher beings, and even the Holy One, blessed be He, accompany him on the way — but one sent out alone is reckoned a mere individual, as though he had no place among mankind, and harms prevail over him. Hence "our hands did not shed this blood, neither did our eyes see it": one who is sent off without food or escort and not attended to is as though he had no share in the community; they have removed him from the collective of mankind, and that is called shedding blood, for they have nullified his strength and impaired his fortune. (מו:) עַל פָּסוּק "יָדֵינוּ לֹא שָׁפְכוּ וְגוֹמֵר":
And they said in Sotah (46b) on the verse 'Our hands did not shed this blood, etc.':
"וְכִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ שֶׁסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְכוּלֵי, אֶלָּא לֹא רְאִינוּהוּ וְכוּלֵי",
"Could it enter your mind that the Sanhedrin murdered him? Rather, we did not see him, etc.,"
פֵּירוּשׁ דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שֶׁהֵם רָאשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּפִי הִתְנַהֲגוּתֵיהֶם בְּמִדּוֹתֵיהֶם כָּךְ מַמְשִׁיכִים בְּכָל הַדּוֹר,
meaning that the Sanhedrin, who are the leaders of Israel, transmit traits to the entire generation according to their own conduct,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרָכִין (יז.)58 Arakhin 17a — "This is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, Jacob, selah." R. Yehuda Nesia and the Rabbis disagree about it: one said, the generation follows its leader; and one said, the leader follows his generation. ... Rather, we say it with regard to sternness and mildness. Rashi: The verse "This is the generation of those who seek Him" sets the generation alongside those who seek Him, comparing the one to the other. In the conclusion, "sternness" means anger, and "mildness" means being easily appeased. Maharsha: "Mildness" — Rashi explains it as humility: if the generation is harsh, the Holy One, blessed be He, sets over them a harsh leader, and if the people of the generation are gentle with one another, He sets over them a leader who guides them gently; and according to the one who says the generation follows its leader, the reverse, for the generation is drawn after its leader. The Sages did not wish to say that "those who seek Him" refers to the generation, as though they were all seekers of the Lord, but rather to the good leaders, who are certainly seekers of the Lord — or else the phrase refers to the leaders as those who seek the good of the generation, as it is said, "seeking the good of his people.": "דּוֹר לְפִי פַּרְנָס".
as they stated in Arachin (17a): 'A generation is shaped according to its leader.'
וּכְשֶׁהֵם דָּנִים דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת וּקְנָסוֹת לַהֲרוֹג וּלְהַעֲנִישׁ עוֹבְרֵי עֲבֵירָה,
And when they judge capital cases and penalties to execute and punish transgressors,
סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ שֶׁהֵם מַמְשִׁיכִים לֵב רַגָּז וְכַעַס וּרְצִיחָה בּוֹ בַּדּוֹר.
you might have thought that they impart a wrathful heart, anger, and murderous impulse into the generation.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ "יָדֵינוּ לֹא שָׁפְכוּ" –
Regarding this they declared: 'Our hands did not shed,' meaning:
דְּאָנוּ לֹא הִמְשַׁכְנוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כֹּחַ שְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים בַּדּוֹר.
we did not, Heaven forbid, draw down an impulse of bloodshed into the generation.
וְעַל זֶה פָּרִיךְ: וְכִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ וְכוּלֵי,
And on this the Gemara challenges: 'Could it enter your mind, etc.?',
דְּוַודַּאי סַנְהֶדְרִין הַהוֹרְגִים בְּמִצְוַת ה' אֵינָם שׁוֹפְכֵי דָמִים לְהַמְשִׁיךְ כֹּחַ שְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים.
for surely the Sanhedrin who execute by Hashem's command are not murderers who draw down bloodlust!
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: אֶלָּא לֹא וְכוּלֵי,
And to this they replied: 'Rather, we did not, etc.',
דְּהַיְינוּ אַדְּרַבָּה שֶׁהִמְשַׁכְנוּ הַהֵיפֶךְ, כֹּחַ הָרַחֲמָנוּת,
meaning that, on the contrary, we drew down the reverse—the power of mercy,
לִהְיוֹת כָּל הָרוֹאֶה חֲבֵירוֹ מְלַוֵּוהוּ וּמִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּהַצָּלָתוֹ מִשְּׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים.
so that anyone seeing his fellow escorts him and exerts himself to save him from bloodshed.
וּלְהַמְשִׁיךְ הַהֵיפּוּךְ בָּזֶה צָרִיךְ כַּוָּנָה לִשְׁמָהּ,
And to bring forth this inverted effect requires intentional performance purely for Heaven's sake,
דְּוַודַּאי מִצְוָה מַגְנָא וּמַצְלָא
for while a mitzvah certainly protects and saves

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סוֹטָה כא59 Sotah 21a — Rav Yosef said: A mitzva, at the time one is engaged in it, protects and saves; at a time one is not engaged in it, it protects but does not save. Torah, whether at a time one is engaged in it or at a time one is not engaged in it, protects and saves. Rabba objected: If so, did Doeg and Ahithophel not engage in Torah? Why did it not protect them? Rather, Rava said: Torah, at the time one is engaged in it, protects and saves; when one is not engaged in it, it protects but does not save. A mitzva, whether one is engaged in it or not, protects but does not save. Rashi: Rav Yosef holds that a mitzva does in fact protect a great deal from sufferings, and the baraita's "only for the moment" refers to sin, that the evil inclination not overpower him: while one is engaged in the mitzva it shields him from sufferings and saves him from the evil inclination lest it make him stumble, but once the mitzva is finished it shields him from punishment and does not save him. And when the baraita says "a transgression extinguishes a mitzva," it means not its shielding from sufferings but the receiving of reward in the time to come. Rabba's "why did it not protect them" means: why did it not save them from the evil inclination, which led them to sin and made them utterly wicked? Tosafos (s.v. "a mitzva, whether one is engaged in it or not"): This is difficult: what then does the baraita mean by comparing the mitzva to a lamp, which protects only for the moment? If it means protection from the evil inclination, [by Rava] a mitzva does not protect at all; if from punishment, it protects forever. Likewise, why did Scripture compare the Torah to light because it protects forever? If from punishment, a mitzva also protects forever; and if from the evil inclination, the Torah saves only for the moment [while one is engaged in it]. Maharsha: There is a slight difficulty: since [by Rava] the Torah still protects forever, why did Doeg and Ahithophel die before their time, as is said in Perek Chelek — why did the Torah not protect them? One may answer that he says the Torah protects only from punishments and sufferings, not from death. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael 14): According to Rav Yosef, while one is engaged in a mitzva he is performing a divine act and is worthy of both protection and rescue, but when he is not, it protects without saving, for the mitzva, being bound to the body, is bound to time — the baraita's "for the moment" refers to saving — whereas the Torah, which is not physical, saves forever. Rava holds that when one is not engaged in the Torah, since he has turned his mind away from the intellectual Torah, it protects but does not save, while a mitzva, engaged in or not, only protects; and that is why the mitzva is called "for the moment": it affords mere protection, and full punishment may still come upon him afterward, since it does not save completely. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 59): Torah is so called from "instructing the way," as the Sages said, "the light within it brings him back to the good"; and the light of Torah — which "protects and saves" from sin, as stated in Sotah, and this is "brings him back to the good" — is only for those who "go to the right" in it, for whom it is an elixir of life. But [one who studies] not for its own sake does not attain the light, and so it does not instruct him or bring him back to the good. Beis Yaakov (Vayeishev 5): Mitzvos protect only while one is engaged in them, for their light is like the light of a lamp, which shines only while it clings to the wick — like wealth stored in a treasury, which gives a man security but no strength to overcome his fellow until he buys food and drink with it and takes it into his body. Words of Torah, however, protect and save even when one is not engaged in them, for a person has strength from them constantly, without interruption, as it is written, "like dew from the Lord," and Torah is likened to dew. Yet in truth the light in the performance of the mitzvos is far greater than the light in words of Torah; only the Blessed One contracted it in garments, so that a person can attain in a single hour, by performing the mitzvah, what he could not attain without the act..)
(as they taught in Sotah 21a)
אַף כְּשֶׁעוֹשֶׂה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
even when performed not for its own sake,
שֶׁהֲרֵי "מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ",
since 'from doing it not for its own sake one comes to do it for its own sake,'
כָּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁלֹּא יוֹלִיד רַע חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בַּלֵּב.
all the more so will it not engender evil in the heart, Heaven forbid.
רַק לִהְיוֹת מוֹלִיד הַהֵיפֶךְ זֶהוּ רַק עַל יְדֵי לִשְׁמָהּ.
However, to generate the absolute opposite holy effect is possible only through selfless intention.
וְעַל זֶה שַׁפִּיר הוּצְרַךְ לוֹמַר "יָדֵינוּ לֹא וְגוֹמֵר" –
And concerning this, it was rightly necessary to declare 'Our hands did not, etc.'—
הַךְ "לֹא" הוּא בְּמַעֲשֶׂה:
this 'not' pertains directly to action:
עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה יָדֵינוּ לֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת נִשְׁפָּךְ,
through the deeds of our hands it was unfitting that blood be shed,
דְּעַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה יָדֵינוּ הִמְשַׁכְנוּ מִדַּת הַמְּנִיעוֹת מִשְּׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים בְּלֵב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
for through the actions of our hands we imparted the restraint against bloodshed into the hearts of the Jewish people,
וְלֹא רְאִינוּהוּ וְכוּלֵי.
and we did not see him, etc.

items.h:
Seif 2 — The Broken Heart and Torah Lishmah
Prayer rises from felt deficiency, while Torah studied for Heaven's sake produces reverence and faithful action.

p: וְכֵן הַתְּפִלָּה עִיקָּרָהּ בְּלֵב נִשְׁבָּר,
Likewise, prayer in its essence is rooted in a broken heart,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תְּהִלִּים נא, יט60 Psalms 51:19 — The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise. Radak: The sacrifices He desires are a broken spirit; and “a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” even though no sacrifice accompanies it — whereas the sacrifice itself You despise when the heart is not broken. Metzudas Dovid: A broken spirit is the sacrifice that finds favor; and if so, You will not despise my broken and contrite heart. Malbim: The essential sacrifice in which God takes pleasure is a broken spirit — that a man break his inner spirit, which raises images upon the heart, so that it no longer forms evil images but only images of wisdom and the fear of the Lord; this the Lord accepts as a sacrifice. And a broken and contrite heart too God does not despise: the heart is the outer vessel in which the spirit dwells, and when it is broken through submission, fasting and affliction, the outer vessel itself is broken so that it no longer craves.):
as it is written (Psalms 51:19):
"לֵב [נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה] וְגוֹמֵר לֹא תִבְזֶה",
"A broken and contrite heart, etc., You will not despise,"

וְאָמְרוּ (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, כג61 Zohar, Bereshit 17:187 — And David, because of the exile, said, "hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness," for he saw the Shekhinah laid waste and parched, and he bore suffering on her account. Afterward, when he saw that Israel were returning in joy, he composed ten kinds of song, and at the end of them all he said, "A prayer of the poor man, when he is faint." This is the prayer that wraps up all the prayers that precede it, [holding them back] until his own prayer enters. For this reason the poor man precedes them all.:):
and they taught (Zohar Part I, 23b):
"תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי אִיהִי מְעַטְּפָא כָּל צְלוֹתִין".
"The prayer of the poor man envelops all prayers."
כִּי עִיקַּר הַתְּפִלָּה מֵעוּמְקָא דְלִבָּא הוּא מִכֹּחַ הַכָּרַת הַחִסָּרוֹן,
For the essence of prayer from the depths of the heart arises from the realization of lack;
וּכְפִי גּוֹדֶל הַכָּרַת חֶסְרוֹנוֹ וְצָרְכּוֹ לִישׁוּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and commensurate with the depth of awareness of one's deficiency and need for the salvation of Hashem, blessed be He,
כָּךְ יִהְיֶה גּוֹדֶל צַעֲקָתוֹ מִקִּירוֹת הַלֵּב כַּיָּדוּעַ.
such will be the intensity of one's outcry from the walls of the heart, as is known.
וְלֵב נִשְׁבָּר הוּא הֵיפֶךְ הַשִּׂמְחָה,
Now, a broken heart is the very antithesis of joy,
כַּאֲשֶׁר מִתְבּוֹנֵן בְּחֶסְרוֹנוֹתָיו בְּכָל דָּבָר בִּפְרָט
for when a person contemplates his flaws in every single detail
וְאֵיךְ צָרִיךְ יְשׁוּעָה גְּדוֹלָה וְרַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם מְרוּבִּים,
and how desperate he is for vast salvation and abundant heavenly mercy,
וַודַּאי יִמָּלֵא עֶצֶב וּדְאָגָה כְּפִי הַסְּבָרָא.
he would logically be overcome with sorrow and anxiety.
אֲבָל מִצְווֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הֵם לְהֵיפֶךְ, מוֹלִידוֹת שִׂמְחָה,
Yet the commandments of Hashem, blessed be He, do the reverse, generating joy;
וְזֶהוּ סִימָן שֶׁהִיא שְׁלֵימָה וּמְקוּבֶּלֶת.
and this constitutes the very sign that the prayer is whole and accepted.
וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֵם בְּעֶצֶם מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב,
Words of Torah, moreover, intrinsically gladden the heart,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט)62 Ecclesiastes 7:19 — Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city. Rashi: "Wisdom gives strength to the wise" — since it had said "do not be overly wicked" [verse 17], meaning that if you have been somewhat wicked do not add to it but examine your deeds and regret the sin, he now says that wisdom gives the wise man strength, for it counsels him to repent. "More than ten rulers" — we find of Josiah that Scripture testified of him that there had been no king like him before him: his wisdom stood by him and he examined his deeds, and it was better for him than ten rulers of Jerusalem who did wickedly and did not turn from their way. Metzudas Dovid: "Gives strength to the wise" — it gives strength to the wise man, more than a man is strengthened by the might of ten rulers set in a city to rule over it; and ten is said because it is a round number.: "הַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם",
as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:19): "Wisdom strengthens the wise,"
שֶׁנּוֹתְנוֹת בּוֹ עֹז וּתְקִיפוּת,
imbuing him with strength and fortitude,

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא עב63 Yoma 72b — R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is meant by "And this is the Torah which Moses set [sam] before the children of Israel"? If he is worthy, it becomes for him a potion [sam] of life; if he is not worthy, it becomes for him a potion of death. And this is what Rava said: To one who is skilled in it, a drug of life; to one who is not skilled in it, a drug of death. Maharsha (s.v. "which Moses set"): The expression "setting" does not fit [the Torah] in its plain sense, just as we say in the first chapter of Sanhedrin of "which you shall set before them" that it should have said "which you shall teach them"; therefore they expounded "sam" here in the sense of a potion of life and a potion of death. And he said: to one who is skilled in it, who studies it for its own sake, it is a potion of life; to one who is not skilled in it, who studies it not for its own sake, it is a potion of death. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 4): Although expounding "sam" [set] as "sam" [potion] seems far-fetched, this derasha is clear: Scripture does not say "the Torah which Moses taught" but "which Moses set," an expression used of a tangible thing, to teach you that the Torah is a real thing acting upon a man, so that just as it brings him life, so it brings him death. One who has merit of soul through the commandments acquires through the Torah, the supreme divine intellect, a yet higher level; but when a sinner whose soul is full of filth enters this supreme level, which is close to the Blessed One, he is like an impure person who eats of sacred offerings; how should it not bring him death? This does not mean one who sinned in the past and no longer sins, for he is called a penitent, but one who is a master of Torah and a sinner.:):
and therefore they taught (Yoma 72b):
"לֹא זָכָה – נַעֲשֵׂית וְכוּלֵי",
"If he did not merit, it becomes a potion of death, etc.,"
כִּי נוֹלָד בּוֹ עַל יְדֵי חָכְמָה קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ
because wisdom can engender levity and arrogance within him,
וְנִקְרָא "חָכָם לְהָרַע" חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
and he is termed 'wise to do evil,' Heaven forbid.

וְהַיְינוּ בְּאוֹתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה64 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 1:2 — R. Yochanan said: One who learns without intending to act — better for him had his afterbirth been turned over his face and he had never come into the world. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "and does he not concede"): Does R. Shimon b. Yochai not concede that one interrupts words of Torah in order to perform a commandment and fulfil it in its proper time, such as making a sukkah or a lulav? And the very purpose of study is in order to act — so why did he not interrupt in order to fulfil the commandment of reciting the Shema? [His reason is] that the Shema is itself "recitation," and one does not set aside the speaking of one study for the sake of another study.
And this applies to that severe form of study not for its own sake of which our Sages of blessed memory said
(יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ב):
(Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:2):
"נוֹחַ לוֹ שֶׁנֶּהֶפְכָה וְכוּלֵי",
"'It would have been better for him had his afterbirth turned over, etc.';"

אֲבָל סְתָם שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים נ65 Pesachim 50b — R. Yehuda said that Rav said: A person should always occupy himself with Torah and with the commandments even not for their own sake, for out of [doing them] not for their own sake he comes to [do them] for their own sake. Rashi (s.v. "those who act for its own sake"): For those who act for its own sake [His kindness is] "above the heavens"; for those who act not for its own sake, "up to the heavens" — for he is at any rate performing a commandment, as Rav Yehuda [taught]. Tosafos (s.v. "and here, those who act not for its own sake, as Rav Yehuda"): This is puzzling, for he himself said in the second chapter of Berakhot (17a): "Whoever engages in Torah not for its own sake, it would have been better for him not to have been created." R. Yitzchak [the Ri] answers that there it speaks of one who studies in order to be haughty, to taunt and to best his fellows in halachah, and not in order to practice; but here it speaks of one like "the lowly one who profits" mentioned above, who does no work all week nor on the eve of the Sabbath — one who intends nothing bad but acts out of laziness — and even so, His kindness is great up to the heavens. Maharsha (s.v. "and it is written: For great above the heavens"): One who acts not for its own sake — that is, for some lower end, though without intending evil, as Tosafot wrote — has his kindness in this world reach only the lower world, "up to the heavens"; but one who acts for its own sake, whose aim reaches above, has his kindness even in this world come from above, "above the heavens." Both verses end "and Your truth unto the skies," for both, those who act for its own sake and those who do not, will merit the reward of the World to Come. Maharal (Derech Chaim 4:5): [Against Tosafot's question from "it would have been better for him not to have been created":] I do not see the difficulty, for the meaning is that if he does not study not for its own sake, he will not study for its own sake either. One who studies not for its own sake is certainly not good, and it would be better for him not to have been created — yet that is better than not studying at all, for of one who does not study at all this is true all the more. So this is what he says: even if he does not study for its own sake he should study nonetheless, for out of not for its own sake he comes to for its own sake. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Ahavas Hashem 2): Although of one who acts not for its own sake it is said that it would have been better for him not to have been created, he nonetheless has great reward — though certainly the essence is to do the commandment out of love of the Holy One, blessed be He, for that is the essence of the deed. A commandment not for its own sake has something that a transgression for its own sake lacks: from a transgression for its own sake one will not come to a commandment for its own sake, but from a commandment not for its own sake one does come to a commandment for its own sake, for the deed is one and the same.:):
whereas for standard learning not for its own sake, concerning which they said (Pesachim 50b):
"לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסוֹק וְכוּלֵי",
"'A person should always engage in Torah even not for its own sake...'",
וַודַּאי אֵין מוֹלִיד קַלּוּת עַל כָּל פָּנִים.
it certainly does not engender levity at any rate.
אֲבָל כַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא לִשְׁמָהּ, הַסִּימָן אַדְּרַבָּה,
However, when Torah study is conducted purely for Heaven's sake, the mark is quite the opposite:
מוֹלִיד יִרְאָה וּזְהִירוּת,
it brings forth reverence and meticulous care,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִדּוּשִׁין מ:)66 Kiddushin 40b — R. Tarfon and the Elders were once reclining in the upper chamber of the house of Nitza in Lod, and this question was put before them: Is study greater, or is action greater? R. Tarfon answered and said: Action is greater. R. Akiva answered and said: Study is greater. They all answered and said: Study is greater, for study brings to action. Rashi: "The house of Nitza" is the name of the man. "For study brings to action" — so that he has both of them in hand. Tosafos (s.v. "Study is greater, for study brings to action"): In tractate Bava Kamma this very statement is adduced to prove that action is greater, which is difficult. The resolution is that for a man himself action is indeed preferable, but teaching others is certainly greater than action — and that is why we say to a man "you have fulfilled" and do not say "you have taught." Others explain that one who has not yet learned and comes to ask whether to study first or to act is told to study first, since an ignoramus cannot be pious; but for one who has already learned, action is better than study. Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot): The word "once" shows that the incident belongs to the mishna here: "anyone who is engaged in Bible and in Mishna" — the two parts of Torah study — "and in the desired mode of behavior," which is the practice of good character. Since Scripture does not say "three cords are not quickly broken" but "a threefold cord is not quickly broken," one of the three must be the principal strand, made threefold by the two that accompany it; and it was over which of them is the principal and greatest that R. Tarfon and the Elders were in doubt. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 40b): R. Tarfon says action is greater because action is the end, and study, which is learning in order to do, is not essential as the deed is; for man is not pure intellect — were he wholly intellect his Torah would be the principal thing, but since he is not, the deed is principal, for every deed is done in the body while Torah is in the intellect. R. Akiva holds that study is greater because it brings to action: study is the beginning, and all is in the power of the beginning, and whatever comes first is of greater rank, since it is the cause, and the cause is greater than that which it causes. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Kedoshim): "Every man shall fear his mother and his father, and keep My Sabbaths": the father is study and the mother is action, and study is greater, for it brings to action, as the Gemara states; "and keep My Sabbaths" — for in these two the essential intent is found, since the essential intent of performing the commandments is called Shabbat, Shabbat being a name of the Holy One, blessed be He, as the holy Zohar states. Tiferes Yosef (Bamidbar 4): As the Talmud says, "Study is greater, for study brings to action" — and my honored grandfather and master, of blessed memory, said that its main intent is not the plain sense: "study" signifies the "hosts of Torah," a person's longing for words of Torah, which, being only longing and not yet firmly fixed, does not yet show the virtue of study. The virtue of study is that it "brings to action": his longing for words of Torah worked so powerfully that it acted upon all the vessels of the body, so that he carried out his will in deed with those very words of Torah, for the inner content of performing the commandments is words of Torah.: "גָּדוֹל תַּלְמוּד שֶׁמֵּבִיא לִידֵי מַעֲשֶׂה".
as they stated (Kiddushin 40b): "Great is study, for it leads directly to action."

sections.en: Fear of Heaven as Beginning and End

items.h: Yirat Shamayim both opens and completes divine service, preserving Torah from distortion and ensuring that wisdom leads to action.

Seif 1 — Fear as the Gate and Goal of Torah
Yirat Shamayim is both the entrance to wisdom and the safeguard that brings Torah to proper action.

p: הַתְחָלַת הָעֲבוֹדָה הִיא הַיִּרְאָה,
The beginning of divine service is fear and awe,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תְּהִלִּים קיא, י67 Psalms 111:10 — The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; all who practice it have good understanding. His praise endures forever. Radak: One who has prepared his heart to occupy himself with wisdom should first occupy himself with the fear of the Lord and make it his root and foundation, and conduct himself by its ways in the wisdom that he learns; for if a man studies speculative wisdom first, he may grow bold and deny the great signs and wonders found in the holy Scriptures. “A good understanding to all who do them” — a good understanding and a good providence belong to one who does both, occupying himself with the fear of the Lord and with wisdom; or “good understanding” means success, that one who engages in both will prosper in this world and in the world to come. Metzudas Dovid: The right course is that at the very beginning of his study of wisdom a man root the fear of the Lord in his heart, and this is reckoned a good understanding for all who do so. For then his praise will stand forever, and he will be renowned for his wisdom, because it will endure — which is not so if the fear does not precede the wisdom. Malbim: The beginning and root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, for since wisdom is received from the Master of wisdom and its statutes and roots are not established by demonstrations, while desire and the inclination entice a man to turn aside from them, he must bind his soul in the bonds of fear, so that fearing the Lord he will not transgress the statutes of wisdom. Then there is “a good understanding to all who do them” — to those who perform the precepts — for the spirit of the Lord will enlighten them to grasp their reasons and their secrets.):
and as it is written (Psalms 111:10):
"רֵאשִׁית [חָכְמָה יִרְאַת ה'] וְגוֹמֵר",
"'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem,' etc.,"

וְאוֹמֵר (דְּבָרִים י, יב68 Deuteronomy 10:12 — And now, O Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul. Rashi: "And now, Israel" — although you did all this, His mercy and His love are still upon you, and for all that you have sinned before Him He asks of you nothing "but to fear [the Lord your God]." Our Rabbis derived from here that everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven. Ramban: "What does the Lord your God ask of you" is joined to "for your good" [in the next verse]: He asks nothing of you for His own need, only for your need, as in "If you are righteous, what do you give Him?" — it is all for your good. And he gave the reason, that the heavens and the heaven of heavens and the earth and all that is in it belong to the Lord and all give honor to His name, so that He has no need of you; only He desired your fathers and chose their seed after them.):
and Scripture states (Deuteronomy 10:12):
"מָה ה' [אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ] כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה",
"'What does Hashem your God ask of you, but to fear...?'"
וְהוּא הַסּוֹף וְהַתַּכְלִית גַּם כֵּן
and it is likewise the end and ultimate objective,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (קֹהֶלֶת יב, יג69 Ecclesiastes 12:13 — The sum of the matter, when all has been heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole man. Rashi: "The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God" — do what you can, and let your heart be directed to Heaven. "And keep His commandments, for this is the whole man" — for it was for this that the whole man was created. Metzudas Dovid: "The end of the matter" — the purpose of everything. "All has been heard" — everything a man does is heard before the Omnipresent, blessed be He, and nothing is hidden from Him; therefore fear God and do not transgress what He warned you not to do. "For this is the whole man" — what was said above of what befalls a man in his life and in his death is the lot of every man without exception, and therefore be very careful in the commandments of the Omnipresent, blessed be He.):
as it is written (Ecclesiastes 12:13):
"סוֹף דָּבָר [הַכֹּל נִשְׁמָע אֶת הָאֱלֹהִים] יְרָא וְגוֹמֵר".
"'The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God,' etc."

וְכֵן הִמְשִׁילוּ70 Shabbat 31a-b — Rabbah bar Rav Huna said: Any man who has Torah in him but has no fear of Heaven is like a treasurer to whom they handed the keys of the inner chamber but did not hand the keys of the outer one — with what is he to enter? R. Yannai used to proclaim: Alas for one who has no courtyard, yet makes a gate for a courtyard. Rashi: [Fear of Heaven] is like the outer doors, by way of which one enters the inner ones: so too, if he is God-fearing he becomes anxious to observe and to do, and if not, he does not care for his Torah. "With what is he to enter?": by which door is he to enter, so as to open the inner ones? Maharsha: Fear precedes wisdom, as we learned, "Anyone whose fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures"; and this is like the preceding [parable], that fear preserves what is within, as the measure of salt-earth preserves the grain in the storehouse. On this [the Gemara] also brings "Alas for one who has no courtyard…": the Torah is only a gate for entering into fear of Heaven, so fear of Heaven must come first — as Rashi explains in chapter Ba Lo [of Yoma]. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 31a): Torah and wisdom are the keys to the inner chambers, by which a person rises level after level through the intellect — but only when he is himself a complete being, for the philosophers' claim that everything depends on the intellect is vanity: the intellect is not the man. Fear of Heaven is the essential thing, through which he is counted a complete being fit for elevation, while the Torah is the elevation that befits him; so one who has wisdom without fear of Heaven is like one handed the inner keys but not the outer. So too "Alas for one who has no courtyard, yet makes a gate for a courtyard": the house is the essential thing and the gate its improvement — without fear of Heaven, which makes him a complete creation, what does wisdom, the improvement of man, avail? Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 4): R. Yannai cries out over a great loss: to make a gate for a dwelling one does not have is a futile, idle act, and so is Torah without fear of Heaven. Torah and wisdom are the opening and gate into the house and courtyard where one dwells, while fear of Heaven is the house itself, for through it a person dwells with the Blessed Name — nothing is with Him but the fear of Him, as it is written, "the fear of the Lord is His treasure"; corporeal man has a screen and partition between himself and the Blessed Name, and through the Torah he has an opening, but this man has no dwelling with the Blessed Name at all, and is further from Him than another man. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 10): One who has no fear of Heaven is separated and set apart from the Blessed Name, and once he is set apart from Him, what inner, higher level can he acquire through wisdom? He has no beginning by which to enter — hence he is like one who holds the inner keys but not the outer. And in R. Yannai's saying, fear of Heaven makes a person a house with the Blessed Name, who is the place and house of all beings that cleave to Him, while wisdom is the gate by which he ascends to his place with Him; so he is like one who makes a gate, which is only the house's preparation, when he lacks the house itself. (שַׁבָּת לא:):
And thus they compared it (Shabbat 31b):
יִרְאָה וְתוֹרָה לְמַפְתְּחוֹת חִיצוֹנוֹת וּפְנִימוֹת וּלְדַרְתָּא וְתַרְעָא,
fear and Torah to external and internal keys, and to an inner courtyard and an outer gate,
דְּהַיְינוּ מַפְתֵּחַ חִיצוֹן שֶׁל הַתַּרְעָא,
namely the outer key of the gateway,
וְגַם הַדַּרְתָּא שֶׁאַחַר הַתַּרְעָא – תְּחִלָּה וָסוֹף.
as well as the inner courtyard beyond the gate—representing beginning and end.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, יז71 Pirkei Avot 3:17 — R. Elazar ben Azariah said: Where there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; where there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. Where there is no wisdom, there is no fear [of Heaven]; where there is no fear, there is no wisdom. Where there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; where there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. Where there is no flour, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no flour.):
And as they stated (Pirkei Avot 3:17):
"אִם אֵין יִרְאָה אֵין חָכְמָה" –
"If there is no fear, there is no wisdom"—
הֲרֵי שֶׁהִיא קוֹדֶם לַחָכְמָה,
which shows that it precedes wisdom;
"וְאִם אֵין חָכְמָה אֵין יִרְאָה" –
"and if there is no wisdom, there is no fear"—
הֲרֵי שֶׁבָּא אַחַר הַחָכְמָה.
which demonstrates that it follows after wisdom.
כִּי הַיִּרְאָה הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ לִזְהִירוּת בְּמִצְווֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה,
For reverence is the foundational root for vigilance in negative commandments,
וּמִי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם בְּוַדַּאי אֵין זָהִיר בְּמִצְווֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה,
and one who lacks fear of Heaven is certainly not vigilant regarding negative prohibitions;

וַאֲפִילּוּ מַאן דְּעָבַר אַדְּרַבָּנָן שָׁרֵי לְמִקְרְיֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי (שַׁבָּת מ סוֹף עַמּוּד א72 Shabbat 40a — Rava said: One who transgresses the words of the Sages — it is permitted to call him a transgressor.),
and even one who transgresses a rabbinic decree may be designated as wicked, etc. (Shabbat 40a end),
וְנִקְרָא רָשָׁע כְּשֶׁעָבַר עַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה,
and he is termed wicked when violating a negative commandment,

וְנֶאֱמַר (תְּהִלִּים נ, טז73 Psalms 50:16 — But to the wicked God said: What right have you to recite My statutes, and to take My covenant upon your lips? Rashi: “And take My covenant upon your mouth” — My Torah. Radak: Until here he reproved those who bring the sacrifice and do not turn from their wickedness; now he reproves those who study and do not practice. A man who shows himself wicked is wicked in the eyes of God and of men, and for that very reason is close to repenting, since men recognize him and reprove him; but one who shows himself good and a servant of God while his heart is evil and his deeds evil in secret is very far from repentance. So too one who studies the Torah and does not practice it: men who see him study and do the opposite of what he studies learn from his deeds and are led to sin, and they come to despise the study of the Torah. Metzudas Dovid: But to the wicked man, who does not confess his transgressions when he brings his sacrifice and does not turn back from them, God says: what have you to do with reciting My statutes — that is, with performing My commandments without the heart’s intent, as a man recites a tale of words with no intention at all? “And take My covenant in your mouth” — the words of the Torah, which were given with a covenant, you bear only upon your mouth, speaking them with the lips alone and not with the heart. Malbim: God says to the wicked man who thinks to bribe Him with the many sacrifices he brings: what have you to do with reciting My statutes? The Lord commanded statutes, which are commandments with no [evident] reason, such as the commandments of the sacrifices, and rational commandments whose reason is known, such as those concerning theft, adultery, slander and the like; and you who act wickedly in the rational commandments “recite My statutes” by bringing sacrifices, and by this “take My covenant upon your mouth,” as though on this account I had made a covenant with you to love you.):
and it is stated (Psalms 50:16):
"וְלָרָשָׁע [אָמַר אֱלֹהִים] מַה לְּךָ לְסַפֵּר [חֻקָּי] וְגוֹמֵר",
"'And to the wicked God says: What right have you to recount My statutes,' etc.,"
כִּי מוּטָב שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲסֹק בַּתּוֹרָה,
for it would be better were he not to occupy himself with Torah,
דַּחֲבָל עַל וְכוּלֵי.
since it is a pity upon him, etc.

וְכֵן בְּהֵיפֶךְ, "שָׁנָה וּפֵירַשׁ קָשֶׁה מִכּוּלָּם" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ פְּסָחִים מט74 Pesachim 49b — Great is the hatred with which the ignorant hate a Torah scholar — greater than the hatred with which the nations of the world hate Israel; and their wives more than they. It was taught: One who studied and then withdrew — more than all of them. Rashi: "One who studied and withdrew": a student who studied and then withdrew from the Torah, and who knows how much Torah scholars disparage the ignorant and how lowly they are in their eyes — he hates more than all of them. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTorah 15): The ignorant man is more material than the gentile: the gentile too is material compared with Israel, who have the Torah, yet he is not reckoned as material as the ignorant man, who ought to acquire intellect and does not want it — for he too received the Torah of Moses and does not study it, and so he is worse than the gentile who never received it, and further from and more opposed to the intellectual. Their wives are more so, for woman is yet more material. And one who studied and withdrew is more than all of them, for having had the Torah and withdrawn from it shows that he is wholly opposed to the intellectual; it is the materiality in him that makes him withdraw from the Torah, and so he is the harshest of all. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 57): Separation from a thing is of a greater degree than [the state of] one who never had need to separate; therefore they said of the Torah (Pesachim 49b) that one who withdraws from the Torah is farther from the Torah than one who never saw Torah in his life. So too, one who withdrew from sin, which inclines toward this physical world, stands higher than one who never inclined after it at all. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Esau, who came from only two of the patriarchs, could renounce himself entirely, and through this exchange he is the root and beginning of the nations; for the beginning of evil always has an affinity with and hold on the end of good, and in that respect it is worse than all, in the manner of what is said (Pesachim 49b), "One who studied and withdrew is worst of all," because he knew and rebelled.:),
And conversely, 'one who studied and then abandoned it is harsher than them all' (as they stated in Pesachim 49b),
וּמוּטָב שֶׁלֹּא עָסַק בַּתּוֹרָה מִקּוֹדֶם,
and it would have been better had he not engaged in Torah beforehand,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ75 Yoma 86a — It was taught: “And you shall love the Lord your God” — that the Name of Heaven should become beloved through you. A man should read Scripture and study Mishnah and attend upon Torah scholars, and his dealings with others should be gentle. What do people then say of him? “Fortunate is his father who taught him Torah, fortunate is his teacher who taught him Torah.” But one who reads and studies and attends upon scholars, yet is not honest in his dealings and does not speak pleasantly with others — what do people say of him? “Woe to so-and-so who studied Torah, woe to his father who taught him Torah, woe to his teacher who taught him Torah. So-and-so who studied Torah — see how corrupt are his deeds and how ugly his ways.” Rashi: "Become beloved through you": to your fellow [men]. "Read": Scripture; "study": Mishnah; "and attend upon Torah scholars": to learn [from them], that is, the working out of the reasons of the mishnayot — what their reasons are and from where they derived them. Maharsha (s.v. "fortunate is his father"): For certainly his father and his teacher taught him Torah for its own sake, and the Name of Heaven is exalted and made beloved thereby; conversely, "woe to his father who taught him" means that they taught him Torah not for its own sake. People do not say woe of everyone who learns not for its own sake, since from learning not for its own sake one comes to learning for its own sake; but in this man they have seen that he did not come to learn for its own sake, and so they say woe of him, and of his father and his teacher as well. Maharsha (s.v. "that the Name of Heaven should become beloved through you"): They seem to have derived this from the particle et [את] in "And you shall love the Lord" because here they did not see fit to expound it as including Torah scholars, as they expounded the et of "The Lord your God you shall fear": with regard to fear, the fear of one's teacher may be equated with the fear of Heaven, but love of one's teacher cannot be equated with love of Heaven. Therefore they expounded the et of "And you shall love" as including that [the Name] should become beloved through you. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Ahavas Hashem 2): He infers this from Scripture's writing "And you shall love the Lord your God" where it could have written "And you shall love the Lord": the name "your God" belongs with fear, for "God" denotes the attribute of justice ("The Lord your God you shall fear"), not with love — hence they expounded that the Name of Heaven should become beloved through you, that is, that people will say that He is your God and the Name of the Lord is called upon you, for He is glorified and made beloved through you. They applied the verse to Torah scholars because they stand first in relation to God, His Godship resting upon them first; and when the scholar, upon whom the Torah of God is called, conducts himself in an upright and fitting way, others too are drawn after him and accept His Godship, until all are drawn after God, blessed be He. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 4): One who belongs to God ought to be acceptable to people, and people take pleasure in him because he is ordered in his deeds — for order in a man is pleasing and acceptable to people — and therefore through such a man the Name of Heaven is sanctified; conversely, the Name of Heaven is desecrated most of all when his deeds are not set right, for this leads [people] away from Him. That is "And you shall love the Lord your God": that you bring about the love of God, blessed be He, because He is your God, called upon you, and your deeds are pleasing — and this is the sanctification of His Name. (יוֹמָא פו.):
and as they stated (Yoma 86a):
"מָה בְּרִיּוֹת אוֹמְרוֹת: פְּלוֹנִי שֶׁעָסַק בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי",
"'What do people say? Look at so-and-so who studied Torah, etc.,'"
וְנִמְצָא שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם מִתְחַלֵּל.
and the Name of Heaven consequently ends up profaned.
וְהַיִּרְאָה צְרִיכָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה בֵּין בִּתְחִלָּה בֵּין בַּסּוֹף,
Thus, fear is essential for words of Torah both at the beginning and at the end,
וְהוּא הָעִיקָּר כְּטַעַם "נַעֲשֶׂה וְנִשְׁמָע",
and it constitutes the primary foundation, mirroring the inner rationale of 'we will do and we will hear,'

פִּרְיוֹ וְעָלָיו76 Shabbat 88a — R. Elazar said: When Israel gave precedence to “we will do” over “we will hear,” a Heavenly voice went forth and said to them: Who revealed to My children this secret, which the ministering angels employ? — as it is written, “Bless the Lord, O His angels, mighty in strength, who do His word, hearkening to the voice of His word”: first “who do,” and only then “hearkening.” And R. Chama son of R. Chanina said: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood” — why are Israel likened to an apple tree? To teach you that just as with the apple tree the fruit comes before the leaves, so Israel gave precedence to “we will do” over “we will hear.” Rashi: ["Who do His word, hearkening":] they are ready to do before they hear, not in the manner of other servants, who first hear the matter to know whether they can take it upon themselves or not. ["Its fruit comes before its leaves":] such is its nature, and in this it differs from other trees: the budding of its fruit precedes its leaves. Tosafos (s.v. "its fruit comes before its leaves"): R. Tam objected that we see it grows like other trees, and explained that the "apple" is the etrog — "the scent of your nose like apples" is rendered [in the Targum] "like the scent of the etrog" — whose fruit stays on the tree from year to year, so that when last year's leaves fall and others come, the fruit precedes those leaves. But it is puzzling that he cites "As an apple tree among the trees of the wood," for in that verse it is not Israel who is likened to the apple tree but the Holy One, blessed be He — "so is my beloved among the sons"; he should rather have cited "the scent of your nose like apples" (Song of Songs 7:9). Maharsha: ["Who revealed to My children this secret":] The angel, being wholly spiritual, has no other mind but to do the will of the Blessed One and is ready as though he had already done it, whereas man, joined of body and soul, has in him also the mind of the evil inclination, which entices him to evil, so that he is not ready to do the will of his Father in Heaven; at the Giving of the Torah this secret was revealed to Israel — that their two hearts, the two inclinations, should have one mind ("O that they had such a heart"), ready like these angels to do before hearing. ["As an apple tree":] In its context the verse likens the Holy One, blessed be He, to the apple tree, but by this exposition it may refer back to "so is my love among the daughters" — Israel among the nations; he likens the doing to the fruit and the hearing to the leaves, for the deed is the main thing, as it is said: "Not study is the main thing, but the deed." Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 29): Doing is carrying out what the Blessed One decrees, and what comes from His side is necessary and so precedes hearing, which is intellect, comes from the side of the recipient, and is only contingent; therefore the angels, created to do their Creator's errand, put "we will do" before "we will hear," and so did Israel, who were created to do the decree the Blessed One decrees upon them. For other men the deed follows from knowing that a thing is good to do, but Israel's very essence is to serve the Blessed One in deed, and the knowledge follows the deed — as with the angels, each created for its own task, which is why it is written first "who do His word" and afterwards "hearkening to the voice of His word." Therefore they are likened to the apple tree: other trees put out their leaves first, since leaves are easy to bring forth, but the apple tree has greater power of bringing forth and yields its fruit, the principal thing, first, and afterwards the leaves, which are subsidiary and guard the fruit. (שַׁבָּת פח.),
fruit and its protective leaves (Shabbat 88a),
וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ.
and this is not the place to elaborate further.

sections.en: Hidden Holiness, Song, and the Imprint of Time

items.h: Divine revelation leaves spiritual imprints in place and time; song, Rosh Chodesh, and inherited custom reveal holiness even before it becomes fully visible.

Seif 1 — Song, Revelation, and the Imprint of Holiness
Song follows direct revelation, while foreknowledge leaves a spiritual imprint even before holiness appears openly.

p: שִׁירָה הוּא רַק כְּשֶׁמַּכִּיר הַנּוֹכָח,
Song is uttered only when one directly perceives the divine Presence,
כְּעִנְיַן "רָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי",
as in the matter of 'a handmaiden saw at the Sea what the prophet Ezekiel did not see, etc.,'
אָז נִפְתַּח פִּיהֶם לוֹמַר שִׁירָה.
only then was their mouth opened to sing praise.
וְלָכֵן אֵין אוֹמְרִים שִׁירָה עַל נֵס שֶׁבְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ,
Therefore, we do not recite song (Hallel) over a miracle occurring outside the Land of Israel,

כִּי "הַדָּר בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ דּוֹמֶה וְכוּלֵי" (כְּתוּבּוֹת קי77 Ketubot 110b — The Sages taught: A person should always dwell in the Land of Israel, even in a city most of whose inhabitants are idolaters, and not dwell outside the Land, even in a city most of whose inhabitants are Jews. For whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God, and whoever dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God, as it is said: "To give you the land of Canaan, to be your God" (Leviticus 25:38). Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot): The Holy One, blessed be He, is of course God of the whole world, but He is called "God of the Land" after the Land of Israel, as Nachmanides writes on the portion of Vayelech. Accordingly, "whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God" is well said with respect to His being God of the Land; but since He is also called God of the whole world, it cannot properly be said of one outside the Land that he has no God, and this is what the Talmud finds difficult. The answer is that he is "like one who has no God" in the sense that it is as though he does not accept the Holy One, blessed be He, as God, but serves idols like the rest of the nations of the lands. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kesuvos 110b): The Holy One, blessed be He, is called God of the Land, for the Land of Israel is called His own land, while the other lands He gave over to the princes appointed over them. Hence one who dwells outside the Land is as one who serves the power appointed over the land in which he dwells, and as one who receives it as a god and a master; being handed over under its dominion is itself reckoned as service to it. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 1): As is said (Ketubot 110b), whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God, and whoever dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God. The word "like" means that it is so in the imagination, for in truth, God forbid — "the whole earth is full of His glory"; but the imagination misleads a person so that he does not grasp that the Blessed One stands before him wherever he is, while in the Land of Israel even the imagination is pure, as is said, "the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise." Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 31): This is also the difference between the Land of Israel and outside the Land: in the Land of Israel there is the union of the name Havayah with the name Elokim, for the Blessed One always seeks it out and in every act there is recognition that the Lord is God, as the Talmud and the holy Zohar state, "whoever dwells in the Land of Israel is like one who has a God." In other lands there is a separation between the name Havayah and the name Elokim, because great distractions there disturb a person's mind so that he does not recognize the Blessed One's rule even over this world, until they said, "whoever dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God"; and this stems from its being the land of the nations, for the nations disturb their own understanding.:)
for 'one who dwells outside the Land of Israel is comparable to one who has no God, etc.' (Ketubot 110b),
שֶׁאֵין מַכִּיר הַנּוֹכָח.
because he lacks immediate perception of the divine Presence.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (יִתְרוֹ עט עַמּוּד ב) עַיֵּין שָׁם,
And as they stated in the Zohar (Yitro 79b), see there,
שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵין נְבוּאָה וְהַשְׁרָאַת שְׁכִינָה בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ,
for there is neither prophecy nor the dwelling of the Shechinah outside the Land of Israel,
דְּהַיְינוּ גִּילּוּי הַכָּרַת נוֹכַח שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמָּשׁ "ה' לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד".
namely the overt perception of the actual presence of His Shechinah, blessed be He, as in 'I set Hashem before me always.'
וְאוֹמְרִים הַלֵּל בָּרְגָלִים,
And we recite Hallel on the pilgrimage festivals,
דְּאָז בָּאִים "לֵירָאוֹת פְּנֵי וְגוֹמֵר"
because then they come 'to appear before the face of the Lord God, etc.,'
וְזָכוּ לִרְאִיָּה,
and merited direct vision;
וּמַה שֶּׁכְּבָר הָיָה אֵיזֶה פַּעַם,
and what already occurred at some past time,

הֲרֵי זֶה כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מוֹעֵד קָטָן כה.)78 Moed Katan 25a — R. Abba opened his eulogy over him: Our master was worthy that the Divine Presence should rest upon him, except that Babylonia caused it not to be. R. Nachman bar Chisda objected: But it is written, "The word of the Lord came [hayo haya] to Ezekiel son of Buzi the priest in the land of the Chaldeans"! His father struck him with his sandal and said to him: Did I not tell you not to trouble everyone? What is meant by "haya"? — That it had already been [before, in the Land of Israel]. Rashi: "Babylonia caused it" — for the Divine Presence does not rest outside the Land. "His father struck him with his sandal" — Rav Chisda tapped Rav Nachman upon his sandal, as a man quietly touches his fellow's foot, so that those standing about Rav Huna's bier should not hear; [he meant:] do not burden everyone with objections. "That it had already been" — that is, it was at that hour alone and no more; and some say that it had already been in the Land of Israel, where the Divine Spirit had rested upon him. Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot, s.v. "What is meant by 'haya'? — that it had already been"): Rashi's second explanation is found in the Midrash [Yalkut] on this matter, and it derives it from the doubled expression "hayo haya, the word of the Lord": "hayo" — that He had spoken with him in the Land; "haya" — that He spoke with him outside the Land. בִּנְבוּאַת יְחֶזְקֵאל בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ:
is in line with what they said (Moed Katan 25a) regarding Ezekiel's prophecy outside the Land of Israel:
"הָיֹה הָיָה" – שֶׁהָיָה כְּבָר.
'It surely came to pass'—meaning it had already begun previously.
וְזֶהוּ בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַנֶּפֶשׁ,
This operates in the holiness of the soul,
וְכֵן בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַזְּמַן:
and likewise in the holiness of time:
כְּשֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן כְּבָר הָיָה קְדוּשָּׁה וְגִילּוּי שְׁכִינָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל,
when during that specific appointed season there was already holiness and revelation of the Shechinah in the Land of Israel,
יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת אַחַר כָּךְ גַּם בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ.
it can subsequently extend even outside the Land.
וְלָכֵן אוֹמְרִים הַלֵּל בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם.
Therefore we recite Hallel on those commemorative days.
וְעִנְיַן הַלֵּל דְּרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ,
And concerning the matter of Hallel on Rosh Chodesh:
כִּי כְּמוֹ שֶׁקְּדוּשָּׁה שֶׁהָיְתָה בֶּעָבָר בַּזְּמַן פַּעַם אַחַת נִקְבַּע לְדוֹרוֹת,
for just as a sanctity that occurred once in the past within time becomes fixed for generations,
וְכֵן בַּנֶּפֶשׁ כְּמוֹ קְדוּשַּׁת הָאָבוֹת בַּבָּנִים,
and likewise in the soul, such as the holiness of the Patriarchs transmitted to their descendants,
וְכֵן בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
and similarly within the entirety of Israel,
כָּל קְדוּשּׁוֹת שֶׁסִּיגְּלוּ דּוֹרוֹת שֶׁקְּדָמוּנוּ
all sanctities amassed by earlier generations
כְּבָר הֵם קְבוּעִים וַחֲקוּקִים בְּלִבָּבוֹת כָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּנּוֹדָע,
are already established and engraved in the hearts of all Jewish people as is known,
כֵּן גַּם אַלְּהַבָּא יֵשׁ רוֹשֶׁם וַחֲקִיקָה בֵּין בַּנְּפָשׁוֹת,
so too looking toward the future, there is an imprint and etching within souls,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: גַּם בַּגּוֹיִם הֵיכָן מָצָאתִי בִּסְדוֹם (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נ79 Bereshit Rabbah 50:10 — "And your two daughters who are present [hanimtza'ot]" — R. Toviyah bar R. Yitzchak said: Two finds — Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. R. Yitzchak said: "I found David My servant" — where did I find him? In Sodom. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): Abraham our father, who chose exile, is the foundation of faith, and with him began the revelation of the trait of King David, as it is said, "Where did I find him? In Sodom" — for there faith was in exile. With the overturning of Sodom Abraham drew the holy sparks out from there and took in the foundation of faith ("and he believed in the Lord"), to root it in his descendants after him.),
as it is written: 'Even among the nations, where did I find a righteous root? In Sodom' (Bereishit Rabbah 50),
דְּנִיצּוֹל לוֹט בִּזְכוּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
for Lot was rescued by the future merit of King David, peace be upon him,
וְכַדּוֹמֶה הַרְבֵּה.
and many similar instances.
רַק בְּעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת הוּא רַק בְּצֶאֱצָאָיו שֶׁעָתִיד לְהוֹלִיד לְבַד,
Yet regarding idolaters, this future merit applies strictly through descendants he is destined to father,

וּפֵירוּשׁ בִּזְכוּת – "וּבְרָא מְזַכֵּי אַבָּא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד80 Sanhedrin 104a — Why did they not count Amon [among those who have no share in the World to Come]? Because of the honor of Josiah. Then let them not count Manasseh either, because of the honor of Hezekiah! A son confers merit upon a father, but a father does not confer merit upon a son, as it is written, "and there is none that can deliver out of My hand" — Abraham cannot deliver Ishmael, Isaac cannot deliver Esau. Rashi (s.v. "a son confers merit upon a father"): Josiah confers merit upon Amon his father, but Hezekiah does not upon Manasseh his son, as it is written, "and there is none that can deliver out of My hand," which is expounded in the aggadah: Abraham cannot deliver [Ishmael], etc. Maharsha (s.v. "a father does not confer merit"): It is the way of some wicked men not to want their sons to be like them, but rather righteous; therefore a son confers merit upon his father, for the father, though wicked, rebuked him and guided him on the good path. But a father does not confer merit upon a son, for the son had someone to learn from and did not learn. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 15): The transgressors of Israel, alluded to by the willow, attain their rectification and eternal life through their offspring after them, for "a son confers merit upon a father"; even those listed in Perek Chelek as having no share in the World to Come, though they have no permanence as individuals, endure through their seed, who are called by their name. Nor is this an empty remembrance: the son is related to the father because something of the father's power is in him — the fathers are the root of the sons' souls — and since the son's soul endures forever, the father's root, which is its root, endures with it. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 229): ["Honor your father and your mother" applies] also to father and mother in the plain sense, in the vein of "a son confers merit upon a father": when one reaches this level, in which the root of his supernal root is refined, the sin at the beginning of his creation ("and in sin did my mother conceive me") is also repaired, and his father and mother are refined as well — and thereby he honors them..),
and the meaning of 'by merit' is 'a son confers merit upon a father' (Sanhedrin 104a),
וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת "בִּזְכוּת" פֵּירוּשׁוֹ הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ מֵאוֹתוֹ זְכוּת הַגָּנוּז בּוֹ בְּהֶעְלֵם.
and thus in multiple sources 'by merit' means when there exists within him a concealed root of that future merit.
דְּכָל מִדּוֹתָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִשְׁפָּט,
For all the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, operate with exact justice,
וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁכֻּלָּם כְּאִישׁ אֶחָד,
whereas in Israel, who are all bound as one single person,
כָּל זְכִיּוֹת שֶׁל הַדּוֹרוֹת הַבָּאִים יֵשׁ בָּהֶם רוֹשֶׁם גַּם כֵּן בַּדּוֹרוֹת שֶׁלִּפְנֵיהֶם.
all merits of coming generations leave a retroactive imprint within the generations preceding them.
כִּי וַדַּאי אִלּוּ הָיָה הַכֹּל בְּחִירָה לְבַד,
For surely, were everything governed solely by human free choice,
לֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת רוֹשֶׁם מִקּוֹדֶם כְּלָל.
there would be no reason for any prior imprint whatsoever.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הַבְּחִירָה הוּא מִצַּד הַגִּילּוּי וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד,
Yet in truth, free choice exists only from the perspective of manifest reality and this physical world,
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת יְדִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִיא מַקֶּפֶת הַכֹּל,
whereas in ultimate truth, the foreknowledge of Hashem, blessed be He, encompasses all,
שַׁפִּיר שַׁיָּיךְ לִהְיוֹת רוֹשֶׁם מִקּוֹדֶם.
so that an anticipatory imprint can rightfully exist.

items.h:
Seif 2 — The Sanctity Embedded in Time
Sacred events leave recurring traces in time, with Rosh Chodesh increasingly revealing its hidden future holiness.

p: וְכֵן מָצִינוּ גַּם בַּזְּמַן,
And similarly we find this principle in time,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י81 Rashi on Genesis 19:3; Rashi on Genesis 27:9 — Rashi on "and he baked unleavened bread": It was Passover. Rashi on "two kids of the goats": And were two kids of the goats Isaac's meal? Rather, it was Passover: the one he offered for his Passover offering, and of the other he made the savory dish — so in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer.)
as our Sages of blessed memory taught (cited in Rashi)
עַל פָּסוּק "מַצּוֹת אָפָה"
on the verse 'he baked unleavened cakes' (Genesis 19:3),
וְעַל פָּסוּק "שְׁנֵי גְּדָיֵי עִזִּים – אֶחָד לַפֶּסַח"
and on the verse 'two kids of the goats'—one as a Passover offering

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפִרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לב82 Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 32:15 — [The night of Passover had come.] He went and brought two kids of the goats. And were two kids of the goats Isaac's meal? Surely one would have been enough for him, as it is said, "The righteous man eats to satisfy his soul." Rather, one corresponded to the Passover offering, and one was to make him the savory dish to eat — for we have learned that the Passover offering is eaten only when one is already sated.).
(as written in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 32).

וְאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה יב83 Sotah 12b — R. Chanina bar Pappa said: That day [on which Moses was cast into the river] was the twenty-first of Nisan. The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, shall the one who is destined to recite the Song at the Sea on this day be stricken on this day? R. Acha bar Chanina said: That day was the sixth of Sivan. The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, shall the one who is destined to receive the Torah at Mount Sinai on this day be stricken on this day? Rashi (s.v. "the Song at the Sea"): It was said on the twenty-first of Nisan, as taught in Seder Olam: from Rameses to Sukkot, from Sukkot to Etham, and from Etham to before Pi-hahiroth — that is three [days]; on the fourth, "it was told to the king of Egypt that the people had fled"; on the fifth and sixth the Egyptians pursued; on the night of the seventh they went down into the sea. In the morning they said the Song, and it was the seventh day, the last festival day of Passover. Maharsha: These two statements are cited as disputing the preceding one: whereas it was said above that [Pharaoh's astrologers] did not know that he would be stricken over the waters of Meribah, these [Sages] hold that they certainly knew, and the principal striking by water that they foresaw was his being cast into the river. But he was saved from that decree through the ministering angels who pleaded for him — on the twenty-first of Nisan according to one, on the sixth of Sivan according to the other — for by the merit the angels invoked the decree was annulled, as it is said at the end of Tractate Shabbat that Israel is not subject to the constellations, since great merit annuls the decree of the constellation.:)
And they stated (Sotah 12b)
עַל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
concerning Moses our teacher, peace be upon him,
שֶׁאָמְרוּ מַלְאָכִים:
that the ministering angels proclaimed:
"בְּיוֹם זֶה עָתִיד לוֹמַר שִׁירָה, בְּיוֹם זֶה עָתִיד לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה",
'On this day he is destined to utter song; on this day he is destined to receive the Torah,'
וְכֵן הַרְבֵּה כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּזֶה.
and many similar instances.
כִּי יֵשׁ רוֹשֶׁם לְמַפְרֵעַ,
For there exists a retroactive spiritual imprint;
וּמִיהוּ רוֹשֶׁם זֶה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת,
however, this imprint does not stem from manifest revelation,
שֶׁהֲרֵי בַּנִּגְלֶה הוּא כֹּחַ הַבְּחִירָה
for in the manifest realm, free choice reigns,
וְאֵין שַׁיָּיךְ רוֹשֶׁם קוֹדֶם מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁמָּא לֹא יִבְחַר בַּטּוֹב,
and no prior imprint is applicable before the deed lest one fail to choose good,
רַק מִצַּד הַהֶעְלֵם.
rather it derives solely from the hidden realm.
וְזֶה עִנְיַן קְדוּשַּׁת רֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ
And this is the essence of the holiness of Rosh Chodesh,
שֶׁלֹּא נִזְכַּר בַּתּוֹרָה כְּלָל,
which is not explicitly defined in the Torah as a day of rest,
כִּי לֹא הָיָה בּוֹ הִתְגַּלּוּת שְׁכִינָה בֶּעָבָר,
because no historical revelation of the Shechinah occurred upon it in the past;
רַק לֶעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר:
rather regarding the ultimate future it is said:
"וְהָיָה מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ וּמִדֵּי שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ יָבוֹא וְגוֹמֵר",
'And it shall come to pass that from one New Moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, shall all flesh come, etc.,'
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גִּלּוּי הַנּוֹכָח גַּם בְּרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ.
signifying that direct revelation of the divine Presence will manifest on Rosh Chodesh as well.
כִּי לֶעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה שִׁיר חָדָשׁ,
For regarding the future it is said there will be a 'new song,'

פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר פז)84 Midrash Tehillim 87:7 — "And singers as well as dancers: all my springs are in you." R. Judah bar R. Simon said in the name of R. Meir: Just as a well wells up with fresh water at every hour, so Israel utter a new song at every hour. That is what is written, "And singers as well as dancers: all my springs are in you." עַל פָּסוּק "וְשָׁרִים כְּחֹלְלִים וְכוּלֵי",
meaning as written in Shocher Tov (Midrash Tehillim 87) on the verse 'And singers as well as dancers, etc.,'
כִּי לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא יִהְיוּ מְשׁוֹרְרִים בְּכָל שָׁעָה שִׁיר חָדָשׁ.
that in the World to Come they will sing a renewed song at every single hour.
כִּי כְּמוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵין לוֹ גְּבוּל וָסוֹף,
Because just as Hashem, blessed be He, has neither boundary nor end,
כָּךְ לְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ אֵין גְּבוּל.
so too His comprehension has no limit.
וּבְכָל רֶגַע יַשִּׂיגוּ הַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכָח בְּמַדְרֵגָה מְחוּדֶּשֶׁת וְנוֹסֶפֶת עַד אֵין קֵץ כְּלָל.
And at every moment they will attain direct perception of His Presence on a newly elevated tier without any end at all.
רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מוּגְבָּל,
Only in this world, which is constrained,
הַהַשָּׂגָה גַּם כֵּן בִּגְבוּל.
is perception likewise bounded.
אֲבָל לֶעָתִיד יִהְיֶה נִקְרָא שִׁיר חָדָשׁ,
However, in the future it will truly be called a 'new song,'
כִּי תָּדִיר יִהְיֶה חָדָשׁ,
because it will constantly be brand new,
כִּי הַשִּׁיר מִצַּד הַהַכָּרָה,
since song emanates directly from cognitive realization;
וּבְכָל רֶגַע יִהְיֶה הַכָּרָה מְחוּדֶּשֶׁת וְשִׁיר חָדָשׁ,
and in every instant there will be fresh realization and a new song,
וְאֵין רֶגַע שֶׁיְּשׁוֹרְרוּ שִׁיר שֶׁכְּבָר אָמְרוּ בְּרֶגַע שֶׁלִּפְנֶיהָ,
with no moment in which they repeat the song recited the moment before,
וְנִמְצָא לְעוֹלָם יִהְיֶה שִׁיר חָדָשׁ.
resulting in an eternally new song.
זֶהוּ עִנְיַן רֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ,
This is the mystical essence of Rosh Chodesh,
וְעַיֵּין זוֹהַר תְּרוּמָה קלח רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א,
and see Zohar Terumah 138a,
וְהוּא רוֹמֵז לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעֲתִידִים לְהִתְחַדֵּשׁ כְּמוֹתָהּ,
alluding to Israel who are destined to renew themselves like the moon,
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּיִחוּד,
and King David, peace be upon him, in particular,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כה85 Rosh Hashanah 25a — Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi] said to R. Chiyya: Go to Ein Tav and sanctify the new month there, and send me the sign: David, king of Israel, lives and endures. Rashi: Rabbi sent R. Chiyya to Ein Tav because he was anxious lest the people of his own town murmur against him when he sanctified the month the next day, since they had seen the old moon all through the twenty-ninth (his teacher explained that a decree had been issued in Rabbi's place forbidding the sanctification of the month). David is the sign because he is likened to the moon, as it is said of him: "His throne as the sun before Me; as the moon it shall be established forever" (Psalms 89:37–38). Tosafos (s.v. "Go to Ein Tav and sanctify it"): There the court was established for sanctifying the month, as the Pesikta says on "Blow the shofar at the new moon": the court sanctifies the month at Ein Tav because it is the house of assembly. And the Yerushalmi says that just as they blew the shofar at Yavneh so they blew it at Ein Tav, which implies that a fixed court sat there, like the one at Yavneh. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 25a): David's kingship resembles the moon: like the moon he is called "small"; of Tamar's twins, Zerach corresponds to the sun and Peretz, from whom the house of David comes, to the moon; and the twenty-eight generations from Peretz to Zedekiah correspond to the twenty-eight days on which the moon's light is seen — for Israel reckon by the moon and the nations by the sun. Hence the sign "David, king of Israel, lives and endures": since the Holy One, blessed be He, likened David's kingdom to the moon, then just as the moon endures forever, so does his kingdom, as it is written, "His throne as the sun before Me; as the moon it shall be established forever." Some explain it as a mystery — David's attribute, on which the sanctification of the month depends (so the Ramban) — but he holds that the words are meant in their plain sense. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 17): Israel, who come from Abraham, called "pious," are not content [with the nations' reckoning by the sun] and count by the moon, the trait of King David, as it is said, "and send me the sign: David, king of Israel…" — the lesser luminary, lowliness. Though the moon belongs rather to the realm of desire, by it they overcome desire, like David "the small," who makes himself small and need not prevail through the opposite, self-exaltation. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): David, king of Israel, is rooted in the attribute of kingship, and his kingship is "established forever as the moon," as is known from "and send me the sign: David, king of Israel, lives and endures": he is likened to the moon, which has nothing of its own. Therefore he called himself "poor," having only what the Blessed One gives him and being unable to do anything at all against His will — and this is the root of the attribute of kingship. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Miketz 10): The abolition of the month [sought by the Greeks] means the sanctification of the month, as we find, "Go to Ein Tav and sanctify it": they were afraid to sanctify it in its proper place, and he said, "send me the sign: David, king of Israel, lives and endures," because they feared to say "sanctification of the month" explicitly, so he told him to send it by allusion..):
as our Sages of blessed memory taught (Rosh Hashanah 25a):
"שְׁלַח לִי סִימָנָא: 'דָּוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל חַי וְקַיָּם'",
'Send me the sign: David, King of Israel, is alive and enduring,'
שֶׁהוּא סִימָן לִקְבִיעוּת הַחוֹדֶשׁ.
which served as the secret watchword for sanctifying the new month.
וְלָכֵן נִזְכַּר עִנְיַן קְדוּשַּׁת הַחוֹדֶשׁ בַּכָּתוּב
Therefore, the communal sanctification of the month is explicitly highlighted in Scripture
רַק בְּעִנְיַן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם עִם שָׁאוּל,
specifically in the narrative of King David, peace be upon him, and Saul (I Samuel 20),
וּמִשָּׁם לְמֵידִין סְעוּדַת רֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ,
and from there we derive the festive meal of Rosh Chodesh,
דְּאָז נִתְחַדֵּשׁ הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר זֶה
because at that moment the revelation of this future light was initiated
בְּעֵת הַתְחָלַת בִּנְיַן הַמַּלְכוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל בִּכְלָל,
at the dawn of establishing royalty for Israel in general,
וּמַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד בִּפְרָט,
and the Davidic dynasty in particular,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַתְחָלַת הִתְגַּלּוּת רְשִׁימַת אוֹר דִּלְעָתִיד.
which represents the dawn of the manifest imprint of that future messianic illumination.
וְנִקְבַּע בְּרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ וְלֹא בְּשַׁבָּת
And this renewal was fixed specifically in Rosh Chodesh and not on Shabbat,
דְּיִהְיֶה גַּם כֵּן גִּלּוּי אוֹר זֶה לֶעָתִיד,
even though this light will also be revealed on Shabbat in the future,
לְפִי שֶׁקְּדוּשַּׁת שַׁבָּת קְבִיעָא וְקַיָּימָא
because the holiness of Shabbat is inherently fixed and immutable,
וְהוּא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
originating purely from Hashem, blessed be He;
וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵאִיר
and so long as He does not actively radiate it,
אֵין שַׁיָּיךְ הַשָּׂגַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָרְשִׁימוּ מִקּוֹדֶם.
it is not possible for the children of Israel to apprehend its prior imprint.
רַק קְדוּשַּׁת רֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ דְּ"יִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי",
Rather, the holiness of Rosh Chodesh is sanctified by the Jewish people ('Israel sanctifies the seasons'),
שֶׁזֶּה יִקְבַּע לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם,
which Hashem fixes for them in recognition of their own initiative,
כְּאִלּוּ הֵם קָבְעוּ קְדוּשָּׁה זוֹ,
as though they established this holiness themselves;
שַׁיָּיךְ שַׁפִּיר גַּם כֵּן רוֹשֶׁם מִקּוֹדֶם.
hence it rightfully admits an anticipatory imprint beforehand.
וְהַכָּתוּב הִקְדִּים גַּם כֵּן "מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ וְגוֹמֵר" לְשַׁבָּת,
Scripture likewise places 'from New Moon to New Moon' before 'from Sabbath to Sabbath'
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת: "אַיְידֵי דַּאֲתְיָא מִדְּרָשָׁא חֲבִיבָא".
in keeping with the Talmudic adage: 'Because it is derived by rabbinic exposition, it is beloved.'
כִּי שַׁבָּת הִיא קְדוּשָּׁה פְּשׁוּטָה קְבוּעָה מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית,
For Shabbat possesses an absolute sanctity fixed since the six days of Creation,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן חוֹדֶשׁ נִתְחַדֵּשׁ עַל יְדֵי סִיגּוּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
whereas the New Moon is innovated through the spiritual achievements of the Jewish people.

וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּפִרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר (פֶּרֶק מה86 Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 45:4 — Aaron reasoned within himself: If I say to Israel, "Give me silver and gold," they will bring it at once; rather I will say to them, "Give me the earrings of your wives and of your sons and daughters," and the matter will come to nothing. The women heard and would not agree to give their earrings to their husbands, but said to them, "You wish to make an abomination and a detestable thing that has no power to save?" They did not listen to them. And the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the women their reward in this world and in the world to come: in this world, that they keep the New Moons, as it is said, "Who satisfies your years with good, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.")
Therefore our Sages of blessed memory stated in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 45)
דְּנִיתַּן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לַנָּשִׁים בִּשְׂכַר שֶׁלֹּא עָשׂוּ עֵגֶל,
that in this world it was granted to women as a reward for not participating in the Golden Calf,
כִּי לוּלֵי אוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה הָיָה כְּבָר חֵירוּת מִמַּלְכֻיּוֹת וּמִיֵּצֶר הָרָע כְּמוֹ לֶעָתִיד,
for had it not been for that sin, there would already have been freedom from exile and from the evil inclination as in the ultimate future,
וְהָיוּ זוֹכִים לְאוֹתוֹ קְדוּשָּׁה.
and all would have merited that elevated sanctity.
וְהַנָּשִׁים שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לָהֶם חֵלֶק בְּאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה,
And the women, having taken no part in that deed,
מַשִּׂיגִים רְשִׁימָה זוֹ יוֹתֵר.
attain this foretaste and spiritual imprint more profoundly.
וּבְוַודַּאי כֵּן בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר הַמִּתְקָרֵב לְעִקְבֵי מְשִׁיחָא
And certainly, in every subsequent generation drawing nearer to the footsteps of the Messiah,
נִתְגַּלָּה קְדוּשַּׁת רֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ יוֹתֵר,
the latent holiness of Rosh Chodesh is revealed ever more,
כְּעִנְיַן קְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת בַּיָּמִים דִּמְקַמֵּי שַׁבַּתָּא.
parallel to the dawning sanctity of Shabbat on the days immediately preceding it.

items.h:
Seif 3 — Custom, Hallel, and Hidden Attachment
Inherited custom can express a bond with Hashem deeper than fully articulated or consciously structured wisdom.

p: וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן הַהַלֵּל שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה87 Taanit 28b — Rav happened to come to Babylonia and saw them reciting Hallel on the New Moon. He thought to stop them; but when he saw that they were skipping portions, he said: I may infer from this that they are holding to the custom of their fathers. Rashi: "Skipping portions": as we do, skipping "Not to us, O Lord, not to us" and beginning [again] from "The Lord has remembered us; He will bless." "They are holding to the custom of their fathers": but the Hallel of Chanukah, for instance on the first of Tevet, certainly does override [the lay delegation's morning service]; for since the prophets instituted that it be said at every season and over every trouble (may it not come upon them), so that when they are redeemed they say it over their redemption, it is as though it were from the Torah. Tosafos (s.v. "they are holding to the custom of their fathers"): Some explain that from here [we learn] that one does not recite a blessing over a custom, as is also implied in Sukkah (44b), where the willow was beaten without a blessing because it is a custom of the prophets. But Rabbeinu Tam ruled that one does: otherwise Rav could have recognized that they were reciting it as a custom from their not blessing (and he was present from the start, since it says "Rav happened to come to Babylonia," not "he happened into a synagogue"), rather than inferring it from their skipping. The willow is different, being merely a custom of handling; but over other customs, such as reading Hallel, one certainly blesses, and so is the halacha in practice. (תַּעֲנִית כח:):
And this clarifies the episode regarding Hallel where our Sages taught (Ta'anit 28b):
"סָבַר לְאַפְסוֹקִינְהוּ" –
Rav 'thought to stop them' from reciting it,
דְּמַה שַׁיָּיכוּת שִׁיר קוֹדֶם שֶׁנִּגְלָה הַנּוֹכָח?
reasoning: what place is there for full song before the divine Presence is openly revealed?
"כֵּיוָן דַּחֲזָא דִּמְדַלְּגִי, אָמַר: מִנְהַג אֲבוֹתֵיהֶם" –
'Once he saw that they skipped sections, he said: It is an established custom of their fathers'—
פֵּירוּשׁ, כִּי מִצְוַת הַתּוֹרָה הוּא מַה שֶּׁהוּא גָּלוּי לִפְנֵי חָכְמָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה,
meaning that a biblical commandment reflects what is overtly revealed before the Supreme Wisdom,
וּמִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר פְּעוּלַת דָּבָר זֶה לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
wherein Hashem directly illuminates the spiritual effect of that deed for Israel.
וּמִצְוַת חֲכָמִים הִיא מַה שֶּׁחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּשֵׂכֶל אֱנוֹשִׁי מֵאִיר לָהֶם שֶׁרָאוּי פְּעוּלָה זוֹ.
And a rabbinic commandment is that which is illuminated to the Sages of Israel through sanctified human intellect that this action is fitting.
וּמִנְהַג יִשְׂרָאֵל תּוֹרָה הוּא,
Yet a sacred custom of Israel (minhag) is itself Torah,
שֶׁמַּה שֶּׁאֵין בּוֹ גִּילּוּי דְּהֶאָרָה לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר זֶה,
whereby even without an overt illumination prompting that action—
לֹא מִצַּד הֶאָרַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּנִּגְלֶה בְּנוֹבְלוֹת חָכְמָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה הַמִּתְגַּלָּה בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁהוּא הַתּוֹרָה,
neither through direct divine revelation via the manifest emanations of supernal wisdom that appear in the Torah,
וְלֹא מִצַּד שֵׂכֶל הַחֲכָמִים,
