There is anger without inward fury, and it has sweeping force, since in his anger he sweeps on and chastises, but not cruelty; and there is fury without anger, which has cruelty but no sweeping force, since he does not punish now. But jealousy, when a man is zealous for his honor that has been profaned, has both cruelty and sweeping force, for the jealous man avenges himself at once. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 233): There is hardly a person entirely free of these three, jealousy, desire, and honor: as it says, "who can stand before jealousy?"; of desire the Sages said, "even the most pious of the pious…"; and needless to say honor, which includes both. Jealousy is the worst of them all and the root of the serpent, and corresponding to it is the leper, who is sent outside the camp of Israel.):
And so Scripture states (Proverbs 27:4):
"וּמִי יַעֲמֹד לִפְנֵי קִנְאָה",
'And who can stand before envy?'
וְהוּא צַד הַשְּׂמֹאל דְּרַע,
which is the left side of evil,
אֵין לְךָ אָדָם יַעֲמֹד כְּנֶגְדּוֹ.
before which no person can stand invulnerable.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קסד112 Bava Batra 164b — Rav Amram said in the name of Rav: There are three transgressions from which no man is spared on any day — sinful thought, want of concentration in prayer, and malicious speech. Malicious speech — can that enter your mind? Rather, the dust of malicious speech. Rashbam: Deliberation in prayer: some explain that after a man has prayed he reckons in his heart that the Holy One, blessed be He, will now pay him his reward, supply his needs and hear his prayer, because he prayed with concentration. Tosafos (s.v. "deliberation in prayer"): One might explain that the fault is looking for one's prayer to be answered, as in Berakhot, where such deliberation brings a man to heartache and is listed among the things that call his sins to mind — which would match sinful thought and malicious speech, neither of them a mitzvah. Tosafot rejects this: many people never look for their prayer to be answered, since they do not concentrate that much, so why should no man escape it on any day? Rather the transgression is the want of deliberation — failing to pray with concentration — and from this no man is spared on any day, for nobody is able to concentrate properly in his prayer. Maharsha: If no man can escape these three, in what sense are they transgressions at all, and why does Rav say "no man [adam]"? Man is called adam after ash, blood and bile: because he is moulded of dust and ash he cannot fix his mind in prayer; because he has blood, its heat brings him to sinful thought; and because he has bile, he comes to malicious speech and evil traits. But one who so conducts himself as to resemble an angel of the Lord can indeed be saved from all three — and it is for that reason that they are properly called transgressions.:):
And as they stated (Bava Batra 164b):
"שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים אֵין אָדָם נִיצּוֹל בְּכָל יוֹם:
There are three things from which a person is not saved each day:
הִרְהוּר עֲבֵירָה וַאֲבַק לָשׁוֹן הָרָע",
sinful thoughts and the dust of slanderous speech,"
הֵם שְׁנֵי קְצוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר,
these being the two extremes mentioned above,
"וְעִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה"
"and calculating expectation in prayer" (iyun tefillah),
הוּא נֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
which corresponds to our father Jacob, peace be upon him,
דְּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה וְאֵין בּוֹ פְּסוֹלֶת כְּלָל,
whose bed was complete, bearing no dross at all,
שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ רָשָׁע שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכוּנֶּה,
such that even a wicked person among Israel is still termed Israel,

"וַאֲפִילּוּ רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבָּךְ וְכוּלֵי" (סַנְהֶדְרִין לז113 Sanhedrin 37a — Reish Lakish said: From here — "Your temples are like a pomegranate split open" (Song of Songs 6:7): even the empty ones among you are as full of commandments as a pomegranate is of seeds. Maharsha: Reish Lakish reads the whole verse [Song of Songs 4:3] as speaking of the niddah: "your lips are like a thread of scarlet" are the bloodstains, red as scarlet, and "your speech is comely" means that although all closeness is forbidden, speech with her is permitted — or that she may still adorn herself in her days of niddah, as R. Akiva holds, lest she become repugnant to her husband. Even so the man does not come to transgress, for "your temples are like a pomegranate split open" — even the empty ones among you, etc.; and "behind your veil" means that beyond this they restrain themselves further so as not to come to transgression — that a man with a discharge may not eat together with a woman with a discharge, and other such distancings. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 37a): This is because Israel are, in themselves, fit for the Torah, and therefore even the empty ones among them are full of commandments like a pomegranate. For what a thing is by its own nature carries great strength: just as the pomegranate is full [of seeds] by the very essence of its creation, so the empty ones are full of commandments by the very essence of theirs. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Esau's heart was full of crookedness, and only through the dimming of his eyes could Isaac think well of him; through that same dimming he afterwards did not recognize Jacob either, but he smelled "the smell of his traitors," for even the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and there is no room at all to accuse him. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:57): Jacob's service was chiefly in intention for the sake of Heaven, and the "garments" of deed began only with Laban, where he began to beget the souls of Israel, who are themselves the commandments of the Torah; hence it says then that [Rebecca] dressed him in Esau's garments. Therefore the Sages read "the smell of his garments" as "the smell of his traitors," meaning, as they said, that even the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate: they too have a garment of the deed of the mitzvot. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 9): Even [Acher] belongs to the secret of the broken vessels, which were also placed in the Ark; thus "R. Meir found a pomegranate," as it is written, "your temples are like a slice of pomegranate," "even the empty ones among you…": one from whom the light has been emptied resembles a pomegranate. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 5): When Jacob donned Esau's garments to receive the blessings, Isaac smelled in him "the smell of his traitors," which come from the mixture of good and evil; but in Israel it is the reverse: the evil is only on the exterior, in the garment, while the interior is good, for even the empty ones and the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate. And scent is something the soul enjoys, which comes from the interior. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In the seed of Jacob none is cast off, for just as evening and morning make one day, so His praise rises from the wicked as from the righteous: even the empty ones of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and the sinners of Israel are full of remorse. Of this the Sages said, "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors," and Bereishis Rabbah applies it to the likes of Yakim of Tzeroros, who in a brief moment preceded Yose ben Yoezer, a perfect tzaddik who had toiled all his days, to the World to Come; for the penitent attains this in a single moment..),
and 'even the empty ones among you are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate' (Sanhedrin 37a),

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שָׁם114 Sanhedrin 37a — R. Zeira said: From here — "And he smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him" (Genesis 27:27): do not read "his garments [begadav]" but "his traitors [bogedav]." Tosafos (s.v. "and he smelled the smell of his garments"): "Smell" is a term that belongs to menstrual blood, as we say at the end of chapter Kol HaYad (Niddah 20b): a certain woman brought blood before R. Elazar; he smelled it and said, "This is blood of desire." Maharsha: Jacob was certainly perfectly righteous, but he was now wearing the garments of the wicked Esau, which Esau had coveted from the wicked Nimrod, and how many bloodstains from the murders of these wicked men were on them; yet when Jacob came before his father even these garments gave off a good fragrance, as it is said, "and he smelled the smell of his garments," for the fragrance of the Garden of Eden entered with him. This is a sign for his children, that even the traitors among them give off a fragrance through the commandments, as with the bloodstains of niddah. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 37a): The garments allude to the empty ones: garments are secondary to the man, and so the empty ones are not the essence of "man" — for the righteous are always likened to man, and Israel, being more righteous than the nations, are called "man" (Yevamot 61a); therefore the wicked are likened to garments, which are not the man himself and are far from him. The good deed that the empty ones do for the sake of Heaven is called "smell" because smell reaches from far away, and so the Holy One, blessed be He, smells the commandments of the empty ones, who are far from Him; further, smell is associated with the attribute of judgment, and the empty ones, who subdue their inclination with great strength and wage war against it, belong to that attribute. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Esau's heart was full of crookedness, and only through the dimming of his eyes could Isaac think well of him; through that same dimming he afterwards did not recognize Jacob either, but he smelled "the smell of his traitors," for even the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and there is no room at all to accuse him. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:57): Jacob's service was chiefly in intention for the sake of Heaven, and the "garments" of deed began only with Laban, where he began to beget the souls of Israel, who are themselves the commandments of the Torah; hence it says then that [Rebecca] dressed him in Esau's garments. Therefore the Sages read "the smell of his garments" as "the smell of his traitors," meaning, as they said, that even the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate: they too have a garment of the deed of the mitzvot. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 10): In Israel the evil stems from the vessels themselves, not from what is drawn out of them, and in the essence of the vessels there is no evil at all; therefore "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors": they too give off a good fragrance, as it says, "the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot." As the Sages said of the myrtle, fragrance without taste, so in Israel there are those who have mitzvot but not Torah. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): The penitent breaks through every bound and in a single moment can rise from the utmost darkness to great light, which is the good name that spreads from one end of the world to the other; and of this it is said, "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors": once they have returned from [their betrayals], theirs is the chief good fragrance, smelled throughout the whole world. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Toldos 5): When Isaac asked, "Are you my son Esau?", he meant that in the smell of his garments he sensed deeds, for which he called him "Esau" [as one who does the will of his Maker]; and the Midrash indeed reads "his garments" as "his traitors." To this Jacob answered "I am": I am the one who performs the deeds of the mitzvot, and what you sensed is the fragrance of Jacob's traitors, for the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and they too give off a good fragrance. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): Even when Israel sins, it is like a myrtle standing among reeds, for the essence of a Jew's heart always gives off a good fragrance like the myrtle, as the Sages said on "he smelled the smell of his garments": "the smell of his traitors." The sins are only like thorns surrounding the rose, which prick it for the moment, and in the future this will be made clear in all Israel, when "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In the seed of Jacob none is cast off, for just as evening and morning make one day, so His praise rises from the wicked as from the righteous: even the empty ones of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and the sinners of Israel are full of remorse. Of this the Sages said, "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors," and Bereishis Rabbah applies it to the likes of Yakim of Tzeroros, who in a brief moment preceded Yose ben Yoezer, a perfect tzaddik who had toiled all his days, to the World to Come; for the penitent attains this in a single moment.):
and as written (there):
"וַיָּרַח אֶת רֵיחַ בְּגָדָיו – בּוֹגְדָיו".
'He smelled the fragrance of his garments (begadav)—his betrayers (bogedav).'
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת.
Nevertheless, there remain distinct spiritual gradations.
וּתְפִלָּה פֵּירוּשׁ הִתְחַבְּרוּת וּדְבֵיקוּת,
Prayer essentially signifies connection and cleaving,
וְזֶהוּ עִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה דְּאֵין אָדָם נִיצּוֹל,
and this explains why no man is spared from iyun tefillah:
דְּבָזֶה גַּם יַעֲקֹב אֵין שָׁלֵם לְגַמְרֵי
for in this, even Jacob's realm is not entirely uniform
לִהְיוֹת כֻּלּוֹ שָׁוֶה וְחַד בְּלֹא מַדְרֵגוֹת בְּעִנְיַן הַשְּׁלֵימוּת וְהַדְּבֵיקוּת,
such that all would be identical and unified without levels in cleaving;
וּכְמוֹ לֶעָתִיד יַעֲשֶׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מָחוֹל לַצַּדִּיקִים וְכוּלֵי
whereas in the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle dance for the righteous, etc.

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב סוֹף תַּעֲנִית לא115 Taanit 31a — In time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance for the righteous, and He will sit among them in the Garden of Eden, and each and every one will point with his finger, as it is said: “And it shall be said on that day: Behold, this is our God, for whom we waited that He might save us; this is the Lord, for whom we waited — let us be glad and rejoice in His salvation.” Rashi: “A circle-dance” [machol]: [a dance] round about, as in the term “the surrounding space [machol] of the vineyard” (Kilayim 4:1). “Points with his finger”: and says, “This is the Lord, for whom we waited that He might save us; this is the Lord, for whom we waited — let us be glad and rejoice in His salvation.” Maharsha: The language [“this is our God… this is the Lord”] is doubled because a person must bless God for the attribute of judgment upon him just as for the attribute of mercy, as it is said, “In God I will praise His word; in the Lord I will praise His word”: when He is “our God” in the attribute of judgment, we waited for Him to save us, and “this is the Lord” in the attribute of mercy toward us, we waited for Him. And it does not say “in our salvation” but “in His salvation,” in the manner of “I am with him in distress”: when He saves us, He too is saved with us, and over this we will be glad and rejoice. Maharal (Be'er HaGolah, Be'er 4): A dance [machol] is a circle, and every point on a circle is turned, along its line, toward the center, which is set apart from the whole circle; so the righteous, raised entirely above materiality, will all be drawn toward and joined to the Holy One, blessed be He, who sits in their midst — joined to Him not from one side but from every side, since the dance goes round — while He remains set apart from them as the center is from the circle. And each points to Him with his finger because one points with the finger at something singular and distinct from all else: the righteous will cleave to His truth as the One who is set apart from all beings. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev 6): The letter samekh points to the future, when the Holy One, blessed be He, will slaughter the evil inclination and make a circle-dance for the righteous, that is, without distinction of levels, like every round thing, which has no head or end. And although there will be levels then too, for Torah scholars "go from strength to strength," since there will be no evil inclination the levels will not come from new service but only from the service of this world. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): Moses, in his blessing, which is the blessing of the time to come, called Dan a lion, by virtue of the revelation of the level of circles, when the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance for the righteous in the time to come; then Dan will be joined together with Judah, so that the end is embedded in the beginning. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Korach): Korach's claim was that no Jew is elevated above another, for "the Lord is in their midst": the Blessed One dwells within all of them equally, as taught that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle-dance for the righteous, a dance being a circle in which no one is closer than his fellow. And Korach claimed that it is so now as well..),
(as written at the end of Ta'anit 31a),
פֵּירוּשׁ עִיגּוּל,
meaning a circle,
דְּיִתְגַּלֶּה מַדְרֵגַת הָעִיגּוּלִים דְּשָׁם אֵין מַדְרֵגוֹת
wherein the realm of Circles will be revealed, where no hierarchical gradations exist
דְּכֻלּוֹ שָׁוֶה בִּשְׁלֵימוּת.
and all are entirely equal in perfection.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קוֹמַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא קוֹמַת הַיּוֹשֶׁר דְּצוּרַת אָדָם,
In contrast, the stature of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, represents the Stature of Linearity (Yosher) in human form,
שֶׁבָּזֶה יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת רֹאשׁ וְסוֹף וּקְצוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע,
wherein there exist gradations of head, feet, and limbs as is known,
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּצֵל דְּהַיְינוּ לְהַגִּיעַ לִשְׁלֵימוּת גָּמוּר,
and it is impossible to be fully spared—that is, to reach absolute perfection—
כִּי כֹּחַ זֶה עֲדַיִן אֵינוֹ בִּשְׁלֵימוּת כַּנִּזְכָּר
because this power is not yet culminated
עַד בִּיאַת מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁהוּא יִהְיֶה בְּתַכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת.
until the coming of the Messiah, who will embody the ultimate perfection.

וּכְפַרְנָס כֵּן דּוֹר (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב עֲרָכִין יז116 Arakhin 17a — "Such is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face, O Jacob. Selah." R. Yehuda Nesia and the Rabbis differ about this. One said: The generation is according to its leader; and one said: The leader is according to his generation. [The dispute] is said with respect to severity and gentleness. Rashi: The verse "This is the generation of those who seek Him" sets the generation alongside those who seek Him, comparing the one to the other. In the conclusion, "severity" means anger, and "gentleness" means being easily appeased. Maharsha: "Gentleness" — Rashi explains it as humility: if the generation is harsh, the Holy One, blessed be He, sets over them a harsh leader, and if the people of the generation are gentle with one another, He sets over them a leader who guides them gently; and according to the one who says the generation follows its leader, the reverse, for the generation is drawn after its leader. The Sages did not wish to say that "those who seek Him" refers to the generation, as though they were all seekers of the Lord, but rather to the good leaders, who are certainly seekers of the Lord — or else the phrase refers to the leaders as those who seek the good of the generation, as it is said, "seeking the good of his people.".),
And as the leader is, so is the generation (Arachin 17a),
כָּל הַדּוֹר יִהְיֶה בְּתַכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת
the entire generation will reach ultimate perfection
וְאָז יִנָּצְלוּ גַּם מֵעִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה
and then they will be spared even from flaw in iyun tefillah,
דְּיִהְיֶה דְּבֵיקוּת הַגָּמוּר,
there being absolute cleaving;
וּמִמֵּילָא יִנָּצְלוּ מֵהִרְהוּר עֲבֵירָה וַאֲבַק לָשׁוֹן הָרָע,
and automatically they will be delivered from sinful thoughts and the dust of slander,
דְּהֵם אֵין שַׁיָּיכִים בֶּאֱמֶת לְגוּף אָדָם.
since these do not truly belong to man's essential self.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק אֵין מִטָּתָן וְכוּלֵי,
And regarding Abraham and Isaac it was said their bed was not complete, etc.,
פֵּירוּשׁ מִטָּה שֶׁפָּרִים וְרָבִים עָלֶיהָ דְּהַיְינוּ בְּתוֹלָדוֹת,
meaning the bed on which they procreate, referring to offspring,
אֲבָל בְּעֶצֶם יֵשׁ שְׁלֵימוּת.
yet in their personal essence there was total perfection.
וְכֵן בְּעֶצֶם אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ שְׁלֵימוּת,
So too within love and fear, in their pristine essence, perfection exists,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (מד117 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned." R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is Israel. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is myrtle, and myrtle they call it. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious..):
and as they stated in Sanhedrin (44a):
"מָשָׁל לְאָסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי חִילְפֵי, אָסָא שְׁמֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי",
'A parable of a myrtle standing among thorns: its name remains myrtle, etc.,'
שֶׁהִמְשִׁילוּ חֲטָאִים הַסּוֹבְבִים לָאָדָם כְּקוֹצִים הַסּוֹבְבִים לַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה,
comparing the sins surrounding man to thorns encircling a rose,
וְאֵינוֹ מֵעֶצֶם הָאָדָם,
showing they are not of the person's essence,
רַק שֶׁסּוֹבְבִים וּמַקִּיפִים אוֹתוֹ מִצַּד הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁל הָאָדָם.
but merely surround and encompass him through outward manifestation.
אֲבָל מִצַּד עֶצֶם נֶפֶשׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי אֵין בּוֹ חֵטְא כְּלָל,
Yet from the perspective of the essential Jewish soul, there is no sin whatsoever,
רַק הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת בְּמַעֲלַת הַדְּבֵיקוּת – בָּזֶה הַחִלּוּקִים הוּא בְּעֶצֶם הַנְּפָשׁוֹת,
only that regarding the gradations of cleaving, differences exist within souls,
שֶׁמִּצַּד קוֹמַת הַיּוֹשֶׁר יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת בַּנְּפָשׁוֹת.
for from the perspective of Linear Stature, souls occupy distinct levels.
וּמַדְרֵגָה הַשְּׁלֵימָה דְּהַיְינוּ לְהִנָּצֵל לְגַמְרֵי מֵעִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה,
And reaching that perfect level—being completely spared from flaw in iyun tefillah—
שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לְסוֹף קוֹמַת הַיּוֹשֶׁר בִּשְׁלֵימוּת,
where one arrives at the very pinnacle of the Stature of Linearity,
אָז תֵּיכֶף מַתְחִיל הָעִיגּוּלִים
the realm of Circles immediately commences,
וְנִגְלָה אוֹר הָעִיגּוּלִים שֶׁאֵין מַדְרֵגוֹת בְּעֶצֶם כְּלָל.
revealing the light of Circles where no essential gradations exist.
וַעֲדַיִן לֹא הִגִּיעַ לָזֶה אָדָם,
And as yet, no man has attained this,
שֶׁהֲרֵי עֲדַיִן לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה אוֹר זֶה בָּעוֹלָם
for this illumination has not yet broken through in the world
עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא אֶחָד מִזַּרְעָא דְּדָוִד
until one arises from the seed of David,
שֶׁהוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּתְפִלָּה
who represents the spiritual level of prayer,
כְּטַעַם "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה",
in the spirit of 'and I am prayer,'
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים,
as written numerous times in the Zohar,
וְיִזְכֶּה לְעִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה בִּשְׁלֵימוּת,
and will attain iyun tefillah in its utter perfection;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (יח118 Megillah 18a — "Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king." And once David has come, prayer has come, as it is said: "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer." And once prayer has come, the Temple service has come, as it is said: "Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon My altar." Rashi: "Afterward the children of Israel shall return" — after they return to the Temple [that is, once Jerusalem has been rebuilt], they will then seek the Holy One, blessed be He, and David their king. Maharsha: He derives the coming of David from this verse, for the Sages said that three commandments were given to Israel upon their entry into the Land — to appoint themselves a king, to cut off the seed of Amalek, and to build the Chosen House — and the conclusion is that the king is appointed first; so it will surely be in the time to come as well, and since "I will bring them to My holy mountain" means the building of the Chosen House, David must necessarily have come before it. And he says "once prayer has come, the Temple service has come" because prayer, which is the service of the heart, precedes the service of the altar — and so Solomon did when he built the Temple: first he prayed that no trouble should come, and only afterward is it written, "And Solomon sacrificed to the Lord twenty-two thousand oxen.".):
and as they stated in Megillah (18a):
"כֵּיוָן שֶׁבָּא דָּוִד, בָּאת תְּפִלָּה".
'Once David came, prayer came.'

sections.en: Prayer at the Height of the World

items.h: Prayer rises above ordinary physical concerns and draws from the deepest spiritual level, especially through the hidden radiance of Israel's Hod.

Seif 1 — Prayer beyond the World
Prayer stands above ordinary physical reality and draws down the hidden radiance of Israel's spiritual splendor.

p: הַתְּפִלָּה הוּא מִדְּבָרִים הָעוֹמְדִים בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם,
Prayer is among those matters that stand at the highest pinnacle of the world,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת119 Berakhot 6b — “When vileness is exalted among the sons of men.” One of the Sages said to Rav Bibi bar Abaye, and some say Rav Bibi said to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: What is this? He said to him: These are matters that stand at the very height of the world, and yet people treat them lightly. Rashi: "When vileness is exalted" is the latter half of the verse quoted just above, "The wicked walk round about." And "matters that stand at the very height of the world" — such as prayer, which ascends on high. Maharsha: This plainly refers back to the opening of the verse: one who prays round about the synagogue, that is, outside it, is called wicked precisely because he treats prayer lightly, prayer being one of those "matters that stand at the very height of the world." Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Tehillim 34): Although in human eyes the deed seems to be the main thing, the chief guarding is truly of the mouth and tongue, for everything is clarified through the tongue — as the Baal Shem Tov explained the Gemara's "things that stand at the height of the world": it is words [spoken words] that stand at the height of the world. As the holy Zohar says, "once he has brought a word out of his mouth, that word becomes a voice, splits the airs and firmaments, and rises on high." (ו:):
as they stated in Berakhot (6b):
עַל פָּסוּק "כְּרוּם זֻלֻּת",
on the verse "when vileness is exalted (kerum zulut),"
פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁהוּא מְרוֹמָם מִכָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
meaning that it is elevated above all affairs of this world;
כַּיָּדוּעַ תְּפִלָּה כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ,
as is known, prayer is like standing before the King,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵירוּבִין120 Eruvin 64a — Rabbah bar Rav Huna said: One who has drunk should not pray; but if he prayed, his prayer is a prayer. One who is intoxicated should not pray; and if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination. What is the case of one who has drunk, and what of one who is intoxicated? One who is intoxicated is anyone unable to speak in the presence of a king; one who has drunk is anyone still able to speak before a king. Tosafos (s.v. "One who is intoxicated should not pray, and if he prayed his prayer is an abomination"): He has not fulfilled his obligation, since he cannot speak in the presence of a king, and he must go back and pray again — as in the case of one who prayed with excrement before him (Berakhot 22b), where the conclusion is that since he sinned, his prayer, though he prayed it, is an abomination and must be repeated. The two are not alike in every respect: one who has merely drunk may not pray until his wine wears off, and even with mixed wine he may not pray after more than a quarter-log; yet it is obvious that one who has drunk does recite Grace after Meals and all the other blessings. Maharsha (Chidushei Halachot): On Tosafot's closing words, that on account of urine it is obvious one need not repeat the blessing: he might better have said the stronger thing, that on account of urine one certainly need not repeat the prayer either, since it is excrement that was taught as an impediment and not urine. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 2): "Abomination" is said of one who inclines to what is alien — as all the forbidden relations, the harlotry of the material, are called "abomination" — so that whoever is drawn after the physical to excess, until he becomes wholly a creature of body and intellect is removed from him, is an abomination to the Blessed Name. Hence the prayer of a drunkard is an abomination: intellect has already left him and he has become physical, and when he asks the Blessed Name to supply his needs it is as though he wanted Him to grant his request to fill his bodily desire, as the body without intellect that he now is. A man ought to pray that the Blessed Name grant his needs so that he may serve Him and study Torah, and then his prayer is surely acceptable; but the drunkard prays at the moment he has inclined most toward the body, and this is surely an abomination. (סד.): "הֵיכִי דָּמֵי שִׁכּוֹר וְכוּלֵי".
as they asked in Eruvin (64a): "What is the definition of a drunkard, etc.?"
וְהָעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
And one who stands before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He,
וַדַּאי מְרוֹמָם מִכָּל חֶמְדַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
is certainly transcendent above all worldly physical desire;
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם יוֹכִיחַ:
and Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, proves this:
"לֶחֶם לֹא אָכַל וְגוֹמֵר",
"bread he did not eat, etc.,"
שֶׁעָמַד בָּהָר לִפְנֵי ה'.
for he stood on the mountain before Hashem.

וְאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת ו:)121 Berakhot 6b — And our father Abraham — whence do we know that he fixed a place [for his prayer]? For it is written, "And Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood"; and "standing" means nothing other than prayer, as it is said, "And Pinchas stood and prayed." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 4): Abraham fixed a place for his prayer, and his cleaving to the Blessed One was therefore fixed and not incidental, as it is written, "to the place where he had stood." For that reason the Blessed One was with him continually and fixedly, with no removal at all, and he was joined to the Divine Presence; and when he went out to war the Divine Presence fought his enemies and was always his help — all because he fixed a place for his prayer, that is, because his prayer, which is his cleaving to Him, was fixed and not incidental, and what is fixed is never removed, unlike the incidental, which does not endure.: "אֵין עֲמִידָה אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה",
And they stated (Berakhot 6b): "There is no 'standing' other than prayer,"
פֵּירוּשׁ עֲמִידָה לִפְנֵי ה' הוּא רַק בִּתְפִלָּה.
meaning that standing before Hashem is achieved specifically in prayer.
דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא אָחִיד בְּגוּפָא דְּמַלְכָּא
For in Torah, one holds fast to the King's essence
וְנִקְרָא "אִישׁ אֱלֹהִים – בַּעֲלָא דְּמַטְרוֹנִיתָא".
and is titled "the man of God – the husband of the Matronita (the Shechinah)".
אֲבָל תְּפִלָּה הִיא מַטְרוֹנָה,
However, prayer itself is the Matronita,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּיקּוּנִים (סוֹף תִּיקּוּן יג)122 Tikkunei Zohar 29b:10 — And therefore a herald goes out every day: Whoever slays that serpent which nests among the great mountains, they give him the daughter of the King — that is prayer — who sits upon the tower of which it is said, "The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous runs into it and is set on high." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 11): The life of the moment comes from the bond of soul and body and dwells in the heart, the place of toil, for the evil inclination sits at the two openings of the heart, and only "whoever prevails in battle, they give him the King's daughter — that is prayer." But the eternal life of Torah, which does not come from the bond with the body and resides in the brain, is free to all: if [the evil one] meets you, drag him to the study house, and one who has not prevailed should engage in Torah, not only after the victory. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 208): A person's main battle with his inclination is over imaginings and thoughts in the heart and mind, and of this the Tikkunim say, "whoever prevails in battle, they give him the King's daughter — that is prayer." For prayer is the recognition of the Presence, as one standing before the King, which requires the heart and mind to stand firm; and one who overcomes his inclination, leaving imagination and stray thoughts, is granted that the Blessed One be present before his eyes at the time of prayer.: "בְּרַתָּא דְּמַלְכָּא דָּא צְלוֹתָא".
as written in the Tikkunim (end of Tikkun 13): "The daughter of the King—this is prayer."
וּבְנֵי אָדָם מְזַלְזְלִים,
And human beings treat it lightly,
פֵּירוּשׁ מִצַּד מַדְרֵגַת בְּנֵי אָדָם קַדְמָאָה הֵיפֶךְ בְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים,
meaning from the mundane level of earthly man—the antithesis of divine beings—
דִּשְׁקוּעִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ זִלְזוּל,
wherein being immersed in this world causes degradation,
דְּחוֹשְׁבִים כָּל עִיקַּר תְּפִלָּה הַיְינוּ רַק שְׁאֵלַת צְרָכָיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
for they assume the entire essence of prayer is merely requesting one's physical needs in this world,
הֲרֵי דְּעִיקָּרָהּ בְּצָרְכֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם.
concluding that its core lies in mundane necessities rather than the heights of the universe.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֵם גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
Yet in truth, all mundane affairs of this world likewise derive from Hashem, blessed be He,
וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֵינָם שְׁנֵי עִנְיָנִים נִפְרָדִים,
and this world and the World to Come are not two disconnected realities,
דִּשְׁנֵיהֶם נִקְרָאִים עוֹלָם,
since both are designated as 'world' (olam);
שֵׁם עוֹלָם רָצָה לוֹמַר כָּל בְּרוּאֵי וְעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם נִכְלָל בָּזֶה.
the term olam indicates that all creations and occurrences of existence are encompassed within it.
רַק הַחִלּוּק בֵּינֵיהֶם:
The only distinction between them is:
זֶה נִקְרָא "הַזֶּה" – פֵּירוּשׁ הַנִּגְלֶה לָעַיִן,
this one is called 'this' (hazeh)—meaning manifest to the eye,
וְזֶה נִקְרָא "הַבָּא" – פֵּירוּשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם.
and that one is called 'to come' (haba)—meaning concealed.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֵישׁ פְּסָחִים (ב123 Pesachim 2b — They raised an objection: “And I said: Surely darkness shall envelop me, and the night shall be light about me” (Psalms 139:11) — evidently “light” means day! There, this is what David said: I had said, surely darkness will envelop me in the World to Come, which resembles day; [but] now this world, which resembles night, is light about me. Rashi: [On the objection:] David had thought in his affliction, when he was pursued, that he would surely die in this darkness, which would "envelop" him — darken over him continually (from the word for twilight) — and instead the night and darkness in which he dwelt became "light about me"; since it is set against "night," "light" means day: the night became day for me. [On the answer:] "I said" that because of my sin I would be driven even from the World to Come; and now that He has forgiven me that sin, even this world, in which I had dwelt in darkness and disgrace, has shone about me — for in Solomon's days, when he sought to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies and the gates cleaved to one another, the Holy One, blessed be He, made known to David's enemies that He had forgiven David (Moed Katan 9a). Maharsha: At first sight, on the Gemara's present assumption that "night" is said figuratively of his being in distress and darkness, as Rashi explains, one could equally say that "light" comes from "to shine" [and does not mean day] — just as the Gemara takes it at the end, where "night" is a figure for this world and "light" is from "to shine," as Rashi explains; and this can be resolved. Maharal (Derashas Shabbos HaGadol): This world, being a physical world, is called "night" because of matter, which does not exist in complete actuality; and what does not [fully] exist is called "night" and "darkness." For whatever stands within turbid matter is said to be in darkness, and what is in darkness is reckoned as though it does not exist at all. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 19): [On "to declare Your kindness in the morning and Your faithfulness in the nights":] "Morning" is the World to Come, which is entirely light, as in the first chapter of Pesachim, where the World to Come is called "morning" and this world "night." In the World to Come the kindness and good that the Holy One, blessed be He, does with the righteous will be seen; but in this world, which is like night and in which the righteous do not dwell in good, one declares His faithfulness — for though he is in distress, he believes in Him that the good will be his in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): Truth is what is clarified and revealed in the heart and needs no faith, but in concealment truth is clothed in faith (the secret of "True and firm" in the morning and "True and faithful" in the evening), so that even in concealment one believes in the Life of the worlds by way of faith. This is the state of all of man in this world, which is likened to night, and all the more so in the time of exile, the full darkness of night; and since this world is full of deceptions and the darkness of the evil inclination, one must at least strengthen himself in faith.:):
And as they stated at the beginning of Pesachim (2b):
דּוֹמִים לְיוֹם וָלַיְלָה,
they are compared to day and night,
פֵּירוּשׁ דִּבְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִצַּד הֶסְתֵּר הָאוֹר נִגְלֶה צָרְכֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה
meaning that in this world, due to the concealment of the divine light, physical needs appear
כְּאִילּוּ הוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
as though they were contrary to the will of Hashem, blessed be He,
כִּי תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַשְׁכִּיחִים.
because worldly desires cause forgetfulness.
אֲבָל מִצַּד הַגִּלּוּי נִגְלֶה דְּכָל מַה שֶּׁבָּרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ – לִכְבוֹדוֹ וּלְקִילּוּסוֹ
Yet from the perspective of ultimate revelation, it is disclosed that all Hashem created was for His glory and praise

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב רֵישׁ מִזְמוֹר יט124 Midrash Tehillim 19:1 — "For the leader. A psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God." This is what Scripture says: "The Lord has made everything for His own sake" (Proverbs 16:4) — for His praise, as it is said, "Sing to the Lord with thanksgiving" (Psalms 147:7). Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): The aim of the whole Torah is to come to a complete apprehension that there is a Creator, Ruler and Overseer, which was the purpose of the creation of the world: "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. All 613 commandments are counsels for reaching this, for the Torah is called truth, being counsels for reaching a clear apprehension in the heart, so manifest that it needs no faith. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 6): Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created for His glory, He created to reveal the glory of His kingship and His Presence among the lower beings, and "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. The building of the Tabernacle and the Temple is man's work of building a place for His Presence after the sin, when the Presence is not revealed everywhere, in the pattern of the Blessed One's work in creation; had man not sinned, the whole world would have been a Tabernacle and a Sanctuary. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The angels cry, "Where is the place of His glory?", but man grasps the Throne of Glory, for "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise; the purpose of creation is the revelation of His glory, and its purpose is man. For the chief revelation of glory is when a person with free choice, whose body inclines toward impurity, nevertheless subdues his inclination and desires for the sake of Heaven's honor, which the angels, who have no evil inclination, cannot attain at all.).
(as written in Shocher Tov at the start of Psalm 19).
וְלֹא בָּרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דָּבָר לְהַשְׁכִּיחוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם,
And Hashem, blessed be He, created nothing to cause Him to be forgotten, Heaven forbid;
וְאִם כֵּן וַדַּאי כָּל צָרְכֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַה שֶּׁבָּרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ נִצְרָכִים לָאָדָם,
and if so, certainly all bodily needs that Hashem created for man to require
הֵם בֶּאֱמֶת עוֹמְדִים בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם,
actually stand at the highest pinnacle of the universe,
פֵּירוּשׁ בַּהַהִתְרוֹמְמוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְעִנְיַן הָעוֹלָם, רָצָה לוֹמַר לְעִנְיַן הַבְּרִיאָה כֻּלּוֹ.
meaning within the spiritual elevation intrinsic to the world, namely to the entirety of Creation.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה, שֶׁהוּא מַכִּיר שֶׁכָּל צְרָכָיו מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
And this is achieved through prayer, wherein one recognizes that all his sustenance is from Hashem, blessed be He,
וְאִם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא יִתֵּן לוֹ אֵין לוֹ כְּלוּם,
and without Hashem providing, he possesses nothing;

הֲגַם דַּ"הֲרֵי שֻׁלְחָן וַהֲרֵי וְכוּלֵי125 Kiddushin 46a — R. Yochanan said: Here is the table, here is the meat and here is the knife — and we have nothing to eat. Rashi (s.v. "Here is the table"): That is to say: we have a mishna taught before us, and we do not know how to explain it." (קִדּוּשִׁין מו.),
and even though 'here is the table and here is the food, etc.' (Kiddushin 46a),
אֵין לָנוּ מַה לֶּאֱכוֹל אֶלָּא אַחַר הַתְּפִלָּה מְבַקְּשִׁים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּתֵּן.
we have nothing to sustain us until, following prayer, we beseech Hashem to grant it.
עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְרוֹמְמִים כָּל צָרְכֵי הָאָדָם וְנִבְרָאֵי הָעוֹלָם לְרוּם הַמַּעֲלוֹת.
Through this, all human needs and the creatures of the world are elevated to the summit of spiritual heights.
וְיֵשׁ חִלּוּק בֵּין אוֹר תּוֹרָה לִתְפִלָּה,
And there is a fundamental difference between the light of Torah and that of prayer,
שֶׁהֵם נִקְרָאִים יוֹם וָלַיְלָה וְשָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ כַּנּוֹדָע.
which are termed day and night, and heaven and earth, as is known.
כִּי הַתּוֹרָה הוּא אוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמַּמְשִׁיךְ בָּעוֹלָם,
For the Torah is the supernal light of Hashem that one draws down into the world,
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת ח.):
and along the lines of what they stated (Berakhot 8a):
"מִשֶּׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ אֵין לוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּלֵי הֲלָכָה בִּלְבַד",
"Since the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has only the four cubits of Halakhah,"
דְּשָׁם שׁוֹפֵעַ אוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ דִּירָה בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים.
for there Hashem's light flows just as in the Temple, establishing a dwelling in lower realms.
וּתְפִלָּה הוּא בְּהֵיפֶךְ,
Prayer, however, operates in the reverse direction,
כִּי אֵין תְּפִלָּה אֶלָּא עַל חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ,
since there is no prayer except over a lack that one endures,
עַל זֶה הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל לְהִוָּושֵׁעַ,
over which he prays for deliverance;
וְנִמְצָא הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי חֲשֵׁיכָה וְשִׁפְלוּת מֵאָרֶץ,
and thus only out of darkness and earthly lowliness
עַל יְדֵי זֶה פִּיו נִפְתָּח בִּתְפִלָּה וּמִתְעַלֶּה וְיוֹשֵׁב בְּרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם.
is his mouth opened in prayer, ascending to dwell at the world's highest peak.

כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר בְּסוֹטָה (ה126 Sotah 5a — "And with him that is of a contrite and lowly spirit." Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: one said, [read] "the contrite one is with Me"; and one said, "I am with the contrite one." And it stands to reason like the one who said "I am with the contrite one," for the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over all the mountains and hills and rested His Presence upon Mount Sinai, and did not raise Mount Sinai upward. Rashi: "The contrite one is with Me" — I raise him up until he dwells beside Me, and this is [the sense of the verse] "I dwell [on high] … with the contrite." "I am with the contrite one" — I lower My Presence to be beside him. Maharsha: The practical lesson [of the view that 'I am with the contrite one'] is that even a distinguished person should lower himself toward one beneath him, and not say that this is beneath his dignity, for there is no honor greater than the honor of Heaven. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 5a): According to the one who says "the contrite one is with Me," the Holy One, blessed be He, raises up the contrite: just as arrogance inclines toward the material, humility is a separate [transcendent] level, as Moses possessed it, so it is fitting that the humble man be elevated to God and be with Him. According to the one who says "I am with the contrite one," God rests His Presence upon what is crushed and lowly, because the lowly are simple — as the Sages hinted that the essence of the Divine Presence was [originally] among the lower beings. [It stands to reason like the latter,] for when God joins Himself to the contrite one the union is according to His power and is complete, whereas when the contrite one is with God the union is not as full. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAnavah 1): On either view the contrite one, as the effect, is joined to God, the Cause: according to "I am with the contrite one" the Cause turns toward the effect, which is prepared to receive His glory, and according to "the contrite one is with Me" the effect is raised to be with the Cause. It stands to reason like "I am with the contrite one," for one who comes to another is wholly with him, since the other receives him entirely, whereas one who comes to the great cannot be joined with him so fully. God comes to the humble man to be with him — passing over all the high mountains to rest His Presence on Mount Sinai — because the humble man possesses something of his Maker's own attribute, and like things are found together..):
This reflects the sage's opinion in Sotah (5a):
"אִתִּי דַּכָּא", דְּ"אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא" הוּא עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
'He brings the contrite with Me'—meaning 'I dwell with the contrite' through Torah study,

וְ"דַכָּא אִתִּי" הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה127 Rashi, Sotah 5a — “I am with the contrite” — I raise him up to dwell beside Me; that is to say, I cause the contrite to dwell with Me. “I am with the contrite” — I lower My Presence to be beside him..
and 'the contrite elevates up to Me' through prayer.
וְאָז "לַיְלָה כַּיּוֹם יָאִיר",
And then 'the night shines like the day,'

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (רֵישׁ שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב תְּהִלִּים128 Midrash Tehillim 1:5 — "May the words of my mouth find favor" — that they be enacted for the generations, and written down for the generations, and inscribed for the generations; and that men not read them as one reads [ordinary] books, but that they read them and receive reward for them as for [the tractates] Nega'im and Ohalot. "May the words of my mouth find favor." R. Yirmeyah bar Shalom said in the name of R. Yochanan: What is meant by "Let me dwell in Your tent forever"? Could it enter your mind that David asked to dwell in two worlds? Rather, David said: Let them make mention of me in the synagogues and study houses, and it will be as though I were alive and enduring in both worlds. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeitzei 7): David asked that the reader of Psalms receive reward as for Nega'im and Ohalot, rather than simply as one engaged in Torah, because the impurities of those tractates correspond to the flaws of jealousy and of the pursuit of honor, the flaws of Doeg and Ahithophel, who disputed with him. His intent was that through Psalms one should be able to rectify even these two flaws, which are grave and hardest to rectify in this world.):
and as written (at the beginning of Shocher Tov on Psalms):
דְּבִקֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁיְּהֵא קוֹרֵא תְּהִלִּים כְּעוֹסֵק בִּנְגָעִים וְאָהֳלוֹת,
that King David, peace be upon him, prayed that reciting Psalms be deemed equal to studying Nega'im and Ohalot,
דְּהַיְינוּ גּוּפֵי הֲלָכוֹת.
namely the core, rigorous bodies of halakhic law.

וְאָמְרוּ בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר כה)129 Midrash Tehillim 25:6 — "Guide me in Your truth and teach me, for You are the God of my salvation; in You do I hope all the day." And is it possible for a man to pray the whole day? Rather, because this world is day for the nations of the world and night for Israel — therefore, "in You do I hope all the day." עַל פָּסוּק "אוֹתְךָ קִוִּיתִי כָּל הַיּוֹם",
And they expounded in Shocher Tov (Psalm 25) on the verse 'For You I hope all the day,'

(וּבְמִזְמוֹר פו)130 Midrash Tehillim 86:2 — "Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to You do I call all the day." And is it possible for a man to pray the whole day? Rather, it is this world, which is day for the nations and night for Israel. Hence, "for to You do I call all the day." עַל פָּסוּק "אֵלֶיךָ אֶקְרָא כָּל הַיּוֹם":
(and in Psalm 86) on the verse 'To You I call all the day':
וְכִי אֶפְשָׁר לְאָדָם לְהִתְפַּלֵּל כָּל הַיּוֹם כֻּלּוֹ?
is it humanly possible for a person to pray the entire day continuously?
אֶלָּא זֶה עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא יוֹם לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְלַיְלָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.
Rather, this refers to this world, which is day for the nations of the world and night for Israel.
וְלִכְאוֹרָה לְפִי הַתֵּירוּץ קָשֶׁה יוֹתֵר,
Now seemingly, according to this resolution the difficulty increases,
דְּכִסְבוּרִים אָנוּ כָּל הַיּוֹם לְבַד,
for we thought it meant only twelve daytime hours,
וְהוּא הוֹסִיף כָּל זְמַן עוֹלָם הַזֶּה – יוֹם וָלַיְלָה תָּמִיד לֹא יִשְׁבֹּות.
yet he expanded it to the entire duration of this world—incessantly day and night without cessation.
וְעוֹד, שֶׁקָּרָא לְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּשֵׁם הַשַּׁיָּיךְ לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
Furthermore, he designated this world by the term 'day' which pertains to the nations,
וְהָיָה לוֹ לִקְרוֹתוֹ לַיְלָה כְּשֵׁם שֶׁהוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.
whereas he should have termed it 'night' as it is experienced by Israel.

אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא מִקֵּץ ט131 Midrash Tanchuma, Miketz 9 — R. Yose bar Chalafta says: There are set times for prayer, as it is said, "But as for me, may my prayer to You, O Lord, be at a favorable time." When is a favorable time? When the congregation is praying.):
However in truth, our Sages of blessed memory stated (Midrash Tanchuma, Miketz 9):
"עִתִּים הֵם לִתְפִלָּה",
"There are designated times for prayer,"
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּתִי וְגוֹמֵר עֵת רָצוֹן".
and as written: 'And as for me, may my prayer come to You, Hashem, at an acceptable time.'
פֵּירוּשׁ "עֵת רָצוֹן" – כְּשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּתְפַּלְּלוּ לְפָנָיו,
An 'acceptable time' means when Hashem, blessed be He, desires that one pray before Him,

כְּטַעַם: "אִם תְּפִלָּתִי שְׁגוּרָה בְּפִי132 Berakhot 34b — R. Chanina ben Dosa used to pray for the sick and say: “This one will live,” or “This one will die.” They asked him: How do you know? He said to them: If my prayer flows fluently in my mouth, I know that it is accepted; and if not, I know that it is rejected. Rashi: "If it is fluent" — if my prayer is ordered in my mouth and runs smoothly and I do not stumble, and my supplication wells up from my heart to my mouth for as long as I wish to prolong my pleading. "That it is rejected [metoraf]" — that the sick man [is doomed]; another explanation, it is the expression "they fling his prayer back in his face" — that is, the prayer offered for him is flung back and driven away from him and is not accepted. Maharsha: See Rashi. The Arukh explains "metoraf" from "tereifa" in its literal sense, like the eighteen tereifot: at the very hour when he prayed for the one who died, that man was already a tereifa and would certainly die, according to the view that a tereifa cannot live. Beis Yaakov (Vayigash 7): As the Talmud relates, R. Chanina ben Dosa would pray for the sick and say, "This one will live and this one will die," and when asked how he knew, answered, "If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know that it is accepted"; he learned this from the verse "Who creates the fruit of the lips: peace, peace." That is, if the lips and the organs of action assist a person in praying his prayer, he may trust in the Lord that his prayer is accepted and heard; and the word used for "fruit" denotes prophecy, from the language of a spring that flows forth and yields produce, meaning that the Blessed One stirs prophecy in him in abundance, and it will surely be fulfilled." (בִּבְרָכוֹת לד:),
mirroring: 'If my prayer flows fluently in my mouth' (Berakhot 34b),
כִּי לוּלֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְאָדָם לְהִתְפַּלֵּל כְּלָל לְפָנָיו.
for without Hashem's enablement, it is impossible for man to pray before Him at all.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁתִּקְּנוּ בַּתְּחִלָּה: "אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וְגוֹמֵר",
And as instituted at the opening: 'O Lord, open my lips, etc.,'
אָז אוּכַל לִפְתּוֹחַ פִּי בִּתְפִלָּה.
only then am I empowered to open my mouth in prayer.
וּכְשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּתְפַּלְּלוּ לְפָנָיו וּפוֹתֵחַ הַפֶּה בִּתְפִלָּה,
And when Hashem desires that prayer be offered and opens one's mouth,
אָז וַדַּאי תְּפִלָּתוֹ שְׁגוּרָה,
then his prayer is assuredly fluent—
פֵּירוּשׁ "שְׁגוּרָה" – שְׁלוּחָה מִלְּמַעְלָה, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁלָחָהּ לְתוֹךְ פִּיו,
meaning 'shgura' signifies dispatched from Above, Hashem having placed it in his mouth,
וְאָז הוּא מְקוּבָּל,
and then it is fully accepted;
דְּהַיְינוּ עֵת רָצוֹן.
which constitutes an 'acceptable time.'
וְיָדוּעַ דְּעִיקַּר הַתְּפִלָּה הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַרְגָּשַׁת הַצַּעַר וְהַחִסָּרוֹן,
And it is known that the catalyst of prayer is the sensation of distress and deficiency,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, קצה עַמּוּד א133 Zohar, Balak 14:188 — Why so? Because the poor man is broken of heart, and it is written, "The Lord is near to the broken-hearted." The poor man is forever contending with the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Holy One, blessed be He, listens and hears his words. Once he has prayed his prayer, He opens all the windows of the firmaments, and all the other prayers that ascend on high are pushed aside by that broken-hearted poor man; as it is written, "A prayer of the poor man when he is enwrapped." It should have said, "when he wraps himself." What is "when he is enwrapped"? Rather, he makes a wrapping about all the prayers of the world, and they do not enter until his own prayer has entered. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 213): One who is lacking and asks for completion cannot fail to be answered by the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, "The Lord is near to the broken-hearted," and as the Zohar says, the prayer of the poor man encompasses all prayers and splits the firmaments. And "there is no poor man except in knowledge": even one who does not know how to pray and appease his Maker "pours out his speech before the Lord," that is, he speaks without knowing how, not deliberately and in order, but out of the brokenness of his heart pours out his soul to God in disordered words, and such a prayer is more acceptable.):
and as written (Zohar Part III, 195a):
"תְּפִלָּה לֶעָנִי דִּמְעַטְּפָא כָּל צְלוֹתִין וּבָקְעֵי רְקִיעִין",
'A prayer of the afflicted man envelops all prayers and cleaves through the heavens,'
לְפִי שֶׁהוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל מֵעוּמְקָא דְּלִבָּא בְּהַרְגָּשַׁת הַחִסָּרוֹן,
because he cries out from the depths of his heart in acute awareness of his lack,
וְזֶה עַצְמוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and this awareness itself originates from Hashem, blessed be He.
דְּכֵן מָצִינוּ בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא,
For so we find regarding Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa:
כַּאֲשֶׁר הָיְתָה תְּפִלָּתוֹ שְׁגוּרָה,
when his prayer was fluent,
הַיְינוּ דְּהָיָה מֵיצַר לוֹ מְאֹד חָלְיוֹ שֶׁל פְּלוֹנִי וְצַעֲרוֹ,
it was because the sickness and agony of the sufferer weighed heavily upon him,
וְאָז הָיָה פִּיו נִפְתָּח לְבַקֵּשׁ עֲבוּרוֹ מֵעוּמְקָא דְּלִבָּא.
and then his mouth opened to plead on his behalf from the depths of his soul.
וְכֵן כָּל צַעַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹלֵחַ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
Likewise, any sorrow that Hashem sends unto man in this world, Heaven forbid,
הוּא עַל זֶה – לְעוֹרְרוֹ לִתְפִלָּה.
is intended for this very purpose: to awaken him to prayer.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כא)134 Shemot Rabbah 21:5 — And why did the Holy One, blessed be He, do this to them? Because He longed for their prayer. R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: To what may the matter be compared? To a king who was travelling on the road, and a princess cried out to him: I beg you, save me from the brigands. The king heard and rescued her. After some time he wished to take her as a wife, and he longed for her to speak with him, but she would not. What did the king do? He incited the brigands against her, so that she would cry out and the king would hear. When the brigands came upon her she began crying out to the king. The king said to her: This is what I longed for — to hear your voice. So too He incited Pharaoh to pursue Israel, as it is said, "And Pharaoh drew near" — immediately, "the children of Israel cried out to the Lord." עַל "וּפַרְעֹה הִקְרִיב":
As our Sages expounded (Shemot Rabbah 21) on 'and Pharaoh drew near':
מָשָׁל לְמַטְרוֹנִית שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ הַמֶּלֶךְ לִשְׁמוֹעַ קוֹלָהּ.
a parable of a noblewoman whose voice the king desired to hear.

וְאָמְרוּ (בִּיבָמוֹת סד135 Yevamot 64a — R. Yitzchak said: Why were our forefathers barren? Because the Holy One, blessed be He, longs for the prayer of the righteous. R. Yitzchak said: Why is the prayer of the righteous likened to a pitchfork? Just as this pitchfork turns the grain over from place to place, so the prayer of the righteous turns the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, from the attribute of anger to the attribute of mercy. Rashi: "Pitchfork [eter]": pala in the vernacular [a shovel]. Maharsha: The comparison seems to be this: just as the pitchfork turns the grain over to separate its bad part, the chaff, from its good part, so the prayer of the righteous turns [the attributes] over to separate the attribute of judgment from the attribute of mercy. This is said of Isaac more than of the other forefathers because his attribute was the attribute of judgment, as it is written, "the Fear of Isaac" (Genesis 31:42), and "Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac" (Genesis 31:53); yet through his prayer he turned the attribute of judgment into the attribute of mercy, changing their natural barrenness. So too in Bereshit Rabbah: he overturned the decree, and therefore [the implement] is called atra, for it overturns the threshing floor. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Yevamos 64a): "Why were our forefathers barren?": Since the Blessed Name is the Cause of all and the forefathers are the beginning and cause of the nation, it had to be found in them that they are themselves caused, created by the Cause; so they were barren and needed the Cause, praying to Him for children — for whoever prays is caused in relation to the Blessed Name, needing the Cause to Whom he prays. He longs for the prayer of the righteous in particular because there is no Cause without a caused, and the righteous man humbles himself and makes himself caused before the Cause, whereas the wicked man does not. "From the attribute of anger to the attribute of mercy": the prayer of the righteous cleaves to complete mercy, and so it turns the attribute of the Blessed Name from judgment entirely to mercy — whereas for other men, even when the Blessed Name grants their request and prayer, He does not turn to the opposite, from the attribute of anger to the attribute of mercy. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach 8): Why does it say "and you shall hold your peace" — why should they not pray, when the Holy One, blessed be He, longs for the prayer of the righteous? But wherever there is a revelation of Atika, there is no place for prayer and arousal from below, as we find that whoever delights in the Sabbath is granted the requests of his heart..):
And they taught (Yevamot 64a):
"מִפְּנֵי מָה הָיוּ הָאָבוֹת עֲקוּרִים? שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְאַוֶּוה לִתְפִלָּתָן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים".
"Why were the Patriarchs barren? Because the Holy One yearns for the prayer of the righteous."

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד136 Sanhedrin 44b — "Would you set out your cry before distress comes?" (Job 36:19). R. Elazar said: A person should always offer his prayer before trouble comes, for had Abraham not offered prayer before the trouble between Bethel and Ai, there would not have been left of the enemies of Israel [a euphemism for Israel itself] a remnant or a survivor. Rashi: So Job's friends were saying to him: Did you set out your cry "not in distress" — before the trouble had come? Had you done so, all would have strengthened your power. Maharsha: They derived this because just before, Scripture states that Abraham built an altar over the tidings of offspring and of the Land, whereas here it says without explanation, "and he pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east, and he built there an altar" (Genesis 12:8), not stating why; hence they concluded that he did so on account of the future, and so the verse ends "and he called upon the name of the Lord" — that is, he prayed there concerning the sin of Achan. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 44b): For when a person offers his prayer in advance, at that time he has no adversaries on high, and then his prayer is heard, since he has no adversaries above; therefore a person should offer prayer before trouble comes.:):
And on this they said (Sanhedrin 44b):
"לְעוֹלָם יַקְדִּים וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: 'הֲיַעֲרֹךְ שׁוּעֲךָ וְגוֹמֵר'",
"A person should always anticipate distress with prayer, as it is said: 'Will your cry avail...?'"
שֶׁיִּתְעוֹרֵר לִתְפִלָּה קוֹדֶם
meaning that he awaken to prayer beforehand
וְלֹא יִצְטָרֵךְ לְצָרָה שֶׁתְּעוֹרְרֶנּוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
and not require hardship to stir him up, Heaven forbid.
וְכָל הַגָּלִיּוֹת וְהַיִּסּוּרִין הוּא רַק עַל זֶה:
And all the exiles and tribulations are directed entirely toward this:
לְהַעֲלוֹת כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם עַל יְדֵי הַתְּפִלָּה,
to elevate all earthly worldly affairs to the highest pinnacle through prayer,
לִהְיוֹת לַיְלָה כַּיּוֹם יָאִיר;
so that 'night shines like day';
כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה בִּשְׁלֵימוּת יִתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר הַיּוֹם,
and when this reaches completion, the light of day shall be revealed,
דְּהַיְינוּ עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְיוֹם.
namely the World to Come, which resembles luminous day.
וְנֶאֱמַר: "נְתָנַנִי וְגוֹמֵר כָּל הַיּוֹם דָּוָה",
And Scripture states (Lamentations 1:13): 'He has made me desolate and faint all the day,'

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, יז עַמּוּד א וְזוֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קטז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב137 Zohar 2:17a — R. Chiya said: The nations have no dominion over Israel save for one day alone, which is a day of the Holy One, blessed be He — and that is a thousand years. This is what is written, "He has made me desolate and faint all the day" (Lamentations 1:13) — one day alone, and no more. R. Yose said: If they are enslaved longer, that is not by decree of the King, but because they do not wish to return to Him.):
and our Sages stated (Zohar II 17a, and Zohar I 116b end):
דְּהַגָּלוּת אֶחָד מִיּוֹמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
that the exile constitutes one divine thousand-year 'day' of the Holy One, blessed be He.
וּבְכָל מָקוֹם קוֹרִין לְצָרוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל חֹשֶׁךְ וְלַיְלָה,
Now in all scriptural contexts, Israel's troubles are termed darkness and night,
דְּ"יוֹם" בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא אוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמֵּאִיר בְּלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם.
for 'day' in biblical vocabulary strictly denotes Hashem's light shining within human hearts.
אֲבָל גִּלָּה בְּכָאן הַסּוֹד,
Yet here the mystical secret is revealed,
דְּכָל הַגָּלוּת אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא יוֹם מִצַּד הִתְגַּלּוּת מִדַּת הַיּוֹם כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה לְהָאִיר לָעוֹלָם,
that all exile is fundamentally 'day' through the unfolding of the daytime attribute, wherein Hashem seeks to illuminate the world,

וּכְדִשְׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ד, יז: וּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה א, ע138 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 — R. Yudan son of R. Aivu said: It happened that a Jew was plowing in the valley of Arbel, and his cow lowed before him. An Arab passed by and heard its voice. He said to him: Jew, Jew, unyoke your ox and loosen your plow, for the Temple has been destroyed. It lowed a second time. He said to him: Jew, Jew, yoke your ox and fasten your plow, for King Messiah has been born. He said to him: What is his name? — Menaḥem. And what is his father's name? — Ḥizkiyah. And where is he? — In the royal capital, in Bethlehem of Judah. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "he was standing and plowing"): He was standing and plowing, and his ox gave one cry; an Arab who passed before him said to him: Jew, unfasten your yoke of oxen and your plow and stop plowing, because today your Temple has been destroyed. And afterwards, when it cried a second time, he said to him: tie up your ox and plow, because on this very day your King Messiah has been born. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael 26): Dumb animals receive impressions from above more readily than man does, whose form is not simple enough to be a mere receiver; one need not wonder, then, that this Arab knew how to understand from a beast that lacks speech that the Temple had been destroyed. The Messiah is called "Menachem" because he is the consolation of Israel in their exile; and since every consolation gives strength to the one who receives it, he is called "son of Chizkiyah" [from chozek, strength]. So too the verse, "For the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me" (Lamentations 1:16) — for he who restores the soul is one who strengthens another out of his weakness.):
and as our Sages expounded (Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:4; Midrash Rabbah Eichah 1:51):
דִּבְתִשְׁעָה בְּאָב נוֹלַד מָשִׁיחַ.
that the Messiah was born on the Ninth of Av.

וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא נד139 Yoma 54b — Reish Lakish said: When the gentiles entered the Sanctuary they saw the cherubs entwined one with the other. They took them out to the marketplace and said: These Israelites, whose blessing is a blessing and whose curse is a curse — shall they occupy themselves with such things? At once they debased them, as it is stated: "All who honored her debase her, for they have seen her nakedness." Rashi: "They took them out to the marketplace": they peeled them off the wall. Maharsha: Israel's blessing is a blessing [for the nations too], for through the sacrifices (the seventy bullocks of the Festival correspond to the seventy nations) Israel's blessing was a blessing for the idolaters as well, and likewise their curse; yet, they said, they occupy themselves with such things, which are unchastity and idolatry, so "all who honored her," the nations for whom the offerings atoned, "debase her, for they have seen her nakedness," thinking it unchastity and idolatry. Alternatively, the cherubs' being entwined was a sign of blessing and love for Israel and their not being entwined a sign of curse and hatred; the gentiles said this was not so, for even at the destruction, a time of curse, they were entwined, and so "all who honored her" as a sign of blessing and curse "debase her, for they have seen her nakedness," that even now they were entwined. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Devarim 13): The Ritva asked about the statement that when the nations entered the Sanctuary they saw the cherubs entwined with one another: is it not said that when Israel do not do the will of the Omnipresent the cherubs face the House, and at the time of the destruction they were not doing His will? The answer is that before the Temple was destroyed they were indeed not doing His will, for it never occurred to them that it would be destroyed; but when they saw the enemies enter the Sanctuary, all Israel at once had thoughts of repentance, only the decree had already been sealed, and at once they were counted among those who do the will of the Omnipresent, and from this the Messiah was born at once; therefore the cherubs immediately turned their faces toward one another, and when the nations entered they found them entwined. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 171): In the place, time and soul in which the Blessed One's payment and reward flow, the very abundance of the flow becomes retribution for evil, as in the breaking of the vessels through the abundance of light. Therefore the Sages said that the cherubs were found entwined although Israel were not doing the will of the Omnipresent: for at that time there was the full force of the abundant flow of light, which is why Ezekiel merited "visions of God," and one who truly merits receives the payment of good then, which is the matter of the Messiah's birth on the Ninth of Av.:):
Similarly they stated (Yoma 54b):
דִּבְחוּרְבָּן מָצְאוּ כְּרוּבִים מְעוֹרִים זֶה בָּזֶה,
that at the destruction of the Temple, they found the cherubim embraced within each other,
וְיָדוּעַ דְּזֶהוּ הִתְחַבְּרוּת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לַאֲבִיהֶם שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם.
and it is known that this reflects the passionate union of the people of Israel with their Father in Heaven.
רַק יֵשׁ יוֹם אֶחָד לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֲשֶׁר הוּא לֹא יוֹם וְלֹא לַיְלָה,
Rather, there is one unique day belonging to Hashem which is neither day nor night,
פֵּירוּשׁ כִּי מִדּוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּל אֶחָד הוּא אוֹר מְיוּחָד בְּמַדְרֵגָה וְעִנְיָן מְיוּחָד.
meaning that each divine attribute is an illumination operating on its own specific level.
וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה דְּ"דָּוָה" בְּהֵיפֶךְ אַתְוָון "הוֹד",
And it is known from the holy Ari, of blessed memory, that the letters of davah
invert to spell Hod
(הוֹד), שֶׁהַגָּלוּת הוּא מִמִּדָּה זוֹ
indicating that exile emanates from this sefirotic attribute,

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, רפב עַמּוּד א וְשִׁיּוּרֵי מִדְרָשִׁים140 Zohar, Ki Teitzei 25:121 — With these the wicked Esau made Edom, and his female counterpart Ma'adim — she is the shedding of Israel's blood — and she caused it to be fulfilled in the Matrona: "The Lord has delivered me into the hands of those I cannot withstand"; "He has made me desolate, faint (davah) all the day" — HOD was turned into DAVAH. For Netzach and Hod correspond to them: Yakhin and Boaz, "the two upon which the House rests.").
(as written in Zohar III 282a, and Shiurei Midrashim).
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הוֹד נִקְרָא זִיו וְיוֹפִי הַבּוֹלֵט מִחוּץ לְעֵין רוֹאִים וְלֹא אוֹר פְּנִימִי לְבַד,
For Hod is defined as external radiance and beauty visible to onlookers, not merely hidden inward light,
וּכְעִנְיַן קַרְנֵי הוֹד דְּמֹשֶׁה,
akin to the radiant beams of Hod upon Moses,
וְכֵן אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן בְּרָזָא דְּהוֹד הוּצְרַךְ לְבוּשִׁים "לְכָבוֹד וּלְתִפְאָרֶת".
and Aaron the Priest, aligned with the secret of Hod, required garments 'for honor and glory.'
וּפְנִימִיּוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל בֶּאֱמֶת דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
The inner core of Israel is truly bound to Hashem, blessed be He;
רַק מִצַּד חוּץ יֵשׁ טַעֲנָה לָרוֹאִים "הַלָּלוּ וְכוּלֵי וְהַלָּלוּ וְכוּלֵי",
yet externally, onlookers challenge: 'these are idolaters and those are idolaters,'

כְּמַאֲמַר זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים141 Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:2 — “Or has God ventured to come and take Him a nation from the midst of a nation?” R. Yehoshua said in the name of R. Chanan: It is not written here “a nation from the midst of a people,” nor “a people from the midst of a nation,” but “a nation from the midst of a nation” — for these were uncircumcised and these were uncircumcised, these grew a forelock and these grew a forelock, these wore mixed kinds and these wore mixed kinds. If so, the attribute of strict justice would never have allowed Israel to be redeemed..
as our Sages have frequently noted.
וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד חֶשְׁכַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
This arises from the pervasive darkness of this world,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת יז.)142 Berakhot 17a — After he had prayed, R. Alexandri would say: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will — and what prevents us? The yeast in the dough and subjection to the kingdoms. May it be Your will to deliver us from their hand, that we may return to perform the statutes of Your will with a whole heart. Rashi: "And what prevents us" — from doing Your will. "The yeast in the dough" — the evil inclination in our heart, which leavens us. Maharsha: He explains it after what Maimonides wrote in the Eight Chapters, that a man must keep to the middle path in his traits and his deeds. The evil inclination drives him to one extreme within what is permitted him — to be arrogant and to indulge in permitted desire — and is therefore likened to the leaven in the dough, which raises the dough and makes it more than its true measure; while subjection to the gentile kingdoms forces him to the opposite extreme, for they do not allow Israel to hold themselves up but abase them utterly and withhold from them every good, even what they need for the service of God. Thus "our will is to do Your will" — to walk the middle path — "and what prevents us?" These two, each pulling toward its own extreme; may it be Your will to subdue them before us and behind us, that is, both extremes, "that we may return" to walk in the middle. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 21): In Israel a thought that is not for its own sake comes only from the [evil] inclination, which accustoms one to seek his own pleasure in everything, but the depths of the hearts of the children of Israel are solely for the sake of Heaven, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will." Hence, when there is an actual deed, that suffices to join it to the will in the depths of the heart, and no account is taken of the thought of the "yeast in the dough" that confuses it. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 1): The sign of the covenant testifies that the holy flesh of Israel does not desire evil, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will … and who prevents us …": this depth of will stems from our father Abraham, while the Torah is the spice against the [evil] inclination and the Land of Israel is the opposite of subjugation to the kingdoms. "Our will," the depth of the will, is freedom from the evil inclination and from subjugation; hence no exile came from Abraham's side, and the sufferings come only from the side of the inclination and the subjugation. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Though Israel sank in exile into the forty-nine gates of impurity, this was a clarification before Him who examines hearts of the difference between the nations' immersion, which stems from the essence of their hearts, and Israel's, which comes only from their being mixed among the nations, whereas in the essence of their hearts "it is revealed and known that our will is to do [Your will]." The essence of Israel's hearts is not immersed in impurity at all, and from this side comes the redemption from the nations. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): Even the wicked of Israel are all righteous, just as all Israel are called circumcised, even one actually uncircumcised; so one who is wicked in deed is so only from the side of the [evil] inclination and not from his heart, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will …," and as the Rambam explains the reason for coercing [a husband] until he says "I want."
