Though he is called wicked for his actual sin, even the sinners of Israel are full of regret, and there is no wicked Jew who does not regret for some moment once the pleasure has passed and the inclination no longer incites him, because of the depth of good in the depths of his heart. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 24): On Atzeres, the time of accepting the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, there is a mitzvah to give pleasure to the body as well, for the yoke is felt mainly by the body, whereas as for the soul, "it is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will." By this we show that although for the body it is a yoke, it nevertheless rejoices in accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, of Torah and of mitzvos. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The holiness of the name Israel at the root of every Jew cannot be uprooted, and even if he multiplies sins it is all from the side of the "yeast in the dough" and the "subjugation to the kingdoms" that surround the root of Judaism, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will …" Therefore he is compared to a myrtle standing among reeds: the sins are only in the reeds surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 263): The reason the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to the deed is that in truth "the hidden things belong to the Lord our God" and "the Lord's portion is His people," as it says, "It is revealed and known … and who prevents us …"; but in idolatry, where one denies [God], God forbid, even an evil thought is joined [to the deed]. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In the depths of the heart "it is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will — and who prevents us …": even the hindrances in a heart that inclines to evil lie only in the revealed part of the heart, from the "yeast in the dough" that sits at the openings of the heart and the "subjugation to the kingdoms" — the thorns that surround the rose and clothe it, one from without and the other from within. But it is all only a garment and not the essence, which is the depth of his heart, where his essential vitality cleaves to the Blessed One.: "גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ וְכוּלֵי וּמִי מְעַכֵּב וְכוּלֵי",
as stated in Berakhot (17a): "It is revealed and known that our true will is to do Your will, but what deters us?"
דִּבְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַפְּנִימִיּוּת נֶעְלָם
for in this world the inner essence remains concealed,
וּבַחִיצוֹנִיּוּת אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת נָקִי וּמַזְהִיר לְגַמְרֵי.
and externally it is impossible to appear completely flawless and pristine.
אֲבָל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה לְהָאִיר גַּם לַחִיצוֹנִית דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל,
However, Hashem desires to illuminate even the external layer of Israel,

דְּ"רָאוּ כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ כִּי שֵׁם ה' וְגוֹמֵר" (דְּבָרִים כח, י143 Deuteronomy 28:10 — And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall fear you.),
so that 'all peoples of the earth shall see that the name of Hashem is called upon you' (Deuteronomy 28:10),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב לֶעָתִיד: "וְנָהֲרוּ וְגוֹמֵר" וְכֵן כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים.
and as written concerning the future: 'and they shall stream, etc.' and multiple other passages.
וְנִמְצָא הֶאָרָה זוֹ הוּא עִיקָּרָהּ לְצוֹרֶךְ חִיצוֹנִים.
Thus, this manifestation of light is primarily intended for outward observers.
דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל עַצְמָם יֵשׁ לָהֶם הַשָּׂגָה בְּאוֹר פְּנִימִי וּדְבֵיקוּתָם בְּעֶצֶם,
For the Jewish people internally possess direct grasp of the inward light and fundamental cleaving;
כְּמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל: עָשִׁיר הַמִּתְלַבֵּשׁ בִּלְבוּשֵׁי כָּבוֹד הוּא רַק לָרוֹאִים,
comparable to a rich man who dons honorable attire solely for onlookers,
שֶׁאֵין יוֹדְעִים עָשְׁרוֹ – יַכִּירוּהוּ עַל יְדֵי בְּגָדָיו.
so that those unaware of his wealth recognize him through his garments.
וְנִמְצָא הוּא לְצָרְכָּן שֶׁל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לְהָאִיר לָהֶם.
Consequently, this illumination serves the nations of the world, shedding light upon them.
וְלֹא אוֹר גָּמוּר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁיִּשְׁפַּע לָהֶם,
Yet it is not a direct influx of ultimate divine light unto them, Heaven forbid;
רַק שֶׁיַּשִּׂיגוּ אוֹרָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְקַרְנֵי הוֹד שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם, וְ"יָרְאוּ מִמֶּךָּ".
merely that they perceive the radiance of Israel and the beams of Hod upon them, and 'revere you.'
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ טוֹבָה, הוּא נִשְׁפָּע בְּכָל עוֹלָם כְּמַדְרֵגָתוֹ.
And when Hashem bestows goodness, it filters into every sphere according to its measure.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה לְהַשְׁפִּיעַ אוֹר זֶה,
When Hashem desires to transmit this illumination,
דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁחִיצוֹנִית יִשְׂרָאֵל – פֵּירוּשׁ כָּל תַּאֲווֹת וְחֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁשְּׁקוּעִים בָּהֶם –
namely that the externality of Israel—the physical appetites and earthly attractions in which they are involved—
יִהְיֶה נִכָּר לַכֹּל שֶׁהוּא לִרְצוֹן שָׁמַיִם לְבַד,
shall be visible to all as dedicated solely to the will of Heaven,
וְשֶׁיַּכִּירוּ גּוֹיִם כֹּחַ מַלְכוּתְךָ.
so that nations recognize the power of Your sovereignty.
פֵּירוּשׁ מַלְכוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא רַק בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל,
For the sovereignty of Hashem rests directly upon Israel alone,
רַק כֹּחַ מַלְכוּתְךָ הוּא כְּעִנְיַן זִיו הַהוֹד,
yet the outward 'power of Your sovereignty' is like the splendor of Hod,
זֶה יוּכְלוּ לְהַכִּיר כִּי שֵׁם ה' נִקְרָא עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
and this the nations can perceive—that Hashem's Name is called upon Israel.
וְיָדוּעַ אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן הוּא עֲבוֹדָה וְאֵין עֲבוֹדָה אֶלָּא תְּפִלָּה,
And Aaron the Priest embodies divine service, which is prayer,
כִּי אוֹר זֶה הוּא שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְעוֹרֵר לְאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדָה וּתְפִלָּה,
for this light is awakened by Hashem within man toward divine service and prayer;
עַל יְדֵי זֶה מַעֲלֶה כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְרוּמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם,
and through this he elevates all matters of this world to the cosmic pinnacle,
וְ"לַיְלָה כַּיּוֹם יָאִיר" בְּקַרְנֵי הוֹד.
and 'night shines like the day' through beams of Hod.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תּוֹרָה הוּא רַק קְדוּשָׁה הַפְּנִימִית שֶׁל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
In contrast, Torah is the intrinsic, inward sanctity of the children of Israel,

דְּאֵין מוֹסְרִין דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב חֲגִיגָה יג144 Chagigah 13a — R. Ami said: Words of Torah are not transmitted to a gentile, as it is said, "He has not done so for any other nation; and as for His ordinances, they have not known them." Tosafos (s.v. "words of Torah are not transmitted to a gentile"): R. Elchanan asked why a verse is needed at all, since a gentile who engages in Torah is liable to death, and one who teaches him already transgresses "do not put a stumbling block before the blind"; and if you say the case is the seven commandments, for which he is not liable, it is a positive duty to transmit those to them. He answers that our passage speaks even where another gentile is ready to teach him — where, as with handing a cup of wine to a nazirite who is not on the far bank of a river, there is no stumbling block — and even so it is forbidden, from "He declares His word to Jacob." Maharsha: He does not say that one may not teach Torah to a gentile, for the seven commandments are certainly taught to them. Rather, as the context shows, what is not transmitted to a gentile is the reason and the inner sense of the commandments; even of their own seven, the reason and the secret are not handed over. That is the force of "He has not done so for any other nation": though they too have ordinances and a civil law they are bound to keep, since law is one of the seven commandments of the sons of Noah, still "His ordinances they have not known" — they do not know their reasons and the secret of these matters..),
for words of Torah are not transmitted to idolaters (as written in Chagigah 13a),
וְאֵין הֵם מַכִּירִים בָּזֶה כְּלָל.
and they possess no perception of it whatsoever.
וְלָכֵן הִתְעוֹרְרוּת יוֹם וְאוֹר זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין וְהַרְגָּשַׁת הַצַּעַר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
Therefore the awakening of this 'day' and light in the world comes through suffering and sorrow, as mentioned above,
וְהוּא יוֹם לְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת.
and it constitutes 'day' for the nations of the world.
וְאֵין הַכְּתוּבִים וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה קוֹרְאִים יוֹם עַל שֵׁם הַדִּמְיוֹן מַה שֶּׁנִּדְמֶה לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לְיוֹם, דְּזֶה הֶבֶל;
Scripture and our Sages do not call it 'day' merely based on the delusion that the nations imagine it as day, for that is vanity;
רַק שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת הוּא יוֹם,
rather in truth it is day,
דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְעַסֵּק בָּזֶה לְהָאִיר גַּם לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁיַּשִּׂיגוּ גְּדוּלַּת יִשְׂרָאֵל,
in that the Holy One occupies Himself to illuminate even the nations that they recognize Israel's greatness.

וּכְטַעַם: "לֹא גָּלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא לְהוֹסִיף גֵּרִים" (פְּסָחִים פז145 Pesachim 87b — And R. Elazar said: The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts should be added to them, as it is stated: "And I will sow her to Me in the land." Does a man sow a se'ah except to bring in many kor? Maharsha: ["He exiled... only":] for had it been as punishment for their sin, He could have punished them with other things; rather, it was so that converts should be added to them — that is, to make the faith known among the other nations as well. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:77): The Sages said, "Israel was exiled only so as to add converts," for the exile is because the Blessed One wished that even in dark places, in the concealment of His countenance, they should find His truth and recognize Him even "from behind," as it were; and from this aspect converts too are added, yet they are nevertheless hard for Israel "like a scab." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 10): The Land, being soft and not rocky, yields more fruit, as the Sages expounded "And I will sow her to Me in the land," that through sowing in the holiness of the Land comes the vast increase; and "they were exiled only so as to add converts" means that each gentile has a particular power that he cannot change at all, nor can the convert change it. What is added in exile is that Israel absorbs the power of the lands of the nations, the particular obstinacy and heart of stone of each place, and by clarifying that in that power they are not obstinate like the nations but can change it for the glory of Heaven as the Blessed One wills, converts are added: the power of the nations' heart of stone is also granted to join Israel and be called by the name of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Parah 3): The Midrash's "Israel from the nations" does not mean their descent from Terah, which is already covered by "Abraham from Terah," but refers to "The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel only so that converts would be added to them," which was explained to mean not actual converts but the holy sparks and vitality within the nations, as in "and You give life to them all," which are brought out through the exiles. All the nations have holy sparks from which their life derives, and for this reason exile among all seventy nations was needed. Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 10): Through the length of their wanderings Israel brings out further holiness that is found [among the nations], as it says, "The Holy One, blessed be He, did righteousness with Israel by scattering them among the nations," and "He exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would be added to them." The matter is that every nation was created for His glory, that the glory of Heaven should come forth from it, only they are its opposite; by entering among the nations Israel clarifies how the glory of Heaven is built even from them, and in this lies great preciousness: to understand and bring forth the glory of Heaven even from its opposite. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 17): The main purpose of the exile is as the Talmud says on "the righteousness of His scattering in Israel": the Holy One, blessed be He, did righteousness with Israel so that converts would be added to them, like one who sows with a scattering hand, the whole aim of whose intention is that a crop should grow from it. So too, in the future the Blessed One will show that the aim of the exile was that souls be added to Israel, and that not a single individual was cast away.:).
And as in: "Israel was exiled solely to add proselytes" (Pesachim 87b).
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא לֹא יִהְיֶה הָעֵסֶק אֶלָּא עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַד,
In contrast, in the World to Come divine interaction will involve Israel alone,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "ה' בָּדָד יַנְחֶנּוּ וְאֵין וְגוֹמֵר",
as written: 'Hashem alone led him, and there was no foreign god with him,'

וְאֵין מְקַבְּלִים גֵּרִים לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב יְבָמוֹת כד146 Yevamot 24b — Our Rabbis taught: Converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah. Similarly, they accepted no converts in the days of David, nor in the days of Solomon. R. Eliezer said: What is the verse? "Behold, one may surely sojourn [as a convert] when I am not [with you]; whoever sojourns with you [now, in your poverty] shall settle beside you" (Isaiah 54:15) — but the other [who comes later], no. Rashi: "Behold, one may surely sojourn": one who comes to convert may sojourn "when I am not" — while I am not with you, let him convert, that is, at the present time. "Whoever sojourns with you": in your poverty, as stated. "Shall settle beside you" (lit. "shall fall upon you"): in the World to Come; "fall" means "rest," as in "he fell [i.e., settled] in the presence of all his brethren" (Genesis 25:18) and "a thousand shall fall at your side" (Psalms 91:7). Tosafos (s.v. "nor in the days of David, nor in the days of Solomon"): Ittai the Gittite, and Pharaoh's daughter in Solomon's days, pose no difficulty, for the only reason [converts were refused then] was the king's table, and these had no need of it; but it is difficult from what we say below (79a) about the Gibeonites, that in David's days a hundred and fifty thousand converts were added to Israel. One may answer that they converted of their own accord, as we find in the days of Mordecai and Esther, "And many of the people of the land became Jews"; and some texts read that they did not accept converts in the days of David and Solomon, but these became converts who attached themselves [unaccepted]. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 46): "Whoever sojourns with you" in your poverty, he "shall fall to you," but otherwise not. Thus you see that converts are not accepted when the days of good arrive, because one does not make a beginning in good days, for in such a case a man certainly serves God, blessed be He, because he sees the good; therefore his beginning must come before, and then he acquires the World to Come even in the good days. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 2): Sin and the serpent's filth come from the Blessed One so that through them there should be additions, absorbed from within the husk into holiness, as in "Israel was exiled only so that converts would be added to them." And the Sages read "whoever sojourns with you [shall fall to you]" as "in your poverty," for the main addition of converts comes specifically in Israel's poverty, through the sins and the serpent's filth, and not in the time to come. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): The love of Torah is revealed most in converts: Israel were brought out of bondage and drawn near by the Holy One, blessed be He, but the convert left the tranquility of this world and the license he had among the nations to follow his desire, and came of his own will to fence himself in and cleave to Israel, afflicted, lowly and downtrodden in this world. For only "in your poverty shall he fall to you," and converts were not accepted in the days of David and Solomon, nor one who converts out of love for some thing; only for love of the Torah does he draw near and enter under the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayakhel 2): The law regarding the mixed multitude was that of "converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah; similarly, they did not accept converts in the days of David or Solomon," that is, because their intention is not desirable for the sake of Heaven. Yet after the fact, as Rambam writes, once they have converted the great court does not reject them, since they have immersed, but neither does it draw them near until their end is seen. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): Of the future it is said that [Esau] will wrap himself in his tallis, and he will surely think then that he truly wishes it and is not merely deceiving; but in truth converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah, because they come then only out of love of reward or fear of punishment. Beis Yaakov (Vayeira 30): In the future the world will be conducted by the attribute of Isaac, as shown by "converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah" and "each righteous man has a dwelling of his own": that is, then the world will be conducted by the measure of "what is mine is mine," each one holding back from yielding his portion, as Isaac restrained himself from bestowing where it is not the will of the Blessed One. Only in the future, after the clarifications are complete, will the attribute of Isaac govern; for now, in this world, a person must conduct himself by the attribute of kindness.:).
and converts will not be accepted in the Messianic era (as written in Yevamot 24b).
וּלְיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא לַיְלָה,
Yet for Israel this state is night,

דְּיִסּוּרִין מַעֲבִירִין עַל דַּעְתּוֹ וְדַעַת קוֹנוֹ (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב עֵירוּבִין מא147 Eruvin 41b — The Sages taught: Three things drive a man out of his own mind and out of the mind of his Maker, and these are they: the nations [that oppress him], an evil spirit, and grinding poverty. What difference does this make? That one should ask for mercy on their behalf. Tosafos (s.v. "out of his own mind and out of the mind of his Maker"): There is also sorcery, which weakens the heavenly retinue, but it seems to be included under "an evil spirit." As for the evil inclination, although it appears in Moed Katan 17a that a man's inclination sometimes overpowers him so that he cannot subdue it, even so a man is able to take care not to come to that. Maharsha: Surely a man must be on his guard that grinding poverty not drive him out of his mind, for it says below, "Three do not see the face of Gehenna, and these are they: grinding poverty …" — which must mean one who guarded himself and did not transgress against his own mind and the mind of his Maker, and that only with great difficulty. This is unlike the evil inclination, against which one must be more careful still, as Tosafot wrote, and which is therefore not counted here; or one may say that those in grinding poverty likewise do not see Gehenna only because mercy is asked on their behalf.:),
for suffering distracts a person from his own sense and the knowledge of his Creator (Eruvin 41b),

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בִּבְרָכוֹת יז.)148 Berakhot 17a — After he had prayed, R. Alexandri would say: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will — and what prevents us? The yeast in the dough and subjection to the kingdoms. May it be Your will to deliver us from their hand, that we may return to perform the statutes of Your will with a whole heart. Rashi: "And what prevents us" — from doing Your will. "The yeast in the dough" — the evil inclination in our heart, which leavens us. Maharsha: He explains it after what Maimonides wrote in the Eight Chapters, that a man must keep to the middle path in his traits and his deeds. The evil inclination drives him to one extreme within what is permitted him — to be arrogant and to indulge in permitted desire — and is therefore likened to the leaven in the dough, which raises the dough and makes it more than its true measure; while subjection to the gentile kingdoms forces him to the opposite extreme, for they do not allow Israel to hold themselves up but abase them utterly and withhold from them every good, even what they need for the service of God. Thus "our will is to do Your will" — to walk the middle path — "and what prevents us?" These two, each pulling toward its own extreme; may it be Your will to subdue them before us and behind us, that is, both extremes, "that we may return" to walk in the middle. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 21): In Israel a thought that is not for its own sake comes only from the [evil] inclination, which accustoms one to seek his own pleasure in everything, but the depths of the hearts of the children of Israel are solely for the sake of Heaven, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will." Hence, when there is an actual deed, that suffices to join it to the will in the depths of the heart, and no account is taken of the thought of the "yeast in the dough" that confuses it. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 1): The sign of the covenant testifies that the holy flesh of Israel does not desire evil, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will … and who prevents us …": this depth of will stems from our father Abraham, while the Torah is the spice against the [evil] inclination and the Land of Israel is the opposite of subjugation to the kingdoms. "Our will," the depth of the will, is freedom from the evil inclination and from subjugation; hence no exile came from Abraham's side, and the sufferings come only from the side of the inclination and the subjugation. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Though Israel sank in exile into the forty-nine gates of impurity, this was a clarification before Him who examines hearts of the difference between the nations' immersion, which stems from the essence of their hearts, and Israel's, which comes only from their being mixed among the nations, whereas in the essence of their hearts "it is revealed and known that our will is to do [Your will]." The essence of Israel's hearts is not immersed in impurity at all, and from this side comes the redemption from the nations. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): Even the wicked of Israel are all righteous, just as all Israel are called circumcised, even one actually uncircumcised; so one who is wicked in deed is so only from the side of the [evil] inclination and not from his heart, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will …," and as the Rambam explains the reason for coercing [a husband] until he says "I want." Though he is called wicked for his actual sin, even the sinners of Israel are full of regret, and there is no wicked Jew who does not regret for some moment once the pleasure has passed and the inclination no longer incites him, because of the depth of good in the depths of his heart. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 24): On Atzeres, the time of accepting the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, there is a mitzvah to give pleasure to the body as well, for the yoke is felt mainly by the body, whereas as for the soul, "it is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will." By this we show that although for the body it is a yoke, it nevertheless rejoices in accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, of Torah and of mitzvos. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The holiness of the name Israel at the root of every Jew cannot be uprooted, and even if he multiplies sins it is all from the side of the "yeast in the dough" and the "subjugation to the kingdoms" that surround the root of Judaism, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will …" Therefore he is compared to a myrtle standing among reeds: the sins are only in the reeds surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 263): The reason the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to the deed is that in truth "the hidden things belong to the Lord our God" and "the Lord's portion is His people," as it says, "It is revealed and known … and who prevents us …"; but in idolatry, where one denies [God], God forbid, even an evil thought is joined [to the deed]. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In the depths of the heart "it is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will — and who prevents us …": even the hindrances in a heart that inclines to evil lie only in the revealed part of the heart, from the "yeast in the dough" that sits at the openings of the heart and the "subjugation to the kingdoms" — the thorns that surround the rose and clothe it, one from without and the other from within. But it is all only a garment and not the essence, which is the depth of his heart, where his essential vitality cleaves to the Blessed One.: "וּמִי מְעַכֵּב וְכוּלֵי".
and as written in Berakhot (17a): "And what deters us, etc."
רַק כַּאֲשֶׁר מִתְעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִתְפִלָּה,
Only when one is aroused through this to prayer,
אָז מִמֵּילָא לַיְלָה כַּיּוֹם יָאִיר,
then spontaneously the night shines as day,
וְנִגְלָה אוֹר זֶה וְקַרְנֵי הַהוֹד,
and this light and the beams of Hod are revealed,
דְּהַגַּם שֶׁשְּׁקוּעִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
showing that even when occupied with worldly pursuits like the nations,
אֵין כֵּן אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
it is entirely different with Israel,
דְּהֵם כָּל צָרְכֵיהֶם מְקַבְּלִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
for they receive all their necessities consciously from Hashem, blessed be He.
וְאָז נִקְרָא "אֵלֶיךָ אֶקְרָא כָּל הַיּוֹם",
And then it is called 'To You I call all the day,'
דִּכְשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִקְרִיאָה מִתּוֹךְ הַצָּרָה,
for when one attains prayer out of distress,
אָז יֵשׁ לִקְרוֹתוֹ יוֹם כְּמוֹ שֶׁהוּא לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
it may rightfully be termed 'day' just as it is for the nations.
דַּהֲרֵי יוֹם וְאוֹר זֶה מֵאִיר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז
For this day and this light Hashem radiates at that moment,
שֶׁיָּאִירוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל כָּךְ
so that Israel shines so brightly
עַד שֶׁ"כָּל רֹאֵיהֶם יַכִּירוּם וְגוֹמֵר",
that 'all who see them shall acknowledge them, etc.,'
גַּם אוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין מַכִּירִין פְּנִימִיּוּת הָאוֹר.
even those incapable of grasping the inner divine light.
וְטַעַם "אֵלֶיךָ אֶקְרָא כָּל הַיּוֹם" כְּטַעַם "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּתִי וְגוֹמֵר",
And the rationale of 'To You I call all the day' mirrors 'And as for me, my prayer, etc.,'
כִּי עֵסֶק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהָאִיר אוֹר יוֹם הַזֶּה הוּא עֵת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת עֵת רָצוֹן,
for Hashem's initiative to radiate the light of this day constitutes an awakening of the acceptable time,
דְּהַיְינוּ רָצוֹן לִתְפִלָּה,
namely a divine willingness to receive prayer,
שֶׁהִתְעוֹרְרוּת זֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי אוֹר הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה
for this awakening is generated by the light of this day
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְעוֹרֵר לְהָאִיר בָּעוֹלָם קַרְנֵי הוֹד דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
which the Holy One, blessed be He, stirs to project the radiant beams of Israel's Hod across the universe.

sections.en: Heart, Mind, Speech, and Torah

items.h: Prayer belongs to the heart, Torah to wisdom, yet both require speech and inner understanding so holiness can move from outward action into the heart.

Seif 1 — From Wisdom to the Heart through Speech
Torah and prayer unite mind, heart, and spoken action so holiness can become inwardly rooted.

p: תְּפִלָּה עִיקָּרָהּ בַּלֵּב,
Prayer in its essence is in the heart,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית ב149 Taanit 2a — As it was taught: "To love the Lord your God and to serve Him with all your heart" — what is the service that is in the heart? You must say: This is prayer. And it is written thereafter, "And I will give the rain of your land in its season, the early rain and the late rain." Maharsha: One may ask why the Gemara must ask, "From where do we know [that rain is mentioned] in prayer?" — it is explicit in Solomon's prayer: "When the heavens are shut up and there is no rain … and they pray" (I Kings 8:35). The answer is that that verse speaks only of prayer in a time of distress, once the heavens are already shut up; here the Gemara seeks a source for [mentioning rain] not in a time of distress but in the fixed prayer of every day, and it derives it from "to serve Him with all your heart" — "what is the service [that is in the heart]?" — which speaks of the service and fixed prayer of every day. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 3): The service of God that Israel has in their exile, in every place, is prayer. Prayer is called "service" because when a person prays to God it shows that he depends upon Him, needs Him, and has no existence apart from Him — and this is His Godhead, that all beings need Him and depend upon Him; therefore prayer, and not the fear of God, is called service, for fear does not show that a person depends upon Him. And when a person depends upon Him it is as though he is brought near to Him, for whatever depends upon another is brought near and given over to it; therefore prayer is complete service to God..):
as they said (Ta'anit 2a):
"עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁהִיא בַּלֵּב וְכוּלֵי – זוֹ תְּפִלָּה",
"'Service that is in the heart, etc.' – this is prayer,"

וְכֵן "הַמִּתְפַּלֵּל צָרִיךְ שֶׁיְּכַוֵּון אֶת לִבּוֹ" (בִּבְרָכוֹת לא.)150 Berakhot 31a — The Sages taught: One who prays must direct his heart to Heaven. Abba Shaul says: A sign for the matter — “You will direct their heart, You will incline Your ear” (Psalms 10:17). Rashi: Read the verse as a condition: if "You will direct their heart," then "You will incline Your ear." Maharsha: In Yevamot 105b the requirement that the heart be directed upward is derived from a different verse, "Let us lift up our heart with our hands"; here the baraita adduces this verse only for the point that direction of the heart is required. וְטוּבָא.
and likewise 'one who prays must direct his heart' (Berakhot 31a), and many similar teachings.
וְתוֹרָה כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה עִיקָּרָהּ בַּמּוֹחַ,
Torah study, seemingly, has its primary seat in the brain,
אֲבָל אָנוּ מְבַקְּשִׁים "וְתֵן בְּלִבֵּנוּ בִּינָה וְגוֹמֵר",
yet we beseech 'and place understanding within our hearts, etc.,'
כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּיֵשׁ חָכְמָה וּבִינָה שֶׁהֵם מוֹחָא וְלִבָּא.
for as is known, there exist Chokhmah (Wisdom) and Binah (Understanding), which correspond to the brain and the heart.
פֵּירוּשׁ, חָכְמָה הוּא כְּלָלֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הַמְּפוֹרָשִׁים,
The explanation is: Chokhmah represents the overarching, explicit principles of the Torah,
וּבִינָה הוּא הִתְבּוֹנְנוּת דָּבָר מִתּוֹךְ דָּבָר הַמְּפוֹרָשׁ לָדוּן וּלְהוֹרוֹת בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה.
while Binah is the cognitive discernment of one thing from another based on what is explicit, in order to adjudicate and instruct at the time of practical deed.

וְכֵן מָצִינוּ בִּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (לה151 Sanhedrin 35a — Shall we try him on the eve of Shabbat and conclude his verdict on Sunday? They will forget their reasons. And even though two scribes of the judges stand before them and write down the words of those who acquit and the words of those who convict — granted that they write down what was spoken aloud, the hearts of men forget. Therefore it is not possible. Rashi: "Let them try him on the eve of the Sabbath and conclude on Sunday" — for as long as the verdict is not concluded there is no torment of judgment, since every moment he hopes to be saved, whereas once it is concluded he spends the whole day awaiting death. "They would forget their reasons" — which they had debated and weighed carefully on the first day. "What is in the heart is forgotten" — what is in men's hearts they do not write, and though one remembers the basis of the reasoning, the way he had worked it out is forgotten from his heart, and he cannot compose it to give a proper reason as at first. Sod Yesharim (Parashas Zachor 15): The full warmth of remembrance is on the very day; on the next day the matter has grown old and is no longer called "remember" but "keep," as we find in the Gemara: "Shall we try him on the eve of Shabbat and conclude on Sunday? They will forget their reasoning; though two court scribes stand before them and write the words of those who acquit and those who convict, granted that they write what is said aloud, the heart of men forgets." That is, even though they remember the matter as on that day, the warmth of the remembrance cannot be on the following day as it was on the very day..):
And so we find in the phrasing of the Sages in Sanhedrin (35a):
"לִיבָּא דְּאִינָשֵׁי אִינָשֵׁי",
'The heart of people makes them men,'
הֲרֵי דְּהַהִתְחַדְּשׁוּת נוֹבֵעַ מִן הַלֵּב.
showing that intellectual renewal and innovation emanate directly from the heart.

וְחָכְמָה וּבִינָה הֵם תְּרֵין רֵעִין דְּלָא מִתְפָּרְשִׁין (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, ד עַמּוּד א152 Zohar, Vayikra 3:37 — R. Shimon said: All of this is well said, but the inner meaning of the matter is: "Eat, O friends" — above; "drink and be drunk, O beloved ones" — below. R. Elazar said to him: Who are those above, and who are those below? He said to him: You have asked well. It is that supernal place where they are in union and in joy and are never parted — these are called "friends." This is what is written, "And a river goes out of Eden": Eden and that river are never parted, and are found forever in desire, in union, in joy. "Drink and be drunk, O beloved ones" — these are the ones below, who are called "beloved," at appointed times. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 1): The essence of thought is chochmah, which makes an impression in the mind that spreads at once to the heart and from it to the whole body; for Abba and Imma are "two companions that never part": a thought that reaches the root of Abba, chochmah in the mind, is joined with binah in the heart, a person's faculty of feeling, and he feels it in his heart at once. Together they give birth to the powers of action, as in "the eye sees, the heart desires, and the instruments of action complete it." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 52): When a person merits the supernal fear that enters the depths of the heart, "binah is the heart," he merits chochmah as well, for they are "two companions that never part." So our master taught that a person's main effort is in the attribute of fear, after which he merits love as a gift from the Blessed One: by bringing fear into the depths of his heart, as "binah is the heart," he merits chochmah, which is love, for chochmah and binah are "two companions that never part" forever.),
Now Chokhmah and Binah are 'two companions that never part' (Zohar Part III, 4a),
כִּי תוֹרָה נִקְרָא רַק מַה שֶּׁמּוֹרֶה לַלֵּב,
for it is termed 'Torah' only when it actually instructs and guides the heart,

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ153 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 1:2 — R. Yochanan said: One who learns without intending to act — better for him had his afterbirth been turned over his face and he had never come into the world. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "and does he not concede"): Does R. Shimon b. Yochai not concede that one interrupts words of Torah in order to perform a commandment and fulfil it in its proper time, such as making a sukkah or a lulav? And the very purpose of study is in order to act — so why did he not interrupt in order to fulfil the commandment of reciting the Shema? [His reason is] that the Shema is itself "recitation," and one does not set aside the speaking of one study for the sake of another study. (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ב, ח.):
and along the lines of what they stated (Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:2, 8a):
"הַלָּמֵד שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲשׂוֹת נוֹחַ וְכוּלֵי",
"'One who studies with no intention to act, it would have been better, etc.,'"
וְ"הָאוֹמֵר אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה – אַף תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי"
and 'one who says he possesses nothing but Torah does not even possess Torah, etc.'

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב יְבָמוֹת קט154 Yevamot 109b — It was taught: R. Yose says, anyone who says he has no Torah has no Torah. That is obvious! Rather: anyone who says he has nothing but Torah has nothing but Torah. That too is obvious! Rather, he does not even have Torah. What is the reason? Rav Pappa said: The verse states, "And you shall learn them and take care to do them" — whoever is included in doing is included in learning; whoever is not included in doing is not included in learning. Rashi: "Anyone who says he has no Torah" — [who says] he does not occupy himself with Torah; "has no Torah" — he receives no reward for study. "Nothing but Torah" — and he does not fulfill [it]. "Not even Torah" — he does not even have the reward for study. Maharsha (s.v. "whoever is included in doing"): Here the Gemara makes the first clause [learning] depend on the second [doing], whereas on "You shall bind them … and you shall write them" it makes the second depend on the first ("whoever is included in binding is included in writing"). The reason is that here the reverse, "whoever is included in learning is included in doing," could not be expounded with respect to reward, for one who is not included in learning is certainly not included in doing at all: study leads to action, and "a boor does not fear sin, nor is an ignoramus pious." Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Yevamos 109b): Rashi's words suggest one who does not observe [the commandments] and commits transgressions, God forbid — but would that need saying? Rather, it means one who keeps himself away from performing the commandments: if he has a sukkah to build, he tells someone else to build it, and although it would not take him from his study he pays it no heed, for all his intent is on Torah. Such a one, having no doing, does not have the Torah in actuality, for through the intellect with which he studies the Torah is not actual, but only through performing the commandments; hence it is written, "And you shall learn them and do them" — whoever is included in doing is included in learning. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on completing the Talmud 5): Without fear of Heaven, which fences the heart against evil desires, one who wants to place his effort in wisdom alone is the one of whom they said, "Whoever says he has nothing but Torah does not have [even Torah]": for effort applies only from chochmah downward, while in chochmah itself effort has no place at all, and one cannot speak of "having" it. Through this he turns heretic, believing not in the Oral Torah but only in the Written Torah, which is the root of chochmah.:).
(as written in Yevamot 109b).
וְנֶאֱמַר: "לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר וְגוֹמֵר וְלֵב אָיִן" –
And it is stated (Proverbs 17:16): 'Why is there a purchase price in the hand of a fool to acquire wisdom... when he has no heart?'
כָּל שֶׁלֵּב אֵין, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִקְרָא כְּסִיל,
so long as there is no engaged heart, even if he knows words of Torah he is still termed a fool;
רַק שֶׁמְּחִיר בְּיָדוֹ לִקְנוֹת חָכְמָה
he merely holds the purchase price in hand to acquire wisdom,
כִּי אַף חָכְמָה אֵין בְּיָדוֹ כָּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּלֵּב.
for he does not truly possess even wisdom so long as it is absent from the heart.

שֶׁזֶּה כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו155 Sanhedrin 106b — And R. Yitzchak said: What is meant by that which is written, "But to the wicked God says: What have you to do to declare My statutes, and that you have taken My covenant in your mouth"? The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Doeg the wicked: What have you to do to declare My statutes? When you reach the section of murderers and the section of slanderers, what do you expound in them? "And you have taken My covenant in your mouth" — R. Ami said: The Torah of Doeg was only from the lips outward. Rashi: "The section of murderers" — for he slew [the city of] Nob. "In your mouth" — but not in the heart. Maharsha: "What have you to do to declare [literally, to count] My statutes": since he counted three hundred laws (as below), all the more did he count the six hundred and thirteen commandments; so He said to him: What is their counting to you, when in your hands the whole section of murderers and the section of slanderers are missing from the count, for you transgress them in their plain sense — and what do you expound in them, to take them out of the plain meaning of Scripture? As for "from the lips outward," beyond Rashi's "not in the heart," it may mean that he did not use even the inner organs of speech, such as the palate and the throat, for words of Torah, only the lips, without making his voice heard — as with Hannah, "only her lips moved," which is the rule for prayer, whereas in Torah study one must make one's voice heard.:):
This is comparable to what they said (Sanhedrin 106b)
בְּדוֹאֵג: "כָּל תּוֹרָתוֹ מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ",
concerning Doeg: 'all of his Torah was from the lip outward,'
פֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁאֵין נִבְלָע בַּלֵּב,
meaning that it was not absorbed into the heart,

כְּעִנְיַן "וְלָרָשָׁע וְגוֹמֵר עֲלֵי פִיךָ156 Psalms 50:16 — “But to the wicked God says: What right have you to recount My statutes, and to take My covenant upon your lips?” Rashi: “And take My covenant upon your mouth” — My Torah. Radak: Until here he reproved those who bring the sacrifice and do not turn from their wickedness; now he reproves those who study and do not practice. A man who shows himself wicked is wicked in the eyes of God and of men, and for that very reason is close to repenting, since men recognize him and reprove him; but one who shows himself good and a servant of God while his heart is evil and his deeds evil in secret is very far from repentance. So too one who studies the Torah and does not practice it: men who see him study and do the opposite of what he studies learn from his deeds and are led to sin, and they come to despise the study of the Torah. Metzudas Dovid: But to the wicked man, who does not confess his transgressions when he brings his sacrifice and does not turn back from them, God says: what have you to do with reciting My statutes — that is, with performing My commandments without the heart’s intent, as a man recites a tale of words with no intention at all? “And take My covenant in your mouth” — the words of the Torah, which were given with a covenant, you bear only upon your mouth, speaking them with the lips alone and not with the heart. Malbim: God says to the wicked man who thinks to bribe Him with the many sacrifices he brings: what have you to do with reciting My statutes? The Lord commanded statutes, which are commandments with no [evident] reason, such as the commandments of the sacrifices, and rational commandments whose reason is known, such as those concerning theft, adultery, slander and the like; and you who act wickedly in the rational commandments “recite My statutes” by bringing sacrifices, and by this “take My covenant upon your mouth,” as though on this account I had made a covenant with you to love you." – הַיְינוּ בַּפֶּה בִּלְבַד.
akin to 'And unto the wicked God said:... upon your mouth' (Psalms 50:16)—meaning exclusively upon the mouth.
וְעִיקַּר הַתּוֹרָה רַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִבְלָע בַּלֵּב,
Indeed, the primary objective of the Torah is strictly that it be absorbed into the heart,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה יז157 Vayikra Rabbah 17:1 — "Happy is the man whose strength is in You" — one might think this applies to all; therefore it says, "in whose heart are the highways" — these are they in whose hearts the paths of the Torah are beaten out. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 7): "To illuminate paths" [in the Zohar's words] is as it is said, "highways in their hearts," of which the Midrash says: these are they in whose hearts the paths of the Torah are beaten. This is [the promise] "I will open for you openings through which wagons and carts can enter": through the awakening from below in the aspect of fear, one merits that the words of Torah become "highways in their hearts," illuminating the paths.)
as written in Vayikra Rabbah (beginning of Parashah 17)
עַל פָּסוּק "מְסִלּוֹת בִּלְבָבָם" –
on the verse 'highways in their heart' (Psalms 84:6):
דִּשְׁבִילִין דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא כְּבִישִׁין בְּלִבְּהוֹן.
'the paths of Torah are paved firmly in their hearts.'

וּבְשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב (מִזְמוֹר קיט)158 Midrash Tehillim 119:7 — "In my heart I have hidden Your word, that I might not sin against You." The evil inclination has no power over the Torah; and whoever has the Torah in his heart, the evil inclination has no power over him and does not touch him. And so it says, "I, Wisdom, dwell with prudence" — and in the place where I dwell, prudence is round about me, and over prudence the evil inclination has no power. And so it says, "The Torah of his God is in his heart; his steps do not slip." And so Moses says, "And you shall place these My words upon your heart and upon your soul." Hence, "In my heart I have hidden Your word." עַל פָּסוּק "בְּלִבִּי צָפַנְתִּי אִמְרָתֶךָ":
And in Shocher Tov (Psalm 119) on the verse 'In my heart I have hidden Your word':
כָּל מִי שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בְּלִבּוֹ, אֵין יֵצֶר הָרָע שׁוֹלֵט וְנוֹגֵעַ בְּלִבּוֹ.
whoever holds the words of Torah in his heart, the evil inclination cannot dominate or touch his heart.

וְאֵינוֹ סוֹתֵר מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה159 Sukkah 52a — “For he has done greatly” — Abaye said: And among Torah scholars more than all of them, as Abaye once heard a certain man saying to a woman, “Let us rise early and go on our way.” Abaye said: I will go and separate them from transgression. He followed them three parasangs through the marshes, and when they were parting he heard them say, “The way is long and the company pleasant.” Abaye said: Had it been I, I could not have restrained myself. He went and leaned against a doorpost in anguish. A certain elder came and taught him: Whoever is greater than his fellow, his evil inclination is greater than his. Rashi (s.v. "had it been the one who hates me"): Had my enemy been alone with the woman, he could not have restrained himself from sinning; and he was speaking of himself. Rashi (s.v. "he leaned"): He leaned against the bolt of the door, like a man who is brooding and in distress. Rashi (s.v. "the way is long, and the company pleasant"): It is a long way between our two places, and we cannot go on together any further; had we been able to go by one road, our company would have been pleasant. Rashi (s.v. "when they were parting from one another"): They were from two towns, and when they reached a fork in the road he turned one way and she the other. Maharsha (on "for he has done greatly"): The verse concludes "for he has done greatly," meaning that he provokes the great more, as Abaye concludes. Alternatively, "he has done greatly" means that he has made himself great in relation to the righteous, [appearing to them] as a mountain, as was said above that at first he resembles a spider's thread and in the end cart-ropes; and "among Torah scholars more than all of them" is then a statement in its own right, as in the incident of Abaye. Maharsha (s.v. "the way is long"): It may also be explained as referring to the past: we have come a long way, but the company was pleasant, so that because of the company the way did not seem so long to us. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 2): The evil inclination provokes the Torah scholar more than all, although he is complete, being a man of intellect: for the intellect a man possesses [in this world] is never in its completeness but is held with deficiency, so that the Torah scholar and Israel lack the completeness fitting for them, whereas other men and other nations, who have only the small level, cannot be called so deficient. Therefore the evil inclination provokes them more and more, and whoever has a higher level must guard himself against the evil inclination. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 48): After Israel received the Torah and reached a supreme level, the evil inclination provoked them to sin, in the manner of "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his": because they had reached a supreme level that the rest of creation had not reached, the evil inclination, which is Satan, seeks to cast them down from their level. For privation clings more to a man who has a supreme level, one not fitting for every man, than it clings to the low level that is found in all. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 19): Just as "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his" (and that elder, who was Elijah according to some commentators in Tosafos, a view I have received as primary, was revealed to Abaye through his anguish to tell him this and console him), so too, when someone's inclination is greater than his fellow's, this is a sign that he is also greater than him in the holy sparks within him, for God has made one opposite the other in each person, and the choice is in his hands. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 6): Such an abundance of light would bring great hardship to those who walk in the way of God, for the same reason as "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his": with a greater abundance of the light of the Blessed One, the evil in that same place grows stronger too, because so much light lies within it, for evil always surrounds the good. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): Since the Blessed One does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, and even one created righteous must choose against an inclination that overpowers him daily, "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his". Therefore the inclination appears to the righteous like a mountain, for its assault on them is enormous, matching the great power of good innate in them. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Terumah 8): The Sages said that the evil inclination provokes Torah scholars more than all and that "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his"; why should this be? The inclination is longing, and the purpose of its creation is to be the delight of Torah; so the one who is greater, in whom the delight of Torah is sunk more deeply, has, since "God has made the one opposite the other," a stronger desire toward the opposite as well, while one who does not magnify the delight of Torah in himself has no strong desire for the opposite either. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 2): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," for the virtue is drawn together with the deficiency: as great and precious wealth needs more guarding than a small thing, being more liable to harm because more people strive after it, so in the soul, the greater its stature, that is, the more divine power it holds (and the will toward the opposite is also a divine power), the greater in it is this power of inclination as well, and it needs guarding. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," for as the strength of the virtue, so is the strength of the deficiency, from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, where evil stands opposite the good and corresponds to it. Hence Dan, the lowest of the tribes in virtue, is lower in his deficiency as well, and the inclination is not as strong in him. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 134): When a person reaches a higher level, by the measure of that level he has not yet begun to repent, and his sin returns in full force; of this it is said, "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his", for the sin is the deficiency in a person, and so is the inclination. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Where the strength of the virtue lies, there lies the strength of the deficiency, for "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his": as is known, in Adam's sin the "man of Belial" ruled over the holy man limb for limb, God having made the one opposite the other, so that corresponding to the holiness of each limb and power is the dominion of the "man of Belial" in enticing to evil. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Mishlei 19): "The desire of a man is his kindness": the desire found in a person's heart is also a kindness from the Blessed One, for "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his", and if he brings the power of his longing and desire into holiness, his stature grows all the more. Beis Yaakov (Vayishlach 4): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," for "God has made the one opposite the other": the power of good against the power of its opposite. Yet every person has the power of good to overcome his inclination, and through this he rises, gathering wealth in holiness little by little, which is the whole purpose of man's creation in this world. Sod Yesharim (Seventh Night of Pesach 16): The vessel [of longing] that a person attains in old age was already in him on the day he was born, only that each time he clarifies himself further, the vessel grows larger in him too, as the Sages said, "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his". (נב.)
Nor does this contradict what they stated in Sukkah (52a)
עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי הִגְדִּיל לַעֲשׂוֹת" – וּבְתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים יוֹתֵר מִכּוּלָּם,
on the verse 'for he has done great things'—that it incites against Torah scholars more than against anyone else,

דְּטַעַם אֵין שׁוֹלֵט כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שִׁילְהֵי חֲגִיגָה (כז160 Chagigah 27a — R. Abbahu said that R. Elazar said: The fire of Gehenna has no power over Torah scholars. This may be inferred a fortiori from the salamander: if the salamander, which is a creature born of fire, is such that one who anoints himself with its blood is immune to fire, then Torah scholars, whose whole body is fire, as it is written "Is not My word like fire, says the Lord" — how much more so. Reish Lakish said: The fire of Gehenna has no power over the sinners of Israel. This may be inferred a fortiori from the golden altar: if the golden altar, which has upon it no more than the thickness of a gold dinar, stood so many years and the fire had no power over it, then the sinners of Israel, who are as full of commandments as a pomegranate, as it is written "Your temples are like a pomegranate split open" — do not read "your temples [rakkatekh]" but "the empty ones among you [reikanin shebakh]" — how much more so. Rashi: The salamander is a creature born of fire, formed when a fire is kept burning in one place for seven years continuously, without interruption. "No more than the thickness of a gold dinar" — a slight thing, and yet its gold was not diminished, for a miracle was performed with it. Tosafos (s.v. "the fire of Gehenna has no power over the sinners of Israel"): This cannot be said of the sinners of Israel in their bodies, for it is taught in Rosh Hashanah that for them Gehenna is consumed but they are not consumed; it speaks rather of those who are transgressors only in part. Tosafos (s.v. "which has upon it no more than the thickness of a dinar"): In the Tanchuma: Moses wondered at this, that the wood could not but be burned; and the Omnipresent said to him, Such is My way with the fire of above — fire consumes fire and yet does not destroy it, as it is written, "and the bush was not consumed" (Exodus 3:2). Maharsha: Because the words of Torah are themselves fire, the bodies of those who learn them become fire, as they said, "A Torah scholar who seethes — it is the Torah within him that makes him seethe." And from the Tosafot it appears that the golden altar's meaning is this: its coating was no thicker than a gold dinar, and even so the wood beneath it was not burned, for the thin gold shielded it — and in like manner the sinners of Israel, who are also full of commandments, as it is written, "like a pomegranate split open"; and these commandments, which are likened to gold, as it is said, "more desirable than gold," shield them so that the fire of Gehenna has no power over them. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 26): At the end of Chagigah the fire of Torah is likened to the fire of Gehenna — therefore the fire of Gehenna has no power over Torah scholars, and they derived it from the salamander, for it is all one fire — and afterwards the fire of Gehenna is likened there to the fire of the altar, a fire from above that consumes yet does not destroy. It is like the purging of an iron vessel in fire, which expels the absorbed flavors while the vessel itself remains: it burns only the evil absorbed in this world, and in Torah scholars the fire of Torah burns it away in this world. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Although the inclination is stronger in Torah scholars, they said at the end of Chagigah that the fire of Gehenna has no power over them because their whole body is fire; for the fire of Gehenna is the fire of the desires — "your spirit is a fire that shall consume you": the fire of Gehenna is made from the sin itself — and the fire of Torah is a fire that consumes the fire of Gehenna. "Their whole body is fire" means that they leave the category of body altogether, for everywhere fire alludes to something spiritual. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 15): Gehenna is chiefly for corruptions of the covenant, and for this there is no repair except through Torah; about this they said that the fire of Gehenna has no power over Torah scholars — for they have surely repented, since the light of Torah brings them back to the good and they repair what came before. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 4): Of Israel who engage in Torah it is said at the end of Chagigah that their whole body is fire, as it says, "Is not My word like fire"; and the sinners of Israel too, of whom it is said there that they are full of mitzvos — when they engage in the Torah's mitzvos they are engaged in Torah and cleave to it and become fire, and therefore the fire of Gehenna has no power over them either. This comes through their cleaving to the Blessed One by engaging in His mitzvos, for He is a fire that consumes the fire of Gehenna, which comes from the burning of evil desires. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 15): Reish Lakish's statement about the sinners of Israel is introduced as "said Reish Lakish," not "Reish Lakish said" as one who comes to disagree, implying that the two do not disagree; but then, if the fire of Gehenna has no power even over all the sinners of Israel, why need R. Elazar say it only of Torah scholars, because their body is fire? They said "has no power," not "they do not enter at all," so clearly they do enter, only the fire does not rule over them — yet this cannot mean that they do not feel the burning at all, for then why would they enter? And from Acher, from whose grave smoke rose, we see that it did rule over him even though his whole body was fire. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 144): The essence of a person is not the body but the soul, which is the power that thinks; wherever his thought is fixed, there the whole person is. So one who cleaves to Torah and thinks of it constantly — all his limbs become so, as the Sages said: the fire of Gehenna has no power over Torah scholars, for their whole body is fire, as it says, "Is not My word like fire." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): Through R. Yochanan, Acher too entered the Garden of Eden: the smoke and fire of the evil desires that surrounded him were extinguished, and the light of his Torah was revealed, though his deeds were not so. When his daughter said to Rebbi, "Remember his Torah," fire licked at [Rebbi's] bench — that is, the fire of his Torah, for "Is not My word like fire," and Torah scholars' whole body is fire, wherefore the fire of Gehenna has no power over them, as they said at the end of Chagigah..):
for the reason it 'does not dominate' mirrors what they taught at the end of Chagigah (27a):
"אֵין אוֹר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֵט",
"the fire of Gehenna has no dominion,"
וְלֹא אָמַר אֵין נִכְנָס לְגֵיהִנָּם,
and it did not state that it never enters Gehenna;
רַק לָמְדוּ מִמִּזְבַּח הַזָּהָב דְּהָיָה אוֹר בּוֹעֵר רַק שֶׁאֵין מְכַלֶּה.
they merely deduced it from the golden Altar, upon which fire burned without ever consuming it.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן דּוֹאֵג דְּנִדְחָה מֵחֵלֶק עוֹלָם הַבָּא,
In contrast, regarding Doeg who was utterly banished from his portion in the World to Come,
הֲרֵי מְכַלֶּה;
the fire indeed consumed him;
עַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "מִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ".
and concerning that state they remarked: 'from the lip outward.'

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם "דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת" אָמְרוּ וְכוּלֵי (סַנְהֶדְרִין קד161 Sanhedrin 104b — The expounders of hidden meanings used to say: All of them enter the World to Come, as it is said, "Gilead is Mine and Manasseh is Mine, Ephraim also is the stronghold of My head, Judah is My lawgiver; Moab is My washpot, upon Edom I will cast My shoe, over Philistia I will shout." "Gilead is Mine" — this is Ahab, who fell at Ramoth-gilead. "Manasseh" — as its plain sense. "Ephraim is the stronghold of My head" — this is Jeroboam, who came from Ephraim. "Judah is My lawgiver" — this is Ahithophel. Rashi: "The expounders of hidden meanings" are expounders of verses, as it is written, "that which is inscribed [ha-rashum] in the writing of truth" (Daniel 10:21); they would say that all of them have a share, even Manasseh, Jeroboam and Ahab. "Gilead is Mine and Manasseh is Mine" — it is upon Me to bear their iniquity so that they may merit [the World to Come]; "Manasseh" in its plain sense is Manasseh son of Hezekiah. Ahithophel [is "Judah"] because he was of the tribe of Judah like David, who called him "my familiar friend," that is, my kinsman. Maharsha: Ahab's fall and death at Ramoth-gilead was itself his atonement, by which he merits the World to Come; and Manasseh alone is named "in its plain sense" because the others are designated by other names, their own names having been names of wickedness all their lives, whereas Manasseh repented in his lifetime and his own name, now in repentance, brings him to the World to Come. Jeroboam is "the stronghold of My head" because he was the first of all the kings of Israel and was made king at the word of the prophet, so he is not fit to be among those who go down to Gehinnom. "Judah is My lawgiver" is spoken by David: Ahithophel was David's teacher — "my lawgiver" — and through David his disciple he merited the World to Come, just as R. Meir, his disciple, brought Acher to the World to Come. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 2): The world was created with measure and limit, with room for choice between good and evil and for reward and punishment, whereas the World to Come has no choice; therefore the dorshei reshumos said that all of them come to the World to Come, for the World to Come is truly without limit, as it is written, "and I will feed you the heritage of Jacob your father," a heritage without boundaries. This world is not so: it is bounded, with time and with deeds good and evil. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): There are many levels of what is called "having no share": such a soul still has existence and is not wholly annihilated like the souls of the nations, enduring forever through its attachment to its root in the living God, only it has no share of its own; and this apart from the dorshei reshumos saying that all of them have a share in the World to Come. Though they said it of the particular souls listed in the Mishnah, from the particular one learns about the whole, for these seven marked individuals correspond to seven kinds of corruption through which one's share in the World to Come can be lost. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): This is the exposition of the dorshei reshumos ["expounders of hidden meanings"] that all of them have a share in the World to Come, all who are of the seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, except Balaam: "reshumos" denotes the level of chochmah above binah, binah being the World to Come and the heart, where feeling lies; chochmah in the mind is not felt, only its impression (reshimu) is felt in the heart. From the standpoint of the attainment of chochmah there is no dross at all in the seed of Jacob, and even things that have no remedy through repentance, which alludes to the World to Come, are rectified by the opening of the gate of chochmah, which is above the level of repentance.:),
Nonetheless, the 'interpreters of subtle impressions' (dorshei reshumot) expounded, etc. (Sanhedrin 104b),
פֵּירוּשׁ, דְּחֵלֶק עוֹלָם הַבָּא נִקְרָא בִּינָה כַּנּוֹדָע,
meaning that the allotted portion of the World to Come is designated as Binah, as is known,
דְּהַיְינוּ רַק עַל יְדֵי הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב.
which is attained solely through understanding rooted in the heart.
אֲבָל יֵשׁ רְשׁוּמוֹת
Yet there exists the realm of 'reshumot' (supernal impressions),
וְהִיא מָקוֹם יוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹן דְּלָא קַיָּימָא לִשְׁאֵלָה,
which is an even higher realm that is beyond inquiry,
וְאֵין הַשָּׂגַת אָדָם שָׁם רַק בִּרְשִׁימוּ שֶׁלּוֹ.
where human comprehension cannot penetrate except via its faint impression.
שָׁם אַף זֶה דְּמִשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ אֵין נִדְחָה,
In that lofty sphere, even one whose Torah was merely 'from the lip outward' is not utterly cast out,
דְּהוּא לְמַעְלָה מִן הַלֵּב,
for that realm transcends the heart,
וְסוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה דָּבוּק בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה
and 'the end of action is bound up in the initial thought'
בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלַם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה,
in this physical world, which constitutes the World of Action;
וַעֲקִימַת שְׂפָתָיו הָוֵי מַעֲשֶׂה,
and the physical movement of one's lips is halakhically deemed an action,
אַף בָּזֶה יֵשׁ קְדוּשָּׁה
so that even within this outward speech holiness abides
וּמוֹעִיל לְהַכְנִיס הַקְּדוּשָּׁה בַּלֵּב עַל יְדֵי כֵּן;
and serves to draw holiness inward into the heart through that mechanism;

וְזֶה טַעַם "וְחַיִּים בְּיַד לָשׁוֹן" (מִשְׁלֵי יח, כא162 Proverbs 18:21 — Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it shall eat its fruit. Rashi: "And those who love it shall eat its fruit" — one who loves his tongue and accustoms it to Torah eats its reward in this world. Metzudas Dovid: Death and life are given over to the power of the tongue: if a man speaks words of Torah he lives, and if he speaks slander he dies. And one who loves to multiply words with it eats its fruit, whether for good or for ill. Malbim: The "tongue" points to the higher, reasoned speech that draws one thing out of another and judges between truth and falsehood, and upon it depend death and life: one who by such reasoning believes in the principles of faith lives, while one who walks crookedly and denies God's existence, His providence, and reward and punishment dies. "And those who love it shall eat its fruit" — he will never be sated but will eat continually, for understanding has no limit and he will always go on deriving one thing from another.).
and this explains the verse (Proverbs 18:21): 'and life is in the power of the tongue.'

sections.en: Deficiency as the Vessel for Greatness

items.h: Every great spiritual potential is matched by a corresponding vulnerability; rectification transforms the very site of deficiency into extraordinary perfection.

Seif 1 — Great Deficiency, Great Potential
The deepest flaws can reveal the capacity for exceptional holiness when their underlying power is rectified.

p: כְּפִי הַמַּעֲלָה וְהַשְּׁלֵימוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאָדָם
Commensurate with the virtue and perfection that a person possesses,
כָּךְ יֵשׁ לְעֻמָּתוֹ חִסָּרוֹן כְּנֶגְדּוֹ מַמָּשׁ כְּפִי עֶרְכּוֹ.
so too is there facing him an exact corresponding deficiency according to his measure.
כִּי מִימוֹת חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן הַכֹּל מְעוֹרָב טוֹב וָרָע
For since the days of the sin of Adam the First, everything is intermingled of good and evil,
וְזֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה שֶׁעָשָׂה אֱלֹהִים הֵם בְּעִרְבּוּבְיָא.
and the one corresponding to the other that God created exist in complete confusion.
וְכָל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן עָצוּם
And whoever contains an immense deficiency
הוּא כְּלִי גַּם כֵּן לִשְׁלֵימוּת מֻפְלָג אִם יִזְכֶּה.
is likewise a vessel for extraordinary perfection, if he merits.

כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רטז סוֹף עַמּוּד א163 Zohar Chadash, More about Parshat Vayera 4 — And we have further learned in this mystery another matter in support of it: "for that he also is flesh" — and we have established that "beshagam" is Moses, who was destined to give the Torah in the generation of the Flood; but they were wicked, and the Holy One, blessed be He, stored it away for the righteous.)
Along the lines of what they said in the Zohar (Part III, 216a end)
בְּדוֹר מַבּוּל שֶׁהָיוּ רְאוּיִים לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה.
concerning the Generation of the Flood, that they were originally fit to receive the Torah.
וְהוּא כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה (נב.):
And it is in accordance with what they taught in Sukkah (52a):
"כָּל הַגָּדוֹל [מֵחֲבֵירוֹ] יִצְרוֹ גָּדוֹל [הֵימֶנּוּ]",
"Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than he,"
פֵּירוּשׁ יֵצֶר דְּתַאֲווֹת שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא שְׁטוּת
meaning the inclination of bodily desires which is termed folly,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה ג.)164 Sotah 3a — Reish Lakish said: A man commits a transgression only if a spirit of folly has entered into him, as it is stated: "If any man's wife goes astray [tisteh]" (Numbers 5:12) — it is written tishteh, from the word for folly. Maharsha: For were it from the sense of "turning aside," it should have been written titeh, and were it from the sense of "straying," as in "I hate the doing of those who turn aside [setim]" (Psalms 101:3), it should have been written with a samekh, tisteh; perforce they expounded it from the word for folly. The Midrash Rabbah derives it from "He who commits adultery with a woman lacks understanding" (Proverbs 6:32), meaning that the adulteress entices him even with words of folly and he does her will; but the Talmud's wording, "a man commits a transgression only if…," implies that this is to be learned of every transgression — that the spirit misleads him and befools him, [turning him] from the good way to the evil way. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 3a): That is, sin is not found in the realm of the intellect; therefore they said that a man sins only if a spirit of folly has entered into him, and then he sins. And so Shlomo calls the wicked man a "fool" throughout the book of Kohelet. עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי תִשְׂטֶה".
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sotah 3a) on the verse 'if she goes astray (tisteh/tishteh).'
וּכְפִי גַּדְלוּת הַחָכְמָה
And commensurate with the greatness of wisdom,
כָּךְ יֵשׁ גַּדְלוּת שְׁטוּת.
so too is there a greatness of folly.
וּבִהְיוֹת יִצְרָא דְּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שַׁלִּיט
And when the inclination for idolatry held dominion,
הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת אוֹר הַנְּבוּאָה נִגְלֶה
it was because the light of prophecy was then manifest,
אָז לִהְיוֹת רוֹאֶה בָּעַיִן מַרְאוֹת אֱלֹהִים,
such that one would perceive visions of God with the physical eye;
מִזֶּה נִמְשַׁךְ יֵצֶר הָרָע לַעֲשׂוֹת אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים הַנִּגְלִים לָעַיִן.
from this was drawn the evil inclination to fashion other gods that are visible to the eye.

וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (סט165 Yoma 69b — "And they cried with a loud voice to the Lord their God" (Nehemiah 9:4). What did they say? Rav said, and some say R. Yochanan: Woe, woe! This is the one that destroyed the Temple, and burned its Sanctuary, and killed all the righteous, and exiled Israel from their land — and still it dances among us. Did You give it to us for anything but that we should receive reward through it? We do not want it, and we do not want its reward. They fasted three days and three nights, and it was delivered to them. A fiery lion cub came forth from the Holy of Holies, and the prophet said to Israel: This is the inclination for idolatry. Rashi: "Woe, woe": an expression of crying out and complaint. "This is the one that destroyed the Temple": they were praying for mercy, that the evil inclination for idolatry be delivered into their hands. "That we should receive reward through it": that we should subdue it and receive reward. "The prophet said to them": Zechariah son of Iddo. Maharsha (Sanhedrin 64a, s.v. "what did they say"): They hurled words toward Heaven with a loud voice, as Elijah did, [pleading] that it is in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, to remove the evil inclination from us, as it is written, "and whom I have made evil" (Micah 4:6). This is no true plea in judgment, since man was given free choice, and the Torah as the antidote [to the inclination]; but it is some plea. And their fasting until the inclination for idolatry was delivered into their hands means that they annulled its power in the heart with the help of Heaven, as "one who comes to purify himself is helped"; for the inclination for idolatry is the evil inclination of the heart. Maharsha (s.v. "like a fiery lion cub"): It is the constellation Leo, the sign of the month of Av, in which the Temple was destroyed because they worshipped idols; therefore he said, "This is the inclination for idolatry," through which the First Temple was destroyed, as is said in the first chapter of this tractate. Maharal (Derech Chaim 5:23): As is stated in Yoma and in Sanhedrin, "Did You give us the evil inclination for anything but to receive reward? We want neither it nor its reward": from this you see that because one fulfills the commandment through the pain of the evil inclination, his reward is greater. For one who fulfills the commandment despite the pain draws near to the Blessed One by his own strength, against what hinders him, and reward is only according to one's nearness to the Blessed One. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 46): When there is no evil inclination there is no merit, as they said in Tractate Yoma, "Did You create the evil inclination for anything but to receive reward…"; therefore [in the days of the Messiah, when the evil inclination is removed,] there will be neither merit nor guilt. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 6): Even if the commandments are for our good, this too is by decree, and not like one who wishes to benefit another, where the recipient, if he does not wish to accept, may exempt himself, in the manner of "Did You give it to us for anything but that we should receive reward? We want neither it nor its reward." That is not so; rather, that good itself is decreed upon Israel. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 33): The only mitzvah of a feast is on Purim, and it seems to me that it was instituted then through the slaughter of the inclination for idolatry, which the Men of the Great Assembly accomplished in the days of the Persian kings. [Israel] were then wholehearted in other matters and merited the slaughter of the inclination, a foretaste of the future, when it will be slaughtered entirely; and then there will be the great feast, on the day He is to bestow kindness on the seed of Isaac. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 15): All [Israel] is one assembly, and a deficiency in part of it is in the whole; this brought about the destruction of the First Temple, until the Men of the Great Assembly arose to repair the assembly by nullifying the inclination for idolatry, and therefore they were called the Great Assembly, for through them the assembly was made great. But the inclination for sexual transgression remained, which causes licentiousness and the casting off of the yoke, and from it derive heresy and the Sadducees. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Yisro 6): Israel put "we will do" before "we will hear" because they longed and desired to do [His will] and wished to be like angels, without free choice; they spoke in the manner of the Men of the Great Assembly, who said, "We want neither it nor its reward." For although reward and punishment rest chiefly on free choice, they declared that they did not want to receive any reward at all, and wished to serve the Blessed One like angels, without any free choice. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares, from the Yerushalmi 16): Seeing the magnitude of the sins, the Men of the Great Assembly said, "We want neither it nor its reward," and nullified the inclination for idolatry. Through subduing that inclination, the opposite of recognizing the Blessed One, [Israel] had attained the revelation of the Shechinah; so once the sin made it necessary to nullify it, prophecy and the Shechinah departed from Israel as a matter of course, for nothing was left through which to attain that revelation, and everything was in concealment. Sod Yesharim (Purim 32): In the days of Ahasuerus the Blessed One handed over to the Men of the Great Assembly the entire conduct [of the world] until the time of the end, as we find that the inclinations for idolatry and for sexual transgression were delivered into their hands. Had they wished, it was within their power to subdue all the forces in the world beneath them and bring them into holiness; but they held themselves back from receiving any good before the time that had arisen in His simple will to grant it to them.:):
Therefore they said in Yoma (69b):
דִּכְשֶׁבִּיטְּלוּהוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה,
that when the Men of the Great Assembly nullified this inclination,

אָמְרוּ: "לָא אִיהוּ בָּעֵינַן וְלָא אַגְרֵיהּ166 Yoma 69b — They fasted three days and three nights, and He delivered the evil inclination for idolatry into their hands. It came forth from the Holy of Holies like a fiery lion cub. The prophet said to Israel: This is the inclination for idolatry. They seized it, and one of its hairs was torn out, and it let out a cry that was heard four hundred parasangs away. They said: What shall we do? Perhaps, Heaven forbid, they will have mercy on it from Heaven. The prophet said to them: Cast it into a lead pot and seal its mouth with lead, for lead absorbs sound. Rashi: "The prophet said to them": Zechariah son of Iddo. "One of its hairs": a hair. "A lead pot": a pot made of lead. "Lead absorbs sound": the sound enters into the lead and does not come out of it. Maharsha (s.v. "like a fiery lion cub"): The fiery lion cub is the constellation Leo, the sign of the month of Av, in which the Temple was destroyed because they worshipped idols; hence he said, "This is the inclination for idolatry," through which the First Temple was destroyed. The hair [se'ar] torn from it alludes to Se'ir, that is Edom, whose power they came to annul, for the Second Temple too was destroyed in Av, under Leo, by the Romans; and its cry alludes to the cry of Esau, "and he cried a great [and exceedingly bitter] cry" (Genesis 27:34), through which he merited to rule over Israel, and over the Land of Israel, which is four hundred parasangs. Casting it into a lead pot means curbing the power of the mouth of wickedness somewhat in this world until the World to Come, as it is said, "and all wickedness shall vanish like smoke," and "iniquity shall shut her mouth." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaLashon 6): In Tractate Yoma and in Tractate Sanhedrin they said that there are two inclinations, the inclination for sexual immorality and the inclination for idolatry, and these correspond to the body and the soul; the body certainly does not incline to idolatry, for idolatry concerns spiritual powers, and this pertains to the soul in particular, not to the body. This was more so in the early days, as is stated in its place; and now this great thing, that the soul should have an inclination toward external powers, has been removed. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 33): The only mitzvah of a feast is on Purim, and it seems to me that it was instituted then through the slaughter of the inclination for idolatry, which the Men of the Great Assembly accomplished in the days of the Persian kings. [Israel] were then wholehearted in other matters and merited the slaughter of the inclination, a foretaste of the future, when it will be slaughtered entirely; and then there will be the great feast, on the day He is to bestow kindness on the seed of Isaac.
