Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 258): Concerning this King Solomon asked, "Give me neither poverty nor riches": not to chase after the excesses of desire, which is called "poverty," and also not to hold back his desire entirely, which is called "riches"; rather one must keep to the middle line, as the Sages said of this: "The inclination — let the left push away and the right draw near." Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Anthology, Sotah; from Dover Tzedek 12b): On "R. Shimon ben Elazar says: The inclination … let the left push away and the right draw near": one may say that the right draws near precisely so that the left may push away, and this is "very good." And I heard that the Sages likened the inclination to the leaven in the dough — and the leaven is what makes the dough right, and it is said of leaven that a little of it is good. Beis Yaakov (Vayechi 12): When a person receives some good or eats some food, he must watch himself not to be drawn too far into that pleasure and desire, setting all his thoughts and desire on it, until it darkens and dims his light and he cannot return to his holiness. Rather, a person must set a law, a measure and a limit for each and every pleasure, how far he will be drawn after it: "and the left pushes away and the right draws near.": "שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה וְיָמִין מְקָרֶבֶת",
in contrast to bodily desires, concerning which our Sages taught (Sotah 47a): "the left hand pushes away while the right draws near,"
וְכֵן לֶעָתִיד לֹא יֵהָרֵג יֵצֶר זֶה,
and so in the ultimate future this inclination will not be destroyed,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א דַּף קלז, קלח)312 Zohar 1:137a — It was taught: R. Shimon said — he is a deceiver and was always a deceiver, and the evil inclination, which is a deceiver, dwells there. This is what is written, "the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean" — the deceitful bone; "from Paddan Aram" — from a yoke of deceivers, as we learned, a "paddan" of oxen is a yoke; "the sister of Laban the Aramean" — the sister of the evil inclination, the deceiver. As we learned: at first, when it was befouled with sins in this world, it was called Lot; in the time to come, when it will no longer be befouled as before, but is like one who has bathed and immersed away his defilement, they call it Laban ["white"]. In any case, the evil inclination is not abolished from the world. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): I heard that Shittim denotes folly [shtut], which will be healed in the future — "a spring shall come forth from the house of the Lord and water the valley of Shittim" — that is, after the slaughter of the evil inclination, which is called Laban because it is whitened, as written in Midrash HaNe'elam, and as the Sages said on the verse "a heart of flesh," that it will be only a heart to bring forth flesh. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 9): The evil inclination was created to serve man in permitted needs that aid the service of the Blessed One — that is, once a person subdues it so that he rules over it and his heart is in his control; then the evil inclination is called Laban, for it has been whitened, as they said in Midrash HaNe'elam of the time to come, that it will not be entirely abolished but only whitened. This is like what they said on "I will give you a heart of flesh" — a heart to bring forth flesh — and this is its servitude to the form of man in all the bad traits within the inclination's power, which also have some needed use. דְּאִקְרֵי לָבָן דְּאִתְלַבַּן, עַיֵּין שָׁם.
as written in the Zohar (Part I, 137b–138a) that it is called Laban because it becomes whitened and purified, see there.
וְעִיקַּר גִּידּוּל עֲמָלֵק וְעֵשָׂו עַל יְדֵי נְפִילַת יִשְׂרָאֵל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּתַאֲווֹת,
And the primary ascendance of Amalek and Esau occurs through Israel's lapse, Heaven forbid, into lusts,
כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ עֵשָׂו "עַל חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה" בִּרְצִיחָה;
for Esau's root is "by your sword you shall live," grounded in murder;
וְהַגַּם דְּאֻמּוֹת כְּלוּלִים מִכָּל רָעוֹת יַחַד,
and even though the nations embody all evils collectively,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַגָּוֶון וַדַּאי בְּרוֹצֵחַ נִרְאֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל תַּאֲוָה.
nonetheless the outward appearance of a murderer makes him seem not to be driven by bodily lust.
וּבָזֶה הוּא פְּשִׁיטַת טְלָפָיו בְּיִחוּד שֶׁיּוּכַל לִטְעוֹן נֶגֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל.
And herein lies his specific display of split hooves, enabling him to prosecute against Israel.
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם הֵם נְקִיִּים מֵרְצִיחָה,
Yet nevertheless, if Israel are pure from murderous hatred,
אָז מִיגַנְיָא מִינֵיהּ מִצַּד שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם עוֹדֶף נֶגְדּוֹ בָּזֶה.
then they are shielded from him because they possess superior spiritual merit against him in that area.
אֲבָל בְּצֵירוּף שְׁנֵיהֶם מִתְגַּבֵּר בְּיוֹתֵר חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
However, in the confluence of both vices, he overpowers severely, Heaven forbid.
וּלְכָךְ אָז דְּהָיָה הִשְׁתַּחֲוָויָה לַצֶּלֶם
Therefore back then, because there was bowing to the idol (in Nebuchadnezzar's days),
וּבְשׁוּשָׁן הָיָה גַּם כֵּן הֲנָאָה מִסְּעוּדָתוֹ, דְּהַיְינוּ הִתְפָּרְצוּת בְּתַאֲווֹת, הִתְגַּבֵּר בְּיוֹתֵר.
and in Shushan there was also indulgence in his banquet, representing an outbreak of lust, Amalek overpowered with tremendous force.

וְהָא דְּשָׁאֲלוּ אֶת רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי: מִפְּנֵי מָה וְכוּלֵי313 Megillah 12a — His students asked R. Shimon bar Yochai: Why were the enemies of Israel of that generation deserving of destruction? He said to them: You say it. They said: Because they took pleasure in the feast of that wicked man. He said: If so, only those in Shushan should have been destroyed, and not those in the rest of the world. They said: Then you tell us. He said to them: Because they bowed to the image. Rashi: "Because they prostrated themselves to the image" — the image of the days of Nebuchadnezzar. Maharsha: Rashi takes "the image" to be Nebuchadnezzar's, since Scripture implies that Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah alone refrained while all the rest bowed down; he is unwilling to explain it of bowing to Haman, which would imply that Mordecai alone refrained while all the rest bowed to him. And this is correct, for prostration to Haman took place only in Shushan, so that the objection would return — let those in Shushan be killed and not those in all the rest of the world — whereas the image in the plain of Dura was evidently set up for the whole world. Maharal (Or Chadash on Esther, introduction): Even according to R. Shimon ben Yochai, what brought the decree out at that time was that they had enjoyed Ahasuerus's feast, for that sin was what caused the earlier sin of prostrating to Nebuchadnezzar's image to be recalled against them. This is why Scripture recounts the feast at such length: taking pleasure in it was itself close to idolatry, since the feast was made in praise of his kingdom, and Ahasuerus's was one of the four kingdoms of the world, which are set against Israel who cleave to God and which themselves cleave to idolatry. When they took pleasure in a feast made for the name and glory of that nation's kingdom, they were thereby giving praise to idolatry — though this is not outright idolatry — and so this sin caused the sin of the image to be remembered, even though only those in Shushan committed it. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 33): Though the Jews were only joining gentiles at a single feast, the Gemara calls this "serving idols in purity," and this was the accusation: that they took pleasure in the feast of that wicked man, which is a trace of idolatry, and likewise that they bowed to the image — though it was only a [royal] statue and they did it only for appearance's sake, it is nevertheless a trace of idolatry, and "round about Him it storms greatly" [He is exacting with those near Him]. Because they then purified themselves in this matter until they had slaughtered the inclination to idolatry entirely, the Blessed One wished to establish a feast for them, to show that even in their drunkenness they need fear nothing, their hearts being already whole with Him. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 255): The Megillah opens with the feast because the decree sprouted from it, as the Sages said, "because they took pleasure"; and although the Gemara concludes that it was because they bowed to the image, they were not punished for that at the time, since in truth they did it only for appearance's sake, and "the Lord sees into the heart" — there was sin only from the human side, for "man sees what is before the eyes." As long as they conduct themselves with a generous eye, the Blessed One too has a generous eye toward them, bestowing on them by His measure of "seeing into the heart"; but on account of "they took pleasure" — the incitement of the power of the narrow eye — the Blessed One too said, "Mine is mine and yours is yours," judging by what is before the eyes. (מְגִילָּה יב.),
And that which the disciples asked Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: "Why did Israel deserve destruction, etc.?" (Megillah 12a),
עַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא: "אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים",
see there in the Gemara: both perspectives are the words of the living God;
דְּהַתְחָלַת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הָמָן הוּא מִפְּנֵי הַהֲנָאָה, דְּמִזֶּה מִתְעוֹרֵר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל;
for the initial awakening of Haman was due to the banquet's pleasure, which roused him as noted above;
וְהִתְעוֹרְרוּתוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת הָיָה רַק בְּשׁוּשָׁן וְעַל מָרְדֳּכַי בְּיִחוּד,
and his initial animosity in truth was centered only in Shushan and specifically against Mordechai,

כְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה שָׁם)314 Megillah 12a — "That they should do according to the will of man and man" (Esther 1:8). Rava said: To do according to the will of Mordecai and Haman — Mordecai, as it is written, "a Jewish man"; Haman, "a man who is an adversary and an enemy." Rashi: "According to the will of Mordecai and Haman" — the two of them were the stewards of the drink at the feast. Maharsha: Rashi's explanation, that they were the stewards of the drink, is not clear to me; on the contrary, the verse implies that the king charged the stewards to act according to the will of each and every man who was drinking. The Targum's rendering seems right: "to do according to the will of the man of the house of Israel and according to the will of the man of every nation and tongue." And since "a man and a man" is a superfluous expression, the Sages said that Scripture made all Israel depend upon Mordecai — that is, upon his will that they be given nothing forbidden to eat or drink, for Mordecai himself certainly took no pleasure whatever in that feast — and made all the nations depend upon Haman, whose will was for every kind of eating. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 33): Jews too were at the feast in Shushan, and so the Sages said "according to the will of man and man — Mordecai and Haman," who were the ones appointed over it; this alludes to "from great to small," for Esau is called "great" and Jacob "small," and they divided this world and the World to Come between them. Thus the gentiles satisfied their appetites at that feast according to their will, lacking none of the desires of this world, while for the Jews who were there it was according to their will in restraining their appetites. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 255): Ahasuerus's feast was an incitement to make them submit to him, for "there is no incitement without eating and drinking," and those close to the king absorb his power most. So the Sages said "according to the will of man and man — Mordecai and Haman": as they were the chief stewards of the drink at the feast, they certainly absorbed the most from this incitement. עַל פָּסוּק "כִּרְצוֹן אִישׁ וָאִישׁ" – מָרְדֳּכַי וְהָמָן,
in accordance with the Sages' exposition (Megillah 12a) on the verse "according to the pleasure of every man (ish va-ish)"—referring to Mordechai and Haman,
דְּהָיָה גַּם הוּא בְּאוֹתָהּ סְעוּדָה.
for Haman was also present at that same banquet.
רַק דְּהִתְגַּבְּרוּתוֹ עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּחֲוָויָה לַצֶּלֶם, בָּזֶה כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁוִים,
Only that his overpowering force stemming from the bowing to the idol applied equally to all Israel;
לְכָךְ נִתְעוֹרֵר עַל כָּל עַם מָרְדֳּכָי.
therefore he was aroused against the entire people of Mordechai.
וְנִקְרָא בְּכָאן "עַם מָרְדֳּכָי",
And they are titled here "the people of Mordechai,"
כִּי כָּל נֶפֶשׁ יֵשׁ לוֹ עִנְיָן מְיוּחָד שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא רֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר,
because every soul possesses a unique spiritual domain in which it is head of the generation,
וּבְעִנְיַן מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק וְהָמָן בְּיִחוּד הָיָה מָרְדֳּכַי כְּנֶגְדּוֹ,
and in the specific mission of obliterating Amalek and Haman, Mordechai stood directly facing him;
וְנִקְרְאוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם "אִישׁ" כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
and both were termed ish ("man") as noted above.
כִּי בְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ יֵשׁ כְּנֶגְדּוֹ, "זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה", נֶפֶשׁ בְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
For opposite every soul exists, "one corresponding to the other," an opposing counterpart among the nations,
וְנֶגֶד מָרְדֳּכַי הָיָה הָמָן;
and opposite Mordechai stood Haman;
וּלְכָךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר גִּדַּל הַמֶּלֶךְ אֶת הָמָן, לְעֻמַּת זֶה גַּם כֵּן הָיָה הִתְנַשְּׂאוּת לְמָרְדֳּכָי.
and therefore when the king promoted Haman, parallel elevation simultaneously accrued to Mordechai.
וּמִצַּד הָמָן שֶׁהָיָה חוֹשֵׁב בְּלִבּוֹ "לְמִי יַחְפֹּץ הַמֶּלֶךְ וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהוּא הָעִיקָּר בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ,
And from the arrogant perspective of Haman who assumed in his heart "whom would the king delight to honor more than myself," viewing himself as the center of the entire world,
נִקְרְאוּ גַּם כֵּן הַיְּהוּדִים לְנֶגְדּוֹ "עַם מָרְדֳּכָי", שֶׁהוּא הָעִיקָּר בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ.
the Jews confronting him were likewise called "the people of Mordechai," he being the true spiritual center of the universe.
וְהִנֵּה יָדוּעַ דְּעִיקַּר יְשׁוּעַת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנִיצּוּחָם אֵיזֶה דָּבָר הוּא עַל יְדֵי נִיצּוּחָם אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ בַּלֵּב,
And behold, it is known that the essential salvation of Israel and their victory over any adversary comes through subduing that very spiritual force within the heart;
וְהָיוּ צְרִיכִים אָז כְּבִישַׁת שְׁנֵי הַכֹּחוֹת:
and they needed at that time to subdue both powers:
הַיְינוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְכַעַס,
namely, all Israel regarding the inclination of idolatry and anger,
וְשֶׁבְּשׁוּשָׁן בְּיִחוּד בְּיִצְרָא דְּתַאֲווֹת גַּם כֵּן.
and those in Shushan specifically regarding the inclination of physical desire as well.
וּלְכָךְ בִּקְּשָׁה אֶסְתֵּר לִינָּתֵן לַיְּהוּדִים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁן עוֹד יוֹם לְנִיצּוּחַ הָאוֹיְבִים.
Therefore Esther requested that the Jews in Shushan be granted an additional day to defeat the enemies.
וּפוּרִים הוּא יוֹם הַנַּיָיחָא שֶׁאַחַר הַטִּרְדָּא, כִּי כָּל זְמַן הַנִּיצּוּחַ הוּא בְּטִרְדָּא;
And Purim is the day of restful relief (neicha) following turmoil, for the entire duration of active combat is filled with agitation;
וְאֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין מַעְצָר לְרוּחָם וְזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף הֵם הַמְּמַהֲרִים בְּנִיצּוּחַ עֲמָלֵק,
and those who have no restraint over their spirit, along with the seed of Joseph, hasten to crush Amalek,
וְדַי לָהֶם יוֹם אֶחָד לְבַד לִשְׁפּוֹךְ חֲמָתָם עֲלֵיהֶם לְבִלְתִּי הַשְׁאִיר שׁוֹרֶשׁ וְעָנָף,
and a single day is sufficient for them to pour out their wrath upon them so as not to leave root or branch;
כִּי מִיָּד שֶׁמִּתְבָּרְרִים שֶׁכַּעַס יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין דּוֹמֶה לְכַעַס הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת,
for as soon as it becomes clarified that Israel's holy anger bears no resemblance to the anger of idolaters—
שֶׁהֵם כּוֹעֲסִים רַק עַל הַגּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת ה' וּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא רוֹצֶה לִכְעוֹס –
in that they rage solely against nations that have not known Hashem and where the Holy One desires wrath—
מִכָּל מָקוֹם שׁוֹפְכִים כַּעֲסָם עַל עֲמָלֵק וְאֵין נִשְׁאָר מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלוּם, כִּי חֲמָתָם הוּא חֲמַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
they pour their wrath upon Amalek until nothing of him remains, for their indignation is the indignation of Hashem, blessed be He.
וְזֶהוּ כָּל עִיקַּר שִׁימּוּשׁ הַכַּעַס וּרְצִיחָה שֶׁנִּבְרָא בָּעוֹלָם,
And this is the sole constructive purpose of anger and lethal force created in the world,
שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ צוֹרֶךְ כְּלָל רַק לְזֶרַע עֲמָלֵק שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהֶם "תִּמְחֶה" – שָׁם צָרִיךְ לְשַׁמֵּשׁ בִּרְצִיחָה.
having no utility whatsoever except against the seed of Amalek of whom it is commanded "you shall blot out"—there lethal violence must be applied.

וְנֶעֱנַשׁ שָׁאוּל עַל שֶׁהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ שָׁם בְּרַחֲמָנוּת (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב יוֹמָא כב315 Yoma 22b — "And he strove in the valley" (I Samuel 15:5). R. Mani said: over the matter of the valley. When the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Saul, "Go and strike Amalek," he said: If for a single life the Torah said to bring a heifer whose neck is broken, then for all these lives how much more so. And if the men have sinned, what have the animals sinned? And if the adults have sinned, what have the little ones sinned? A heavenly voice went forth and said to him: "Do not be overly righteous" (Ecclesiastes 7:16). Maharsha (s.v. "Do not be overly righteous"): That is, by having mercy even on the wicked. Maharsha (s.v. "over the matter of the valley"): That is, he contended with his Maker: when He commanded him, "Go and strike Amalek … infant and suckling, ox and sheep," he argued, "If for a single life …" The Sages took "he strove in the valley" out of its plain sense (that he fought and strove with Amalek in the valley) because Scripture implies that Amalek dwelt in the mountain ("Then the Amalekite came down, and the Canaanite who dwelt in that mountain"); and although Scripture records his pity only for Agag and the best of the flocks and herds, since he pitied Agag he presumably pitied the little ones as well, who had not sinned at all.:),
And Saul was penalized for exercising misplaced compassion there (Yoma 22b),
וּלְעָתִיד דְּיִמָּחוּ וְיִתְבַּטְּלוּ, יִתְבַּטֵּל גַּם יֵצֶר זֶה מֵהָעוֹלָם.
and in the future when Amalek is blotted out and erased, this destructive inclination will likewise be eliminated from the world.
וּדְכְרַכִּים דְּמִיגַנְיָא שֶׁנְּקִיִּים מִזֶּה וְלֹא יוּכַל לְקַטְרֵג כָּל כָּךְ נֶגְדָּם,
And regarding the inhabitants of walled cities who are shielded, being clean of unbridled rage so that he cannot prosecute heavily against them,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶגֶד זֶה אִם מָצָא מְקוֹם קִטְרוּג, נִיצּוּחוֹ מִתְאַחֵר אֶצְלָם יוֹתֵר,
nevertheless, if he does find grounds for prosecution, his defeat is delayed longer among them,
וּצְרִיכִים לְהִתְבָּרֵר גַּם בְּתַאֲווֹת.
and they must undergo spiritual clarification regarding bodily lusts as well.
וּפוּרִים הוּא הַנַּיָיחָא שֶׁאַחַר מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק,
And Purim is the holy repose following the erasure of Amalek,

דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרַשׁ מִשְׁלֵי פָּרָשָׁה ט)316 Midrash Mishlei 9 — "She has also set her table" (Prov. 9:2) — she set a table for herself in this world and in the world to come. And what is this? The good name she acquired for herself in this world and in the world to come. For all the festivals are destined to be nullified, but the days of Purim will never be nullified, as it is said, "And these days of Purim shall not pass from among the Jews" (Esther 9:28). R. Elazar said: The Day of Atonement, too, will never be nullified, as it is said, "And this shall be for you an everlasting statute, to atone for the children of Israel from all their sins once a year." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): The festivals will be nullified — so that one will no longer say "as the Lord lives, who brought out" — because each marks a going out from some particular immersion in evil, and the holiness of each, revealed through its particular miracle, is nullified when a greater holiness is revealed, like a candle in daylight; but Purim is not a going out from a particular immersion — it is the going out from the general root of evil, Amalek, "the first of the nations," and it clarifies the root of Israel: that even when they are in every evil, it is not truly so. Every redemption is a going out from evil to good, but Purim shows that even while in evil they are not evil at all; and this holiness is not nullified by a greater holiness, for all the others come from the side of virtue, whereas the virtue of the days of Purim comes from the side of lack, and the greater the lack, the greater the virtue. דִּלְעָתִיד גַּם כֵּן לֹא יִתְבַּטֵּל;
which is why our Sages stated (Midrash Mishlei, Parashah 9) that in the future it will never be nullified;
כִּי בִּיטּוּל דִּלְעָתִיד הַכֹּל נִתְלָה בִּמְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק שֶׁיִּתְחַדֵּשׁ אָז, שֶׁיִּמָּחֶה לְגַמְרֵי,
for the future nullification of the evil impulse depends entirely upon the eradication of Amalek which will then be completed, when he is utterly erased,
דְּהוּא עַצְמוֹ בִּיטּוּל יִצְרָא דְּכַעַס וְלִיבּוּן יֵצֶר דְּתַאֲוָה, דְּהַכֹּל נִמְשָׁךְ מִזֶּה.
which itself constitutes the eradication of anger and the purification of desire, everything flowing from this.
וּפוּרִים הוּא הַנַּיָיחָא שֶׁיֵּשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ.
And Purim is the serene rest that follows afterward.
וְהַנַּיָיחָא שֶׁל בִּיטּוּל הַכַּעַס וּרְצִיחָה מִן הַלֵּב הוּא קְדוּשַּׁת הַפּוּרִים דְּאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר,
And the repose of removing anger and violence from the heart is the sanctity of Purim on the fourteenth of Adar,
שֶׁמִּתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם בְּעֵת הַבִּיסּוּם עַד דְּלָא יָדַע אֵין לוֹ רְצִיחָה אֶלָּא עַל עֲמָלֵק, וּבְרָכָה וְטוֹבַת עַיִן לְזֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל.
wherein it is clarified that even while intoxicated 'until he knows not,' he harbors lethal fury solely against Amalek, and blessing and goodwill toward the seed of Israel.
וּקְדוּשַּׁת יוֹם חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר מְאִירָה דְּכָל תַּאֲווֹתָיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמָיִם.
And the sanctity of the fifteenth day (Shushan Purim) radiates the realization that all of his bodily desires are dedicated purely for the sake of Heaven.

sections.en: Darkness before Light

items.h: Creation advances through darkness that becomes the condition for greater light; even sin and collapse can become the ground from which Torah, awe, and holiness emerge.

Seif 1 — Light that Emerges from Darkness
The pattern of creation is descent before ascent, so prior failure can become the condition for deeper holiness.

p: הַסֵּדֶר שֶׁיִּסַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה: "בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא" (שַׁבָּת עז317 Shabbat 77b — R. Zeira found Rav Yehuda standing at the door of his father-in-law's house, and saw that he was in a cheerful mood, such that had he asked him about all the hollows of the world he would have told him. He said to him: Why do the goats walk at the front and the sheep after them? He said to him: It is as in the creation of the world — first darkness and afterward light. Rashi: "All the hollows of the world": that is, the things that happen throughout the space of the world. "First darkness": goats are generally black, and ewes generally white. Maharsha: Although the natural philosophers gave reasons for how each thing is formed, and the Talmud too has a few such ("why is the whole ear hard and the lobe soft"), these reasons are forced in their plain sense, so they must be meant as a parable on matters of Torah: Greece is likened to a goat ("and the he-goat grew exceedingly great", Daniel 8:8) and Israel to a sheep ("Israel is a scattered sheep", Jeremiah 50:17), and he asked why in the Second Temple the goats — the kings of Greece, Alexander of Macedon and those after him — reigned first, and only afterward the sheep, the kings of Israel. He answered that this was already alluded to in the creation of the world: first darkness — "and darkness was upon the face of the deep", which Bereshit Rabbah expounds of Greece, who darkened Israel's eyes — and afterward light, the Hasmonean kingdom, who came to reign through the miracle of the Chanukah lights. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 77b): The goats derive from the power of the attribute of judgment, which is the attribute of night; and night came before day because the attribute of judgment, by the very strength of that attribute, hastens to go forth into actuality. So too the goats walk at the head of the flock because of the swiftness of action they receive from the attribute of judgment — and this is what he answered him: as at the creation of the world. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 1): With respect to night, which is darkness, cessation and darkness come before day, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness...": for one who stands in darkness, darkness comes first and afterward light, and so there were two thousand years of chaos and afterward two thousand of Torah. But for one who stands in the day, day comes first and afterward night, to rest from his toil; and so once the Torah was given there was light for the world, and light comes before darkness. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 61): Esau was the firstborn in birth, which is the emergence into actuality, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness": on the side of the refuse the left is the right and comes first, and the this-world of Esau, in which darkness prevails, comes first. But in formation [yetzirah], which is the hidden world, the thought of creation and the conception of the world, the right comes first. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): The creation of the world was "first darkness and afterward light": first comes the portion of Bereishis, in the knowledge of the vessels, and afterward the attainment of the light of Abraham our father through knowledge, in the manner of "the advantage of light over darkness." Such too is the order of man's attainment of the light of the Blessed One, like the creation of the world: first the six days of work and afterward Shabbos; but for man's own action the light must come first and afterward the making of the vessel. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): This light [of the soul's root] can be attained in this world only through repentance, for such is the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light." Thus for certain righteous men, such as King David in the trial of Bathsheba, the Blessed One arranged a deed of the wicked in order to establish the yoke of repentance, for this cannot come about except through a preceding darkness. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): [In the Oral Torah and the innovation of laws not yet clarified] it is impossible to stand at all without a prior stumbling, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light," for so is the light attained by created beings: specifically out of darkness and concealment. Therefore Esau was formed before Jacob, being the preceding darkness that leads to the attainment of the light of Torah afterward. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 21): On "Why do the goats go first... as at the creation of the world, first darkness and afterward light," Rashi explains that goats are ordinarily black. So Teves, whose sign is the kid, is the aspect of darkness, and specifically then [the Hasmoneans] brought about their miracle through their self-sacrifice, to shine out of the darkness with greater excellence, as the Zohar says, "there is no light except that which comes out of darkness"; and this is like the creation of the world. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Sheidim 1): Since it is of the working of the Blessed One that it be so, "first darkness and afterward light," for the advantage of light is recognized only from darkness, [the forces of evil] therefore begin to act first, and from this the light shines forth, as in "He made darkness His hiding place," for there He is hidden. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): Such is the way of the Blessed One in the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light"; and so [the Sages] said that He would create worlds and destroy them, these being the worlds of chaos, until the world of rectification emerged. So it is in everything: all the incarnations of the Messiah that have already been in the world are akin to "creating worlds and destroying them," and specifically through those destructions the world of rectification is built, by raising up the lights of the broken vessels. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 174): Since in natural things the Blessed One established this order, "first darkness and afterward light," it is certainly the essence of His will, as [the Sages said], "In the place where penitents stand...". Although, Heaven forbid, one may not say "I will sin and repent" and do so by choice, it nonetheless happens of itself, for "there is no righteous man on earth..."; and such is the order: "the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light," far beyond one who did not walk in darkness. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): From the standpoint of this world's imagination it seemed at first that everything belonged to Esau, for such is the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light," as [the Sages] said at the beginning of Berakhos, which is why the evening Shema was placed first. For the Shema, the recognition of [God's] unity, was the essence of the creation of the world, and first one must recognize it out of darkness and concealment, for that was the whole matter of creation. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Shabbos): This is as it is written, "The Lord my God illuminates my darkness": after a person recognizes his sin and is pained over it, he merits that the Blessed One shines for him a rectification for it. Through the darkness, the remorse and pain he felt over the deed, he merits the light that reveals its rectification; and this is "first darkness and afterward light." Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 71): The Blessed One set the light in this world surrounded and encompassed by darkness, to leave man room to distinguish himself, that he remove the darkness and shine even within it. Therefore, when the Blessed One shines His bright light, He will shine it only for one who on his part walked in the light and did His will; He created the darkness only for the sake of one who desires the light, that for his sake He will illuminate the darkness too. Tiferes Yosef (Shavuos 7): It is written, "who forms light and creates darkness," yet at the creation of the world "there was evening and there was morning," first darkness and afterward light, so here too it should have said "creates darkness" first. The explanation: the first light was not yet within creation's capacity to receive, and light that creation cannot receive is called darkness from creation's standpoint; therefore it says "forms light and creates darkness," for from creation's standpoint it begins with day, since in the first evening creation had no grasp at all. Sod Yesharim (Shabbos HaGadol 6): As my father and teacher explained, the whole purpose of the darkness that the Blessed One set first is only that the light afterward be the more explicit; therefore "it was evening" is said first and then "it was morning." So too with Abraham our father: all the concealment he had at first, until he said, "Shall you say the palace has no master?", was the darkness that came first, only so that the Blessed One would afterward shine to him with greater clarity, "I am the master of the palace.":).
The order that Hashem, blessed be He, established in Creation is: "first darkness and then light" (Shabbat 77b).
כָּךְ הוּא בְּכָל יְמוֹת עוֹלָם,
So it is throughout all the days of the world:
אֵין לְךָ שׁוּם אוֹר מִתְגַּלֶּה אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ הַחֹשֶׁךְ הַקָּדוּם לוֹ.
you have no light revealed except out of the darkness that preceded it.
דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל: מַתַּן תּוֹרָה קָדַם לוֹ יְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם,
By way of example: the Giving of the Torah was preceded by the Exodus from Egypt,
וְעַד שֶׁשָּׁקְעוּ וְכוּלֵי;
and until they had sunk into the forty-nine gates of defilement, etc.;
וּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ עַל יְדֵי שְׁבִיַּת הָאָרוֹן לִפְלִשְׁתִּים, שֶׁהוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ לְגַמְרֵי,
and the building of the Holy Temple came about through the capture of the Ark by the Philistines, which was the total opposite;
וְהַגּוֹרֵם לָזֶה חֵטְא בְּנֵי עֵלִי,
and the cause of this was the sin of the sons of Eli,
הוּא מַמָּשׁ חֵטְא דְּנָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא שֶׁגָּרְמוּ קְדוּשָּׁה לַמִּשְׁכָּן,
which was literally like the sin of Nadav and Avihu who caused holiness to rest upon the Mishkan,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (זְבָחִים קטו:)318 Zevachim 115b — "And there I will meet with the children of Israel, and it shall be sanctified by My glory" — read not "by My glory" but "by My honored ones." This the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, but they did not know its meaning until the sons of Aaron died. Once the sons of Aaron died, he said to him: Aaron my brother, your sons died only to sanctify the name of the Holy One, blessed be He. When Aaron knew that his sons were beloved of the Omnipresent, he was silent and received a reward, as it is stated, "And Aaron was silent." Rashi: "And it shall be sanctified by My glory": this was said to Moses on the day he was commanded concerning the work of the Tabernacle, hinting to him that on the day He caused His Presence to rest upon the House it would be sanctified through His honored ones; but the hint was not such that he could understand what it meant until they died. "Only so that the glory of the Omnipresent be sanctified through them": to make known that He is awesome over those who fear Him and those intimate with Him — and this is "This is what the Lord spoke" [Leviticus 10:3]: [what He spoke] to me on the day I was commanded concerning the Tabernacle, "and it shall be sanctified by My glory," that is, through those honored and near to Me I will be sanctified. "As it is stated, And Aaron was silent": thus he was silent and received the reward, which Bereshit Rabbah explains was that on this account he merited to have the Divine word addressed to him alone, for the section on those who have drunk wine, stated after that episode, mentions not Moses but only Aaron. Tosafos (s.v. "and he received a reward for his silence"): It is taught in Torat Kohanim that as the reward for this the Divine word was addressed to him alone, for in the section "Do not drink wine or strong drink" it is written "And the Lord spoke to Aaron," and not "to Moses." This is puzzling, since the Sifrei, on "And [the Lord] spoke to Aaron" in the section of Korach, learns from "as the Lord spoke to him by the hand of Moses" that such speech was to Moses, to tell Aaron; perhaps, then, what it calls "addressed to him alone" is that Scripture writes "to Aaron," and not [a command] for him to tell the children of Israel. Tosafos (s.v. "the Holy One, blessed be He, hinted it to Moses, but he did not know it"): That is, he did not know through whom; but he did know that the Holy One, blessed be He, was going to sanctify the Tabernacle through a great man, for it is said in the Midrash that Moses said to Aaron, 'I had thought it would be through me or through you.' Maharsha (s.v. "the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, but he did not know"): Moses' words, 'your sons died only to sanctify the Name,' cannot mean that they died without sin, for there is no sanctification or glory of the Omnipresent in that — far be it from Him to execute judgment without justice; rather, it is His glory to exact punishment from the righteous in this world for the few transgressions in their hands, and thereby He is exalted, sanctified and feared: if so with the righteous, how much more with the wicked. The meaning, then, is that they did not die on account of this sin [as such], but because "round about Him it storms mightily" (Psalms 50:3) [— He is exacting with those near Him], and through them His Name is sanctified and feared. This is why Moses said, 'I had thought it would be through me or through you,' we being the nearer; but when he saw their death he said that they were the more honored, and that it was of them He had hinted "sanctified by My glory" — by My honored ones — to exact punishment from them for light transgressions. Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:2): Of Aaron it is written "And Aaron was silent": he accepted the attribute [of justice] of the Blessed Name in silence, and at once received a reward, as the Sages expounded (Torat Kohanim) from the next section, "And the Lord spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them" — to Elazar and Itamar — because they had been alike in silence and accepted the decree of the Omnipresent with love. For whoever accepts the decree of the Blessed Name is fit for recompense, since he takes the yoke upon himself; every yoke is the essence of service, and all service stands to be recompensed — so the acceptance of the decree is fit above all to receive a reward. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 18): Since man is physical, what he is to know must be made clear to him in a manner fitting a physical being; so, that all might know the sanctity of the Tabernacle, He said "and it shall be sanctified by My glory" — 'by My honored ones,' Nadav and Avihu, who would commit a sin and the House be sanctified through them. For He, blessed be He, who dwells in this House is separate from all beings, and that is the sanctity of the House; and this is shown in that even with the righteous He does not unite and has no joining with them. Were He joined to beings, He would surely be joined to those who love Him and are honored by Him, and then He would not execute judgment upon them; the judgment He executes upon the righteous shows that He, blessed be He, is entirely separate even from those who love Him. עַל פָּסוּק "וְנִקְדַּשׁ בִּכְבֹדִי".
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Zevachim 115b) on the verse "and it shall be sanctified by My glory."
וְעִיקַּר בִּנְיַן הַמִּשְׁכָּן גָּרַם חֵטְא הָעֵגֶל,
And the very building of the Mishkan was caused by the sin of the Golden Calf,
שֶׁבִּקְשׁוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל "אֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר יֵלְכוּ וְגוֹמֵר" מוּרְגָּשׁ לָעַיִן,
wherein Israel sought "gods that will walk before us, etc." tangible and sensible to the physical eye,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה פָּעֲלוּ קְדוּשַּׁת מִשְׁכָּן וְאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד,
and through this they brought about the sanctity of the Mishkan and the Tent of Meeting,
שֶׁהוּא מָקוֹם מוּרְגָּשׁ לָעַיִן הוֹלֵךְ לִפְנֵיהֶם שֶׁשָּׁם הַשָּׂגַת אֱלֹהוּת, "וְהָיָה כָּל מְבַקֵּשׁ ה' וְגוֹמֵר".
which is a tangible place apparent to the eye going before them where divine perception resides, "and it came to pass that everyone who sought Hashem, etc."
וְאַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן נִבְחַר עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִכְהֻנָּה גְּדוֹלָה,
And Aaron the Priest was chosen through this for the High Priesthood,
כִּי מֹשֶׁה אָמַר לוֹ: "הֵבֵאתָ עָלָיו חֲטָאָה גְדֹלָה",
for Moses said to him: "You have brought a great sin upon them,"
וּמִתּוֹךְ צְעָקָה זוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה בְּלִבּוֹ עַל כָּךְ
and out of this anguished cry that was in his heart over it,
וְהָיָה צוֹעֵק לַה' לְתַקֵּן זֶה
and he would cry out to Hashem to rectify this,
וּמְבַקֵּשׁ לְהָבִיא עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל זְכִיּוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת,
and sought to bring great merits upon Israel,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ319 Pirkei Avot 1:12 — Hillel says: Be of the disciples of Aharon — loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah. (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק א): "מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן וְכוּלֵי וּמְקָרְבָן לַתּוֹרָה",
and as they said (Avot 1:12): "the trait of Aaron, etc., and drawing them near to the Torah,"
עַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה לִכְהֻנָּה גְּדוֹלָה, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁהוּא הַמְכַפֵּר שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
through this he merited the High Priesthood, meaning that he serves as the atoner for all Israel.
וְכֵן כָּל דָּבָר, מִתּוֹךְ חֹשֶׁךְ יוֹצֵא אוֹר שֶׁהוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵיפֶךְ אוֹתוֹ הַחֹשֶׁךְ,
And so with every matter, out of darkness emerges a light that is the literal opposite of that very darkness,
בֵּין בַּדּוֹרוֹת בֵּין בִּפְרָטֵי נְפָשׁוֹת.
whether across the generations or within individual souls.
וְגוּף עִנְיַן הַמִּשְׁכָּן וּמִזְבֵּחַ וְסֵדֶר עֲבוֹדָה
And the essential nature of the Mishkan, the altar, and the sacrificial order
הוּא הוֹרָדַת הַשְּׁכִינָה בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים,
is the drawing down of the Shechinah into the lower realms,
וְסֵדֶר הַתִּיקּוּנִים וְכַפָּרוֹת שֶׁל חֲטָאִים,
and the order of rectifications and atonements for sins,
וְקִינּוּחַ לְכָל מִינֵי לִכְלוּכִים,
and the wiping away of all types of defilements,
וְיִפּוּי וְקִישּׁוּטֵי הַכַּלָּה,
and the beautification and adornments of the Bride;
וְהוּא נִמְשָׁךְ עַל יְדֵי שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים,
and this is drawn down through the dwelling of His Shechinah, blessed be He, in the lower world;
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁיֵּשׁ גִּלּוּי שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּקֶרֶב לִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
for once there is a revelation of His Shechinah within the hearts of the children of Israel,
מִמֵּילָא מִתְנַקֶּה כָּל לִכְלוּךְ וְנִדְחֶה הָרַע וְהַחֹשֶׁךְ,
automatically every impurity is cleansed and evil and darkness are dispelled,
דְּ"עִמֵּיהּ שְׁרֵי נְהוֹרָא",
for "light dwells with Him" (Daniel 2:22),
וְזֶהוּ "מִשְׁכָּן" – רָצָה לוֹמַר מְקוֹם שְׁכִינָה.
and this is Mishkan—meaning the dwelling place of the Shechinah.
אֲבָל "מִקְדָּשׁ" – רָצָה לוֹמַר מְקוֹם קְדוּשָּׁה,
However, Mikdash—meaning a place of kedushah (holiness)—
הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵיפֶךְ מִשְׁכָּן,
is the literal antithesis of Mishkan;
דִּקְדוּשָּׁה רָצָה לוֹמַר הַבְדָּלָה וְהַפְרָשָׁה שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר נִבְדָּל,
for kedushah denotes transcendence, separation, and withdrawal as a secluded entity,
אֲבָל שְׁכִינָה הוּא הַשּׁוֹכֵן וּמִתְחַבֵּר וְאֵין נִבְדָּל,
whereas Shechinah represents that which indwells, connects, and does not remain separate,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "הַשֹּׁכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טֻמְאֹתָם" (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב יוֹמָא נו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב320 Yoma 56b — "Who dwells with them in the midst of their impurity" (Lev. 16:16) — even at a time when they are impure, the Divine Presence is with them. Maharsha (Yoma 57a, s.v. "now you are certainly impure"): [The Sadducee] meant: even if you were once pure, now in exile you have certainly become impure, as it is written, "Her impurity is in her skirts," and He separates Himself from you as one keeps apart from the impurity of a menstruant. [R. Chanina] answered him from what is written of them, "that dwells with them [in the midst of their impurity]," that He does not separate entirely, but as a man keeps apart from his wife while she is a menstruant yet lives with her in one house; so the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells with us even now in exile, as it is said, "I will be with him in distress." Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 4): The Blessed One does not dwell in the midst of their impurity unless the sin was unwitting, and of that it is written, "And so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them in the midst of their impurity." [Hence the First Temple, whose distinction was that the Divine Presence rested in it,] was destroyed when they defiled the Sanctuary through idolatry, sexual immorality and bloodshed, the three sins that are called impurity. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 1): The Divine Presence does not depart even toward evening, in the time of darkness, as it is likewise said, "who dwells with them amid their impurity." For the souls of all Israel are bound and linked together as in a chain, so that the revelation of the Divine light — in concealment, hiddenness and great contraction — is not absent from the heart of any Jew; even the lowest of the low has in him a portion of life, a portion of God from above. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Regarding spiritual holiness it is said, "who dwells with them amid their impurity," and "the Divine Presence never departed from the Western Wall": in concealment it never departed, even in every kind of sinking into evil bitterer than death — "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." We suppose this a deficiency, but in truth it is the strength of completeness and the ultimate clarification: that wherever a person sinks, his heart remains bound to the Blessed One with a bond that cannot be severed. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The Holy One, blessed be He, as it were entered Egypt, the place of impurity, and this was the great miracle and the first of the miracles: the clarification of "I am the Lord who dwells with them amid their impurity," from their beginning and root in the Patriarchs, who are truly holy seed with no connection to any impurity, so that it was revealed that impurity has no real existence. Esther is the end: even in the lowest levels, where the nations hold sway, the Blessed One is with them, even in the place of impurity's greatest strength, as when Esther entered the house of Ahasuerus. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 4): Raising the holy sparks out of the matters of this world, by engaging in them for the sake of Heaven, is like a king's son returning from captivity, whose joy exceeds that of one who was always in the palace; of this it is said, "I am the Lord who dwells with them amid their impurity" — amid it precisely. Over this that wicked one [Bilaam] was blinded when he spoke of "the fourth of Israel" and said "He who is holy…," for he did not know that there is holiness even in bodily matters. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): So too the souls of Israel outside the Land are like the Tabernacle [dismantled in order to be rebuilt], for the Blessed One dwells with them amid their impurity and His Presence is within the hearts of Israel: wherever they were exiled the Divine Presence went into exile with them, and that place became their place. Through the exile they gather in the bit of good among the nations and return it all to holiness, and that place too becomes sanctified with the holiness of the air of the Land of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Even when sin caused Israel to be exiled among the nations, outside even the holiness of the Land, wherever they were exiled the Divine Presence went with them — for even "in the lands of their enemies I have not rejected them," and "I am the Lord who dwells with them amid their impurity." Nonetheless they are never separated from the root of holiness, and in the end all will be redeemed, even those wholly assimilated among the nations.),
as it is written: "Who dwells with them in the midst of their uncleanness" (and as written in Yoma 56b),
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קְדוּשָּׁה הוּא הַבְדָּלָה מִטֻּמְאָה.
in contrast to kedushah, which is separation from impurity.

וּמָצִינוּ מִשְׁכָּן דְּאִקְרֵי מִקְדָּשׁ, וּמִקְדָּשׁ אִקְרֵי מִשְׁכָּן (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רֵישׁ עֵירוּבִין321 Eruvin 2a — We find that the Tabernacle is called a Temple and that the Temple is called a Tabernacle. Granted, the Temple is called a Tabernacle, as it is written, "And I will set My Tabernacle among you" (Lev. 26:11). But whence do we know that the Tabernacle is called a Temple? Shall we say, from what is written, "And the Kohathites, bearers of the Sanctuary, set forward, and they set up the Tabernacle against their coming" (Num. 10:21)? Rashi: "And I will set My Tabernacle among you": when this verse was spoken the Tabernacle had already been erected, for it is written in Leviticus, and that whole book was spoken in the Tent of Meeting, as it is written, "And the Lord spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting." What Tabernacle, then, was He still promising them, if not the Temple? Tosafos (s.v. "We find that the Tabernacle is called a Temple"): The consequences of the equation are that its building does not override the Sabbath, and that a man may not enter it with the dust on his feet — which shows that Tabernacle and Temple are derived one from the other. But elsewhere (Shevuot 16b, Sotah 16a, Yoma 44a) the Gemara requires two separate verses for this; R. Nethanel answered that here no verse is needed, since the exposition really concerns the Temple alone, the Tabernacle having had no doors. Maharsha (Chidushei Halachot): As for Tosafot's first consequence, that the building does not override the Sabbath: although for the Tabernacle itself this is expounded from the juxtaposition of the Sabbath to the work of the Tabernacle, that is a mere support, and the Gemara does not cite it; the real derivation concerns the Temple, from "You shall keep My Sabbaths and revere My Sanctuary" (Yevamot 6a). And by Tosafot's own conclusion — that the two are derived from one another only in a matter that does not depend on the sanctity of the Tabernacle — these very two examples do depend on sanctity and are not so derived; Tosafot listed them only in passing, being sure that there are other consequences that do not depend on that sanctity. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 1): "We find the Tabernacle called a Temple" is the matter of "for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He [and His Shechinah]," whose meaning the Chavos Yair wrote he did not know. The Shechinah is the portion of God dwelling within the hearts of Israel, as in "I will set My Tabernacle among you"; the title "the Holy One" denotes holiness, which everywhere means separation — God's light, separate from human hearts and too great to be grasped, which He contracted into the light of His Shechinah within the hearts of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 2): [On "These are the accounts of the Tabernacle, the Tabernacle of the Testimony":] although the Sages said, "We find the Tabernacle called a Temple and the Temple called a Tabernacle," each is nevertheless called principally by its own particular name.),
And we find that the Mishkan is called Mikdash, and the Mikdash is called Mishkan (as written at the beginning of Eruvin 2a),
דְּכוּלָּא חַד וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת בְּיַחַד,
for all is one and both truths coexist simultaneously:
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגַם נִבְדָּל מֵהֶם,
that the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells within the children of Israel and is also transcendent above them,

כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁאִיתָא בְּתַנָּא דְבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ג322 Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 3:1 — King David further said: My fear came out of my joy and my joy out of my fear, and my love rose above them both. Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, made a covenant with me that I should be versed in Scripture, in Mishnah, in the laws and in the aggadot, as it is stated: "For is not my house so with God? For He has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure" (II Samuel 23:5). And there is no covenant other than Torah, as it is stated: "My covenant was with him, life and peace" (Malachi 2:5). Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The joy the Blessed One desires is possible only when the separating screen is removed; therefore Tanna DeBei Eliyahu says, "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear," for the joy of Israel is only that which comes out of fear, and so it says both "Serve the Lord in fear" and "Serve the Lord in joy," since both are needed together. This is the proper joy, as opposed to the frivolous joy of filling the appetites of this world. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): Fear of Heaven in the heart arouses one to wisdom, leading to the Torah of the mind and then back to the fear in the heart from which good deeds issue; this is also what Tanna DeBei Eliyahu says, "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear" — the joy is in Torah, as it is written, "The precepts of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart." Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 79): The unification and interweaving of the two Divine Names is what Tanna DeBei Eliyahu says, "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear": in truth the Blessed One's essence is one, single and unique, and there are only two lights, that is, two kinds of perception for the human soul — when it perceives the Shechinah of the Blessed One within it, fear and shame come upon it, and when it perceives the infinite light, it attains joy. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 13): With the Blessed One love and fear are mixed together, in the sense of "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear"; in truth everything was said in a single utterance, and only from man's side does he use sometimes the one and sometimes the other, as needed to overcome the inclination. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 13): [Isaac's laughter, drawn from joy,] belongs to holiness, as Tanna DeBei Eliyahu says, "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear": the holy gevuros are the full force of the fear of the Blessed One, because He is Master and Ruler, and one has joy from this as well; whereas the evil gevurah of anger and murder is the opposite of joy, and the laughter that comes from it is only mockery of His creatures. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 4): Every other fear is dread of some harm, and one wishes to be free of it; but of the fear of God it says, "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear": joy in God brings one to fear Him for His exaltedness, which he recognizes through his joy, as in "rejoice with trembling"; and out of the fear, which comes from sensing the light of the revelation of His Presence within his heart, he comes to joy. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 147): [The vine signifies fear, and] "wine gladdens the heart," as Tanna DeBei Eliyahu says, "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear": for when one knows that the Blessed One does everything and that it is He who gives him strength and might, from this flow both fear and joy. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Berakhos): Joining redemption to prayer means joining joy and trust to fear; and since uniting joy and fear — as in "My fear out of my joy and my joy out of my fear" — is not within man's grasp but comes only from the Blessed One's salvation, one in whose hand God has made this succeed has a sign that he is a son of the World to Come.):
like that which is found in Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah (beginning of Chapter 3):
"אֲנִי יָרֵאתִי מִתּוֹךְ שִׂמְחָתִי, וְשָׂמַחְתִּי מִתּוֹךְ יִרְאָתִי".
"I feared out of my joy, and I rejoiced out of my fear."
הַשִּׂמְחָה הוּא אִישׁ בְּרֵעֵהוּ וְכַדּוֹמֶה מִתּוֹךְ הָאַהֲבָה וְהַהִתְחַבְּרוּת,
Joy arises between a man and his friend and the like out of love and intimacy,
וְהַיִּרְאָה הוּא מִצַּד הַדֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ מֵאָדָם שֶׁגָּדוֹל וְנִבְדָּל מִמֶּנּוּ.
while fear/awe stems from respectful deference toward one who is great and elevated above him.
וְאֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הֵם שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחַד,
And regarding Hashem, blessed be He, both aspects exist together,
וְהָא בְּלֹא הָא לָא סַגִּי,
and neither can suffice without the other;
דְּיִרְאָה לְבַד מֵבִיא שְׁטוּת, כְּעִנְיַן "הֲלֹא יִרְאָתְךָ כִּסְלָתֶךָ וְגוֹמֵר",
for awe alone brings folly, in the vein of "Is not your fear your foolish confidence, etc." (Job 4:6),
וְשִׂמְחָה לְבַד מֵבִיא קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ,
and joy alone brings frivolity,

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ323 Shabbat 31a — Rava said: When a man is brought in for judgment they say to him — Did you deal faithfully in business? Did you set fixed times for Torah? Did you engage in procreation? Did you hope for salvation? Did you debate matters of wisdom? Did you understand one thing from another? And even so, only if the fear of the Lord is his treasure — yes; if not — no. This may be compared to a man who said to his messenger: Take up a kor of wheat to the upper storey for me. He went and took it up. He said to him: Did you mix into it a kav of preservative? He said: No. He said to him: Better that you had not taken it up at all. Rashi: "Did you set fixed times": since a person must occupy himself with worldly affairs — for if there are no worldly affairs there is no Torah — he must set times for Torah, a fixed measure, so that the whole day is not drawn after worldly affairs. "Procreation" is the verse's "strength" and "understood one thing from another" is its "knowledge"; "hope for salvation" — as the prophets foretold. The "kav of preservative" is salty earth, which keeps the produce from becoming wormy. Maharsha: The verse just before — "The Lord is exalted… He has filled Zion with justice and righteousness" (Isaiah 33:5) — speaks of the judgment of the future, when these things are asked. The "fixed times" are two, one by day and one by night; he says not "did you fulfill" but "did you engage in procreation", that is, by marrying off an orphan boy and girl; "salvation" answers to the verse's plural "salvations", for one who hopes for it every hour hopes many times; and "debated in wisdom" excludes empty pilpul — the aim must be to reason with intellect, wisdom and knowledge. The parable means that wheat taken up to the storehouse does not keep without the preservative, and so all of these endure in that storehouse only through the fear of the Lord. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 2; similarly Netzach Yisrael 29): The judgment asks whether a man lived as befits one who bears a soul from the separate, higher beings: they take nothing from one another, so he is asked first whether he dealt faithfully and took nothing not due to him; fixed times for Torah show that the intellect is his essence and not incidental; through procreation he is no longer a mere individual, just as the separate beings are not; hoping for the salvation, when the world will pass wholly from potential into actuality, places him in actuality as they always are; and debating wisdom and understanding one thing from another are wholly of the separate intellect. Yet even with all these he needs the fear of the Lord, for man is an effect with no existence of his own except through his Cause, and only through fear, which shows that he has a Cause whom he fears, is he sustained by it — hence it is called his "treasure", for a storehouse preserves, like the kav of preservative without which even the finest grain does not keep. It does not say "the love of the Lord is his treasure", for only in fear does a man know himself to be an effect sustained by its Cause. Sha'ar HaEmunah (Entrance to the Gate 1): The fear of the Lord is the vessel for receiving the Torah, as it says, "the fear of the Lord is his treasure"; so in Shabbat, "Faithfulness" is the Order of Zera'im (as Tosafos explain, for he believes in the Life of the worlds and sows), and the Gemara concludes, "even so, if the fear of the Lord is his treasure, yes; if not, no." The matter is that the beginning of judgment is about faith, for faith is the root of fear and fear is the vessel that holds the faith: a person believes in the Blessed One, and through faith in His surpassing power and exaltedness [comes to fear Him]. (שַׁבָּת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד א): "מוּטָב שֶׁלֹּא הֶעֱלֵיתָ",
and concerning this they said (Shabbat 31a end): "It were better you had not brought it up,"
דְּבַתּוֹרָה נֶאֱמַר: "מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב",
for regarding Torah it is said: "gladdening the heart,"
וְעַל יָדָהּ הוּא הַהִתְחַבְּרוּת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and through it comes intimate connection to Hashem, blessed be He.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּתְפִלָּה נִקְרָא: "וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל",
In contrast, regarding prayer it is called: "and I will be sanctified among the children of Israel,"
דְּלָכֵן מִצְוַת תְּפִלָּה בְּצִבּוּר,
which is why the mitzvah of communal prayer,
שֶׁהוּא הַכָּרַת הַקְּדוּשָּׁה וְשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִבְדָּל,
which represents the recognition of holiness and that Hashem is transcendent,
הוּא עַל יְדֵי רִיבּוּי הַמִּתְאַחֵד;
is actualized through a unified plurality;

וְ"כָל בֵּי עֲשָׂרָה שְׁכִינְתָא שַׁרְיָא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין לט.)324 Sanhedrin 39a — The emperor said to Rabban Gamliel: You say that wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests. How many Divine Presences are there? Rabban Gamliel summoned the emperor's servant and struck him on the neck. He said to him: Why did you let the sun into the emperor's house? He said to him: The sun rests upon the whole world. He said to him: And if the sun, which is one of a thousand thousand myriads of attendants who stand before the Holy One, blessed be He, rests upon the whole world, the Divine Presence of the Holy One, blessed be He, how much more so. Rashi: Rabban Gamliel summoned the servant of the heretic [i.e., the emperor] and struck him on his neck; and the reply, "The sun rests upon the whole world," was the heretic's own. Maharsha: This is explained by what I wrote on the aggadot of the Elders of Athens [Bekhorot 8b]: the Holy One, blessed be He, has no bound of place, as it is said, "the whole earth is full of His glory," and "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place" — for He is the place of the world, and the world is not His place. The heretic, who believes in corporeality, will not accept this, and the emperor inclined to that belief; hence he asked how many Divine Presences there must be in so many places, if it rests wherever there are ten. So Rabban Gamliel brought him an analogy and a proof from the sun, which is a body and a single simple element and yet rests upon the whole world: all the more does the Divine Presence, which is not a body, rest upon the whole world, bounded by no place. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:4): "Wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests" means that [ten] is called Knesses Yisrael, of which it is said, "I am the Lord who dwells with them in the midst [of their impurity]": the Blessed One testifies that the depth of their longing is for Him alone, even when the heart is full of ulterior motives and stray thoughts, and so their prayer is a complete unification. With an individual, by contrast, the Blessed One does not yet set His seal at once, and until He testifies it is not clear that his desire is truly for God alone. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 55): [Rebecca's] bracelets, the ornament of the hands that signifies completeness of deed, weighed ten, as in "Wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests" — that is, even without any act of mitzvah; for ten denotes general completeness, the good brought into the heart in full once evil has been removed, so that the Divine Presence rests within him until he needs no deed at all. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Before [Joseph's] soul could be revealed in this world there had to be a complete congregation devoted to the Blessed One, for "Wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests" — since they bear the name of a congregation, the Shechinah rests among the seed of Jacob, who are a congregation; Isaac and Jacob, the fathers who beget the congregation, are not within it but above it. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Kedoshim): "The congregation of the children of Israel" is wherever Israel gather as an assembly for the sake of Heaven, as the Gemara says, "Wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests"; there the Shechinah necessarily dwells with them. Therefore we were commanded to be refined and holy, like a king who says to his friend: since you have obliged me to go with you, see that you do not lead me through filthy places. Beis Yaakov (Toldos 29): Holiness everywhere is at ten, as the Gemara says, "Wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests": that is, from man's side it is ten; somewhat above his grasp it is a hundred; and higher still, with the Blessed One, it is a thousand, which is why it says "Holy, holy, holy.",
and "wherever ten gather, the Shechinah rests" (Sanhedrin 39a),
שֶׁהֵם קוֹמָה שְׁלֵימָה,
for they constitute an entire spiritual stature,
דִּבְנֵי אָדָם אֵין דַּעְתָּן שָׁוָה,
since people's minds are not identical,
וְכָל עֶשֶׂר דֵּעוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת,
and there are ten distinct viewpoints;
כַּאֲשֶׁר הֵם עֶשֶׂר נְפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, שְׁכִינְתָא שַׁרְיָא מִמֵּילָא,
yet when they are ten Jewish souls, the Shechinah rests upon them automatically,

דְּקָדְמָה וְאָתְיָא (בְּרָכוֹת ו.)325 Berakhot 6a — And whence do we know that when ten pray, the Divine Presence is with them? For it is said, "God stands in the congregation of God." And since [the Divine Presence rests] even upon three [who sit in judgment], was it necessary to state ten? For ten, the Divine Presence comes ahead and is already there; for three, not until they are seated. Rashi: "Whence do we know [that when] ten [pray]" — a congregation is constituted by ten, as it is said, "How long shall this evil congregation [murmur against Me]" — Caleb and Joshua being excluded [from the twelve spies]. "The Divine Presence comes ahead" — before all ten have assembled, for "stands in the congregation of God" implies from the outset; "until they are seated" — as it is written "He judges," that is, at the time of judgment. Maharsha: All these — ten, three, two and one — are already a complete mishnah in the third chapter of Avot, which brings them from these same verses; but there they are all cited with regard to Torah study, whereas here each verse is genuinely needed, as the Gemara's series of questions shows. The explanation is that of ten who pray it says "God stands," as it were standing there with those who pray, for one may not sit within four cubits of a man praying; while of three sitting in judgment, whose mitzvah is performed seated, it says "in the midst of the judges He judges," as they are seated — whence the conclusion, "for three, not until they are seated." Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:6): Ten are wholly fit for the Divine Presence, so that there is no difference between ten, a hundred and a thousand; therefore the Divine Presence comes ahead of them, as it is written, "their king passed on before them and the Lord at their head." One should not say that a recipient is needed here, for a recipient would be required only for a number less than ten, which belongs to the lower world; but the number ten is everywhere set apart for holiness, reaching the rank of the separate world, and so it needs no one to receive the glory of the Presence. When they are three, however, the man counts as the recipient of the Divine Presence, and the recipient must come first — hence "not until they are seated." בְּלִי שׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
having preceded and arrived (Berakhot 6a) without any human exertion,
וְהוּא מִצַּד קְדוּשַּׁת הַמִּקְדָּשׁ;
and this derives from the transcendent holiness of the Mikdash;
דְּיָחִיד הָעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה שְׁכִינָה עִמּוֹ,
whereas regarding an individual studying Torah with whom the Shechinah rests,
הַיְינוּ כְּפִי הַשָּׂגָתוֹ וְדַעְתּוֹ לְבַד,
this corresponds solely to his personal intellectual capacity and mind;
זֶהוּ קְדוּשַּׁת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד שֶׁהָיָה עִיקָּרוֹ לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
this being the immanent sanctity of the Mishkan and the Tent of Meeting which was primarily dedicated to words of Torah,
וְהַבְּלִיטָה בִּקְדוּשָּׁה זוֹ הוּא שֵׁם "מִשְׁכָּן", דַּ"אֲנִי ה' שֹׁכֵן וְגוֹמֵר",
and the prominent feature of this sanctity is the name Mishkan, as in "I am Hashem Who dwells, etc.,"
וְזוֹ אֵינָהּ קְבוּעָה.
and this degree is not permanent.

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים פא326 Nedarim 81a — And why is it not common for Torah scholars to have Torah scholars issue from their sons? Rav Yosef said: So that people should not say that the Torah is an inheritance for them. Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi says: So that they should not lord it over the community. Mar Zutra says: Because they domineer over the community. Rav Ashi says: Because they call ordinary people "donkeys." Ravina says: Because they do not first recite the blessing over the Torah. Rashi: "So that they should not say" — so that people should not say that the Torah is an inheritance for them and that we need not trouble ourselves to learn it; "so that they should not lord it over the community" — that they should not assume authority when they see that they and their fathers and their sons are all Torah scholars. "Because they call ordinary people donkeys" — because they do not treat them with respect but despise them on account of the Torah they possess. "Because they do not first recite the blessing over the Torah" — when they rise early for study; scholars who are the sons of scholars, being diligent and accustomed in Torah, are not careful to bless when they begin. Tosafos: "The Torah is an inheritance" — for the Torah scholars, and [people say] we need not trouble ourselves to learn it; and "so that they should not lord it over the community." "They do not first recite a blessing over the Torah" — when they rise early to study they do not recite "to engage in words of Torah," "make pleasant," and "who chose us." Maharsha: "Because they domineer over the community" — the Arukh reads here too "lord themselves"; the two opinions differ in this, that one holds it is not a punishment but a safeguard, to keep them from coming to self-aggrandizement, while the other holds it is a punishment for the offense of domineering over the community. "Because they call ordinary people donkeys" — as though by the very nature of their creation they were unfit for wisdom, like this donkey; and on their own premise that one begets his like, the objection follows: since they themselves are scholars, why are their sons not scholars? Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 81a): "So that they should not say that the Torah is an inheritance for them": intellectual wisdom is separate from man, and inheritance does not apply to it, for a man bequeaths to his son only what is bodily, since his kinship to his son is on the side of the body alone; he bequeaths stature and beauty and the like, but not a thing entirely separate from bodily man, as the Torah is. As for "they do not first recite the blessing over the Torah" — Heaven forbid that they did not bless at all; they blessed with the mouth, but they did not bless the Holy One for the giving of the Torah with the whole intention of heart that so great a good deserves, and so they were not cleaving to the Torah as they should, and therefore no scholars issue from them. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:145): Hence the difference between "Torah scholars' sons are not Torah scholars" and what they said in Eduyos, "a father confers merit on his son in wisdom": "confers merit" means by virtue of his righteousness, not by virtue of his wisdom. For the Torah scholar and the righteous man who serves God, the pillars of Torah and of service, correspond to mind and heart; from the heart "are the issues of life," the extension of the seven lower [attributes] into the body, and these are the seven things in which a father confers merit on his son, whereas from the side of the mind there is no such extension. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): From the standpoint of Torah, inheritance by one's offspring does not apply, for it is ownerless to all; on the contrary, the Blessed One is particular that people should not say the Torah is an inheritance, as they said, "Why is it not common for Torah scholars [to have sons who are Torah scholars]..." Therefore Moses our teacher did not bequeath his crown to his sons — not on his own account, although a father confers merit on his son in wisdom, but because the Blessed One did not wish it on account of the generation, which was not worthy and could have erred [into thinking] that Torah is an inheritance. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, Thirteen Principles of Conduct 10): One who is righteous, his offspring too is not forsaken, and is a Torah scholar; and though "Torah scholars are not commonly succeeded by sons who are Torah scholars," that refers to [sons who are] likewise exceedingly great. And it returns to the seed of their seed: whoever is a Torah scholar, and his son and his grandson, is assured that it will not cease..):
And in line with what they said (Nedarim 81a):
דְּאֵין תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מְצוּיִים לִהְיוֹת בְּנֵיהֶם תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים,
that it is uncommon for the children of Torah scholars to become Torah scholars,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ קְבִיעוּת בְּמָקוֹם מְיוּחָד לְבַד,
for it is not fixed in one exclusive place,
שֶׁהוּא קְדוּשָּׁה מִצַּד הִתְחַבְּרוּת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּדְבֵיקוּת,
being a sanctity born of intimate union and cleaving to Hashem, blessed be He;
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהִתְחַבְּרוּת אֵינוֹ בִּקְבִיעוּת,
and it is known that passionate union is not constant,
וְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת אַהֲבָה וּדְבֵיקוּת הוּא רַק לִפְרָקִים,
and the arousal of love and cleaving occurs only intermittently,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּתְמִידוּת הוּא הַיִּרְאָה.
whereas constant and enduring throughout is awe.
וּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ נִקְרָא "בֵּית תְּפִלָּתִי",
And the Holy Temple is designated "the house of My prayer,"
וְכֵן דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּטַעַם "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה",
and likewise the spiritual rung of King David, peace be upon him, mirroring "and I am prayer,"
וְכֵן כֹּהֵן בַּעֲבוֹדָה דְּהַיְינוּ תְּפִלָּה,
and so too the priest in the sacrificial service, which is prayer,
זֶה נִכְרַת בְּרִית עוֹלָם וְהוּא קְדוּשָּׁה קְבוּעָה.
this was forged as an eternal covenant, constituting an immutable, permanent sanctity.
וּמֶלֶךְ דּוֹמֶה לְצִבּוּר,
And a king is comparable to the community,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
as they said in Rosh Hashanah

(יְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ג: מֶלֶךְ וְצִבּוּר נִדּוֹנִין בְּכָל יוֹם וְכוּלֵי, "מִשְׁפַּט עַבְדּוֹ וּמִשְׁפַּט עַמּוֹ וְגוֹמֵר דְּבַר יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ327 Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 1:3 — R. Isaac the Elder in the name of Rabbi: A king and a community are judged every day. What is the reason? "To maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel, each day's matter in its day" (I Kings 8:59)."),
(Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 1:3: a king and the community are judged every day, "the cause of His servant and the cause of His people, as every day shall require"),
דְּהוּא הַמְאַסֵּף הָעָם,
for the king unites and gathers the entire people,
וְהַכָּרָתוֹ קְדוּשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִצַּד דֵּעוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁל כָּל אָדָם,
and his perception of Hashem's sanctity encompasses the diverse viewpoints of all men;
זֶהוּ הַכָּרַת קְדוּשָּׁה דְּמִקְדָּשׁ מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא נִבְדָּל,
this being the comprehension of the Mikdash's holiness—that He is transcendent,
וְלֹא בְּהִתְחַבְּרוּת כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ לְבַד.
and not merely through intimate communion according to his personal intellect alone.
וְזֶה עִנְיַן "וְנִקְדַּשׁ בִּכְבֹדִי" דְּמִשְׁכָּן אִקְרֵי מִקְדָּשׁ,
And this is the secret of "and it shall be sanctified by My glory," wherein the Mishkan is called Mikdash,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גַּם קְדוּשָּׁה זוֹ שֶׁל מִדַּת הַכָּבוֹד וְדֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה יִרְאָה;
in that it also contains this transcendent holiness of the attribute of Glory, reverent etiquette, and awe;
זֶה נַעֲשָׂה עַל יְדֵי מִיתַת נָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא שֶׁהֵבִיא יִרְאָה גְּדוֹלָה,
and this was effected through the death of Nadav and Avihu which generated profound awe;
כִּי תְּחִלַּת בְּלִיטַת קְדוּשָּׁה זוֹ דִּשְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּקִרְבֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגַם בְּטֻמְאוֹתָם,
for the initial emergence of this indwelling sanctity of Hashem within the midst of Israel, even in their uncleanness,
הוֹלִיד שִׂמְחָה וְתֹקֶף אַהֲבָה וְחֵשֶׁק וְהִתְקָרְבוּת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
bored forth joy, intense love, passion, and drawing near to Hashem, blessed be He.
וְזֶה עִנְיַן (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב)328 Vayikra Rabbah 12:1 — R. Shimon says: Aharon's sons died only because they entered the Tent of Meeting drunk with wine. "שְׁתוּיֵי יַיִן נִכְנְסוּ" –
And this is what is meant by (Vayikra Rabbah 12:1) "they entered drunk with wine"—
פֵּירוּשׁ בְּשִׂמְחָה יְתֵירָה, כִּי "יַיִן יְשַׂמַּח וְגוֹמֵר",
meaning in excessive ecstatic joy, for "wine gladdens, etc.",
וְלֹא שִׁיתְּפוּ הַיִּרְאָה עִמָּהּ;
and they failed to join awe together with it;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה פָּרָשַׁת בְּהַעֲלֹתְךָ)329 Bamidbar Rabbah 15:24 — They too had been light-headed when they went up to Mount Sinai and saw the Divine Presence: "And they beheld God, and they ate and drank" (Ex. 24:11). Was there eating and drinking there? To what may the matter be compared? To a servant attending his master with his rations in his hand, and he keeps biting at them. So did they act light-headedly, as though eating and drinking. The elders, and Nadab and Abihu, deserved to be burned at that very hour; but because the day of the giving of the Torah was precious before the Holy One, blessed be He, He did not wish to strike them on that day and make a breach among them — as it is written, "And upon the nobles of the children of Israel He did not lay His hand," implying that they deserved to have a hand laid upon them. But after a time He exacted it from them: Nadab and Abihu were burned when they entered the Tent of Meeting. גַּם כֵּן
and as our Sages of blessed memory also taught (Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Beha'alotekha)
דִּכְבָר נִגְזַר עֲלֵיהֶם מִקּוֹדֶם עַל "וַיֶּחֱזוּ [אֶת] הָאֱלֹהִים וַיֹּאכְלוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
that judgment had already been decreed upon them previously regarding "and they beheld God and ate, etc.",
דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן מִיעוּט דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְיִרְאָה,
which was likewise a deficiency in reverent etiquette and awe,
וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתֹּקֶף שֶׁנִּתְעוֹרֵר בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה דַּ"ה' עֹז לְעַמּוֹ יִתֵּן",
stemming from the sheer intensity awakened at the Giving of the Torah, "Hashem gives strength unto His people,"
וְנִתְעוֹרֵר עוֹד יוֹתֵר בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַמִּשְׁכָּן.
and stirred even more vigorously within the immanent holiness of the Mishkan.

אֶלָּא דְּאָז הִתְחִיל לְהוֹפִיעַ גַּם כֵּן אוֹר הַמִּקְדָּשׁ (זְבָחִים קטו330 Zevachim 115b — "And there I will meet with the children of Israel, and it shall be sanctified by My glory" — read not "by My glory" but "by My honored ones." This the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, but they did not know its meaning until the sons of Aaron died. Once the sons of Aaron died, he said to him: Aaron my brother, your sons died only to sanctify the name of the Holy One, blessed be He. When Aaron knew that his sons were beloved of the Omnipresent, he was silent and received a reward, as it is stated, "And Aaron was silent." Rashi: "And it shall be sanctified by My glory": this was said to Moses on the day he was commanded concerning the work of the Tabernacle, hinting to him that on the day He caused His Presence to rest upon the House it would be sanctified through His honored ones; but the hint was not such that he could understand what it meant until they died. "Only so that the glory of the Omnipresent be sanctified through them": to make known that He is awesome over those who fear Him and those intimate with Him — and this is "This is what the Lord spoke" [Leviticus 10:3]: [what He spoke] to me on the day I was commanded concerning the Tabernacle, "and it shall be sanctified by My glory," that is, through those honored and near to Me I will be sanctified. "As it is stated, And Aaron was silent": thus he was silent and received the reward, which Bereshit Rabbah explains was that on this account he merited to have the Divine word addressed to him alone, for the section on those who have drunk wine, stated after that episode, mentions not Moses but only Aaron. Tosafos (s.v. "and he received a reward for his silence"): It is taught in Torat Kohanim that as the reward for this the Divine word was addressed to him alone, for in the section "Do not drink wine or strong drink" it is written "And the Lord spoke to Aaron," and not "to Moses." This is puzzling, since the Sifrei, on "And [the Lord] spoke to Aaron" in the section of Korach, learns from "as the Lord spoke to him by the hand of Moses" that such speech was to Moses, to tell Aaron; perhaps, then, what it calls "addressed to him alone" is that Scripture writes "to Aaron," and not [a command] for him to tell the children of Israel. Tosafos (s.v. "the Holy One, blessed be He, hinted it to Moses, but he did not know it"): That is, he did not know through whom; but he did know that the Holy One, blessed be He, was going to sanctify the Tabernacle through a great man, for it is said in the Midrash that Moses said to Aaron, 'I had thought it would be through me or through you.' Maharsha (s.v.
