Maharsha: Scripture need not have said "on the seventh day"; it comes to teach that it was on the Sabbath, which is called "the seventh," that his heart was merry with wine. Not so Israel, whose heart is not then merry with wine; rather, once they have eaten and drunk they begin with words of Torah, whereas the nations begin with words of licentiousness. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar 4): We do find songs and praises even in this world, and Israel are praised for beginning with words of Torah and words of praise when they eat and drink on the Sabbath; yet from "Then our mouth will be filled with laughter and our tongue with song" the Sages derive that one may not fill one's mouth with laughter in this world, and by the same token song should be forbidden. [He answers that] the full revelation of joy belongs to the future, which is called "then"; but on the Sabbath, when the Ancient One is revealed, the mouth too is opened to say songs and praises, and this also falls under "then our mouth will be filled." (יב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב):
and as they stated in Megillah (12b):
"יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּשֶׁאוֹכְלִין וְשׁוֹתִין עוֹסְקִים בְּשִׁירוֹת וְתִשְׁבָּחוֹת, וְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְכוּלֵי",
"When Israel eat and drink they engage in songs and praises of God, whereas the nations of the world engage in frivolity, etc.",
שֶׁאָז אָדָם נִיכָּר בְּכוֹסוֹ וְגוֹבֵר כֹּחַ הַדִּמְיוֹן, נִיכָּר שָׁרְשׁוֹ.
for at that moment when a man is tested in his cup and his imagination takes over, his holy soul-root is openly revealed.
וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן פּוּרִים: "וְנַהֲפוֹךְ הוּא וְגוֹמֵר",
And this is the inner meaning of Purim: "and it was turned to the contrary, etc." (Esther 9:1),
"דְּלָא יָדַע",
"that he did not know"

דִּבְשִׁבְעָה בַּאֲדָר מֵת מֹשֶׁה וּבְשִׁבְעָה בַּאֲדָר נוֹלָד (שָׁם יג421 Megillah 13b — "They cast pur, that is, the lot" (Esther 3:7). It was taught: Once the lot fell in the month of Adar, he rejoiced greatly. He said: The lot has fallen for me in the month in which Moses died. But he did not know that on the seventh of Adar Moses died, and on the seventh of Adar he was born. Rashi: “They cast pur” — and what is the pur? It is the lot, cast “from day to day,” as to which day of the month the lot would fall upon, and likewise “from month to month”; and he cast the lot for them all on a single day. That Moses died on the seventh of Adar is reckoned back from “the people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month” (Joshua 4:19), deducting the thirty days of mourning for Moses and the three days in which they prepared provisions; and that he was born on the seventh of Adar is learned from “I am a hundred and twenty years old this day” (Deuteronomy 31:2) — this day my days and my years are fulfilled — and the birth is fit to atone for the death. Maharsha: That Moses died on the seventh of Adar is in some measure explicit in the verses, but that he was born on that day is only an exposition of the Sages, from “I am a hundred and twenty years old this day,” which teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, fills out the years of the righteous from day to day — and this exposition Haman did not know. It appears further, from the precision of “on the seventh of Adar he died,” that Haman rejoiced over the day as well: the lot he cast “from day to day” fell on the thirteenth of Adar, which lies within the seven days of mourning for Moses, who died on the seventh. Maharal (Ohr Chadash, Esther 3:7): When Haman cast lots to learn which time was the end of Israel and the lot fell on Adar, he rejoiced, for in that month Moses died, the master of Israel who is reckoned the form of all Israel, and he thought that this month, the last of the months, signified, Heaven forfend, the end of Israel as well. But he did not know that Moses was also born on the seventh of Adar: a thing that is complete has its end joined to its beginning, as in a sphere, so that Moses' end signified not cessation but completion, and what is complete returns to the Holy One, blessed be He, from whom it began. So too Israel: though they have an end, that end is only a completion, joined to their beginning in Nisan, when the Holy One, blessed be He, brought them out of Egypt, and from His side they have eternal existence. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Therefore [Haman] rejoiced when the lot fell on Adar, for on this basis he imagined he had a claim against Israel, his proof being that Moses died then — for he understood death as it is among the nations, where the power is cut off entirely. But with Israel it is not so — "the sun rises and the sun sets": the earlier setting is what brings about the rising that follows, through the spreading of that power, and the proof is that Moses was also born then; on the contrary, that month is set apart for Israel's triumph over the nations. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar 2): Moses represents the revelation of the light "that it was good" of the Written Torah — as it says, "she saw him, that he was good," and when he was born the whole house was filled with light. When Haman saw that Moses died in Adar — that is, that the light of the Written Torah was hidden away — he thought he would thereby be able to prevail; but he did not know that this was precisely the cause of the revelation of the "light sown for the righteous" from the Oral Torah, as indeed at Moses' passing the Oral Torah at once shone forth through Osniel ben Kenaz, who restored the forgotten laws through his dialectic. This is "on the seventh of Adar he was born": precisely then the light sown for the righteous was born.:);
that on the seventh of Adar Moses died and on the seventh of Adar he was born (Megillah 13b);
הַיְינוּ דְּמִיתַת מֹשֶׁה הוּא גְּנִיזַת אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה וְהַחָכְמָה, וּמִמֵּילָא גּוֹבֵר הַדִּמְיוֹן;
meaning that the death of Moses represents the concealment of the light of Torah and wisdom, automatically causing illusion to surge;
וּבֶאֱמֶת אָז נוֹלָד,
yet in deeper truth, he was then reborn,
כִּי אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יְדֵי הִתְגַּבְּרוּת הַדִּמְיוֹן
for within Israel, through the very intensification of illusion
עַד שֶׁכְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה הַדִּמְיוֹן שׁוֹלֵט וְגוֹבֵר,
to the point where outwardly illusion appears completely dominant,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְהַפֵּךְ לְהִיוָּלֵד אוֹר הַחָכְמָה שֶׁהֵיפוּךְ לַדִּמְיוֹן מַמָּשׁ.
through that very descent it inverts to birth the divine light of wisdom, the exact opposite of illusion.
כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר מִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁגַּם בְּעֵת הַדִּמְיוֹן הוּא דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת,
For once it becomes clear that even amid illusion a person remains bound to Hashem in ultimate truth,
וְהוּא שָׂם אֶל לְבָבוֹ זֶה,
and he takes this deeply to heart,
לָדַעַת כִּי מֵאַיִן לוֹ כֹּחַ לַחְשׁוֹב וּלְהַרְהֵר שׁוּם דָּבָר אִם לֹא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
realizing that from where could he possess the capacity to think or imagine anything were it not empowered by Hashem,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִמֵּילָא נִתְתַּקֵּן הַדִּמְיוֹן,
through this consciousness the imaginative faculty is automatically rectified,

כִּדְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת פח422 Shabbat 88b — R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is meant by "My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh that lies between my breasts"? The Congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the Universe, though my Beloved presses and embitters me, still "he lies between my breasts." "My beloved is to me a cluster of henna in the vineyards of Ein Gedi" — He to whom everything belongs atones for me for the sin of the kid [the golden calf] that I gathered for myself. Rashi: ["Though my Beloved presses and embitters me":] at the [sin of the] calf, when He said, "Take off your ornaments." ["He lies between my breasts":] He at once said to make Him a Tabernacle, so that His Presence would be concentrated between the two staves [of the Ark], which in the First Temple appeared like two breasts pressing and protruding through the curtain opposite the entrance. ["Ein Gedi":] the sin of the calf, which is a kind of animal; alternatively, a term for idolatry, as in "who prepare a table for Gad" (Isaiah 65:11). ["That I gathered":] that I gathered to myself in lusting after many gods, as it is written, "These are your gods, O Israel" (Exodus 32:4). Maharsha: ["Though He presses me":] Besides Rashi's explanation, one may explain it in the sense of "In all their affliction He was afflicted" — the Blessed Name is with us in every exile: though He presses and embitters me in exile, "He lies between my breasts (shadai)," in the sense of "He shall abide in the shadow of the Almighty (Shaddai)." ["He to whom everything belongs":] The Yalkut's reading, "the man (ish) to whom everything (kol) belongs" [expounding eshkol], is more correct, "man" being fitting for the Holy One, blessed be He, of whom it is said, "The Lord is a man of war"; and since "kid" means any young tender offspring, the calf included, as Rashi explains in the Torah, "Ein Gedi" suits the sin of the calf even in its plain sense. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 88b): "For the sin of the kid" seems to me to mean: that I became a kid — after I had been a full-grown he-goat, and great, I became low and inferior; this is the reverse of "the kids have become he-goats" (Berakhot 63a), for here the he-goats became kids. And "that I gathered for myself" should be taken as a term of pressing: the sin is pressed into a person and fixed in him. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 14): When it is revealed in the hearts of Israel that the Blessed One extends through all creatures and gives life to them all, and that everything is His, this brings atonement for all sins, as they said, "He to whom everything belongs will atone for the sin of the kid." For since everything is His and nothing exists apart from Him, there is no iniquity or sin there at all, since all is from the truth of His will and there is none besides Him. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 5): One must understand why precisely here the Blessed One is called "cluster" [eshkol], "He to whom everything belongs," more than elsewhere. As in "Who makes peace and creates evil," where "evil" is written and "everything" is read as a euphemism, evil is called "everything"; so "cluster, He to whom everything belongs" means He who creates "everything," the aspect of evil, and "atones for me for the sin of the kid" refers to the darkness of creation, which will be turned into "very good.":):
just as our Sages stated (Shabbat 88b):
"מִי שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ מְכַפֵּר לִי עַל עֲווֹן גְּדִי וְכוּלֵי",
"He to Whom all belongs atones for me regarding the sin of the kid/calf, etc.",
שֶׁמִּי שֶׁהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ – כָּל הַמַּעֲשִׂים וְהַפְּעֻלּוֹת וְהַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת וְהָרְצוֹנוֹת,
in that since everything belongs to Him—all deeds, actions, thoughts, and inner desires—
אִם כֵּן גַּם הֶעָווֹן הוּא שֶׁלּוֹ, וּמִמֵּילָא מְכַפֵּר וְכוּלֵי.
then the lapse too is enfolded within His providence, and consequently atoned for.
וּבְכֹחַ הַמְדַמֶּה עַצְמוֹ שֶׁבּוֹ גּוֹבֵר הַדִּמְיוֹן,
And through the very faculty of imagination wherein fantasy surges,
בְּכֹחַ זֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו לְכַלּוֹתוֹ וּלְבַטְּלוֹ.
through that very faculty does one prevail over it to dissolve and annul it.
וְנִמְצָא שֶׁמִּתְהַפֵּךְ לִהְיוֹת שׁוֹרֶשׁ עֲמָלֵק הָרוֹדֵף – נִרְדָּף מֵעַצְמוֹ;
Thus the overarching root of the pursuing Amalek inverts into being pursued by his own device;
שֶׁמִּכְתָּב שֶׁכָּתַב "לִהְיוֹת הַיְּהוּדִים וְגוֹמֵר",
so that the decree Haman wrote "that the Jews should be ready for that day",
נִתְהַפֵּךְ הַפֵּירוּשׁ שֶׁבֵּאֲרוּ בַּכְּתָבִים שְׁנִיִּים,
the interpretation became inverted as clarified in the second royal letters,
הַכַּוָּנָה הָיָה שֶׁיִּשְׁלְטוּ בְּשׂוֹנְאֵיהֶם;
the intent becoming that the Jews should rule over their adversaries;
וְהָעֵץ שֶׁהֵכִין לְמָרְדֳּכַי נִתְהַפֵּךְ שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ;
and the gallows he prepared for Mordechai inverted into being erected for him;
הַיְינוּ דְּהַהִתְגַּבְּרוּת שֶׁל הַדִּמְיוֹן עַצְמוֹ נִתְהַפֵּךְ אַחַר כָּךְ,
meaning that the initial triumph of the imagination itself later turned inside out,
שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה הִתְגַּבְּרוּת דִּמְיוֹן כּוֹזֵב כְּלָל,
when it became evident that this was not the victory of a deceitful illusion at all,
רַק דְּבַר אֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ,
but rather ultimate, absolute Truth,
כְּמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל חֲלוֹמוֹת יוֹסֵף,
comparable, by way of example, to the dreams of Joseph,
שֶׁבִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה הָיָה נִרְאֶה דִּמְיוֹן,
which at the time appeared to be mere self-aggrandizing fantasy,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁרָאוּ שֶׁהָיָה כֵּן, הֲרֵי נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה דִּמְיוֹן כְּלָל.
yet later when everyone witnessed its exact fulfillment, it became proven that it was never an illusion at all.
וְזֶהוּ הַמָּשָׁל בַּנִּגְלֶה,
And this is the parable on the overt plane,
וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה הַרְבֵּה מַדְרֵגוֹת גָּבוֹהַּ עַל גָּבוֹהַּ
and within this dynamic exist many sublime ascending rungs
בְּהַעֲלָאַת הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת וְהַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת וְתִיקּוּנָן לִהְיוֹת נַעֲשֶׂה מִדִּמְיוֹן – אֱמֶת.
in elevating thoughts and fantasies, rectifying them so that out of illusion emerges absolute Truth.
וְהָעִיקָּר רַק עַל יְדֵי הַהַכָּרָה הַבְּרוּרָה שֶׁ"אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ" וְהַכֹּל שֶׁלּוֹ,
And the core attainment proceeds solely through the distinct perception that "there is none else beside Him" and all is His,
וְכָל חָכְמַת אֱנוֹשׁ וְתַחְבּוּלוֹתָיו אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם.
and that all mortal wisdom and human stratagems are nothingness.
וְכָךְ הוּא בְּעֵת שִׁכְרוּתוֹ,
And so it is at the moment of intoxication on Purim,
שֶׁאָז אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם דַּעַת וְחָכְמָה כְּמוֹ כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּדַעְתּוֹ,
when a person possesses no calculated intellect or deliberate wisdom as in his sober state,
כִּי רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמּוֹלִיד בּוֹ עֵצָה וּמַחֲשָׁבָה וְרָצוֹן,
realizing that Hashem, blessed be He, alone engenders counsel, thought, and desire within him,
מִמֵּילָא נִתְקָן הַכֹּל.
whereby everything automatically becomes rectified.
– וְנֶאֱמַר עַל זֶה: "וְהָיָה בְּהָנִיחַ וְגוֹמֵר",
And concerning this Scripture states: "And it shall be when Hashem has given you rest, etc." (Deuteronomy 25:19),
כִּי מִקּוֹדֶם צָרִיךְ הָאָדָם לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּבִיעוּר שֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת רָעוֹת שֶׁבְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ,
for beforehand a person must strive to eradicate the seven corrupt emotional traits manifest in his conscious heart,
שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לִידֵי אֵיזֶה עֲבֵירָה בַּפּוֹעַל
so that he never comes, Heaven forbid, to any actual sin in deed,
וְלֹא לִידֵי הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה שֶׁבְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ;
nor unto conscious sinful fantasies within his heart;
וּכְשֶׁנָּקִי מִזֶּה, אָז יִשְׁתַּדֵּל לִמְחוֹת מִקֶּרֶב לְבָבוֹ דִּמְיוֹנוֹת שֶׁל הֶבֶל].
and once pure of that, he may then exert himself to blot out from the depths of his soul the root fantasies of vanity.

sections.en: Torah against Imagination

items.h: Torah guards a person from the distortions of imagination in action, sleep, and waking thought, while Purim reveals a holiness beyond calculated human effort.

Seif 1 — Torah against the Power of Imagination
Torah guards thought across waking, sleep, and action, while Purim reveals holiness beyond deliberate calculation.

p: הַתּוֹרָה מַצֶּלֶת מִדִּמְיוֹנוֹת,
The Torah rescues a person from illusions,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן423 Avot d'Rabbi Natan 20 — R. Chananyah, deputy of the priests, says: Whoever takes words of Torah to heart has many intrusive thoughts removed from him — thoughts of hunger, thoughts of folly, thoughts of immorality, thoughts of the evil inclination, thoughts of an evil wife, thoughts of idle matters, thoughts of the yoke of flesh and blood. For so it is written in the book of Psalms by David king of Israel: “The precepts of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.” (רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כ):
and as it is written in Avot DeRabbi Natan (beginning of Chapter 20):
"הַמְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל תּוֹרָה מַעֲבִירִין מִמֶּנּוּ הִרְהוּרֵי וְכוּלֵי",
"Whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him stray thoughts of, etc.,"

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ [תַּנְחֶה אֹתָךְ, בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ תִּשְׁמֹר עָלֶיךָ, וַהֲקִיצוֹתָ הִיא תְשִׂיחֶךָ]" (מִשְׁלֵי ו, כב424 Proverbs 6:22 — “When you walk, it shall lead you; when you lie down, it shall watch over you; and when you awake, it shall talk with you.” Rashi: “When you walk” — in your lifetime; “when you lie down” — in the grave; “and when you awake” — at the resurrection of the dead, to stand in judgment. “It shall talk with you” — it shall speak on your behalf. Metzudas Dovid: “It shall lead you” — it shall conduct you on the straight path; “it shall watch over you” — from those who plunder by night; “it shall talk with you” — it shall converse with you like a good friend who speaks with his companion to take delight in him. Malbim: He is speaking of the three situations mentioned above [in 3:23–25] — a man walking on the road, lying down, and rising in his house. On the road, where there is the danger of the way, “it shall lead you” on the straight path; lying down, where there is danger because he is not then using his senses and his mind, “it shall watch over you”; and when you rouse from sleep, it will be the matter of your talk.).
and as it is written (Proverbs 6:22): "When you walk it shall lead you; when you lie down it shall watch over you; and when you awake it shall converse with you."
פֵּירוּשׁ, כִּי בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּרָכִים מִתְגַּבֵּר הַמְדַמֶּה:
The explanation is that the imaginative faculty (ha-medameh) overpowers in three ways:
הָאֶחָד – בְּעִסְקוֹ בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ דִּמְיוֹן,
The first: when he is occupied in affairs of this physical world which is entirely an illusion,
צָרִיךְ לִיזָּהֵר שֶׁלֹּא יִשְׁקַע בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹתָיו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
wherein he must be cautious not to drown in its illusions, Heaven forbid,
וְיִתְעַסֵּק רַק מַה שֶּׁלְּצָרְכּוֹ.
and engage only in that which is truly necessary for his upkeep.
וְזֶה נִקְרָא "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ",
And this stage is called "when you walk" (be-hithalekhekha),

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת יא.)425 Berakhot 11a — If so, let the Merciful One write "in sitting and in walking"; what is meant by "when you sit and when you walk"? It is in your own sitting and in your own walking that you are obligated, but in that of a commandment you are exempt. Rashi (s.v. "Are we not dealing [with one who walks to perform a commandment]"): Rashi explains the difficulty that these words answer: from where do we know that the verse speaks only of an optional journey? Scripture writes "on the way" without qualification, so that a journey undertaken for a commandment is implied by it as well, and even so the Merciful One said that he should recite the Shema. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 3): "I considered my ways" — my own way, in the sense of what [the Sages] said, "when you walk" — in your own walking — you are obligated; and even so, "I turned my feet to Your testimonies." So too "If you walk in My statutes" says simply "walk," not mentioning walking for a mitzvah as in "those who walk in the Torah of the Lord," and unqualified walking means one's own walking. The meaning is: "if in My statutes" — if the words of Torah are engraved in the heart — "you walk": even your own walking will be to words of Torah, to the house of study.: "'וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ' – בְּלֶכֶת דִּידָךְ וְכוּלֵי";
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Berakhot 11a): "'And when you walk'—in your own secular pursuits, etc.";
הֲגַם דִּסְתָם דֶּרֶךְ בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁלֵי דֶּרֶךְ ה',
and even though 'way' in the Book of Proverbs generally denotes the path of Hashem,
רַק "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ" הַיְינוּ לֶכֶת דִּידָךְ בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
yet "when you walk" implies your own conduct amidst the affairs of this world,
וּבָזֶה צָרִיךְ "תַּנְחֶהוּ", בְּאֵיזֶה דֶּרֶךְ יֵלֵךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִשְׁקַע בַּדִּמְיוֹן.
and in this he requires "it shall lead you," showing in which path to walk so as not to sink into illusion.
וְזֶה הָיָה מְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, "אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְגוֹמֵר",
And this was the nature of the blotting out of Amalek under Moses our teacher, peace be upon him: "who met you by the way, etc.",
שֶׁאָז הָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעֵסֶק וְלֹא בְּעַצְלוּת וְיוֹשֵׁב בָּטֵל,
for then Israel were actively engaged, not in indolence or sitting idly,
וּבָא הוּא לְהַכְנִיס מַחֲשֶׁבֶת דִּמְיוֹן בְּלִבָּם.
and Amalek came to inject illusory thoughts into their hearts.
וְזֶהוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ עֲמָלֵק:
And this is the essential root of Amalek:
לֹא בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת כְּיוֹשֵׁב בָּטֵל,
not generating illusions like one who sits around idly,
רַק לְהַשְׁקִיעַ בְּדִמְיוֹנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
rather to plunge a person into active worldly illusions;
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה הוּא עִיקַּר צִיוּוּי הַזְּכִירָה לְהִתְגַּבֵּר,
and along this line lies the primary commandment of remembrance, to prevail against him;
כִּי מִיְּשִׁיבָה בָּטֵל כְּיָשֵׁן מִמֵּילָא הָאָדָם מֵקִיץ וְיָכוֹל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר בְּקַל,
for from idle slumber a person naturally awakes and can easily overcome,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּשִׁיקּוּעַ בִּזְרִיזוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
unlike immersion accompanied by fervent energetic activity, Heaven forbid.
אֲבָל אֲגַג בִּימֵי שָׁאוּל לֹא נִתְעוֹרֵר כְּלָל נֶגְדָּם,
However, Agag in the days of King Saul did not arouse himself against Israel at all,
רַק יִשְׂרָאֵל הִתְעוֹרְרוּ נֶגְדּוֹ,
rather Israel initiated against him,
כִּי אָז הָיָה הַמְדַמֶּה מֵעַצְמוֹ גּוֹבֵר מִטַּעַם הַבַּטָּלָה,
because then the imaginative faculty overpowered on its own due to idle dormancy,
כְּטַעַם "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ תִּשְׁמֹר וְגוֹמֵר",
mirroring the verse: "when you lie down it shall watch over you, etc.",
כִּי בְּשֵׁינָה הַמְדַמֶּה גּוֹבֵר
for during sleep the imagination intensifies,
וְצָרִיךְ רַק שְׁמִירָה שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה דִּמְיוֹן כּוֹזֵב,
and one merely requires protection so that it does not become a deceitful illusion,
רַק דּוּגְמַת חֲלוֹמוֹת יַעֲקֹב וְיוֹסֵף.
but rather resembles the truthful prophetic dreams of Jacob and Joseph.
וְזֶה אֵינוֹ מִמַּעֲשֵׂה אָדָם כְּלָל,
And this preservation does not stem from human effort at all,
כִּי הַמְדַמֶּה מְדַמֶּה מֵעַצְמוֹ,
for the imagination imagines spontaneously,
רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹמֵר.
and Hashem, blessed be He, alone protects.
וְהַתְחָלַת הַמְּלוּכָה הוּא הַתְחָלַת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַשֵּׁינָה.
And the inauguration of monarchy corresponds to the initial stirring from sleep.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הָמָן הָיָה מֵעִנְיַן "וַהֲקִיצוֹתָ וְגוֹמֵר",
And afterward Haman pertained to the category of "and when you awake, etc.",

כַּיָּדוּעַ דִּבְרֵי הָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה עַל "אֱלֹהֵיהֶם יָשֵׁן וְכוּלֵי" (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֶסְתֵּר פָּרָשָׁה ז426 Esther Rabbah 7:12 — "And Haman said to King Ahasuerus: There is [yeshno] one people" — He of whom it is said "the Lord is one" has fallen asleep [yashen] toward His people. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Before Me there is no sleep, as it is written, "Behold, the Guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps"; yet you have said that there is sleep before Me. By your life, out of that very sleep I shall rouse Myself against that man and destroy him from the world, as it is written, "Then the Lord awoke as one asleep, and He smote His adversaries backward." Sod Yesharim (Purim 25): On the Gemara's "they are asleep from the commandments" and the Midrash's "[Haman] said, their God is asleep," the holy Arizal wrote that this was also the matter at the beginning of creation, "And the Lord God cast a deep sleep." When a person nullifies himself completely and hands all the power of his own being over to the Blessed One, the Blessed One returns to him a sprouting of salvation all the more, and before every sprouting of salvation there must first be such a nullification. So the destruction and exile were a nullification in which Israel handed back to the Blessed One all the might they had from performing the commandments, until they seemed asleep from the commandments, and this is the deep sleep.),
as known from the teachings of the holy Ari, of blessed memory, on the verse "their God is asleep, etc." (Esther Rabbah 7),
שֶׁהָיָה כֵּן אָז בְּסוֹד הַדּוּרְמִיטָא,
that this cosmic state then occurred in the esoteric mystery of the supernal slumber (dormita),

וּכְטַעַם דִּבְרֵי אֶסְתֵּר: "אוּלַי יַרְגִּישׁ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּלֵי" (מְגִילָּה טו427 Megillah 15b — The Sages taught: What did Esther see that she invited Haman? R. Shimon ben Menasya says: Perhaps the Omnipresent will take notice and work a miracle for us. Rashi (s.v. "Perhaps the Omnipresent will take notice"): That the Holy One, blessed be He, will notice that even I am drawing the enemy of Israel near me; or else that He will notice that I am reduced to flattering this wicked man and to slighting my own honour. Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot): Rashi's first explanation — that He will notice that even she is drawing the enemy of Israel near — is difficult: would she for that reason bring the trouble still closer and help him accomplish his design? Rather, that the Holy One, blessed be He, would notice and see that "there is none shut up or left at large" [and Israel has no helper at all]. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 1, on "What did Esther see"): From this passage it is proved that Solomon's counsel, "If your enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat," is said even of a thoroughly wicked enemy, since the Sages applied it here to Esther's inviting Haman. The reason is that once an enemy takes his sustenance from you he can no longer stand opposed to you, for whoever receives from another passes under him — and so "you heap coals of fire upon his head." "And the Lord shall repay you": the Holy One, blessed be He, who desires no opposition at all, will deliver him into your hand, and will help and assist in this.:),
and reflecting Esther's reasoning: "Perhaps the Holy One, blessed be He, will take note, etc." (Megillah 15b),
פֵּירוּשׁ, יָקִיץ מִשְּׁנָתוֹ כְּטַעַם "עוּרָה, לָמָּה תִישַׁן".
meaning He will awaken from His slumber, mirroring (Psalms 44:24): "Awake! Why do You sleep, O Lord?"
וּבָזֶה עִיקַּר הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם עַל הַתְחָלַת יְקִיצָה מִשְּׁנָתוֹ,
And in this phase lies man's primary spiritual exertion: at the initial awakening from his sleep,
הַיְינוּ הַתְחָלַת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְהוֹצִיא עַצְמוֹ מִדִּמְיוֹן,
namely the initial awakening to extract himself from illusion,
כְּשֶׁעֲדַיִן אֵין הַלֵּב מָלֵא מֵהַכָּרָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
when the heart is not yet completely filled with the conscious perception of Him, blessed be He,
שֶׁאָז נִקְרָא "שִׂיחָה",
which is then designated as sichah (casual speech),

דְּיָדוּעַ מִדִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֲגִיגָה ה:)428 Chagigah 5b — R. Ila was going up the stairway of the house of Rabba bar Sheila. He heard a child reading: "For behold, He who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his speech." He said: A servant whose master declares to him what is his speech — what remedy has he? What is meant by "what is his speech"? Rav said: Even the idle speech between a man and his wife is declared to a person at the hour of death. Rashi: "Idle speech" — words of levity before marital relations. Maharsha: "He who forms the mountains and creates the wind" takes in both the body and the soul: the body was formed from the center of the world, from the Temple Mount, and the soul was created from the spirit of God, as it is said, "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life"; and a man's speech issues from the two together, since the organs of speech belong to the body and to the spirit alike. Hence "and declares to man what is his speech" — what remedy has he, seeing that He Himself formed and created them both? The verse could have said simply "his speech"; the word "what [mah]" was therefore expounded, since it denotes something slight, as in "and what are we" — that is, even the slightest speech between a man and his wife. עַל פָּסוּק "מַה שֵּׂחוֹ",
as is known from the words of our Sages (Chagigah 5b) on the verse (Amos 4:13) "what is his sicho",
דְּשִׂיחָה נִקְרָא רַק שִׂיחַת חוּלִין;
that sichah refers specifically to ordinary mundane speech;

וּבְוַדַּאי אֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר דְּשִׂיחַת חוּלִין שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים תּוֹרָה (סֻכָּה כא429 Sukkah 21b — R. Acha bar Adda said, and some say R. Acha bar Adda said in the name of Rav Hamnuna in the name of Rav: From where is it derived that even the ordinary talk of Torah scholars requires study? As it is stated: "And its leaf does not wither" (Psalms 1:3). Rashi: "Requires study": those who hear them must give their attention to them. "Its leaf": the least weighty thing about him. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 59): The essence of intellect is called "fruit," and the ordinary talk of Torah scholars is called "leaves," because leaves are the garment of the fruit: the leaves are on the outside and the fruit within. So too the intellect of a Torah scholar is something inward, while his ordinary talk, being something outward, is called "leaves," for it is a garment to the intellect. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 118): A Torah scholar, of whom even his ordinary talk requires study, as the Sages said, has the power even through his ordinary talk to rectify souls, for it is actual words of Torah — just as the Torah contains a number of narratives, and the Talmud many things that look like mundane stories, yet they are Torah in the full sense. And whoever is greater than his fellow, his ordinary talk is greater than his fellow's Torah, as it says, "The conversation of the patriarchs' servants is finer than the Torah of the sons." This was said in Sukkah of Rabban Gamliel's talk in his sukkah, which suggests that in the sukkah, through being in "the shade of faith," they merit to be so.:),
and surely they did not mean that 'the mundane conversation of Torah scholars is Torah' (Sukkah 21b)
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם כַּוָּנָה פְּנִימִית לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
refers to an utterance where they held a conscious internal intention for words of Torah,
דְּזֶה נִקְרָא תּוֹרָה בֶּאֱמֶת וְלֹא שִׂיחַת חוּלִין,
for that is genuinely categorized as Torah and not mundane speech;
דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל מַאֲמָרֵי רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ סִפּוּרֵי מַעֲשִׂיּוֹת
such as, for example, the allegorical narratives of Rabbah bar Bar Chana in Bava Batra and similar tales,
רַק שֶׁגָּנוּז בָּהֶם כַּוָּנָה פְּנִימִית, הוּא דְּבַר תּוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ וְלֹא שִׂיחַת חוּלִין;
which conceal a deep esoteric meaning, being literal Torah and not secular conversation;
רַק שִׂיחַת חוּלִין נִקְרָא מַה שֶּׁבֶּאֱמֶת אֵין כַּוָּנָתוֹ רַק לְדִבְרֵי חוֹל.
rather, sichat chulin is that whose overt intent is truly directed only toward mundane matters.
וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְשׁוֹן "שִׂיחָה" הוּא דִּבּוּר שֶׁמִּן הַשָּׂפָה וְלַחוּץ,
And it appears that the term sichah signifies speech from the lips outward,
וְלֹא מִמַּעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא "דִּבּוּר".
and not from the innermost depths of the heart, which is termed dibbur.

וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלַּת יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא "לָשׂוּחַ" (בְּרָכוֹת כו430 Berakhot 26b — Abraham instituted the morning prayer, as it is stated: “And Abraham rose early in the morning to the place where he had stood” (Genesis 19:27), and “standing” means nothing other than prayer, as it is stated: “Then Pinchas stood and prayed” (Psalms 106:30). Isaac instituted the afternoon prayer, as it is stated: “And Isaac went out to converse in the field toward evening” (Genesis 24:63), and “conversation” means nothing other than prayer, as it is stated: “A prayer of the afflicted, when he faints and pours out his converse before the Lord” (Psalms 102:1). Tosafos (s.v. "Isaac instituted the afternoon prayer"): Even though we say (Yoma 28b) that Abraham's prayer was from the hour when the walls darken — that is, he too prayed in the afternoon — one may answer that this was only after Isaac had instituted it. Tosafos (s.v. "and 'conversation' means nothing other than prayer"): This is difficult, for in Avodah Zarah 7b the Gemara proves the reverse, that "conversation" means prayer, from "And Isaac went out to converse in the field." One may answer that we find the like elsewhere: in Megillah 13a "and he raised Hadassah" is expounded from "and he stood among the myrtles," while in Sanhedrin 93a the derivation runs the other way. Maharsha: The patriarchs did not institute the order of the eighteen blessings, for that was arranged at Yavne; rather, from the patriarchs we learn that a man must pray three prayers each day, fulfilling what is said, "Evening and morning and noon I speak and moan" (Psalms 55:18). And Abraham surely prayed the afternoon and evening prayers as well, since we are told (Yoma 28b) that he observed even the eruv tavshilin; it is only that from each of the patriarchs we learn the prayer in connection with which Scripture records of him that he prayed. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 3): The patriarchs instituted the prayers because they were the beginning of the whole world, as it were the first effect proceeding from the Blessed One, and prayer is the joining of the effect to its Cause; so each instituted [a prayer] according to his own attribute. Abraham instituted the morning prayer at the beginning of the day, for he was the beginning among the patriarchs and so resembled the morning, the beginning of the day, and the Blessed One is the beginning of the world; and Isaac instituted the afternoon prayer, after midday, which is the completion [of the day], as the Blessed One is also the completion of the world.:),
And therefore the prayer of our father Isaac, peace be upon him, is termed "lasuach" (Berakhot 26b),
כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הַמַּתְחִיל בִּתְפִלָּה – הַיְינוּ דַּוְוקָא בְּכַוָּנָה שְׁלֵימָה – נִקְרָא "עֲמִידָה",
for our father Abraham, peace be upon him, who initiated prayer—specifically with complete intentional focus—is called "standing" (amidah),

כְּטַעַם מַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה יג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב431 Sotah 13b — And some say: Moses did not die. It is written here, "And Moses died there" (Deuteronomy 34:5), and it is written elsewhere, "And he was there with the Lord" (Exodus 34:28). Just as there he stood and served, so here he stands and serves. Maharsha: It is because of the difficulty raised in the first chapter of Bava Batra — could Moses have been dead and [yet] written "And Moses died"? — that they said he did not die, basing it on the verbal analogy of "there" [in both verses]. It speaks of his "serving" because, as is said elsewhere, serving [the Torah] is greater than studying it; and in the same vein they said in Ta'anit, "Jacob our father did not die." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Beha'aloscha 8): Moses our teacher did not die — "just as there he stands and serves, so here he stands and serves" — and the Zohar says he rejoiced that this perfection was found in him, since through him came the manna, which is from the side of the Tree of Life, in which death does not dwell. And although they expounded that he did not die, it is nevertheless written of him "and no man knows his burial": no person can grasp how the term burial applies to Moses, yet at least the term is written of him — unlike Elijah, of whom no term of death is written at all, even outwardly.):
mirroring the teaching of our Sages (Sotah 13b end):
"מַה לְּהַלָּן עוֹמֵד וּמְשַׁמֵּשׁ וְכוּלֵי",
"Just as there he stands and ministers, etc.",
כִּי עֲמִידָה הוּא רַק לַעֲבוֹדָה.
for 'standing' designates dedicated sacrificial service.
וְיִצְחָק בָּא וְהוֹסִיף, דְּגַם תְּפִלָּה שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּנָה הוּא תְּפִלָּה;
Isaac came and added that even prayer uttered without active conscious focus is nonetheless valid prayer;

וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דִּידֵיהּ דְּ"מַחֲוֵי לְהוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ432 Shabbat 89b — In time to come the Holy One, blessed be He, will say to Avraham: Your children have sinned against Me. He will say before Him: Master of the Universe, let them be wiped out for the sanctification of Your Name. He will say: I will tell it to Yaakov, who had the pain of raising children; perhaps he will ask mercy for them. He will say to him: Your children have sinned. He will say before Him: Master of the Universe, let them be wiped out for the sanctification of Your Name. He will say: There is no sense in the old, and no counsel in the young. He will say to Yitzchak: Your children have sinned against Me. He will say before Him: Master of the Universe — my children and not Your children? When they put “we will do” before “we will hear,” You called them “My son, My firstborn”; and now they are my children and not Your children? … They begin and say [to Yitzchak]: “For you are our father.” Yitzchak says to them: Before you praise me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He. … Immediately they lift their eyes on high and say: “You, O Lord, are our Father; our Redeemer from of old is Your name.” Rashi: "Let them be wiped out" — since they have sinned; and Your Name will be sanctified in the world when You execute judgment upon those who transgress Your words. "For you are our father" — they said this facing Yitzchak, and he told them: Point toward the Holy One, blessed be He, for He is your father. Maharsha: Since the end of the verse says "You, O Lord, are our Father," the Gemara understood that "For you are our father" at its beginning, which lacks the Divine Name, refers not to the Holy One, blessed be He, but to Yitzchak — and not to Avraham and Yaakov, of whom it says "does not know us" and "does not acknowledge us." For Avraham's answer, "let them be wiped out for the sanctification of Your Name," can be taken for ill — that Israel be wiped out, God forbid — or for good — that their sins be wiped out, as in "atone for our sins for Your Name's sake"; Yaakov answered in the same words, and so it is said, "There is no sense in the old and no counsel in the young," for their words cannot be decided either way, and this is "Avraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us." Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 13): Avraham and Yaakov, the first and last of the Patriarchs, each say "let them be wiped out," because Israel can be vindicated only by going into the depth of judgment, and theirs is not the attribute of judgment: "There is no sense in the old and no counsel in the young," for sense and counsel belong to judgment, whose strength lies in the middle — as the Levites serve only between thirty and fifty — and among the Patriarchs that is Yitzchak. Therefore Yitzchak answers, "My children and not Your children?": Israel are caused by the Blessed One essentially and first of all, which is why they are called "My son, My firstborn," and whatever is joined to the Pure ought to be free of sin. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): "And if You say it is all upon me," that is, that the existence of the dross comes only from my side, because there is dross in me, "I offered up my soul," and I am a perfect burnt-offering before You, with no dross in me from myself; it comes only from the spreading-forth that the Blessed One willed in creating the world. When it is revealed that everything comes from the root, from the Blessed One, the screen that the sins made between Israel and their Father in Heaven is removed, and through this "the Holy One, blessed be He, is shown to them before their eyes," even though "man shall not see Me and live": for the Sages said that at the time of death they see, since then the screen of this world is removed, and so too with this revelation of "half upon You" the screen of this world will be removed. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:83): The Torah was given specifically to the earth, the place of concealment, where face-to-face recognition is not known, and so one must judge only by the intellect of one in concealment; and face-to-face recognition comes from the side of strength [gevurah], in the sense of "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes." Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The recognition of "I am the Lord your God" is the recognition of "You are with me," and this is from the side of Isaac, as they said, "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes": complete seeing, face to face, comes through Isaac, for this apprehension, clear to the eye and in distinct levels, is from the attribute of contraction, which contracts apprehension into measures and levels. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 190): The root of Joseph is fear of sin, which is guarding the eye, and [fear, yirah,] has the letters of "seeing" [reiyah], in the sense of "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes," for this comes from the power of Isaac and from his attribute. Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 17): [The blessing "Who revives the dead" is in the mystery of Isaac,] as the Gemara says: Isaac said to them, "Before you praise me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He," and Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes. This alludes to the resurrection of the dead: it is not in the power of any creature in the world to show a person his foundation and the root from which he was hewn, to heal the root of his deficiency and comfort him in his grief; this was entrusted to no intermediary but given into the hand of the Blessed One alone. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 73): Isaac's attribute is always to hear from the depth of the supernal root, and the sight of the surface hue was a small thing to him; so the Gemara says that the Holy One says to Abraham and to Jacob, "Your children have sinned," but Isaac answered, "[They are] Your children, and not mine," for he always looked to the depth of the supernal root, where Israel are always called children of the Omnipresent, and therefore every kind of salvation for Israel is aroused from his side. Even the salvation that cannot be recognized in this world except by hearing, Isaac will show in the future to sight as well, so that it will be explicitly recognized upon all the hues of Israel's garments how His light dwells within them, as the Gemara says, "And Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes."" (שַׁבָּת פט:)
and this was his exalted spiritual level, wherein "the Holy One showed them with their own eyes" (Shabbat 89b)
אֵיךְ "מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ" מַמָּשׁ לְנוֹכַח הָעַיִן.
how "the whole earth is full of His glory" literally stood visible before their eyes.
וּבְהַכָּרָה בְּרוּרָה כָּזוֹ אֵין שׁוּב נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ בְּכַוָּנַת לִבּוֹ,
And with such palpable clarity, the specific transient intention of his heart no longer makes a difference,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ד)433 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 2:4 — The great R. Ḥiyya said: In all my days I never prayed with intent. Once I tried to concentrate, and I mused in my heart and said: Who enters before the king first, the commandant of the fortress or the Exilarch? Samuel said: I counted chicks. R. Bun bar Ḥiyya said: I counted courses of stone. R. Mattaniah said: I am grateful to my head, for when it reaches "We give thanks" it bows of itself. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "In all my days I never prayed with intent"): It was because he was preoccupied with meditating upon Torah — and so with all those that follow. The "arkafta" is the alkafta, an officer who ranks above the Exilarch, and his musing was whether those who enter before the king are presented from the lower rank upward or from the higher downward, since the alkafta precedes the Exilarch. "Courses" are courses of a building; and R. Mattaniah's head bows of itself even though he is preoccupied with meditating upon Torah.: "אֲנָא מִן יוֹמַי לָא כַּוֵּונִית וְכוּלֵי",
as stated (Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:4): "In all my days I never directed my heart with conscious intent, etc.";
כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר יֵשׁ לוֹ הַכָּרָה בְּרוּרָה כָּזוֹ, זוֹ כַּוָּנָה כּוֹלֶלֶת עַל כָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹתָיו וְדִבּוּרָיו וּמַעֲשָׂיו;
for once a person possesses such constant fundamental perception, it serves as an overarching, encompassing intention over all his thoughts, words, and deeds;
אַף שִׂיחַת חוּלִין שֶׁלּוֹ הַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ,
even his casual mundane conversation is experienced as originating from Hashem alone, there being none beside Him;
וְאֵין שׁוּם נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ בְּכַוָּנָה כָּךְ אוֹ כָּךְ לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל עַל זֶה,
and it makes no difference to toil over this or that granular concentration,
רַק לְהַנִּיחַ הַכֹּל עַל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
save to cast everything upon Hashem, blessed be He,
וּלְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל רַק בְּעִיקַּר הַכַּוָּנָה דְּ"שִׁוִּיתִי ה' לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" – מַמָּשׁ לְנֶגְדִּי.
and exert oneself solely in the core orientation: "I have set Hashem always before me"—literally facing me.

וְאָז מִמֵּילָא, כַּאֲשֶׁר מְקַיֵּים "גּוֹל [עַל ה' מַעֲשֶׂיךָ] וְגוֹמֵר", "וְיִכֹּנוּ [מַחְשְׁבֹתֶיךָ434 Proverbs 16:3 — “Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts shall be established.” Rashi: "Roll your deeds upon the Lord" — roll and cast your needs upon Him, and your plans will be established, that is, founded and enduring. Another explanation: pray before Him for all your needs. Metzudas Dovid: Turn your deeds toward the Lord, so that they bring you to His service, and then your plans will be established and made firm. Malbim: Thoughts are many and sweep across the soul with nothing to fix or ground them; but if a man does all his deeds only for the Lord, to magnify God's honor and do His will, so that God is the purpose of his acts, then his thoughts have a base and foundation, for he will think only of doing what is God's honor and His will.]".
And then automatically, when one fulfills: "Commit your works unto Hashem," then "your thoughts shall be established" (Proverbs 16:3).
וְזֶה נִקְרָא "דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין" וְלֹא "מִתְעַסֵּק בְּעָלְמָא",
And this is designated as davar she-eino mitkaven (an unintentional consequence) rather than mit'asek be-alma (a completely oblivious act),
דַּהֲרֵי מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כַּוָּנָה כּוֹלֶלֶת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
for in any event an overarching general intention is required, as mentioned above,
וְצָרִיךְ לֵידַע שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ לְהִתְפַּלֵּל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיֵּצֵא יִצְחָק לָשׂוּחַ".
and he must recognize that he is setting out to pray, as it is written: "And Isaac went out to meditate (lasuach) in the field" (Genesis 24:63).
שֶׁבְּאַבְרָהָם הָיָה עֲמִידָה, דְּהַיְינוּ כָּל הַתְּפִלָּה,
For with Abraham there was 'standing', which embodied the entire prayer,
וּבְיִצְחָק רַק יְצִיאָה;
whereas with Isaac there was merely the 'going out';
אֲבָל בְּיַעֲקֹב גַּם יְצִיאָה לֹא, רַק "וַיִּפְגַּע",
yet with Jacob there was not even a planned setting out, but rather "and he encountered (va-yifga) the place",
וּפְגִיעָה הוּא כְּמוֹ מִקְרֶה וּכְמִתְעַסֵּק בְּעָלְמָא
and encountering is like an unexpected occurrence and akin to mit'asek,
דְּגָרַע מִדָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין, שֶׁאַף כַּוָּנָה כּוֹלֶלֶת אֵין כָּאן.
which is even below davar she-eino mitkaven, since even an overarching premeditated intention is absent here.
וְהוּא תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית בְּחֶשְׁכַּת לַיְלָה שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם אוֹר בָּהִיר כְּלָל,
And this corresponds to the evening prayer (Arvit) amid the darkness of night where no bright illumination shines at all,
דַּרְגָּא דִּידֵיהּ "הַמַּבְרִיחַ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה"
this being Jacob's spiritual level that "crosses from one end to the other",
שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ אֱמֶת וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר מִלְּבַר;
which is entirely truth, leaving nothing outside;
אַף הַחֲלוֹמוֹת שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם כַּוָּנָה בָּהֶם לֹא מִלְּפָנֶיהָ וְלֹא מֵאַחֲרֶיהָ,
even dreams, which possess no conscious human intent beforehand or afterward,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ בִּידִיעַת אָדָם כְּלָל, גַּם כֵּן הוּא רַק לַה',
being completely outside mortal forethought, are likewise consecrated purely to Hashem,
כִּי מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁאֵין פְּסוֹלֶת כְּלָל.
because his bed is whole, containing no spiritual defect whatsoever.

כִּי אַבְרָהָם נִקְרָא "תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים" (חֲגִיגָה ג435 Chagigah 3a — Rava expounded: What is meant by "How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O daughter of the noble"? How beautiful are the feet of Israel when they go up for the pilgrimage festival. "Daughter of the noble" — the daughter of Abraham our father, who is called noble, as it is said, "The nobles of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham." "The God of Abraham," and not the God of Isaac and Jacob? Rather, "the God of Abraham," for he was the first of the converts. Rashi: "Who is called noble" — because his heart moved him of its own accord to recognize his Creator. "The nobles of the peoples" — these are the converts, who volunteer from among the nations to take upon themselves the yoke of the commandments. Tosafos (s.v. "the first of the converts"): Because he was commanded concerning circumcision, unlike all those who came before him. Maharsha: "How beautiful are the feet of Israel" — for whoever's foot is not sound does not go up at all, as below, "excluding one who is lame." And their beauty is made to depend on their going in sandals, because one who goes barefoot goes in pain, as it is said, "Withhold your foot from being unshod" (Jeremiah 2:25), whereas these went up on foot in gladness, with their offerings of rejoicing; and so the Targum renders it, "How lovely are your steps, three times a year, in sandals." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 3): Tractate Avodah Zarah serves to clarify the distinctions between Israel and the idolaters, and Abraham's Avodah Zarah "was four hundred chapters," for Abraham is called "father of a multitude of nations" — as stated at the beginning of Chagigah, he is called "the first of the converts" — and, as it is said, he "recognized his Creator," implying that at first he did not. Hence [on Pesach night] one "begins with disgrace": "at first our fathers were idol worshippers." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Abraham our father too is called "father of a multitude of nations," for he was not born from the womb of the seed of Israel, who are borne from the womb with the Blessed One as the rock of their heart by birth; for he is called "the first of the converts," since it was through his own effort that he merited the understanding of the heart and to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite" — like a native in Israel, who is an Israelite from the womb. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 14): [If Israel cannot resemble Isaac, who was born in holiness, circumcised at eight days without his own knowledge, and so became Israel,] the deeds of Abraham suffice: for Abraham is called "the first of the converts" and sought to bring the whole world under the wings of the Shechinah, being "father of a multitude of nations" — the father of all converts — whereas Isaac is not found to have made converts. And although Abraham's converts were helped only in his lifetime, for after his passing they broke the covenant, his covenant helped at least his own seed, so that whoever is of the seed of Israel is in any case superior to a convert. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 9): Abraham our father, who is called "the first of the converts," is the beginning of the holiness that comes from below — fencing all his limbs and faculties within holiness — and he had to draw himself near, as is said of converts in Kiddushin; he was tested with ten trials so that every level would be clarified in him through his own holiness from below, in battle with the inclination. And although he afterwards merited to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite," reckoned as a native in Israel, that was after Jacob came forth from him..),
For Abraham is designated the "first of the converts" (Chagigah 3a),
שֶׁהוּא רֹאשׁ הַמִּשְׁתַּדְּלִים,
being the foremost of those who exert personal striving,
וְנֶאֱמַר בּוֹ: "הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי" –
and concerning him it was said: "Walk before Me" (Genesis 17:1)—
הִילּוּךְ הוּא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּ"בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ וְגוֹמֵר".
walking signifying human exertion, representing the level of "when you walk, etc."
וְזֶה נִקְרָא גֵּר,
And this is termed the category of the convert (ger),

שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (ע סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)436 Kiddushin 70b — "And they shall be My people" (Jeremiah 30:22). Rabba bar Rav Huna said: This is a further distinction between Israelites and converts. Of Israelites it is written, "And I will be their God, and they shall be My people" (Ezekiel 37:27); but of converts it is written, "For who is he that has pledged his heart to approach Me, says the Lord — and you shall be My people, and I will be your God" (Jeremiah 30:21–22). Rashi (s.v. "Of Israelites it is written"): "And I will be their God" — even though they are not yet His people; and since He draws them near, they come to be His people. Converts, however, are not drawn near from Heaven unless they first draw themselves near by becoming good. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 70b): Israel derive by an unbroken chain from the First Cause; and just as they derive from the First Cause, so the First Cause is their God and seeks after them, for there is no cause without its effect. As a father seeks after his son, so does He seek after Israel, who are called sons because they are His effects essentially and from the first; but the convert, in whom this is not so, must cleave to Him, blessed be He, of himself. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 8): This is the distinction between Israel and converts of which they said in Kiddushin, "this is a further superiority": of Israel it is written first "And I will be their God" and afterwards "and they shall be My people," meaning that the Blessed One is their God perforce, whether they wish it or not — as at the giving of the Torah, when He held the mountain over them like a barrel, and likewise in the future, "with a strong hand … will I reign." This is only in Israel, by virtue of the holiness they have from birth from their fathers, which is not so with converts. דִּתְחִלָּה "וִהְיִיתֶם לִי וְכוּלֵי",
as our Sages of blessed memory stated in Kiddushin (70b end) that initially "and you shall be unto Me, etc.",
שֶׁרַק עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ זוֹכֶה;
meaning that solely through his exertion does he merit;
וּבָזֶה צָרִיךְ לָצֵאת פְּסוֹלֶת,
and within this mode of striving, waste/dross must inevitably be extruded;
דַּהֲרֵי מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם נִרְאֶה כְּאִילּוּ יֵשׁ דָּבָר חוּץ שֶׁהוּא מִשְׁתַּדֵּל וְעוֹבֵד
for from the perspective of human striving, it appears as though there exists an external entity who strives and serves
כְּעֶבֶד לְאָדוֹן שֶׁאֵינוֹ עַצְמוּת הָאָדוֹן.
like a servant to a master, not being the very essence of the Master Himself.
וְזֶהוּ יִשְׁמָעֵאל שֶׁנִּקְרָא "פֶּרֶא אָדָם",
And this represents Ishmael who is called "a wild ass of a man" (Genesis 16:12),
פֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ אָדָם יַעֲרִי שֶׁהוּא דְּמוּת אָדָם וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מִין בְּהֵמָה;
meaning like a wild jungle creature possessing human silhouette while yet belonging to the beast species;

וְכָךְ לָמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק לא)437 Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 31 — He said to Ishmael and to Eliezer: Do you see anything on one of these mountains? They said to him: No. He accounted them as the donkey. He said: Since you see nothing, "Stay here with the donkey" (Genesis 22:5) — with those who resemble a donkey.: "עַם הַדּוֹמֶה לַחֲמוֹר" עַל יִשְׁמָעֵאל.
and so our Sages taught (Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 31): "a people likened unto a donkey" applied to Ishmael.
כִּי יֵשׁ צוּרַת אָדָם לְמַעְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּיחֶזְקֵאל וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "בְּצַלְמֵנוּ",
For there exists the divine Form of Man on High, as written in Ezekiel and in "in Our image",
דְּהַיְינוּ צוּרַת אָדָם הוּא שֶׁיַּכִּיר שֶׁאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ,
signifying that the true Form of Man is to recognize that there is none else beside Him,
גַּם עֶצֶם גּוּפוֹ וּבְשָׂרוֹ הַמַּמָּשִׁיִּים אֵינָם דָּבָר שֶׁחוּץ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and that even his physical body and flesh are not an entity outside of Hashem, blessed be He.
וְזֶהוּ צוּרַת אָדָם דִּלְמַעְלָה,
And this is the Form of Man Above,
דְּתַכְלִית הַבְּרִיאָה הָיָה לְהַכָּרָה זוֹ, שֶׁיַּכִּיר הָאָדָם שֶׁאֵין הוּא נִפְרָד כְּלָל
for the purpose of Creation was this very awareness: that man recognize he is not severed at all,
הֲגַם שֶׁנִּרְאֶה נִפְרָד;
even though he appears separate;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַבְּהֵמָה אֵין לָהּ הַכָּרָה זוֹ שֶׁהִיא גַּם כֵּן אֵין נִפְרֶדֶת,
whereas the beast lacks this consciousness that it is likewise unseparated,
וְיֵשׁ לְמַעְלָה פְּנֵי נֶשֶׁר וְכוּלֵי וְהַכֹּל מֵאֲמִיתָּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ;
and there exist Above the face of the eagle, etc., all deriving from His divine truth;
זֶה מַכִּיר רַק הָאָדָם וְלֹא הֵם,
yet this is recognized solely by man and not by them,
וְאֵין זֶה שַׁיָּיךְ "כְּצַלְמֵנוּ", שֶׁהֲרֵי הֵם כְּנִפְרָדִים מִצַּד עַצְמָם,
and they cannot be called "in Our image," since they operate as detached beings from their own perspective,
רַק הָאָדָם מַכִּיר, וְאֵין הֵם עֶצֶם הָאָדָם רַק נִפְרָדִים מִמֶּנּוּ.
man alone perceiving this, while they are not the essence of man but separate from him.
אֲבָל הָאָדָם שֶׁמַּכִּיר זֶה בְּעַצְמוּתוֹ מַמָּשׁ,
However, the person who recognizes this within his literal essence,
שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא: "וְאַתֶּם הַדְּבֵקִים וְגוֹמֵר", דָּבוּק מַמָּשׁ לֹא דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל,
which is termed: "And you who cleave, etc." (Deuteronomy 4:4)—cleaving literally and not merely allegorically—
זֶה נִקְרָא "כְּצַלְמֵנוּ",
this is what is meant by "in Our image",
זֶה עִיקַּר צֶלֶם אָדָם שֶׁזָּכָה לוֹ אַבְרָהָם עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ,
this being the essential Divine Image that Abraham merited through his personal exertion,

הִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ שֶׁנִּקְרָא "הָאָדָם הַגָּדוֹל" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יד438 Bereshit Rabbah 14:6 — "The man" — by the merit of Abraham. R. Levi said: "The greatest man among the giants" — this is Abraham. Why does it call him great? Because he was fit to have been created before Adam the first man; but the Holy One, blessed be He, said: Perhaps he will bring ruin, and there will be no one to come and set it right in his place. Rather, I will create Adam first, so that if he brings ruin, Abraham will come and set it right in his place.).
attaining this level of being called "the greatest man" (as written in Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 14).
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, מִצַּד הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַצְמוֹ הֲרֵי עֲדַיִן נִרְאֶה כְּדָבָר נִפְרָד,
Yet nonetheless, by virtue of the exertion itself, he still appears as a separate actor,
וּמִזֶּה יוֹצֵא פֶּרֶא אָדָם.
and from that aspect of separateness emerged the 'wild ass of a man' (Ishmael).
אֲבָל יִצְחָק נִימּוֹל לִשְׁמוֹנָה,
However, Isaac was circumcised at eight days,
שֶׁהוּא מִלֵּידָה, מִבֶּטֶן קָדוֹשׁ לַה',
being consecrated from birth, holy to Hashem from the womb,
אַף "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ" בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת.
even in the state of "when you lie down," without active exertion.

וְגַם עֵשָׂו נִקְרָא "יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר" בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (יח.)439 Kiddushin 18a — R. Chiyya bar Avin said that R. Yochanan said: A gentile inherits from his father by Torah law, as it is written, "Because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as an inheritance" (Deuteronomy 2:5). But perhaps an apostate Israelite is different? Rather, [it is derived] from here: "Because I have given Ar to the children of Lot as an inheritance" (Deuteronomy 2:9). Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Isaac taught Torah only to his sons, and even among them there was one who was unworthy, except that he is called an "apostate Israelite" in Kiddushin, for he had a root of Jewishness from birth — his head is buried in the Cave of Machpelah in Isaac's bosom — and therefore he too had some hold on words of Torah; yet in the end he too was waste. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 4): [Isaac, the first to be circumcised at eight days, was the one in whom holiness began to take root in all his offspring;] and his wish to draw Esau near was because Esau had free choice, being called an "apostate Israelite," so that the matter stood in the balance whether he could enter into the holiness of Israel.;
And even Esau is initially classified as an "apostate Israelite" in Kiddushin (18a);
רַק הַחִלּוּק: כְּשֶׁהֵמִיר יָצָא מִתּוֹרַת יִשְׂרָאֵל,
the only difference being that once he apostatized he exited the status of Israel,

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּזֶרַע יַעֲקֹב, "אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא – יִשְׂרָאֵל" (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד440 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned" (Joshua 7:11). R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is an Israelite. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is still myrtle and people call it myrtle. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious..),
which is not the case with the seed of Jacob, where "even though he has sinned, he remains Israel" (Sanhedrin 44a),

וְנֶאֱמַר: "רֵיחַ בְּגָדָיו" – רֵיחַ בּוֹגְדָיו (שָׁם לז441 Sanhedrin 37a — R. Zeira said: From here — "And he smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him" (Genesis 27:27): do not read "his garments [begadav]" but "his traitors [bogedav]." Tosafos (s.v. "and he smelled the smell of his garments"): "Smell" is a term that belongs to menstrual blood, as we say at the end of chapter Kol HaYad (Niddah 20b): a certain woman brought blood before R. Elazar; he smelled it and said, "This is blood of desire." Maharsha: Jacob was certainly perfectly righteous, but he was now wearing the garments of the wicked Esau, which Esau had coveted from the wicked Nimrod, and how many bloodstains from the murders of these wicked men were on them; yet when Jacob came before his father even these garments gave off a good fragrance, as it is said, "and he smelled the smell of his garments," for the fragrance of the Garden of Eden entered with him. This is a sign for his children, that even the traitors among them give off a fragrance through the commandments, as with the bloodstains of niddah. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 37a): The garments allude to the empty ones: garments are secondary to the man, and so the empty ones are not the essence of "man" — for the righteous are always likened to man, and Israel, being more righteous than the nations, are called "man" (Yevamot 61a); therefore the wicked are likened to garments, which are not the man himself and are far from him. The good deed that the empty ones do for the sake of Heaven is called "smell" because smell reaches from far away, and so the Holy One, blessed be He, smells the commandments of the empty ones, who are far from Him; further, smell is associated with the attribute of judgment, and the empty ones, who subdue their inclination with great strength and wage war against it, belong to that attribute. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Esau's heart was full of crookedness, and only through the dimming of his eyes could Isaac think well of him; through that same dimming he afterwards did not recognize Jacob either, but he smelled "the smell of his traitors," for even the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and there is no room at all to accuse him. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:57): Jacob's service was chiefly in intention for the sake of Heaven, and the "garments" of deed began only with Laban, where he began to beget the souls of Israel, who are themselves the commandments of the Torah; hence it says then that [Rebecca] dressed him in Esau's garments. Therefore the Sages read "the smell of his garments" as "the smell of his traitors," meaning, as they said, that even the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate: they too have a garment of the deed of the mitzvot. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 10): In Israel the evil stems from the vessels themselves, not from what is drawn out of them, and in the essence of the vessels there is no evil at all; therefore "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors": they too give off a good fragrance, as it says, "the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot." As the Sages said of the myrtle, fragrance without taste, so in Israel there are those who have mitzvot but not Torah. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): The penitent breaks through every bound and in a single moment can rise from the utmost darkness to great light, which is the good name that spreads from one end of the world to the other; and of this it is said, "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors": once they have returned from [their betrayals], theirs is the chief good fragrance, smelled throughout the whole world. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Toldos 5): When Isaac asked, "Are you my son Esau?", he meant that in the smell of his garments he sensed deeds, for which he called him "Esau" [as one who does the will of his Maker]; and the Midrash indeed reads "his garments" as "his traitors." To this Jacob answered "I am": I am the one who performs the deeds of the mitzvot, and what you sensed is the fragrance of Jacob's traitors, for the sinners of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and they too give off a good fragrance. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): Even when Israel sins, it is like a myrtle standing among reeds, for the essence of a Jew's heart always gives off a good fragrance like the myrtle, as the Sages said on "he smelled the smell of his garments": "the smell of his traitors." The sins are only like thorns surrounding the rose, which prick it for the moment, and in the future this will be made clear in all Israel, when "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In the seed of Jacob none is cast off, for just as evening and morning make one day, so His praise rises from the wicked as from the righteous: even the empty ones of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate, and the sinners of Israel are full of remorse. Of this the Sages said, "he smelled the smell of his garments — the smell of his traitors," and Bereishis Rabbah applies it to the likes of Yakim of Tzeroros, who in a brief moment preceded Yose ben Yoezer, a perfect tzaddik who had toiled all his days, to the World to Come; for the penitent attains this in a single moment..).
and it was expounded: "the smell of his garments (begadav)"—the fragrant spark of his traitors (bogedav; Sanhedrin 37a).
וְהַיְינוּ דִּבְשֵׁינָה הוּא הֶעְדֵּר הִתְעַסְּקוּת,
And this means that in sleep there is an absence of active occupation,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב442 Bereshit Rabbah 50:3 — R. Levi said: The Holy One, blessed be He, judges the nations of the world only at night, when they are asleep; and He judges Israel only by day, when they are occupied with the commandments. This is the meaning of the verse, “And He shall judge the world in righteousness.” (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ג וּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נ)
and as written (Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 1:3; Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 50)
דְּאַף כְּשֶׁהֵן יְשֵׁנִים שֶׁאֵין וְכוּלֵי,
that even when they are asleep and not performing mitzvot, etc.,
וְהוּא מִלֵּידָה יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כְּשֶׁאֵין עוֹשֶׂה טוֹב.
he remains an Israelite from birth even when not actively doing good.
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה רַע גַּם כֵּן,
Yet nonetheless, it is required that he also refrain from doing evil,
וּלְכָךְ צָרִיךְ "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ תִּשְׁמֹר וְגוֹמֵר" – שְׁמִירָה מֵרַע,
and therefore he requires "when you lie down it shall watch over you"—protection from evil,
וְצָרִיךְ עֲדַיִן לְהַתְחָלַת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַל כָּל פָּנִים,
and he still requires an initial minimal exertion at least,
הַיְינוּ יְדִיעָה בַּתְּחִלָּה לִשְׁמוֹר עַצְמוֹ מֵרַע.
namely, conscious awareness at the outset to safeguard himself from wrongdoing.
וְאִם כֵּן, עֲדַיִן אֵין כָּאן הַכָּרַת הָאֱמֶת בִּידִיעָה בְּרוּרָה שֶׁאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ,
And if so, there is still not yet present here the recognition of Truth with clear perception that there is none else beside Him,
דְּאָז מַה מָּקוֹם לָרַע?
for if there were, what possible place could remain for evil?
רַק כְּטַעַם "בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ",
Rather, this mirrors the rung of "seeing with their eyes",
שֶׁהוּא רַק כְּעֵין "שִׁוִּיתִי ה' לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" –
which is like setting Hashem before oneself,

דְּהַיְינוּ לְנֶגְדּוֹ לְבַד, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִמְשָׁךְ הַיִּרְאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ שׁוּלְחָן עָרוּךְ אֹרַח חַיִּים443 Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1 (Rema) — “I have set the Lord before me always” — this is a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. For a man’s way of sitting, his movements and his dealings while he is alone in his house are not as his sitting, his movements and his dealings before a great king; nor is his speech and free expression while among his household and relatives as his speech in a king’s court. All the more so when a man takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds — as it is said, “If a man hides himself in secret places, shall I not see him? says the Lord” — at once he attains awe and submission in dread of the Blessed One, and is abashed before Him always.,
namely, facing Him from opposite, whence awe is drawn as stated at the beginning of the Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim;
וְהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ "סוּר מֵרָע" כַּאֲשֶׁר מַכִּיר שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ.
and this is the root of "turn away from evil," recognizing that one stands before the King.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן דַּרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב הוּא "בְּקִרְבְּךָ קָדוֹשׁ" –
In contrast, the spiritual level of Jacob is "the Holy One in the midst of you" (Hosea 11:9)—

מַמָּשׁ קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָיו (תַּעֲנִית יא רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב444 Taanit 11b — R. Elazar said: A man should always regard himself as though a holy one dwelt within his innards, as it is said, "The Holy One is in your midst, and I will not come into the city." Rashi: "As though a holy one dwelt within his innards": as though all his innards were holy, and it is forbidden to weaken them — for this is the sense of "the Holy One is in your midst," that is, that it is forbidden to fast. "The Holy One is in your midst": he is expounding the beginning of the verse, [whose sense is]: because the Holy One dwells in distress, "I will not come into the city" above until I build Jerusalem below; and [his use of it] is a mere allusion. Tosafos (s.v. "as though a holy one"): [That is,] the Holy One, blessed be He. The objection is: but [R. Elazar] said above that he is called holy — that is, that one who sits in a fast is called holy. Maharsha: "Within his innards": one may further explain [that he is called holy] because eating a meal is itself called holiness, as is said in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah on "purity leads to holiness": a person must sanctify himself in his eating, for so it is written concerning the forbidden foods, "Sanctify yourselves and be holy." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 7): He should regard [himself] as though a holy one were within his innards — that is, holiness is with him, as though he himself were holy, and he ought not to fast. Though his innards hold his eating and drinking, let him regard it as though a holy one were there: let him not say, "I am a man and not holy, and I will follow my desire," but regard [himself] as though a holy one were within his innards, and not be drawn after his desire. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): It says in Ta'anis that one should regard oneself as though a holy one dwelt within his innards, and that therefore it is forbidden to fast; that is, through this his eating has the holiness of the sacrifices, and [one who fasts] is like one who removes sacrifices from the altar of God. And the murderer, who causes the Shechinah to depart from all Israel — all the more so it does not dwell within his innards. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Eikev): Great is the eating of Israel, and everything requires divine help to become fit for Israel's eating and to enter the innards of Israel, for the innards too are written "between two letters" [i.e., two Divine Names] — "For the Lord your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God" — "your midst" meaning the innards. And this is what the Gemara says: "as though a holy one dwelt within his innards, as it is said, 'the Holy One is in your midst.'" Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Ta'anis 9): [Reconciling R. Elazar's statements, as his father taught:] when a person sees that enjoying a thing will not hold him back from the will of the Blessed One, and will even help him fulfil it, he is forbidden to fast from it, because it is said, "the Holy One is in your midst," and he must draw out the honor of Heaven that is in that thing, for the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing in vain.).
literally the Holy One dwelling deep within his inward chambers (Ta'anit 11a).
דְּמִצַּד שֶׁצָּרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת דְּ"סוּר מֵרָע",
For from the perspective that requires exertion to turn from evil,
הֲרֵי דְּיֵשׁ עַל כָּל פָּנִים רַע בָּעוֹלָם,
it implies that there exists at least some reality of evil in the world,
וּמִזֶּה יָצָא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרַע וְהוּא עֲמָלֵק שֶׁנִּקְרָא "רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם",
and from that perception emerged the root of evil, which is Amalek, designated "the first among nations",
דְּגוֹיִם הֵם הָרַע וְהוּא הָרֵאשִׁית וְהַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְקוֹם מְצִיאוּת לָרַע.
for the nations represent the manifestations of evil, and he is the primal archetype asserting that evil possesses autonomous existence.
וְהוּא הַתּוּכָא דִּדְהָבָא,
And this is the dross of gold (tucha de-dahava),
דִּבְכָל דָּבָר יָקָר יֵשׁ פְּסוֹלֶת גַּם כֵּן,
for within every precious substance dross is likewise found,

כְּטַעַם "כָּל הַגָּדוֹל מֵחֲבֵירוֹ יִצְרוֹ גָּדוֹל וְכוּלֵי" (סֻכָּה נב445 Sukkah 52a — Abaye heard a certain man say to a woman: Let us rise early and go on the road together. Abaye said: I will go and keep them from transgression. He followed them three parasangs through the marshes. As they parted from one another he heard them say: The way was long, and the company pleasant. Abaye said: Had it been the one who hates me [that is, I myself], I could not have restrained myself. He went and leaned against the bolt of a door in anguish. A certain elder came and taught him: Whoever is greater than his fellow, his evil inclination is greater than his. Rashi (s.v. "had it been the one who hates me"): Had my enemy been alone with the woman, he could not have restrained himself from sinning; and he was speaking of himself. Rashi (s.v. "he leaned"): He leaned against the bolt of the door, like a man who is brooding and in distress. Rashi (s.v. "the way is long, and the company pleasant"): It is a long way between our two places, and we cannot go on together any further; had we been able to go by one road, our company would have been pleasant. Rashi (s.v. "when they were parting from one another"): They were from two towns, and when they reached a fork in the road he turned one way and she the other. Maharsha (on "for he has done greatly"): The verse concludes "for he has done greatly," meaning that he provokes the great more, as Abaye concludes.
