Alternatively, "he has done greatly" means that he has made himself great in relation to the righteous, [appearing to them] as a mountain, as was said above that at first he resembles a spider's thread and in the end cart-ropes; and "among Torah scholars more than all of them" is then a statement in its own right, as in the incident of Abaye. Maharsha (s.v. "the way is long"): It may also be explained as referring to the past: we have come a long way, but the company was pleasant, so that because of the company the way did not seem so long to us. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 2): The evil inclination provokes the Torah scholar more than all, although he is complete, being a man of intellect: for the intellect a man possesses [in this world] is never in its completeness but is held with deficiency, so that the Torah scholar and Israel lack the completeness fitting for them, whereas other men and other nations, who have only the small level, cannot be called so deficient. Therefore the evil inclination provokes them more and more, and whoever has a higher level must guard himself against the evil inclination. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 48): After Israel received the Torah and reached a supreme level, the evil inclination provoked them to sin, in the manner of "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his": because they had reached a supreme level that the rest of creation had not reached, the evil inclination, which is Satan, seeks to cast them down from their level. For privation clings more to a man who has a supreme level, one not fitting for every man, than it clings to the low level that is found in all. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 19): Just as "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his" (and that elder, who was Elijah according to some commentators in Tosafos, a view I have received as primary, was revealed to Abaye through his anguish to tell him this and console him), so too, when someone's inclination is greater than his fellow's, this is a sign that he is also greater than him in the holy sparks within him, for God has made one opposite the other in each person, and the choice is in his hands. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 6): Such an abundance of light would bring great hardship to those who walk in the way of God, for the same reason as "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his": with a greater abundance of the light of the Blessed One, the evil in that same place grows stronger too, because so much light lies within it, for evil always surrounds the good. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): Since the Blessed One does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, and even one created righteous must choose against an inclination that overpowers him daily, "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his". Therefore the inclination appears to the righteous like a mountain, for its assault on them is enormous, matching the great power of good innate in them. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Terumah 8): The Sages said that the evil inclination provokes Torah scholars more than all and that "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his"; why should this be? The inclination is longing, and the purpose of its creation is to be the delight of Torah; so the one who is greater, in whom the delight of Torah is sunk more deeply, has, since "God has made the one opposite the other," a stronger desire toward the opposite as well, while one who does not magnify the delight of Torah in himself has no strong desire for the opposite either. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 2): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," for the virtue is drawn together with the deficiency: as great and precious wealth needs more guarding than a small thing, being more liable to harm because more people strive after it, so in the soul, the greater its stature, that is, the more divine power it holds (and the will toward the opposite is also a divine power), the greater in it is this power of inclination as well, and it needs guarding. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," for as the strength of the virtue, so is the strength of the deficiency, from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, where evil stands opposite the good and corresponds to it. Hence Dan, the lowest of the tribes in virtue, is lower in his deficiency as well, and the inclination is not as strong in him. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 134): When a person reaches a higher level, by the measure of that level he has not yet begun to repent, and his sin returns in full force; of this it is said, "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his", for the sin is the deficiency in a person, and so is the inclination. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Where the strength of the virtue lies, there lies the strength of the deficiency, for "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his": as is known, in Adam's sin the "man of Belial" ruled over the holy man limb for limb, God having made the one opposite the other, so that corresponding to the holiness of each limb and power is the dominion of the "man of Belial" in enticing to evil. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Mishlei 19): "The desire of a man is his kindness": the desire found in a person's heart is also a kindness from the Blessed One, for "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his", and if he brings the power of his longing and desire into holiness, his stature grows all the more. Beis Yaakov (Vayishlach 4): "Whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his," for "God has made the one opposite the other": the power of good against the power of its opposite. Yet every person has the power of good to overcome his inclination, and through this he rises, gathering wealth in holiness little by little, which is the whole purpose of man's creation in this world. Sod Yesharim (Seventh Night of Pesach 16): The vessel [of longing] that a person attains in old age was already in him on the day he was born, only that each time he clarifies himself further, the vessel grows larger in him too, as the Sages said, "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his"..),
mirroring "whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater, etc." (Sukkah 52a),
כְּפִי הַיַּקְרוּת כָּךְ הַפְּסוֹלֶת.
commensurate with the preciousness, so is the extracted dross.
וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הוּא דָּבָר יָקָר שֶׁצָּרִיךְ עֲבוֹדָה,
And exertion is a precious thing requiring toil,
וְלֹא כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה,
which not every person merits,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין צט:)446 Sanhedrin 99b — R. Elazar said: Every man was created for toil, as it is stated, "For man is born to toil." And when it says, "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth," you must conclude that he was created for the toil of Torah. And this is what Rava said: All bodies are carriers of burdens; happy is he who merits to be a carrier of the Torah. Rashi: "Carriers of burdens" — toilers; that is, all bodies were created for toil. "Happy is he who merits" — happy is he who merited that his toil and labour be in Torah. Another explanation: a "druftek" is a long purse into which money is put — all bodies are receptacles for receiving and taking things in, and happy is he who merited to become a receptacle for the Torah. Maharsha: One might have thought man was created for the toil of conversation, even idle talk, since the purpose of his creation is that he is called "a speaking living being," and in this his form differs from the other living creatures; but it is not so — his speech is to be not idle talk but words of Torah, as it is said, "This book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth." "Happy is he who merits" — who merits the purpose for which he was created. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 99b): Man, being a bodily creature, cannot be at rest — rest befits only what is separate from matter — and, being in potential and not in actuality like every material thing, he needs toil, which is his going out into actuality; therefore "man is born to toil." Yet he was not created for the toil of conversation, for speech does not bring a man into actuality, but for the toil of the intellect, for it is through the Torah that man is in actuality. Hence Rava: every body, being in potential, cannot be without toil; but happy is he whose burden-bearing is in the Torah, for he toils in the very thing for which he was created — his final perfection, to be in actuality through the intellectual Torah. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): This world is the world of toil: "man is born to toil," and "happy is he who merits to be a carrier of Torah," for it was for this that the Torah was given — that man's toil should be in words of Torah, just as the Blessed One's work in the act of Creation was entirely through words of Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 2): Israel are called "those who engage in Your Torah," for one should have an engagement in Torah, since man "is born to toil" — that is, he should have an occupation and not go idle; and truly he was created for the toil of Torah, and "happy is he who merits to be a carrier of Torah." In any case, one who must also engage in the toil of worldly occupation should know that he was created only to serve his Maker, his chief intent being to fix times for Torah, or, if he is not capable of that, to raise his children to Torah study.: "טוּבֵיהּ לִדְזָכֵי וְהָוֵי דְּרוֹפְתְּקֵי דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא447 Rashi, Sanhedrin 99b — Fortunate is he who merited it, who laboured in Torah and toiled in it.".
as written (Sanhedrin 99b): "Happy is he who merits to be an enduring vessel for Torah."
וְכֶסֶף, הֲגַם דְּאֵין יָקָר כָּל כָּךְ כְּזָהָב,
And silver, even though not as intrinsically precious as gold,

מִכָּל מָקוֹם לְגַבֵּי דַּהֲבָא נִקְרָא "טִבְעָא" (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא מד:)448 Bava Metzia 44b — In his old age he held: silver, which circulates readily, is the currency; gold, which does not circulate readily, is the commodity — and it is the commodity that effects the acquisition of the currency. Rashi: "Which circulates" — it is spent freely and passes current with the merchant. שֶׁהוּא מַטְבֵּעַ הַיּוֹצֵאת;
is nonetheless termed currency (tiv'a) relative to gold (Bava Metzia 44b), being coin in active circulation;
וְזֶה דֶּרֶךְ כָּל אָדָם בְּעֵסֶק וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים.
and such is the path of every person in active engagement in Torah, mitzvot, and good deeds.

וְיֵשׁ לָזֶה מַצְרֵף449 Proverbs 17:3; 27:21 — “The refining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold, but the Lord tests hearts.” And there: “The refining pot is for silver and the furnace for gold, and a man according to his praise.”,
And for this there is the refining pot (matzref),
וְנִרְאֶה דְּפֵירוּשׁ הַמִּלָּה שֶׁהוּא מְצָרֵף וּמְלַקֵּט כָּל גַּרְגִּירֵי הַכֶּסֶף הַנָּקִי
and it appears that the meaning of the word is that it joins and collects all grains of pure silver
וְהַנִּשְׁאָר יוֹצֵא לַחוּץ;
while the remainder is discarded outside;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כּוּר לַזָּהָב הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ,
whereas the furnace (kur) for gold operates in the reverse,
שֶׁהוּא מַדְחֶה הַפְּסוֹלֶת מִתּוֹכוֹ וְהַנִּשְׁאָר כֻּלּוֹ זַךְ.
casting the dross out from within itself so that what remains is entirely pure.
וּבְמַצְרֵף וָכוּר שָׁם נִבְחָנִים כָּל מִינֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת:
And in the refining pot and the furnace, all categories of spiritual exertion are tested:
אִם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת פְּרָטִי בְּכָל עִנְיָנָיו,
whether in detailed exertion throughout all one's daily matters,
שֶׁבָּזֶה צָרִיךְ צֵירוּף מְרוּבֶּה לְלַקֵּט כָּל פְּרָטֵי מַעֲשָׂיו אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ לַה';
wherein much refining is needed to gather every detail of one's actions that were truly dedicated unto Hashem;
וְאִם בַּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הַכְּלָלִי לְהַכִּיר אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא נִכְחוֹ.
or in overarching general striving to recognize that Hashem stands directly facing him.
וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן פְּשִׁיטַת טְלָפַיִם,
And within this sphere there also exists the hypocritical extension of hooves,

כְּשִׁבְעָה מִינֵי פְּרוּשִׁים שֶׁזָּכְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה כב450 Sotah 22b — The Sages taught: There are seven kinds of Pharisee: the Pharisee of Shechem, the bruised Pharisee, the bloodletting Pharisee, the pestle Pharisee, the Pharisee of "What is my duty, that I may do it?", the Pharisee out of love, and the Pharisee out of fear. The Pharisee of Shechem — this is one who acts as the men of Shechem acted. The bruised Pharisee — this is one who bruises his feet [dragging them to appear humble]. The bloodletting Pharisee — R. Nachman bar Yitzchak said: this is one who draws his blood against the walls [walking with his eyes shut]. The pestle Pharisee — Rabba bar Sheila said: one who stoops over like a pestle. Rashi: "The deed of Shechem": they circumcised themselves not for the sake of Heaven; so too this one's deeds are for his own benefit, that people should honor him, and not for the sake of Heaven. "Bruises his feet": he walks humbly, heel beside toe, without lifting his feet from the ground, and so strikes his toes against the stones; "draws blood against the walls": he makes himself like one who shuts his eyes so as not to look at women, and thereby strikes his head against the wall until the blood flows. "Stoops like a pestle": he walks bent over, like a pounder shaped like a mallet whose head is bent. Tosafos (s.v. "the Pharisee out of love, the Pharisee out of fear"): The Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot, ch. 9) explains the seven differently: the Pharisee of Shechem carries his mitzvot on his shoulder; the "bruised" one says, "Wait for me while I do a mitzva"; the "bloodletting" one does one sin and one mitzva and offsets the one against the other; another says, "Whatever I have, I deduct from it and do mitzvot"; the one of "What is my duty, that I may do it?" asks, "What sin have I committed, that I may do a mitzva to match it?"; the Pharisee out of fear is like Job and the Pharisee out of love like Abraham — and none of them is beloved but the Pharisee out of love, like Abraham, as it is written: "the seed of Abraham who loved Me" (Isaiah 41:8). There too it teaches: act out of love and act out of fear — out of love, for should you come to hate, know that you love, and one who loves does not hate; out of fear, for should you come to rebel, know that you fear, and one who fears does not rebel. Maharsha: The Gemara does not object here, as it does shortly after, that a person should engage in mitzvot even not for their own sake, because the "not for its own sake" of Shechem was worse and notorious, since they had already sinned and he had violated her, for which they were liable to death. The bruised Pharisee may also be understood through the teaching in Chullin that the blood of a bruise suffered on the way to a mitzva atones like the blood of a burnt-offering: he bruises his own feet so that people will think him a righteous man atoned for as by such blood. And though one should walk with head bowed, stooping like a pestle is excessive; perhaps all these refer to those who display abstinence before people without being abstinent, whereas a true Pharisee who does these things is praiseworthy. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 22b): The name "Pharisee" is said of one who separates himself from a thing although he is not obligated to, and does so; and there are seven, because such separations beyond obligation, by which people appear righteous in others' eyes, number seven. For anything that must be kept entirely distant, and after which people tend to be strongly drawn, has seven levels, from what is near to what is farthest, since this number is suited to such a thing.:),
like the seven types of hypocritical ascetics recorded by our Sages (Sotah 22b),
שֶׁמַּרְאֶה אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּרוֹצֶה לְהַכִּיר אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהוּא מְאַנֶּה אֶת עַצְמוֹ.
who displays himself as seeking to know Hashem while merely deceiving himself.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר נֶחְפַּשׂ עֵשָׂו נִבְעוּ מַצְפּוּנָיו,
And when Esau is searched out his hidden schemes are laid bare,

וּמְפַרְסְמִין הַחֲנֵפִים (יוֹמָא פו451 Yoma 86b — The hypocrites are exposed on account of the desecration of the Name, as it is stated: "When a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will lay a stumbling block before him." Rashi: "The hypocrites are exposed": those who are wicked yet present themselves as righteous — if anyone knows his deeds, it is a commandment to expose him because of the desecration of the Name, for people learn from his deeds, thinking him righteous; and moreover, when punishment comes upon him, people say, "What did his merit avail him?" "As it is stated, When a righteous man turns from his righteousness": the end of the verse is "I will lay a stumbling block before him" — I bring his way a sin, open to all, on which he stumbles, and they come to know his deeds. Maharsha: As Rashi explains, they show themselves openly as righteous while their heart is not with them; and this is why it says "and commits iniquity," for the word "iniquity" [avel] is used of one who acts so in secret, the source of them all being "Indeed, in your heart you work iniquities" (Psalms 58:3).:),
and hypocrites are publicly exposed (Yoma 86b),

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וָאֵרָא ט) עַל פָּסוּק "אִם יִסָּתֵר אִישׁ וְגוֹמֵר452 Midrash Tanchuma, Vaera 9 — The Holy One, blessed be He, displays the arrogance of the haughty to all creatures. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: “Can a man hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? says the Lord.” R. Binyamin bar Levi said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let a man sit in a corner of his house and occupy himself with Torah — I display him to all creatures; all the more so if a man hides himself to worship idols or to commit a transgression, I display him to all creatures, as it is said, “Can a man hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? says the Lord.”",
and as our Sages expounded (Midrash Tanchuma, Va'era 9) on the verse "Can any hide himself, etc." (Jeremiah 23:24),
הוּא נִדְחֶה מִמֵּילָא.
such false devotion being automatically rejected.
וְכָל זֶה הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה כְּשֶׁאָדָם מַתְחִיל לִיכָּנֵס לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
And all of this represents the preliminary stages when a person begins entering divine service,
דְּעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לַעֲבוֹר מִקּוֹדֶם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת הַלָּלוּ,
requiring him to pass through these two lower levels beforehand;
דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ לִתְמִימוּת שֶׁהוּא פְּשִׁיטוּת
for it is impossible to arrive at wholeness (temimut), which is pure simplicity,
וְאֵינוֹ דָּבָר יָקָר כְּלָל,
and is not an ostentatious, costly thing at all,
רַק "כִּי קָרוֹב אֵלֶיךָ הַדָּבָר וְגוֹמֵר",
but rather "for the thing is very near unto you, etc." (Deuteronomy 30:14),
שֶׁהוּא נְחֹשֶׁת שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סוּסְפִיתָא,
symbolized by copper which contains no dross (susfita),
כִּי הַפָּשׁוּט אֵין בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן
for what is simple possesses no deficiency,
וּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת פְּסוֹלֶת כְּלָל,
and his bed is intact such that no waste can possibly emerge,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן בְּקִרְבּוֹ מַמָּשׁ,
since Hashem, blessed be He, dwells literally within his very inward core,

וְאַף "בְּתוֹךְ טֻמְאֹתָם" (יוֹמָא נו453 Yoma 56b — The Sages taught: "And so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them in the midst of their impurity" — even at a time when they are impure, the Divine Presence is with them. Maharsha (Yoma 57a, s.v. "now you are certainly impure"): [The Sadducee] meant: even if you were once pure, now in exile you have certainly become impure, as it is written, "Her impurity is in her skirts," and He separates Himself from you as one keeps apart from the impurity of a menstruant. [R. Chanina] answered him from what is written of them, "that dwells with them [in the midst of their impurity]," that He does not separate entirely, but as a man keeps apart from his wife while she is a menstruant yet lives with her in one house; so the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells with us even now in exile, as it is said, "I will be with him in distress." Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 4): The Blessed One does not dwell in the midst of their impurity unless the sin was unwitting, and of that it is written, "And so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting that dwells with them in the midst of their impurity." [Hence the First Temple, whose distinction was that the Divine Presence rested in it,] was destroyed when they defiled the Sanctuary through idolatry, sexual immorality and bloodshed, the three sins that are called impurity. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 1): The Divine Presence does not depart even toward evening, in the time of darkness, as it is likewise said, "who dwells with them amid their impurity." For the souls of all Israel are bound and linked together as in a chain, so that the revelation of the Divine light — in concealment, hiddenness and great contraction — is not absent from the heart of any Jew; even the lowest of the low has in him a portion of life, a portion of God from above. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Regarding spiritual holiness it is said, "who dwells with them amid their impurity," and "the Divine Presence never departed from the Western Wall": in concealment it never departed, even in every kind of sinking into evil bitterer than death — "I will fear no evil, for You are with me." We suppose this a deficiency, but in truth it is the strength of completeness and the ultimate clarification: that wherever a person sinks, his heart remains bound to the Blessed One with a bond that cannot be severed. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The Holy One, blessed be He, as it were entered Egypt, the place of impurity, and this was the great miracle and the first of the miracles: the clarification of "I am the Lord who dwells with them amid their impurity," from their beginning and root in the Patriarchs, who are truly holy seed with no connection to any impurity, so that it was revealed that impurity has no real existence. Esther is the end: even in the lowest levels, where the nations hold sway, the Blessed One is with them, even in the place of impurity's greatest strength, as when Esther entered the house of Ahasuerus. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 4): Raising the holy sparks out of the matters of this world, by engaging in them for the sake of Heaven, is like a king's son returning from captivity, whose joy exceeds that of one who was always in the palace; of this it is said, "I am the Lord who dwells with them amid their impurity" — amid it precisely. Over this that wicked one [Bilaam] was blinded when he spoke of "the fourth of Israel" and said "He who is holy…," for he did not know that there is holiness even in bodily matters. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): So too the souls of Israel outside the Land are like the Tabernacle [dismantled in order to be rebuilt], for the Blessed One dwells with them amid their impurity and His Presence is within the hearts of Israel: wherever they were exiled the Divine Presence went into exile with them, and that place became their place. Through the exile they gather in the bit of good among the nations and return it all to holiness, and that place too becomes sanctified with the holiness of the air of the Land of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Even when sin caused Israel to be exiled among the nations, outside even the holiness of the Land, wherever they were exiled the Divine Presence went with them — for even "in the lands of their enemies I have not rejected them," and "I am the Lord who dwells with them amid their impurity." Nonetheless they are never separated from the root of holiness, and in the end all will be redeemed, even those wholly assimilated among the nations.:),
and even "in the midst of their uncleanness" (Yoma 56b),
מִמֵּילָא אֵין טֻמְאָה.
meaning that impurity has no true dominion.
וְזֶהוּ הַכָּרַת הַיִּחוּד הַגָּמוּר שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם לְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת כְּלָל,
And this is the perception of absolute Divine Unity wherein self-conscious striving has no place at all,
רַק כְּטַעַם "וַהֲקִיצוֹתָ הִיא תְשִׂיחֶךָ" מֵעַצְמָהּ,
operating rather in the manner of "and when you awake it shall converse with you" entirely on its own,

כְּטַעַם (בְּרָכוֹת טז:)454 Berakhot 16b — After he had concluded his prayer, R. Elazar would say: May it be Your will, Lord our God, to cause love and brotherhood, peace and companionship to dwell in our lot; to make our borders rich in disciples; to prosper our end with a future and a hope; to set our portion in the Garden of Eden; and to provide us with a good companion and a good inclination in Your world. And may we rise early and find our heart’s longing to fear Your name, and may the contentment of our soul come before You for good. Rashi: Rashi glosses "in our lot [pureinu]" as "in our portion," and "a future and a hope" as: that our end be good and that we see what we have hoped for. On "may we rise early and find our heart's longing to fear Your name": that the evil inclination not overcome us through the thoughts of the night and so turn us from You by day; rather, when we rise each morning may we find our heart yearning toward You. "May the contentment of our soul come before You" means the supplying of our needs and our peace of mind. Maharsha: Beside Rashi's rendering of "pureinu" as "our lot," Maharsha offers a second reading: it is our marriage bed, that our household be whole in love — and it is for this reason that the same words, love and brotherhood and peace and companionship, were fixed in the seven wedding blessings. On "and may we find the longing [yichul] of our heart" he prefers to read the word with a yod, from trembling and dread, as in "my heart trembles within me," and he hears in "the contentment [korat] of our soul" an allusion to "as cold water [mayim karim] to a faint soul." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3): Kerias Shema is the constant acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, in which one must be so bound up in thought that even lying on his bed he knows before Whom he lies, so that it will be as in "may we rise early and find our heart's yearning": as soon as he rises he finds himself in the place where he lay down, in that same thought. So it was with Jacob, "and behold, the Lord stood over him," for all day the Lord was before him and even at night his heart did not lie down in another thought. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim Katan 2): The Shulchan Aruch opens with "one should strengthen himself like a lion," for the main thing is to overcome the evil inclination and rise in the morning to the service of one's Creator; this is akin to "may we rise early and find our heart's yearning to fear Your name," meaning that without any preparation or deeds our heart's longing should be for the fear of Heaven and His service. Only afterward can the evil inclination gain strength, and for this the Rema opened with "I have set the Lord before me always.": "וְנַשְׁכִּים וְנִמְצָא יִחוּל לִבֵּנוּ",
mirroring the prayer (Berakhot 16b): "and may we awake to find our heart yearning for You,"
שֶׁמִּיָּד בְּהַשְׁכָּמָה מִשֵּׁינָה אָז הוּא הַתְחָלַת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת.
for the instant of awakening from sleep marks the threshold of human exertion.
וְדַרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב, שֶׁגַּם הַהַתְחָלַת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אֵינוֹ מִשֶּׁלּוֹ כְּלָל, רַק "הִיא תְשִׂיחֶךָ".
And the spiritual rung of Jacob is that even this initial awakening is not generated by him at all, but rather "it shall converse with you."
וְזֶהוּ פּוּרִים "עַד דְּלָא יָדַע וְכוּלֵי",
And this is the meaning of Purim: "until he knows not, etc.",
שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְשִׁכְרוּתוֹ שֶׁל לוֹט,
reaching the total intoxication of Lot,
שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו כְּמִתְעַסֵּק בְּעָלְמָא,
wherein all a person's actions are performed like one acting purely oblivious,
שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם דַּעַת לֹא בַּתְּחִלָּה וְלֹא בַּסּוֹף,
possessing no calculating intellect either at the beginning or at the end,
וְעִם כָּל זֶה דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and nevertheless remaining cleaving unto Hashem, blessed be He.
כִּי הָמָן בָּא מִכֹּחַ טַעֲנָה שֶׁהִשְׁתַּחֲווּ וְכוּלֵי,
For Haman attacked by virtue of the accusation that they had bowed to the idol, etc.,
וְאָמַר שֶׁצָּרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עַל כָּל פָּנִים לָסוּר מֵרָע;
arguing that one must at least demonstrate human effort to turn from evil;
וּבֶאֱמֶת אֵין כֵּן, דְּהֵם לֹא עָשׂוּ אֶלָּא לִפְנִים,
yet in truth it is not so, for they only acted superficially for appearance,
כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לָרַע כְּלָל רַק לִפְנִים.
since the essential root of Israel holds no connection to evil whatsoever, save externally.
וּבְכָל פּוּרִים זוֹכִין לְאוֹר זֶה,
And on every Purim we merit this transcendent illumination,
וְהוּא מֵעֵין שַׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא,
which is an inkling of Shabbat which is an inkling of the World to Come,
דְּאֵין שָׁם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת דְּ"יִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי",
where the effort of 'Israel sanctifies the seasons' does not operate,
רַק קְדוּשָּׁה קְבִיעָא וְקַיָּימָא.
rather an inherent, fixed, and enduring holiness.
וְכֵן פּוּרִים אֵין צָרִיךְ קְדוּשַׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל,
And likewise Purim does not depend upon the conscious sanctification of Israel,
שֶׁהֲרֵי מִצְוָתוֹ בְּשִׁכְרוּת "עַד דְּלָא יָדַע",
for its central mitzvah is observed through intoxication 'until he knows not',
שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם לְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת;
leaving no room for calculated striving;
רַק אוֹתוֹ יוֹם זָכָה בַּגּוֹרָל מֵעַצְמוֹ,
rather that day was chosen through the lot on its own,
כְּמוֹ מִי שֶׁמַּרְוִיחַ בַּגּוֹרָל בְּלֹא יְגִיעָה כְּלָל.
like one who wins through a lottery without any toil whatsoever.

sections.en: Ahasuerus's Feast and the Hidden King

items.h: The Megillah's royal banquet conceals a deeper divine feast, where intoxication, reversal, and hidden providence prepare the cure before the affliction appears.

Seif 1 — The Feast before the Cure
Ahasuerus's banquet conceals divine providence, preparing Purim's salvation through the very setting that seems to threaten Israel.

p: עִנְיַן מִשְׁתֵּה אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ שֶׁנִּזְכַּר בַּמְּגִילָּה וּדְרָשׁוֹת רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בּוֹ, וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ דָּבָר רֵיק,
The matter of the feast of Ahasuerus recorded in the Megillah and our Sages' homilies concerning it are certainly not an empty thing,
וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ עִנְיַן מִשְׁתֵּה פוּרִים עַכְשָׁיו אַחַר הָרְפוּאָה.
and it is intrinsically the archetype of the Purim feast now observed following the cure.

וְאוֹתוֹ מִשְׁתֶּה הָיָה הָרְפוּאָה שֶׁקָדַם לַמַּכָּה, כְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה יג455 Megillah 13b — "After these things" (Esther 3:1) — after what? Rava said: After the Holy One, blessed be He, had created the remedy for the blow. For Reish Lakish said: The Holy One, blessed be He, does not strike Israel unless He first creates a remedy for them, as it is stated: "When I would heal Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim is uncovered" (Hosea 7:1). But with the nations of the world it is not so: He strikes them, and only afterward does He create a remedy for them, as it is stated: "And the Lord shall smite Egypt, smiting and healing" (Isaiah 19:22). Rashi: “After these things the king promoted Haman” is written after the episode of Bigthan and Teresh, and the Gemara asks “after what?” — that is, what is Scripture testifying in telling us that he did not promote him until this affair had come about. “After the Holy One, blessed be He, had created the remedy for the blow” — for the blow that was destined to come later. And “when I would heal Israel” means: only afterward “is the iniquity of Ephraim uncovered,” through the blow that I bring upon them. Maharsha: The Holy One, blessed be He, has already assured us, “I will make a full end of all the nations … but of you I will not make a full end, and I will chastise you in measure” (Jeremiah 46:28); the sufferings that come upon Israel do not come to destroy them but to scour away their sin, and this is their remedy, prepared before the blow, for they will certainly be healed. Not so the nations of the world, for it is possible that they be utterly destroyed and never come to a remedy at all; only if they repent may healing come to them afterward, as it is said of them, “smiting and healing, and they shall return to the Lord” (Isaiah 19:22). Maharal (Ohr Chadash, Esther 3:1): With Israel, were there no remedy the Holy One, blessed be He, would not strike them at all, for He does not destroy Israel, and the blow can never rest upon them except where there is a remedy for them; thus the remedy is the cause of the blow, and without the remedy there would be no blow. And since the cause of a thing precedes the thing it causes, the remedy comes first. With the nations, however, the remedy is not the cause of the blow; on the contrary, the blow is the cause of the remedy and the remedy follows upon it, and therefore the blow comes first.:),
And that very feast was the remedy that preceded the affliction, in accordance with the words of our Sages (Megillah 13b),
דְּוַדַּאי בְּדֵעָה מְיוּשֶּׁבֶת לֹא הָיָה הוֹרֵג לְוַשְׁתִּי
for surely with a settled mind he would never have executed Vashti,
רַק עַל יְדֵי מִשְׁתֶּה, דְּפֵירוּשׁוֹ סְעוּדָה שֶׁל שִׁכְרוּת,
save through a drinking feast, which denotes a feast of drunkenness,
דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא כָּל הַסְּעוּדָה עַל שֵׁם הַשְּׁתִיָּה.
which is why the entire meal is designated by the term for drinking.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שָׁם יב456 Megillah 12a — [R. Shimon ben Yochai said that the Jews of that generation were liable to destruction because they had prostrated themselves to the image.] They said to him: But is there favoritism in the matter [that they were nevertheless delivered]? He said to them: They did it only for appearance's sake, and so too the Holy One, blessed be He, dealt with them only for appearance's sake. And this is what is written: "For He does not afflict from His heart" (Lamentations 3:33). Rashi: "But is there favoritism in the matter?" — that is, how then did they merit a miracle? "They did it only for appearance's sake" — out of fear. Maharsha: That is, they acted so only from fear of being killed, as is set out in the book of Daniel, and did not intend in their hearts to serve the idol; so too the Holy One, blessed be He, dealt with them only outwardly, frightening them that they deserved destruction so that they should take alarm and repent on that account. And this is the sense of "For He does not afflict from His heart": when a man commits a transgression with his heart not in it, the Holy One, blessed be He, "grieves the children of men" only in order that he should repent and be delivered from the trouble. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 33): Though the Jews were only joining gentiles at a single feast, the Gemara calls this "serving idols in purity," and this was the accusation: that they took pleasure in the feast of that wicked man, which is a trace of idolatry, and likewise that they bowed to the image — though it was only a [royal] statue and they did it only for appearance's sake, it is nevertheless a trace of idolatry, and "round about Him it storms greatly" [He is exacting with those near Him]. Because they then purified themselves in this matter until they had slaughtered the inclination to idolatry entirely, the Blessed One wished to establish a feast for them, to show that even in their drunkenness they need fear nothing, their hearts being already whole with Him. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): The acceptance of the Torah in the days of Ahasuerus, though out of love, was in concealment, for in what was revealed there were claims against them, as the Sages said that "they did it only for appearance's sake" — that is, only in the outward, revealed deed, while the inwardness of their heart is for God. This was the redemption of that time, which made clear concerning Israel's sins that even when they sin, the inwardness of their heart is for Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 255): The Megillah opens with the feast because the decree sprouted from it, as the Sages said, "because they took pleasure"; and although the Gemara concludes that it was because they bowed to the image, they were not punished for that at the time, since in truth they did it only for appearance's sake, and "the Lord sees into the heart" — there was sin only from the human side, for "man sees what is before the eyes." As long as they conduct themselves with a generous eye, the Blessed One too has a generous eye toward them, bestowing on them by His measure of "seeing into the heart"; but on account of "they took pleasure" — the incitement of the power of the narrow eye — the Blessed One too said, "Mine is mine and yours is yours," judging by what is before the eyes..): יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא עָשׂוּ אֶלָּא לִפְנִים וְכוּלֵי,
And as written (there, 12a): Israel acted only externally, etc.,
שֶׁהַחֵטְא שֶׁלָּהֶם לֹא הָיָה בְּדַעַת מְיוּשֶּׁבֶת וּשְׁלֵימָה, וְהָיָה לִפְנִים עוֹנֶשׁ;
in that their sin did not stem from settled and mature consciousness, and likewise their punishment was only outward;
וְהַהַצָּלָה גַּם כֵּן שֶׁלֹּא עַל יְדֵי דַּעַת מְיוּשֶּׁבֶת
and their salvation likewise unfolded not through settled deliberation,
וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי יַיִן,
rather through wine,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין עא457 Sanhedrin 71b — Wine and sleep for the wicked are a benefit to them and a benefit to the world; and for the righteous they are an evil to them and an evil to the world. Rashi: As long as they are drinking and sleeping they do not sin and do no harm to people. For the righteous it is an evil to them, for [then] they are not occupied with Torah; and an evil to the world, for the Torah with which they occupy themselves protects the generation, and when they are idle from it, punishment comes to the world. Maharsha: From the pleasure of the wine on which he becomes drunk he comes to the pleasure of sleep in the morning until the fourth hour, as is said of the gentile kings. So it is with the rebellious son: wine and sleep are a benefit to him and a benefit to the world, for as long as he has the means to buy wine and is asleep he does not rob people, until he has used up his property. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): "Wine and sleep for the wicked are a benefit to them, etc., but for the righteous an evil, etc." — for wine "was created only to comfort mourners and to give reward to the wicked," who through it are sunk in lust as they please, which is their whole desire and their benefit; and it is also a benefit to the world that they are sunk in lust and do no harm to others. For the righteous, however, it is the beginning of a fall: even when wine causes no outright evil, it brings on sleep and a slackening of the hands from the service of the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 238): Sleep too is good for re-awakening after the mind has fallen into a confusion of alien thoughts: in sleep the mind departs and afterwards a new soul returns, so that one can strengthen himself anew and forget all that was the day before. This is the reason for "sleep for the wicked, etc." and the reverse for the righteous: the mind and holy thoughts they held all day depart, and the next day they need a fresh strengthening and a new beginning, and all beginnings are hard, whereas within the day the thought remains bound and continues. With the wicked it is the reverse: their scheming thought continues all day, so that it can hardly cleave to words of Torah except with great difficulty, so strongly is it bound to the alien things he thinks of.:): "יַיִן וְשֵׁינָה לָרְשָׁעִים וְכוּלֵי, לַצַּדִּיקִים וְכוּלֵי",
as written (Sanhedrin 71b): "Wine and sleep are beneficial for the wicked, etc., while for the righteous, etc.,"
שֶׁאֵין לוֹ דַּעַת לַעֲשׂוֹת, וְרָשָׁע אֵין עוֹשֶׂה רַע.
because the wicked person loses cognitive capacity to act, thereby desisting from doing evil.

אֲבָל גַּבֵּי יִשְׂרָאֵל, "עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים", אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת מ458 Berakhot 40a — It was taught: The tree from which Adam ate — R. Meir says it was the vine, for nothing brings wailing upon a man but wine, as it is said, "And he drank of the wine and became drunk." R. Nechemiah says it was the fig, for by the very thing they were ruined by they were set right, as it is said, "And they sewed fig leaves." R. Yehudah says it was wheat, for a child does not know how to call "father" and "mother" until he has tasted the taste of grain. Rashi: "Nothing brings wailing upon a man but wine" — and this [tree] brought death [into the world]. "A child does not know how to call father and mother [until he has tasted grain]" — and this [tree] is called the Tree of Knowledge. Maharal (Derech Chaim 4:21): All three powers of man were in the Tree of Knowledge, as the verse says, "that the tree was good for food" — against the appetite; "and that it was a delight to the eyes" — against the vital power of the soul; "and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise" — against the intellect; and the Sages differ only over which of them was the chief cause of death. R. Meir says the vine, since it is the vital power, in which sight resides, that is drawn after wine — "look not upon wine when it is red"; R. Yehudah says wheat, since eating grain gives understanding, and the sin lay in the intellect going out beyond its proper measure; R. Nechemiah says the fig, since of all fruits the fig is most desired for eating, and the death came through his being drawn after the natural power from which desire arises..):
However, regarding Israel, of whom it is said 'Your people are all righteous,' our Sages stated (Berakhot 40a):
"אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁמֵּבִיא יְלָלָה וְכוּלֵי",
"There is nothing that brings lamentation like wine, etc.,"
דְּגַם בְּלֹא דַּעַת נֶפֶשׁ לֹא טוֹב,
for 'without knowledge the soul is not good' (Proverbs 19:2),

וְאֵין "לֹא טוֹב" אֶלָּא רָע (שַׁבָּת קמט459 Shabbat 149b — Rather, it is derived from here: "Also, for a righteous man to bring punishment is not good" — and "not good" means nothing other than evil; and it is written, "For You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You" — You are righteous, Lord, and evil shall not dwell in Your dwelling. Rashi: "Also to punish the righteous is not good": a righteous man who brings about punishment is not good, and since he is not good, he is evil. "And it is written, evil shall not dwell with You": thus he does not enter His enclosure. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 149b): Though the Holy One, blessed be He, punishes the sinner for his sin, because true justice requires that judgment be done — and all of it is for good, since even the evil that comes from Him serves the purpose of good — a man intends only the evil; therefore one through whom his fellow is punished, bringing his fellow to privation, himself inclines toward privation. So he is not brought into the enclosure of the Holy One, blessed be He, with whom there is no privation or lack: having been the cause of an evil thing, of which it is written "evil shall not dwell with You," he has no bond or connection with Him, for privation cannot join with Him who is complete existence.:).
and 'not good' signifies literal evil (Shabbat 149b).
אֲבָל בְּפוּרִים צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת "עַד דְּלָא יָדַע", הֶעְדֵּר הַדַּעַת,
Yet on Purim there must be the state of 'until he knows not,' an absence of conscious intellect,
וְזֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם רַע?
and is this, Heaven forbid, evil?
רַק מוּבָן עַל פִּי דִּבְרֵי הָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה בִּפְרִי עֵץ חַיִּים בְּטַעַם זֶה,
Rather, it is understood through the words of the holy Ari, of blessed memory, in Pri Etz Chayim concerning this reason:
כְּדֵי לְהַשְׁפִּיעַ לַנִּיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ שֶׁבַּקְּלִיפָּה,
in order to channel divine light unto the holy spark trapped within the kelipah (husk),

וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר אֶלָּא בְּלֹא דַּעַת, דִּבְלָאו הָכִי וְכוּלֵי, יְעֻיַּין שָׁם460 Pri Etz Chaim, Sha'ar HaPurim ch. 6 — See Pri Etz Chaim, the Gate of Purim, chapter six, on the inner meaning of the day and its obligation of rejoicing..
and this is achievable solely in a state transcending conscious intellect, for otherwise, etc., see there.
וְהַכַּוָּנָה: כִּי בְּכָל עִנְיַן רַע וּמִדָּה רָעָה יֵשׁ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר טוֹב, לְוּלֵי כֵן לֹא הָיָה בָּעוֹלָם;
And the inner meaning is: within every evil phenomenon and negative trait exists a divine point of goodness, without which it could never exist in the universe;
וּכְמוֹ כֵן בָּאֻמּוֹת, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "גָּלוּת הַשְּׁכִינָה" כַּיָּדוּעַ.
and similarly among the gentile nations, and this is designated as 'the exile of the Shechinah,' as is known.
וְהַיְינוּ: כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בָּרַע הֲרֵי הַטּוֹב כָּפוּף לוֹ,
Namely: as long as one utilizes evil, the good remains subjugated beneath it,
וְכָל כֹּחַ שִׁימּוּשׁ הָרַע בְּוַדַּאי אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי מְעַט הַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ, כִּי הַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and the active capacity of evil to operate is derived strictly from the kernel of good embedded within it, for all originates from Hashem, blessed be He.
דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל, הָרוֹצֵחַ וְהוֹרֵג אָדָם,
By way of example: regarding a murderer who slays a human being,
הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁיּוּכַל לִשְׁלוֹט אָדָם בְּאָדָם לְהָרְגוֹ לְעִנְיַן הַטּוֹב –
Hashem created this potential for man to hold lethal power over man for a sanctified purpose—
לַהֲרוֹג שִׁבְעָה עֲמָמִין וַעֲמָלֵק וְכָל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין.
to execute the seven nations, Amalek, and those condemned to death by the court.
וְעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִיתַּן כֹּחַ זֶה לָאָדָם, וְזֶה הוּא הַמְכֻוָּון בִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבָּרָא כֹּחַ זֶה.
And for this purpose was this capacity endowed unto man, this being the primary divine will in creating this power.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בּוֹ לְרַע, נִמְצָא כֹּחַ זֶה שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּפוּף לְשִׁימּוּשׁ דְּרַע;
Yet when one employs it for wickedness, this divine faculty from Hashem becomes subjugated to the operation of evil;
וְכֹחוֹתָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ הַשּׁוֹכְנִים בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים נִקְרָא "שְׁכִינָה", וְזֶהוּ "גָּלוּת הַשְּׁכִינָה".
and His divine powers indwelling within lower realms are termed the Shechinah, and this constitutes the 'exile of the Shechinah.'
וְהִנֵּה בַּעֲמָלֵק נֶאֱמַר "תִּמְחֶה", וְאֵין מְקַבְּלִים גֵּרִים מִמֶּנּוּ
Now regarding Amalek it is commanded 'you shall utterly blot out,' and we accept no converts from him

(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מְכִילְתָּא סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח461 Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Amalek 2 — R. Eliezer says: The Omnipresent swore by His throne that if one of any of the nations of the world comes to convert, Israel shall accept him, but from the house of Amalek they shall not accept him, as it is stated: "And David said to the young man who told him: Where are you from? And he said: I am the son of a stranger, an Amalekite" (II Samuel 1:13). At that moment David recalled what had been said to Moses, and said: "Your blood be upon your head, for your own mouth has testified against you" (II Samuel 1:16). Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 5): Amalek is excluded from all the nations, in that Israel were commanded to wipe it out entirely and converts are not accepted from it, as stated in the Mekhilta. For each nation is a particular power of evil, and there is no evil trait in the world without some side of good, for otherwise it would not exist; but Amalek, "the first of the nations" and the beginning of the spread of every kind of evil, has no particular power of evil at all — it is the root of evil, for its whole power is that it is the opposite of good, and its whole will is to destroy the name of Israel, Heaven forbid, from the world.);
(as written in the Mekhilta, end of Parashat Beshalach);
נִמְצָא שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ טוֹב כְּלָל,
meaning that he harbors no redeemable good whatever,
וְאֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר זֶה, וּמִנַּיִן לוֹ חַיּוּת וְקִיּוּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּלָל?
how then is this possible, and from where does he derive vitality and existence in this world at all?
וְנִרְאֶה כִּי הוּא הַדַּעַת דְּרַע,
And it appears that he embodies the Da'at (Consciousness) of evil,
דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא "רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם",
which is why he is titled 'the first of the nations,'
כִּי דַּעַת הוּא חִבּוּר חָכְמָה וּבִינָה שֶׁהֵם רֵאשִׁית.
for Da'at is the synthesis of Chokhmah and Binah which are the Beginning.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁבָּא נֶגֶד מֹשֶׁה שֶׁהוּא הַדַּעַת,
And this explains why he attacked opposite Moses who embodies Da'at,
וּבָא מִיָּד בְּרִפּוּי יָדַיִם מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא הַדַּעַת אֶת ה', גּוֹבֵר דַּעַת אַחֶרֶת רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן.
striking immediately upon the slackening of hands from Torah, which is the knowledge of Hashem, whereby alien consciousness surges, Heaven preserve us.

וּבֶאֱמֶת יָדוּעַ דְּ"אֵל אַחֵר אִסְתָּרַס וְלָא עָבִיד פֵּירִין" (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, קג עַמּוּד א462 Zohar 2:103a — Come and see: it is written, "And a river went out of Eden to water the garden" (Genesis 2:10). That river never rests from spreading and increasing and bearing fruit. But the alien god is castrated, and has no desire at all, and does not increase, and bears no fruit — for were it to bear fruit, it would lay the whole world waste. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 29): "The other god is castrated and bears no fruit," as is known, because in the kelipah there is no Da'as to join Chochmah and Binah. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:54): The Sava of Mishpatim states that "the other god is castrated," which Etz Chaim explains to mean that it has no Da'as; therefore the nations have only a feminine nefesh, and therefore Moses has no counterpart among the nations at all — only Pharaoh, who is the Keser of evil, whereas Moses, on the side of holiness, is the nourishment of Da'as. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): The souls of Israel renewed at every time, and the words of Torah and wisdom that a seasoned student is destined to innovate, exist only in Israel, for "the other god is castrated and bears no fruit" and has no increase at all. Every kind of wisdom that the sages of the nations innovate is drawn through the wisdom of Israel, and even the increase among the nations comes only through the deeds of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 5): The Zohar says that "the other god is castrated and bears no fruit," for it would lay the world waste if the spiritual power of evil could increase beyond what it was at the beginning of creation: all sins only empower and strengthen that evil power and conceal the good, but add no offspring to it, and all the offspring and increase of the nations is only physical, like the multiplying of animals. Only "you are called 'man'" — to be fruitful and multiply the Divine image and the spiritual — and through the multiplying of the children of holiness, holiness grows. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 107): "A person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly enters him" — that is the other god of which the Zohar says it "is castrated and bears no fruit," which the Arizal explained as meaning that it has no Da'as; therefore Moses, who is the secret of Da'as, is its rectification. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Since "the other god is castrated and bears no fruit," all the blessing of the nations lies in something that bears no fruit, like mules, which do not give birth. Sod Yesharim (Yom Kippur 23): [That the goat belonging to that side is one that has not joined with a female] is explained by the Zohar's words, "the other god is castrated and bears no fruit": although they too have a complete stature, the whole existence of their stature lasts only as long as some trace of choice still stirs in their heart, and once every trace of choice is gone from them — once they are entirely settled in the view that they exist of necessity — they are nullified completely.),
Yet in truth it is known that 'the other god is castrated and bears no fruit' (Zohar II 103a),
שֶׁאֵין שָׁם מִדַּת הַדַּעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָאֲרִ״י זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה.
meaning that the true attribute of Da'at is absent there, as the holy Ari wrote.

וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (אֶסְתֵּר רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א)463 Esther Rabbah 1:11 — "As the king sat [keshevet] on his royal throne" (Esther 1:2). R. Yitzchak said: The nations of the world have no sitting. They objected to him: But is it not written, "as the king sat"? He said to them: It is not written here "when the king sat [beshevet]," but "as the king sat [keshevet]" — a sitting that is not a sitting. But the sitting of Israel is a sitting, as it is stated: "While Israel dwelt in Cheshbon and its hamlets" (Judges 11:26). עַל פָּסוּק "כְּשֶׁבֶת הַמֶּלֶךְ" –
And this is what is expounded in the Midrash (Esther Rabbah 1) on the verse 'when the king sat'—
דְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אֵין לָהֶם יְשִׁיבָה,
that the nations of the world possess no stable sitting;
פֵּירוּשׁ, "יְשִׁיבָה" נִקְרָא שֶׁהַדֵּעָה מְיוּשֶּׁבֶת,
the explanation being: 'sitting' denotes a settled mind,
וְהֵם אֵין לָהֶם יִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת כְּלָל.
and they possess no true settled consciousness at all.
כִּי דַּעַת נִקְרָא חִבּוּר מוֹחָא וְלִבָּא,
For Da'at is defined as the unification of brain and heart,
הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁמֵּבִין בְּשִׂכְלוֹ שֶׁטּוֹב וְשֶׁרָאוּי לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ,
meaning that a person desires solely what he understands in his intellect to be good and proper to do,
וְלֹא מְחַשֵּׁב רַק מַה שֶּׁרוֹצֶה;
and contemplates only what is aligned with upright will;
וְהוּא מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ,
being one whose heart is under his sovereign control,

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בָּרְשָׁעִים: "הֵן בִּרְשׁוּת לִבָּן" (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה לד464 Bereshit Rabbah 34:10 — "The Lord said to His heart" — the wicked are in the power of their heart: "The scoundrel said in his heart"; "Esau said in his heart"; "Yeravam said in his heart"; "Haman said in his heart." But the righteous, their heart is in their power: "Hannah was speaking upon her heart"; "David said to his heart"; "Daniel set it upon his heart"; "the Lord said to His heart." Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Beshalach): The righteous rule over their heart, for "their heart is in their power": whatever first occurs to their mind they reconsider afterward, and if it is not proper before them they do not do it. The wicked are the opposite, for "they are in the power of their heart."),
unlike the wicked of whom it is said: 'they are in the control of their heart' (Bereishit Rabbah 34),
הַיְינוּ אַף עַל גַּב שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ שֶׁזֶּה לֹא טוֹב, לִבּוֹ מִתְאַוֶּוה לָזֶה
meaning that even though he knows a matter is corrupt, his heart lusts for it
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַטּוֹת מִתַּאֲוַות לִבּוֹ, וְזֶה נִקְרָא שֶׁאֵין לוֹ דַּעַת.
and he cannot redirect his heart's craving, which is termed having no Da'at.
וְהוּא מִתְבָּרֵר בְּבֵירוּר בְּאוֹתָן שֶׁהֵם מִדַּעַת שֶׁבָּרַע כְּמוֹ בִּלְעָם,
And this becomes clearly demonstrated in those rooted in the counterfeit Da'at of evil like Balaam,
שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
who likewise stood directly opposite Moses our teacher, peace be upon him,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּסִּפְרֵי (סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בְּרָכָה)465 Sifrei Devarim 357 — "And there never arose a prophet in Israel like Moses" (Deuteronomy 34:10) — in Israel none arose, but among the nations of the world one arose. And who was he? Bilaam son of Beor. But there is a difference between the prophecy of Moses and the prophecy of Bilaam: Moses did not know Who was speaking with him, whereas Bilaam knew Who was speaking with him, as it is stated, "The saying of him who hears the words of God" (Numbers 24:16).: "אֲבָל בְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם קָם".
as written in the Sifrei (end of Parashat Vezot HaBerachah): 'yet among the nations of the world there did arise one like Moses—Balaam.'
וְכֵן יָדוּעַ דְּבִלְעָם וַעֲמָלֵק חַד, וְאוֹתִיּוֹתֵיהֶן מִצְטָרְפִין;
And it is known that Balaam and Amalek are one entity, their letters combining;
וְכֵן אָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ: "וְיֹדֵעַ דַּעַת [עֶלְיוֹן] וְגוֹמֵר",
and so he claimed concerning himself: 'and knows the knowledge of the Most High, etc.' (Numbers 24:16),
וּבוֹ נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר בְּעַצְמוֹ,
and in him it was demonstrated that even though he knew the exalted virtue of Israel as he confessed,
עִם כָּל זֶה לֹא יָכוֹל לְהַטּוֹת מִתַּאֲוַות לִבּוֹ לְבַקֵּשׁ לְעָקְרָם.
nonetheless he could not turn away from his heart's lust to seek to uproot them.
וְכֵן הָמָן, שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: "לֹא תוּכַל לוֹ כִּי נָפוֹל תִּפּוֹל",
And likewise Haman, to whom his advisors warned: 'you shall not prevail against him, but shall surely fall,' (Esther 6:13),
וְעִם כָּל זֶה לֹא זָז מֵרְצוֹנוֹ, הֲגַם שֶׁמֵּבִין שֶׁאֵין זֶה בִּיכָלְתּוֹ כְּלָל.
and despite this he did not budge from his obsessive will, even though understanding it was entirely beyond his capability.
כִּי זֶהוּ עִנְיַן הַדַּעַת דְּרַע:
For this is the definition of the Da'at of evil:
הַיְינוּ שֶׁרָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִבְרוֹא זֶה גַּם כֵּן בָּעוֹלָם,
namely, that Hashem desired to create this phenomenon in the world as well,
כֹּחַ זֶה הַמְבָרֵר שֶׁהָרַע אֵין בּוֹ מַמָּשׁוּת,
this force demonstrating that evil possesses no actual substance,
וְשֶׁהַדַּעַת שֶׁלָּהֶם מְבָרֵר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ דַּעַת.
and that their pseudo-knowledge proves they lack true knowledge.
וְזֶהוּ בְּרִיאַת עֲמָלֵק, שֶׁהוּא בְּרִיָּה כְּדֵי לְמַחוֹתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁאִיר לוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ וְעָנָף,
And this was the creation of Amalek, being created solely to be blotted out without leaving root or branch,

וְהַהַמְחָאָה שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא עַל יְדֵי עַצְמוֹ, כְּטַעַם (מְגִילָּה טז466 Megillah 16a — "The gallows that he had prepared for him." A Sage taught: for himself he had prepared it. Rashi: "For himself he had prepared it" — for his own need. Maharsha: The word "for him" is superfluous in the verse; Scripture is thereby announcing to him that he had prepared it for himself and not for Mordecai. Maharal (Ohr Chadash, Esther 6:4): The Sages inferred this because Scripture should have said "that he had made": the term "prepare" applies even where one did not intend it, for in the end, through his own deeds, it stands prepared for him; or else from the superfluous "for him," which is written to say that he prepared it for himself. Such was the way of Haman: all that he thought to do to Mordecai was turned upon himself, and it stood ready to be turned upon him from the very first, not only once the gallows were found. For when he thought to destroy Israel, whose existence is in God, blessed be He, Himself, it recoiled upon him, like a stone hurled with great force at an iron wall, which rebounds upon the thrower..): "לוֹ הֵכִין467 Esther 6:4 — “And the king said: Who is in the court? Now Haman had come into the outer court of the king’s house, to speak to the king about hanging Mordechai on the gallows he had prepared for him.” Malbim: "Who is in the court?" — Scripture is making known the force of the miracle, that it was not natural but providential: at that very moment Haman came to hang Mordecai, so that He who orders all causes had already prepared for him the instrument of death.".
and his destruction is brought about through himself, mirroring (Megillah 16a): 'the gallows which he had prepared for himself.'
וְהַתְחָלַת עִנְיַן פּוּרִים הָיָה מֵעֵת "כְּשֶׁבֶת הַמֶּלֶךְ וְגוֹמֵר",
And the beginning of the Purim narrative dates from 'when the king sat, etc.,'
שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ: "כְּשֶׁבֶת" וְלֹא "שֶׁבֶת",
of which they noted in the Midrash: 'keshevet' (as he sat) and not 'shevet' (settled),
שֶׁהָיָה רַק בְּדִמְיוֹן יִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת;
for it was merely an illusory imagination of settled peace;
כִּי הַדַּעַת דְּרַע אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּדִמְיוֹן לְבַד, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ קִיּוּם בֶּאֱמֶת כְּלָל.
because the Da'at of evil is nothing but fantasy, possessing no true endurance.
וְנֶגֶד זֶה בַּמִּדּוֹת רָעוֹת בַּנֶּפֶשׁ הוּא שִׁכְרוּת,
And corresponding to this among the soul's corrupt traits is drunkenness,
שֶׁהוּא בְּלֹא דַּעַת וְהִיפּוּךְ הַדַּעַת הָאֲמִיתִּי.
which is void of Da'at and the exact antithesis of authentic consciousness.
וְהִנֵּה מִכָּל מִדָּה רָעָה אֶפְשָׁר לִקְלוֹט הַטּוֹב מִמֶּנָּה כְּשֶׁיִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בָּהּ לְטוֹב,
Now from every negative trait it is possible to extract the good within it when one redirects it toward good,
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בָּזֶה בָּאֻמּוֹת עַל יְדֵי גֵּרִים.
and likewise among the nations through righteous proselytes.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּעֲמָלֵק שֶׁאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּרִים;
In contrast to Amalek from whom we accept no converts;

אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ (גִּיטִּין נז468 Gittin 57b — Some of Haman's descendants taught Torah in Bnei Brak; some of Sisera's descendants taught children in Jerusalem; some of Sennacherib's descendants taught Torah in public — who were they? Shemaya and Avtalyon. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 7): What is recounted here of the wicked whose seed converted within Israel and taught Torah in public is a wondrous thing. For when the wicked are extreme in wickedness and possess very great power, as these men did, it is impossible that their power was not joined to a higher power, the power of the Blessed One — only that with them it stood in impurity. But with the sons, once they converted, that power was refined and purified and made white, and therefore their sons were great men who taught Torah in public. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:135): None of these three gifts flows to the nations except through Israel: Haman's wealth came because he issued from the power of Saul, who let Agag live, and Saul's rectification came through [Haman's] descendants who learned Torah in Bnei Brak. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Saul's compassion was not, Heaven forbid, of an evil kind; he sensed something good in [Agag], as the Sages said, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in public" — namely Rav Shmuel bar Shilat. It is clear to me that this came about through one of the seed of Amalek coming upon a daughter of Israel, since converts are not accepted from Amalek, and the child is fit; yet he is still called a descendant of Haman, just as the Torah calls [the blasphemer] "the son of an Egyptian man." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 5): "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah": for the commandments of the Torah one needs faith in free choice, which lies in man's hand and is the opposite of [Divine] knowledge. Since some measure of the withdrawal of knowledge [that is Haman's root] is of use for words of Torah and the fulfilment of the commandments, Saul thought this was a root that must not be destroyed — it was this that he pitied, and from this side came [Haman's] descendants who learned Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 2): As I heard on "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah": it came about because Saul let Agag live that night, when Agag grieved that his seed would be cut off, and in reward Haman issued from him. And I heard that such grief over one's seed is the yearning of the seed of Israel — the nations do not grieve at all over the extinction of their line — and it came to Agag from the root within him of Haman's descendants who would emerge and cleave to Israel [which is why they are called by Haman's name]. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 2): One must ask how "To the sinner He gives the task of gathering and amassing, to give to the one who is good" can be said of Haman, since nothing may be taken from Amalek. But it is as the Sages said, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak" — namely Rav Shmuel bar Shilat; and although converts are not accepted from Amalek, it appears that Rav Shmuel bar Shilat came from one of them who came upon a daughter of Israel, and so issued from Haman unwittingly. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The feminine aspect of Amalek can be absorbed [into holiness] only in this way: of Amalek it is written "you shall blot out," and converts are not accepted from it, yet some of Haman's descendants taught children in Jerusalem — so it must have been that a gentile of his descendants came upon a daughter of Israel, for the child is fit and is an Israelite, though he is still called the son of the gentile, as the Torah says, "the son of an Egyptian man." Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Vayechi): Although Saul's compassion on Agag was reckoned to him as a sin, the Blessed One nonetheless intended that a good thought remain from that act, as the Gemara says, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak"; through this Saul's intention was made clear — that he meant to bring out the good and the holiness that was in Agag. Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Ta'anis 2): From the side of the Blessed One everything was created only for the purpose of good, and the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing in vain — to the point that the Sages said, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak; some of Sisera's descendants learned Torah in Jerusalem." Sod Yesharim (Parashas Zachor 7): In truth, all the grace that King Saul perceived in Agag is what the Gemara says, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak"; but Agag, on his own part, had to be nullified entirely.:): "מִבְּנֵי בָנָיו שֶׁל הָמָן לָמְדוּ תוֹרָה בִּבְנֵי בְּרַק",
yet nonetheless they stated (Gittin 57b): 'the descendants of Haman taught Torah in Bnei Brak,'
נִרְאֶה דְּהֲגַם דְּמִצְוָה לְהָרְגוֹ וַאֲפִילּוּ יֹאמַר שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְהִתְגַּיֵּיר,
showing that even though it is a mitzvah to slay him even if he claims he wishes to convert,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם נִתְגַּיֵּיר וְקִבְּלוּהוּ דִּין יִשְׂרָאֵל עָלָיו.
nevertheless if he succeeded in converting and was accepted, the full legal status of an Israelite applies to him.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי כְּשֶׁיִּרְצוּ לִקְלוֹט מִמֶּנּוּ הַנִּיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ לֹא יוּכְלוּ,
And this is because if they consciously seek to extract the holy spark from him they cannot,
כִּי הַנִּיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ שֶׁבּוֹ הַמְחַיֵּיהוּ הַיְינוּ כֹּחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּרְצוֹנוֹ
for the holy spark sustaining him is Hashem's transcendent power and will
שֶׁרָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ דַּעַת אֱמֶת,
desiring that there exist an entity devoid of authentic Da'at,
וְעַל יָדָהּ יִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁהַדֵּעוֹת וּמִדּוֹת הָרָעוֹת אֵינָן דַּעַת כְּלָל.
through which it becomes demonstrated that wicked ideologies and corrupt traits are not knowledge at all.
וְנִמְצָא רָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דָּבָר רַע,
Thus He willed that an evil entity appear,
וְדָבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ אֱמֶת, כִּי אֵין רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרַע כְּלָל;
yet this formulation is not absolute truth, for Hashem has no intrinsic desire for evil;
רַק לָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְפִי הַדִּמְיוֹן נִרְאֶה שֶׁהָיָה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ,
only to the eye in this world according to illusion does it appear as though Hashem willed this,
אֲבָל עַל הָאֱמֶת אֵין לוֹ מְצִיאוּת כְּלָל.
whereas in ultimate truth it possesses no independent reality at all.
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, הֲלֹא הַדִּמְיוֹן גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
Yet nevertheless, is not illusion itself created by Hashem, blessed be He?
וְזֶה: כָּל זְמַן שֶׁעֲמָלֵק בָּעוֹלָם אֵין הַשֵּׁם שָׁלֵם;
And this explains why so long as Amalek exists in the world, the Name is not complete;
כִּי שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה הוּא מִדַּת אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב,
for the Name Havayah is the attribute of Truth belonging to Jacob,
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁעֲמָלֵק בָּעוֹלָם נִרְאֶה שֶׁיֵּשׁ דִּמְיוֹן שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֱמֶת וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
whereas while Amalek is in the world it appears as though there exists an illusion that is not true yet emanates from Hashem,
וְזֶה וַדַּאי אִי אֶפְשָׁר;
and this is an impossibility;
וּלְכָךְ שְׁתֵּי אוֹתִיּוֹת אַחֲרוֹנוֹת שֶׁהֵם מוֹרוֹת עַל עוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין נִשְׁלָמוֹת,
therefore the final two letters indicating this physical world remain incomplete,
כִּי הֲרֵי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בַּדִּמְיוֹן נִרְאֶה דִּמְיוֹן שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֱמֶת וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן נִבְרָא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
for in this world, within illusion, there appears an untruth that was also created by Hashem.
וּבֶאֱמֶת אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהָבִין זֶה כְּלָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:
And in truth it is impossible to fathom this in this world:
אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר זֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְצִיאוּת שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְצִיאוּת כְּלָל?
how can there be an entity whose entire reality is nonexistence?
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן "אֵין הַכִּסֵּא שָׁלֵם" –
And this also explains why 'the Throne is not complete'—
הַכִּסֵּא הוּא עוֹלַם הַבְּרִיאָה,
for the Throne is the World of Beriah (Creation),
כְּמוֹ מוֹשַׁב אָדָם הוּא עַל כִּסֵּא וְהוּא מָקוֹם מְקַבֵּל לָאָדָם,
just as a man sits upon a chair which serves as a receptacle for him,
וְכָךְ יְשִׁיבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל הַנִּבְרָאִים שֶׁבָּהֶם הוּא הַכָּרָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ;
so is Hashem's sitting upon creations through whom His reality is perceived;
דִּבְעַצְמוּתוֹ הוּא בִּלְתִּי בַּעַל תַּכְלִית וְאֵין שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹ מָקוֹם וּמוֹשָׁב,
for in His essence He is Infinite, admitting no concept of place or seat,
רַק מִצַּד הַנִּבְרָאִים הַמַּשִּׂיגִים כְּבוֹדוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהַשָּׂגָתָם הוּא בִּגְבוּל,
save from the perspective of creatures grasping His glory whose perception is bounded,
וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא "כִּסֵּא";
and therefore it is termed 'Throne';
וְאֵין הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁבִּשְׁלֵימוּת עַל יְדֵי עֲמָלֵק.
and Creation cannot achieve wholeness so long as Amalek remains.
כִּי שְׁלֵימוּת הַבְּרִיאָה כַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
For the perfection of Creation occurs when it fulfills the will of Hashem,
וְגַם כָּל מִינֵי רַע, מֵאַחַר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם אֵיזֶה נְקוּדָּה מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְעִנְיָן זֶה, הֲרֵי זֶה כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
and all forms of evil, since they contain a spark of divine will for a purpose, are considered aligned with divine will,
[לֹא] לְקִיּוּמוֹ רַק לְמַחוֹתוֹ,
not for their preservation, but solely to be blotted out,
וְאִם כֵּן כָּל זְמַן שֶׁקַּיָּים, הֲרֵי אֵין הַבְּרִיאָה שְׁלֵימָה עֲדַיִן.
and if so, as long as he exists, Creation is not yet whole.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּהָאָלֶ״ף שֶׁהוּא עֹמֶק רֵאשִׁית נֶעְלָם,
And that is the letter Alef which represents the concealed depth of the Beginning,
דְּאֵין נִגְלֶה אֶלָּא הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת וְלֹא עֹמֶק רֵאשִׁית דִּבְרִיאָה שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ נִמְשָׁךְ "רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם".
wherein only the external expansion is revealed and not the primal depth of Creation whence emerges the 'first of the nations.'
כִּי הַתְחָלַת מַחֲשֶׁבֶת הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ דְּבָרִים נִרְאִים כְּנִפְרָדִים מֵאֲמִיתַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
For the initial thought of Creation was that entities appear separate from Hashem's truth
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מַכִּירִים יִחוּדוֹ;
and nevertheless consciously recognize His absolute Unity;
וּמִצַּד רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיַּכִּירוּ יִחוּדוֹ,
and from Hashem's desire that they recognize His Unity,
מִמֵּילָא מוּבָן שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר גַּם כֵּן לְהֵיפֶךְ,
it naturally follows that the opposite possibility must also exist,
רַק שֶׁרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן.
except that Hashem's will is that they choose good.
וְזֶה הָאֶפְשָׁרוּת לְהֵיפֶךְ, שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר הַמּוּבָן מִמֵּילָא מִצַּד רָצוֹן זֶה,
And this very possibility for the opposite, inherently generated by this will,
מִזֶּה נִמְשַׁךְ הָרֵאשִׁית דְּגוֹיִם.
from this emerges the 'first of the nations' (Amalek).

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (חֻלִּין קלט469 Chullin 139b — Where is Haman [indicated] in the Torah? "Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?" [the word being spelled as Haman is spelled]. Rashi: "From where" — for the affair of Haman. "Of [hamin] the tree" — that he would be hanged upon the tree. Maharsha: Each of these four — Moses, Haman, Esther and Mordecai — is known by a further name as well, and one might have argued that the familiar name is not the one rooted in the Torah, since Moses was so named by Pharaoh's daughter in the Egyptian tongue, while Haman, Mordecai and Esther appear to be Persian names; the Gemara therefore asks in each case from where in the Torah that particular name comes. For Haman it answers "Of the tree," from the episode of the serpent, because he was a viper's brood out of Esau and Amalek, whose power is the power of the primeval serpent; and the Midrash says that Haman and the serpent both opened with "af," and that both set their eyes upon what was not fitting for them. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Chullin 139b): This too is an exceedingly profound matter. For Haman was of the seed of Amalek, whose power is that of Samael the wicked, who rode upon the serpent and enticed the woman to eat of the tree of knowledge and brought death into the world; and just so did Haman seek to bring annihilation and death upon Israel, who in particular are called "man." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Therefore they said in Chullin, "Where is Haman indicated in the Torah? 'Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree'" — this was the first accusation of the attribute of judgment, over the first sin in the world, for the questioning and the accusation began with the word hamin. And this is the root of Haman "from the Torah": there is nothing without a root in holiness, for otherwise it would have no existence in the world, and since all the worlds were created through the Torah, the blueprint of all the works of creation, everything must have its root in the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 5): The root of Haman, which the Sages said in Chullin is alluded to in the verse "Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree": the word hamin expresses a question, and this opened the way to the error that the Blessed One needs to ask — and the Blessed One willed it so, that whoever wishes to err may come and err. From this extends the root of Haman, the root of the error of thinking that the Blessed One has withdrawn His knowledge from the lower worlds, the root and beginning of sinking into imaginings and separation from the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 3): Haman did not believe there could be any holiness in bodily enjoyments such as eating and drinking, and this grew from the root of the serpent who enticed Adam in this. There is a hint of it in the Gemara, "Where is Haman indicated in the Torah? 'Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree,'" for there it is written, "of which I commanded you not to eat, have you eaten" — and this is the root of the kelipah of Haman: to be immersed in the lust of eating for bodily pleasure, as the serpent enticed.:): "הָמָן מִן הַתּוֹרָה מִנַּיִן? 'הֲמִן הָעֵץ וְגוֹמֵר470 Genesis 3:11 — “And He said: Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?” Rashi: "Who told you?" — from where would you know what shame there is in standing naked? And "Have you eaten of the tree" is asked as a question. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Therefore they said in Chullin, "Where is Haman indicated in the Torah? 'Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree'" — this was the first accusation of the attribute of judgment, over the first sin in the world, for the questioning and the accusation began with the word hamin. And this is the root of Haman "from the Torah": there is nothing without a root in holiness, for otherwise it would have no existence in the world, and since all the worlds were created through the Torah, the blueprint of all the works of creation, everything must have its root in the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 5): The root of Haman, which the Sages said in Chullin is alluded to in the verse "Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree": the word hamin expresses a question, and this opened the way to the error that the Blessed One needs to ask — and the Blessed One willed it so, that whoever wishes to err may come and err. From this extends the root of Haman, the root of the error of thinking that the Blessed One has withdrawn His knowledge from the lower worlds, the root and beginning of sinking into imaginings and separation from the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 3): Haman did not believe there could be any holiness in bodily enjoyments such as eating and drinking, and this grew from the root of the serpent who enticed Adam in this. There is a hint of it in the Gemara, "Where is Haman indicated in the Torah? 'Have you eaten of [hamin] the tree,'" for there it is written, "of which I commanded you not to eat, have you eaten" — and this is the root of the kelipah of Haman: to be immersed in the lust of eating for bodily pleasure, as the serpent enticed.'",
And on this they taught (Chullin 139b): 'Where is Haman indicated in the Torah? From the verse: Is it from (ha-min) the tree, etc.',
שֶׁמִּצַּד הַצִּיוּוּי שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלֹּא יֹאכַל, מִזֶּה נִמְשַׁךְ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָמָן;
for from the divine prohibition not to eat, the root of Haman was drawn down;
דּמִזֶּה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְצַוּוֹת לָמַדְנוּ דְּיֵשׁ אֶפְשָׁרוּת גַּם כֵּן לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּהֵיפֶךְ,
because the very need to issue a commandment demonstrates the inherent potential to act inversely,
וְזֶה כֹּחַ אֶפְשָׁרוּת הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ עֲמָלֵק וְהוּא דָּבָר הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵעַצְמוֹ.
and this potentiality is the root of Amalek, developing as an automatic corollary.
וּכְמוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין וּמִתְעַסֵּק, דְּעֶצֶם הַכַּוָּנָה לֹא הָיָה לָזֶה,
Just like an unintended consequence and detached action, where the primary intent was never directed toward it,
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִמְשַׁךְ כֹּחַ זֶה מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
yet nonetheless this capacity was derived from His divine will.
וּלְכָךְ קְלִיטָתוֹ לִקְדוּשָּׁה הוּא גַּם כֵּן שֶׁלֹּא בְּמִתְכַּוֵּין,
Therefore, his absorption into holiness likewise occurs unintentionally,
וְאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּרִים מֵהֶם, רַק כְּשֶׁמִּתְגַּיְּירִים מֵעַצְמָן וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּמִתְכַּוֵּין;
and we accept no converts from them, save when they convert spontaneously and without premeditated contrivance;
כִּי עִיקַּר בִּנְיַן הַנִּיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ שֶׁבָּהֶם הוּא לֹא-דַּעַת.
for the essential fabric of the holy spark within them is non-consciousness (lo-da'at).
וְכֵן עַל יְדֵי שִׁכְרוּת "עַד דְּלָא יָדְעֵי",
And likewise through intoxication 'until they know not,'
כִּי לְבָרֵר דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁגַּם הַכֹּחַ זֶה שֶׁבְּלֹא דַּעַת –
because to clarify that even this force of non-knowledge—
הַיְינוּ הָאֶפְשָׁרוּת לִמְצִיאוּת הָרַע – הוּא גַּם כֵּן מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
namely the cosmic potential for evil—is also an offshoot of Hashem's will,
דָּבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל לְבָרֵר עַל יְדֵי הַדַּעַת וְהַהֲבָנָה הַבְּרוּרָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
this truth cannot be resolved through conscious human reason in this world,
שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהָבִין כְּלָל אֵיךְ יִהְיֶה שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים בְּנוֹשֵׂא אֶחָד.
for mortal intellect cannot fathom how two opposites can coexist within a single subject.
וְהוּא מַמָּשׁ כְּעֵין קוּשְׁיַת יְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה
And this is literally like the paradox of Divine Foreknowledge and Free Will,
שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לַשֵּׂכֶל לְהָבִין כְּלָל תֵּירוּץ מוּסְבָּר בַּלֵּב עַל זֶה,
where human intellect cannot conceive an intellectually satisfying resolution,
רַק תַּכְלִית הַיְּדִיעָה בָּזֶה הוּא שֶׁלֹּא נֵדַע, וּכְדִבְרֵי רַבֵּינוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן.
the pinnacle of knowledge here being that we know not, as taught by Maimonides.
וְכֵן רְפוּאָה לְשׁוֹרֶשׁ עֲמָלֵק וּמְחִיָּתוֹ הוּא עַל יְדֵי מִשְׁתֶּה,
And so too the remedy for Amalek's root and his annihilation is wrought through a feast,
וְזֶה טַעַם מִשְׁתֵּה אֶסְתֵּר וְשֶׁהִזְמִינָה אֶת הָמָן לְהַשְׁפִּיעַ גַּם לוֹ;
which explains Esther's banquets and her inviting Haman to extend illumination unto him as well;
כִּי בַּמִּשְׁתֶּה אֶפְשָׁר לְהָאִיר לְאוֹתוֹ נִיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ –
