for "Hashem alone led him, and there was no strange god with him" (Deuteronomy 32:12), there being no evil remaining to require fences and boundaries of "hitherto shall you come" or hedging with roses.
דְּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, שֶׁאֵין שַׁיָּיךְ חִלּוּק כְּלָל בֵּין רַע לְטוֹב בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאֵין מָקוֹם לְהֶבְדֵּל כְּלָל, מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין מְצִיאוּת לָאֻמּוֹת וְלִפְסֹלֶת מִצִּידּוֹ כְּלָל.
For Jacob's bed is whole, no division between evil and good applying within Israel, and no place for separation remaining, since the nations and dross possess no reality from his perspective.
וְזֶהוּ יִחוּד הַגָּמוּר דִּ"שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר" – יִשְׂרָאֵל סָבָא, דְּהַיְינוּ סְעוּדָתָא דִּזְעֵיר אַנְפִּין,
And this is the absolute Unity of "Hear, O Israel, Hashem is our God, Hashem is One"—Israel the elder patriarch, which is the feast of Ze'eir Anpin,

שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד קֵירוּב בָּשָׂר, שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו493 Sanhedrin 106a — "And he took up his parable and said: Alas, who shall live when God appoints him?" R. Shimon ben Lakish said: Woe to him who keeps himself alive by the name of God. R. Yochanan said: Woe to the nation that will be found there at the hour when the Holy One, blessed be He, brings redemption to His children. Who casts his garment between a lion and a lioness at the hour when they couple with one another? Rashi: "Who keeps himself alive by the name of God" — who makes himself a god, like Pharaoh and Hiram; alternatively, woe to those who sustain and pamper themselves in this world and cast off the yoke of Torah from their necks. "When God appoints [mi-sumo El]" — when the Holy One, blessed be He, sets redemption for Himself and pays the reward of the righteous in the time to come (so I have heard); woe to the nation that exists in those days and thinks to hold Israel back. "Who casts his garment between a lion and a lioness" to keep them from coupling, which is dangerous — that is, who can hold Israel back when the Holy One, blessed be He, is bringing them in? Maharsha: "Who keeps himself alive by the name of God" may also mean by the actual name of God: when evil comes upon them to destroy them for their sin, they keep themselves alive and save themselves by working with divine names, as the Midrashim relate they did at the time of the Destruction — and woe to those who do so, for they are not fit to be saved by the working of names. "When God appoints [mi-sumo El]" means when the Holy One, blessed be He, again sets the name El that is shared in their name, Isra-el, so that they are joined to one another through that shared name; and the letters of lavi and levi'ah [lion and lioness] hint at this. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 106a; Netzach Yisrael, ch. 60): R. Shimon ben Lakish speaks of the nation that keeps itself alive by the name of God — that diminishes His divinity and magnifies itself, making itself a god — an allusion to the fourth kingdom, which says "Whom have I in heaven?" R. Yochanan's "woe" is likewise said of the fourth kingdom, which interposes and separates between Israel and their Father in Heaven, so that as long as it exists Israel is distant and separated from Him. When the Blessed Name joins Israel to Himself, woe to the nation that separates them — "who casts his garment between a lion and a lioness" — so great is His desire for that union. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 8): Had Israel kept two Sabbaths they would be redeemed at once and no nation or tongue would rule over them, "for who puts his head between a lion and a lioness when they are joined to one another?" — and that union is the holiness of the Sabbath, in complete union, as in "you who cleave to the Lord your God.".): "אוֹי לְמִי שֶׁיַּכְנִיס רֹאשׁוֹ בֵּין לָבִיא לִלְבִיאָה בְּשָׁעָה וְכוּלֵי".
operating through physical intimacy, concerning which our Sages stated (Sanhedrin 106a): "Woe to him who thrusts his head between a lion and lioness when they are mating."
וְזֶהוּ הַכֹּל מִצַּד קְדוּשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
And this entirely stems from the holiness of Shabbat which is an inkling of the World to Come.

וְתֵיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ מַתְחִילִים יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, וְאוֹמֵר הַבְדָּלָה, לִהְיוֹת מוֹנֶה סֵדֶר הַבְדָּלוֹת (פְּסָחִים קג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב494 Pesachim 103b — He said to him: I hold in accordance with that which R. Elazar said that R. Oshaya said: One who reduces [the distinctions in the havdalah] should not reduce them to fewer than three, and one who adds should not add more than seven. Rashi (Rashbam): "More than seven" — the Gemara sets out further on [which seven distinctions these are]. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Pesachim): This is why it says, "One who reduces should not reduce to fewer than three, and one who adds should not add more than seven," while the son of the holy ones says one: one adds distinctions when he has not merited the breadth of understanding to sense the substance of the distinction, and must clarify it to himself with proofs, adducing the other things that likewise depend on human perception, until he recognizes a distinction between things that look alike outwardly. The son of the holy ones needed no proof; at first glance, from the very matter he stood in, he recognized and understood the distinction.):
And immediately following Shabbat the six days of action begin, and one recites Havdalah, enumerating the order of distinctions (Pesachim 103b end):
הַפּוֹחֵת לֹא יִפְחוֹת מִשָּׁלֹשׁ, נֶגֶד שְׁלֹשָׁה אָבוֹת, שֶׁהֵם שָׁרְשֵׁי הַהַבְדָּלוֹת בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּרָכִים שֶׁזָּכַרְנוּ:
he who shortens shall not recite fewer than three blessings of distinction, corresponding to the three Patriarchs who are the roots of distinction in the three aforementioned ways:
שֶׁהֵם מִצַּד הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, וּמִצַּד הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, וּמִצַּד הָרָצוֹן [רַעֲוָא דְּרַעֲוִין];
which are from the aspect of deed, thought, and transcendent will (Ra'ava DeRa'avin);
וְהַמּוֹסִיף לֹא יוֹסִיף עַל שֶׁבַע, נֶגֶד שֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת דִּימֵי הַבִּנְיָן, שֶׁהֵם שָׁרְשֵׁי כָּל הַכֹּחוֹת שֶׁבְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, וּבִכְלַל בִּנְיַן הָאָדָם;

and he who adds shall not exceed seven, corresponding to the seven sefirotic attributes of cosmic building, which are the source of all powers throughout the entire universe, and encompass the spiritual structure of man;
וּבְכָל כֹּחַ פְּרָטִי שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן וְכֹחוֹת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה יַכִּיר הַהֶבְדֵּל שֶׁבֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי.
and through each individual force belonging to the days of building and active weekdays, one recognizes the fundamental distinction between Israel and the nations.

sections.en: Tzitzit, Royal Dignity, and Jacob's Humility

items.h: Sacred garments conceal and dignify the human form, cultivating a joyful humility that synthesizes the spiritual powers of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Seif 1 — Tzitzit and the Dignity of Sacred Garments
Sacred clothing conceals vulnerability and creates a joyful, royal humility rather than self-negating sadness.

p: מִצְוַת צִיצִית הוּא לְבוּשׁ לְקוֹמַת אָדָם שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נִגְלֶה עֶצֶם הָאָדָם,
The commandment of tzitzit serves as a garment covering the human stature so that the naked essence of man is not exposed;
לְכָךְ מִתְעַטְּפִין בִּשְׁעַת תְּפִלָּה כְּדֵי לְהִתְכַּסּוֹת מִן הַמְקַטְרְגִים,
therefore one enwraps oneself during prayer to be concealed from the accusing angels,
שֶׁיָּדוּעַ כִּי כָּל עוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים הֵם מַמָּשׁ בְּצֶלֶם וּדְמוּת הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
for it is known that all supernal worlds correspond literally to the image and likeness of man in this world,
כִּי כָּל הָעוֹלָמוֹת נִתְלִים בָּאָדָם,
since all the worlds are suspended upon man,
הַיְינוּ מִצַּד נֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם שֶׁהִיא בַּגּוּף מִסְּתָמָא עִנְיָנָהּ בְּדוֹמֶה לוֹ.
meaning that from the aspect of the human soul enclothed in the body, its nature functions analogously to it.
וּכְמוֹ הַגּוּף מִתְכַּסֶּה בִּלְבוּשִׁים וְאֵין נִיכָּר מוּמָיו וְנֶגַע שֶׁבַּבָּשָׂר,
And just as the physical body is shrouded in garments so that its blemishes and bodily afflictions are not apparent,

וּ"מָאנֵי מְכַבְּדוּתָא" (שַׁבָּת קיג495 Shabbat 113a — "And you shall honor it by not doing your own ways." "And you shall honor it" — that your Shabbat garment should not be like your weekday garment; and this is as R. Yochanan would call his garments "my honorers." "By not doing your own ways" — that your walking on Shabbat should not be like your walking on a weekday. "From pursuing your affairs" — your affairs are forbidden, the affairs of Heaven are permitted. Rashi: [R. Yochanan's garments were] "my honorers" because they honor their owners. "From pursuing your affairs" — as we say in Eruvin (38b): a person may not stroll to the end of his field on Shabbat to see what it needs [after Shabbat]; "the affairs of Heaven are permitted" — such as pledging charity and arranging the betrothal of children (below, 150a). Maharsha: R. Yochanan's calling his garments "my honorers" accords with the Gemara's later derivation of changing garments [for Shabbat] from Aaron, of whose garments this same expression is used: "for honor and for glory." "Your walking on Shabbat" is, as the Gemara concludes, a large stride, which is forbidden even on a weekday because of danger, and the verse teaches that on Shabbat it is also prohibited; and the Gemara does not expound here, as it does of "your affairs," that "your ways are forbidden, the ways of Heaven are permitted," because even where there is no prohibition there is still danger. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 113a): Shabbat is holy, and what is holy is separate from the material; therefore it is fit for honor, for honor belongs to what is removed from the material — as the elder is honored for the wisdom he has acquired, which is not physical — and so the Shabbat garment should not be like the weekday one, that a person be honored in his dress. The affairs of Heaven are permitted because the essence of Shabbat is removal from physical activity, and the affairs of Heaven are not physical. A large stride is forbidden on Shabbat, for it is movement beyond the ordinary measure — unlike normal walking, which is simply a person's way — and on Shabbat there should be rest, not physical movement..),
and "clothes are an honor" (Shabbat 113a),
כָּךְ כְּלַל הַתּוֹרָה הִיא לְבוּשֵׁי הַנֶּפֶשׁ, כַּיָּדוּעַ בְּסוֹד "חֲלוּקָא דְּרַבָּנָן",
so the totality of the Torah provides the garments of the soul, known in the mystical secret of the 'Rabbinic Cloak' (Chaluka DeRabbanan),
וְזֶהוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, כַּאֲשֶׁר הַנֶּפֶשׁ שָׁבָה לְשָׁרְשָׁהּ,
and this manifests in the World to Come, when the soul returns to its root,
אָז לְבוּשִׁים שֶׁלָּהּ הֵם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָהּ בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
its spiritual garments then being its diligent exertion in Torah and mitzvot within this world.

וּבְגַן עֵדֶן יֵשׁ בָּזֶה חִלּוּקִים בֵּין גַּן עֵדֶן עֶלְיוֹן לַתַּחְתּוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, רי רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב)496 Zohar 2:210b — Happy is the portion of one who merits those garments of which we have spoken, in which the righteous are clothed in the Garden of Eden. These come from the good deeds a man performs in this world through the commandments of the Torah; by them the soul abides in the lower Garden of Eden and is clothed in these precious garments. And when the soul ascends through that opening of the firmament above, other garments are made ready for it, precious and supernal, which come from the desire and the intention of the heart in Torah and in prayer. The Holy Lamp learned thus from Elijah: the garments below, in the earthly Garden, are from deeds; the garments above, from the desire and intention of the spirit within the heart. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר497 Tzidkas HaTzaddik §155 — A person's honor in this world accords with his purity in his permitted affairs, which in this world are the garments of the matters of mitzvah. … And [the Sages] said (Shabbos 113a) that [garments] are "things that bring honor." That is, after Adam was driven from the Garden of Eden, which was his [proper] place, garments were made for him, and honor goes according to them. So in this world the deeds of Torah and mitzvos are called the person's body and his permitted affairs are his garments; but in the Garden of Eden the garment is made from the deeds of Torah and mitzvos, as the Zohar says (Vayakhel 210a), for there the person's body means only the thoughts and desires of the mind and heart … and there honor accords with his deeds in Torah and mitzvos. Higher still, as the Zohar says (ibid. 210b), the garment is made from the intentions of the heart and the desires for Torah and mitzvos, and there each one's honor accords with his good intention..
And in the Garden of Eden there are distinctions between the Upper and Lower Eden in this regard, as written in the Zohar (II 210b) and elsewhere.
וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּפִי עִנְיַן הַמִּצְווֹת לַגּוּף כָּךְ הֵם לַנֶּפֶשׁ;
And in this world, just as mitzvot relate physically to the body, so do they relate spiritually to the soul;
וְדֶרֶךְ מָשָׁל, מִצְווֹת דַּאֲכִילָה שֶׁמּוֹסִיפִים חַיּוּת לַגּוּף, כָּךְ הַמִּצְוָה שֶׁבָּהּ מוֹסִיף חַיּוּת לַנֶּפֶשׁ,
by way of example, dietary mitzvot that add physical vitality to the body similarly impart spiritual life-force to the soul,

וְעַל יְדֵי כְּזַיִת פִּסְחָא נִפְתַּח הַפֶּה לוֹמַר הַלֵּל עַד שֶׁפָּקַע אִגָּרָא (פְּסָחִים פה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב498 Pesachim 85b — Rav said: The roofs and the upper stories [of the Temple] were not sanctified. Is that so? But did not Rav say in the name of R. Chiyya: An olive's bulk of the Paschal offering — and the Hallel splits the roof. Rashi: “An olive’s worth of the Paschal lamb” — the groups were so large that each man received no more than an olive’s worth of it. “And the Hallel split the roofs” — at the sound of the crowd’s clamour from the Hallel, their roofs seemed as though they were splitting, as they recited the Hallel over the Paschal offering. Rashi: ["Roofs and upper stories were not sanctified":] neither the roofs of Jerusalem with the sanctity of Jerusalem, for [eating] offerings of lesser sanctity, nor the roofs of the chambers of the Temple Court with the sanctity of the Court, for [eating] offerings of the highest sanctity. ["An olive's bulk of the Paschal offering":] they would register in such large groups that no more than an olive's bulk of the Paschal offering reached each one. ["The Hallel splits the roof":] at the tumult of the multitude from the Hallel it seemed as though the roofs were splitting, for they would recite the Hallel over the Paschal offering, as we learn below (95a): the first [Passover] requires Hallel while it is eaten. Maharsha (on 86a, s.v. "they eat on the ground and recite on the roof"): Because [each received only] an olive's bulk of the Paschal offering and the eaters were many, the house may have been too tight for them to sit in at the time of eating, so many of them went up to the roof at the time of the Hallel, not at the time of eating. And in saying that the Hallel "splits the roof" they intended this: as for their eating in the house, it is possible that one ate it for the sake of the Paschal offering and another ate it as gluttonous eating, as explained in Tractate Horayot (10b); but the Hallel was certainly entirely for the sake of Heaven — and this is the allusion of "splits the roof": that the force of their recitation rose upward to heaven.),
and through eating an olive-sized portion of the Paschal offering the mouth opened to recite Hallel so loudly it broke the roof (Pesachim 85b),
שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הוֹסָפַת חִיזּוּק וְכֹחַ וְחַיּוּת.
which stemmed from this infusion of strength, power, and vitality.
וּמִצְווֹת דִּמְקוֹם מְזוּזָה וּמַעֲקֶה וְכַדּוֹמֶה הֵם גּוֹדְרִים מָקוֹם לַנֶּפֶשׁ גַּם כֵּן,
And spatial mitzvot such as mezuzah, a rooftop parapet, and the like establish a sanctified boundary for the soul as well,
וּכְטַעַם: "וּכְתַבְתָּם עַל מְזוּזֹת וְגוֹמֵר", "לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ וְגוֹמֵר עַל הָאֲדָמָה",
reflecting: "And you shall write them upon the doorposts, etc.," "so that your days may multiply... upon the land" (Deuteronomy 11:20–21),
וְהֲגַם שֶׁגָּלוּ הָעִנְיָן מִתְקַיֵּים בַּנֶּפֶשׁ.
and even though Israel was exiled, the spiritual reality endures within the soul.
כִּי עִיקַּר אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הַיְינוּ מָקוֹם קָבוּעַ לִקְדוּשָּׁה,
For the essential core of the Land of Israel is a permanent, established abode for holiness,

וּכְטַעַם "הַקּוֹבֵעַ מָקוֹם לִתְפִלָּתוֹ אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם בְּעֶזְרוֹ" (בְּרָכוֹת ו499 Berakhot 6b — R. Chelbo said that Rav Huna said: Whoever fixes a place for his prayer — the God of Abraham is his help. And when he dies they say of him: Where is the humble one, where is the pious one, of the disciples of our father Abraham? Rashi: "The God of Abraham" — who himself fixed a place for his prayer; "is his help" — in the manner in which He used to help Abraham. Maharsha: It is evident that one who keeps changing the place of his prayer receives an influx and a divine power according to that particular place and direction, as they said, "one who wishes to become wise should face south, and to become rich should face north"; but one who fixes a single place for his prayer, without change, directs the divine powers to the one true Name. This is "the God of Abraham is his help," for it was through Abraham, to whom the Holy One said "and be a blessing," that His Name was made one in the world. And it is fitting to say of such a man "where is the pious one," for it is a mark of piety that he asks his needs of the attribute of mercy and does not turn his face to seek great things by some other route. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 4): Prayer is the cleaving of a man to the Blessed One, and if that cleaving is merely incidental it is not reckoned cleaving at all, for whatever is incidental belongs to a moment and an hour and is not continual. Hence the admonition to fix a place for one's prayer: fixing a place shows that his prayer is not incidental, since the incidental has no fixity; and if he sits one time in this place and another time in that, there is no fixity at all, and this is no essential cleaving but only a chance occurrence. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Pekudei 2): There is the voice of prayer, the portion of King David, as it is written, "and I am prayer," and for it a place is needed, as it is said, "until I find a place for the Lord"; and so [the Sages] said, "Whoever fixes a place for his prayer…" — "…to the place where he had stood." Hence when Israel entered the Land and came to fixity of place, the Temple was needed as a place for the Lord, a fixed place for the indwelling of the Shechinah, whereas in the wilderness, following Moses' portion of Torah, they had no fixed place and the Shechinah rested in the Tabernacle, which is called a tent. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Berakhos): "Whoever fixes a place for his prayer, the God of Abraham is his help": he should pray that the Blessed One bestow on the whole world the salvation he himself lacks, and not pray for himself alone, for that is called a narrow eye; rather he should pray that the whole world receive good in this matter. This is "the God of Abraham is his help," for such was Abraham's prayer, as the Midrash says that many barren women were remembered together with [Sarah] — in truth it all came through Abraham's prayer, only it was hidden from the eyes of the world.:),
mirroring the teaching: "Whoever fixes a designated place for his prayer, the God of Abraham helps him" (Berakhot 6b),
כִּי זֶה עִיקַּר עִנְיַן אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם – לִהְיוֹת קְבִיעוּת מָקוֹם לִקְדוּשָׁתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ אֶצְלוֹ,
for this was the essential achievement of Abraham our father: establishing an enduring place for His holiness within him,
לֹא כְּבַתְּחִלָּה שֶׁאֵין קְבִיעוּת, פְּעָמִים זֶה צַדִּיק וּבְדוֹר אַחֵר צַדִּיק אַחֵר מִזֶּרַע אַחֵר;
not like the prior eras where holiness had no permanent lineage, one righteous man arising and in another generation another from a different line;
אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קָבַע מָקוֹם לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רַק אֶצְלוֹ.
rather Abraham established an enduring spiritual dwelling place for Hashem to remain anchored within his lineage alone.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי אָדָם נִקְרָא "הוֹלֵךְ", שֶׁאֵין לוֹ מָקוֹם קָבוּעַ,
And this is because man is termed a dynamic "walker" who lacks a static place,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ קָבוּעַ תָּמִיד בְּמַדְרֵגָה אַחַת, פַּעַם כָּךְ וּפַעַם כָּךְ;
never remaining fixed at one identical level, shifting at different times;
אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא "אַב הָעוֹלָם", הַיְינוּ יְסוֹד הַבִּנְיָן שֶׁעָלָיו עִיקַּר הַקְּבִיעוּת מָקוֹם.
yet Abraham is titled the "Father of the World," the bedrock foundation upon which permanent spiritual rootedness rests.
וּכְמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל, אָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בַּיִת וּמָקוֹם,
Just as, by way of analogy, a man who owns a home and fixed place,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ תָּדִיר בַּשְּׁוָוקִים וּרְחוֹבוֹת, לְעוֹלָם דַּעְתּוֹ לַחֲזוֹר לִמְקוֹמוֹ וּלְקִיבְעָא קַמָּא,
even though he traverses markets and streets, his mind is ever set on returning to his home and original base,
וְנִקְרָא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מָקוֹם וְדַעְתּוֹ תָּמִיד אַמְּקוֹמוֹ.
and he is defined as having a home, his focus tethered to his home.
וְזֶה כָּל עִיקַּר עֵסֶק אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: לִבְנוֹת יְסוֹד קַיָּים בַּלֵּב שֶׁזֶּה לֹא יִמּוֹט לְעוֹלָם,
And this was Abraham's foundational work: erecting an unshakeable foundation in the heart that never totters,
אַף אִם יֵלֵךְ בְּכָל אֲשֶׁר יֵלְכוּ מַחְשְׁבוֹתָיו וּרְצוֹנוֹתָיו,
even if his thoughts and impulses wander wherever they may,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַיְסוֹד קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּים בַּלֵּב מִדְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא יִמּוֹט.
nonetheless this firm foundation of cleaving to Hashem established within the heart remains immovable.
וּלְפִיכָךְ נִתְבָּרֵךְ בִּירוּשַּׁת הָאָרֶץ, שֶׁהוּא הַבְטָחַת קְבִיעוּת מָקוֹם,
Therefore he was blessed with the inheritance of the Land, which is the promise of an enduring spiritual home,
שֶׁאַף שֶׁגָּלוּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם דַּעְתָּם לְהָתָם,
so that even when exiled, their longing remains bound there,
וּלְעוֹלָם כָּל מַחֲשֶׁבֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל רַק עַל עִנְיַן יַהֲדוּתָם,
and the essential contemplation of Israel remains focused upon their Jewishness,
וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיַּהֲדוּת תָּקוּעַ בְּלִבָּם אַף אִם יֵלְכוּ לְמָקוֹם שֶׁיֵּלְכוּ בְּגוּף וּבְנֶפֶשׁ.
the root of Judaism being deeply implanted in their hearts wherever they wander in body and soul.
וְעַל יְדֵי מִצְוַת מְזוּזָה בְּיִחוּד זוֹכֶה לִקְדוּשַּׁת קְבִיעוּת מָקוֹם לַנֶּפֶשׁ, וְכַיּוֹצֵא בְּכָל הַמִּצְווֹת.
And specifically through the mitzvah of mezuzah one merits this holiness of an established home for the soul, and so with all mitzvot.
וּמִצְוַת צִיצִית בִּבְגָדָיו הִיא לְהַלְבִּישׁ וּלְכַסּוֹת כָּל הַמּוּמִין שֶׁבַּגּוּף, וְרוּבּוֹ כְּכוּלּוֹ,
And the mitzvah of tzitzit on one's garments is to clothe and cover all bodily defects, the majority considered like the whole,
וּלְכָךְ דַּי בַּעֲטִיפַת רֹאשׁוֹ וְרוּבּוֹ,
and therefore enwrapping the head and majority of the torso suffices,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה כּוּלּוֹ מְכֻסֶּה בְּכִסּוּי גָּמוּר,
because through this a person is enveloped in complete covering,
עַד שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם בְּרִיָּה מַכֶּרֶת מַה שֶּׁבְּלִבּוֹ רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּלְבַד, וְאֵין מָקוֹם לְקִטְרוּג.
so that no creature recognizes what is inside his heart except Hashem alone, leaving no foothold for spiritual accusation.

וּמָצִינוּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "וִידֻעִים לְשִׁבְטֵיכֶם" – שֶׁאֵין מַכִּירָם כְּשֶׁבָּא מְעוּטָּף בְּטַלִּיתוֹ500 Deuteronomy 1:13 with Rashi — “Provide for yourselves men who are wise and understanding and known to your tribes, and I will set them as heads over you.” Rashi explains: “Known to your tribes” — men recognizable to you. If one were to come before me wrapped in his cloak, I should not know who he is, or of what tribe, or whether he is fitting; but you know him, for you have raised him. Therefore it says, “known to your tribes.”;
And we find that Moses our teacher said on "and known unto your tribes": that one cannot scrutinize them when enwrapped in a tallit;
וְיָדוּעַ דִּבְרֵי הַזֹּהַר עַל פָּסוּק "וְאַתָּה תֶחֱזֶה", שֶׁמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה יוֹדֵעַ לְהַכִּיר אָדָם בִּרְאִיָּה בִּלְבַד,
and known is the Zohar on "and you shall discern," that Moses could assess a man's spiritual state through sight alone,
רַק עַל יְדֵי עֲטִיפַת טַלִּית שֶׁל מִצְוָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַכִּיר עוֹד.
yet through the enwrapment of the tallit of mitzvah he could no longer be scrutinized from without.
וְזֶהוּ עַל הֶעָבָר – הוּא כִּסּוּי מוּמָיו;
And this relates to the past: it conceals his prior spiritual blemishes;
וְעַל לְהַבָּא – "מָאנֵי מְכַבְּדוּתָא" הוּא מַה שֶּׁגּוֹרֵם: "וּזְכַרְתֶּם אֶת כָּל מִצְוֹת [ה'] וְגוֹמֵר", "וְלֹא תָתֻרוּ וְגוֹמֵר",
while regarding the future, honorable clothing inspires: "and you shall remember all the commandments of Hashem, etc.," and "do not spy out after your own heart, etc.",
כְּדֶרֶךְ הַתִּינוֹק הַמִּתְחַבֵּר לִבְזוּיִים, עוֹשִׂים לוֹ בְּגָדִים יָפִים,
like a youth who befriends base company, whose parents dress him in dignified clothes,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִפְרָשׁ מֵעַצְמוֹ מִלְּהִתְחַבֵּר לְרֵיקָנִים וְלַעֲשׂוֹת כְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם, רַק מִתְחַבֵּר לִנְכְבָּדִים כְּעֶרְכּוֹ.
whereby he naturally withdraws from idle ruffians and associates with honorable peers commensurate with his attire.

וְעִנְיַן רַב קְטִינָא וּמַלְאָכָא501 Menachot 41a — An angel found Rav Katina wearing a linen wrap, which is exempt from tzitzit because it is a night garment. He said to him: Katina, Katina — a linen wrap in summer and a cloak in winter, and what of the commandment of tzitzit? He said to him: Do you then punish a man for a positive commandment he was not obliged to perform? He said to him: At a time when there is divine anger, we do punish — for at a time of anger, even one who neglects a positive commandment is liable to punishment. Rashi: The angel's words disagree with Rabbah bar Rav Huna, for the angel holds that ritual fringes are an obligation upon the man. A linen wrap had no fringes, as was said above, because it is a night garment; and a cloak is like ours, which are round and have only two corners, and is therefore exempt from fringes. Tosafos (s.v. "Do you then punish a man for a positive commandment?"): For a positive commandment such as this one, since a man is not obliged to buy a garment that carries the obligation if he has none; but for an outright positive commandment, even the court below would flog him until his soul departed. Maharsha: So Tosafot explained; and so it is proved in the chapter HaKones, that the judgment of Heaven is stricter than the judgment of man, for many things are reckoned there in which one is liable by the laws of Heaven and exempt by the laws of man. And what the angel said, that at a time of anger we do punish, means that at a time of anger in the world the righteous ought to shield their generation by their prayer and by their commandments, and therefore they ought to multiply commandments in order to bring merit to their generation and not seek ploys to exempt themselves — and so it is fitting that righteous men such as these be punished for it. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Menachos 41a): That a man has nullified a positive commandment means only that he has not acquired a further degree and elevation; it is not like a negative commandment, where he sins and does what ought not to be done. It is enough that one who does not fulfil a positive commandment is given no reward for it in the World to Come; to punish him for it is not fitting. But at a time of anger, when strict judgment rules the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, punishes even for a positive commandment, because the man ought to have acquired that elevation — and it is for this that man was created, that he should always acquire more. (מְנָחוֹת מא.), מַה שֶּׁלֹּא לָבַשׁ צִיצִית,
And regarding the incident of Rav Ketina and the angel (Menachot 41a) where he did not don four-cornered garments with tzitzit,
נִרְאֶה דִּשְׁמוֹ מֵעִיד עָלָיו, דְּהָיָה לְקַטְנוּתוֹ וְשִׁפְלוּתוֹ בְּעֵינֵי עַצְמוֹ שֶׁאֵין רָאוּי לְהִתְכַּבֵּד כְּלָל,
it appears that his name Ketina ("the small one") testifies to his deep humility and self-effacement, feeling unworthy of honorable attire,
וְ"חַטָּאתִי נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד", וְלֹא רָצָה לְכַסּוֹתָהּ,
and "my sin is ever before me," being unwilling to shroud it,
כִּי עַל יְדֵי כִּסּוּי הַצִּיצִית הִיא נִכְסֵית גַּם מֵעֵינֵי עַצְמוֹ, וְזֶה שִׁפְלוּת יְתֵירָה.
for through the protective cover of tzitzit his spiritual blemish is hidden even from his own eyes, reflecting extreme self-effacement.
וּבֶאֱמֶת נִקְרָא "רַב", וְתֹאַר "רַב" רַק כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ תַּלְמִיד,
Yet in truth he was titled "Rav," and the title "Rav" applies only when a disciple exists,

עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא קַמָּא ב502 Bava Kamma 2a — From the fact that it teaches "primary categories" [literally, fathers], it follows that there are subcategories [literally, offspring]. Are their subcategories like them, or are they not like them? Rashi (on the Mishnah, s.v. "four primary categories of damage"): He calls "primary categories" [literally, fathers] those that are written explicitly in the verse, and the Gemara explains which are their subcategories [literally, offspring]..): "אָבוֹת – מִכְּלָל דְּאִיכָּא תּוֹלָדוֹת",
along the lines of what they stated (Bava Kamma 2a): "primary categories imply secondary offshoots,"
וְכָךְ תֹּאַר "רַב" – תֹּאַר הַיַּחַס שֶׁהוּא רַב שֶׁל אֵיזֶה אָדָם וְאֵינוֹ קָטָן.
and thus "Rav" is a relational title indicating that he is the master of someone, not a small individual.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה503 Moed Katan 17a — R. Yochanan said: What is meant by the verse, “For the priest’s lips shall guard knowledge, and Torah shall they seek from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord of Hosts”? If the teacher resembles an angel of the Lord of Hosts, let them seek Torah from his mouth; and if not, let them not seek Torah from his mouth. Rashi (s.v. "and if not, let them not seek Torah from his mouth"): Since his reputation is bad, the fact that the Sages need him counts for nothing, for it is better that they not learn from him at all. Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot; here he refers the reader to his comment at Chagigah 15b): This is the meaning of the verse: the priest, of the tribe of Levi, is the one who instructs in the Torah and teaches it to Israel, as it is said, "They shall teach Your ordinances to Jacob." And it says: even though he keeps knowledge upon his lips to teach you Torah, if you would learn Torah from his mouth, look first whether he resembles an angel in his deeds. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTorah 8): This matter is plain, for we have explained that student and teacher are bound and joined together more closely than any two men; there is no joining like that of student and teacher. Hence if a man learns Torah from a scholar who is not fitting, he becomes bound and joined to a wicked man, and that is a debased condition, for they said, "Do not associate with a wicked man." (מוֹעֵד קָטָן יז.): "אִם הָרַב דּוֹמֶה לְמַלְאַךְ ה' צְבָאוֹת וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: כִּי מַלְאַךְ וְגוֹמֵר",
And our Sages taught (Moed Katan 17a): "If the rabbi resembles an angel of the Lord of Hosts, etc., as it is said: 'For he is an angel of the Lord of Hosts'",
תֵּאֲרוּ כָּל רַב בְּמַלְאָךְ,
equating every authentic master with an angel,
כִּי הַמַּלְאָכִים הֵם כְּפִי הַדּוֹרוֹת,
for angels manifest according to the capacity of the generations,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה אֵיכָה פָּרָשָׁה א, ו וְסִפְרֵי הַאֲזִינוּ)504 Eikhah Rabbah 1:33; Sifrei Devarim 319 — "And they went without strength before the pursuer." R. Azariah said in the name of R. Yehuda son of R. Simon: When Israel do the will of the Omnipresent, they add strength to the might above, as it says, "Through God we shall do valiantly"; and when Israel do not do the will of the Omnipresent, they, as it were, weaken the great power above, as it is written, "You weakened the Rock that bore you." And in the Sifrei on Haazinu: "You weakened the Rock that bore you" — whenever I seek to do good for you, you weaken the power above. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on completing the Talmud 5): Insofar as the mind cleaves to its source no corruption can touch it; it becomes deficient only through its connection downward to the heart, when it turns not to its source but downward, for, as is known, the arousal below brings about the arousal above, and so the desire of the heart begets the thoughts of the mind. [And this is the meaning of] "You weakened the Rock that bore you": that they weaken the power of the household above. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 2): All the supernal forces of holiness also depend on man, as is said on "You weakened the Rock that bore you," that [Israel] weaken the power of the household above, and that at the Destruction the wings of the Chayyos and the household above were diminished; for these too are part of the whole of creation, all of which exists for the sake of man, who is the likeness upon the Throne, riding upon all of creation. עַל "תֶּשִׁי" – שֶׁמַּתִּישִׁין כֹּחַ פַּמַלְיָא שֶׁל מַעְלָה,
as our Sages expounded on "teshi" (Deuteronomy 32:18)—that Israel's deeds weaken or elevate the heavenly host,
כְּפִי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבַּדּוֹר כָּךְ הַמַּלְאָכִים.
the heavenly angels reflecting the stature of Israel in that generation.
וּמִצַּד בַּקָּשַׁת הַתּוֹרָה מֵרַב הוּא רַק מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא שְׁלִיחַ ה',
And seeking Torah from a master is legitimate solely because he functions as Hashem's emissary,
כִּי עִיקַּר קַבָּלַת תּוֹרָה הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי ה' יִתֵּן חָכְמָה מִפִּיו וְגוֹמֵר",
for the reception of Torah derives fundamentally from Hashem, as written: "For Hashem gives wisdom; out of His mouth, etc.",
וְהַמְקַבֵּל מֵרַב צָרִיךְ שֶׁיֵּדַע שֶׁהוּא מַלְאַךְ ה' צְבָאוֹת.
and a disciple receiving from a master must recognize that he is an emissary of the Lord of Hosts.
תֹּאַר "צְבָאוֹת" בְּכָאן שֶׁהוּא עַל צִבְאֵי צְבָאוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת, כִּי "רִבּוֹא רִבְבָן קֳדָמוֹהִי",
The title Tzva'ot (Hosts) here denotes diverse heavenly legions, for "myriads of myriads stand before Him",
וְכָךְ בָּעוֹלָם יֵשׁ הַרְבֵּה מַשְׁפִּיעִים וּמְקַבְּלִים דּוּגְמַת רַב וְתַלְמִיד.
and similarly in the world there are varied channels of givers and receivers like teacher and disciple.
וְתֹאַר "צְבָאוֹת" הוּא מִצַּד הָרִיבּוּי,
And the Name Tzva'ot stems from this plural diversity,
וְשַׁיָּיךְ לְעִנְיַן הַקַּבָּלָה שֶׁמְּקַבְּלִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי שָׁלִיחַ;
pertaining to receiving divine illumination from Hashem through an emissary;
וּלְכָךְ חַנָּה קְרָאַתְהוּ כֵן שֶׁהוֹלִידָה שְׁמוּאֵל רַבָּן שֶׁל נְבִיאִים,
which is why Hannah was the first to invoke this Name when praying for Samuel, master of prophets,
שֶׁיָּדוּעַ שֶׁקַּבָּלַת הַנְּבִיאִים מִשֵּׁם זֶה.
it being known that prophetic transmission derives from this Name.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה א)505 Vayikra Rabbah 1:1 — Another interpretation: the prophets are called angels. This is what is written, “And He sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt” — and was it an angel of the Lord? Was it not Moshe? Why then does Scripture call him an angel? Rather, from here we learn that the prophets are called angels. R. Yochanan said: It is from their father's house that the prophets are called angels, as it is written, “And Chaggai, the messenger of the Lord, spoke in the Lord's message to the people.” דְּהַנָּבִיא נִקְרָא "מַלְאָךְ",
And as our Sages stated (Vayikra Rabbah 1), a prophet is termed an angel (mal'akh),
שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "חַגַּי מַלְאַךְ ה' בְּמַלְאֲכוּת ה'".
as it is said (Haggai 1:13): "Haggai the angel of Hashem on the mission of Hashem."

כִּי עִיקַּר שֵׁם "נָבִיא" מִלְּשׁוֹן "נִיב שְׂפָתַיִם", שֶׁהוּא דִּבּוּר לַזּוּלַת, כְּמוֹ "אַהֲרֹן יִהְיֶה נְבִיאֶךָ506 Exodus 7:1-2 — “And the Lord said to Moshe: See, I have set you as a god to Pharaoh, and Aharon your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and Aharon your brother shall speak to Pharaoh, that he send the Children of Israel from his land.” Rashi: "I have made you a god to Pharaoh" — a judge and chastiser, to chastise him with plagues and afflictions; "shall be your prophet" is rendered by the Targum "your spokesman," for every term of prophecy denotes one who proclaims and makes heard to the people words of rebuke. "You shall speak" — you shall say each message once, just as you heard it from My mouth, and Aaron your brother will render it and make it palatable in Pharaoh's ears.";
For the title navi derives from niv sefatayim (spoken expression) addressed unto another, as in "Aaron your brother shall be your speaker";

וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד רִיבּוּי צְבָאָיו וְלֹא מִצַּד הַיִּחוּד דְּ"אָז לֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד וְגוֹמֵר507 Jeremiah 31:33 — “And no longer shall a man teach his fellow or a man his brother, saying, Know the Lord — for they shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord; for I shall forgive their iniquity, and their sin I shall remember no more.” Radak: The verse is plain; his only note is on the vocalization of "I will inscribe it," which Ben Asher reads with a qamatz and Ben Naftali with a sheva and a patach. Metzudas Dovid: "After those days" means after they return from the exile. "I have put My Torah within them" is a past form standing for a future: I will incline their heart to fulfil the Torah; and "upon their heart I will write it" means that it will not be forgotten from their heart, as though it were engraved there. Malbim: "I will put My Torah within them" — they will keep My Torah at the prompting of their own understanding, until it becomes something natural to them, found within them. "And upon their heart I will write it" — it will not need to be written in a book with ink, for it will be written on their heart; the heart stands for the power of choice and of rule within the soul, so that no choice contrary to the Torah will arise in them, their heart being full of the Torah's statutes implanted within it.".
and this belongs to the multiplicity of His hosts, not to the ultimate Unity where "no longer shall every man teach his brother, etc."
וְכָל רַב – מַלְאָךְ, וּמַמָּשׁ דּוֹמֶה לַמַּלְאָךְ שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר.
And every true rabbi is an emissary angel, literally mirroring the spiritual angel of that generation.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהַקּוּשְׁיָא עַל רַב קְטִינָא הוּא מִצַּד תֹּאַר "רַב" שֶׁעָלָיו,
And since the rebuke against Rav Ketina was predicated upon the title "Rav" he bore,
דְּעַל יְדֵי שִׁפְלוּתוֹ זֶה זָכָה לְתֹאַר "רַב",
for specifically through his radical humility did he merit this title of "Rav",
דְּ"מַאן דְּאִיהוּ זְעֵיר אִיהוּ רַב", וּמִמֵּילָא אֵין כָּאן עוֹד שִׁפְלוּת;
since "he who is small is great," meaning that debilitating self-abasement no longer belongs there;
וְתֹאַר "רַב" קוֹדֵם דּוּגְמַת שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה,
and the title of master takes precedence just as on High,
דְּרַק בִּמְקוֹם גְּדוּלָּתוֹ שָׁם אַתָּה מוֹצֵא עַנְוְתָנוּתוֹ, וּגְדוּלָּתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת.
for only where His greatness is established do you find His humility, His greatness coming first.
וְלָכֵן נִגְלָה עָלָיו מַלְאָכָא לְהוֹכִיחוֹ עַל זֶה,
Therefore an angel appeared to him to admonish him regarding this,
דְּהוּא "רַב" וְדוֹמֶה לְמַלְאַךְ ה' צְבָאוֹת,
telling him that he is a "Rav" resembling an angel of the Lord of Hosts,
וְאֵין רָאוּי לֵילֵךְ בְּשִׁפְלוּת כָּזֶה,
and it is not fitting to carry oneself in such extreme self-effacing negligence,
וְ"צִיצִית מַה תְּהֵא עָלֶיהָ?",
challenging him: "What will become of tzitzit?"
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ לִהְיוֹת מְצוּיָּינִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בִּלְבוּשׁ כָּבוֹד.
since Hashem desires that Israel be distinguished in this world by garments of honor.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "בְּעִדָּן רִתְחָא עָנְשִׁינַן" –
And this explains the angel's statement: "In a time of divine wrath we penalize"—
חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּעֵת זַעַם וּשְׁלִיטַת מְקַטְרְגִים אָז עָנְשִׁינַן, וְצָרִיךְ לְכִסּוּי דִּלְבוּשׁ;
meaning, Heaven forbid, during moments of celestial anger when accusers hold sway, punishment is exacted and the covering of tzitzit is vital;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּעֵת רָצוֹן, דְּ"אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ" וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַכִּיר הַלֵּב,
unlike in times of divine favor when "there is none else beside Him" and Hashem looks directly into the heart,

"אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא אֶשְׁכּוֹן" (סוֹטָה ה508 Sotah 5a — "[I dwell in the high and holy place,] and also with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: one said, the contrite one is with Me; and one said, I am with the contrite one. And it stands to reason like the one who said, I am with the contrite one, for the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over all the mountains and hills and rested His Presence upon Mount Sinai, and He did not raise Mount Sinai up to Himself. Rashi: "The contrite one is with Me" — I raise him up until he dwells beside Me, and this is [the sense of the verse] "I dwell [on high] … with the contrite." "I am with the contrite one" — I lower My Presence to be beside him. Maharsha: The practical lesson [of the view that 'I am with the contrite one'] is that even a distinguished person should lower himself toward one beneath him, and not say that this is beneath his dignity, for there is no honor greater than the honor of Heaven. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 5a): According to the one who says "the contrite one is with Me," the Holy One, blessed be He, raises up the contrite: just as arrogance inclines toward the material, humility is a separate [transcendent] level, as Moses possessed it, so it is fitting that the humble man be elevated to God and be with Him. According to the one who says "I am with the contrite one," God rests His Presence upon what is crushed and lowly, because the lowly are simple — as the Sages hinted that the essence of the Divine Presence was [originally] among the lower beings. [It stands to reason like the latter,] for when God joins Himself to the contrite one the union is according to His power and is complete, whereas when the contrite one is with God the union is not as full. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAnavah 1): On either view the contrite one, as the effect, is joined to God, the Cause: according to "I am with the contrite one" the Cause turns toward the effect, which is prepared to receive His glory, and according to "the contrite one is with Me" the effect is raised to be with the Cause. It stands to reason like "I am with the contrite one," for one who comes to another is wholly with him, since the other receives him entirely, whereas one who comes to the great cannot be joined with him so fully. God comes to the humble man to be with him — passing over all the high mountains to rest His Presence on Mount Sinai — because the humble man possesses something of his Maker's own attribute, and like things are found together..),
as in "I dwell with the contrite" (Sotah 5a),
וְצָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת שִׁפְלוּתוֹ עַל פָּנָיו וּמִתְגַּעְגֵּעַ כְּבֵן לִפְנֵי אָבִיו בְּהַכָּרַת חֶסְרוֹנוֹ.
where one's humility must be manifest upon his face, yearning like a son before his father in conscious awareness of his lack.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּעִידָּן וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁנֶּגֶד זֶה חוּט שֶׁל צִיצִית: "רְצוּעָה בִּישָׁא לְאַלְקָאָה וְכוּלֵי" (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, קעה עַמּוּד א509 Zohar 3:175a — It is written, "From the uttermost part [kanaf] of the earth we have heard songs: Glory to the righteous one; and I said, My secret is mine" (Isaiah 24:16). "From the kanaf of the earth" — this is the corner of the tzitzit. "We have heard songs" — these are the other threads, which issue and hang from the supernal place. And when I looked at the sky-blue thread and saw in it a strap for flogging, a place of dread that must be feared, I said: Woe is me, that people do not know to look and consider for what they are punished.),
In contrast to times of wrath where the fringed cord of tzitzit wards off the demonic lash (Zohar III 175a),
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הִיא מַקִּיפָתוֹ אֵין מִתְיָירֵא עוֹד.
and when enveloped in it one no longer fears external accusers.
וְצָרִיךְ לְהִתְעַטֵּף בִּלְבוּשׁ שֶׁל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם,
And one must enwrap oneself in the garment of the fear of Heaven,
שֶׁעַל זֶה רוֹמֵז הַצִּיצִית,
to which tzitzit allude,
דִּמְהַפֵּךְ הַיִּרְאָה דְּעוֹנָשִׁים לְיִרְאָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
transforming base fear of punishment into pure, exalted awe of Hashem,
וְזוֹכֶה לְתֹקֶף הָאַהֲבָה עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה בְּדַרְגָּא דְּ"וַיִּגְבַּהּ לִבּוֹ בְּדַרְכֵי ה'"
and meriting intense love through awe, reaching: "and his heart was lifted up in the ways of Hashem" (II Chronicles 17:6),
הָאָמוּר בִּיהוֹשָׁפָט שֶׁנִּקְרָא כֵן לְשׁוֹן "מִשְׁפָּט", כִּי זֶה מַדְרֵגָתוֹ,
said of Jehoshaphat whose name derives from mishpat (judgment), which was his spiritual station,
וְכֵן הוּא הֵקִים שׁוֹפְטִים כִּמְפוֹרָשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב.
and who established judicial courts as recounted in II Chronicles.
וְ"הַמִּשְׁפָּט לֵאלֹהִים הוּא", שֶׁכֵּן נִקְרָאִים הַדַּיָּינִים, דַּרְגָּא דִּגְבוּרָה,
And "judgment belongs to God," judges being called Elohim, embodying the level of Gevurah,
כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה הִיא הַגְּבוּרָה דִּכְבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר,
for through awe comes the inner might to conquer the base inclination,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּבַעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ",
and as it is written: "and that His fear may be upon your faces, that you sin not" (Exodus 20:17),
וְאוֹמֵר: "רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹהִים בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה וַהֲרָגוּנִי וְגוֹמֵר".
and Scripture states: "Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me, etc." (Genesis 20:11).
כִּי הַיִּרְאָה דּוּגְמַת צִיצִית, דְּעַל יָדָהּ בָּא לְ"וְלֹא תָתֻרוּ",
For divine awe functions like tzitzit, through which one reaches "do not spy out after your own heart",
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁמַּכִּיר כְּבוֹדוֹ שֶׁלָּבוּשׁ בְּמַלְבּוּשֵׁי כָּבוֹד כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
by recognizing one's dignity when attired in garments of honor as mentioned above,
כָּךְ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הַחוֹפֶפֶת עַל פְּנֵי הָאָדָם.
so operates the fear of Heaven hovering upon a person's countenance.

וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ (נְדָרִים כ510 Nedarim 20a — It was taught: "That His fear may be upon your faces" — this is shame. "That you sin not" — this teaches that shame brings one to fear of sin. From here they said: It is a good sign in a man that he is bashful. Others say: Anyone who feels shame will not readily sin. And one who has no shame upon his face — it is known that his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 20a): That shame brings one to fear of sin is plain, and he derives it precisely from the wording of the verse, "that His fear may be upon your faces," which implies shame; for otherwise why say "upon your faces"? — rather, it is shame that brings one to fear, and shame shows itself in the face, as though He had said: be ashamed before Me and stand in awe of Me. "He will not readily sin," because one who feels shame is far from brazenness; the brazen man may be called wicked, as it is said, "A wicked man hardens his face," since by his brazenness he departs from the straight measure, while the bashful man stands within it and finds it hard to depart from uprightness. And "his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai" — for at Sinai they accepted His Godhood, and one who has a God over him is an effect of a cause and so bears shame upon his face; the brazen man, by force of his brazenness, is reckoned no effect at all, and so it is evident that his forefathers did not accept His kingship and Godhood there, for had they accepted it His fear would have been upon their faces and no brazen man would have come forth from them. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 17): This is [the meaning of] "That His fear may be upon your faces" — "this is shame": because the Blessed One then revealed Himself to the eyes of all Israel, as it says, "Face to face the Lord spoke with you," there remained from it for all generations the capacity of a person to picture in his heart that the King of kings stands over him and sees his deeds, so that fear and shame before Him come upon him constantly. Beis Yaakov (Vayeira 34): The essence of shame is that a person be ashamed before the Blessed One even when he is in his innermost chambers, and this was fixed in the heart of Israel from the Giving of the Torah, as it is written, "That His fear may be upon your faces," on which the Gemara says, "This is shame," and "one who has no shame, it is known that his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai." Shame before people is the lowest level, yet even this shame has good in it, for through it one can come back to complete repentance, being like a remnant of life through which one can return to life. Tiferes Yosef (Pesach 5): Even after the great clarity of the revelation at Mount Sinai was hidden, something remained, as it is written after the Giving of the Torah, "That His fear may be upon your faces, that you sin not," which the Sages expounded, "This is shame": that is, there remained in the heart of each one of Israel a fixed point by which he is ashamed to act against the will of the Blessed One. So although that light was hidden from them, at the root something of it remained, while on the outer garment the great revelation of that time was concealed..) עַל פָּסוּק "בַּעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" – זוֹ הַבּוּשָׁה;
And our Sages expounded (Nedarim 20a) on "that His fear may be upon you": this is shame/modesty (boshet);

וְהַיְינוּ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת כח511 Berakhot 28b — His disciples said to him: Our teacher, bless us. He said to them: May it be [His] will that the fear of Heaven be upon you as the fear of flesh and blood. His disciples said to him: Only that far? He said to them: Would that it were so! Know that when a man commits a transgression he says, “May no man see me.” Rashi: "Only that far?" is said in astonishment — and no more than the fear of flesh and blood? "Would that it were" — that it be like the fear of flesh and blood, for then you would refrain from many transgressions. A man commits the transgression in secret out of fear of people, though he knows that everything lies open before the Holy One, blessed be He, and that does not restrain him. Maharsha: Even granted what we say, that everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven [so that praying for it seems out of place], he said this to them by way of admonition — that they should act, and Heaven would then assist them, as it is said, "In the way a man wishes to go, he is led," and "one who comes to purify himself is assisted." Maharal (Derech Chaim 2:1): Man in this world does not have the Blessed One before him, and therefore he comes to sin — so much so that on this account the Sages said, "May it be His will that the fear of Heaven be upon you as the fear of flesh and blood." For man is on earth and sees a king of flesh and blood before him, and so there is fear of flesh and blood; but man does not see the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 2): [Fear] is the attribute of Isaac, "the Fear of Isaac," who always saw that the Holy One, blessed be He, actually stood over him; this is in the manner of what they said, "May the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood ... know that when a man commits a transgression he says, May no man see me," implying that the fear of Heaven, too, means seeing that the King of kings stands and actually sees him. Rav Tzadok (Sefer HaZichronos 4): R. Yochanan ben Zakkai already said, "Know that when a man commits a transgression he says, Would that no man see me"; were his faith true that the Blessed One fills the whole earth with His glory and watches over him and sees his deeds, he would surely never sin. But although everyone believes this, it is not fixed in his heart, and it is forgotten at the time of sin.:): כְּשֶׁאָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אוֹמֵר: "וּלְוַאי שֶׁלֹּא יִרְאַנִי אָדָם",
and this connects to what they taught (Berakhot 28b): when a person sins he thinks: "if only no man sees me",
וְהוּא מִצַּד הַבּוּשָׁה מִמּוֹרָא בָּשָׂר וָדָם;
which stems from shame before the sight of flesh and blood;
וּמִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ יִרְאָתוֹ – הַיְינוּ מוֹרָא הַמָּקוֹם – הוּא מִתְבַּיֵּישׁ מִלְּפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ לַעֲבוֹר.
and one who possesses true fear of Heaven feels bashful before Hashem to transgress.
וְהַבּוּשָׁה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד הַשִּׁפְלוּת,
And noble shame does not arise from degraded self-effacement,
דְּהַבְּזוּיִים בְּיוֹתֵר אֵינָם בְּנֵי בּוֹשֶׁת,
for the basest individuals possess no shame,
וְעִיקַּר הַבּוּשָׁה הוּא לְפִי הַמַּעֲלָה וְהַכָּבוֹד.
rather authentic shame exists in proportion to dignity and stature.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַהִתְקָרְבוּת כְּבֵן לִפְנֵי אָבִיו, שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַשְׁפִּיל אֶת עַצְמוֹ,
And through drawing close like a child before a parent, where the Holy One lowers Himself in love,
כָּךְ הָאָדָם לְעוּמָּתוֹ בְּתַכְלִית הַשִּׁפְלוּת,
so does man stand opposite Him in total humility,
וְאָז "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא", כְּטַעַם "ה' צִלְּךָ".
and then, "I am with the contrite," mirroring "Hashem is your shadow."
אֲבָל הַיִּרְאָה הוּא כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי אָדוֹן,
However, awe is like a servant standing before his master,
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְרוֹמָם וּמְנוּשָּׂא,
wherein Hashem is exalted and transcendent,
אָז הָאָדָם כְּדֻגְמָתוֹ גַּם כֵּן מַכִּיר כְּבוֹדוֹ –
so man, reflecting His image, also recognizes his own elevated dignity—
לֹא כָּבוֹד מְדוּמֶּה,
not illusory pride,
רַק אֵיךְ הוּא מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי יוֹצֵר הַכֹּל יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ,
rather understanding that he is the handiwork of the Creator of all, blessed be His Name,
וְנִזְכָּר מִשָּׁרְשׁוֹ שֶׁהוּא מִמָּקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ,
remembering that his soul originates from an exalted supernal source,
וְאֵיךְ יְשַׁקַּע עַצְמוֹ בִּדְבָרִים פְּחוּתִים.
and how then could he plunge himself into base trivialities?

וּכְטַעַם (שְׁבוּעוֹת מז512 Shevuot 47b — "As far as the great river, the river Euphrates" (Deuteronomy 1:7) — Shimon ben Tarfon says: Draw near to one anointed with oil, and you too will be anointed. The school of R. Yishmael taught: The servant of a king is like a king. Rashi: "Draw near to one anointed with oil, and you will be anointed" — if you touch one anointed with oil, you too will be anointed by touching him. That is: the Euphrates is smaller than the three [other] rivers, being listed last among them — "and the fourth river is the Euphrates" (Genesis 2:14) — yet here it is called "the great river" because it is mentioned here on account of the Land of Israel, which is important, and so it too is mentioned with importance. Dehina denotes oil and anointing: the Targum renders "it is made fat with fat" (Isaiah 34:6) with the same word. Maharsha: Tosafot in chapter Maaser Behemah [Bechorot 55b] raise a difficulty from this passage, which implies, as Rashi explains, that the Euphrates is smaller than the three [other] rivers, whereas there it is said that the three rivers are below the Euphrates, since "it is the Euphrates from the beginning." But were it not for Rashi's explanation, it would seem that here too [the Gemara] holds that the Euphrates is the greatest of them all, [and only asks why] it is called "great" here and not in Genesis, where the four rivers are mentioned; and it says that since here it is mentioned in connection with the Land of Israel, it is therefore called "great" — on account of "draw near to one anointed.":): "עֶבֶד מֶלֶךְ – מֶלֶךְ",
Reflecting (Shevuot 47b): "the servant of a king is like a king,"
כִּי מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא עֶבֶד מֶלֶךְ הוּא מִתְנַהֵג גַּם כֵּן בְּטַכְסִיסֵי מַלְכוּת
for as a servant of the King he must conduct himself with royal dignity
וּבְדֶרֶךְ כָּבוֹד כָּרָאוּי לְעֶבֶד מֶלֶךְ.
and honorable decorum becoming a royal attendant.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה לְהַכְנָעָה וַעֲנָוָה דְּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
And through this he merits authentic humility, the trait of Jacob our father,
שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִצַּד שִׁפְלוּתוֹ הַמֵּבִיא לְהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁגּוֹרֵם מָרָה שְׁחוֹרָה,
which does not stem from self-abnegation that leads to paralysis and melancholy, Heaven forbid,
רַק עַל יְדֵי שִׂמְחַת לֵב דִּמְבַקְשֵׁי ה' הוּא מַכִּיר עֶרְכּוֹ.
rather through the gladness of heart of those who seek Hashem he perceives his true spiritual worth.

items.h:
Seif 2 — Jacob as the Synthesis of Abraham and Isaac
Jacob integrates love and fear, and these patriarchal powers remain active within every Jewish soul and prayer.

p: וּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִיא הִתְחַבְּרוּת מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק,
And the attribute of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, is the synthesis of the attributes of Abraham and Isaac,
דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה שִׁפְלוּת יְתֵירָה, שֶׁאָמַר: "אָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר"
for our father Abraham, peace be upon him, possessed extreme humility, declaring: "I am dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27)

[וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם זָכוּ בָנָיו וְכוּלֵי (סוֹטָה יז513 Sotah 17a — Rava expounded: As a reward for what Abraham our father said, "And I am but dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27), his children merited two commandments — the ashes of the [red] heifer and the dust of the sota. Maharsha (Chiddushei Aggados, Chullin 88b): At first glance this is difficult — had Abraham not said "And I am but dust and ashes," would there have been no purification for corpse-impurity? Rather, without Abraham's merit the purification of one defiled by the dead would have required remote things, hard to obtain; but in reward for his lowering himself they merited that its preparation and sprinkling be through things readily found, dust and ashes. The merit corresponds like to like: for "I am dust," [referring to] the beginning of man's formation, they merited the dust of the sota, through which she merits to bear a son like Abraham; and for "ashes," [man's state] at death, they merited to purify corpse-impurity with ashes. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Chullin 88b): Abraham called himself "dust," for man is formed from dust, and "ashes," for every man's end is ashes at his death; since in his humility he counted himself wholly as ashes — and humility is complete simplicity, which, like a simple vessel, cannot receive impurity — his children merited the ashes of the heifer, which, joined with living water, remove the impurity of the dead. And for "I am dust" they merited the dust of the sota: woman is likened to the earth, and rain is as a husband to the earth, and these two are never false to one another, for the earth receives from no other; and it must be dust of the Tabernacle floor, for that dust is holy. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 17a): By saying "And I am but dust and ashes," Abraham showed humility carried to its utmost, and one who carries a good attribute to its extreme is brought near to God by that exalted attribute; therefore his children merited through it a commandment, which is complete nearness to God — a commandment of the same kind as the attribute in which he excelled. Since Abraham so excelled in this exalted attribute, his children could not but acquire through it complete cleaving to God, and so they merited the commandments most akin to it, the ashes of the heifer and the dust of the sota..), שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּשִׁפְלוּת כָּזֶה טָהֳרָה מֵחֲטָאִים, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ],
and nevertheless his descendants merited, etc. (Sotah 17a), for in such lowliness there is purification from sins, but this is not the place to elaborate,
וְהוּא קָצֶה הָאַחֲרוֹן דְּאַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּבֵן לְאָבִיו,
and it is the ultimate extremity of the love of Hashem, blessed be He, as a son to his father,
שֶׁבַּפְּסֹלֶת שֶׁלּוֹ יָצָא יִשְׁמָעֵאל, "פֶּרֶא אָדָם",
from whose dross emerged Ishmael, "a wild ass of a man",
דְּהַיְינוּ בְּהֵמָה בִּדְמוּת אָדָם שֶׁמְּשׁוּקָּע בְּכָל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַמָּשׁ כִּבְהֵמָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדַע בֹּשֶׁת.
meaning a beast in the guise of a man, submerged in all the lusts of this physical world literally like an animal that knows no shame.
אַךְ יִצְחָק דַּרְגָּא דִּילֵיהּ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הָעוֹצֶרֶת בְּעַד תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת,
Whereas with Isaac, his spiritual level is the fear of Heaven that restrains wicked lusts,
אֲבָל בַּפְּסֹלֶת שֶׁלּוֹ יָצָא חֶרֶב דְּעֵשָׂו
yet from his dross issued the sword of Esau,
הַבָּא מִצַּד בַּקָּשַׁת הִתְנַשְּׂאוּת עַל הַזּוּלַת שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד רְדִיפַת כָּבוֹד,
originating from seeking dominance over others, which stems from the pursuit of honor,
דְּזֶה עִיקַּר עֵשָׂו "פּוֹשֵׁט טְלָפָיו", שֶׁגַּם הוּא מַכִּיר הַבּוּשָׁה בָּרָע וְרוֹצֶה לִהְיוֹת טוֹב,
for this is the essence of Esau 'extending his split hooves', recognizing the shame of evil and desiring to appear good,
רַק לֹא בֶּאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ וּמִבּוּשַׁת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אֶלָּא בּוּשַׁת בָּשָׂר וָדָם שֶׁיַּחֲזִיקוּהוּ לְטוֹב.
only not in genuine truth out of shame before Hashem, but rather out of shame before flesh and blood so they deem him virtuous.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, "מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה",
In contrast, regarding our father Jacob, peace be upon him, "his bed is whole",
דְּדַרְגָּא דִּילֵיהּ עֲנָוָה וּתְמִימוּת שֶׁאֵין חָפֵץ בְּכָבוֹד מְדוּמֶּה
for his spiritual level is authentic humility and wholeness, desiring no illusory honor
וְגַם אֵין מַשְׁפִּיל עַצְמוֹ בְּשִׁפְלוּת מְדוּמֶּה,
nor debasing himself with artificial self-abnegation,
רַק "תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", שֶׁהוּא הַדְּבֵיקוּת בֶּאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ,
rather "You grant truth unto Jacob" (Micah 7:20), which is cleaving to absolute truth,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה אֵין מָקוֹם לְבַקָּשַׁת כָּבוֹד אוֹ שִׁפְלוּת מֵאַחַר שֶׁ"אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ".
whereby there is no room to seek honor or wallow in lowliness, since "there is none else beside Him."
וּמִדָּתוֹ רַק "תָּמִים תִּהְיֶה עִם ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ".
And his attribute is solely "You shall be wholehearted with Hashem your God" (Deuteronomy 18:13).
וְזֶהוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁאַחַר הַצִּיצִית הָרוֹמֵז לִדְבֵיקוּת כַּיָּדוּעַ:
And this is the secret of tefillin donned after tzitzit, alluding to divine cleaving as is known:
תְּפִלִּין שֶׁל רֹאשׁ מִצַּד הַהִתְנַשְּׂאוּת שֶׁמַּנִּיחַ רֹאשׁוֹ תַּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּשְׁמָא דְּמָארֵיהּ עֲלֵיהּ,
the head-tefillin corresponds to supernal elevation, placing one's head beneath Hashem with the Master's Name resting upon him,
וּמִצַּד זֶה: "וְרָאוּ כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר",
and from this perspective: "And all the peoples of the earth shall see, etc." (Deuteronomy 28:10),
שֶׁאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם רוֹדְפִים כְּבוֹד עַצְמָן, אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין מְבַקְּשִׁים אֶלָּא כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם,
for the nations pursue self-glorification, while Israel seek only the glory of Heaven,
מִמֵּילָא: "שֵׁם ה' נִקְרָא עָלֶיךָ וְיָרְאוּ מִמֶּךָּ",
consequently: "that the Name of Hashem is called upon you, and they shall revere you",
שֶׁזֶּה עִיקַּר כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁאֵין שַׁיָּיךְ לָהֶם תֹּאַר "אָב", רַק תֹּאַר "מֶלֶךְ" הוּא רַק בְּיִרְאָה.
for this constitutes Heaven's glory recognized by the nations, to whom the appellation "Father" does not apply, but only the title "King" through fear.
וּתְפִלִּין שֶׁל יָד הוּא הִשְׁתַּעְבְּדוּת כֹּחַ הַבַּהֲמִי,
And the arm-tefillin represents the subjugation of the animalistic bodily faculty,
שֶׁעִיקַּר פְּעֻלַּת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מְכוּנָּה עַל שֵׁם הַיָּדַיִם בְּכָל מָקוֹם;
for man's primary practical action in this world is designated everywhere by the hands;
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין מִשְׁתַּקֵּעַ גַּם כֵּן בְּשִׁפְלוּת יוֹתֵר מִדַּאי לִהְיוֹת "נִמְשַׁל כַּבְּהֵמוֹת נִדְמוּ",
meaning that one does not sink excessively into debasement to become "likened unto the beasts that perish",
רַק שְׁמָא דְּמָארֵיהּ עֲלֵיהּ לָדַעַת שׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁמָתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה מַעְלָה, וְאֵין רָאוּי לָהּ לְהִשְׁתַּקֵּעַ בִּדְבָרִים שְׁפֵלִים.
rather the Master's Name is bound upon him to remember that his soul originates from on high, making it unfitting to wallow in lowliness.
וְזֶהוּ "וְהָיָה לְךָ לְאוֹת" – וְלֹא לַאֲחֵרִים לְאוֹת,
And this is "and it shall be for a sign unto you" (Exodus 13:9)—and not a sign unto others,
דְּרַק תְּפִלִּין שֶׁל רֹאשׁ הוּא לְאוֹת לַאֲחֵרִים שֶׁלֹּא יִתְנַשֵּׂא עַל הַזּוּלַת,
for only the head-tefillin is an outward sign unto others that one should not pride himself over another,
דְּעִיקַּר בַּקָּשַׁת הַכָּבוֹד הוּא עַל הַזּוּלַת, וְכֵן חֲלוּקַּת הַכָּבוֹד עַל יְדֵי "וְרָאוּ כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְגוֹמֵר", דְּ"אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם".
since the pursuit of honor is directed toward others, and the imparting of honor comes through "all the peoples shall see, etc.", for "there is no king without a nation."
אֲבָל תְּפִלִּין שֶׁל יָד הוּא "לְךָ לְאוֹת" מַה שֶּׁבֵּינוֹ לְבֵין עַצְמוֹ,
However, the arm-tefillin is "a sign unto you" in what is between a person and himself,
שֶׁלֹּא לְהִשְׁתַּקֵּעַ בְּשִׁפְלוּת, לִהְיוֹת לְאוֹת וּלְזִכָּרוֹן כָּךְ בְּלִבּוֹ וּמוֹחוֹ דָּבָר זֶה, וְאֵין שַׁיָּיכוּת לַזּוּלַת בָּזֶה.
not to drown in base lowliness, serving as a personal sign and memory within his heart and mind, having no external relation to others.
וּתְפִלִּין שֶׁל יָד קוֹדֵם כְּמוֹ שֶׁהַצִּיצִית קוֹדֶמֶת.
And the arm-tefillin takes precedence just as tzitzit takes precedence.
וּלְפִי שֶׁיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מְחוּבָּר מִשְּׁנֵי הַקְּצוֹת, לְכָךְ הֵם שְׁתֵּי מִצְווֹת וְאֵין מְעַכְּבוֹת זוֹ אֶת זוֹ כַּיָּדוּעַ,
And because our father Jacob synthesizes both extremes, they constitute two independent mitzvot that do not invalidate one another,
דְּהַגַּם דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא קַו הַיּוֹשֶׁר,
for even though Jacob embodies the straight central middle path,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בַּיְצִיאָה בִּפְרָטֵי נְפָשׁוֹת יֵשׁ נְטִיּוֹת לְכָאן וּלְכָאן.
nonetheless in their unfolding within individual souls there exist leanings to this side and to that.
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעַל הָאֱמֶת הַכֹּל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב וּנְטוּעִים עַל קַו יוֹשֶׁר,
Even though in truth all are Jacob's seed and planted upon the central path of rectitude,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד שֶׁהֵם גַּם כֵּן זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, יֵשׁ בָּהֶם גַּם כֵּן נְטִיּוֹת מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת.
nonetheless, since they are likewise the offspring of Abraham and Isaac, they also exhibit distinct leanings in their outward manifestation.
וּמִצַּד שֶׁחֲלוּקִים לִשְׁנַיִם הֵם נֶגֶד שְׁנֵי אָבוֹת,
And being divided into two, they correspond to the two Patriarchs (Chesed and Gevurah),
וְהַטַּלִּית נַעֲשָׂה אַחַר כָּךְ דּוּגְמַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
and the tallit enwrapment afterward reflects our father Jacob (Tiferet),
כְּטַעַם: "יִרְאָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ – חָכְמָתוֹ מִתְקַיֶּימֶת",
mirroring: "if one's fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures" (Avot 3:9),
וְנֶאֱמַר: "הֵן יִרְאַת ה' הִיא חָכְמָה", וְהוּא אַחַר כָּךְ בְּקִיּוּמָהּ.
and it is said: "Behold, the fear of Hashem, that is wisdom" (Job 28:28), which is attained afterward in its enduring realization.
כִּי בַּהַתְחָלָה מַתְחִילִין מִמִּצְוַת צִיצִית, דַּרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל הַנִּימּוֹל לִשְׁמוֹנָה;
For at the outset one begins with the mitzvah of tzitzit, the level of Isaac who marks the initial inception of the name Israel circumcised at eight days;

אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא "תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים" (חֲגִיגָה ג514 Chagigah 3a — Rava expounded: What is meant by "How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O daughter of the noble"? How beautiful are the feet of Israel when they go up for the pilgrimage festival. "Daughter of the noble" — the daughter of Abraham our father, who is called noble, as it is said, "The nobles of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham." "The God of Abraham," and not the God of Isaac and Jacob? Rather, "the God of Abraham," for he was the first of the converts. Rashi: "Who is called noble" — because his heart moved him of its own accord to recognize his Creator. "The nobles of the peoples" — these are the converts, who volunteer from among the nations to take upon themselves the yoke of the commandments. Tosafos (s.v. "the first of the converts"): Because he was commanded concerning circumcision, unlike all those who came before him. Maharsha: "How beautiful are the feet of Israel" — for whoever's foot is not sound does not go up at all, as below, "excluding one who is lame." And their beauty is made to depend on their going in sandals, because one who goes barefoot goes in pain, as it is said, "Withhold your foot from being unshod" (Jeremiah 2:25), whereas these went up on foot in gladness, with their offerings of rejoicing; and so the Targum renders it, "How lovely are your steps, three times a year, in sandals." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 3): Tractate Avodah Zarah serves to clarify the distinctions between Israel and the idolaters, and Abraham's Avodah Zarah "was four hundred chapters," for Abraham is called "father of a multitude of nations" — as stated at the beginning of Chagigah, he is called "the first of the converts" — and, as it is said, he "recognized his Creator," implying that at first he did not. Hence [on Pesach night] one "begins with disgrace": "at first our fathers were idol worshippers." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Abraham our father too is called "father of a multitude of nations," for he was not born from the womb of the seed of Israel, who are borne from the womb with the Blessed One as the rock of their heart by birth; for he is called "the first of the converts," since it was through his own effort that he merited the understanding of the heart and to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite" — like a native in Israel, who is an Israelite from the womb. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 14): [If Israel cannot resemble Isaac, who was born in holiness, circumcised at eight days without his own knowledge, and so became Israel,] the deeds of Abraham suffice: for Abraham is called "the first of the converts" and sought to bring the whole world under the wings of the Shechinah, being "father of a multitude of nations" — the father of all converts — whereas Isaac is not found to have made converts. And although Abraham's converts were helped only in his lifetime, for after his passing they broke the covenant, his covenant helped at least his own seed, so that whoever is of the seed of Israel is in any case superior to a convert. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 9): Abraham our father, who is called "the first of the converts," is the beginning of the holiness that comes from below — fencing all his limbs and faculties within holiness — and he had to draw himself near, as is said of converts in Kiddushin; he was tested with ten trials so that every level would be clarified in him through his own holiness from below, in battle with the inclination. And although he afterwards merited to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite," reckoned as a native in Israel, that was after Jacob came forth from him..),
whereas our father Abraham is called "the first of converts" (Chagigah 3a),
וְהוּא הַהַתְחָלָה לְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהַיְינוּ רַק כְּמוֹ הֲכָנָה,
being the preliminary starting point unto the name Israel, functioning like a preparatory phase,
וְהוּא מַה הָאָדָם מֵכִין עַצְמוֹ לְקַיֵּים הַמִּצְוָה.
which is how man prepares himself to fulfill the commandment.

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה סג)515 Bereshit Rabbah 63:2 — R. Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said: Abraham was saved from the fiery furnace only through the merit of Jacob. This is like a man sentenced by the governor to be burned, but the governor foresaw by his astrology that he was destined to beget a daughter who would marry the king, and said: He is worthy to be saved through the merit of that daughter. So too, sentence went out from Nimrod that Abraham be burned, and the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that Jacob was destined to arise from him, and said: Abraham is worthy to be saved through the merit of Jacob. That is what is written: “Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, who redeemed Abraham” — Jacob redeemed Abraham.: "יַעֲקֹב אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם" כַּיָּדוּעַ;
And concerning this our Sages expounded (Bereishit Rabbah 63:1): "Jacob who redeemed Abraham," as is known;
וְהַיְינוּ דְּאַבְרָהָם מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ נִרְאֶה כְּגֵר הַמִּתְגַּיֵּיר,
meaning that Abraham viewed from his personal origins resembles a convert,

אֲבָל מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת יַחַס אֻמָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית מִמֶּנּוּ, הֲרֵי גַּם הוּא נִקְרָא אֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל וְ"אֵיתָן הָאֶזְרָחִי" (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טו516 Bava Batra 15a — Rav said: Ethan the Ezrahite — this is Abraham. It is written here, "Ethan the Ezrahite" (Psalms 89:1), and it is written there, "Who roused one from the east [mizrach], whom righteousness meets wherever he sets his foot" (Isaiah 41:2). Rashi: The words "or say Jacob" are not our reading here. On the alternative reading, the baraita above, in its enumeration of the ten elders, does count both Abraham and Ethan the Ezrahite, and does not count Asaph, since it holds that he is one of the three sons of Korah. Tosafos (s.v. "and by Solomon and by the sons of Korah"): Some texts count Abraham and Ethan the Ezrahite as two separate names among the ten, and read below: "it counts Abraham and it counts Ethan — but did not Rav say that Ethan the Ezrahite is Abraham? — the Ethan the Ezrahite counted here is Jacob." That reading is difficult, for on it we would have no source that David wrote his book by the hand of Abraham, since Ethan the Ezrahite would then not be Abraham. Maharsha: One may object that this exposition by itself does not show that Ethan the Ezrahite is Abraham — one could equally say that Heman the Ezrahite is Abraham. Rav may have relied on the identification of "Ethan" with Abraham drawn from "the month of Eitanim" (I Kings 8:2), which is expounded as the month in which the mighty ones [eitanim] of the world, the Patriarchs, were born; and that it is Abraham rather than Isaac or Jacob he learns from the exposition of "Ezrahite" as "from the east [mizrach]." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeira 9): Abraham merited to be a citizen [ezrach] in Israel, for he is called "Ethan the Ezrahite," as stated in Bava Basra, and he is called Israel, as stated in Bereishis Rabbah; he was the root of Israel, the first father. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): Once Jacob was clarified as the Lord's portion, his "bed" complete, Abraham and Isaac too were called fathers only of the seed of Jacob, and even Abraham is called Israel, as the Sages said that he is called "Ezrahite" because he merited to be a citizen [ezrach] in Israel..),
yet through the lineage of the nation of Israel issuing from him, he too is termed a native citizen in Israel and "Eitan the Ezrachi (native)",

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שָׁם)517 Bereshit Rabbah 63:3 — Abram was called Abraham. Isaac was called Abraham, as it is stated: “These are the generations of Isaac son of Abraham; Abraham.” Jacob’s name was called Israel, as it is written: “No longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel.” Isaac’s name was called Israel, as it is written: “These are the names of the children of Israel who came to Egypt, with Jacob.” Abraham was called Israel. R. Natan said: This is a deep matter — “And the dwelling of the children of Israel who dwelt in Egypt” and in the land of Canaan and in the land of Goshen “was four hundred and thirty years.”: אַבְרָהָם נִקְרָא "יִשְׂרָאֵל" וְכוּלֵי.
and as our Sages stated (Bereishit Rabbah there): Abraham was called "Israel, etc."
וְזֶהוּ אַחַר שֶׁנּוֹלַד יַעֲקֹב, אָז יֵשׁ קְדוּשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם בִּנְטִיַּת הַקָּצֶה דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
And this was actualized once Jacob was born, establishing Israel's sanctity even within Abraham's extreme leaning of love.
וּקְדוּשַּׁת נְטִיַּת שְׁנֵי הַקְּצוֹת, שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּנוֹטֶה בֶּאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ נוֹטֶה,
And the sanctity of both polar leanings, which though appearing one-sided are fundamentally balanced in truth,
הוּא קְדוּשַּׁת שְׁנֵי אֲבָהָן לְאַחַר שֶׁנּוֹלַד יַעֲקֹב,
is the sanctity of the two Patriarchs revealed after Jacob's birth,
וְנִתְגַּלָּה דְּגַם בָּהֶם אֵין פְּסֹלֶת,
demonstrating that within their pure root there is no dross,

כִּי "בְּיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע" – וְלֹא כָּל יִצְחָק (נְדָרִים לא518 Nedarim 31a — One who vows: I will not benefit from the seed of Abraham — is prohibited from deriving benefit from a Jew and permitted to benefit from the nations of the world. But is there not Ishmael [who is also of Abraham's seed]? It is written: "For in Isaac shall seed be called to you." But is there not Esau [who is of Isaac]? "In Isaac" — and not all of Isaac. Rashi: "But is there not Ishmael" — he too is of Abraham's seed, and he is among the nations of the world [so benefit from him should have been forbidden as well]. "For in Isaac shall seed be called to you" — and it is by that seed that the man vowed; and "in Isaac, and not all of Isaac" teaches that Esau is not called the seed of Isaac, and therefore the one who vowed is permitted to derive benefit from the nations of the world. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The very essence of Abraham and Isaac was not yet wholly transformed until the birth of Jacob, when the promise "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac" was fulfilled, and Ishmael and Esau were pushed away from being called the seed of Abraham and Isaac. Then Abraham and Isaac too were perfected, their "bed" complete, for from then on only the seed of Jacob is called and traced to them. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): The titles "father" and "mother" refer only to their power that extends into the child; therefore they said in Nedarim, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you" — and not Esau and Ishmael, who are not called Abraham's seed: though he begot them, his power is not discernible in them after the begetting, unless one converts, for [a convert] is called a son of Abraham. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 13): The angels, who said "Sarah your wife shall have a son" [attributing him to the feminine side], saw that Esau's evil severities would also issue from him; but they did not know the depths revealed afterwards in the Torah in "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you," which the Sages expounded in Nedarim, "and not all of Isaac" — Esau is not called his seed at all, so that in truth [Isaac] was entirely holy. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Emor 6): Although Abraham and Isaac are also called by the name Israel, that is only after Jacob was born and named Israel, for then it was clarified that "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac," since Ishmael and Esau are not called their seed; then they too were called by the name Israel, but not before. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 78): Sometimes some good may come to a father even from wicked sons, as with Abraham, from whom Ishmael and the sons of Keturah issued, through whom the dross went out; but for this the father must merit that the status of "his seed" be stripped from them, as it says of Abraham, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In truth the "bed" of Abraham and Isaac too was complete, for only "in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac": Esau and Ishmael are not their seed at all, only Jacob, whose bed was complete. Once Jacob was clarified as having a complete bed without dross, they too were clarified, for the dross was pushed away from being called their seed at all.
