Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 13): "If You say all are upon me, I offered my life before You": since Yitzchak gave himself over to the Blessed One, he belongs to Him entirely, and therefore he bears their iniquity entirely. Israel lift their eyes to Yitzchak as though he were their redeemer, but this is not so — through his attribute they are joined to the Blessed One, but the atonement itself is His; and Yitzchak, who is never separated from Him, shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, "in their eyes," that is, through the attribute of judgment, which is his. Then they lift their eyes on high and say "our Redeemer," for He Himself redeems them, and not through another. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): "And if You say it is all upon me," that is, that the existence of the dross comes only from my side, because there is dross in me, "I offered up my soul," and I am a perfect burnt-offering before You, with no dross in me from myself; it comes only from the spreading-forth that the Blessed One willed in creating the world. When it is revealed that everything comes from the root, from the Blessed One, the screen that the sins made between Israel and their Father in Heaven is removed, and through this "the Holy One, blessed be He, is shown to them before their eyes," even though "man shall not see Me and live": for the Sages said that at the time of death they see, since then the screen of this world is removed, and so too with this revelation of "half upon You" the screen of this world will be removed. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:83): The Torah was given specifically to the earth, the place of concealment, where face-to-face recognition is not known, and so one must judge only by the intellect of one in concealment; and face-to-face recognition comes from the side of strength [gevurah], in the sense of "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes." Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The recognition of "I am the Lord your God" is the recognition of "You are with me," and this is from the side of Isaac, as they said, "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes": complete seeing, face to face, comes through Isaac, for this apprehension, clear to the eye and in distinct levels, is from the attribute of contraction, which contracts apprehension into measures and levels. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 190): The root of Joseph is fear of sin, which is guarding the eye, and [fear, yirah,] has the letters of "seeing" [reiyah], in the sense of "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes," for this comes from the power of Isaac and from his attribute. Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 17): [The blessing "Who revives the dead" is in the mystery of Isaac,] as the Gemara says: Isaac said to them, "Before you praise me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He," and Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes. This alludes to the resurrection of the dead: it is not in the power of any creature in the world to show a person his foundation and the root from which he was hewn, to heal the root of his deficiency and comfort him in his grief; this was entrusted to no intermediary but given into the hand of the Blessed One alone. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 73): Isaac's attribute is always to hear from the depth of the supernal root, and the sight of the surface hue was a small thing to him; so the Gemara says that the Holy One says to Abraham and to Jacob, "Your children have sinned," but Isaac answered, "[They are] Your children, and not mine," for he always looked to the depth of the supernal root, where Israel are always called children of the Omnipresent, and therefore every kind of salvation for Israel is aroused from his side. Even the salvation that cannot be recognized in this world except by hearing, Isaac will show in the future to sight as well, so that it will be explicitly recognized upon all the hues of Israel's garments how His light dwells within them, as the Gemara says, "And Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes.":),
And this is what the Holy One demonstrates before their eyes (Shabbat 89b),
כִּי הוּא לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁשָּׁם הָאוֹר שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לִרְאוֹת עַיִן בְּעַיִן.
for this stands before Him where the light shines to perceive eye to eye.
וְלָכֵן מַזְכִּירִין עֲקֵידַת יִצְחָק וְהוּא עִיקַּר הַזִּכְרוֹנוֹת.
Therefore we invoke the Binding of Isaac, which is the heart of Zikhronot.
וְעִיקַּר הַזִּכָּרוֹן בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא – אֵיזֶה לַחַיִּים,
And the primary remembrance on that day is who shall live,
כִּי מִצַּד הַזִּכָּרוֹן לְטוֹבָה מִמֵּילָא נִמְשָׁךְ חַיִּים, כְּטַעַם "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם".
for from favorable remembrance life is spontaneously bestowed, mirroring "and You preserve them all."
וּזְכִירַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּאֵיזֶה דָּבָר אֵינוֹ כִּזְכִירַת בָּשָׂר וָדָם שֶׁהוּא נִבְדָּל מִן הַדָּבָר שֶׁזּוֹכֵר;
And Hashem's remembrance of an entity is unlike human memory which remains separate from the object recalled;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הֲרֵי עַל יְדֵי הַזְּכִירָה נִדְבָּק בִּמְקוֹר הַחַיִּים יִתְבָּרַךְ.
rather with Hashem, through His divine remembrance the soul becomes bound directly unto the Source of Life.
"וּבַמֶּה? בַּשּׁוֹפָר" – הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ קִיּוּם הַחַיִּים שֶׁהוּא בִּמְזוֹנֵי,
"And through what? Through the shofar"—functions like the preservation of life through food;
כָּךְ קִיּוּם הַזִּכָּרוֹן הוּא בַּשּׁוֹפָר שֶׁהוּא הַמְעוֹרֵר הָאָדָם וּמַזְכִּיר אֶת הָאָדָם,
so is remembrance sustained through the shofar which awakens man and reminds him,
וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ זוֹכְרוֹ.
whereby Hashem likewise remembers him.
וְזֶהוּ עִיקָּר שֶׁצָּרִיךְ אָדָם לְקִיּוּם חַיֵּי עוֹלָם שֶׁבּוֹ:
And this is the vital necessity for man to sustain eternal life within himself:
לִהְיוֹת לוֹ קוֹל שׁוֹפָר הַמְּעוֹרְרוֹ מִשְּׁנָתוֹ תָּדִיר, וְהוּא הַמַּמְשִׁיךְ לוֹ חַיִּים.
to have the blast of the shofar continuously rousing him from spiritual slumber, channeling life unto him.
וּמְשַׁל זֶה בְּחַיֵּי הַגּוּף הוּא הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁעַל יָדָהּ הוּא הַמְשָׁכַת חַיֵּי הַגּוּפָנִים.
And the parallel in bodily life is food through which physical existence is sustained.
וְנֶאֱמַר: "תִּקְעוּ בַחֹדֶשׁ שׁוֹפָר וְגוֹמֵר כִּי חֹק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים פא, ד–ה),
And it is written: "Blow the horn at the new moon... for it is a statute (chok) for Israel, etc." (Psalms 81:4–5),

וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּבֵיצָה (טז564 Beitzah 16a — A man's entire livelihood is allotted to him from Rosh HaShana until Yom Kippur, except for the expenses of Sabbaths, the expenses of Festivals, and the expenses of his sons' Torah study: if he spends less, he is given less, and if he spends more, he is given more. R. Abbahu said: What is the verse? "Sound the shofar at the new moon, at the covered time for our festival day" — which is the festival on which the moon is covered? You must say this is Rosh HaShana. And it is written: "For it is a statute [chok] for Israel, an ordinance of the God of Jacob." How do we know that this word "statute" is a term for food? For it is written: "And they ate their allotment [chukkam] which Pharaoh gave them." Rashi: Everything a man is destined to earn in the coming year, from which he will be sustained, is fixed for him — so much and no more; he must therefore take care not to spend lavishly, since they will not add to his earnings for food beyond what was decreed for him. For the expenses of Sabbaths and Festivals, by contrast, no sum was fixed and no source assigned; rather, according to what he is accustomed to spend they furnish it to him, whether at once or after a time. "If he spends less, he is given less" means that they furnish him only a meagre income. Tosafos (s.v. "A man's entire livelihood is allotted to him ... and the expenses of his sons' Torah study"): R. Yitzchak explained that all three are derived from the verses cited just above: the expenses of Sabbath from what was said there, "Borrow on My account and I will repay"; and Torah from "the joy [chedvah] of the Lord is your strength" — for "joy" means Torah, as it is written, "The precepts of the Lord are upright, gladdening the heart." Tosafos (s.v. "which is the festival on which the moon is covered"): Tosafot objects to Rashi's explanation, that the moon is not visible, for on that reading the verse should have said that the moon is covered and not that the month is covered. Rabbeinu Tam therefore takes "kese" as a term for an appointed time, as in "at the appointed day [yom hakese] he will come home"; Rabbeinu Meshullam explained that the New Moon is "covered" on Rosh HaShana in that its offering is not stated explicitly in Scripture. Maharsha: Maharsha asks how this accords with the opinion in the first chapter of Rosh HaShana that the world is judged on Passover with regard to grain, and answers that there the judgment concerns the grain of the world at large, whether the crop will prosper, whereas here it is each individual's own sustenance — whether he will have it in plenty — that is settled from Rosh HaShana until Yom Kippur. He further asks why the Gemara proves that "statute" is a term for food from the end of the verse, "and they ate their allotment," rather than from its opening, "for it was a statute for the priests from Pharaoh": the opening could be read as a fixed allowance of money with which they bought what they needed, whereas "they ate their allotment" shows that the allotment itself was what they ate, namely bread. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Yevamos 105a): Explaining why the decree against the house of Eli could be atoned for through Torah, he writes that the Torah, being intellectual, stands above the decree, "as we explained concerning 'a man's sustenance is allotted to him from Rosh HaShanah' (Beitzah 16a), that the Torah is not subject to the decree, for it stands above the decree" [which is why the expenses of his sons' Torah study are outside the yearly allotment]. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 10): From "For it is a statute for Israel" the Sages expounded that all of a man's sustenance is allotted to him from Rosh HaShanah; "man" without qualification means Israel, who are called "man," and "statute" is a term for food. That is, the Blessed One allots to each one of Israel as much sustenance as will benefit him for the service of the Blessed One, and this is the "allotted bread" that King Solomon requested, even though his daily meal was very large. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 1): On "Which festival is it on which the moon is concealed? It is Rosh HaShanah," [the author's] father explained that "at the concealing" alludes to the fact that a person does not see his actions joined all the way up to the Supernal Sun: he sees only that "according to the effort is the reward," but not their connection up to the infinite light. Therefore the commandment of this day is to sound the shofar, which arouses the Great Shofar, signifying that Israel raises all its actions up to the Supernal Sun, to the place where the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Divine Presence..): "חֹק" – זֶה לִישָּׁנָא דִּמְזוֹנֵי,
which our Sages expounded in Beitza (16a): chok denotes sustenance,
וּמִכָּאן דִּמְזוֹנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם קְצוּבִים מֵרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה;
deriving thence that a person's livelihood is apportioned on Rosh Hashanah;
וַהֲרֵי מְפוֹרָשׁ בַּכָּתוּב כִּי "חֹק" זֶה טַעַם עַל "תִּקְעוּ" הַקּוֹדֵם.
and Scripture explicitly provides this chok as the rationale for the preceding command to blow.
וְהַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁאָז קוֹצְבִין מְזוֹנוֹת, לָכֵן בָּאִים הַשּׁוֹפָרוֹת
Namely, because sustenance is then decreed, the shofar blasts are sounded,
שֶׁהוּא הַקּוֹל – "קוֹל יַעֲקֹב", שֶׁזֶּה כָּל כֹּוחוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב בַּקּוֹל.
which represents the voice—"the voice of Jacob," whose entire strength resides in voice.
וְעִיקַּר תְּפִלַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "וְנָתַן לִי לֶחֶם לֶאֱכֹל וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, כ),
And the core plea of our father Jacob was: "and will give me bread to eat, etc." (Genesis 28:20),
וְזֶה כָּל יְגִיעָתוֹ וַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ: עַל מְזוֹנֵי וְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים;
and this was his toil: praying for sustenance and the preservation of life;
שֶׁכְּבָר זָכָה לְבָנֵי מִסִּטְרָא דְּאַבְרָהָם, וְחַיֵּי מִסִּטְרָא דְּיִצְחָק,
having already merited children from Abraham and life from Isaac,
אֲבָל צָרִיךְ לְדָבָר הַמְקַיֵּים הַחַיִּים –
yet requiring that which preserves life—
דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יוּפְסַק חַס וְשָׁלוֹם וְיִמָּצֵא דֹּפִי בְּזַרְעוֹ כְּמוֹ אֵצֶל אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, רַק מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה.
namely that life never be severed, Heaven forbid, with no defect in his seed as occurred with Abraham and Isaac, his bed being whole.
וְהַקִּיּוּם דְּחַיִּים הוּא בַּפֶּה:
And the preservation of life operates through the mouth:
חַיִּים הַגּוּפָנִיִּים בַּוֶּשֶׁט הַמַּכְנִיס מִינֵי אוֹכָלִים וּמַשְׁקִים,
physical life through the esophagus (veshet) that ingests food and drink,
וְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם בַּקָּנֶה הַמּוֹצִיא קוֹל.
and eternal life through the windpipe (kaneh) that produces vocal sound.
וּשְׁנֵיהֶם קְרוּיִים "סִימָנִים", שֶׁהֵם סִימָנֵי הַחַיּוּת שֶׁעַל יָדָם הוּא קִיּוּם הַחַיּוּת.
And both are termed "signs" (simanim), being indicators through which vitality is preserved.
וּבָהֶם נִיכָּר סִימַן הַחַיּוּת, שֶׁבְּקִלְקוּל הַחַיּוּת נֶחְלַשׁ אוֹ נֶעְדַּר לְגַמְרֵי כֹּחַ הָאֲכִילָה וְכֹחַ הַדִּבּוּר וְהַשְׁמָעַת הַקּוֹל.
And in them the sign of life is recognized, for with declining vitality eating, speech, and voice weaken or cease.
וְהַקָּנֶה עִם הָרֵיאָה וְלֵב וְכָבֵד הַנִּתְלִים בָּהּ,
And the trachea together with lungs, heart, and liver suspended from it,
וְהַוֶּשֶׁט עִם אֵבָרֵי הַמָּזוֹן הַנִּתְלִים בּוֹ,
and the esophagus with digestive organs attached to it,
הֵם מַמָּשׁ דּוּגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ וָגוּף,
literally mirror soul and body,
שֶׁאֵלּוּ מְשַׁמְּשִׁים לַכֹּחוֹת הַנַּפְשִׁיִּים וּמִדּוֹת שֶׁבַּנֶּפֶשׁ, וְאֵלּוּ לַכֹּחוֹת הַגּוּפָנִים.
these ministering to the spiritual traits of the soul, and those to bodily faculties.
וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶה דָּבָר נֶעְלָם מִשֵּׂכֶל בְּנֵי אָדָם: חִבּוּר הַנֶּפֶשׁ בַּגּוּף,
And in truth the fusion of soul and body is hidden from human reason,
וְלָכֵן לֹא יָבִינוּ גַּם כֵּן אֵיךְ הַמָּזוֹן יְקַיֵּים הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
which is why people likewise fail to grasp how physical food sustains the spiritual soul.
אַךְ הָאֱמֶת שֶׁהֵם מְחוּבָּרִים וְכוּלּוֹ חַד,
Yet the truth is that they are unified as one,
וְהַדָּם הוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ הֹוֶוה מִן הַמָּזוֹן וּמִשְׁכָּנוֹ בַּלֵּב,
and the blood which is the soul is generated from food, residing in the heart,
וּמִמֶּנּוּ חַיּוּת כָּל הָאֵיבָרִים,
from which all limbs draw vitality,
וְהָרֵיאָה וְהַקָּנֶה הַמּוֹצִיא קוֹל תְּלוּיִים בּוֹ.
and the lungs and trachea producing sound depend upon it.
וְעַל יְדֵי קִיּוּם שׁוֹפָרוֹת בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה הוּא חוֹק וָקֶצֶב הַמְּזוֹנוֹת שֶׁל כָּל הַשָּׁנָה כֻּלָּהּ,
And through the mitzvah of Shofrot on Rosh Hashanah the measure of sustenance for the entire year is established,
דְּיָהֵיב מְזוֹנֵי לְחַיֵּי לְקִיּוּם הַחַיִּים, לִהְיוֹת לוֹ כֹּחַ לְתוֹרָה וּתְפִלָּה.
He giving food for life to sustain existence, that man have strength for Torah and prayer.
וְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת דְּ"עוּרוּ יְשֵׁנִים" בְּכָל הַשָּׁנָה כֻּלָּהּ הַבָּא עַל יְדֵי הַמָּזוֹן –
And the awakening of "awake, sleepers" throughout the entire year mediated through food—

שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יב565 Bava Batra 12b — R. Avdimi of Haifa said: Before a person eats and drinks he has two hearts; after he eats and drinks he has but one heart, as it is stated: "A hollow man will get a heart" (Job 11:12) — and it is written, "hollow of boards" (Exodus 27:8), which we render [in Aramaic]: hollowed out with boards. Rashi: "A hollow man" — when he is hollow, without a full stomach. "Will get a heart" — he has several hearts, in that he does not settle upon one complete mind. Maharsha: At first sight the statement sounds like praise and a mark of superiority, since "two hearts" would then match the sense of "hollowing" in the verse adduced alongside it, "and new wine opens [yenovev] the virgins," where the word is expounded favorably. But Rashi explained it as a defect, in line with the teaching that thirteen things were said in praise of bread eaten in the morning, among them that it makes the simple wise. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggadot, Bava Batra 12b): There is a man whose heart is deficient and a man whose heart is whole. Before he has eaten and drunk his heart is in its wholeness, and after he eats and drinks his heart is deficient, for eating and drinking confuse a man's intellect — as is well known, before a man has eaten and drunk his mind is at its clearest and purest.:): "לְאַחַר שֶׁאָכַל אֵין אֶלָּא לֵב אֶחָד",
concerning which our Sages stated (Bava Batra 12b): "after one has eaten he has but one heart",
וּכְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: לְטוֹבָה;
and as Rashi interprets: directed toward good;
כִּי כֵן מִדַּת הָאֲכִילָה הָרְאוּיָה:
for such is proper eating:
לִהְיוֹת קִיּוּם הַחַיִּים הָאֲמִיתִּיִּים דְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם עַל יָדָהּ,
that through it authentic eternal life is sustained,
שֶׁאֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא לֵב אֶחָד לְאָבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם.
having solely a single, undivided heart devoted unto his Father in Heaven.

sections.en: Israel, the Nations, and the Middle Path of Torah

items.h: Each nation embodies an extreme spiritual tendency, while Israel receives Torah's enduring middle path and reveals its essential cleaving to Hashem.

Seif 1 — Torah's Middle Path and Israel's Essential Will
Unlike the nations' spiritual extremes, Torah gives Israel an enduring middle path rooted in direct cleaving to Hashem.

p: כָּל אֻמָּה יֵשׁ לָהּ כֹּחַ מְיֻחָד דְּרַע שֶׁבּוֹ תָּלוּי עִקַּר חַיּוּתָם,
Every nation possesses a specific power of evil upon which the core of their vitality depends,
דְּלָכֵן לֹא נִתְּנָה תוֹרָה,
which is why the Torah was not given to them,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ב עַמּוּד ב566 Avodah Zarah 2b — It is written: "And he said: The Lord came from Sinai and rose from Seir unto them," and it is written: "God comes from Teman." What did He seek in Seir, and what did He seek in Paran? R. Yochanan said: This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, took the Torah round to every nation and tongue, and they did not accept it, until He came to Israel and they accepted it. Rashi: "Paran" is the land of Ishmael, as it is written of Hagar, "and she dwelt in the wilderness of Paran." Tosafos (s.v. "What did He seek in Seir, and what did He seek in Paran?"): Paran is the land of the Ishmaelites, as it is written of Hagar, "in the wilderness of Paran," and the exposition relies on the end of the verse, "and the Holy One from Mount Paran, selah"; one should not read "what did He seek in Teman," since Teman belongs to Seir, as it is written, "And your mighty men, O Teman, shall be dismayed." R. Elchanan, however, reads "what did He seek in Seir, and what did He seek in Teman," holding that Teman here is not the name of a nation but the southern quarter, as the Sifrei expounds that the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself to Israel from the four directions — and on that reading the verse from Habakkuk was indeed needed. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 2b): As for the statement that the Holy One, blessed be He, took the Torah round to all the nations: the Torah is from the side of the Blessed One, and therefore it belongs to all, for the Torah is the supreme wisdom and pertains to all the nations; only from the side of the recipient does it belong to Israel specifically. From the side of the Torah itself there is no limit to it, and it lies before all, if there is but a recipient; but from the side of the recipient, none receives it save Israel.):
as our Sages of blessed memory said (Avodah Zarah 2b):
שֶׁהֶחֱזִירָהּ כֻּלֵּהּ וְלֹא קִבְּלוּהָ,
He offered it around, etc., and they did not accept it;
כִּי הַתּוֹרָה הִיא קַו הָאֶמְצָעִי דֶּאֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב,
for the Torah is the middle line, as in 'truth unto Jacob,'

אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תוֹרָה (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ח567 Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 3:8 — "And it cast truth to the ground" — whenever Israel casts the words of the Torah to the ground, this wicked kingdom decrees and succeeds. What is the reason? "It cast truth to the ground, and it acted and succeeded" (Daniel 8:12). And there is no truth but Torah, as you say, "Buy truth and do not sell it, wisdom and instruction and understanding" (Proverbs 23:23). Pnei Moshe (s.v. "through the transgression of the Torah"): When transgressors grow slack and cast the Torah aside, then "a host is given over" against them. And because the verse "they encamped in Rephidim" is likewise expounded to mean that they let their hands go slack from the Torah, and therefore "Amalek came," these verses too are expounded here in the same manner.),
and there is no truth other than Torah (Talmud Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 3:8),
כִּי הַהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת בְּאֵיזֶה צַד זֶה שֶׁקֶר,
because sinking entirely into any single extreme is falsehood,
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁלֹּא תִּכּוֹן לָעַד,
meaning that it cannot endure eternally;
שֶׁהַקִּיּוּם לָעַד נַחֲלָה בְּלֹא מְצָרִים,
for eternal existence is an inheritance without boundaries,
דְּהַיְנוּ גְּבוּל וּמֵיצַר הַמַּפְסִיק וּמְסַמֵּן סוֹף הַדָּבָר,
meaning a border and boundary that interrupts and marks the end of a thing,
זֶהוּ רַק מִדַּת קַו הָאֶמְצָעִי.
this belongs solely to the measure of the middle line.
וְהוּא יְסוֹד כָּל מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה עֵטִין שֶׁלֹּא לִהְיוֹת שָׁקוּעַ בְּשׁוּם דָּבָר.
And this is the foundation of all the commandments of the Torah: counsels ensuring one does not become submerged in anything.
וְזֶהוּ כָּל הַגָּלוּת בָּאֻמּוֹת
And this is the purpose of the entire exile among the nations:
לְבָרֵר שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל אֵין שְׁקוּעִים בְּאוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ הָרַע שֶׁל אוֹתָהּ אֻמָּה,
to clarify and prove that Israel is not submerged in that specific evil power of that nation;
כִּי הֵם מִתְגַּבְּרִים בְּטַעֲנָה שֶׁגַּם יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁקִּבְּלוּהָ לֹא קִיְּמוּהָ,
for the nations prevail with the accusation that even Israel, who accepted the Torah, did not fulfill it,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּאוֹמְרִים שֶׁגַּם הֵם שְׁקוּעִים.
as stated at the beginning of Avodah Zarah, where they claim that they too are submerged.
וְנֶגֶד הִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת בְּאֵיזֶה כֹּחַ מִתְגַּבֶּרֶת אֵיזֶה אֻמָּה שֶׁחַיּוּתָן אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ כְּנֶגְדָּם לְהִשְׁתַּעְבֵּד בָּם,
And corresponding to any submergence in a power, whichever nation derives its vitality from that specific power asserts dominance against them to enslave them,
עַד שֶׁמִּתְבָּרֵר שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָם כֵּן וְאָז נִגְאָלִים מֵהֶם.
until it becomes clarified that Israel is not so, and then they are redeemed from them.
וַעֲמָלֵק נִקְרָא רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם שֶׁהוּא תַּמְצִיתָם,
And Amalek is called the 'first of the nations' because he is their quintessence,
כְּמוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל רֵאשִׁית תְּבוּאָתֹה שֶׁהֵם תַּכְלִית הַמְּכֻוָּן בַּבְּרִיאָה,
just as Israel is 'the first of His harvest,' being the ultimate intended purpose of Creation;
וְהַתַּכְלִית נִקְרָא רֵאשִׁית דְּסוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה,
and the ultimate purpose is called 'first,' because 'the end of action was first in thought';
וְתַכְלִית בְּרִיאַת כָּל כֹּחוֹת דְּרַע שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל יְנַצְּחוּם וּלְהַרְאוֹת אַבְדָנָם.
and the purpose for creating all powers of evil is for Israel to conquer them and demonstrate their destruction.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּהַגַּם דְּיֵשׁ כֹּחַ הִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת אֲשֶׁר לְמַרְאִית עַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא כֹּחַ נִבְדָּל,
That is to say, even though there exists a force of submergence which, to outward appearance in this physical world, is an independent power,
בֶּאֱמֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּעַל הַכֹּחוֹת כֻּלָּם,
in truth Hashem, blessed be He, is the Master of all forces,
וְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁדְּבוּקִים בּוֹ וְכָל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם מִמֶּנּוּ,
and Israel, who cling to Him and whose entire actions derive from Him—
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁמְּבַטְּלִים כָּל כֹּחוֹתֵיהֶם לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
meaning they nullify all their faculties completely to Hashem, blessed be He—
דְּזֶהוּ עִקַּר כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ:
which is the core of the entire Torah:
"אָנֹכִי ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ" – פֵּרוּשׁ בַּעַל כֹּחוֹתֶיךָ,
'I am Hashem your God' – meaning the Master of your powers,

שֶׁזֶּהוּ הוֹרָאַת שֵׁם אֱלֹהִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּטוּר אֹרַח חַיִּים (סִימָן ה568 Tur, Orach Chayim 5 — In his blessings he should have in mind the meaning of the words he utters. When he mentions the Name, he should have in mind the meaning of its pronunciation with alef-dalet, a term of lordship — that He is Lord of all; and he should further have in mind the meaning of its spelling with yod-heh, a term of being — that He was, is, and will be. And when he mentions "Elohim," he should have in mind that He is mighty and strong, who has the power over the upper worlds and the lower, for "El" is a term of power and strength, as in "and the mighty of the land he took." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 1): The four-letter Name indicates the Holy One, blessed be He, as He extends beyond our grasp, which has limits, for it denotes "He was, is, and will be," as written in the Tur, Orach Chayim 5: an expansion without end that is hidden from us. The Name of lordship indicates that He is Lord of all and His kingship rules over all: the attribute of kingship, for whose sake creation was made bounded and contracted, as though there were separate beings, to reveal His kingship, for there is no king without a people; and this is the power of contraction and of the existence of bounded beings.'),
which is the precise meaning of the Name Elohim, as written in Tur, Orach Chaim (Siman 5),
יְכוֹלִים עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְנַצֵּחַ כָּל מִינֵי הַכֹּחוֹת.
are able through this to overcome all varieties of forces.
וְנִצּוּחַ הַגָּמוּר דִּזְבִיחַת הַיֵּצֶר הוּא כִּלָּיוֹן כָּל עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת,
And the complete triumph of slaughtering the evil inclination is the annihilation of all idolaters,
וְנִמְצָא הַתַּכְלִית שֶׁלָּהֶם רַק לְהַאֲבִידָם.
so that their ultimate end is solely for their destruction.
וְכָל הַגֵּרִים שֶׁמֵּהֶם וְכֵן הַנִּשְׁאָרִים לֶעָתִיד לַעֲבָדִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אָז אֶהְפֹּךְ וְגוֹמֵר",
And all converts who emerge from them, as well as those remaining in the future as servants, as it is written: 'For then will I turn, etc.,'

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כד569 Avodah Zarah 24a — The colleagues of R. Eliezer answered him from the verse "All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you; they shall come up with acceptance upon My altar." R. Eliezer said to them: In the time to come they will all be converts who attach themselves of their own accord. Rav Yosef said: What is the verse? "For then will I turn to the peoples a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord." Rashi: "Converts who attach themselves of their own accord" — they drag themselves along to convert on their own initiative, even though [the court] does not accept them. And [Abaye objects that] "that they may all call upon the name of the Lord" shows only that they will withdraw from idolatry, not that they will withdraw from bestiality. Maharsha: Since converts will not be accepted in the time to come, the nations will not be able to serve Him with all His commandments as Israel does, but only with that one portion of the Torah which they are able to keep — and the prohibition of bestiality belongs to that portion, since the descendants of Noah were already commanded concerning it. "For then will I turn to the peoples a pure language": at the beginning of the settlement of the world all men had one language, the holy tongue, and when the generation of the dispersion rebelled He confounded it for them; the verse promises that when the nations return to serve the Lord that pure language, the holy tongue, will be restored to them, for no other tongue is "pure speech" beside it. עַמּוּד א): "כֻּלָּם גֵּרִים גְּרוּרִים וְכוּלֵי570 Rashi, Avodah Zarah 2b — “Hangers-on” — those who attach themselves of their own accord in order to convert, even though we do not accept them.",
and our Sages of blessed memory taught (Avodah Zarah 24a): 'they all become dragged-along converts, etc.,'
אֵינוֹ מִצַּד תַּכְלִית הַמְּכֻוָּן בִּבְרִיאָתָם, רַק מִצַּד הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת.
this is not by virtue of the primary purpose intended in their creation, but merely from external extension.
כִּי כָּל נִבְרָא שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל גְּבוּל בְּהֶכְרֵחַ יֵשׁ לוֹ שְׁנֵי קְצָווֹת וְאֶמְצָעִי,
For every finite creature inevitably possesses two extremes and a middle;
וְקַו אֶמְצָעִי הוּא הַתַּכְלִית הַמְּכֻוָּן בּוֹ,
and the middle line is the primary purpose intended for it,
וְהַקְּצָווֹת הֵם הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ מִתַּכְלִית הַזֶּה.
while the extremes are the peripheral extensions stemming from this purpose.
וְהַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁל אָבְדַן אוֹתָן כֹּחוֹת הוּא לִהְיוֹת עֲבָדִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.
And the extension of the destruction of those powers is their becoming servants to Israel.
דְּהַתַּכְלִית הוּא הַכָּרַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּעַל הַכֹּחוֹת כֻּלָּם,
For the ultimate end is the recognition of Hashem, blessed be He, as Master of all forces,

דְּכָל פָּעַל לְמַעֲנֵהוּ לְקִלּוּסוֹ (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב רֵישׁ מִזְמוֹר יט571 Midrash Tehillim 19:1 — "For the leader. A psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God." This is what Scripture says: "The Lord has made everything for His own sake" (Proverbs 16:4) — for His praise, as it is said, "Sing to the Lord with thanksgiving" (Psalms 147:7). Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): The aim of the whole Torah is to come to a complete apprehension that there is a Creator, Ruler and Overseer, which was the purpose of the creation of the world: "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. All 613 commandments are counsels for reaching this, for the Torah is called truth, being counsels for reaching a clear apprehension in the heart, so manifest that it needs no faith. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 6): Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created for His glory, He created to reveal the glory of His kingship and His Presence among the lower beings, and "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. The building of the Tabernacle and the Temple is man's work of building a place for His Presence after the sin, when the Presence is not revealed everywhere, in the pattern of the Blessed One's work in creation; had man not sinned, the whole world would have been a Tabernacle and a Sanctuary. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The angels cry, "Where is the place of His glory?", but man grasps the Throne of Glory, for "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise; the purpose of creation is the revelation of His glory, and its purpose is man. For the chief revelation of glory is when a person with free choice, whose body inclines toward impurity, nevertheless subdues his inclination and desires for the sake of Heaven's honor, which the angels, who have no evil inclination, cannot attain at all.),
that 'everything was made for His sake,' for His praise (Shocher Tov, beginning of Psalm 19);
וּמִצַּד הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל הֵם הַמַּכִּירִים זֶה וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם הִתְעַלּוּת עַל אוֹתָן כֹּחוֹת,
and from the extension wherein Israel are those who recognize this and rise above those forces,
הֵם קוֹנִים אוֹתָן לַעֲבָדִים.
they acquire them as servants.
אֲבָל עֲמָלֵק שֶׁהוּא רֵאשִׁית וְתַכְלִית הַמְּכֻוָּן דְּגוֹיִם לְבַד,
However, Amalek, who represents the very beginning and apex solely of the gentile nations,
לָכֵן אַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד וּמָחֹה תִּמְחֶה וְגוֹמֵר.
therefore 'his end shall be destruction,' and 'you shall utterly blot out, etc.'
וְאָמְרוּ בַּמְּכִילְתָּא (סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח) דְּאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּר מֵעֲמָלֵק,
And they said in the Mekhilta (end of Parashat Beshalach) that no convert is accepted from Amalek,

וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין572 Sanhedrin 99b — Timna was a royal princess. She wished to convert; she came to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, and they did not accept her. She went and became a concubine to Elifaz son of Esav, saying: Better to be a maidservant to this nation than a noblewoman of another nation. From her came forth Amalek, who afflicted Israel. What is the reason? Because they should not have distanced her. Rashi: "Royalty without a crown" — a great prince, only not crowned; and since Timna was the sister of a chief, she was certainly a king's daughter. "Better to be a maidservant to this nation" — to the children of Abraham and Isaac, who fear Heaven, rather than a mistress to another nation; therefore she became a concubine to Eliphaz son of Esau, who was of the seed of Isaac. "To push her away" — from beneath the wings of the Shechinah, for they ought to have converted her. Maharsha: They derived this exposition from Scripture's taking care to state that Amalek's mother was Timna, who bore him to Eliphaz — "And Timna was a concubine to Eliphaz" — whereas for Eliphaz's other sons, Teman, Omar, Zepho and the rest, it does not mention who their mother was. They expounded that because Abraham [Isaac and Jacob] did not accept her, she had to become a concubine to Eliphaz, saying, "Better to be a maidservant," and for this they were punished in that Amalek, who afflicted Israel, was born of her. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 99b): Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did not accept Timna because, owing to her importance and royalty, she would not enter conversion as is fitting: one is a convert only when he joins himself wholly to those to whom he converts, and while the Patriarchs humbled themselves before God, blessed be He, Timna, being royal, would not regard herself as a convert. Once pushed away she was distanced all the more, for whatever is pushed away is pushed away entirely: had she not come to convert there would have been no distancing, but since she came to convert and was rejected by the Patriarchs, who are the very beginning, this was the utmost distancing, leaving no share or connection at all. Therefore Amalek came forth from her, for no nation could be as opposed to Israel as Amalek was except one born of such distancing. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 20): Among the nations, those with a greater connection to holiness are the worse, and Amalek has more connection to holiness than all the nations: besides issuing from two patriarchs and matriarchs, his mother Timna went around to the doors of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to convert, and they did not accept her, for they sensed the force of impurity of "the first of the nations" destined to come from her. Yet she still yearned to convert and went around their doors — surely because of a holy spark stirring within her. (צט עַמּוּד ב) דְּתִמְנַע בָּאתָה לְאַבְרָהָם יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב לְאִגַּיּוֹרֵי וְלֹא קִבְּלוּהָ.
and therefore they stated in Sanhedrin (99b) that Timna came to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to convert, and they did not accept her.
כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ דְּרַע בָּאָדָם הוּא מִצַּד הָאֵם,
For the root of evil in man stems from the maternal side,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וּבֵן כְּסִיל תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ",
as it is written: 'and a foolish son is the grief of his mother,'
כִּי הִיא מַכְנֶסֶת בָּאָב כַּיָּדוּעַ מֵחֵטְא הָרִאשׁוֹן.
for she instills it into the father, as is known from the Primordial Sin.
וְהִיא בָּאת לְאִגַּיּוֹרֵי וְאָמְרָה: "מוּטָב שֶׁאֶהְיֶה שִׁפְחָה וְכוּלֵי",
And she came seeking to convert, saying: 'It is better that I be a maidservant, etc.,'
הֲרֵי חָשְׁקָה לִכְאוֹרָה לְהִדָּבֵק בֶּאֱמֶת.
seeming seemingly to desire to cleave unto the Truth.
וְזֶה שֹׁרֶשׁ עֲמָלֵק,
And this is the root of Amalek,
שֶׁהוּא תַּמְצִית כָּל מִינֵי כֹּחוֹת,
who is the synthesis of all categories of forces,
וְנִמְצָא יֵשׁ לוֹ כָּל כֹּחוֹת הַהֲפָכִיּוֹת,
so that he possesses all opposing powers,
וְהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ תַּכְלִיתָן שֶׁהוּא לְהַאֲבִידָן,
and he is the root of their ultimate end, which is to destroy them,
וְנִמְצָא יֵשׁ לוֹ גַּם כֹּחַ זֶה וְיוּכַל לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּכָל מִינֵי כֹּחוֹת.
so that he possesses this power as well, and can utilize every variety of force.
וְאֵינוֹ מִכְּלַל זֶרַע עֵשָׂו
And he is not within the general seed of Esau,

שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סִפְרֵי בְּרָכָה פִּסְקָא שמג)573 Sifrei Devarim 343 — When the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed Himself to give the Torah to Israel, He revealed Himself not to Israel alone but to all the nations. First He went to the children of Esau and said to them: Will you accept the Torah? They said to Him: What is written in it? He said to them: "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13). They said: The whole being of those men and of their father is murder, as it is said, "and the hands are the hands of Esau" (Genesis 27:22), and "by your sword you shall live" (Genesis 27:40). דְּאָמַר: "מַה כְּתִיב בָּהּ? לֹא תִרְצַח וְכוּלֵי",
about whom our Sages of blessed memory said (Sifrei Berachah, section 343) that he asked: 'What is written in it? Do not murder, etc.,'
שֶׁהוּא שָׁקוּעַ בָּזֶה כִּי הוּא פְּסֹלֶת דְּיִצְחָק.
for he is submerged in this, being the byproduct of Isaac.
אֲבָל עֲמָלֵק נֶגֶד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
Amalek, however, is set directly against our father Jacob, peace be upon him,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ גַּם כֵּן כֹּחַ זֶה לָלֶכֶת בְּקַו יֹשֶׁר,
having likewise this capacity to walk in a straight path,
וְיֵשׁ לוֹ גַּם כֵּן כֹּחַ לָלֶכֶת בִּשְׁנֵי קְצָווֹת.
and possessing also the capacity to veer into both extremes.
וּלְכָךְ בָּאת אֵצֶל כָּל שְׁלֹשָׁה אָבוֹת לְאִגַּיּוֹרֵי.
Therefore Timna approached all three Patriarchs to convert.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם וְלֹא רֵאשִׁית תְּבוּאָתוֹ דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
Yet in truth he is the 'first of the nations' and not the 'first of His harvest' belonging to Hashem, blessed be He,
דְּתַכְלִיתוֹ לְמַעֲנֵהוּ לְקִלּוּסוֹ,
whose purpose is for His sake and praise,
אֲבָל כַּוָּנַת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת לְגַרְמַיְהוּ.
whereas the intention of idolaters is for their own self-interest.
וְזֶה עִקַּר הַחִלּוּק בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים
And this is the essential distinction between Israel and the nations,

שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ד574 Rosh Hashanah 4a — And one who acts in this way — is it not exemplary? But it was taught: One who says, "This sela is for charity so that my sons may live," or "so that I may merit thereby life in the World to Come," is a wholly righteous man. This is not difficult: here — with a Jew; there — with gentiles. Rashi: "With respect" [literally, "from your burden"]: from the very text with which you came against us to refute us I give you an answer — see what is written in it: "that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons"; you learn that he did it not for the sake of Heaven but for his own benefit. "Such a man is wholly righteous": if he is accustomed to this. "Here, of an Israelite": whose heart is directed to Heaven, and if it goes ill with him in his life he does not complain but ascribes the suffering to his sin; but a gentile, if he is not repaid in kind, complains. Tosafos (s.v. "so that my sons may live"): And what we learned in the first chapter of Avos, "Do not be like servants who serve the master in order to receive a reward", refers to the nations of the world, who come to regret their earlier [good deeds]. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos, on Tosafot s.v. "so that my sons may live"): The reading [in Tosafot] should be "like the nations of the world", as in Tosafot Yeshanim; for it is unreasonable that the Mishnah [in Avos] speaks only of the nations of the world, since Tzadok and Baitus, who erred in [Antigonos's] words, were Israelites. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 4a): This does not contradict "Do not be like servants who serve the master in order to receive a reward" (Avos 1:3), which speaks of one who performs a commandment for the sake of the reward of that very commandment, so that the aim of his service is not the Blessed One but himself; this man performs the commandment as it should be, out of love of the Blessed One, only that the aim of his love is that it should go well with him — and since in the end he loves the Blessed One and serves Him as is fitting, he is wholly righteous. As for the distinction between Israel and a gentile: the very being and rank of Israel is righteousness and goodness, so that an Israelite who performs a commandment for his own benefit is wholly righteous, for "righteous" means only one who is drawn along the path of uprightness (to look to nothing but love of the Blessed One is the rank of the pious man, not a condition of the righteous); but the nations are not in their essence of the rank of righteousness, so a gentile is righteous only when his whole intention is for the sake of Heaven. עַמּוּד א):
concerning which our Sages of blessed memory said (Rosh Hashanah 4a):
"הָאוֹמֵר סֶלַע וְכוּלֵי בִּשְׁבִיל וְכוּלֵי הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר",
'One who declares: this coin is for charity so that my son may live, is a completely righteous person,'
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּאֻמּוֹת עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת.
which is not so among the nations of the idolaters.

כִּי חֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים אֵצֶל רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד575 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned" (Joshua 7:11). R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is an Israelite. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is still myrtle and people call it myrtle. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious. עַמּוּד א) "אָסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי הִיצֵי",
For the sins of Israel are termed by our Rabbis of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 44a) 'a myrtle standing among thorns,'
שֶׁהֵם רַק סוֹבְבִים אוֹתוֹ אֲבָל שָׁרְשׁוֹ אֵין כָּךְ,
which merely encircle it while its core root remains pristine;
וְהוּא כְּמוֹ "כּוֹפִין עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר רוֹצֶה אָנִי",
and it is analogous to 'we coerce him until he says: I am willing,'

דְּיָדוּעַ טַעַם הָרַמְבַּ"ם (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ב מֵהִלְכוֹת גֵּרוּשִׁין576 Mishneh Torah, Divorce 2:20 — One whom the law requires to be compelled to divorce his wife, and who does not wish to divorce her — the Jewish court in every place and at every time beats him until he says “I am willing,” and he writes the bill of divorce, and it is valid. Why is this bill of divorce not void — for he is under duress, whether at the hands of gentiles or at the hands of Jews? Because we call a man coerced only when he is pressed and driven to do a thing which the Torah does not oblige him to do — as one who is beaten until he sells or gives. But one whose evil inclination has overpowered him to annul a commandment or to commit a transgression, and who is beaten until he does what he is obliged to do or until he distances himself from what is forbidden — he is not under duress from us; rather he has brought the duress upon himself by his own evil intent. Therefore this man, who does not wish to divorce — since he wishes to be of Israel, and wishes to perform all the commandments and to keep far from transgressions, and it is only his inclination that has overpowered him — once he is beaten until his inclination is weakened and he says “I am willing,” he has already divorced willingly. And why is this bill of divorce not void, seeing that he is coerced, whether by gentiles or by Jews? Because we call a man coerced only when he is pressed and forced to do a thing that the Torah does not obligate him to do. But one whose evil inclination has overpowered him to annul a commandment or to commit a transgression, and who was beaten until he did what he is obligated to do, or until he withdrew from what is forbidden — he is not coerced by them; rather, he has coerced himself by his own evil intent. Therefore this man who does not wish to divorce, since he wishes to be of Israel and wishes to perform all the commandments and to keep far from transgressions, and it is his inclination that has overpowered him — once he has been beaten until his inclination is weakened and he says "I consent," he has already divorced willingly. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 21): This follows the Rambam's reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing'": in the depths of the heart everyone wishes to heed the words of the Sages and only the leaven in the dough holds him back, so once he has been beaten and his inclination has weakened until he also says with his mouth, "I am willing," it suffices. So too, intention not for the sake of Heaven in a Jew comes only from the inclination, which accustoms him to seek his own benefit in everything, whereas the depths of the heart of the children of Israel are solely for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): That the name Israel can never be uprooted from a Jew seems to take away his free choice; this is the mountain held over them at Sinai, that he will be Israel against his will. But when they accepted [the Torah] again in the days of Ahasuerus it was clarified that this is not coercion, for at his root he truly chooses the Blessed One of his own will; as the Rambam wrote on the reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing,'" even if he is wicked and unwilling to accept the words of the Sages, his true will is not so. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): "All Israel have a share in the World to Come" includes even the wicked of Israel, for all are called righteous, just as all Israel are called circumcised even one who is in fact uncircumcised. One who is wicked in deed is so only because of the evil inclination and not from his heart, as it says, "It is revealed and known before You that our will [is to do Your will]," and as is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing.'" Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 3): There was a "great protest" against the Torah [since it was accepted under coercion] until they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus, when the Blessed One clarified that the point of the heart is truly good; consequently there is no "great protest," as is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing'": since in truth he wants it, it is not called duress, and so they were already acquired as a people and for eternal life. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Even the wicked and the sinners of Israel have this: although they sin through the incitement of the inclination, the leaven in the dough, in their true will there is this point, that they can abandon all the desires of this world for the will of the Blessed One. That is why "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing'" is effective, as is known from the Rambam's reason; and this is an inheritance from our father Isaac. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 7): Therefore, although he has sinned, he is still Israel in every respect, for all of it comes only from the leaven in the dough and not from the truth of the point of the heart, as is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing,'" which holds even for one who apostatizes from the whole Torah out of spite. This stems from the root of Jewish holiness that was fixed as a lasting acquisition in the heart of all Israel at the giving of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from a Jew however many his sins: even when he multiplies sins, it all comes from the leaven in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness, as it says, "It is revealed and known before You that our will...," and similarly in the Rambam on the reason for "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing.'" Therefore [the Sages] compared [the sinner of Israel] to a myrtle standing among reeds: the sins are only in the reeds surrounding the myrtle, while the myrtle itself has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): As is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing,'" what in the heart is unwilling is so only because of the evil inclination. On this it says, "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable [ratzon]," and I received the interpretation that even when one sees that his heart's will is not yet in it, speaking good with the mouth, which is called "the lips of the righteous," helps to teach and to draw the will into the heart as well. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Mishlei 10): "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable [ratzon]": as the Sages said, "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing,'" that is, through his speech he brings the will into his heart as well. What he says with his lips while his heart is not yet clarified helps him to clarify his heart toward the will wholeheartedly: for instance, when anger at his fellow sprouts in his heart, his counsel is first to speak kindly to his fellow even if not wholeheartedly, and by this he gradually brings love into his heart in place of hatred. Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 57): When a person shortchanges himself in divine service, this is "the buyer was defrauded," and a buyer defrauded by less than a sixth is like what the Talmud says, "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing'": in truth the depth of the heart of Israel is drawn after the will of the Blessed One, but on the outer garment there are impediments that keep him from serving God, and he is shortchanged by them. Yet this is only less than a sixth, which is wholly waived [and the sale stands].).
following the known rationale of Maimonides (end of chapter 2 of the Laws of Divorce).
כָּךְ מַה שֶּׁעוֹשֶׂה לְכַוָּנָה אַחֶרֶת,
Similarly, whatever an Israelite performs with an ulterior motive,
דְּמִתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ הַיְנוּ הַתּוֹכִיּוּת וּפְנִימִיּוּת הוּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
the inner core and essence beneath the 'not for its own sake' is truly for Heaven's sake,
וּלְכָךְ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר,
and therefore he is a completely righteous person,
כְּמוֹ דְּהַגֵּט כָּשֵׁר וְנֶחְשָׁב מֵרְצוֹנוֹ הַגָּמוּר,
just as the bill of divorce is valid and counted as his genuine will,
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שָׁרְשָׁם כָּךְ.
unlike the nations of the world whose fundamental root is selfish.
וְזֶהוּ שַׁבָּת אוֹת וּבְרִית בֵּינִי וְגוֹמֵר, וְגוֹי שֶׁשָּׁבַת וְכוּלֵי,
And this explains: 'Shabbat is a sign and covenant between Me, etc.,' and 'a gentile who observed Shabbat is liable, etc.,'
כִּי נִיחַת יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא בְּהֶעְדֵּר הַפְּעֻלָּה וּבִטּוּל כָּל הַכֹּחוֹת לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַד שֶׁאֵין לוֹ כְּלוּם.
for the rest of Israel is in the cessation of action and the nullification of all faculties to Hashem until one possesses nothing.
אֲבָל נִיחַת אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הוּא רַק כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ,
The rest of the nations, however, exists only when one retains ego;
וְהַיֵּשׁוּת הוּא מִצַּד הַפְּעֻלָּה וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
and individual existence is rooted in action and effort,
וְהֶעְדֵּר כֹּחוֹתָיו הוּא מִיתָתוֹ,
and the surrender of his faculties is his demise,
דְּקִיּוּמוֹ הוּא רַק הִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת בְּכֹחַ.
since his entire subsistence is merely submergence in individual force.
וּמַה שֶּׁבִּזְמַן שַׁבָּת וִימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הוּא בְּנַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגֵרִים,
And that which divides Shabbat and the weekdays parallels the division in souls between Israel and converts,

שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין577 Kiddushin 70b — Rabbah bar Rav Huna said: This is a superiority that Israel has over converts. For of Israel it is written, “And I shall be to them a God and they shall be to Me a people”; but of converts it is written, “Who is this that has pledged his heart to approach Me, says the Lord — and you shall be to Me a people, and I shall be to you a God.” Rashi (s.v. "Of Israelites it is written"): "And I will be their God" — even though they are not yet His people; and since He draws them near, they come to be His people. Converts, however, are not drawn near from Heaven unless they first draw themselves near by becoming good. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 70b): Israel derive by an unbroken chain from the First Cause; and just as they derive from the First Cause, so the First Cause is their God and seeks after them, for there is no cause without its effect. As a father seeks after his son, so does He seek after Israel, who are called sons because they are His effects essentially and from the first; but the convert, in whom this is not so, must cleave to Him, blessed be He, of himself. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 8): This is the distinction between Israel and converts of which they said in Kiddushin, "this is a further superiority": of Israel it is written first "And I will be their God" and afterwards "and they shall be My people," meaning that the Blessed One is their God perforce, whether they wish it or not — as at the giving of the Torah, when He held the mountain over them like a barrel, and likewise in the future, "with a strong hand … will I reign." This is only in Israel, by virtue of the holiness they have from birth from their fathers, which is not so with converts. (ע סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) הַחִלּוּק:
concerning which they stated in Kiddushin (70b end) the distinction:
דְּאֵלּוּ הַגֵּרִים בְּרֵישָׁא "וִהְיִיתֶם לִי לְעָם" וְכוּלֵי,
that converts are initially included under 'and you shall be My people, etc.,'
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָן דַּוְקָא בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יִכָּנוּ שֶׁבָּאִים לְהִתְגַּיֵּר.
since specifically through their active exertion do they become titled with the name of Israel when coming to convert.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מִלֵּדָה מִבֶּטֶן בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ,
Israel, by contrast, is from birth and the womb without human effort,

דַּאֲפִלּוּ חָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד עַמּוּד א578 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned" (Joshua 7:11). R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is Israel. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle standing among thorns, its name is still myrtle, and myrtle they call it. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious.).
such that 'even though he sinned, he remains Israel' (Sanhedrin 44a).
רַק מִצַּד עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
Only from the vantage point of this world is exertion primary,
שֶׁהָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נֶגֶד יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה,
for this world corresponds to the six working days,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה: "מִי שֶׁטָּרַח וְכוּלֵי579 Avodah Zarah 3a — They said before Him: Master of the Universe, give us the Torah anew and we shall perform it. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: Fools of the world! One who took trouble on the eve of the Sabbath eats on the Sabbath; one who took no trouble on the eve of the Sabbath — from where shall he eat on the Sabbath? Even so, I have one easy commandment, and sukkah is its name — go and perform it. At once each of them took and went and made a sukkah on his roof; and the Holy One, blessed be He, made the sun blaze upon them as at the summer solstice, and each of them kicked his sukkah and went out. Rashi: "On the eve of the Sabbath" means in this world. "On the top of his roof" — because they made most use of their roofs, which were not sloped. "Made the sun blaze [makdir]" is an expression of piercing: it bores through with the force of great heat, as in "one may cut through [makdirin] the hills" (Eruvin 58a), a matter of boring and cutting. Maharsha: Every sukkah is made for shade, to shield from the sun, and one may make its covering as thick as one likes and it is still valid; so He blazed the sun upon them until the covering's leaves withered. That is the force of "made blaze [makdir]" — that holes opened in the covering, and the sun tormented them through them. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a, s.v. "and sukkah is its name"): Since the nations claim to be fit for the Torah, which is intellectual and beyond nature, He gave them the commandment that shows a person going out of his nature: leaving his fixed, natural dwelling to sit in the shade of the sukkah. The nations, whose whole conduct is natural, cannot bear this and kick at it; Israel too are somewhat natural, for man is not an angel, and are exempt from the sukkah when it causes them suffering, yet they do not kick, for they desire and love to go beyond nature, only that at such times it is impossible for them. This shows that the Torah, the whole of which is beyond nature, is not fit for the nations at all. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a, s.v. "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat"): That is, this world is the physical world, which is always in potential, and therefore commandments and good deeds belong to it, for in it things go out from potential into actuality. But in the World to Come a person is already in actuality, and going out into actuality has no place there, since it is not physical; the World to Come is therefore cessation and rest. Hence he said that one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat, the day of action, will eat on Shabbat, the day of rest, on which nothing goes out into actuality — and so the commandments pertain to this world alone. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 25): Shabbat is [the day on which God Himself is one's light, needing no fire of fear]; nevertheless one must toil to cook the food on the eve of Shabbat, for "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, what will he eat on Shabbat?" and "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward": this light does not come to a person by itself. So too the Shabbat lamp must be lit from the eve of Shabbat, for on Shabbat there is no longer time to arouse fear, the day being entirely love and cleaving to God. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): This world is the world of toil, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat" refers to the world to come, the day that is entirely Shabbat, where there is no doing even of Torah and mitzvot, as they said, "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; and Shabbat is a semblance of the world to come, the time of the Blessed One's rest. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Sukkah): Shabbat alludes to the future, when there will be no labor, but only what a person acquired in this world through his deeds will then be fixed in his heart, according to how much he toiled in this world. Therefore all labors are forbidden on Shabbat in this world, and only what one toiled for on the eve of Shabbat does one eat on Shabbat. Beis Yaakov (Vayeishev 3): All the possession a person acquires for himself in the world of action comes only from performing the mitzvot, and clarity [of understanding] alone does not suffice; by this he acquires the life of the world to come, for this world is like the eve of Shabbat and the world to come like Shabbat, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will have what to eat on Shabbat." Tiferes Yosef (Shemini Atzeres 4): A person calls his labor "toil" only where he does not see its purpose; on Shabbat he attains the light of the Blessed One and recognizes that he attained it through the work of the six days. This is "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat": through the toil and labor he expended he attains this light, and so he recognizes retroactively that all the activity of the six weekdays was not futile toil for him either. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 18): In the future the nations will want to begin from the start, without first entering the gate of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Blessed One answers that this is impossible: "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat" means that had they first refined themselves to be included in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, within "every citizen in Israel" [which includes converts], they too could have kept the mitzvah of sukkah. But to begin now without that prior inclusion is impossible, for one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat has nothing to eat on Shabbat, and from where would he gain a share in the mitzvah of sukkah?",
as written at the beginning of Avodah Zarah: 'He who toiled, etc.,'
וְכָל הַמִּצְוֹת בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
and all commandments require exertion,
כִּי שַׁבָּת מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְבָּרְרוּ,
for Shabbat is a foretaste of the World to Come after souls have been clarified,
אֲבָל הַבֵּרוּר בְּנִצּוּחַ הַכֹּחוֹת הוּא בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת.
yet the clarification in subduing the forces occurs through active exertion.

דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים פז580 Pesachim 87b — R. Elazar said: The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would join them, as it is stated: "And I will sow her to Me in the land" (Hosea 2:25). Does a man sow a se'ah of grain for any purpose other than to bring in many kor? R. Yochanan said it is derived from here: "And I will have compassion upon her that had not received compassion" (ibid.). Maharsha: ["He exiled... only":] for had it been as punishment for their sin, He could have punished them with other things; rather, it was so that converts should be added to them — that is, to make the faith known among the other nations as well. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:77): The Sages said, "Israel was exiled only so as to add converts," for the exile is because the Blessed One wished that even in dark places, in the concealment of His countenance, they should find His truth and recognize Him even "from behind," as it were; and from this aspect converts too are added, yet they are nevertheless hard for Israel "like a scab." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 10): The Land, being soft and not rocky, yields more fruit, as the Sages expounded "And I will sow her to Me in the land," that through sowing in the holiness of the Land comes the vast increase; and "they were exiled only so as to add converts" means that each gentile has a particular power that he cannot change at all, nor can the convert change it. What is added in exile is that Israel absorbs the power of the lands of the nations, the particular obstinacy and heart of stone of each place, and by clarifying that in that power they are not obstinate like the nations but can change it for the glory of Heaven as the Blessed One wills, converts are added: the power of the nations' heart of stone is also granted to join Israel and be called by the name of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Parah 3): The Midrash's "Israel from the nations" does not mean their descent from Terah, which is already covered by "Abraham from Terah," but refers to "The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel only so that converts would be added to them," which was explained to mean not actual converts but the holy sparks and vitality within the nations, as in "and You give life to them all," which are brought out through the exiles. All the nations have holy sparks from which their life derives, and for this reason exile among all seventy nations was needed. Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 10): Through the length of their wanderings Israel brings out further holiness that is found [among the nations], as it says, "The Holy One, blessed be He, did righteousness with Israel by scattering them among the nations," and "He exiled Israel among the nations only so that converts would be added to them." The matter is that every nation was created for His glory, that the glory of Heaven should come forth from it, only they are its opposite; by entering among the nations Israel clarifies how the glory of Heaven is built even from them, and in this lies great preciousness: to understand and bring forth the glory of Heaven even from its opposite. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 17): The main purpose of the exile is as the Talmud says on "the righteousness of His scattering in Israel": the Holy One, blessed be He, did righteousness with Israel so that converts would be added to them, like one who sows with a scattering hand, the whole aim of whose intention is that a crop should grow from it. So too, in the future the Blessed One will show that the aim of the exile was that souls be added to Israel, and that not a single individual was cast away. עַמּוּד ב): "לֹא גָּלוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא כְּדֵי לְהוֹסִיף גֵּרִים",
Hence they said (Pesachim 87b): 'Israel was exiled solely to add converts,'

וְאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּרִים לֶעָתִיד (יְבָמוֹת כד581 Yevamot 24b — Our Rabbis taught: Converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah. Similarly, they accepted no converts in the days of David, nor in the days of Solomon. R. Eliezer said: What is the verse? "Behold, one may surely sojourn [as a convert] when I am not [with you]; whoever sojourns with you [now, in your poverty] shall settle beside you" (Isaiah 54:15) — but the other [who comes later], no. Rashi: "Behold, one may surely sojourn": one who comes to convert may sojourn "when I am not" — while I am not with you, let him convert, that is, at the present time. "Whoever sojourns with you": in your poverty, as stated. "Shall settle beside you" (lit. "shall fall upon you"): in the World to Come; "fall" means "rest," as in "he fell [i.e., settled] in the presence of all his brethren" (Genesis 25:18) and "a thousand shall fall at your side" (Psalms 91:7). Tosafos (s.v. "nor in the days of David, nor in the days of Solomon"): Ittai the Gittite, and Pharaoh's daughter in Solomon's days, pose no difficulty, for the only reason [converts were refused then] was the king's table, and these had no need of it; but it is difficult from what we say below (79a) about the Gibeonites, that in David's days a hundred and fifty thousand converts were added to Israel. One may answer that they converted of their own accord, as we find in the days of Mordecai and Esther, "And many of the people of the land became Jews"; and some texts read that they did not accept converts in the days of David and Solomon, but these became converts who attached themselves [unaccepted]. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 46): "Whoever sojourns with you" in your poverty, he "shall fall to you," but otherwise not. Thus you see that converts are not accepted when the days of good arrive, because one does not make a beginning in good days, for in such a case a man certainly serves God, blessed be He, because he sees the good; therefore his beginning must come before, and then he acquires the World to Come even in the good days. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 2): Sin and the serpent's filth come from the Blessed One so that through them there should be additions, absorbed from within the husk into holiness, as in "Israel was exiled only so that converts would be added to them." And the Sages read "whoever sojourns with you [shall fall to you]" as "in your poverty," for the main addition of converts comes specifically in Israel's poverty, through the sins and the serpent's filth, and not in the time to come. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): The love of Torah is revealed most in converts: Israel were brought out of bondage and drawn near by the Holy One, blessed be He, but the convert left the tranquility of this world and the license he had among the nations to follow his desire, and came of his own will to fence himself in and cleave to Israel, afflicted, lowly and downtrodden in this world. For only "in your poverty shall he fall to you," and converts were not accepted in the days of David and Solomon, nor one who converts out of love for some thing; only for love of the Torah does he draw near and enter under the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayakhel 2): The law regarding the mixed multitude was that of "converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah; similarly, they did not accept converts in the days of David or Solomon," that is, because their intention is not desirable for the sake of Heaven. Yet after the fact, as Rambam writes, once they have converted the great court does not reject them, since they have immersed, but neither does it draw them near until their end is seen. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): Of the future it is said that [Esau] will wrap himself in his tallis, and he will surely think then that he truly wishes it and is not merely deceiving; but in truth converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah, because they come then only out of love of reward or fear of punishment. Beis Yaakov (Vayeira 30): In the future the world will be conducted by the attribute of Isaac, as shown by "converts are not accepted in the days of the Messiah" and "each righteous man has a dwelling of his own": that is, then the world will be conducted by the measure of "what is mine is mine," each one holding back from yielding his portion, as Isaac restrained himself from bestowing where it is not the will of the Blessed One. Only in the future, after the clarifications are complete, will the attribute of Isaac govern; for now, in this world, a person must conduct himself by the attribute of kindness. עַמּוּד ב),
and converts will not be accepted in the Messianic future (Yevamot 24b),
שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם לְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם, רַק מִי שֶׁמִּלֵּדָה וּמִבֶּטֶן כָּךְ.
for there is no place then for human striving, only for one who is so from birth and the womb.
אֲבָל הַגָּלֻיּוֹת שֶׁהוּא לְבָרֵר נִצּוּחַ הַכֹּחוֹת כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
Yet the exiles, which serve to clarify the conquest of the forces as mentioned above,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לְגֵרִים,
through this open a place for converts,
שֶׁהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת יֵשׁ גַּם לַגּוֹיִם
for exertion belongs to gentiles as well,
וְיוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ לְהִתְכַּנּוֹת בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל.
and a person can attain through his exertion to be titled with the name of Israel.
כִּי מִצַּד עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָעִקָּר הוּא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
For from the perspective of this world the primary focus is exertion,
וְזֶהוּ הֲכָנָה לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
and this serves as the preparation for the World to Come,
כִּי מִי שֶׁלֹּא טָרַח וְכוּלֵי;
for he who did not toil, etc.;

וַאֲפִלּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת וְכוּלֵי (סַנְהֶדְרִין לז582 Sanhedrin 37a — Reish Lakish said: From here — "Your temples are like a pomegranate split open" (Song of Songs 6:7): even the empty ones among you are as full of commandments as a pomegranate is of seeds. Cf. Eruvin 19a, where Reish Lakish speaks of "the sinners of Israel, who are full of commandments like a pomegranate." Maharsha: Reish Lakish reads the whole verse [Song of Songs 4:3] as speaking of the niddah: "your lips are like a thread of scarlet" are the bloodstains, red as scarlet, and "your speech is comely" means that although all closeness is forbidden, speech with her is permitted — or that she may still adorn herself in her days of niddah, as R. Akiva holds, lest she become repugnant to her husband.
