רָצָה לוֹמַר כְּנַף דְּצִיצִית הַמְּעוֹרֵר הַזְּכִירָה.
meaning the corner of the tzitzit which awakens remembrance.

וְזֶה הָיָה בַּתְּחִלָּה כְּשֶׁהָיָה רַחְמָן עַל הָאַכְזָרִים (קֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ז פָּסוּק יז608 Kohelet Rabbah 7:16 — R. Shimon ben Lakish says: Whoever becomes merciful where he ought to be cruel will in the end become cruel where he ought to be merciful. And whence do we know that he became cruel where he ought to have been merciful? As it is stated, "And Nov, the city of the priests, he smote with the edge of the sword" — was Nov, then, like the seed of Amalek? And the Rabbis say: Whoever becomes merciful where he ought to be cruel, in the end the attribute of justice strikes him, as it is stated, "And Saul died, and his three sons." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 28): The refinement of every trait is through its opposite: one merciful by nature is refined by being cruel to Amalek and the like among the enemies of God, as it is written, "Whoever is merciful to the cruel will in the end become cruel to the merciful," for such mercy is in truth cruelty. One who shows mercy only from his inborn nature and not for the sake of Heaven is merciful even where it is fitting to be cruel, and so, one transgression drawing another, in the end it becomes clear, Heaven forbid, that he is merciful only where there is no need and cruel where mercy is needed.),
And this occurred initially when he was compassionate toward the cruel (Kohelet Rabbah 7:17),
וּבַסּוֹף כְּשֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אַכְזָר עַל הָרַחְמָנִים,
and in the end, when he turned cruel against the merciful,
כָּרַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּנַף מְעִילוֹ גַּם כֵּן לְרֶמֶז זֶה.
King David, peace be upon him, cut off the skirt of his robe likewise as an allusion to this.
כִּי זֶהוּ כּוֹפֵל: "זָכוֹר וְגוֹמֵר לֹא תִשְׁכָּח",
For this is why Scripture duplicates: 'Remember, etc., do not forget' (Deuteronomy 25:17, 19),
כִּי עֲבֵירָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה לַעֲשׂוֹת בַּפֹּעַל,
because 'a transgression drags another transgression' to be committed in physical action,
דְּעָבַר וְשָׁנָה הֻתְּרָה לוֹ.
for once a person transgresses and repeats it, it appears to him as permitted.
רַק הַהַתְחָלָה הוּא בְּהִזְדַּמְּנוּת,
Only the inception occurs through sudden opportunity,

כְּטַעַם (סֻכָּה נב609 Sukkah 52b — Rava said: At first [Scripture] calls it a wayfarer, then it calls it a guest, and finally it calls it a man, as it is said, "And there came a wayfarer to the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd to prepare for the guest," and it is written, "And he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him." Rashi: "Wayfarer": one who passes him on the road and does not lodge with him; "guest": a lodger; "man": the master of the house. "And there came a wayfarer": this is said of David and Bathsheba, the prophet speaking to David of the evil inclination that had come upon him. Maharsha (s.v. "it calls it a wayfarer"): The incident itself follows this pattern: at first, "David arose ... and walked about on the roof" — it is called "wayfarer," as explained in Perek Chelek on this verse, where Satan appeared to him in the likeness of a bird; then, "he took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her ... and she returned to her house" — it is called "guest"; and afterwards, when Uriah was killed at David's command and he took her as his wife, it is called "man." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 2): At man's creation deficiency clung to him, but not wholly, for were it wholly attached to him man could not exist at all; so it is called a "wayfarer," who passes by a man and is joined to him only somewhat, without lodging with him. If a man is drawn after it, the deficiency clings to him further and it is called a "guest," who lodges with him; and if he is drawn after it still more, it is called "man," that is, the master of the house, for then the man is not merely joined to evil but is himself deficient and evil. עַמּוּד ב):
mirroring the concept (Sukkah 52b):
בַּתְּחִלָּה קְרָאוֹ "הֵלֶךְ" שֶׁהוּא מִקְרָאִי,
initially Scripture terms the evil inclination a 'wayfarer' who arrives by chance,
וּפַעַם ג' דְּהֻתְּרָה לוֹ הוּא "אִישׁ" וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת עַצְמוֹ.
and on the third occasion when it becomes deemed permitted, he is called a 'man' and the master of the house itself.
וְעַל יְדֵי זְכִירָה בַּתְּחִלָּה
And through mindful remembrance at the beginning,
לֹא בָּא לִידֵי שִׁכְחָה שֶׁבַּסּוֹף.
one does not arrive at the total forgetfulness of the end.

וְכֵן בְּפָרָשַׁת צִיצִית כָּפַל: "וּזְכַרְתֶּם וְגוֹמֵר לְמַעַן תִּזְכְּרוּ וְגוֹמֵר610 Numbers 15:39-40 — “And it shall be for you as fringes, and you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them, and not stray after your heart and after your eyes, which lead you astray — so that you shall remember and do all My commandments, and be holy to your God.” Rashi: The fringes remind one of all the commandments because the letters of "tzitzit" have the numerical value six hundred, and with the eight threads and the five knots this comes to six hundred and thirteen. "You shall not stray (תתורו) after your heart" has the sense of "from scouting out (מתור) the land": the heart and the eyes are the body's spies, procuring its sins for it — the eye sees, the heart covets, and the body commits the transgression. Ramban: Scripture says "you shall not stray after your heart" to warn a man not to err through it [the blue thread, which alludes to the all-inclusive attribute]. Hence the Sages expounded: "after your heart" — this is heresy; "after which you go astray" — this is idolatry; that is, one should not let the blue thread draw him into heretical or idolatrous speculation, but rather "it shall all be for you as fringes, and you shall look upon it and remember."",
And so in the section of tzitzit Scripture duplicates: 'and you shall remember, etc., that you may remember, etc.',
וְכַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דִּכְמוֹ כֵן מִצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה.
and as mentioned above, just so does a mitzvah drag another mitzvah in its wake.
וְהִנֵּה שָׁאוּל בֶּאֱמֶת זָכוּר הָיָה,
Now Saul was in truth mindful,
רַק שֶׁחָמַל וּכְסָבוּר עוֹשֶׂה מִצְוָה,
except that he had compassion, presuming that he was performing a mitzvah;
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן אֶחָד דְּהַתְחָלַת כְּנִיסַת הַיֵּצֶר
and this too is one of the initial entries of the evil inclination,
דְּמַרְאֶה שֶׁזֶּה מִצְוָה,
whereby he portrays that an act is a mitzvah,
וּבַסּוֹף נַעֲשָׂה אַכְזָר וְכוּלֵי חָשַׁב גַּם כֵּן זֶה מִצְוָה.
and in the end when he became cruel, etc., he likewise rationalized that to be a mitzvah.
וְעִנְיַן טָעוּתוֹ,
And the nature of his error,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (גִּטִּין מג611 Gittin 43a — Rabba bar Rav Huna then set an interpreter before him and expounded: "And let this stumbling block be under your hand" — a man does not stand upon words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them. Although they said that one who betroths half a woman, she is not betrothed, still a woman who is half maidservant and half free who was betrothed, her betrothal is a valid betrothal. Rashi (s.v. "and let this stumbling block be under your hand"): He set up an interpreter before him in order to expound a second time, and he opened from the verse, which was said of the men of Jerusalem when Torah had ceased among them, so that they would say to one another, "You have a cloak, be our chief" — that is, matters covered over like your cloak, in which you are expert, tell them to us and be our chief. "And let this stumbling block be under your hand" means words of Torah, upon whose truth a man does not stand until he has stumbled in them by ruling in error and is put to shame, and then he sets his heart to it and understands. So I too stumbled in my ruling, and therefore I retract. Maharsha: When he first taught this ruling it is not said that he set an interpreter before him. Perhaps an interpreter was set up only for the exposition of a verse that was published to the many, as here with "and let this stumbling block be under your hand," whereas earlier he had published to the many only the ruling itself. עַמּוּד א):
is like what they taught (Gittin 43a):
"אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל",
'A person does not stand firmly upon words of Torah unless he stumbles first,'
וּלְכָךְ בִּיאַת עֲמָלֵק הֲכָנָה לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה,
and for this reason the assault of Amalek was the prerequisite preparation for the Giving of the Torah,
כִּי עִנְיַן עֲמָלֵק הוּא הַמִּכְשׁוֹל שֶׁאֵֵרַע חֵטְא בְּהִזְדַּמְּנוּת שֶׁלֹּא בְּמִתְכַּוֵּן,
for the archetype of Amalek is the stumbling block wherein sin occurs through incidental circumstance without premeditation,
וְכַאֲשֶׁר מִתְעוֹרֵר מִזֶּה עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
and when a person awakens from this, he stands firmly upon the words of Torah.
וְנִמְצָא לִכְאוֹרָה הוּא לְצֹרֶךְ,
Thus it seemingly appears to serve a necessary constructive purpose,

וְזֶהוּ "וַיַּחְמֹל וְגוֹמֵר עַל מֵיטַב וְגוֹמֵר612 I Samuel 15:7-9 — “And Shaul smote Amalek from Chavilah as far as Shur, which faces Egypt. And he seized Agag king of Amalek alive, and all the people he destroyed by the edge of the sword. But Shaul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fatlings and the lambs, and all that was good, and they were unwilling to destroy them; but every despised and worthless thing they destroyed.” Rashi: "And the seconds" — the word has no parallel; they are the well-fed beasts, so called, I say, as in "double money" [Genesis 43:12], because such an animal is doubled in flesh and fat. "Despised and worthless" — this is the same as "despised," the mem being an added letter. Radak: "From Havilah as you come to Shur" — perhaps [Amalek] dwelt there together with the sons of Ishmael, or took the land from them. "And the seconds" — Jonathan renders it as though the letters were transposed, "and the fat ones": the beasts that grow fat of themselves on their pasture, as against those fattened by man; and it may also be explained as the yearling lambs. Metzudas Dovid: "As you come" — until you come to Shur, the verse speaking as though to a man who knows the place. "And he spared" — they had pity on Agag and on the best of the flock and on everything good they found there, and would not destroy them; they destroyed only the worthless livestock. Malbim: "And Saul spared" — to spare is not the same as to pity or to have compassion: those are movements of feeling, which a man may feel and still carry out God's command, but sparing is a judgment of the mind, that it is not right or just to destroy the thing at all — and that is what he was warned against, for it sets a man's own wisdom against God. This was Saul's failure, and from that judgment came the deed, "and they were not willing to destroy them": they left the best and the middling and destroyed only the poorest.",
and this explains 'and he spared, etc., the best of, etc.' (I Samuel 15:9) –
פֵּרוּשׁ שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם גַּם כֵּן מֵיטָב וְאֵיזֶה דָּבָר טוֹב
meaning he reasoned that they also contained a choice element and some good,
"לִזְבֹּחַ לַה'" – פֵּרוּשׁ לִהְיוֹת הַכַּוָּנָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם.
'to sacrifice unto Hashem' – meaning his intent was for the sake of Heaven.
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל מִדָּה רָעָה אֵיזֶה דָּבָר טוֹב,
And along the lines that within every negative trait there resides some good,
שֶׁהֵם הַגֵּרִים שֶׁבְּכָל הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת.
namely the proselytes who emerge from all the idolaters.
וְלָכֵן גֵּר עֲמָלֵקִי הָרַג לְשָׁאוּל,
Therefore an Amalekite convert was the one who killed Saul,

וְאָמְרוּ בַּמְּכִילְתָּא (סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח613 Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Amalek 2:50 — R. Eliezer says: The Omnipresent swore by the throne — if one of all the nations of the world comes to convert, Israel shall accept him; but from the house of Amalek they shall not accept him. As it is stated: "And David said to the young man who told him: Where are you from? And he said: I am the son of an Amalekite convert." At that moment David recalled what had been said to Moses — that if one of all the nations of the world comes to convert, Israel shall accept him, but from the house of Amalek they shall not accept him. As it is stated: "And David said to him: Your blood be upon your own head, for your own mouth has testified against you." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 20): Among the nations, those with more connection to holiness are the worse and hold a greater force of impurity, so that one must keep further from them; and Amalek has more connection to holiness than any nation — sprung from two of the patriarchs and matriarchs, his mother Timna having gone round the doors of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob seeking to convert, and his father Eliphaz raised in Isaac's lap. Therefore he was distanced more than all the nations, his name to be blotted out from under the heavens, and the Mekhilta says that no convert is accepted from Amalek. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): I have explained elsewhere that in my view it is clear that [the descendants of Haman who studied Torah] came through one of the seed of Amalek coming upon a Jewish woman, since converts are not accepted from Amalek; rather, it happened through a woman taken captive among them, or otherwise by force. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 5): Apart from [a child born to a Jewish woman forced by one of Haman's seed], no convert is accepted from Amalek, as the Mekhilta says, for once the name Amalek has come upon them in actuality there is no trace of the moisture of holiness in them: his whole root is the evil latent and hidden, to be drawn into action, and were there room to turn him to good he would not be evil at all. A nation whose root of evil lies in outward action can be transformed, but Amalek himself cannot be transformed at all, for the essence does not change, only its outward extension. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 2): In Egypt the task was to extract the holy sparks, and many of the mixed multitude were fit to cleave to Israel; not so Amalek, for the Mekhilta says that the Blessed One swore that no convert would be accepted from Amalek, and likewise the command was to destroy "from ox to sheep." As for "of Haman's descendants studied Torah in Bnei Brak," though converts are not accepted from Amalek, it seems that Rav Shmuel bar Shilat descended from one of them who came upon a Jewish woman, and so issued from Haman unintentionally. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): Of Amalek it is written "you shall blot out," and the Sages said in the Mekhilta that converts are not accepted from Amalek; yet "of Haman's descendants taught children in Jerusalem," so it must have come about through a gentile of his descendants coming upon a Jewish woman, for the offspring is fit and is a Jew, though he is also called the son of the gentile. Absorbing anything from Amalek is possible only in this way, by force and without intent. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 264): Every evil trait includes some good, since it is also set within Israel, and from its good side come the pious of the nations; but the only good in mockery is the mocking of idolatry, which belongs to this world alone. In the future, when the evil inclination is abolished and there is no place for idolatry, there is no place for mockery at all — no remnant of it in the World to Come and no turning into "a clear language," only "you shall blot out" — as the Sages said in the Mekhilta, that no convert is accepted from Amalek. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): Hence the Mekhilta says that converts are not accepted from Amalek, for he is the root of evil in which there is no good; even when he comes to convert and says he wishes to be good, it is only a "spreading out of the hooves" [the pig's display of a false sign of purity], which is the root of Esau.):
and they said in the Mekhilta (end of Parashat Beshalach):
בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה נִזְכַּר דָּוִד דְּאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּר מֵעֲמָלֵק.
at that very moment David recalled that we do not accept a convert from Amalek.
וְהַיְנוּ אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה דְּרָאָה עֹנֶשׁ שָׁאוּל עַל דָּבָר זֶה
That is, the very moment he witnessed Saul's punishment on this account,
נִזְכַּר בִּזְכִירָה גְּמוּרָה
he recalled with complete clarity
דְּבֶאֱמֶת אֵין דָּבָר טוֹב בַּעֲמָלֵק לִקְלֹטוֹ מִדַּעַת יִשְׂרָאֵל,
that in truth there is no good in Amalek to be absorbed through Israel's conscious initiative,
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁיְּקַבְּלוּהוּ.
meaning that they should willingly accept him.
כִּי וַדַּאי הַכְּתוּבִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ "עַל מֵיטַב וְגוֹמֵר" לֹא דִּבְּרוּ שֶׁקֶר
For surely the verses declaring 'the best, etc.' did not utter falsehood,
וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ מֵיטָב,
and there indeed is a choice element within him,

וּכְמַאֲמַר זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (גִּטִּין נז614 Gittin 57b — Some of Haman's descendants taught Torah in Bnei Brak; some of Sisera's descendants taught children in Jerusalem; some of Sennacherib's descendants taught Torah in public — who were they? Shemaya and Avtalyon. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 7): What is recounted here of the wicked whose seed converted within Israel and taught Torah in public is a wondrous thing. For when the wicked are extreme in wickedness and possess very great power, as these men did, it is impossible that their power was not joined to a higher power, the power of the Blessed One — only that with them it stood in impurity. But with the sons, once they converted, that power was refined and purified and made white, and therefore their sons were great men who taught Torah in public. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:135): None of these three gifts flows to the nations except through Israel: Haman's wealth came because he issued from the power of Saul, who let Agag live, and Saul's rectification came through [Haman's] descendants who learned Torah in Bnei Brak. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Saul's compassion was not, Heaven forbid, of an evil kind; he sensed something good in [Agag], as the Sages said, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in public" — namely Rav Shmuel bar Shilat. It is clear to me that this came about through one of the seed of Amalek coming upon a daughter of Israel, since converts are not accepted from Amalek, and the child is fit; yet he is still called a descendant of Haman, just as the Torah calls [the blasphemer] "the son of an Egyptian man." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 5): "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah": for the commandments of the Torah one needs faith in free choice, which lies in man's hand and is the opposite of [Divine] knowledge. Since some measure of the withdrawal of knowledge [that is Haman's root] is of use for words of Torah and the fulfilment of the commandments, Saul thought this was a root that must not be destroyed — it was this that he pitied, and from this side came [Haman's] descendants who learned Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 2): As I heard on "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah": it came about because Saul let Agag live that night, when Agag grieved that his seed would be cut off, and in reward Haman issued from him. And I heard that such grief over one's seed is the yearning of the seed of Israel — the nations do not grieve at all over the extinction of their line — and it came to Agag from the root within him of Haman's descendants who would emerge and cleave to Israel [which is why they are called by Haman's name]. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 2): One must ask how "To the sinner He gives the task of gathering and amassing, to give to the one who is good" can be said of Haman, since nothing may be taken from Amalek. But it is as the Sages said, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak" — namely Rav Shmuel bar Shilat; and although converts are not accepted from Amalek, it appears that Rav Shmuel bar Shilat came from one of them who came upon a daughter of Israel, and so issued from Haman unwittingly. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The feminine aspect of Amalek can be absorbed [into holiness] only in this way: of Amalek it is written "you shall blot out," and converts are not accepted from it, yet some of Haman's descendants taught children in Jerusalem — so it must have been that a gentile of his descendants came upon a daughter of Israel, for the child is fit and is an Israelite, though he is still called the son of the gentile, as the Torah says, "the son of an Egyptian man." Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Vayechi): Although Saul's compassion on Agag was reckoned to him as a sin, the Blessed One nonetheless intended that a good thought remain from that act, as the Gemara says, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak"; through this Saul's intention was made clear — that he meant to bring out the good and the holiness that was in Agag. Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Ta'anis 2): From the side of the Blessed One everything was created only for the purpose of good, and the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing in vain — to the point that the Sages said, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak; some of Sisera's descendants learned Torah in Jerusalem." Sod Yesharim (Parashas Zachor 7): In truth, all the grace that King Saul perceived in Agag is what the Gemara says, "Some of Haman's descendants learned Torah in Bnei Brak"; but Agag, on his own part, had to be nullified entirely. עַמּוּד ב):
and as the Sages of blessed memory stated (Gittin 57b):
"מִבְּנֵי בָּנָיו שֶׁל הָמָן לָמְדוּ תוֹרָה בִּבְנֵי בְּרַק",
'Descendants of Haman studied Torah in Bnei Brak,'
וְהֵם מִזֶּרַע אֲגָג,
and they descended from the seed of Agag,
וְזֶה הִרְגִּישׁ שָׁאוּל.
and this potential Saul intuitively sensed.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: "שְׁמֹעַ מִזֶּבַח טוֹב וְגוֹמֵר" (שְׁמוּאֵל א טו, כב),
And concerning this Samuel said: 'Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, etc.' (I Samuel 15:22),
הַכַּוָּנָה: הֲגַם דִּלְפִי דַּעַת שָׁאוּל זֶה מִצְוָה,
the meaning being: even though according to Saul's rationale this was a mitzvah,
עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "וְאָהַבְתָּ וְגוֹמֵר בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ" –
regarding this Scripture commands: 'and you shall love Hashem with all your soul' –
פֵּרוּשׁ לֹא בַּגּוּף לְבַד, רַק גַּם בַּנֶּפֶשׁ,
meaning not with the physical body alone, but also with your very soul,
שֶׁיַּסְכִּים גַּם לְאַבֵּד הַנֶּפֶשׁ בִּשְׁבִיל רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
that one consent even to lose his spiritual soul for the will of Hashem, blessed be He.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּאַף שֶׁמַּרְגִּישׁ שֶׁזֶּה מִצְוָה וְדָבָר גָּדוֹל לְקַיְּמוֹ לָזֶה דְּנָפֵיק מִנֵּיהּ
That is: even though he senses that it is a mitzvah and a magnificent deed to preserve the one destined to emerge from him

[בְּאוֹתוֹ לַיְלָה מִסְּתָמָא, שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ615 Megillah 12b-13a — Rava said: The Assembly of Israel said it from the other side — See what a Judean did to me, and what a Benjaminite repaid me. “What a Judean did to me” — that David did not kill Shimi, from whom Mordechai descended, whom Haman envied. “And what a Benjaminite repaid me” — that Shaul did not kill Agag, from whom Haman descended, who afflicted Israel. Rashi (s.v. "on the other side"): As a cry [of complaint], and not as praise: a man of Judah and a man of Benjamin caused me this suffering. Rashi (s.v. "that David did not kill Shimi"): Who was liable to death. Maharsha (s.v. "the Assembly of Israel said on the other side"): The expression "what a Benjaminite repaid me" seems imprecise, for what repayment is there here? The sense is that at first glance the Judahite, David, did a good deed in not killing Shimi, from whom was born Mordechai, who brought the redemption through his prayer, and the Benjaminite, Mordechai, repaid and repaired what Shaul had spoiled in not killing Agag, as the Rabbis said above; but Rava says that it is not so. The Judahite repaired nothing by causing Mordechai to be born, for without Mordechai there would have been no calamity, since Haman was provoked only by Mordechai; and the Benjaminite did not repay what Shaul spoiled, for had Shaul killed Agag, Haman would not have been born. Maharal (Ohr Chadash, Esther 2:5): Rava holds that the redemption came only by virtue of Israel as a whole, who were fit for it, and not by virtue of the tribes, for from the side of the tribes there was rather a predisposition to the calamity. Judah is the tribe to which rule belongs and which seeks to rule, and so Mordechai, as a man of Judah, would not submit to Haman, which provoked Haman to seek to rule over him; while Benjamin, the smallest of the tribes, has no great share in rule, so that Shaul, a Benjaminite, did not prevail over Agag to kill him but let him live. Thus the tribes, on the contrary, were the cause of Haman's opposition, and the redemption came from the Holy One, blessed be He, who redeemed them from his hand. (מְגִלָּה יג עַמּוּד א): "מַה שִּׁלֵּם לִי וְכוּלֵי"],
(presumably during that fateful night, concerning which they said (Megillah 13a): 'What did he pay me, etc.')
מִכָּל מָקוֹם "שְׁמֹעַ וְגוֹמֵר",
nonetheless, 'to obey is better, etc.,'
דְּיֵשׁ לִשְׁמֹעַ לִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
for one must obey the explicit will of Hashem, blessed be He,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מְבַטֵּל מִצְוָה וַעֲבוֹדָה וְתִקּוּן לַנֶּפֶשׁ.
even though through this he forfeits an apparent mitzvah, spiritual service, and soulful rectification.
וּמִי שֶׁבּוֹחֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה וּרְדִיפָה אַחַר מִצְוֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים
And one who focuses on his own spiritual service and pursuit of mitzvot and good deeds
יוּכַל לָבוֹא לִידֵי טָעוּת זֶה
can easily stumble into this error
שֶׁיַּסִּיתֶנּוּ הַיֵּצֶר רָע עַל עֲבֵירָה שֶׁהִיא מִצְוָה.
where the evil inclination seduces him concerning a transgression, framing it as a mitzvah.
אֲבָל מִי שֶׁמְּבַטֵּל רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לִרְצוֹת רַק רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
However, one who nullifies his personal will to desire nothing other than the will of Hashem, blessed be He,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לוֹ לִהְיוֹת בֶּאֱמֶת הַכֹּל כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
through this Hashem illuminates his path so that everything in truth aligns with the divine will,
וַאֲפִלּוּ כְּשֶׁשּׁוֹכֵחַ,
even when he forgets;

כְּטַעַם616 Pirkei Avot 2:4 — He used to say: Make His will your will, so that He may make your will His will. Nullify your will before His will, so that He may nullify the will of others before your will. (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ב מִשְׁנָה ד): "בַּטֵּל וְגוֹמֵר כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה וְגוֹמֵר",
mirroring the principle (Pirkei Avot 2:4): 'Nullify your will, etc., so that He may do your will, etc.,'

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (יוֹמָא כב617 Yoma 22b — Rav Huna said: How little does a man suffer or even feel it, when his Master helps him! Saul failed in one matter and it was counted against him; David in two, and they were not counted against him. What was Saul's one? The affair of Agag. What were David's two? The affair of Uriah, and the incitement [to number the people]. Rashi: "How little does a man feel …": how secure and confident, with no need to be troubled or to worry about any evil, is one whom the Holy One, blessed be He, aids! For we find that Saul stumbled in one [matter] and it was counted against him for ill, to penalize him with death and annul his kingship, while David stumbled in two and it was not counted against him for ill. "Of Uriah and of the incitement": that he was incited to count Israel at the end of his days, and so brought a pestilence upon them. Maharsha (s.v. "How little does a man feel"): The commentators already found this difficult (is there favoritism in the matter?) and answered that Saul's sin was graver because it touched on the kingship, whereas David's was a sin common to all Israel; but the words "a man whom his Master aids" do not imply this. Rather, it is to be explained by the dictum "one who comes to purify himself is aided from Heaven": David came to purify himself, confessing his sins and accepting sufferings upon himself, and so Heaven aided him to return in complete repentance, as several verses in Psalms make explicit; whereas we do not find that Saul confessed this sin before the Blessed One or accepted sufferings upon himself, and therefore it was counted against him. Maharsha (s.v. "It is the affair of Agag that Scripture records"): And if you ask why Saul is said to have stumbled in one matter, the affair of Agag, when Scripture has already recorded the burnt offering he brought before Samuel came, of which Samuel told him, "You have acted foolishly … and now your kingdom shall not endure": Samuel told him this [as a warning], that if he did not keep the Lord's commandment further his kingdom would not endure. The sin of the burnt offering was not enough for the kingship to be taken from him, unlike the affair of Agag, of which the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Samuel, "I regret that I made Saul king." Maharal (Gevuros Hashem, ch. 9): This is because David was fit for kingship in his own right, the Blessed One having given the kingship to the seed of Judah, and therefore he was not easily thrust aside and punished; but Saul, who was not fit for kingship in his own right as David was, was punished. This shows that punishment does not come, even when deserved, where [a person] is not predisposed to punishment. עַמּוּד ב): "דָּוִד בִּשְׁתַּיִם וְלֹא עָלְתָה לוֹ".
and as written (Yoma 22b): 'David stumbled in two sins, yet it did not count against him.'
פֵּרוּשׁ: דְּהֵם שְׁנֵי מִינֵי שִׁכְחוֹת:
The explanation: these correspond to two categories of forgetfulness:
הָא' – שִׁכְחָה דְּהִזְדַּמְּנוּת,
the first is the forgetfulness of sudden opportunity,
וְהוּא כֹּחַ עֲמָלֵק כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל,
which is the force of Amalek as mentioned above,
זֶהוּ חֵטְא דְּבַת שֶׁבַע שֶׁהָיָה בְּמִקְרֶה שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן לִרְאוֹתָהּ,
this being the sin of Bathsheba which occurred accidentally when the opportunity arose to see her,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה618 Sanhedrin 107a — “And he walked upon the roof of the king’s house, and he saw from the roof a woman bathing, and the woman was of very fair appearance.” Bat Sheva was washing her hair beneath a screen. The Satan came and appeared to him in the form of a bird; he shot an arrow at it, and it struck the screen and split it, and she was uncovered and he saw her. At once — “And David sent and inquired about the woman, and it was said: Is this not Bat Sheva daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?” Rashi: "Screen" — a beehive [i.e., a wicker hive serving as a screen]. "He shot an arrow" — at the screen, that is, he struck it and broke it; another reading, "opened it": he broke it and it came open. Maharsha: "She was washing her head" — they may have derived this from "he saw from the roof a woman bathing": what one sees from a roof, on a level, is the washing of the head, whereas the washing of the body could not be seen on a level from the roof, only from the side. "Behind a screen" — for Bat Sheva was certainly bathing in privacy beneath the screen, but the Satan appeared to David as a bird perched on the screen, and when he shot an arrow at it, it broke the screen and Bat Sheva was exposed. "At once, And David sent" — that is, the evil inclination did not leave him. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 107a): For a man of Torah such as David, the Torah is the partition between him and a woman's beauty, which arouses the evil inclination, so that he does not perceive it; hence she washed "behind a screen," literally a beehive, which holds sweet honey and stinging bees, just as the Torah holds both "If you walk in My statutes" and "If you do not walk in My statutes." The Satan appeared as a bird because what accustoms a man to lewdness is idleness, all the more when joined to leisure pursuits he longs for, such as hunting birds and beasts; the Satan first draws a man into such pursuits, which removes the partition, and then brings him to sin outright — so the arrow shot after the bird, the following after leisure, cast down the screen until no partition remained, and the evil inclination ruled over him. (סַנְהֶדְרִין קז עַמּוּד א): "צִפּוֹר נְדָדַתּוּ".
and as our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 107a): 'A bird flew and diverted him.'
וְאַחַר שֶׁמִּזְדָּרֵז בָּזֶה, צָרִיךְ עוֹד זְכִירָה שֶׁלֹּא יַחְשֹׁב לַעֲבֵירָה מִצְוָה.
And after one exercises vigilance in this, he requires additional mindfulness so as not to mistake a transgression for a mitzvah.
וְזֶהוּ כֹּחַ אֲגָג,
And this is the power of Agag,
דְּמִסְּתָמָא כֹּחוֹ הוּא הַגּוֹרֵם הַהַסָּתָה בְּלֵב שָׁאוּל.
whose spiritual force presumably caused the incitement within Saul's heart.
וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁלַּעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי רוֹדֵף אַחֲרָיו,
That is, to perform a mitzvah the Israelite man passionately pursues,
וְצָרִיךְ בָּזֶה בְּחִינָה וְדִקְדּוּק לָדַעַת אִם זוֹ מִצְוָה בֶּאֱמֶת.
and regarding this he requires careful examination and scrutiny to determine whether it is truly a mitzvah.
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם, כֵּיוָן שֶׁהַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה הוּא מִצַּד הַטּוֹב,
Nevertheless, since the arousal to perform a mitzvah stems from the good,
נִמְצָא אֵין הִזְדַּמְּנוּת דְּרַע.
there is no presence of an evil opportunity.
רַק הָאָדָם הַבּוֹחֵר בַּטּוֹב עָלָיו לְשָׁרֵשׁ אַחַר רֵאשִׁית הָרָע שֶׁבַּלֵּב לִמְחוֹת אֶבֶן הַטּוֹעִים.
Only the person who chooses good must root out the inception of evil within the heart to blot out the stone of the straying.
וַעֲוֹן דְּהַסָּתָה וַדַּאי חֲשָׁבוֹ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לְמִצְוָה
And the sin of the census David certainly considered a mitzvah,
לִמְנוֹת כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁעָשָׂה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
to count Israel in the manner that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, had done,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "עוֹד תַּעֲבֹרְנָה וְגוֹמֵר".
and as it is written: 'the flocks shall pass again, etc.' (Jeremiah 33:13).
וְנִמְצָא שֶׁאֵֵרַע לוֹ שְׁנֵי הַמִּכְשׁוֹלוֹת
Thus both stumbling blocks occurred to him,
וְעָלְתָה לוֹ לַעֲמֹד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה,
yet it enabled him to stand firmly upon words of Torah through this,
דְּהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּמָרֵיהּ סַיְּעֵיהּ
for he was a man whose Master assisted him,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין צג619 Sanhedrin 93b — Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: Doeg spoke this entire verse — "who knows how to play, and a mighty man of valor, and a man of war, and prudent in speech, and a comely man, and the Lord is with him" — only as slander. "Who knows how to play," that he knows how to ask; "a mighty man," that he knows how to answer; "a man of war," that he knows how to give and take in the war of Torah; "a comely man," that he presents the reasoning of the halakhah; "prudent in speech," that he infers one matter from another; "and the Lord is with him," that the halakhah accords with him in every place. Rashi: Doeg — whom the Gemara below identifies as "one of the young men" — recounted David's praise only so that Saul would envy him and kill him. "To give and take in the war of Torah" means to debate in the Talmud, and "presents the reasoning of the halakhah" means that he brings proof for his words. Maharsha: Doeg departed from what had been asked: Saul's servants had said, "Let them seek a man who knows how to play on the lyre," but he said "knows how to play" without "on the lyre," and added qualities — "a mighty man of valour" and the rest — that no one had asked of him. From this they expounded that "knows how to play" refers not to the lyre but to knowing how to ask, and that he went on to say what had not been asked — "a mighty man," mighty in Torah, to answer, and so "a man of war"; and his intent was slander, as it says in perek Get Pashut: whoever recounts his fellow's praise excessively comes to speak of his faults. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 32): "Knows how to play" is "knows how to ask," for the one who knows how to play and the one who asks share a single quality: the Torah gladdens a man's heart, and one who asks gladdens the heart of the listener and opens it until he rejoices, as one who knows how to play does; the answer that defeats the questioner is "a mighty man of valour," and one who gives and takes in Torah, raising difficulties and resolving them, is "a man of war." "And the Lord is with him" — the halakhah accords with him everywhere — because He, blessed be He, is truth, and when a man's words are true according to the halakhah, the Holy One, blessed be He, is with him. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 3): The Sages said, "and the Lord is with him — that the halakhah accords with him": to arrive at the true halakhah one must be holy within, with the Lord truly with him, free of any bodily self-interest; then he can arrive at the truth of the halakhah. The test of "the Lord is with him" is purity in these three chief traits, for all bad traits stem from matter and from self-interest. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 1): [Knowing the fitting practice for each soul and each generation] comes through complete cleaving to the Blessed One, as in Sanhedrin: "and the Lord is with him — that the halakhah accords with him in every place." That is, bringing the teaching out in accordance with the halakhah comes about because the Lord is always with him, as it says, "I have set the Lord before me always," his heart's whole aim being only to be an agent of the Merciful One in His service, not drawn after any worldly matter. עַמּוּד ב): "'וַה' עִמּוֹ' – שֶׁהֲלָכָה כְּמוֹתוֹ",
as written (Sanhedrin 93b): ''and Hashem was with him' – meaning the halakhah is in accordance with his ruling,'
דִּבְדִידֵיהּ לֹא הֲוָה.
which was not through his own virtue alone.
כִּי זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר רַק עַל יְדֵי שֶׁה' עִמּוֹ
For this is impossible except through Hashem being with him,
דְּ"אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי".
since 'a person does not stand firmly upon words of Torah, etc.'
וְהַיְנוּ דְּעַל יְדֵי הַמִּכְשׁוֹלָה לְבָבוֹ נִשְׁבָּר בְּקִרְבּוֹ
That is: through the stumbling his heart broke within him,
וְאָז זוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת ה' עִמּוֹ,
and then he merits that Hashem be with him,

כְּטַעַם (סוֹטָה ה620 Sotah 5a — "[I dwell in the high and holy place,] and also with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). Rav Huna and Rav Chisda: one said, the contrite one is with Me; and one said, I am with the contrite one. And it stands to reason like the one who said, I am with the contrite one, for the Holy One, blessed be He, passed over all the mountains and hills and rested His Presence upon Mount Sinai, and He did not raise Mount Sinai up to Himself. Rashi: "The contrite one is with Me" — I raise him up until he dwells beside Me, and this is [the sense of the verse] "I dwell [on high] … with the contrite." "I am with the contrite one" — I lower My Presence to be beside him. Maharsha: The practical lesson [of the view that 'I am with the contrite one'] is that even a distinguished person should lower himself toward one beneath him, and not say that this is beneath his dignity, for there is no honor greater than the honor of Heaven. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 5a): According to the one who says "the contrite one is with Me," the Holy One, blessed be He, raises up the contrite: just as arrogance inclines toward the material, humility is a separate [transcendent] level, as Moses possessed it, so it is fitting that the humble man be elevated to God and be with Him. According to the one who says "I am with the contrite one," God rests His Presence upon what is crushed and lowly, because the lowly are simple — as the Sages hinted that the essence of the Divine Presence was [originally] among the lower beings. [It stands to reason like the latter,] for when God joins Himself to the contrite one the union is according to His power and is complete, whereas when the contrite one is with God the union is not as full. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAnavah 1): On either view the contrite one, as the effect, is joined to God, the Cause: according to "I am with the contrite one" the Cause turns toward the effect, which is prepared to receive His glory, and according to "the contrite one is with Me" the effect is raised to be with the Cause. It stands to reason like "I am with the contrite one," for one who comes to another is wholly with him, since the other receives him entirely, whereas one who comes to the great cannot be joined with him so fully. God comes to the humble man to be with him — passing over all the high mountains to rest His Presence on Mount Sinai — because the humble man possesses something of his Maker's own attribute, and like things are found together. עַמּוּד א): "אֲנִי אֶת דַּכָּא".
mirroring (Sotah 5a): 'I dwell with him that is contrite.'
וְזֶה רַק לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה.
And this belongs solely to the penitent, the spiritual rung of David who established the yoke of repentance.
אֲבָל שָׁאוּל בְּאַחַת וְעָלְתָה לוֹ,
Saul, however, stumbled in only one and it counted against him,
הַיְנוּ דְּחָטָא רַק בְּאֶחָד לַחְשֹׁב אַעֲבֵירָה מִצְוָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
meaning he sinned only in the one error of mistaking a transgression for a mitzvah as mentioned above.
רַק דְּמַלְכוּתוֹ לֹא הָיָה דֹּפִי וְשׁוּם עֲבֵירָה
Yet in his kingdom there was neither blemish nor sin,

דְּלֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב יוֹמָא שָׁם621 Yoma 22b — "Saul was one year old when he began to reign" (I Samuel 13:1). Rav Huna said: like a one-year-old, who had never tasted the taste of sin. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: Why did the kingship of the house of Saul not endure? Because there was no flaw in him. For R. Yochanan said in the name of R. Shimon ben Yehotzadak: One appoints a leader over the community only if a box of creeping things hangs behind him, so that if he grows haughty they may say to him: Turn around and look behind you. Rashi: "Did not endure": for length of days. "Because there was no flaw in him": [no flaw] of lineage, so the kings descended from him would have grown haughty over Israel; but David came from Ruth the Moabite. "A box of creeping things": a flaw in the family. Maharsha (s.v. "hangs behind him"): He says "behind him" to teach that this refers only to a flaw that is not so evident and well known, like one's back: a flaw in the mother's family, such as the flaw Rashi explains in the royal house of David. A flaw on the father's side, which is well known in the family, is a disgrace to kingship, just as one who judges capital cases must have an Israelite father, and one whose mother alone is an Israelite is unfit. This is perhaps also why he says "a box of creeping things," for the creeping things in it are not so exposed; and so "Turn around" is said of a disqualification that is not so evident. Maharsha (s.v. "like a one-year-old, who had never tasted sin"): For after he became king he sinned in one matter, the affair of Agag; but "when he began to reign," that is, before he became king, there was no sin in him at all. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAnavah 7): The trait of pride calls for greater warning in one who has stature and greatness, that he not grow proud in his greatness. For a leader ought to be within the collective and not set apart from it by his pride: if in his pride he is set apart from the people, the standing of a leader, who is weighed as equal to the whole people, no longer applies to him, and he does not prosper as a leader should, since all his success is on account of the collective. Therefore a leader is appointed over the community only if a box of creeping things hangs behind him, for then he will not grow proud and is not set apart from the collective.),
having never sinned in his life (as written in Yoma 22b),
וְחָשַׁב דְּזֶהוּ עַצְמוֹ חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁאֵין לוֹ אוֹתוֹ סִכְלוּת מְעַט שֶׁרָאוּי לָאָדָם,
and he thought that this itself was a deficiency—that he lacked that 'little folly' (Ecclesiastes 10:1) appropriate to man,
וְזֶהוּ הַדָּבָר טוֹב שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁיֵּשׁ בַּעֲמָלֵק,
and this was the good element he presumed to exist in Amalek,
וְחָשַׁב דְּרָאוּי לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְחֵטְא בְּיָדַיִם
reasoning that it was appropriate to bring himself to sin deliberately
כְּדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה לַעֲמֹד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּוְקָא.
in order to do repentance and thereby stand firmly upon words of Torah specifically through this.
וְנִמְצָא לְפִי דַעְתּוֹ,
Thus according to his view,
חֶמְלָתוֹ עַל עֲמָלֵק הָיָה עַל דֶּרֶךְ "עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה' וְגוֹמֵר",
his sparing of Amalek was in the spirit of 'it is time to act for Hashem, etc.'
הֲגַם דְּעָבַר עַל דִּבְרֵי נָבִיא
even though he transgressed the command of the prophet,
חָשַׁב דְּכָךְ רָאוּי לָאָדָם לִהְיוֹת בּוֹ סִכְלוּת מְעָט.
he reasoned that it is fitting for a human being to possess a little folly.
וְזֶהוּ הַמֵּיטָב שֶׁבַּעֲמָלֵק "לִזְבֹּחַ לַה'",
And this was the choice aspect in Amalek 'to sacrifice unto Hashem' –
הַיְנוּ לִהְיוֹת ה' עִמּוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַלֵּב נִשְׁבָּר דְּזוֹבֵחַ יִצְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי אַחַר הַחֵטְא,
meaning that Hashem be with him through a broken heart wherein one slaughters his inclination after sinning,
וְחָשַׁב דְּהִיא בָּא לְיָדוֹ וְנִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ שֶׁיַּעֲבֹר דָּבָר זֶה
and he thought that this opportunity had presented itself before him that he might transgress this matter,
שֶׁבּוֹ עַצְמוֹ יְתֻקַּן חֶסְרוֹנוֹ
through which his deficiency would be rectified,
שֶׁהוּא מַה שֶּׁאֵין לוֹ חִסָּרוֹן.
which was the very fact that he lacked any deficiency.
וֶאֱמֶת הוּא שֶׁחָטָא אָז.
And it is true that he sinned then.

אַךְ לְפִי שֶׁחֶטְאוֹ הָיָה כְּעִנְיַן "אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (יוֹמָא פה622 Yoma 85b — One who says: I will sin and repent, I will sin and repent — he is not given the opportunity to repent. [One who says:] I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone — Yom Kippur does not atone. Rashi (Yoma 87a): [The mishnah says "I will sin and repent" twice, as Rav Huna taught:] once he has sinned twice he is no longer given the opportunity to repent, because the transgression seems to him permitted. ["Yom Kippur does not atone":] since it is on it that he relies in order to sin, it does not atone. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 8): [Among the things that impede repentance:] how can there be repentance for this sin, when the repentance itself is what causes him to sin? And likewise here Yom Kippur, a day of atonement and forgiveness, causes the sin, which is entirely improper; for repentance atones for a person when the repentance itself is free of sin, and Yom Kippur when that day is for him a day of atonement and forgiveness of iniquity — not when the repentance is the very substance of the sin. Yom Kippur is the removal of sin, not the bringing of sin. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shelach 6): The gatherer of wood reckoned that the Blessed One might wish them first to go wrong and then repent, so that deliberate sins become merits; but he erred, for that holds only after the fact, when one has gone wrong and then repented, whereas at the outset it is certainly forbidden to think so or to rely on it, and "one who says, 'I will sin and repent,' is not given the opportunity to repent." Yet he did not [truly] say "I will sin and repent," for he intended it for the sake of Heaven, as the Midrash cited says; he merely erred in his judgment. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 15): Even where the case is unlike "one who says, 'I will sin and repent,' is not given the opportunity [to repent]," since here he does not sin on the strength of repenting afterward, nevertheless at that moment he transgresses something the Blessed One does not want, namely that a person sin even for a time, though he will repent. Perhaps this is why [such a person] is not given the opportunity to repent, though the Gemara arrives at it for another reason, and only when it is twice. עַמּוּד ב),
Yet because his sin was analogous to 'I will sin and repent, he is not given the opportunity, etc.' (Yoma 85b),
וְעָלְתָה לוֹ.
it was held against him.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּמֵאַחַר דְּהוּא חָשַׁב בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה לְמִצְוָה לְדַעְתּוֹ,
That is: since during the act he considered it a mitzvah according to his own judgment,
אִם כֵּן אֵינוֹ מִכְשׁוֹל אֶצְלוֹ,
it was not a genuine stumbling block for him;
וְ"אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה" הַיְנוּ רַק כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּדֶרֶךְ מִכְשׁוֹל.
and 'a person does not stand firmly upon words of Torah' applies only when it comes by way of an authentic stumble.
וְכֵן קְלִיטַת הַטּוֹב דַּעֲמָלֵק גַּם כֵּן הוּא רַק בְּדֶרֶךְ זֶה,
And likewise, the absorption of any good from Amalek occurs solely in this manner:
דְּאֵין מְקַבְּלִין גֵּרִים מֵהֶם אִם לֹא בְּדֶרֶךְ מִכְשׁוֹל.
for we do not accept converts from them unless it occurs through an accidental stumbling.
דְּעַל כֵּן כָּךְ הָיוּ בְּנֵי בָּנָיו שֶׁל הָמָן דְּלָמְדוּ תוֹרָה בִּבְנֵי בְּרַק:
Therefore, such was the case with the descendants of Haman who learned Torah in Bnei Brak:
אוֹ דְּלֹא יָדְעוּ כְּשֶׁקִּבְּלוּם שֶׁהֵם מִזֶּרַע עֲמָלֵק
either they did not know when accepting them that they were of Amalek's seed,
וּבְדִיעֲבַד שֶׁקִּבְּלוּהוּ הֲרֵי זֶה גֵּר
and bedieved (ex post facto), once accepted, he is a valid convert –
וְהָא דְּדָוִד שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ הַיְנוּ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁפִּיו עָנָה בוֹ שֶׁחַיָּב מִיתָה עַל הֲרִיגַת שָׁאוּל כִּמְפֹרָשׁ בַּכָּתוּב,
(and that which David executed the Amalekite was because his own mouth testified against him that he was liable to death for killing Saul, as explicit in Scripture,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ לְעַיֵּן;
and nevertheless the matter requires further study);
וְהַקָּרוֹב יוֹתֵר בְּעֵינַי שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי גּוֹי מִבְּנֵי בֵּיתוֹ שֶׁל הָמָן
and what appears closer to my view is that it occurred through a gentile from Haman's household

שֶׁבָּא עַל בַּת יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאֹנֶס דְּהַוָּלָד כָּשֵׁר (יְבָמוֹת מה עַמּוּד ב וְעַיֵּין שָׁם כג עַמּוּד א רַשִׁ"י וְתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל קָסָבַר623 Yevamot 45b — The Sages of Neharde'a said in the name of R. Ya'akov: According to the one who disqualifies the offspring, he disqualifies it even when the mother is unmarried; and according to the one who declares it fit, he declares it fit even when she is a married woman... And the law is: a gentile or a slave who had relations with a Jewish woman — the offspring is of unflawed lineage, whether she was unmarried or a married woman. Rashi: "According to the one who declares it fit": concerning a slave who had relations with a Jewish woman, he declares [the offspring] fit even [when she is] a married woman, and [the Gemara] goes on to explain the reason. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): In my view it is clear that [Haman's descendants who studied Torah] came from one of the seed of Amalek coming upon a Jewish woman, through a woman taken captive among them or otherwise by force, since converts are not accepted from Amalek; and we hold that the offspring is fit. Nevertheless we find that the Torah called such a one "the son of an Egyptian man," and so too he is called one "of the descendants of Haman." Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): Converts are not accepted from Amalek, yet "of Haman's descendants taught children in Jerusalem"; so it must have come about through a gentile of his descendants coming upon a Jewish woman, for the offspring is fit and is a Jew, though he is also called the son of the gentile, as the Torah says, "and he was the son of an Egyptian man." The feminine aspect can be absorbed from Amalek only under duress and without intent, and even then only as a gentile upon a Jewish woman, where the offspring is fit; but when a Jew comes upon a gentile woman, her offspring is like her.),
who violated an Israelite woman under duress, where the offspring is halakhically valid (Yevamot 45b; and see there 23a, Rashi and Tosafot s.v. Kasavar),
וְאַף לְמַאן דְּאָמַר הַוָּלָד מַמְזֵר
and even according to the authority who maintains the child is a mamzer,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר אִם קִבְּלוּהוּ וְנִתְגַּיֵּר וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹדַע שֶׁהוּא מִזֶּרַע עֲמָלֵק,
one can say that if they accepted him and he converted, and only later was it discovered that he was from Amalek's seed,
הֲגַם דְּנֵאמַר דְּגַם דִּיעֲבַד צָרִיךְ לְקַיֵּם בּוֹ מִצְוַת תִּמְחֶה אַף שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּר,
even if we maintain that ex post facto one must still fulfill the mitzvah to blot him out despite having converted,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בָּזֶה לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל הַוָּלָד כָּשֵׁר וְיִשְׂרָאֵל גָּמוּר הוּא.
nonetheless in this case all agree the child is kosher and a full Israelite.
וְכָךְ הוּא קְלִיטַת הַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ עַל יְדֵי אֹנֶס אוֹ טָעוּת,
And such is the absorption of good from him: through coercion or mistake,

כְּמוֹ עִקַּר טַעֲנַת הָמָן שֶׁנִּצְמַח עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לַצֶּלֶם אוֹ נֶהֱנוּ מִסְּעֻדָּתוֹ (מְגִלָּה יב624 Megillah 12a — The disciples of R. Shimon ben Yochai asked him: Why were the enemies of Israel [a euphemism for Israel themselves] of that generation liable to destruction? He said to them: You say it. They said to him: Because they partook of the feast of that wicked one. [He said to them:] If so, let those in Shushan be killed, but let those in all the rest of the world not be killed. They said to him: Then you say it. He said to them: Because they prostrated themselves to the image. Rashi: "Because they prostrated themselves to the image" — the image of the days of Nebuchadnezzar. Maharsha: Rashi takes "the image" to be Nebuchadnezzar's, since Scripture implies that Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah alone refrained while all the rest bowed down; he is unwilling to explain it of bowing to Haman, which would imply that Mordecai alone refrained while all the rest bowed to him. And this is correct, for prostration to Haman took place only in Shushan, so that the objection would return — let those in Shushan be killed and not those in all the rest of the world — whereas the image in the plain of Dura was evidently set up for the whole world. Maharal (Or Chadash on Esther, introduction): Even according to R. Shimon ben Yochai, what brought the decree out at that time was that they had enjoyed Ahasuerus's feast, for that sin was what caused the earlier sin of prostrating to Nebuchadnezzar's image to be recalled against them. This is why Scripture recounts the feast at such length: taking pleasure in it was itself close to idolatry, since the feast was made in praise of his kingdom, and Ahasuerus's was one of the four kingdoms of the world, which are set against Israel who cleave to God and which themselves cleave to idolatry. When they took pleasure in a feast made for the name and glory of that nation's kingdom, they were thereby giving praise to idolatry — though this is not outright idolatry — and so this sin caused the sin of the image to be remembered, even though only those in Shushan committed it. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 33): Though the Jews were only joining gentiles at a single feast, the Gemara calls this "serving idols in purity," and this was the accusation: that they took pleasure in the feast of that wicked man, which is a trace of idolatry, and likewise that they bowed to the image — though it was only a [royal] statue and they did it only for appearance's sake, it is nevertheless a trace of idolatry, and "round about Him it storms greatly" [He is exacting with those near Him]. Because they then purified themselves in this matter until they had slaughtered the inclination to idolatry entirely, the Blessed One wished to establish a feast for them, to show that even in their drunkenness they need fear nothing, their hearts being already whole with Him. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 255): The Megillah opens with the feast because the decree sprouted from it, as the Sages said, "because they took pleasure"; and although the Gemara concludes that it was because they bowed to the image, they were not punished for that at the time, since in truth they did it only for appearance's sake, and "the Lord sees into the heart" — there was sin only from the human side, for "man sees what is before the eyes." As long as they conduct themselves with a generous eye, the Blessed One too has a generous eye toward them, bestowing on them by His measure of "seeing into the heart"; but on account of "they took pleasure" — the incitement of the power of the narrow eye — the Blessed One too said, "Mine is mine and yours is yours," judging by what is before the eyes. עַמּוּד א)
just as Haman's primary accusation arose because they bowed to the idol or enjoyed Ahasuerus' feast (Megillah 12a),
וְזֶה בְּאֹנֶס.
and this was under coercion.
וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵגָה שְׁלִישִׁית בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ עֲמָלֵק:
And this constitutes the third gradation in the root of Amalek:
שֶׁהָא' הוּא שִׁכְחָה וְקָרוֹב לְמֵזִיד,
the first being forgetfulness borderlining intentional transgression,
וְהַב' שׁוֹגֵג,
and the second is inadvertent sin,
וְהַג' אֹנֶס,
and the third is coercion;
וְזֶה רַחֲמָנָא פַּטְרֵיהּ מִלְּבַד בְּג' עֲבֵירוֹת,
and in coercion the Merciful One exempts man, except within the three cardinal transgressions,
וְזֶהוּ בְּאֹנֶס דְּגוֹיִם.
and this refers to coercion imposed by gentiles.
וְיֵשׁ גַּם בַּלֵּב דְּיֵצֶר אֲנָסֵיהּ,
And there is likewise coercion within the heart where the base inclination overpowers him,

כְּעִנְיַן "תְּחִלָּתוֹ בְּאֹנֶס וְסוֹפוֹ בְּרָצוֹן" שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּכְתֻבּוֹת (נא625 Ketubot 51b — Rava said: In any case that began under coercion and ended willingly — even if she says, "Leave him be," and that had he not forced himself upon her she would have hired him — she is permitted [to her husband]. What is the reason? The evil inclination clothed itself in her. Rashi (s.v. "the evil inclination clothed itself in her"): "Began" and "ended" refer to the beginning and the end of the act itself. This too counts as coercion: since the act began by force, it was the ravisher who clothed her in the [evil] inclination. עַמּוּד ב) דְּנֶחְשָׁב לְאֹנֶס,
as in 'its beginning was under duress and its end with consent' which they ruled in Ketubot (51b) is reckoned as duress,
וּבִכְהַאי גַּוְנָא מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא רַע
and in such a manner it is nonetheless negative –

וּכְהַאי דְּיוֹמָא (פג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א)626 Yoma 83a — A certain pregnant woman smelled [food on the Day of Atonement and craved it]. They came before R. Chanina. He said to them: Whisper to her [that today is the Day of Atonement]. They whispered to her, but the whisper did not avail. He read this verse about [the child she carried]: "The wicked are estranged from the womb" (Psalms 58:4). Shabbetai the hoarder of produce came out of her. [In the parallel case, they whispered to the woman and the whisper availed; R. Yehuda HaNasi read about her child, "Before I formed you in the belly I knew you" (Jeremiah 1:5), and R. Yochanan came out of her.] Rashi: "A pregnant woman smelled" [food] when it was Yom Kippur; "whisper to her" — in her ear, that today is Yom Kippur, so that perhaps she might restrain herself; [in the parallel case,] "the whisper availed" — she accepted the whisper, in that the fetus left off its craving. "The wicked are estranged from the womb": they became strangers, estranged from their Father in Heaven. "The hoarder of produce": [he hoarded] to drive up prices, and it is taught that one may not hoard produce in the Land of Israel, nor anything that sustains life, because it drives up prices. Maharsha: The sense of smell is a faculty of the soul — as they say in Berachos on "Let every soul praise the Lord": what is it that the soul enjoys? This is fragrance — whereas taste is a bodily faculty; hence on Yom Kippur, which is akin to the World to Come, where there is no eating or drinking, the spiritual sense, smell, is permitted and the bodily faculty of taste is forbidden. So the woman on whom the whisper availed was satisfied, she and her child, with fragrance, the soul's faculty that is permitted on Yom Kippur, and R. Yochanan issued from her; but the one on whom it did not avail could not be satisfied with what is permitted, fragrance, and craved what is forbidden on Yom Kippur, the bodily sense of taste. דְּנָפֵק מִנַּהּ שַׁבְּתַאי וְכוּלֵי,
(and like the incident in Yoma 83a where from a pregnant woman who craved on Yom Kippur emerged the wicked Shabsai, etc.,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִתִּירוּ לָהּ לֶאֱכֹל מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ פֹּרֶה וְכוּלֵי לְהִתְאַוּוֹת כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁתִּהְיֶה מְסֻכֶּנֶת וַאֲנוּסָה,
for even though they permitted her to eat, it nonetheless reflects a poisonous root to lust so violently as to become critically ill and coerced),
אֶלָּא דְּמַאי הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֶעְבַּד.
save that what could he have done?
וּרְפוּאָה שֶׁקָּדְמָה לַמַּכָּה דְּהָמָן אַף הוּא בְּחֵטְא אֶסְתֵּר בְּאֹנֶס,
And the remedy preceding the blow of Haman likewise occurred through the sin of Esther under coercion,

כִּי כָּךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא מַכֶּה בּוֹ הוּא מַרְפֵּא (מִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת וַיַּקְהֵל627 Shemot Rabbah 50:3 — Another interpretation: "And Betzalel made" — this is what is written, "For I will bring you healing" (Jeremiah 30:17). The ways of the Holy One, blessed be He, are not like the ways of flesh and blood. Flesh and blood wounds with a knife and heals with a bandage; but the Holy One, blessed be He, heals with the very thing with which He wounds, as it is stated: "And they came to Marah, and could not drink the waters of Marah, for they were bitter" (Exodus 15:23)... "And he cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a tree" (Exodus 15:25) — and it was a bitter tree; he took it and cast it into the water, and at once the waters were sweetened. Thus, "and from your wounds I will heal you.").
for such is the manner of Hashem, blessed be He: with the very instrument He strikes, He heals (Midrash Rabbah, end of Parashat Vayakhel).
פֵּרוּשׁ: הַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ הוּא הַתִּקּוּן,
The explanation: the sin itself becomes the rectification,
כִּי נִתְבָּרֵר דִּרְצוֹן מְלָכִים בְּיַד ה',
for it became clarified that the will of monarchs is in Hashem's hand,
מַה שֶּׁהֵם אוֹנְסִים לַעֲבֵירָה כָּךְ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and that which they coerce unto transgression is itself the will of Hashem.
וּלְכָךְ קְלִיטַת הַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי אֹנֶס,
Therefore the absorption of the good within him occurs likewise through coercion,
דְּמִסְּתָמָא זֶה כֹּחוֹ לְהַסִּית הָאָדָם בְּדֶרֶךְ אֹנֶס,
since this is presumably his demonic force—to entice man by way of overwhelming coercion—
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִקְלֹט גַּם כֵּן הַטּוֹב שֶׁבַּכֹּחַ הַהוּא גַּם כֵּן רַק בְּאֹנֶס.
and it is impossible to absorb the good within that power except through coercion.

וְזֶהוּ: "חַיָּב לִבְסוֹמֵי וְכוּלֵי" (מְגִלָּה ז628 Megillah 7b — Rava said: A man is obliged to become intoxicated on Purim until he no longer knows the difference between "cursed is Haman" and "blessed is Mordecai." Rashi: "To become intoxicated" means to become drunk with wine. Tosafos (s.v. "that he does not know the difference between 'cursed is Haman' and 'blessed is Mordecai'"): In the Jerusalem Talmud [the formula runs]: "Cursed is Zeresh, blessed is Esther; cursed are all the wicked, blessed are all the Jews." Maharsha: There is a righteous man who suffers in this world — one not wholly righteous, who receives his punishment here — and a wicked man who prospers here — one not wholly wicked, so that he may be driven out of the World to Come; but the wholly righteous man is granted both tables, as Mordecai was granted all his greatness in this world too, and the wholly wicked man, like Haman of the seed of Amalek and Esau, loses even this world. "Until he does not know" therefore means that he no longer sets his heart to discern the vast distance between "cursed is Haman," who was wholly wicked and lost both worlds, and "blessed is Mordecai," who was wholly righteous and was granted both worlds. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): Even in drunkenness "until he does not know," when he has no understanding to act from, the depths of [a Jew's] heart are steeped in love of Israel. This is the whole clarification of Purim — that Israel's sins and their seeming like all the nations are only external: even when one is intoxicated "until he does not know between 'cursed is Haman' and 'blessed is Mordecai,'" not recognizing openly the difference between Israel and the nations, they bear no likeness at all and are utterly distinct in the depths of their hearts. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 3): Haman's eye was evil toward Israel's festivals, for he did not believe there could be any holiness in bodily enjoyment such as eating and drinking. Hence "a person is obliged to become intoxicated on Purim until...": precisely through drunkenness with wine, without conscious understanding, the inner holiness of Israel is made clear — that even their enjoyment of food and drink is in holiness — after the manner of "wine enters, the secret comes out." עַמּוּד ב) דְּהַיְנוּ בְּלֹא דַּעַת,
And this is: 'one is obligated to become intoxicated, etc.' (Megillah 7b), meaning without conscious intellect,

וְאֹנֶס נִקְרָא בְּלֹא דַּעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרוּבִין (ק629 Eruvin 100b — Rami bar Chama said in the name of Rav Assi: It is forbidden for a man to force his wife in the matter of the commandment [of marital relations], as it is stated: "And he who hastens with his feet sins" (Proverbs 19:2). And R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: Whoever forces his wife in the matter of the commandment will have unworthy children. Rav Ika bar Chinnana said: What is the verse? "Also, without knowledge the soul is not good" (Proverbs 19:2). Rashi: "The matter of the commandment" means marital relations, and "with his feet" is an expression for relations, as it is written, "Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay" (Judges 5:27). "Also, without knowledge" — the first half of that same verse is "And he who hastens with his feet sins"; and "the soul is not good" means that the children conceived without the wife's knowledge, when her husband hastened with his feet, are not good children. Maharsha: At the end of the chapter "And these are permitted" [Nedarim 20b] the children of a woman who was coerced are reckoned among those of whom it is said, "And I will purge out from among you the rebels" (Ezekiel 20:38) — and for this same reason, that they are not worthy children. עַמּוּד ב):
and coercion is classified as 'without intellect' as they said in Eruvin (100b):
"הַכּוֹפֶה אִשְׁתּוֹ וְכוּלֵי גַּם בְּלֹא דַעַת וְכוּלֵי".
'He who coerces his wife, etc., also without knowledge, etc.'
וְנִיחָא דְּפוּרִים הוּא שֶׁגַּם שֶׁחוֹטְאִים בְּלֹא יְדִיעָתָם הוּא טוֹב.
And the divine rest of Purim reveals that even when they sin without their knowledge it is ultimately for the good.
וְנַהֲפֹךְ מִמַּחֲשֶׁבֶת הָמָן לִהְיוֹת עַל רֹאשׁוֹ מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר וְגוֹמֵר,
And the opposite of Haman's scheme resulted, with his plot returning upon his own head,
כְּטַעַם: "עֵת אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַט וְגוֹמֵר",
mirroring: 'there is a time wherein one man rules over another to his own hurt' (Ecclesiastes 8:9),
שֶׁהוּא חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁמַּחֲטִיא,
for he thinks he induces sin,
וּבֶאֱמֶת זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשִׂים זְכִיּוֹת וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מוֹסִיפִים זְכוּת.
yet in truth willful sins become transformed into merits, and through this they increase spiritual credit.
וְאַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה נַעֲשָׂה מִסְּעֻדַּת אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע שֶׁנֶּהֱנוּ מִמֶּנָּה הַמִּצְוָה דִּסְעֻדַּת פּוּרִים.
And following repentance, out of the feast of that wicked king from which they derived pleasure emerged the mitzvah of the festive meal of Purim.
וּמֵהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה לַצֶּלֶם לְפָנִים
And from their outward bowing down to the idol for mere show,

כְּאִלּוּ לֹא יָדַע בֵּין "אַבָּא דְּיָהֵיב מִיטְרָא וְכוּלֵי630 Taanit 23b — Chanan the Hidden was the son of the daughter of Choni the Circle-Drawer. When the world needed rain, the Sages would send schoolchildren to him, and they would seize the hem of his cloak and say to him: Father, Father, give us rain! He said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the Universe, act for the sake of these, who cannot distinguish between a father who can give rain and a father who cannot give rain. Rashi: "Schoolchildren": [were sent] to soften his heart, so that he would pray with intent. "Father, Father": so they used to call him, as an orphan cries, "My father, my father!" "Who cannot distinguish": they suppose that I am their father. Maharsha: [The Gemara] explains why they did not send a pair of Sages to him to ask for mercy, as they did above with Choni the Circle-Drawer and Abba Chilkiyah, but had to send him schoolchildren: when he sensed that Sages were coming to him he would hide himself in the privy so that they would not find him, in order not to take credit for himself, as was said above of Abba Chilkiyah. Therefore they had to send schoolchildren, who would follow him even to the place in the privy where he was hiding and say, "Father, Father..."" (תַּעֲנִית כג עַמּוּד ב),
acting as though one knew not between 'Father Who gives rain, etc.' (Ta'anit 23b),
הַבִּסּוּם "עַד דְּלָא יָדַע בֵּין וְכוּלֵי",
emerged the sacred intoxication 'until he knows not between cursed is Haman and blessed is Mordechai,'
וְהָאוֹמֵר לְהֵיפֶךְ הוּא דּוֹמֶה לָזֶה.
and one who recites the reverse is comparable to this.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בָּזֶה הֲרֵי עוֹשֶׂה מִצְוָה,
And nonetheless in this he performs a mitzvah,
שֶׁקִּיֵּם בָּזֶה מִצְוַת חֲכָמִים: "חַיָּב וְכוּלֵי".
having fulfilled thereby the rabbinic injunction: 'A person is obligated to become intoxicated, etc.'

sections.en: World, Year, Soul, and the Twelvefold Order

items.h: Space, time, and soul share patterned differences; the months and tribes express distinct spiritual qualities that culminate in thought becoming embodied in action.

Seif 1 — World, Year, Soul, and the Pattern of Elul
Differences in place, time, and soul follow one spiritual order, culminating in thought that becomes embodied in habitual action.

p: כָּל עִנְיָנִים חֲלוּקִים בְּעוֹלָם שָׁנָה נֶפֶשׁ כַּיָּדוּעַ מִסֵּפֶר יְצִירָה.
All matters are differentiated across World, Year, and Soul, as is known from Sefer Yetzirah.
וּבַנְּפָשׁוֹת יָדוּעַ דְּאֵין שׁוּם נֶפֶשׁ דּוֹמָה לַחֲבֶרְתָּהּ,
And regarding souls, it is known that no soul resembles another,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת נח631 Berakhot 58a — The Sages taught: One who sees multitudes of Israel says, "Blessed is He who knows secrets" — for their minds are not alike one to another, nor are their faces alike one to another. Rashi: "Multitudes" — a great host of six hundred thousand. "Who knows secrets" — He who knows what is in the heart of all of these. Maharsha: Since the Gemara concludes that a multitude is no fewer than six hundred thousand, there are among them six hundred thousand distinct minds, and these comprise every mind; this is why the Torah was given to six hundred thousand in the wilderness, so that the Torah should include every mind and every wisdom and nothing could be added to it. And what the Sages said, that whatever any sage originates in his generation was already given at Sinai, is because that very matter was already in the mind of one of those six hundred thousand who stood at Sinai, since there can be no further mind beyond six hundred thousand. Maharal (Derech Chaim 4:20): The baraita is framed as "not only this, but even this": even their faces are not alike, and all the more so is it not fitting that their minds should be alike. This is a deep matter belonging to the multiplicity of individuals — since they are many, there must of necessity be difference and distinction among them. עַמּוּד א) שֶׁאֵין דַּעְתָּן דּוֹמָה זֶה לָזֶה.
and as our Sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 58a), that their minds do not resemble one another.
וּמִסְּתָמָא הוּא הַדִּין בְּעוֹלָם אֵין שׁוּם מָקוֹם דּוֹמֶה לַחֲבֵירוֹ,
And presumably the same applies to World—space—where no place resembles another,

כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (מַכּוֹת ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב, י רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א)632 Makkot 9b-10a — Three [cities of refuge] beyond the Jordan and three in the land of Israel? Abaye said: In Gilead murderers are common, as it is written: "Gilead is a city of those who work iniquity, it is covered [akubah] with blood" (Hosea 6:8). What is "covered with blood"? R. Elazar said: They would lie in ambush [okevin] to kill people. And what is different about the cities on this side and on that side, which are distant, and about the middle ones, which are near? Abaye said: In Shechem too murderers are common, as it is written: "And as troops of robbers wait for a man, so does the band of priests; they murder on the way toward Shechem" (Hosea 6:9). Rashi (s.v. "in Gilead"): In Gilead, which is beyond the Jordan, murderers are common. Rashi (s.v. "on this side and on that side, which are distant"): Hebron and Kedesh are far from the borders of the land, so that one who kills at the edge of the border must flee a quarter of the land; but one who kills between Hebron and Shechem, or between Shechem and Kedesh, is near a city of refuge on either side. Rashi (s.v. "they would lie in ambush"): That is, they would lie in wait. Rashi (s.v. "three beyond the Jordan"): This is asked in astonishment: three [cities of refuge] in the inheritance of two tribes, as many as in the inheritance of ten tribes? Tosafos (s.v. "in Gilead murderers are common"): That is, this is why cities of refuge were needed there: when people kill deliberately without witnesses, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings [such a murderer and an unwitting killer] together at a single inn, as is said below [so that the murderer dies at the hand of the unwitting killer, who must then go into exile]. Maharsha (s.v. "Abaye said: In Shechem too murderers are common"): Nevertheless, murderers were not as common in Shechem as in Gilead, for otherwise the question would return to its place: three [cities] beyond the Jordan and [only] three in the land of Israel? Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 80): There is the "Fear of Isaac," a holy severity that is good, like the Torah scholar who "boils" [with anger], and that is the city of refuge. So in Gilead and Shechem, where murderers are common, cities of refuge were multiplied, as in Makkot, for the Blessed One does not deal tyrannically [with His creatures]: since by their native disposition murderers are common there, presumably this same thing is common there in holiness, the "boiling," that is, the cities of refuge; and when it spreads outward it turns into evil murder.: בְּגִלְעָד וּשְׁכֶם שְׁכִיחֵי רוֹצְחִים,
in the manner that they said (Makkot 9b end, 10a beginning): in Gilead and Shechem murderers were prevalent;

וַאֲוִירָא דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל מַחְכִּים (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קנח633 Bava Batra 158b — R. Ila said: [The property remains] in the possession of the mother's heirs. R. Zeira said: In the possession of the son's heirs. When R. Zeira went up [to the Land of Israel], he took his stand with the view of R. Ila; Rabba took his stand with the view of R. Zeira. R. Zeira said: Learn from this that the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise. Rashbam: "In the possession of the mother's heirs" — as is explained below, because the inheritance was already established with that tribe: throughout the woman's life after her husband's death all her property was in her own possession, and she is reckoned to her father's tribe; "in the possession of the son's heirs" — because once her husband died the son was fit to inherit from her before all her relatives on her father's side. "R. Zeira said: learn from this that the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise" — for from the time I went up to the Land of Israel I set my mind to abandon my first view and to reach the truth of the matter. The clause "Rabba took his stand with the view of R. Zeira" is not our reading, and Rabbenu Chananel likewise does not read it. Maharal (Netivot Olam, Netiv HaTorah 10): One who dwells in the Holy Land dwells in a place that possesses holiness, and this is what they meant by "the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise"; for the whole character of the Land of Israel and its excellence is that it is separate from the physical, since it is holy. He says this in explaining why one who dwells in the Land of Israel is counted among those who inherit the World-to-Come: the World-to-Come is itself separate, and dwelling there inclines a man to be separate from the physical. עַמּוּד ב),
and 'the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise' (Bava Batra 158b);
וּבָבֶל וּבוֹרְסִיף סִימָן רַע לַתּוֹרָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קט עַמּוּד א),
and Babylon and Borsippa are an ominous omen for Torah (Sanhedrin 109a);

וּבְקִדּוּשִׁין634 Kiddushin 49b — Ten measures of wisdom came down to the world; the Land of Israel took nine and all the rest of the world one. Ten measures of beauty came down to the world; Jerusalem took nine and all the rest of the world one. Ten measures of wealth came down to the world; the ancient Romans took nine and all the rest of the world one. Ten measures of poverty came down to the world; Babylonia took nine and all the rest of the world one. Ten measures of arrogance came down to the world; Eilam took nine and all the rest of the world one. Ten measures of might came down to the world; Persia took nine, and so on. Ten measures of vermin came down to the world; Media took nine, and so on. Ten measures of sorcery came down to the world; Egypt took nine, and so on. Ten measures of licentiousness came down to the world; Arabia took nine, and so on. Ten measures of insolence came down to the world; Meishan took nine, and so on. Ten measures of drunkenness came down to the world; Kush took nine and one took all the rest of the world. Rashi: "Wisdom" here means Torah together with proper worldly conduct. "Insolence" means bastardy — Meishan took nine, for most of them are of flawed lineage. Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot): Of all of these he says that they "came down," that is, came down from heaven by decree — as is said of the wise man, the mighty man and the rich man, that the angel appointed over this sets the drop before the Holy One, blessed be He, and He decrees: this one shall be wise, this one mighty, this one rich; only that such a decree is readier in one land than in another, according to the angel and the constellation of each country. For this reason he does not also say that ten measures of righteousness came down to the world, or ten of wickedness, since that is not decreed from heaven — all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 49b): These sayings make known to you that He, blessed be He, apportioned all existence according to His wisdom, so that some incline toward one particular thing until they are set apart from all the rest; yet since all things are mingled and included together, it is impossible that the others should not take one portion, and that is the tenth — for the tenth is a subordinate portion drawn after that which is principal, as is known of the tenth in relation to the nine. Wisdom is the separate intellect, and it is fitting that it be in the Land of Israel, which is the holy land, and therefore the holy land is distinguished in wisdom above all other lands; and beauty likewise belongs to Jerusalem, for beauty is the radiance of light, and light is not corporeal. (מט עַמּוּד ב): תִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין וְכוּלֵי עַיֵּין שָׁם,
and in Kiddushin (49b): 'nine measures, etc.,' see there,
דְּכָל אֻמָּה יֵשׁ לָהּ כֹּחַ מְיֻחָד
that each nation possesses a distinct spiritual force,
וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן מִצַּד הַמָּקוֹם אוֹתָן שֶׁנִּקְרָאִים עַל שֵׁם מְקוֹמָן.
and this also corresponds to location for those identified by their geographical locale.
וְכָךְ בְּשָׁנָה אֵין רֶגַע דּוֹמָה לַחֲבֶרְתָּהּ,
And so within Year—time—no moment resembles another,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה635 Sanhedrin 102a — “In a time of favour I answered you” — it was taught in the name of R.
