Chiyya bar Abba said: Where do we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, is called the heart of Israel? From this verse: "God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever" (Psalms 73:26). Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar 8): The theme of this month [Adar] is that even in sleep Israel are holy, since they are bound at their root to the Blessed One — as the Midrash says, "I am asleep from the commandments ... but my heart is awake to perform them ... where do we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel? 'God is the rock of my heart.'" From the side of the Blessed One, "the voice of my beloved knocks, open for me": "my heart is awake" means that the Blessed One, the heart of Israel, rouses Israel from their sleep to perform the commandments. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): The Congregation of Israel boasts, "I am asleep but my heart is awake," which the Sages expounded as referring to the Holy One, blessed be He — "rock of my heart." Even when they are asleep from the commandments and have no "eyes," as in sleep when the eyes are shut and the heart is sunk in imaginings, since the root of the soul is a portion of God and the depths of the heart cleave to the Blessed One, all the imaginings too cleave to Him; even at the height of immersion in the imaginings of this world, which hide the truth, there remains in him a power of awakening to the Blessed One through the heart's cleaving to the living God. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 68): All the service of the body's limbs, and the commandments performed with them, serve only to set the heart straight; the essential thing is the heart, the dwelling place of the Blessed One, as the Sages said, "the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel, as it says, 'rock of my heart.'" Therefore these [outward acts] are not to be a person's goal in themselves, but only things that lead to the goal, as the Zohar calls the 613 commandments "613 counsels."): הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
and reflecting (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2): Hashem, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel;
הַיְנוּ עֹמֶק הַלֵּב דִּלְכָל נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ נְקֻדָּה וְחֵלֶק מַה מִצּוּרַת אָדָם.
meaning the depth of the heart, wherein every Jewish soul possesses a distinct spark and part of this Form of Adam.
וְהִשְׁתַּלְּמוּת הַצּוּרָה עַל יְדֵי כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת שֶׁבַּדּוֹר:
And the ultimate completion of this Form is achieved collectively through all the souls of the generation:

חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם הָעֵינַיִם שֶׁנִּקְרָאִים "עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה" ([בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ד658 Bava Batra 4a — Some say that this is what he said to him: He blinded the eye of the world, as it is written [of the Sages], "And if it be done unwittingly by the eyes of the congregation"; let him go and occupy himself with the eye of the world, as it is written, "Behold, I profane My Sanctuary, the pride of your strength, the delight of your eyes." Rashi: "Behold, I profane My Sanctuary" — the proof lies in the end of the verse, "the delight of your eyes." Maharsha: One may find the absence of light without the absence of eyes — a sighted man at night — and the absence of eyes without the absence of light — a blind man by day; but Herod had caused both, for the Torah is the light and the Torah scholars are the eyes. On this second version Bava ben Buta told him that he could repair the loss of the eyes, since the Temple he would build stands as the eye of the world in place of the Sages he had killed — but the loss of the light, the Torah he extinguished by putting them to death, he could not restore by building it. עַמּוּד א]);
the Sages of Israel are the eyes, who are designated 'the eyes of the congregation' (Bava Batra 4a);
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ הוּא הַלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה;
and the king is the heart, as written in Sefer Yetzirah;
וְתוֹמְכֵי אוֹרַיְתָא הֵם הַשּׁוֹקַיִם, וְכַדּוֹמֶה בְּכָל אֶבְרֵי הַגּוּף.
and the supporters of Torah are the thighs, and so forth across all the limbs of the body.
וְאֵין שׁוּם נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל מִלְּבַר שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ מִמַּעַל,
And there is no soul among Israel from without that does not contain a portion of God from Above,
וְהוּא מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ הָאָבוֹת אֲשֶׁר בְּשֵׁם יַעֲקֹב יְכֻנֶּה.
and it derives from the root of the Patriarchs which is titled with the name Jacob.
אֶלָּא שֶׁבְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַמַּעֲשִׂים אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא עַד שֶׁמִּתְחַלֵּשׁ אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ מוּעָט שֶׁל קְדֻשָּׁה.
Only that in the external spreading forth of physical actions one may sin until that slight force of holiness weakens.
וְזֶהוּ הַתַּשִּׁי שֶׁמּוֹלִיד לְמַעְלָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם,
And this is the enfeeblement caused Above, Heaven forbid,

אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלְּעוֹלָם: "אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא" (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד659 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned" (Joshua 7:11). R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is an Israelite. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is still myrtle and people call it myrtle. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious. עַמּוּד א)
even though eternally: 'even though he sinned, he remains Israel' (Sanhedrin 44a)
וְלֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח,
and no banished soul remains permanently cast off;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לִשְׁעָתוֹ תַּשׁ כֹּחַ.
nonetheless, for that moment it becomes enfeebled.
וְעִנְיָן זֶה שֶׁמְּדַמִּין הַצּוּרָה לְיוֹצְרָהּ,
And this concept that they liken the form to its Creator,
הַיְנוּ כִּי בְּהַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּנִּבְרָאִים הוּא מִצַּד הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ בָּהֶם,
means that Hashem's providence over creatures operates through His immanent expansion within them,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ"ם כִּי יְדִיעָתוֹ הַבְּרוּאִים מִצַּד יְדִיעָתוֹ אֶת עַצְמוֹ.
just as Maimonides wrote that His knowledge of creations stems from His knowledge of Himself.
וְהַיְנוּ כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין חוּץ מִמֶּנּוּ,
That is: in absolute truth there is nothing outside of Him,
וּכְטַעַם: "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם" (נְחֶמְיָה ט, ו);
mirroring: 'and You preserve them all' (Nehemiah 9:6);
וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ נְקֻדָּה שֶׁל חַיּוּת הַקָּבוּעַ בַּלֵּב
and within Israel there is a focal point of vitality permanently embedded in the heart
שֶׁעַל יָדָהּ הֵם דְּבוּקִים בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים,
through which they cleave unto the living God,
הַיְנוּ שֶׁיְּכוֹלִים לְהַרְגִּישׁ זֶה בַּלֵּב.
meaning they are capable of consciously sensing this in their heart.
וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית בְּרִיאַת אָדָם:
And this is the ultimate purpose of man's creation:
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִבְרָא מַכִּיר וּמַרְגִּישׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא.
that there exist a created being who recognizes and feels that there is a Creator.
וְהַכָּרָה זוֹ, מֵאַחַר שֶׁהִיא מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת בָּאָדָם,
And this perception, once it clothes itself within man,
הֲרֵי הִיא קְרוּיָה דְּמוּת אָדָם,
is appropriately termed the Likeness of Adam,
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁהִיא אֲצִילוּת הַשָּׂגָה כְּפִי כֹּחַ הַשָּׂגַת אָדָם.
meaning that it is an emanated comprehension structured according to the human capacity of perception.
וְכֵן הִתְחַלְּקוּתָהּ בַּנְּפָשׁוֹת כְּפִי כֹּחַ הִתְחַלְּקוּת הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי אָדָם,
And likewise its differentiation among souls reflects the multifaceted division of human souls,
שֶׁגַּם זֶה הוּא כְּפִי דְּמוּת אָדָם שֶׁהוּא מוֹלִיד בְּדוֹמֶה לוֹ.
which also mirrors the form of man who fathers offspring in his own likeness.
וּמִסְפַּר הַנְּפָשׁוֹת הוּא כְּפִי הִתְחַלְּקוּת הַקּוֹמָה שֶׁלּוֹ בְּכָל פְּרָטֵי כֹּחוֹתֶיהָ,
And the sum total of souls corresponds to the detailed division of his complete stature throughout all its particular faculties,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּשְׁמוֹת רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה מ660 Shemot Rabbah 40:3 — While Adam still lay an unformed mass, the Holy One, blessed be He, showed him every righteous man destined to arise from him. Some hang from Adam's head, some from his hair, some from his forehead, some from his eyes, some from his nose, some from his mouth, some from his ear, and some from his earlobe. Know this: when Job sought to argue with the Holy One, blessed be He, and said, "Would that I knew where I might find Him... I would lay my case before Him" (Job 23:3-4), the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him: "Where [eifoh] were you when I laid the earth's foundations?" (Job 38:4). What is "eifoh"? R. Shimon ben Lakish said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him — Job, tell Me from what place your soul's origin [eifah] hung: from his head, from his forehead, or from which of his limbs? If you know where your eifah was, then you may argue with Me.):
and as written in Shemot Rabbah (Parashah 40):
בְּאֵיזֶה אֵיפָה הָיָה תָּלוּי וְכוּלֵי, יֵשׁ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ וְכוּלֵי.
in which limb was he suspended, etc., some in his head, etc.

וְזֶהוּ עֹמֶק לְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ661 Midrash Tehillim 1:4 — Chizkiyah bar Chiya said: Fortunate are the prophets, who liken the form to its Former, as it is said, “For the Lord God is a sun and a shield.” And so he says: “A lion has roared — who shall not fear?” And it is written, “Behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east, and His voice was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory.” They cause the ear to hear what it is able to hear, and show the eye what it is able to see. (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר א פָּסוּק א):
And this is the profound depth of the rabbinic idiom (Shocher Tov, Psalm 1:1):
מְדַמִּין צוּרָה לְיוֹצְרָהּ וּנְטִיעָה לְנוֹטְעָהּ,
they liken the form to its Creator, and the plant to its Planter,
וְלֹא אָמְרוּ בְּהֵיפֶךְ.
and they did not articulate it in reverse.
וְהַיְנוּ כִּי אֲמִתּוּת הַדָּבָר הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַשָּׂגָה זוֹ הוּא שֶׁל הַיּוֹצֵר וְהַנּוֹטֵעַ,
For in ultimate truth, this unfolding comprehension belongs intrinsically to the Creator and Planter,
אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵם מְדַמִּין הַצּוּרָה לְיוֹצֵר;
save that they liken the created form to the Creator;
וְהָבֵן כִּי הַדָּבָר עָמֹק וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְפָרֵשׁ יוֹתֵר.
and understand this, for the matter is exceedingly profound and cannot be explained further.
וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן הַיִּחוּד שֶׁאָמְרוּ הַשְּׁבָטִים לְיַעֲקֹב:
And this is the essence of the Divine Unity which the tribes proclaimed to Jacob:

"כְּשֵׁם שֶׁאֵין בְּלִבְּךָ אֶלָּא אֶחָד וְכוּלֵי662 Pesachim 56a — Yaakov sought to reveal to his sons the end of days, and the Divine Presence departed from him. He said: Perhaps, Heaven forbid, there is a flaw in my offspring, as with Avraham from whom Yishmael issued, and with my father Yitzchak from whom Esav issued. His sons said to him: “Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One” — just as there is only One in your heart, so is there only One in ours. At that moment Yaakov our father opened and said: Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever. Rashi: [Reading "the end of days" as "the end of the right hand":] when He will bring His right hand back before Him, for "He has drawn back His right hand before the enemy." "Hear, O Israel": they were saying it to their father. Maharsha: Since Scripture does not go on to tell that he revealed to them the time of the end and of the ingathering of the exiles, [the Sages] said that the Divine Presence departed from him lest he reveal the end, as Daniel too was told "the words are closed up and sealed"; but Yaakov supposed another cause — that one of his sons did not believe in the One God (as the Semag explains) — and so he told them "hearken unto Israel your father," that is, accept the kingship of Heaven as your father did. They answered in that very language, "Hear, O Israel": just as you have accepted the Lord, the name of unity, so is "the Lord our God, the Lord One." And Yaakov said "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom" on hearing his sons mention the name of Heaven, just as they would respond after the High Priest when he mentioned the Name on Yom Kippur (Yoma). Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 7): The acceptance of the kingship of Heaven began with the twelve tribes, the sons of Yaakov, and not with Yaakov himself: given his level — his image engraved on the Throne of Glory — His kingship through him is not reckoned as kingship over the lower beings, which is complete only through Israel. Yet they accepted it only through Yaakov, who is entirely one and through whom the tribes too became one: Yaakov corresponds to the alef of echad ["one"], and with the eight sons of the matriarchs and the four sons of the handmaids they are thirteen, the numerical value of echad. When he heard their acceptance he said "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom," a blessing beyond what the tribes said, fitting only for what is not physical — the upper beings who are without body, and Yaakov, who was holy. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 44): Yaakov was fit to reveal the end, which is closed and utterly hidden, for his level reached the inner, hidden level — a merit he had because there was no flaw in his offspring; but since it is not fitting to reveal it, the world of the Messiah being as it were a new world, the Divine Presence departed, and he feared a flaw in his offspring that would have cut them off from that hidden level. They answered "Hear, O Israel" because Yaakov cleaves entirely to the unity of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the twelve tribes are united through Yaakov their father as the twelve chief limbs of a man are united through the soul, so that through him they too cleave to His unity. Hearing their acceptance of the unity, Yaakov said "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom," which blesses His name insofar as it indicates the truth of His essence — a praise fitting only for one who is holy, as Yaakov was. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Hashanah 12): Jacob our father recognized in the attribute of truth, plainly as daylight, that the Lord is One after the world was created just as before it was created, which is what the Name Havayah signifies. The tribes said, "So there is only One in our hearts": we attain, at least through faith, also plainly, that the Lord is One, as the Zohar says, "He is truth and She is faith." Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 252): "Just as there is only One in your heart ..." is the upper unity in Jacob's heart and the lower unity in the hearts of his sons. The upper unity is that all our deeds, too, You have wrought; this is the beginning, and of it is said "Hear, O Israel": you, Israel, who strive to attain Godliness, know that the Lord is One and that your striving too is from the Blessed One. Afterwards "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever" is in the sense of "after a blessing, the earth He has given to mankind": the unity in reverse, that the Blessed One too is his. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Anthology, Vayigash; from Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 17): Only Jacob our father, a chariot for the Name Havayah, attained fear in the aspect of truth, seeing plainly that the King of kings stands over him; and of this the tribes said, "Just as there is only One in your heart, so there is only One in ours." As we have said many times, the intent is that through faith we can attain the faith of His unity, until it is as plain before the eye that all is from the Blessed One as before the world was created, which is attaining the Lord in the aspect of truth. Beis Yaakov (Vayechi 11): The sons told Jacob, "Just as there is only One in your heart," meaning that the self-limitation that comes through choice is joined to the root of His unity, "so there is only One in ours": as far as our hand reaches we walk by choice, and where our power of choice cannot reach to clarify, there we are bound to the root of His unity above the bounds of choice. At once Jacob said "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever," the lower unity, signifying the clothing of the light of His unity: one who cleaves to His unity, the Blessed One desires him even in the extension of His garments." ([פְּסָחִים נו עַמּוּד א]),
'Just as there is in your heart nothing but the One, etc.' (Pesachim 56a),
שֶׁאַף שֶׁאָנוּ נְפָשׁוֹת חֲלוּקִים, הַכֹּל אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא אֶחָד וְקוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה.
for even though we are differentiated souls, everything is fundamentally one single, integrated stature.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר יַעֲקֹב: "בָּרוּךְ שֵׁם כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד",
And upon this Jacob answered: 'Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever,'
שֶׁהוּא יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה מִצַּד מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ,
which is the Lower Unity (yichuda tata'ah) from the perspective of His Sovereignty (Malchut),
שֶׁאֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם שֶׁהוּא רִבּוּי נִפְרָדִים,
for there is no king without a nation, which involves a multitude of separate individuals,
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַכֹּל עַם אֶחָד מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּעְבְּדוּתָם לַמֶּלֶךְ.
yet nonetheless all constitute one nation through their shared subjugation to the King.
אֲבָל מֹשֶׁה לֹא אֲמָרוֹ,
Moses, however, did not utter it aloud,

דְּמֹשֶׁה מִלְּגָאו, יַעֲקֹב מִלְּבַר (תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּקּוּן יג663 Tikkunei Zohar 29a — When the sukkah was made whole in its thigh, it was said of Jacob, "And Jacob came whole" (Genesis 33:18). And Jacob is certainly the likeness of the central pillar from the outer side; and Moses was there as well, but from the inner side — this one from the body and that one from the soul. And therefore the two thighs of the central pillar, when it is whole, are Netzach and Hod.):
for 'Moses is from within, Jacob is from without' (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13):
מִצַּד הַפְּנִימִיּוּת הוּא רַק יִחוּדָא עִלָּאָה,
from the inward perspective there is solely the Higher Unity (yichuda ila'ah),
דְּהַיְנוּ יִחוּד הַגָּמוּר שֶׁאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ כְּלָל.
namely absolute Unity where there exists nothing at all besides Him.
אֲבָל מִצַּד הַחִיצוֹנִיּוּת דְּיֵשׁ בְּרוּאִים נִפְרָדִים
However, from the outward perspective wherein separate creations exist,
אֶלָּא שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם פְּנִימִיּוּתָם אֶחָד,
yet one recognizes that their inner reality is nonetheless one,
זֶהוּ יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב מִצַּד הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ שֶׁל זַרְעוֹ אַחֲרָיו.
this is the Lower Unity of Jacob through the expansive branching of his seed after him.

וְזֶהוּ "צִיקֵי קְדֵרָה שֶׁהֵרִיחָה בַּת מֶלֶךְ" (פְּסָחִים שָׁם664 Pesachim 56a — The Sages said: What shall we do? Shall we recite it? Moses our teacher did not say it. Shall we not recite it? Jacob said it. They ordained that it be said in an undertone. R. Yitzchak said, they say in the school of R. Ami: This may be compared to a king's daughter who smelled the aroma of a spiced dish [a lowly food]. If she asks for it, she is disgraced; if she does not ask, she suffers. Her servants began to bring it to her in secret. Rashi: "Shall we recite it": this "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom" in the reading of the Shema. "A spiced dish": fried, seasoned meat (Old French arsdure). "She suffers": bodily suffering, from the craving. Maharsha: Moses did not say it — that is, in the passage "Hear, O Israel" written in the Torah — because he did not say it as one who recites the Shema to accept upon himself the kingship of Heaven, but wrote it as instruction for Israel, and so responding "Blessed be the name..." did not apply to it. We, who recite the Shema to accept upon ourselves the yoke of the kingship of Heaven, ought to say it as Jacob did at his sons' acceptance; but since Moses did not say it in the Torah it would be a disgrace to add to his words and interrupt aloud between "the Lord is One" and "And you shall love," and since Jacob said it, let us at least say it quietly. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 7): "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom" is the completion of the acceptance of the kingship of Heaven, which we must accept as completely as Jacob did; hence "if she does not ask, she suffers" — that is, there is a deficiency — for by virtue of the soul man resembles the angels, who say it by virtue of their holiness, and only the body holds him back. Therefore they enacted that it be said quietly, corresponding to the soul, which dwells in concealment just as the Holy One, blessed be He, dwells in concealment; and so he likened the soul to a king's daughter, for she is the daughter of the Holy One, blessed be He. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 44): Moses said "Hear, O Israel" to all Israel, that is, to every person, and not every person is fit for this praise, which belongs only to one who is holy; yet Jacob in his holiness said it, and every person has something of holiness, so a person is in some measure fit to say it. The king's daughter is the soul, emanated from the Holy One, blessed be He, alone, while the body is from the earth; being holy, the soul yearns for this praise, which befits her ("smelled," for smell pertains above all to the soul) — if she asks, it is a disgrace, for she is in the body, from whose side the praise is unfitting, and if she does not, she suffers, for from her own side it is fitting. Therefore they enacted that it be said quietly, not openly, for it befits man only by virtue of the soul, which dwells hidden in the innermost chambers — except on Yom Kippur, when bodily things are set aside and Israel may say it openly.),
And this is the allegory of 'the remnants of the dish which the king's daughter smelled' (Pesachim ibid.),
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֶהֱנֶה מִזֶּה,
meaning that Hashem, blessed be He, takes delight in this,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלְּאָמְרוֹ יֵשׁ גְּנַאי שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ יֵשׁ נִפְרָדִין,
even though to articulate it openly bears a certain indignity, as it appears as though independent entities exist;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם עִקַּר כְּבוֹד מֶלֶךְ בָּזֶה וּמְבִיאִין בַּחֲשַׁאי.
nonetheless, the primary glory of the King is achieved through this, and so they recite it in a whisper.
וְזֶהוּ עִקַּר הַיַּהֲדוּת שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לוֹמַר פַּעֲמַיִם בְּכָל יוֹם תָּמִיד,
And this is the core essence of Judaism which must be recited twice every single day,
דְּזֶהוּ עִקַּר שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיַּהֲדוּת:
for this is the bedrock root of Judaism:
מַה שֶּׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ נְקֻדָּה זוֹ שֶׁבַּלֵּב שֶׁדָּבוּק בָּהּ בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבָהּ מַכִּיר יִחוּדוֹ הָאֲמִתִּי.
that he possesses this inner point in the heart through which he clings to Hashem and perceives His true Unity.
וְעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִתְקַנֵּא בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע,
And regarding this reality the wicked Balaam became envious,
שֶׁבְּכָל נְבִיאוֹתָיו גִּלָּה דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁל הַדְּבֵקוּת וְהַיִּחוּד הַגָּמוּר;
for in all his prophetic utterances he exposed this truth of complete cleaving and absolute Unity;
דְּלָכֵן בִּקְּשׁוּ לִקְבֹּעַ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק בִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע
which is why the Sages sought to institute Parashat Balak within the daily Shema,

לְפִי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהּ: "כָּרַע שָׁכַב כַּאֲרִי וְגוֹמֵר" (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת יב665 Berakhot 12b — R. Abbahu ben Zutarti said in the name of R. Yehuda bar Zevida: They sought to fix the portion of Balak within the recitation of the Shema. And why did they not fix it? Because of the burden on the congregation. ... R. Yose bar Avin said: Because this verse is written in it — "He crouched, he lay down like a lion, and like a lioness; who shall rouse him?" Rashi: "He crouched, he lay down" was chosen because it resembles "when you lie down and when you rise": the Holy One, blessed be He, guards us in our lying down and our rising, so that we lie down tranquil and at ease like a lion and a lioness. Tosafos (s.v. "They sought to fix the portion of Balak within the recitation of the Shema"): It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 1:5) that the three portions were fixed in the recitation of the Shema because the Ten Commandments are contained in them; look there and you will find it all. Maharsha: "He crouched, he lay down" corresponds to the evening Shema, of which "when you lie down" is written, as Rashi explained, and "like a lioness, who shall rouse him" corresponds to the morning Shema, of which "when you rise" is written — for surely no one rouses him: he rises of himself with alacrity, and so a man should rise of himself with alacrity at the time of the morning Shema, that its time not pass. Maharsha adds that he afterwards found in Tanchuma that the preceding verse is cited — "Behold, a people that rises up like a lioness ... he shall not lie down until he devours the prey" — which suits this exposition of the morning and evening Shema better. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:12): When Bilam spoke them, his words were surely counted as profane among Israel, and so they truly were; only when Moses wrote them in the Torah scroll did they become holy and words of the living God — so much so that the Sages sought to fix the portion of Balak in the recitation of the Shema, for it holds great holiness, like the verse "Hear, O Israel." And it is good to bear these words on one's lips evening and morning, every day, constantly. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Balak 3): On the Gemara's statement that they sought to fix the portion of Balak in the Shema because of the verse "He crouched, he lay down like a lion," he asks what this verse — which, as Rashi explains, resembles "when you lie down and when you rise," for the Holy One, blessed be He, guards us when we lie down and rise — has to do with the Shema, which is the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and of the commandments. But the Midrash says that Bilam flattered Israel in his prophecies and made their hearts proud, so that they fell at Shittim — and this was through his saying "He crouched, he lay down"; and the Gemara there says that one who recites the Shema on his bed is as though holding a two-edged sword, whose main purpose is to slay the evil inclination. Sod Yesharim (Purim 3): My grandfather explained the verse "He crouched, he lay down like a lion": what might is evident in a lion once it has lain down, when a lion's might is praised only when it rises? But one who is not truly mighty cannot restrain himself from avenging himself at once upon his enemies, whereas one truly mighty and confident in his strength does not hasten, and can hold back until their measure is full and then repay them; so from his very crouching and lying down and refraining from vengeance, the greatness of his might is evident. עַמּוּד ב),
because it is stated therein: 'He couched, he lay down as a lion, etc.' (Numbers 24:9; as written in Berakhot 12b),
דְּגַם בִּשְׁעַת שְׁכִיבָה וְשֵׁינָה הוּא כַּאֲרִי,
signifying that even during lying down and sleep Israel remains mighty like a lion,
כְּטַעַם: "אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר" (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ה, ב),
mirroring: 'I sleep, but my heart is awake' (Song of Songs 5:2),

שֶׁעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה666 Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2 — "I am asleep, but my heart is awake" (Song of Songs 5:2). The congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, I am asleep with respect to the commandments, but my heart is awake for acts of kindness; I am asleep with respect to the redemption, but the heart of the Holy One, blessed be He, is awake to redeem me. R. Chiyya bar Abba said: Where do we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, is called the heart of Israel? From this verse: "God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever" (Psalms 73:26). Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The Blessed One always dwells in the depths of one's heart, as Shir HaShirim Rabbah says that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel — "the Rock of my heart and my portion" — and on this they expounded "I am asleep but my heart is awake": though a person is sunk in imagination, which is the sleep, the imagination does not reach the depths of the heart, where the point of "the Rock of his heart" is always awake, and through it he can awaken from his slumber and merit the complete redemption. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Sisa 7): [The Zohar reads] "Many of those who sleep in the dust shall awaken" with "I am asleep but my heart is awake": when the Blessed One dwells in the heart of Israel, as they said that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel ("God is the Rock of my heart and my portion forever"), death is only like sleep. Even though the flaw that brought death has not been repaired in the world at large, one who merits that his heart be a dwelling for the Shechinah is redeemed completely, and his death is only like sleep followed by awakening.): הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
concerning which our Sages said (Shir HaShirim Rabbah): the Holy One is the heart of Israel;
וַ"ה' יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב" (שְׁמוּאֵל א טז, ז) – אֵין מִסְתַּכֵּל אֶלָּא לִנְקֻדָּה זוֹ שֶׁבַּלֵּב.
and 'Hashem looks on the heart' (I Samuel 16:7)—He gazes exclusively into this inner point of the heart.

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "לֹא הִבִּיט אָוֶן וְגוֹמֵר" (בַּמִּדְבָּר כג, כא667 Numbers 23:21 — “He has beheld no iniquity in Yaakov, nor has He seen perverseness in Israel; the Lord his God is with him, and the King’s trumpet-blast is among him.” Rashi: Understand it as the Targum does; and by its plain sense it also yields a fine exposition. The Holy One, blessed be He, does not look at the iniquity in Jacob: when they transgress His words He does not deal strictly with them to scrutinize their misdeeds, "amal" meaning transgression, since sin is a vexation before the Omnipresent. "The Lord his God is with him" — even when they provoke Him and rebel before Him He does not stir from their midst; and "the teru'ah of a king is in him" is an expression of love and friendship, as Onkelos renders, "the Shekhinah of their King is among them." Ramban: The subject is God, mentioned above: He has beheld no iniquity or falsehood in Jacob, and has seen in them no perversity or provocation committed before Him, and therefore He is with them and the shout of His kingship is among them; this is the view of R. Abraham ibn Ezra, and it is correct. It may also be explained that "aven" and "amal" here mean deceit and falsehood: no one has seen in Israel any lie — their trust is not false and their hope is not vain, for all their blessings will be fulfilled forever. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 15): Bilam recognized Israel's virtue from the very beginning of their root: even though their sins have grown great, the root is good and was never entirely severed. Hence "How shall I curse whom God has not cursed" — even, as the Sages said, at a time when they deserved a curse — for "He has not beheld iniquity": that is, even though there is toil and iniquity in them. Sod Yesharim (Rosh Hashanah 51): "He has not beheld iniquity [aven] in Yaakov": even in the lowest level of Israel, when one looks into the depth of his heart, there is no obstinacy of the serpent's kind that would remove him entirely from the Blessed One's will, so as to be called aven; and "nor has He seen toil [amal] in Israel": when they are in the good state of "Israel," one can see plainly that they have no place for the deficiency of habit called amal. The reason is "the Lord his God is with him": in every soul of Israel there is a point by which it is bound to the Blessed One, and this point always goes with it, so that however far it strays it can never be removed from it.),
And concerning this Balaam proclaimed: 'He has not beheld iniquity, etc.' (Numbers 23:21),
שֶׁאֵין מִסְתַּכֵּל עַל הֶעָמָל וְהָאָוֶן כְּלָל,
meaning He looks not upon the outward labor and sin at all,
רַק אֶל אוֹתָהּ הַנְּקֻדָּה שֶׁ"ה' אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ וּתְרוּעַת מֶלֶךְ" וּרְצוֹנוֹ הוּא בוֹ בְּאוֹתָהּ נְקֻדָּה,
rather solely unto that inner point wherein 'Hashem his God is with him, and the shout/will of a king' is within him,
שֶׁבָּזֶה הוּא שְׁלֵמוּת מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת.
for in this resides the ultimate completion of the attribute of Sovereignty.
וְאֶפְשָׁר לְשׁוֹן "וּתְרוּעַת" לְשׁוֹן קוֹל תְּרוּעָה,
And it is possible that 'teruat' is an expression of the sound of the blast,
וְהוּא קוֹל שׁוֹפָר הַמְּעוֹרֵר הוּא בוֹ,
which is the voice of the shofar awakening him within,
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְעוֹרְרוֹ גַּם בְּלֹא דַּעְתּוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ,
wherein the Holy One stirs him even without his conscious knowledge and will,
וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ נְקֻדָּה שֶׁבַּלֵּב שֶׁדְּבוּקָה בְּכָל אִישׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and this operates through that point of the heart which remains clinging in every Jew unto Hashem.
וְנִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיַן שׁוֹפָר דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לְעוֹרֵר אוֹתָהּ נְקֻדָּה,
And it appears that this is likewise the purpose of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah: to awaken that point;
כִּי בְּכָל הַשָּׁנָה "ה' יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב" לְבַד,
for throughout the year 'Hashem looks on the heart' alone,
וְהַיְנוּ דְּמַבִּיט אֶל צוּרַת אָדָם שֶׁל כְּלַל הַקּוֹמָה.
meaning He looks upon the Form of Adam representing the collective stature.
אֲבָל בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כָּל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם עוֹבְרִים כִּבְנֵי מָרוֹן,
However, on Rosh Hashanah all who enter the world pass before Him like bnei maron,

וּמְפָרְשִׁים בַּגְּמָרָא668 Rosh Hashanah 18a — Two men took to their sickbeds with the same illness; one recovered and one did not. Why? This one prayed a complete prayer and was answered; that one did not pray a complete prayer, and was not answered. Rashi: "To the scaffold" — a house of assembly where capital cases are tried for execution. "And their judgment was the same" — both had been seized on the same charge. "This one came down" — from the bed; "this one was saved" — from the tribunal. "A complete prayer" — he directed his intent. Maharsha (s.v. "two who went up to bed"): They are compared in the same way in chapter Bameh Madlikin [Shabbat 32a], where it is said that one who went up to his bed and fell ill should regard himself as though he had been brought up to the scaffold, and it concludes there, "These are a man's advocates: repentance and good deeds"; the same holds for prayer, as we say here, "this one prayed and was answered, and that one prayed and was not answered." [The baraita] could just as well have said "and that one did not pray at all," but it teaches that even if he prayed, if [his prayer] was not complete he was not answered. (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח עַמּוּד א): דְּהַיְנוּ בְּזֶה אַחַר זֶה.
and they explain in the Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 18a): meaning one by one in single file.
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם נִסְקָרִים בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת,
Yet nonetheless they are surveyed in a single glance,
דִּכְתִיב: "הַיֹּצֵר יַחַד לִבָּם, הַמֵּבִין אֶל כָּל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם" (תְּהִלִּים לג, טו).
for it is written: 'He fashions their hearts together, He considers all their deeds' (Psalms 33:15).
פֵּרוּשׁ: דְּמִצַּד הַלֵּב הֵם יַחַד לְקוֹמָה אֶחָד וְנִסְקָרִים כְּאֶחָד גַּם בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה,
The explanation: from the aspect of the heart they are bound together as one stature, surveyed as one on Rosh Hashanah;
רַק מִצַּד מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם הֵם עוֹבְרִים כָּל אֶחָד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ לִהְיוֹת לְקוֹמָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ.
only from the aspect of their deeds do they pass individually, each standing as a separate stature in his own right.
וְלָכֵן נִרְאֶה חֶסְרוֹנוֹ בִּפְרָט,
Therefore his specific deficiency becomes exposed,
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ מַעֲלָה מְיֻחֶדֶת שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא מְדֻגָּל לִקָּבַע בִּכְלַל הַקּוֹמָה בְּמָקוֹם מְיֻחָד,
even though each individual possesses a unique virtue through which he is distinguished to be set within the collective stature in a specific place;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ לְקוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁהוּא מָלֵא חֶסְרוֹנוֹת.
nonetheless, viewed as an independent complete stature, he may be full of shortcomings.
וְלָכֵן בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ב, לג עַמּוּד ב)
Therefore on Rosh Hashanah the Zohar teaches (Part II, 33b)
עַל פָּסוּק "בְּתוֹךְ עַמִּי אָנֹכִי יֹשָׁבֶת" (מְלָכִים ב ד, יג): שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה מְדֻגָּל בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ.
on the verse 'I dwell among my own people' (II Kings 4:13): that one should not stand out alone.
וְגַם דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: "וְנִסְקָרִים בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת" הוּא הַמְתָּקָה לְמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּשְׁנָה "כִּבְנֵי מָרוֹן",
And our Sages' dictum that 'they are surveyed in a single glance' sweetens the Mishnah's statement 'like bnei maron';
דְּמִצַּד מִדַּת הַמִּשְׁפָּט הוּא לְפַקֵּחַ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה כָּל אֶחָד בִּפְרָט,
for strict Justice scrutinizes the deeds of each person in detail,
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם לְפִי שֶׁהֵם בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת מַה שֶּׁחָסֵר זֶה מַשְׁלִים זֶה.
yet because they are viewed in a single glance, what one lacks the other completes.

וְרַק בְּמִנְיָן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי אָדָם צָרִיךְ כֹּפֶר נֶפֶשׁ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בָהֶם וְגוֹמֵר669 Exodus 30:12 — “When you take the sum of the Children of Israel according to their numbers, each man shall give a ransom for his soul to the Lord when counting them, so that there shall be no plague among them when they are counted.” Rashi: "When you take" is an expression of receiving, as the Targum renders it: when you wish to receive the sum of their number, to know how many they are, do not count them by heads, but let each one give a half-shekel, and you shall count the shekels and know their number. "That there be no plague among them" — because a count is subject to the evil eye and pestilence comes upon them, as we find in the days of David. Ramban: The Holy One, blessed be He, commanded that whenever Moses takes the head-count of Israel they are to give a ransom for their souls, a half-shekel, and He told him "you shall take the atonement money and give it for the service of the Tent of Meeting"; Scripture did not need to add that he should count them now, since that is understood of itself, and so the commandment is framed generally, to take in every occasion on which he counts them. And because it was not made explicit here whether this is a commandment for the generations or only for Moses in the wilderness, David erred and numbered the people without shekels, and the plague came upon them.,
And only in a census conducted by human hands is an atonement ransom required 'that there be no plague, etc.,'
וְהוּא מִטַּעַם זֶה דִּבְמִנְיָן כָּל אֶחָד נִמְנֶה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ וְכָל אֶחָד מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ מָלֵא חֶסְרוֹנוֹת.
and this is because in a human count each individual is enumerated separately, and on his own he is full of deficiencies.
אֲבָל אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אַף שֶׁ"עוֹד תַּעֲבֹרְנָה הַצֹּאן עַל יְדֵי מוֹנֶה" שֶׁזֶּהוּ "כִּבְנֵי מָרוֹן" לְמַאן דְּאָמַר כִּבְנֵי אִמְּרָנָא,
However, before Hashem, even though 'the flocks shall pass again under the hands of him who counts them'—which is bnei maron according to the authority who defines it as sheep—
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין זֶה מוֹנֶה גָּמוּר כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הֵם בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת.
nonetheless it is not an absolute mortal count, for in truth they are perceived in a single glance.
כִּי עִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁבְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כָּל אֶחָד נִדּוֹן בִּפְרָט,
For the reason why on Rosh Hashanah each person is judged individually
לְפִי שֶׁאָז מִתְעוֹרֶרֶת מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁהִיא הַגּוֹרֶמֶת לִבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם,
is because then the attribute of Sovereignty awakens, which prompted the creation of the world;
דְּאֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם וּ"בְּרָב עָם הַדְרַת מֶלֶךְ" (מִשְׁלֵי יד, כח),
for there is no king without a nation, and 'in the multitude of people is the king's glory' (Proverbs 14:28),
וּמִצַּד זֶה צָרִיךְ רִבּוּי עָם.
and from this perspective an expansive multitude of people is required.
וְהָרִבּוּי הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַרְבֵּה בְּנֵי אָדָם שׁוֹנִים וְנִפְרָדִים זֶה מִזֶּה וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי קוֹמָה אֶחָד שְׁלֵמָה,
And multitude exists through many human beings who are distinct and differentiated from one another, not through a single merged stature;
וּמִצַּד זֶה הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת לְפָנָיו בְּכָל פְּרָטֵי הַיְּצוּרִים.
and from this perspective His consideration focuses upon all the particulars of creations.
וְזֶהוּ מַאן דְּאָמַר: "כְּחַיָּלוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית דָּוִד", דְּהַיְנוּ הַדְרַת מֶלֶךְ כַּנִּזְכָּר.
And this explains the opinion 'like the legions of the house of David'—which embodies the king's glory as mentioned.
וּמַאן דְּאָמַר: "כְּמַעֲלוֹת בֵּית מָרוֹן",
And the opinion 'like the ascent of Beit Maron' reflects that
כִּי אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְבּוֹנֵן בְּכָל מַה שֶּׁפָּעַל בִּבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם וְנִבְרָאִים וְנוֹצָרִים וְנַעֲשִׂים עַד קְצֵה עוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה.
Hashem then contemplates all that He wrought in Creation, across all entities through to the edge of the World of Action.
וְזֶה נִקְרָא מַעֲלוֹת בֵּית מָרוֹן:
And this is termed the steep ascent of Beit Maron:
שֶׁאֲצִילוּת קָדְשׁוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת עַד אֵין קֵץ,
for His holy Atzilut is an infinite, boundless expansion,
רַק נִבְרָאִים הוֹלְכִים וּמִצְטַמְצְמִים.
whereas created beings become progressively constricted.
וְהָעֲלִיָּה לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא רַק עוֹלִין מַעְלָה מַעְלָה בְּדֶרֶךְ צַר מְאֹד,
And the ascent before Him proceeds upward along an exceedingly narrow ridge,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב670 Berakhot 6a — It was taught: Abba Binyamin says — were permission given to the eye to see, no creature could withstand the harmful spirits. Abaye said: They outnumber us, and they stand about us like the ridge around a field. Rashi: like the ridge of a trench that is made around the vines. Rashi: "To see" — all the demons that stand before him. "Like the ridge around a field" — like the line of digging that surrounds the basin made beneath vines, as we learned, "one may not make basins for vines," that is, to gather water there to irrigate the vine; the ridge is the furrow of a plough running all around the mound of the basin, the vine being planted on the mound. Tosafos (s.v. "like the ridge around a field"): Like the furrows that surround a garden bed, as we say at the beginning of Nedarim, "let this bed be [designated as] pe'ah." ([בְּרָכוֹת ו עַמּוּד א]): "וְקָיְמָא עֲלַן כִּכְסָלָא לְאוּגְיָא",
as written (Berakhot 6a): 'and they stand around us like a trench around a garden bed',
"יִפֹּל מִשִּׂמְאלְךָ אֶלֶף וּרְבָבָה מִימִינֶךָ אֵלֶיךָ לֹא יִגָּשׁ" (תְּהִלִּים צא, ז),
'A thousand may fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but it shall not approach you' (Psalms 91:7),
וְזֶהוּ צִמְצוּם מְקוֹם הַדָּרֶךְ.
and this illustrates the constriction of the path.
וְנִמְצָא: הַפֵּרוּשׁ דְּחַיָּלוֹת בֵּית דָּוִד הוּא שֶׁמִּצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וַהֲדָרָתוֹ הוּא לִהְיוֹת הָעִיּוּן בִּפְרָטִים;
Thus the legions of David mean that from Hashem's perspective and His glory scrutiny is cast upon particulars;
וּפֵרוּשׁ דְּבֵית מָרוֹן הוּא מִצַּד הַמָּקוֹם,
while Beit Maron is from the vantage point of location,
לְפִי שֶׁהַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה הוּא בָּעוֹלָמוֹת הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים וּמְקוֹמוֹת הַשְּׁפֵלִים,
since on Rosh Hashanah Hashem's providence reaches into the lower worlds and humble realms,
וְשָׁם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בָּהֶם אֶלָּא אֶחָד אֶחָד.
where it is impossible to scrutinize them except one by one.
וּפֵרוּשׁ דִּכְבְנֵי אִמְּרָנָא הוּא מִצַּד הַנִּבְרָאִים עַצְמָם:
And the interpretation of bnei imrana (sheep) is from the perspective of the creatures themselves:
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהוּא מְחַיֶּה הַכֹּל,
for since Hashem is the heart of Israel and animates all,
כַּאֲשֶׁר מִתְעוֹרֵר מִדָּה זוֹ לְמַעְלָה כֵּן מִתְעוֹרֶרֶת בְּלִבּוֹת כָּל הַנִּבְרָאִים לִהְיוֹת כָּל אֶחָד מְצֻיָּן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
when this attribute stirs Above it stirs in the hearts of all creatures to stand distinct,
וּבָזֶה הֲרֵי הֵם מִתְרָאִים כָּךְ לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּל אֶחָד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ.
and so they present themselves before Hashem, each one separately.
וְאוֹרַיְתָא יָהֲבָא עֵיטִין לַכֹּל,
And the Torah provides counsels for all,

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה טז671 Rosh Hashanah 16a — The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Recite before Me on Rosh HaShana Kingships, Remembrances, and Shofarot — Kingships, so that you crown Me as king over you; Remembrances, so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good; and with what? With the shofar. Tosafos (s.v. "with a ram's shofar"): In chapter Ra'uhu Beit Din (26a) the Mishnah records that R. Yosei validates even a cow's horn; but we hold in accordance with R. Yehuda that one sounds with bent rams' horns, as the Gemara rules there (26b). Maharsha (s.v. "recite before Me Kingships"): The Sifrei derives them from the verse "And you shall sound… and they shall be to you for a remembrance… I am the Lord your God" (Numbers 10:10): "you shall sound" — these are Shofarot; "for a remembrance" — these are Remembrances; "I am the Lord your God" — this is Kingships. The intent of Kingships, Remembrances and Shofarot is explained in the chapter "How is the order of fasts" [Taanit, ch. 2]. Maharsha (s.v. "why do we sound a ram's horn"): The Ran explains that [R. Abbahu] asks this about the mere custom of sounding with a ram's horn; but it seems to me that he asks it on the Mishnah in chapter Ra'uhu Beit Din, "R. Yehuda says: On Rosh Hashanah one sounds with [the horns] of males," which is the accepted halachah. This follows the Midrash that Rashi cites on the Torah, that the yovel is a ram's horn (for in Arabic a ram is called yovla), since we derive the shofar of Rosh Hashanah below [in chapter 2] from the shofar of the Jubilee. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 16a, s.v. "Kingships, Remembrances, Shofarot"): Kingships: the Blessed One is King, and as King He comes to judge; therefore Remembrances follow, for remembrance is not judgment — on the contrary, it recalls what was forgotten, and since He remembers everything, reaching what is deep and inward, He remembers Israel for good, and by this they are saved from the attribute of judgment. And this is "by the shofar," for the tekia signifies elevation, and all elevation is mercy, as the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 29): when Israel take up their shofars and sound them, the Holy One, blessed be He, rises from the throne of judgment and sits upon the throne of mercy. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 16a, s.v. "with a ram's shofar"): Rosh Hashanah is the day of judgment, and when they sound a ram's horn it is as though the judgment had already been carried out, for He remembers the binding of Yitzchak, who was bound before the Holy One, blessed be He, as though judgment had been executed upon him. "I shall account it to you" because the father is the root of the son: when the father, the root of the lineage, was bound, the branch resembles him, for Israel too give themselves over to the honor of the Blessed One. In sum, the ram signifies binding and submission to the attribute of judgment, and by giving over our souls to the Blessed One we are saved from the Accuser — which is also why [the shofars] must be bent. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 13): Rosh HaShanah is the Day of Remembrance, for when a person remembers the Blessed One, the Blessed One remembers the person; this too is the matter of the shofar, of which the Sages said, "so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good — with what? With the shofar." Rambam wrote that the shofar hints, "Awake, sleepers, from your slumber … remember your Creator," for it was their way to rouse the people by sounding the shofar; and it is all one — their remembering the Blessed One and their remembrance rising before Him. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeitzei 3): The holiness of Rosh HaShanah, the Day of Remembrance — "so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good, and with what? With the shofar" — is present on the Sabbath to a greater degree; therefore when Rosh HaShanah falls on the Sabbath there is no need to raise our remembrance before Him for good through the act of the shofar, for [the Sabbath] is in itself a day of remembrance. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Rosh HaShanah): In Remembrances the benefit is explicit, but what is the benefit in reciting Kingships? Though a person imagines that the yoke of Heaven's kingship is servitude, in truth it is the true freedom from every servitude in the world, for where the Blessed One dwells no evil draws near, and one who crowns the Blessed One over himself is entirely free; so the Blessed One counsels Israel that in the days of Rosh HaShanah the word "King" be habitual on their lips, a safeguard from all evil. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh HaShanah 15): "Recite before Me Kingships... so that you crown Me": since the Blessed One desires Israel's crowning of Him, a person is obligated to crown Him over himself in every detail. "Remembrances, so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good" — but what has remembrance to do with the Blessed One, when there is no forgetting before His Throne of Glory? Rather it is from the human side, for a person has many distractions and must fix in himself that none will divert him, and "with what? With the shofar" — only through the shofar can he fix this recognition, for the shofar indicates that a person stations himself in the inner voice. Sod Yesharim (Rosh HaShanah 17): "Recite before Me Remembrances" — that you always bring yourselves near before Me and do not stand far off, behind; as much as a person fixes in his heart the awareness that he always stands before the Blessed One and is watched over every moment, so does the Blessed One truly watch over him. "With what? With the shofar" — a person fixes such awareness by contracting his own desires so as to want only the simple will of the Blessed One, and this contraction is called shofar. עַמּוּד א):
and on this they said (Rosh Hashanah 16a):
אִמְרוּ לְפָנַי מַלְכִיּוֹת שֶׁתַּמְלִיכוּנִי עֲלֵיכֶם –
Recite before Me Kingship verses so that you make Me King over you –
זֶהוּ נֶגֶד כְּחַיָּלוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית דָּוִד,
this corresponds to 'legions of the house of David',
מֵאַחַר שֶׁאָנוּ מַמְלִיכִים אוֹתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עָלֵינוּ וְאָנוּ מֵחֵילוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ,
since we crown Him King over us and count as the King's soldiers;

וְאֵין בּוֹדְקִין אַחַר הַמֻּכְתָּב בָּאִסְטְרַטְיָא שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ בְּחַיָּלוֹת שֶׁל בֵּית דָּוִד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (עו672 Kiddushin 76a — R. Chanina ben Antigonus says: Even one who was enrolled in the king’s army — for such a one is not appointed to the priesthood without examining his lineage. And in the Gemara: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel — in the forces of the house of David. Rav Yosef said: What is the verse? “And they mustered themselves in the army for war.” And what is the reason? Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: So that their merit and the merit of their fathers should aid them. Rashi (76b, s.v. "in the military troops of the House of David"): They served in rotation, month by month in a recurring cycle — and this is the sense of "army list" — and they were entered by name, such and such a family in such a month; and they were careful to record their lineage as free of any blemish, as the Gemara goes on to explain, so that the merit of their fathers should aid them in battle. עַמּוּד א)],
and we do not scrutinize the lineage of one enlisted in the King's army in the legions of David, as in Kiddushin (76a),
וְגַם עַל יְדֵי זֶה אָנוּ חוֹזְרִים לְהִתְאַחֵד לִהְיוֹת צָבָא וְלִגְיוֹן אֶחָד מִצִּבְאוֹתָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ,
and through this we reunite into one single legion among His supernal hosts,
וְאָנוּ גּוֹי אֶחָד בָּאָרֶץ.
standing as 'one nation in the earth.'
וְאָמְרוּ: "זִכְרוֹנוֹת שֶׁיַּעֲלֶה זִכְרוֹנֵיכֶם לְפָנַי וְכוּלֵי" –
And they taught: 'Recite Remembrances that your remembrance ascend before Me, etc.' –
זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַזְּכִירָה עַצְמָהּ וְנֶגֶד מַעֲלַת בֵּית מָרוֹן,
this corresponds to the remembrance itself and counterbalances the steep ascent of Beit Maron;
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁאוֹמְרִים שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַזּוֹכֵר מִמֵּילָא נִתְרַחֵב הַמָּקוֹם וְאֵין שָׁם צִמְצוּם,
for by proclaiming that Hashem is the One Who remembers, the space broadens and constriction vanishes,
וַהֲרֵי הַזִּכָּרוֹן לְטוֹבָה כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צוֹפֶה רַק לְטוֹבָה וְ"לֹא הִבִּיט אָוֶן וְגוֹמֵר".
and remembrance is always for good, for Hashem gazes only for good and 'has not beheld iniquity, etc.'
וּבַמֶּה? בְּשׁוֹפָר, הוּא אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּנְבְרָאִים.
And through what? Through the shofar, which represents the awakening of created beings.
נֶגֶד כִּבְנֵי אִמְּרָנָא תּוֹקְעִין בְּשׁוֹפָר שֶׁל אַיִל לְהַזְכִּיר עֲקֵדַת יִצְחָק שֶׁהוּא הַמְּסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
Countering bnei imrana (sheep) we sound the ram's horn to evoke the Binding of Isaac, which is self-sacrifice unto Hashem.
כִּי תְּקִיעַת שׁוֹפָר הוּא לֶאֱסֹף הָעָם שֶׁיִּהְיוּ יַחַד,
For sounding the shofar gathers the people to be united,
וְגַם לְהַחֲרִיד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְהָעָם לֹא יֶחֱרָדוּ" (עָמוֹס ג, ו);
and inspires trembling awe, as it is written: 'shall not the people tremble?' (Amos 3:6);
וּמִתּוֹךְ הַחֲרָדָה הֵם מִתְאַסְּפִין יַחַד,
and out of this trembling they assemble together,
וְכָל אֶחָד מְבַטֵּל עַצְמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה מְצֻיָּן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ.
and each person nullifies his ego so as not to stand out independently.
וְזֶהוּ הַמְּסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ:
And this is the true essence of self-sacrifice unto Hashem:
שֶׁהָאִתְעָרוּתָא אָז הוּא לְהִצְטַיֵּן כָּל אֶחָד בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
though the natural impulse then is for each to assert himself individually,
רַק שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ הַהַכָּרָה דְּעֹל מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְחֶרְדַּת הַיּוֹם הוּא מִתְבַּטֵּל מֵעַצְמוּתוֹ וְהִצְטַיְּנוּתוֹ,
yet through awareness of His Kingship and the dread of the Day he nullifies his selfhood and distinctiveness,
וּבָזֶה מִמֵּילָא הַכֹּל לְטוֹבָה.
and through this all things spontaneously resolve for the good.

sections.en: Torah, Mitzvot, and the Light of Teshuvah

items.h: Torah and mitzvot illuminate the path through this world's darkness, while repentance transforms darkness itself into a greater and more penetrating light.

Seif 1 — The Lamp, the Light, and the Power of Teshuvah
Torah and mitzvot guide through darkness, while teshuvah converts darkness itself into a more intense light.

p: הַתּוֹרָה וְהַמִּצְוֹת הֵם רַק הֶאָרוֹת לְגוּף הַמְּכֻוָּן שֶׁיֵּשׁ מִבְּרִיאַת הָאָדָם.
The Torah and the commandments are merely illuminations guiding toward the core objective of the creation of man.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "נֵר מִצְוָה וְתוֹרָה אוֹר673 Proverbs 6:23 — “For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light, and reproofs of instruction are the way of life.” Rashi: Just as light gives light to the world always, so does the merit of the Torah stand for a man forever, while the merit of a commandment lasts only for a time, like the light of a lamp. “And reproofs of instruction are the way of life” — reproofs of instruction incline a man toward life, so they are found to be the way of life. Metzudas Dovid: The commandment a man performs gives him light like a lamp, and the Torah he studies is to him as the light of day; and one who listens to reproofs of instruction — this is for him a way that brings him to life. Malbim: The commandment, which is particular, is likened to a lamp, which is particular, and the Torah, which is general, is likened to light, which is general. The lamp burns only so long as there are oil and wick, and so the commandment belongs to a man only while he is confined in a body; but light shines of itself, and so the light of the Torah cleaves to the soul, since the soul is divine. And though a man has light and lamp he must still walk in the way of life, and what leads him there is “reproofs of instruction”." (מִשְׁלֵי ו, כג),
And as it is written: 'For a commandment is a lamp, and Torah is light' (Proverbs 6:23),
שֶׁהֵם מְאִירִים לְהַגִּיעַ אֶל הַמְּכֻוָּן שֶׁהוּא דֶּרֶךְ חַיִּים,
meaning they illuminate the path to reach the ultimate intent, which is the way of life,

שֶׁמְּהַלְּכִין בְּדֶרֶךְ זֶה בְּאִישׁוֹן לַיְלָה וַאֲפֵלָה (סוֹטָה כא674 Sotah 21a — This is comparable to a man walking in the blackness of night and the darkness, who fears the thorns and the pits and the thistles, and the wild beasts and the bandits, and does not know which way he is walking. If a torch of fire comes his way, he is saved from the thorns and the pits and the thistles, but he still fears the wild beasts and the bandits, and still does not know which way he is walking. Once the light of dawn rises, he is saved from the wild beasts and the bandits, but he still does not know which way he is walking. When he reaches the crossroads, he is saved from them all. Rashi: The torch: so too one who merited to fulfill a mitzva is saved from some of the punishments, yet he still fears the wild beasts and bandits, whose way is to prowl at night, as it is written: "You make darkness and it is night, in which all the beasts of the forest creep forth" (Psalms 104:20). Even after dawn he "still does not know" — lest his inclination compel him to neglect [the Torah] and so bring the evil inclination and punishment back upon him. At the crossroads he recognizes his way: so too one who reaches the day of his death without having departed from the Torah is saved from them all, as the Gemara explains below. Maharsha: Man is composed of body and soul: the body performs the mitzvot and the soul, which is his intellect, engages in contemplation, which is the Torah. Just as a torch at night saves one from thorns, pits and thistles, so the mitzvot, the perfection of the body, save a person in this world, which is likened to night, from the three calamities that befall the body — famine (the thorns, as in "thorns and thistles shall it bring forth"), pestilence (the pits, the grave into which one falls) and the enemy's sword (the thistles). The wild beasts and bandits allude to the two things that bar the perfection of the soul and bring a man to sin — the evil inclination and the enticement of a wicked man — and from these he is saved not by the merit of the mitzva but only by the merit of the Torah, the perfection of the soul, likened to dawn, as they said of the evil inclination: "If this repulsive one meets you, drag him to the study hall." Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 21a): Thorns and pits are what a man walks into of his own accord in the dark, and a torch keeps him from them, whereas wild beasts and bandits pursue him though he does not go to them, and only day, when they have no dominion, rids him of them. So too man, in the dark physical world, goes of himself toward evil: the mitzvot of the Torah, which are called a light, guard him like a torch from the evil that stems from himself but cannot save him from the harms that pursue him, while the Torah, which is "light" — and "God called the light day" (Genesis 1:5) — saves him from those as well. And "he still does not know which way he is walking," for even the Torah does not set him on the path directly facing the Holy One, blessed be He, without veering right or left; only when he reaches the crossroads does he know that he walks the straight path before Him. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 15): This world is likened to night, and so in Sotah [the parable] of one walking in the blackness of night and darkness until he reaches the crossroads, which is the day of death — that is, from the standpoint of the man who walks in it. So too the Blessed One, whose kingship rules over all: in this world it is in darkness, for His light is not revealed and His rule is only concealed, as it is said, "He made darkness His hiding place." עַמּוּד א),
for one travels upon this path in the dark of night and gloom (Sotah 21a),
שֶׁעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִמְשַׁל לְלַיְלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ פְּסָחִים,
since this world is allegorized to night as written at the beginning of Pesachim,
כִּי אֵין אָדָם רוֹאֶה וְיוֹדֵעַ כְּלָל מַה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ מִמֶּנּוּ בְּיִחוּד וְעַל מַה הוּא נִבְרָא בָּעוֹלָם.
for man cannot see or know at all what Hashem, blessed be He, uniquely desires of him and for what purpose he was created in the world.
וְ"כָל דֶּרֶךְ אִישׁ יָשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו" (מִשְׁלֵי כא, ב),
And 'every way of a man is right in his own eyes' (Proverbs 21:2),

וְהוּא כְּטַעַם (בְּרָכוֹת מג675 Berakhot 43b — R. Zutra bar Toviya said in the name of Rav: What is meant by "He has made everything beautiful in its time"? It teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, made each and every man's own craft seem fine in his eyes. Rashi: "His craft seems fine to him" — even a tanner finds his craft pleasing in his own eyes; and the Holy One, blessed be He, made it so in order that the world should not lack any craft. Maharsha: "In its time" means at the hour of the decree, when it was decreed what a man's occupation should be, it was decreed together with it that his craft should seem fine to him — even a craft that is despised and lowly, as they said (Kiddushin 82b), the world cannot exist without a perfumer and without a tanner. And the verse continues, "He has also set the world in their heart" — He set it in the heart of every craftsman that his craft is fine for him, "so that man should not find out the work" — that is, some other work and craft; for what God has done is that a man stand by his craft from beginning to end. עַמּוּד ב): יִפָּה לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְכָל אֶחָד אֻמָּנוּתוֹ בְּפָנָיו.
mirroring (Berakhot 43b): the Holy One, blessed be He, made each person's trade seem pleasant to him.
כִּי כָּל אָדָם נִבְרָא לְצֹרֶךְ מְיֻחָד בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
For every person was created for a specific purpose in this world,
וּלְקִלּוּס מְיֻחָד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ מִמֶּנּוּ בְּיִחוּד לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and for a distinct praise that should ascend specifically through him unto Hashem, blessed be He.

כִּי "כֹּל פָּעַל לַמַּעֲנֵהוּ" – לְקִלּוּסוֹ (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר יט676 Midrash Tehillim 19:1 — "For the leader. A psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God." This is what Scripture says: "The Lord has made everything for His own sake" (Proverbs 16:4) — for His praise, as it is said, "Sing to the Lord with thanksgiving" (Psalms 147:7). Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): The aim of the whole Torah is to come to a complete apprehension that there is a Creator, Ruler and Overseer, which was the purpose of the creation of the world: "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. All 613 commandments are counsels for reaching this, for the Torah is called truth, being counsels for reaching a clear apprehension in the heart, so manifest that it needs no faith. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 6): Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created for His glory, He created to reveal the glory of His kingship and His Presence among the lower beings, and "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. The building of the Tabernacle and the Temple is man's work of building a place for His Presence after the sin, when the Presence is not revealed everywhere, in the pattern of the Blessed One's work in creation; had man not sinned, the whole world would have been a Tabernacle and a Sanctuary. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The angels cry, "Where is the place of His glory?", but man grasps the Throne of Glory, for "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise; the purpose of creation is the revelation of His glory, and its purpose is man. For the chief revelation of glory is when a person with free choice, whose body inclines toward impurity, nevertheless subdues his inclination and desires for the sake of Heaven's honor, which the angels, who have no evil inclination, cannot attain at all.).
For 'Hashem has made everything for His sake' (Proverbs 16:4)—for His praise (Shocher Tov, Psalm 19).
וְכָל חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִקְרָא הִלּוּךְ
And all of life in this world is designated 'walking,'

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה כא677 Sotah 21a — The Torah is compared to light, to tell you: just as light protects forever, so too the Torah protects forever. And it says: "When you walk, it shall lead you; when you lie down, it shall watch over you; and when you awake, it shall talk with you" (Proverbs 6:22). "When you walk, it shall lead you" — this is in this world. "When you lie down, it shall watch over you" — this is death. "And when you awake, it shall talk with you" — this is in the world to come. Rashi: "It shall talk with you" — it will plead your merit on your behalf. Maharsha: This verse, which immediately precedes "For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light," also speaks of the Torah and teaches that it protects forever: in this world "it shall lead you" — in the sense of giving you rest from all troubles; when you lie in the grave "it shall watch over you" against the beating of the grave; and in the World to Come "it shall talk with you," pleading on your behalf against the judgment of Gehinnom. As for Tosafot's difficulty — that by the Gemara's conclusion a mitzva too protects forever — a mitzva protects forever only in this world, whereas the Torah protects even in the World to Come from the judgment of Gehinnom, as the verse "and when you awake it shall talk with you" shows. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 21a): The Torah is intellectual, and whatever is intellectual does not fall under time; therefore it protects forever, as befits that which is beyond time and has no change, whereas the mitzva, like everything physical, falls under time and comes to an end, and so protects only for the moment. And since light signifies complete existence — without light nothing has existence, which is why a blind man is considered as though dead — one who holds fast to the Torah, which is complete light, cannot be abandoned by it to nonexistence: in this world, where a man is a "walker" who has no rest and may do something that brings him to ruin, it leads him; after death, the time of dissolution, it guards him from loss and gives him existence; and in the time to come, when he returns to life, it gives him speech, which is life — "it shall talk with you." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 10): Death stems from the first corruption of Adam, and its repair is through occupation with words of Torah, of which it is said: "When you walk it shall lead you" — this is this world; "when you lie down it shall watch over you" — this is death; "and when you awake it shall talk with you" — in the time to come. For then, at the resurrection of the dead, the clarification will be complete, [showing] that death was only like sleep in this world, as the Sages called death "when he lay down to sleep," and the dew of Torah revives him. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): The world is full of turmoil and has no rest; therefore they said, "When you walk it shall lead you" — in this world, for this world is the time of walking, since "man is born to toil." But there are those whose toil is with knowledge and skill in deed, and whose walking is in holiness. The angels are called "standing," for they remain on the one level at which they were created, but man walks constantly from level to level and has no rest, like the righteous mentioned above — and this is truly the ultimate rest. Beis Yaakov (Vayeishev 5): One who has no words of Torah has none of the good itself, for through words of Torah a person is awakened to all good things, as they expounded: "When you walk it shall lead you" — in this world; "when you lie down it shall watch over you" — this is death; "and when you awake it shall talk with you" — in the time to come. In the time to come the Blessed One will fill the treasuries of Israel and reveal to their eyes the light hidden in the performance of the mitzvos, and then they will see that all the knowledge, intentions and lights Israel had in this world were like a dream compared to its interpretation. עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ",
as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sotah 21a) on the verse 'when you walk',
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי הֹלֵךְ הָאָדָם אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת יב, ה),
and as it is stated: 'because man goes to his eternal home' (Ecclesiastes 12:5),

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב)678 Shemot Rabbah 52:3 — She said to him: Rabbi, does a man see his fellow in the World to Come? Does not each and every righteous man have a world to himself, as it is said, "For the man goes to his eternal home [beit olamo], and the mourners go about the streets"? It is not written olamim, in the plural, but olamo — his own world. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 3): [Against those who believe only in the creation before their eyes,] the Sages explained in several places that there exist different worlds, clear and recognizable to the eyes of the discerning though not to the fleshly eyes of fools — as on the verse "for man goes to his eternal home": "each righteous man has a world of his own.": כָּל אָדָם יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
and our Sages taught (Shemot Rabbah, Parashah 52): each person possesses a world unto himself,
וְהוּא שְׁלֵמוּת נַפְשׁוֹ בְּכָל קוֹמָתָהּ,
which is the perfection of his soul throughout its entire stature;

שֶׁהָאָדָם נִקְרָא עוֹלָם קָטָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּקּוּנִים (רֵישׁ תִּקּוּן סט679 Tikkunei Zohar 100b — This is a great secret that I have heard. And as for what He said [to R. Pedat], "Would you have Me destroy the world? Perhaps you would then be born in an hour of sustenance" — thus indeed have I heard: every single righteous man has a world of his own, and that is a person's body, which is called a small world. Therefore He said: Would you have Me destroy his world and bring him back in another body, and perhaps you would then fall in an hour of sustenance.).
for man is termed a microcosm, as written in Tikkunei Zohar (beginning of Tikkun 69).
וּמִסְפַּר יְמֵי חַיִּים הַקְּצוּבִים לְכָל אָדָם
And the number of lifespan days allocated to each person
הֵם מִסְפַּר הַיָּמִים שֶׁקָּצַב לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
are the exact days Hashem, blessed be He, decreed for him,
שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ בָּהֶם בְּהִלּוּכוֹ מֶשֶׁךְ זְמַן הַהוּא אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ, הַיְנוּ שְׁלֵמוּת נַפְשׁוֹ.
wherein during that lifespan he can arrive through his journey unto his eternal home—meaning the perfection of his soul.

וְנֶאֱמַר: "נֵר לְרַגְלִי וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קה680 Psalms 119:105 — “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” Rashi: When I come to render a decision of law, I look into the Torah and it keeps me apart from what is forbidden, like a lamp that saves a man from falling into pits. Radak: Like one who walks in the dark and will not stumble on his way if there is a lamp before him, so are Your words as a lamp before me, warning me not to sin. Metzudas Dovid: Just as a lamp saves a man in the darkness of night from every obstacle, so that his foot not strike against it, so does Your word save me from every stumbling block of transgression; “and a light to my path” repeats the matter in other words. Malbim: One who walks on a road needs a great light shining from afar to show him the path he is to take, and a small lamp to light the ground beside his foot so that he not walk upon thorns and stones of stumbling. So Your words are “a lamp to my feet,” that I not stumble, as I walk in the way of the Lord, over one of the obstacles — such as studying in order to provoke, or being arrogant in rendering decisions — and a great light to show him the path, that he not stray into the ways of death.),
And it is said: 'Your word is a lamp unto my feet, etc.' (Psalms 119:105),
שֶׁהַנֵּר מֵאִיר רַק לִמְקוֹם הַעֲמָדַת הָרֶגֶל לָדַעַת הֵיכָן לְהַעֲמִידָהּ שָׁם בִּמְקוֹמוֹ,
for a lamp illuminates only the immediate stepping place to know where to set one's foot there in its place,
וְאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּרִחוּק מָקוֹם דֶּרֶךְ יוֹתֵר טוֹב
and it is possible that further along there lies a better route
וְצָרִיךְ לְהִתְרַחֵק מִמְּקוֹם עֲמִידַת רַגְלוֹ לְיָמִין אוֹ לִשְׂמֹאל,
requiring him to shift from where his foot currently stands toward the right or left,
וְזֶה אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר כָּל הַנָּתִיב.
and this he cannot know except through the broad light that illuminates the whole path.
וְכֵן הַמִּצְוָה הוּא נֵר לָרֶגֶל אֲבָל אֵין מֵאִיר כָּל הַנָּתִיב,
Similarly, the mitzvah is a lamp to the foot, but it does not illuminate the entire path;

וְלִפְעָמִים: "גְּדוֹלָה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ מִמִּצְוָה וְכוּלֵי" (נָזִיר כג681 Nazir 23b — R. Nachman bar Yitzchak said: A transgression for its own sake is greater than a commandment not for its own sake. But did not Rav Yehuda say in the name of Rav: A man should always occupy himself with Torah and the commandments even not for their own sake, for out of doing them not for their own sake he comes to do them for their own sake? Rather say: it is like a commandment not for its own sake — as it is written, "Blessed above women shall Yael the wife of Chever the Kenite be, above women in the tent shall she be blessed." Rashi (s.v. "for out of doing them not for their own sake he comes to do them for their own sake"): This shows that a commandment not for its own sake is of account, since it brings one to a commandment for its own sake — and yet you say that a transgression for its own sake is greater than it. Rashi (s.v. "rather say: like a commandment not for its own sake"): That the two are of equal worth. "Blessed above women shall Yael be" — that is, like those women of whom we find that they performed a commandment not for its own sake, and of every one of them the word "tent" is used; and she is blessed for having committed a transgression for its own sake, in order to sap the strength of that wicked man so that she might be able to kill him. Tosafos (s.v. "for out of doing them not for their own sake he comes to do them for their own sake"): If you ask: but it is said elsewhere that of one who occupies himself with a commandment not for its own sake it were better for him had he not been created! One may answer that there it speaks of one who occupies himself with Torah not for its own sake in order to browbeat others, whereas here it speaks of one who does so in order to make himself great and to acquire a name. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Ahavas Hashem 2): The objection is this: how can one say that a transgression for its own sake is greater than a commandment not for its own sake, when the commandment not for its own sake has in it what the transgression lacks — for from a transgression for its own sake one will not come to a commandment for its own sake, whereas from a commandment not for its own sake one does come to it for its own sake, since the deed itself is one and the same. The answer is therefore that they are equal: in the transgression for its own sake there is one point in its favour, that it is for its own sake, and one against it, that one cannot say it leads on to commandments; and in the commandment not for its own sake there is one point in its favour, that out of not for its own sake one comes to for its own sake, yet for all that it is not for its own sake. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 9): Esther's going [to the king], though outwardly it seemed the very opposite, since this time it was of her own will, was in truth [a case of] "a transgression for its own sake is greater than a commandment not for its own sake"; nor did she derive benefit from the transgression, since "all their good [is evil for the righteous]." It thus became for her a garment of commandment and holiness, and a means of attaining the holy spirit that comes through complete cleaving to His kingship. עַמּוּד ב),
and at times: 'greater is a sin for Heaven's sake than a mitzvah not for Heaven's sake, etc.' (Nazir 23b),
וְ"עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת וְגוֹמֵר" (תְּהִלִּים קיט, קכו).
and 'it is time to act for Hashem; they have voided Your law' (Psalms 119:126).
אֲבָל הַתּוֹרָה מְאִירָה כָּל מְקוֹם הַהִלּוּךְ,
Torah, however, illuminates the entire scope of the journey,
