וְעַל יְדֵי אוֹר זֶה יוֹדֵעַ לְכַוֵּן וְלֵילֵךְ אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ,
and through this light he knows how to direct his steps toward his eternal home,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִקַּר הַמְּכֻוָּן שֶׁיַּשְׁלִים קוֹמַת נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁתִּהְיֶה כֻּלָּהּ דְּבוּקָה בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
which is the primary objective: that he complete the stature of his soul so that it clings entirely to Hashem, blessed be He,
שֶׁבָּזֶה נִקְרָא בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ שֶׁעוֹלָם שֶׁלּוֹ הוּא.
for through this it is called 'his eternal home,' being his own personalized world.

כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יט682 Avodah Zarah 19a — And Rava said: At first it is called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and in the end it is called by his own name, as it is said: "His delight is in the Torah of the Lord," and then, "and in his Torah he meditates day and night." Rashi: "It is called by his own name" — by the name of the student who toiled in it, as it is written "and in his Torah," which implies the Torah of the man himself. Maharsha: That a Torah scholar's Torah is his own is set out in the first chapter of Kiddushin from this very verse, "and in his Torah he meditates": at the beginning of study it is called "the Torah of the Lord," and once he has learned it and made it fluent it is called "his Torah." This is of a piece with the teaching that at first Moses would learn the Torah and forget it, until it was given to him as a gift — that is, he kept learning it from his teacher until it became an acquisition in his soul. So too with what Rava adds, that a person should first study and only then analyze: until his learning is fluent in his mouth it is not yet his own Torah, and only when he afterwards meditates and delves into it himself does it become his Torah, given to him as a gift. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 19a): This comes to say that the Torah has a relation to the man, until it is called his Torah. Before he has received it, it is called "the Torah of the Lord," for it is the wisdom and order of the Blessed One by which He created all; but once he has received it, it is called the Torah of the man, for it is his Torah and his completion — the way in which he is to walk and the deed he is to do — and it belongs to him entirely, since the Torah is his completion. עַמּוּד א):
Just as our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Avodah Zarah 19a):
בַּתְּחִלָּה נִקְרָא "תּוֹרַת ה'" וּלְבַסּוֹף "תּוֹרָתוֹ",
initially it is called 'the Torah of Hashem,' and ultimately 'his Torah';
כִּי הַהַתְחָלָה הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
for the inception is from Hashem, blessed be He,
כִּי לֹא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לִקְרַב לַהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַלְמָלֵא קֵרְבָנוּ הַמָּקוֹם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְפָנָיו בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה.
for it would have been impossible for man to draw near to Hashem had the Omnipresent not drawn us near before Him at the Giving of the Torah.
וְהַפְּתִיחָה בְּ"אָנֹכִי" שֶׁאֵינוֹ לְשׁוֹן צִוּוּי דְּמַשְׁמַע הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת כְּמוֹ "לֹא יִהְיֶה",
And the opening with 'I am' is not phrased as a command implying human effort like 'you shall not have',
דְּהַהַתְחָלָה הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד, וְזֶהוּ "תּוֹרַת ה'",
for the inception is from Hashem alone, and this is 'the Torah of Hashem';
וְאַחַר כָּךְ "תּוֹרָתוֹ" – הַיְנוּ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם.
and afterward 'his Torah'—meaning human effort.
וְזֶהוּ מַעֲלָה יְתֵרָה שֶׁבֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לְגֵרִים,
And this is the distinct advantage between Israel and converts,

שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין683 Kiddushin 70b — Rabbah bar Rav Huna said: This is a superiority that Israel has over converts. For of Israel it is written, “And I shall be to them a God and they shall be to Me a people”; but of converts it is written, “Who is this that has pledged his heart to approach Me, says the Lord — and you shall be to Me a people, and I shall be to you a God.” Rashi (s.v. "Of Israelites it is written"): "And I will be their God" — even though they are not yet His people; and since He draws them near, they come to be His people. Converts, however, are not drawn near from Heaven unless they first draw themselves near by becoming good. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 70b): Israel derive by an unbroken chain from the First Cause; and just as they derive from the First Cause, so the First Cause is their God and seeks after them, for there is no cause without its effect. As a father seeks after his son, so does He seek after Israel, who are called sons because they are His effects essentially and from the first; but the convert, in whom this is not so, must cleave to Him, blessed be He, of himself. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 8): This is the distinction between Israel and converts of which they said in Kiddushin, "this is a further superiority": of Israel it is written first "And I will be their God" and afterwards "and they shall be My people," meaning that the Blessed One is their God perforce, whether they wish it or not — as at the giving of the Torah, when He held the mountain over them like a barrel, and likewise in the future, "with a strong hand … will I reign." This is only in Israel, by virtue of the holiness they have from birth from their fathers, which is not so with converts. (ע עַמּוּד ב): דִּבְגֵרִים תְּחִלָּה "וִהְיִיתֶם וְגוֹמֵר" וְאַחַר כָּךְ "וְאָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר",
as they taught in Kiddushin (70b): with converts first comes 'and you shall be My people' and afterward 'and I will be your God',
שֶׁהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם תְּחִלָּה וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְקָרְבָם.
meaning their exertion comes first and only afterward does Hashem draw them near.

וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁנִּקְרָא תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים (חֲגִיגָה ג684 Chagigah 3a — Rava expounded: What is meant by "How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O daughter of the noble"? How beautiful are the feet of Israel when they go up for the pilgrimage festival. "Daughter of the noble" — the daughter of Abraham our father, who is called noble, as it is said, "The nobles of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham." "The God of Abraham," and not the God of Isaac and Jacob? Rather, "the God of Abraham," for he was the first of the converts. Rashi: "Who is called noble" — because his heart moved him of its own accord to recognize his Creator. "The nobles of the peoples" — these are the converts, who volunteer from among the nations to take upon themselves the yoke of the commandments. Tosafos (s.v. "the first of the converts"): Because he was commanded concerning circumcision, unlike all those who came before him. Maharsha: "How beautiful are the feet of Israel" — for whoever's foot is not sound does not go up at all, as below, "excluding one who is lame." And their beauty is made to depend on their going in sandals, because one who goes barefoot goes in pain, as it is said, "Withhold your foot from being unshod" (Jeremiah 2:25), whereas these went up on foot in gladness, with their offerings of rejoicing; and so the Targum renders it, "How lovely are your steps, three times a year, in sandals." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 3): Tractate Avodah Zarah serves to clarify the distinctions between Israel and the idolaters, and Abraham's Avodah Zarah "was four hundred chapters," for Abraham is called "father of a multitude of nations" — as stated at the beginning of Chagigah, he is called "the first of the converts" — and, as it is said, he "recognized his Creator," implying that at first he did not. Hence [on Pesach night] one "begins with disgrace": "at first our fathers were idol worshippers." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Abraham our father too is called "father of a multitude of nations," for he was not born from the womb of the seed of Israel, who are borne from the womb with the Blessed One as the rock of their heart by birth; for he is called "the first of the converts," since it was through his own effort that he merited the understanding of the heart and to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite" — like a native in Israel, who is an Israelite from the womb. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 14): [If Israel cannot resemble Isaac, who was born in holiness, circumcised at eight days without his own knowledge, and so became Israel,] the deeds of Abraham suffice: for Abraham is called "the first of the converts" and sought to bring the whole world under the wings of the Shechinah, being "father of a multitude of nations" — the father of all converts — whereas Isaac is not found to have made converts. And although Abraham's converts were helped only in his lifetime, for after his passing they broke the covenant, his covenant helped at least his own seed, so that whoever is of the seed of Israel is in any case superior to a convert. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 9): Abraham our father, who is called "the first of the converts," is the beginning of the holiness that comes from below — fencing all his limbs and faculties within holiness — and he had to draw himself near, as is said of converts in Kiddushin; he was tested with ten trials so that every level would be clarified in him through his own holiness from below, in battle with the inclination. And although he afterwards merited to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite," reckoned as a native in Israel, that was after Jacob came forth from him. עַמּוּד א),
And our father Abraham, peace be upon him, who is called the first of the converts (Chagigah 3a),
הוּא הִכִּיר אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ תְּחִלָּה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ,
recognized his Creator initially through his own personal exertion,
וְאָמַר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "לֶךְ לְךָ מֵאַרְצְךָ וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, א) –
and Hashem said to him: 'Go forth from your land, etc.' (Genesis 12:1) –
פֵּרוּשׁ: מֵהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת שֶׁלְּךָ,
meaning: depart from your self-reliant exertion,
"אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ" – לִהְיוֹת צוֹפֶה רַק מַה שֶּׁאֲנִי מַרְאֶה אוֹתְךָ כְּטַעַם תּוֹרַת ה'.
'unto the land that I will show you'—to look solely toward what I show you, in the spirit of 'the Torah of Hashem.'
וְהִיא אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל,
And this is the Land of Israel;
כִּי בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ זָכָה לְמַדְרֵגַת יִשְׂרָאֵל,
for through his exertion he merited the spiritual level of Israel,
שֶׁהוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ: תְּחִלָּה "אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר",
which is the reverse: first 'I am, etc.',
שֶׁיְּבַטֵּל כָּל כֹּחוֹת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ רַק לְהַבִּיט מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר לוֹ.
nullifying all independent exertion solely to gaze upon what Hashem illuminates for him.
וְזֶה כָּל כֹּחַ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּהַקְדָּמַת "נַעֲשֶׂה" לְ"נִשְׁמָע",
And this is the entire power of Israel in giving precedence to 'we will do' over 'we will hear':
כִּי "גַּם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ" (יְשַׁעְיָהוּ כו, יב),
for 'all our works You have wrought for us' (Isaiah 26:12),
וְהַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת שֶׁלָּנוּ גַּם כֵּן רַק מִמֶּנּוּ,
and our exertion likewise derives solely from Him;
וּמִמֵּילָא כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ הוּא מִמֵּילָא רַק כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּשְׁמַע אַחַר כָּךְ,
and spontaneously all our actions naturally unfold only as we will hear afterward,
כִּי מַה שֶּׁאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה לֹא נוּכַל לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ כְּלָל.
for whatever Hashem, blessed be He, does not desire, we could never execute at all.
וְהוּא הַתְחָלַת הַכְּנִיסָה לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה,
And this is the initial entrance into the words of Torah,
אֲבָל תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ נֶעְלָם אוֹר זֶה,
yet immediately afterward this initial light becomes concealed,
דִּלְבַסּוֹף הוּא "תּוֹרָתוֹ",
for in the end it must become 'his Torah',
וְ"הֵמָּה יִהְיוּ לִי לְעָם" עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם.
and 'they shall be My people' through their own exertion.
וְכֵן אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִיָּד אַחַר כָּךְ: "וַיְהִי רָעָב בָּאָרֶץ" (בְּרֵאשִׁית יב, י),
And so it was with our father Abraham, peace be upon him: immediately afterward 'there was a famine in the land' (Genesis 12:10),
וְזֶה לִכְאוֹרָה הֵיפֶךְ הַהַבְטָחָה.
which seemingly contradicted the divine promise.
רַק כָּךְ הוּא הַמִּדָּה בְּהַנְהָגַת יִשְׂרָאֵל:
Rather, such is the principle in guiding Israel:
בַּתְּחִלָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְקָרֵב מְאֹד וּמֵאִיר בַּלֵּב הַרְבֵּה,
at first Hashem draws one very near and illuminates intensely within the heart,
וְאַחַר כָּךְ מִתְרַחֵק וּמַנִּיחַ הָאָדָם לְעַצְמוֹ,
and afterward He withdraws and leaves man to himself,
שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהִתְקָרֵב כְּקֵרְבוּת הַקּוֹדֵם מֵעַצְמוֹ,
so that he may re-attain that initial closeness on his own initiative,
כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִקְרָא עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁהוּא קֵרַב אֶת עַצְמוֹ.
in order that it be credited to his own name, as though he drew himself near.

וּבְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶאֱמַר: "לֹא אֶעֱזָבְךָ עַד אֲשֶׁר אִם עָשִׂיתִי וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כח, טו685 Genesis 28:15 — “And behold, I am with you, and I will guard you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land; for I will not forsake you until I have done what I have spoken of to you.” Rashi: "I am with you" was said to him because he was afraid of Esau and of Laban. "Until I have done": the word here has the force of "when," not "if." "What I have spoken to you" means for your sake and concerning you — whatever I promised Abraham concerning his seed I promised concerning you and not concerning Esau.),
And concerning our father Jacob, peace be upon him, it is said: 'I will not leave you until I have done, etc.' (Genesis 28:15),
וְנִרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ יַעַזְבֶנּוּ, וְאֵין זוֹ הַבְטָחָה טוֹבָה לִכְאוֹרָה.
making it appear as though afterward He would leave him, which seemingly is not a reassuring promise.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם זֶה הַבְטָחָה טוֹבָה,
Yet in truth, this too is a benevolent promise,
כִּי הָעֲזִיבָה אַחַר כָּךְ הִיא הֶכְרֵחִית בְּהַנְהָגַת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
for the subsequent withdrawal is essential to the governance of this world,
הַדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה וְהֶעְדֵּר הֶאָרָה הַבְּרוּרָה,
which is compared to night and the absence of manifest clarity,
רַק כָּל יָמָיו בְּנִסְיוֹנוֹת,
where all of one's days are fraught with trials;

וְזֶה נִקְרָא עֲזִיבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּחִזְקִיָּהוּ: "כִּי עֲזָבוֹ וְגוֹמֵר לְנַסּוֹתוֹ686 II Chronicles 32:31 — “And so with the envoys of the officers of Babylon, who were sent to him to inquire about the wonder that had occurred in the land — God left him, to test him, to know all that was in his heart.” Rashi: "And so with the envoys" — messengers, the word being as in "for there was an interpreter between them" [Genesis 42:23], since a messenger interprets between the sender and the one sent to. This follows upon the verse "And Hezekiah prospered in all his works" [II Chronicles 31:21]: after all this good with which the Holy One, blessed be He, had prospered him, God left him, to test him and know all that was in his heart, through the envoys of the princes of Babylon sent to him. "To inquire of the wonder" — he did not stand the test, but showed them his whole treasure house. Radak: "The envoys of the princes of Babylon" — a construct upon a construct; "envoys" is from the word for speech. "To know all that was in his heart" — he rejoiced over them and showed them his whole treasure house, and all this for his own honor, and he took pride in it, and God reckoned it to him as a sin; and "to know" means that men should know. Metzudas Dovid: "And so" — this looks back to what precedes: in most things he prospered, but once he was tested and did not prosper, and that was in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon. "To inquire of the wonder" — to ask about the truth of the wonder that had been done in the land at the time of his illness. "God left him" — that is, He did not then incline his heart, neither to good nor to evil, in order to test him and know all that was in his heart. Malbim: "And so with the envoys" — this too was a test in which he did not stand, in that he boasted before the princes of Babylon, as I have explained at length on Isaiah 39." (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב לב, לא).
and this is termed abandonment, as written of Hezekiah: 'God left him, etc., to try him' (II Chronicles 32:31).
וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ כָּל אֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית
And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, who is the root of the entire nation of Israel,
הֻבְטַח "לֹא אֶעֱזָבְךָ עַד וְגוֹמֵר" –
was promised 'I will not leave you until, etc.' –
שֶׁמִּקֹּדֶם יִהְיֶה הַהֶאָרָה כָּל כָּךְ
meaning that the prior illumination would be so powerful
עַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּטוּחַ שֶׁבְּעֵת הָעֲזִיבָה דְּאַחַר כָּךְ גַּם כֵּן לֹא יִהְיֶה צַדִּיק נֶעֱזָב
that he was guaranteed that even during the subsequent withdrawal the righteous would not be forsaken,
וּבְכָל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה יַצְלִיחַ, כִּי הוּא מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה.
and in all that he does he would prosper, for his bed was wholly pure.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק הָיָה עֲדַיִן פְּסֹלֶת,
In contrast, with Abraham and Isaac dross still emerged,
הַיְנוּ שֶׁהָיוּ צְרִיכִים עֲדַיִן הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בֶּאֱמֶת בְּעֵת הָעֲזִיבָה
meaning they still truly required intense exertion during the time of withdrawal
שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נֶעֱזָב חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְגַמְרֵי,
so that the seed would not become entirely abandoned, Heaven forbid,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּעֶזְבוּ בֶּאֱמֶת עֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל,
just as Esau and Ishmael were indeed cast aside,
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹצְאֵי חֲלָצָם לֹא נִקְרְאוּ זַרְעָם
and even though they issued from their loins they were not termed their true seed,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה687 Nedarim 31a — Mishnah: One who vows not to benefit from the seed of Avraham is forbidden to benefit from a Jew and permitted from a gentile. Gemara: But is there not Yishmael? — “For through Yitzchak shall your seed be called” is written. But is there not Esav? — “Through Yitzchak,” and not all of Yitzchak. Rashi: "But is there not Ishmael" — he too is of Abraham's seed, and he is among the nations of the world [so benefit from him should have been forbidden as well]. "For in Isaac shall seed be called to you" — and it is by that seed that the man vowed; and "in Isaac, and not all of Isaac" teaches that Esau is not called the seed of Isaac, and therefore the one who vowed is permitted to derive benefit from the nations of the world. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The very essence of Abraham and Isaac was not yet wholly transformed until the birth of Jacob, when the promise "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac" was fulfilled, and Ishmael and Esau were pushed away from being called the seed of Abraham and Isaac. Then Abraham and Isaac too were perfected, their "bed" complete, for from then on only the seed of Jacob is called and traced to them. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): The titles "father" and "mother" refer only to their power that extends into the child; therefore they said in Nedarim, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you" — and not Esau and Ishmael, who are not called Abraham's seed: though he begot them, his power is not discernible in them after the begetting, unless one converts, for [a convert] is called a son of Abraham. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 13): The angels, who said "Sarah your wife shall have a son" [attributing him to the feminine side], saw that Esau's evil severities would also issue from him; but they did not know the depths revealed afterwards in the Torah in "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you," which the Sages expounded in Nedarim, "and not all of Isaac" — Esau is not called his seed at all, so that in truth [Isaac] was entirely holy. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Emor 6): Although Abraham and Isaac are also called by the name Israel, that is only after Jacob was born and named Israel, for then it was clarified that "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac," since Ishmael and Esau are not called their seed; then they too were called by the name Israel, but not before. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 78): Sometimes some good may come to a father even from wicked sons, as with Abraham, from whom Ishmael and the sons of Keturah issued, through whom the dross went out; but for this the father must merit that the status of "his seed" be stripped from them, as it says of Abraham, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In truth the "bed" of Abraham and Isaac too was complete, for only "in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac": Esau and Ishmael are not their seed at all, only Jacob, whose bed was complete. Once Jacob was clarified as having a complete bed without dross, they too were clarified, for the dross was pushed away from being called their seed at all. Beis Yaakov (Bereishis 28): Isaac thought to bless Esau because he reasoned that the Blessed One can shine even within darkness, and if the Holy One, blessed be He, consented to Esau's deeds they would be very exalted; but the Holy One, blessed be He, did not consent, for He had already sealed the name of Jacob, as it is written, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you." (נְדָרִים לא עַמּוּד א) עַל פָּסוּק "כִּי בְיִצְחָק וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית כא, יב).
as our Sages of blessed memory taught (Nedarim 31a) on the verse 'for in Isaac, etc.' (Genesis 21:12).
כִּי הֵם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם זָכוּ לְהוֹלִיד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
For through their exertion they merited to father our father Jacob, peace be upon him,
שֶׁשְּׁמוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל וִישֻׁרוּן עַל שֵׁם יַשְׁרוּת נַפְשׁוֹ בְּקַו הַיֹּשֶׁר מַמָּשׁ
whose name is Israel and Yeshurun on account of the integrity of his soul aligned upon the true line of uprightness,
שֶׁלֹּא יִטֶּה יָמִין וּשְׂמֹאל מִדֶּרֶךְ הַמֶּלֶךְ מַלְכּוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם.
swerving neither right nor left from the King's Highway of the Sovereign of the universe.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סג)688 Bereshit Rabbah 63:2 — R. Shmuel bar R. Yitzchak said: Abraham was saved from the fiery furnace only through the merit of Jacob. A parable: a man was tried before the governor and his sentence went out to be burned; but the governor saw by his astrology that he was destined to father a daughter who would marry the king, and he said, He is worthy to be saved through the merit of the daughter he will father. So too Abraham: his sentence went out from Nimrod to be burned, and the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that Jacob was destined to come from him and said, Abraham is worthy to be saved through the merit of Jacob. That is what is written: "Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, who redeemed Abraham" — Jacob redeemed Abraham. עַל פָּסוּק "בֵּית יַעֲקֹב אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם" (יְשַׁעְיָהוּ כט, כב):
And our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 63) on the verse 'the house of Jacob who redeemed Abraham' (Isaiah 29:22):
שֶׁבִּזְכוּתוֹ נִצּוֹל,
that in Jacob's future merit was Abraham saved,

פֵּרוּשׁ כֹּחוֹ שֶׁהָיָה גָּנוּז בְּאַבְרָהָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שָׁם)689 Bereshit Rabbah 63:3 — Abram was called Abraham. Isaac was called Abraham, as it is written, "And these are the generations of Isaac son of Abraham" — Abraham. Jacob's name was called Israel, as it is written, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel." Isaac's name was called Israel, as it is written, "And these are the names of the children of Israel who came into Egypt — Jacob." Abraham was called Israel: R. Natan said, this is a deep matter — "And the dwelling of the children of Israel who dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan and in the land of Goshen was four hundred and thirty years.": אַבְרָהָם נִקְרָא יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכֵן יִצְחָק.
meaning his potential power was latent in Abraham, as written (there): Abraham was called Israel, and likewise Isaac.
כִּי כֻּלָּם זָכוּ בְּאַחֲרִית הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם לְכֹחַ זֶה,
For all of them attained this power at the culmination of their exertion,
כִּי אֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר אֶצְלָם מִלְּבַר,
since nothing external clung to their essence,
וּמִמֵּילָא זֶה הַפְּסֹלֶת מִלְּבַר אֵינוֹ קָרוּי שֶׁלָּהֶם כְּלָל
and spontaneously that outer dross was not reckoned as theirs at all
אַחַר שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגַת מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה שֶׁזֶּהוּ לְבַסּוֹף דְּנִקְרָא "תּוֹרָתוֹ".
once one reached the level of a completely pure bed, which is the final stage termed 'his Torah.'
וְכֵן הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרֵאת עַל שֵׁם כָּל הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה אָבוֹת:
And so the Torah is titled after all three Patriarchs:
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "תּוֹרַת חֶסֶד" (מִשְׁלֵי לא, כו) וְהוּא חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם;
as it is written: 'the Torah of lovingkindness' (Proverbs 31:26), which is the kindness unto Abraham;

וְאָמְרוּ (מְגִלָּה לא690 Megillah 31b — Abaye said: They taught this only of the curses in Leviticus, but with the curses in Deuteronomy one may break off. What is the reason? These are stated in the plural, and Moses spoke them from the mouth of the Almighty; and those are stated in the singular, and Moses spoke them of himself. Rashi: “Moses spoke them from the mouth of the Almighty” — he was made a messenger to say, “Thus the Holy One, blessed be He, said to me,” for they are phrased “and I will give,” “and I will appoint,” “and I will send,” the words of One who has the power to do so. But in Deuteronomy it is written “The Lord will smite you,” “The Lord will make the pestilence cleave to you” — Moses said them of himself: if you transgress His commandments, He will appoint them over you. Tosafos (s.v. “Moses said them of himself”): Moses said them of himself — but by the holy spirit. Maharsha: These are two distinct reasons. Since the curses in Leviticus are stated in the plural, there is reason to fear a curse addressed to the many, which is not so of one addressed to an individual; and further, those in Leviticus come from the mouth of the Almighty, whose curse is the more to be feared than curses spoken by Moses — even though Moses too certainly spoke by the holy spirit, as Tosafot wrote. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 43): Heaven forbid that Moses should have said anything of his own, even a single letter. In all the rest of the Torah the Holy One, blessed be He, placed the speech in Moses’ mouth, so that although Moses uttered it, it was as though God Himself were speaking; Deuteronomy, however, Moses spoke of himself, as an emissary speaks what the one who sent him has charged him with. This is the meaning of “the curses in Deuteronomy Moses said of himself”: God did not place the speech in his mouth, because Deuteronomy stands on the side of the receiving of the Torah, and receiving comes through one who is near to the receiver — and Moses is near to Israel. עַמּוּד ב): מֹשֶׁה מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה,
and they said (Megillah 31b): Moses uttered from the mouth of Might (Gevurah),

וּבַזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, פ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)691 Zohar 3:80b — And purity is found in the Torah, as it is written, “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever.” He said to him: It says “the fear of the Lord,” and not “Torah.” He said to him: So it certainly is, for the Torah comes from the side of Gevurah. He said to him: And does it issue from there? It issues from here, as it is written, “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord,” and it is written, “The fear of the Lord is pure.” Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 21): There was still lacking one more Sabbath, that of the attribute of Gevurah, which is the essential one for the Giving of the Torah, since "the Torah issues from the side of Gevurah." As long as they had not received the Torah and brought it down to earth, the revelation of the supernal holiness of that attribute's Sabbath, namely its inclusion within the attribute of Chesed, so that "from His right hand [went] a fiery law for them," was not yet within their reach; that came about on the Sabbath of the Giving of the Torah.: אוֹרַיְתָא מִסִּטְרָא דִּגְבוּרָה מִדַּת יִצְחָק;
and in the Zohar (Part III, 80b): the Torah emerges from the side of Gevurah, the attribute of Isaac;

וְאָמְרוּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ח692 Jerusalem Talmud Rosh Hashanah 3:8 — "And it cast truth to the ground" — whenever Israel casts the words of the Torah to the ground, this wicked kingdom decrees and succeeds. What is the reason? "It cast truth to the ground, and it acted and succeeded" (Daniel 8:12). And there is no truth but Torah, as you say, "Buy truth and do not sell it, wisdom and instruction and understanding" (Proverbs 23:23). Pnei Moshe (s.v. "through the transgression of the Torah"): When transgressors grow slack and cast the Torah aside, then "a host is given over" against them. And because the verse "they encamped in Rephidim" is likewise expounded to mean that they let their hands go slack from the Torah, and therefore "Amalek came," these verses too are expounded here in the same manner.): אֵין אֱמֶת אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה וְהוּא מִדַּת אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב.
and they taught (Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 3:8): there is no truth other than Torah, which is the attribute of truth unto Jacob.
וְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וְאוֹרַיְתָא וְיִשְׂרָאֵל כּוּלָּא חַד,
And the Holy One, blessed be He, the Torah, and Israel are all one;
כִּי הַהַתְחָלָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַיִּפַּח בְּאַפָּיו וְגוֹמֵר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב, ז),
for the inception is from Hashem, blessed be He, as written: 'and He breathed into his nostrils, etc.' (Genesis 2:7),
וְאָמְרוּ: מַאן דְּנָפַח מִתּוֹכוֹ נָפַח.
and the masters taught: whoever breathes, breathes from his innermost essence.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַהֶאָרָה הוּא הַתּוֹרָה וְהִיא מְאִירָה אֶל הַנֶּפֶשׁ, וְהַכֹּל אֶחָד,
And afterward the illumination is the Torah, which shines into the soul, and all is one;

כִּי הָאָבוֹת הֵן הֵן הַמֶּרְכָּבָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה מז693 Bereshit Rabbah 47:6 — Reish Lakish said: The patriarchs are themselves the chariot, as it is said: "God ascended from upon Abraham"; "God ascended from upon him"; "and behold, the Lord stood upon him."),
for the Patriarchs themselves are the divine Chariot (Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 47),

וְצוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד (מִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה בַּמִּדְבָּר רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה ד694 Bamidbar Rabbah 4:1 — "Since you were precious in My eyes, you were honored" (Isaiah 43:4). The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Jacob: Jacob, you are exceedingly precious in My eyes, for, as it were, I have fixed your image upon My throne, and by your name the angels praise Me and say, "Blessed is the Lord, God of Israel, from eternity to eternity" (Psalms 41:14). Hence, "since you were precious in My eyes, you were honored.") –
and the form of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, is engraved upon the Throne of Glory (Midrash Rabbah, Bamidbar, Parashah 4) –
דְּמוּת אָדָם שֶׁעַל הַכִּסֵּא שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל דְּנַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל
the Likeness of Adam upon the Throne, which encompasses all the souls of Israel,
שֶׁהֵם הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַמְּכֻוֶּנֶת בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם.
who are the intended soul in the creation of the cosmos.
וּכְמוֹ הַתּוֹרָה בַּתְּחִלָּה "תּוֹרַת ה'" וְכוּלֵי,
And just as the Torah is initially 'the Torah of Hashem, etc.',
כָּךְ הַנֶּפֶשׁ בַּתְּחִלָּה "וַיִּפַּח וְכוּלֵי" מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי",
so the soul is initially 'and He breathed, etc.' from Hashem, as written: 'the soul You placed within me',
וּלְבַסּוֹף נִקְרָא בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ שֶׁהוּא שֶׁלּוֹ,
and in the end it is called his eternal home, being his own;
דְּהַנֶּפֶשׁ נִקְרֵאת עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁהוּא בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ זָכָה לָזֶה.
for the soul is titled in his name, since through his exertion he attained this.

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה לה695 Vayikra Rabbah 35:7 — "And you shall keep My commandments and do them" — R. Chama son of R. Chanina said: If you keep the Torah, I account it to you as though you had made them. "And do them" — R. Chanina bar Pappa said: He said to them, if you keep the Torah, I account it to you as though you had made yourselves.):
And this is what our Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashah 35):
כְּאִלּוּ אַתֶּם עֲשִׂיתֶם אֶת עַצְמְכֶם עַל פָּסוּק "וַעֲשִׂיתֶם אֹתָם" (וַיִּקְרָא כו, ג),
it is as though you fashioned yourselves, expounded on the verse 'and do them' (Vayikra 26:3),
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה הַתּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת זוֹכֶה לָזֶה.
for through the active performance of the Torah and mitzvot one attains this.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שָׁם פָּרָשָׁה לו696 Vayikra Rabbah 36:4 — "And now, thus says the Lord, He who created you, Jacob, and He who formed you, Israel." R. Pinchas said in the name of R. Reuven: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to His world — My world, My world, shall I tell you who created you, who formed you? Jacob created you, Jacob formed you, as it is written: "He who created you, Jacob, and He who formed you, Israel." Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 5): The Holy One, blessed be He, created the world closed, so that it is not known why it was created, and all of creation is from His goodness and kindness. "He who created you, Jacob": the term "creation" denotes contraction, and the name Jacob too denotes contraction, for he contracted himself exceedingly and desired only the honor of Heaven; "and He who formed you, Israel": "formation" and the name Israel both allude to expansion — the Holy One, blessed be He, began to reveal the expansion of His light and showed him that the whole world is full of His glory, until Jacob compelled even Esau's angel, the great accuser, to acknowledge the honor of Heaven revealed through him.):
And our Sages said (there, Parashah 36):
עוֹלָמִי מִי בְּרָאָךְ? יַעֲקֹב בְּרָאָךְ!
My world, who created you? Jacob created you!
שֶׁהַגַּם דְּהַתְחָלַת הַבְּרִיאָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
For even though the inception of creation is from Hashem, blessed be He,
לְבַסּוֹף נִקְרָא הַכֹּל עַל שֵׁם יַעֲקֹב שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ אֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית,
in the end all is called by the name of Jacob who is the root of the Jewish people,
הַכֹּל נִקְרָא עַל שְׁמָם שֶׁהוּא שֶׁלָּהֶם וּבְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם.
everything being titled in their name, belonging to them and through their exertion.
כִּי הַגֵּרִים הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם פּוֹעֵל עַל לְהַבָּא:
For with converts, their exertion operates toward the future:
בַּתְּחִלָּה "וִהְיִיתֶם וְגוֹמֵר"
first 'and you shall be My people',
וְאַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת זֶה יִזְכּוּ דְּ"אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר".
and afterward through this exertion they merit 'and I will be your God'.
אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת שֶׁלָּהֶם פּוֹעֵל עַל הֶעָבָר:
Israel, however, their exertion operates retroactively upon the past:
וּבַתְּחִלָּה "אָנֹכִי וְגוֹמֵר"
first comes 'I am Hashem your God',
וְאַחַר כָּךְ בָּא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת שֶׁלָּהֶם לְהַגִּיד כִּי בְּדִין הָיָה הִתְקָרְבוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָהֶם,
and afterward comes their exertion to demonstrate that Hashem's initial approach to them was justified by law,
שֶׁהֵם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם מַגִּיעַ לָהֶם כֵּן.
for through their exertion they truly deserve it.
וְזֶה עִקַּר כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל,
And this is the core power of Israel's repentance,

שֶׁיְּכוֹלִים לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם עַד דִּזְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשִׂים כִּזְכִיּוֹת (יוֹמָא פו697 Yoma 86b — Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for one's intentional sins become for him like unwitting transgressions, as it is stated, "Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity" — "iniquity" is an intentional sin, and yet He calls it a stumbling. But did not Reish Lakish say: Great is repentance, for one's intentional sins become for him like merits, as it is stated, "And when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does what is lawful and right, he shall live by them"? This is no difficulty: here, one who repents out of love; there, one who repents out of fear. Rashi: "For you have stumbled in your iniquity": your iniquity will be reckoned as a stumbling, which is an unwitting sin. "He shall live by them": by all that he did — even by the transgressions. Maharsha: That intentional sins become like unwitting ones may be taken literally, as Rashi explained "Return, backsliding children" above: when one repents, He accounts it as though the sin began in youthful folly. That they become like merits is on its face astonishing, for the sinner would then profit; but one who repents out of love, of whom the Gemara concludes it speaks, surely repents fully and adds good deeds beyond what that sin required, and those added deeds become merits for him — as the verse shows: "and does what is lawful and right, he shall live by them," by the justice and righteousness he added to his repentance. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2): Since repentance reaches the Throne of Glory, by the exalted level the penitent now attains all he did before is reckoned unwitting — as one who was ignorant and later became wise calls his earlier deeds unwitting — for unwitting error stems from the material, and the penitent has raised himself from the material level at which he sinned to the level separate [from matter]. His intentional sins become merits because repentance is the very order of the world, all beings existing only by returning to God, from Whom they came; so the sinner's distance from God, which calls for his return, itself becomes merit for him when he returns. This holds only when the return is out of love, for there is no cleaving to Him except through love ("to love the Lord your God … and to cleave to Him"); one who returns out of fear has not come to cleave to Him, and so his intentional sins become only like unwitting ones. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev 11): Then "they shall be white as snow," for deliberate sins become like merits: the Blessed One will then make clear that the deed was not done by the person's choice at all — as the Arizal wrote, where there is [Divine] knowledge there is no choice; choice is given in the seven lower attributes, but in the upper three, in Atika, there truly is no choice — as will become clear once they merit repentance out of love, through which deliberate sins become like merits. עַמּוּד ב).
that they can rectify the past until willful sins become transformed into merits (Yoma 86b).

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן גֵּר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּר כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד (יְבָמוֹת כב698 Yevamot 22a — And how does this differ from forbidden relations? Forbidden relations are entrusted to all; testimony is entrusted to the court — and a convert who converts is like a newborn child. Rashi: "How does it differ": testimony from forbidden relations, regarding which it is stated below (98a) that a convert who was married to his maternal sister must send her away. "Entrusted to all": everyone marries, so if you let him keep her, people will come to permit a forbidden relation among Israelites as well, for not everyone knows that the convert's reason is that he is like a newborn child. "Entrusted to the court": even if you validate the testimony of convert brothers, it will not lead to validating that of Israelite brothers, for the court knows that a convert who converts is like a newborn child. Tosafos (s.v. "forbidden relations are entrusted to all"): Earlier the reason given for the decree regarding converts was "lest they say: we have come from a stricter sanctity to a lesser one," whereas here, as Rashi explains, the reason implied is that it would be confused with Israelites. Both reasons are needed: for paternal relations that were forbidden to them before [conversion], confusion is no concern, since all know that the Torah disregarded [a gentile's] paternal lineage, and the reason is "lest they say"; but maternal relations, which were not forbidden before, are forbidden for fear of confusion — which is also why maternal brothers should not testify in the first instance, while paternal brothers may. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos, on Tosafot s.v. "forbidden relations are entrusted to all"): [Tosafot's inference that the reason here is the fear of confusion] means that regarding testimony the reason "lest they say: we have come from a stricter sanctity [to a lesser one]" does not apply, since among gentiles a relative's testimony is valid, as stated in chapter Arba Mitot [Sanhedrin 57b]; and so the Nimukei Yosef explains in our sugya. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 14a): A convert who converts is as though newly born, for at first he was not reckoned a [true] creation, as they said, "A convert who converts is like a newborn child": before, he was not reckoned a complete human being, and now he is. [Hence his sins are forgiven:] sin belongs to a person by virtue of his materiality, and the gentile who rises to the level of Israel is thereby raised above sin. Maharal (Gevuros Hashem, ch. 42): A gentile cannot make himself into [a member of] another nation — just as an Israelite who apostatizes remains an Israelite, for one cannot change oneself — but because Israel is set apart from all the nations and not included among them, being supreme and holy above them all, it is possible to cleave to them, for one ascends in holiness. And one who converts, because he goes out to cleave to that supreme level, is like a newborn child. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 28): [R. Meir descended from Nero, of Esau's seed.] Before the Torah was given and the nation of Israel chosen, the converts destined to come from Esau were reckoned as his seed; but in truth "a convert who converts is like a newborn child," and he is called by the name of Israel and is no longer called the seed of Esau. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 5): [R. Akiva,] the son of converts, became holy flesh and an Israelite soul through his own effort; for one can attain heavenly mercy so that one's flesh returns like the flesh of the living child — as with "a convert who converts is like a newborn child" — and becomes holy flesh again. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Lech Lecha 6): After his circumcision Abraham merited to become a new creation, whose eyes and ears would see and hear only matters of mitzvah. And although one becomes a new creation only after circumcision, as they said, "a convert who converts is like a newborn child," with the Blessed One, since He had promised him "I will make you a great nation" — creating him anew — he merited it at once. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): By their root, [the offspring of Lot's daughters] are [akin to the mule, born of a mixture]; only after [Ruth] separated from her root — for "a convert who converts is like a newborn child" — did the kingship of Israel, the root of the Congregation of Israel that is likened to a dove, come forth from them. עַמּוּד א),
In contrast, a convert who converts is like a newborn infant (Yevamot 22a),
וּפוֹעֵל שֶׁהַקּוֹדֵם נִשְׁכָּח וּכְאִלּוּ אֵינָם.
which effects that the past is forgotten as though it never existed;
אֲבָל אֵין יְכוֹלִים לְתַקֵּן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַקּוֹדֵם גַּם כֵּן טוֹב,
yet they cannot rectify the past so that it too becomes retroactively good,
כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ אֻמּוֹת אֵין בּוֹ טוֹב,
for the root of the nations contains no intrinsic holy good,
וְהַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ רַק שֶׁמִּתְהַפֵּךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכֻנֶּה וְנִשְׁתַּקַּע שֵׁם עַמְמִין מִמֶּנּוּ.
and whatever good is in him merely shifts to be titled with the name of Israel, drowning out the gentile status from him.
אֲבָל שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָא אַף הַיּוֹתֵר רָשָׁע שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם,
The name of Israel, however, is retained even by the most wicked in the world;
אֲפִלּוּ הַמֵּמִיר דָּת נִקְרָא יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר.
even one who converts out of the faith is still designated an 'apostate Israelite.'

וּבְפֶרֶק נִגְמַר הַדִּין (מד699 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned" (Joshua 7:11). R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is still Israel. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is myrtle and myrtle they call it. "They have also transgressed My covenant which I commanded them, and they have also taken of the devoted thing, and have also stolen, and have also dissembled, and they have also put it among their own goods." R. Ile'a said in the name of R. Yehuda bar Masparta: This teaches that Achan transgressed all five books of the Torah, for "also" is stated five times. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious. עַמּוּד א) לָמְדוּ דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵעָכָן,
And in the chapter Nigmar HaDin (Sanhedrin 44a) they derived 'even though he sinned, he remains Israel' from Achan,
שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּעָבַר עַל חֲמִשָּׁה חֻמְּשֵׁי תוֹרָה,
concerning whom they stated there that he violated all five books of the Torah,
דְּאֵין כָּל זֶה מַפְקִיעַ מִמֶּנּוּ שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי לֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח.
and none of this stripped from him the name of Israel, for no banished one remains cast out.
וְזֶהוּ הַבְטָחַת "כִּי לֹא אֶעֱזָבְךָ עַד וְגוֹמֵר":
And this is the promise: 'for I will not leave you until, etc.':
שֶׁבְּכָל עֲזִיבוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין עֲזִיבָה שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לְהִתַּקֵּן,
that among all abandonments of Israel, there is no withdrawal that cannot be rectified,
דֻּגְמַת יְצִיאַת עֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ בִּכְלַל אֻמּוֹת
unlike the divergence of Esau and Ishmael who became subsumed within the nations,
לִהְיוֹת גֵּר הַמִּתְגַּיֵּר בָּהֶם כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד.
such that a convert from among them is merely like a newborn child.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּבָר נַעֲשָׂה הֲכָנָה בְּכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל מֵהַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
In contrast, within Israel a permanent foundation was established across all Jewish souls by Hashem's providence,
לִהְיוֹת לָהֶם לֵאלֹהִים בְּיָד חֲזָקָה וּבְחֵמָה שְׁפוּכָה גַּם טֶרֶם הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
to be their God with a strong hand and outstretched fury even prior to human exertion;
בְּעִנְיָן שֶׁגַּם בְּכָל מַחְשַׁךְ מַעֲשֵׂהוּ, שֶׁיֵּלֵךְ בַּחֹשֶׁךְ מַמָּשׁ בְּהֶעְדֵּר נֵר מִצְוָה וְתוֹרָה אוֹר,
such that even in the utter darkness of his deeds, where he walks in literal blackness lacking the mitzvah-lamp and Torah-light,
גַּם עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "הָעָם הַהֹלְכִים בַּחֹשֶׁךְ רָאוּ אוֹר גָּדוֹל" (יְשַׁעְיָהוּ ט, א).
concerning this too it is stated: 'The people walking in darkness have seen a great light' (Isaiah 9:1).
וְהוּא כְּטַעַם זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ זְכִיּוֹת,
And this reflects the principle that intentional sins become transformed into merits,
וְנַעֲשָׂה מֵאוֹתוֹ חֹשֶׁךְ אוֹר גָּדוֹל.
and out of that very darkness a great light emerges.
כִּי אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַנִּיחַ לְהִשְׁתַּקֵּעַ כָּל כָּךְ לְזֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּשִׁקּוּעַ כָּזֶה
For Hashem, blessed be He, never permits the seed of Israel to become submerged to such an extent
שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לְהִתְהַפֵּךְ עוֹד לְאוֹר גָּדוֹל.
that it can no longer be transformed into a great light.
פֵּרוּשׁ "גָּדוֹל" – שֶׁהוּא גָּדוֹל מִשְּׁאָר אוֹר,
The meaning of 'great'—it is greater than ordinary light,
כִּי יִתְרוֹן הָאוֹר מִן הַחֹשֶׁךְ,
for the preeminence of light shines out of darkness,
וְלָכֵן חֹשֶׁךְ שֶׁנִּתְהַפֵּךְ לְאוֹר הוּא אוֹר יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל.
and therefore darkness converted to light becomes a vastly greater light.
וְלָכֵן בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין אֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִים לַעֲמֹד
Hence in the place where ba'alei teshuvah stand, the completely righteous cannot stand,
מִפְּנֵי גֹּדֶל הָאוֹר הַמֵּאִיר יוֹתֵר מִכְּפִי כֹּחָם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים.
on account of the vast magnitude of the light shining far beyond the capacity of the completely righteous.

sections.en: Shabbat and Amalek: Opposing Roots of Remembrance

items.h: Shabbat fixes holiness through remembrance; Amalek embodies the opposite root, and Parashat Zachor strengthens the heart by joining both acts of memory.

Seif 1 — Two Remembrances: Shabbat and Amalek
Remembering Shabbat roots holiness in the heart, while remembering Amalek repels the opposing root of forgetfulness.

p: שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע דַּעֲמָלֵק הוּא לְעֻמַּת שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַקְּדֻשָּׁה דְּשַׁבָּת,
The root of evil in Amalek stands directly opposite the root of holiness in Shabbat,
שֶׁהִיא קְדֻשָּׁה קְבִיעָא וְקַיָּמָא וְאֵינָהּ בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם כְּלָל.
which is an intrinsically fixed and enduring holiness that does not depend on human effort at all.
וּפְעֻלַּת אָדָם בָּזֶה הוּא רַק הַזְּכִירָה,
And man's only active role in this is remembrance,
שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ בַּפֶּה וְזוֹכֵר מִקְּדֻשָּׁה זוֹ.
in that he articulates its holiness verbally and keeps this sanctity in mind.
כִּי יָדוּעַ בְּכָל דָּבָר שֶׁהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה קְבוּעָה שָׁם, הוּא קְבִיעוּת כָּל הַגּוּף,
For it is known that wherever a person's thought is anchored, there the entirety of his being is situated,

כַּיָּדוּעַ מִמַּקְלוֹת דְּיַעֲקֹב700 Genesis 30:37-39 — “And Yaakov took himself rods of fresh poplar, almond and plane, and peeled white streaks in them, laying bare the white on the rods. And he set the rods he had peeled in the troughs, in the watering channels where the flocks came to drink, facing the flocks, and they mated as they came to drink. And the flocks mated by the rods, and the flocks bore streaked, speckled and spotted young.” Rashi: "Rods of poplar" is a tree of that name, whose wood is white, and he took it while it was still moist, peeling it so that the white beneath showed through in stripes. "The runnels" are the channels of water, the troughs made in the ground for watering the flocks there; the animal would see the rods and start backward, and the male would then mate with her, so that she bore young of like appearance. "Ring-streaked" (עקודים) means marked differently at the place where they are bound, that is, at the ankles of the fore and hind legs. Ramban: Once they had agreed that his wages would be the animals of these colors, Jacob was permitted to do whatever he could to make them give birth in that manner; perhaps he had even stipulated that he might do with them as he wished, since Laban did not understand the working of this device. Only "when the flocks were feeble," in the days of Tishri, did he not set the rods in — for otherwise not a hoof would have been left to Laban..
as is known from the incident of Jacob's peeled rods.
וּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֵר מִקְּדֻשָּׁה זוֹ, הַיְנוּ שֶׁמַּחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ שְׁקוּעָה בָּזֶה,
And when he remembers this holiness—meaning his consciousness is fully immersed in it—
מִמֵּילָא הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הַהִיא שׁוֹרָה עָלָיו.
that holiness automatically rests upon him.
אֲבָל גּוּף קְדֻשָּׁתָהּ נִקְרָא (שַׁבָּת י:): "מַתָּנָה טוֹבָה יֵשׁ לִי בְּבֵית גְּנָזַי",
However, the very essence of its holiness is termed (Shabbat 10b): "a precious gift I have in My treasury,"

פֵּרוּשׁ:701 Shabbat 10b — Rava bar Mechasya said in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav: One who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him, as it is stated, "to know that I, the Lord, sanctify you." This was likewise taught in a baraita: "To know that I, the Lord, sanctify you" — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name, and I wish to give it to Israel; go and inform them. Rashi: "Must inform him": [he should say,] "I will give you such-and-such a gift" — this is the respectful way, for otherwise he might be ashamed to accept it, whereas this way they come to terms in words beforehand and he is not ashamed of it; and likewise, if he left it in his house without his knowledge, he must let him know that it came from his hand, for through this he will love him. "To know that I, the Lord, sanctify you": I come to inform them that I wish to sanctify them. Tosafos (s.v. "one who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him"): This applies only to a gift given out of love, at which the recipient is not ashamed; but one who gives charity, at which the recipient is ashamed, [should give in secret, as it says,] "A gift in secret pacifies anger" (Proverbs 21:14). Maharsha (s.v. "in My treasure house"): According to the conclusion, which refers [the need to inform] to Shabbat's reward, which does not become known of itself, the "good gift" is the Shabbat of the World to Come, which is wholly good and wholly Shabbat, and "My treasure house" is the great good hidden away for the righteous, of which it is said, "No eye has seen, O God, besides You." On the initial supposition, that it speaks of the Shabbat of this world, which does become known, the good gift is the rest itself — for the labor of the six days belongs to Adam's curse, "by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread," which is why a Noahide who rests is liable — and "My treasure house" is the rest that Adam had on all days before he sinned. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 10b): Just as the one is a giver, the other must be a complete receiver of the gift — otherwise there is no giving here — and one who does not know from whom he receives is not called a receiver; therefore he must inform him, unless the recipient is poor and in need of sustenance, for then [the giver] intended only to sustain him. Shabbat in particular had to be made known because, unlike the other commandments, whose reward merely follows from them, its gift is itself the World to Come — for Shabbat is a semblance of the World to Come, "the day that is entirely Shabbat" — and so He said, "I have a good gift in My treasure house," that is, the good hidden away for the righteous, which is the World to Come. Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:14): When one makes his love known to another, he seeks that one's love in return, like one who says, "See, I have done you this kindness; it is fitting that you love me for it." For this reason they said, "One who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him": whoever receives a gift ought to love the one who gives it, and therefore one must let him know that one is giving him the gift, so that there may be peace between the giver and the receiver. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parashas Shekalim 15): Haman's offer "to bring into the king's treasuries" alludes to "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name": the horn exalted through the shekels and charity reaches without limit up to Atika [the Ancient One], and this is the holiness of Shabbat — the revelation of Atika that one merits on Shabbat — and this is "in My treasure house." Haman claimed that he too could "bring into the king's treasuries" by giving such lavish charity that his horn would be exalted. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): On "to know that I, the Lord, sanctify you," the Gemara says, "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name"; and of its reward, which He is not wont to reveal, He said "to know" — perforce, with "that I [the Lord sanctify you]" He informed them of its reward, for the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah, the holiness it brings into the heart. This is the good gift the Blessed One gave Israel: a root of holiness fixed and enduring in their hearts, from the light of His Presence that dwells with them even amid their impurity, without human effort. Beis Yaakov (Toldos 41): "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name; go and inform them" — that is, that Israel should know that the Blessed One sanctifies them, as it is written, "to know that I, the Lord, sanctify you"; this is a sign that Shabbat is exceedingly good and great, and the Blessed One said "go and inform them" because the main thing is recognition. When Israel wish to taste the holiness of Shabbat they must give over their recognition too to the Blessed One, and this is called "Ayin" [nothingness]. Sod Yesharim (Purim 10): My father explained that the supreme will, above human grasp, by which the Blessed One chose Israel even before their service, is the light called Atika, far above the grasp of creation; the Blessed One concealed this light in this world, and it is to this light that the Sages alluded: "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name." בָּעוֹלָם הַגָּנוּז וְנֶעְלָם.
meaning: rooted in the primordial hidden and concealed realm.
כִּי שַׁבָּת אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
For Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World to Come,
שֶׁהוּא עוֹלָם הַנֶּעְלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
which is the realm concealed within this physical world,
וְאֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים הוּא הָרְשִׁימוּ שֶׁנִּתְגַּלָּה מִמֶּנּוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּמַתָּנָה.
and that one-sixtieth is the spiritual imprint revealed from it into this world as a pure gift.

כִּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא גּוּפֵיהּ נִקְרָא (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.)702 Avodah Zarah 3a — R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is meant by "which I command you this day"? This day to do them, and not tomorrow to do them; this day to do them, and not this day to receive the reward. Rashi: "This day to do them" — in this world; "and not tomorrow" — because one cannot perform them in the World to Come. Tosafos (s.v. "this day to do them, and not tomorrow to do them"): Tosafot asks why the Sages objected to the men of Jericho, who ran the words of the Shema together and did not pause at "this day, upon your heart," so that it sounded like "this day upon your heart and not tomorrow upon your heart" (Pesachim 57a) — what harm is there in that, seeing that it is true, as is implied here? He answers that there one might err and take "this day" and "tomorrow" quite literally, whereas here "this day to do them" stands in a verse that speaks of the payment of reward — "and repays them that hate Him" [Deuteronomy 7:10] — and the reward of the righteous is paid in the World to Come. Maharsha: The objection could have been raised from the Holy One's own words just above, "Fools of the world! One who took trouble on the eve of the Sabbath..." — except that even so He deals with them beyond the letter of the law and tells them to make a sukkah. It may therefore be that the objection is drawn not from "this day to do them and not tomorrow to do them" but from "this day to do them, but not this day to receive the reward": since the nations have already received the reward of their commandments in this world — "and repays them that hate Him to their face" — they receive nothing further in the World to Come, for otherwise justice would be impaired, Israel receiving only the reward of the World to Come. And by the commandment of sukkah He hinted to them that they should have kept the commandments in this world, which is like a sukkah, a temporary dwelling. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a): The Gemara’s objection from this teaching [to the nations’ being offered the sukkah in the time to come] is the very same difficulty as above — "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, from where will he eat on Shabbat?" — only that here it is written in the Torah, and since it is written in the Torah, it cannot possibly be otherwise at all. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 1): Tefillin, the recognition of God's name upon a person in actual deed, belong only to the weekdays and not to Shabbat and festivals, when the recognition in the heart must be clear without any deed, like the world to come, a day [of clear intellectual illumination] that is entirely Shabbat, a cessation from deeds, as it says, "today to do them and not tomorrow." Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 25): Shabbat is [the day on which God Himself is one's light, needing no fire of fear]; nevertheless one must toil to cook the food on the eve of Shabbat, for "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, what will he eat on Shabbat?" and "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward": this light does not come to a person by itself. So too the Shabbat lamp must be lit from the eve of Shabbat, for on Shabbat there is no longer time to arouse fear, the day being entirely love and cleaving to God. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): This world is the world of toil, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat" refers to the world to come, the day that is entirely Shabbat, where there is no doing even of Torah and mitzvot, as they said, "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; and Shabbat is a semblance of the world to come, the time of the Blessed One's rest. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Savo 16): The verse ["all these blessings will come upon you"] certainly does not speak of the reward and punishment for the mitzvot, which are not in this world, for it is only "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; it speaks of the blessings of this world, that God will give every assistance so that one can serve Him all the more. And if, Heaven forbid, they do not listen, the reverse too will serve as an assistance, through which they will take it to heart to return and mend their ways. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares, from the Yerushalmi 14): The world to come is likened to day because there will be no departure there from the [fixed] order, such departure coming about through changes in deeds, as they said, "today to do them and not tomorrow to do them." But in this world, the day of action, where choice is in man's hand, the order changes through deeds: toward evil, as troubles and exile, through evil deeds, and toward good through cleaving to the Blessed One.: "לְמָחָר לְקַבֵּל שְׂכָרָם",
For the World to Come itself is described (Avodah Zarah 3a) as: "tomorrow, to receive their reward,"
מַשְׁמָע שֶׁהֵם בָּאִים בִּשְׂכַר הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם לוֹ.
implying that souls arrive there as a direct recompense for their spiritual toils.
אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין שָׁם תַּשְׁלוּם שָׂכָר,
In this world, however, there is no dispensing of fundamental reward;
רַק שֶׁמִּמֵּילָא, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהוּא לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְנַחַת רוּחַ מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם, מִזֶּה בָּא קְדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת,
rather, solely because their actions bring pleasure before Hashem, blessed be He, does the holiness of Shabbat emerge,
שֶׁהוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי "וַיַּרְא וְגוֹמֵר וְהִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד וְגוֹמֵר",
which arises only from the divine contemplation: "And God saw... and behold, it was very good,"
וְנֶאֱמַר: "שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַשׁ",
and it is stated: "He rested and was refreshed,"

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (הוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י703 Rashi on Exodus 31:17 — "And He rested [va-yinafash]" — as the Targum renders it, "and He rested." Every form of nofesh is an expression of nefesh, soul: one restores his soul and his breath when he takes his ease from the toil of labor. And He of whom it is written, "He does not faint nor grow weary" (Isaiah 40:28), and whose every act is accomplished by a mere word — Scripture ascribed rest to Him only in order to let the ear hear what it is able to hear.):
and our Sages of blessed memory explained (cited in Rashi):
כְּמִי שֶׁמִּתְנַפֵּשׁ מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ וְשׁוֹאֵב רוּחוֹ אֵלָיו.
like one who draws his breath back to himself after his labor.
שֶׁזֶּה סוֹד עֲלִיַּת הָעוֹלָמוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת כַּיָּדוּעַ,
This is the mystical secret of the elevation of the worlds on Shabbat as is known,
וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַנִּיחָא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מֵהַנִּבְרָאִים,
and it is produced through the contentment Hashem derives from created beings,
מִזֶּה נִתְהַוָּה קְדֻשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת.
from which the active holiness of Shabbat is generated.
וְנִמְצָא שֶׁזֶּה גַּם כֵּן כְּעֵין שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
Thus it turns out that this too is somewhat akin to an outcome of human effort,

וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.)704 Avodah Zarah 3a — They said before Him: Master of the Universe, give it to us anew and we will perform it. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: Fools of the world! One who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat; one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat — from where will he eat on Shabbat? Rashi: "On the eve of Shabbat" means in this world. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a, s.v. "and sukkah is its name"): Since the nations claim to be fit for the Torah, which is intellectual and beyond nature, He gave them the commandment that shows a person going out of his nature: leaving his fixed, natural dwelling to sit in the shade of the sukkah. The nations, whose whole conduct is natural, cannot bear this and kick at it; Israel too are somewhat natural, for man is not an angel, and are exempt from the sukkah when it causes them suffering, yet they do not kick, for they desire and love to go beyond nature, only that at such times it is impossible for them. This shows that the Torah, the whole of which is beyond nature, is not fit for the nations at all. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a, s.v. "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat"): That is, this world is the physical world, which is always in potential, and therefore commandments and good deeds belong to it, for in it things go out from potential into actuality. But in the World to Come a person is already in actuality, and going out into actuality has no place there, since it is not physical; the World to Come is therefore cessation and rest. Hence he said that one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat, the day of action, will eat on Shabbat, the day of rest, on which nothing goes out into actuality — and so the commandments pertain to this world alone. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 25): Shabbat is [the day on which God Himself is one's light, needing no fire of fear]; nevertheless one must toil to cook the food on the eve of Shabbat, for "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, what will he eat on Shabbat?" and "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward": this light does not come to a person by itself. So too the Shabbat lamp must be lit from the eve of Shabbat, for on Shabbat there is no longer time to arouse fear, the day being entirely love and cleaving to God. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): This world is the world of toil, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat" refers to the world to come, the day that is entirely Shabbat, where there is no doing even of Torah and mitzvot, as they said, "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; and Shabbat is a semblance of the world to come, the time of the Blessed One's rest. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Sukkah): Shabbat alludes to the future, when there will be no labor, but only what a person acquired in this world through his deeds will then be fixed in his heart, according to how much he toiled in this world. Therefore all labors are forbidden on Shabbat in this world, and only what one toiled for on the eve of Shabbat does one eat on Shabbat. Beis Yaakov (Vayeishev 3): All the possession a person acquires for himself in the world of action comes only from performing the mitzvot, and clarity [of understanding] alone does not suffice; by this he acquires the life of the world to come, for this world is like the eve of Shabbat and the world to come like Shabbat, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will have what to eat on Shabbat." Tiferes Yosef (Shemini Atzeres 4): A person calls his labor "toil" only where he does not see its purpose; on Shabbat he attains the light of the Blessed One and recognizes that he attained it through the work of the six days. This is "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat": through the toil and labor he expended he attains this light, and so he recognizes retroactively that all the activity of the six weekdays was not futile toil for him either. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 18): In the future the nations will want to begin from the start, without first entering the gate of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the Blessed One answers that this is impossible: "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat" means that had they first refined themselves to be included in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, within "every citizen in Israel" [which includes converts], they too could have kept the mitzvah of sukkah. But to begin now without that prior inclusion is impossible, for one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat has nothing to eat on Shabbat, and from where would he gain a share in the mitzvah of sukkah?: "מִי שֶׁלֹּא טָרַח בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת, מַה יֹּאכַל בְּשַׁבָּת?",
along the lines of the adage (Avodah Zarah 3a): "He who did not toil on Friday, what will he eat on Shabbat?"
דְּצָרִיךְ הֲכָנָה לְשַׁבָּת בִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ,
for one requires preparation for Shabbat on a literal level,
וְיָדוּעַ דְּכָל הֲכָנוֹת שֶׁבְּמַעֲשֶׂה יֵשׁ לָהֶם רְמִיזוֹת גַּם כֵּן בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה וּבְהַשָּׂגַת אוֹר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה.
and it is known that all physical preparations allude to internal states of thought and the perception of holy light.

וְהַיְנוּ דְּבֶאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִלָּה כו705 Megillah 26b — Concerning a gift [of a synagogue], R. Acha and Ravina disagree: one forbids it and one permits it. The one who forbids says: By what means would its sanctity lapse? And the one who permits says: Had he not received some benefit from him, he would not have given it to him; the gift therefore reverts to being like a sale. Rashi: A gift — that is, where the townspeople gave the synagogue away to someone for ordinary, non-sacred use. Sod Yesharim (Eighth Day of Pesach 26): This free gift is as the Gemara says of a gift, "had he not derived benefit from him he would not have given it to him, so the gift becomes like a sale." A sale is what the Blessed One gives a person in exchange for his service, and a gift is what He gives beyond his service: when, after all his service, a person recognizes that he has accomplished nothing before the Blessed One for which reward would be due, the Blessed One gives him as a free gift even what service cannot attain. Thus the gift becomes like a sale — not that the Holy One, blessed be He, is lax, but He grants this free gift by strict justice, measure for measure: as this person gave himself over to the Blessed One entirely, not for any particular thing, so the Blessed One bestows all good things on him entirely, not for any particular service.:):
And this matches what our Sages of blessed memory taught (Megillah 26b):
"מַתָּנָה כְּמֶכֶר, דְּאִי לָאו דַּהֲוָה לֵיהּ הֲנָאָה מִנֵּיהּ לָא יָהֵיב לֵיהּ מַתָּנָה",
"A gift is like a sale; were the giver not deriving pleasure from him, he would not present the gift,"
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא מַתָּנָה,
yet it is still termed a gift nonetheless,
שֶׁאֵין זוֹ תְּמוּרַת הַהֲנָאָה כְּלָל,
because it is not direct payment for that pleasure at all,
רַק שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַהֲנָאָה נִתְקָרְבָה דַּעְתּוֹ אֵלָיו עַד שֶׁחָפֵץ בּוֹ לָתֵת לוֹ מַתָּנָה.
rather, through that pleasure the giver's heart is drawn close enough to desire bestowing the gift upon him.
וְכֵן הוּא קְדֻשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת,
So too is the holiness of Shabbat:
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַהֲנָאָה שֶׁרוֹאֶה שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה "וְהִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד"
that through Hashem's pleasure in seeing that all Creation was "very good" –
וְלָכֵן אָמְרוּ כָּאן לְשׁוֹן "מְאֹד",
and therefore Scripture uses the word "very,"

שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה706 Genesis 1:31 — “And God saw all that He had made, and behold it was very good. And it was evening and it was morning, the sixth day.” Rashi: "The sixth day": the definite article was added at the completion of the work of Creation, to say that He made a condition with them — that they endure only if Israel accept upon themselves the five books of the Torah. Another interpretation: all of them stood suspended until "the sixth," that is, the sixth of Sivan, the day appointed for the giving of the Torah. Ramban: "And behold, it was very good" denotes their enduring permanence, as he explained on the earlier verses, and "very" (מאד) has the sense of abundance. He added the word on this day because He is speaking of the creation as a whole, in part of which evil is found, and He declares that even its "very" is good — which is the ground of the Sages' saying that "behold, it was very good" refers to death, since the evil is needed for the preservation of the good. (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט) עַל יֵצֶר הָרָע,
which our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Bereishit Rabbah 9) as referring to the evil inclination,
כִּי קְדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת קְבִיעָא אַף בְּלֹא הֲכָנַת אָדָם בֶּאֱמֶת,
for the holiness of Shabbat is fixed even without man's preparation in truth,
כִּי גַּם הָרָע בֶּאֱמֶת הוּא טוֹב מְאֹד,
since even evil in its ultimate depth is "very good,"
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם לִשְׁעָתוֹ כְּפִי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִרְאֶה רָע,
only that temporarily, within the framework of this world, it appears evil,
וְנִרְאֶה כְּבִטּוּל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לִקְדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת,
and seems like a disruption of Shabbat's sanctity, Heaven forbid,
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "שִׁכַּח ה' בְּצִיּוֹן מוֹעֵד וְשַׁבָּת",
and regarding this it is written: "Hashem has caused festival and Sabbath to be forgotten in Zion,"
לֹא שֶׁבִּטֵּל לְגַמְרֵי, רַק שֶׁשִּׁכַּח]
not that He eliminated it completely, merely that He caused it to be forgotten
מַגִּיעַ קְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ.
does this transcendent holiness descend.

וַאֲפִלּוּ חַיָּבֵי גֵּיהִנָּם נָחִים בְּשַׁבָּת (סַנְהֶדְרִין סה707 Sanhedrin 65b — This very question the wicked Turnus Rufus asked R. Akiva. He said to him: What makes this day different from other days? He said to him: And what makes this man different from other men? He said to him: Because my master wishes it so. [R. Akiva said:] The Sabbath too — because my Master wishes it so. He said to him: This is what I am saying to you — who says that today is the Sabbath? He said to him: The river Sambatyon proves it; the necromancer proves it; your father's grave proves it, for it sends up no smoke on the Sabbath. He said to him: You have demeaned him, you have shamed him, you have cursed him. Rashi: "Because my master wishes it" — the king, Caesar, wished to make me great and made me ruler; "the Sabbath too — because my Master wishes it": the Holy One, blessed be He, wishes it and commanded concerning its honor. The Sambatyon is a river of stones that rushes along all the days of the week and on the Sabbath is quiet and rests; the necromancer's [dead] does not come up on the Sabbath; and the grave of Turnus Rufus's father sent up smoke all week, for he was being judged and burned, but on the Sabbath the sinners in Gehinnom rest. "You have cursed him" — this "curse" is only reviling, as was their usage. Maharsha: His question, "Who says that today is the Sabbath?", was threefold: who says this is the Sabbath of Creation, on which God rested from all His work; the day on which you were commanded to rest; and the Sabbath of the future, the rest of the World to Come. The Sambatyon, which has rested on the Sabbath since Creation, proves the first; the necromancer, who even now does not perform his work on it, proves the second; and his father's grave proves that in the World to Come they rest on this day — hence [Turnus Rufus's] three expressions: "You have demeaned him, you have shamed him, you have cursed him.":),
And even the condemned souls in Gehenna rest on Shabbat (Sanhedrin 65b),
הַיְנוּ שֶׁמִּתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת בְּכָל הַנִּבְרָאִים אַף בְּעֹמֶק רָע,
meaning that this holiness permeates all creatures even in the depths of evil,
כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא מֵעַצְמוֹ בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בֶּאֱמֶת,
because in truth it manifests autonomously without requiring human effort,
דְּהַיְנוּ אַחַר הַמִּיתָה שֶׁאָז נִגְלָה הָאֱמֶת,
namely after death when the ultimate truth is laid bare;
רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה צָרִיךְ הֲכָנָה.
only in this physical world is personal preparation required.
וּבְגֵיהִנָּם הֵם רַק נָחִים מִיִּסּוּרִים,
And in Gehenna they merely rest from active torment,
דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר חַשְׁכוּת וְהַהֶעְדֵּר מֵאוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
which means darkness and deprivation from Hashem's light;
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין נִכְנָסִים גַּם כֵּן לְגַן עֵדֶן,
yet nevertheless they still do not enter Gan Eden,
דְּהַיְנוּ הַשָּׂגַת הָאוֹר.
which represents the active attainment of that divine light.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַזְּכִירָה הוּא פּוֹעֵל הַשָּׂגַת הָאוֹר בַּלֵּב.
