Therefore they are called "adam" in particular and in completeness, for they have all that befits a man, "adam" denoting specifically one who possesses a divine and not merely natural quality. For this reason the commandments, which are divine actions, belong in particular to Israel.
Therefore they are not called adam (Yevamot 61a),
שֶׁהוּא עֶצֶם הַמְכוּוָּן בַּבְּרִיאָה.
who is the essential purpose of Creation.
אִם כֵּן אֵינָם בְּצֶלֶם וּבִדְמוּת לִהְיוֹת חֵלֶק אֱלוֹהַּ
Consequently, they do not possess that image and likeness as a portion of the Divine,
שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהִתְאַחֵד עִם הַכֹּל.
through which they could become united with the whole.

וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא תִּשָּׂא לד)757 Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 34 — R. Yehudah bar Shalom said: When the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, "Write these words," Moses asked that the Mishnah too be put in writing. But the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that the nations of the world were destined to translate the Torah and read it in Greek, and to say, "We are Israel." Until now the scales are balanced. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the nations: You say that you are My children — I do not know; only those who hold My mysteries are My children. And which are they? This is the Mishnah, which was given orally, and from which everything is to be expounded. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): After prophecy departed, the sages of the Oral Torah began, and the Sages said, "He has set me in dark places — this is the Talmud of Babylonia"; but this is the mysteries of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it says in Tanchuma, "Those who hold My mysteries are Israel." For it is written, "He made darkness His hiding place" — there are His hidden things; and though it is darkness and the hiding of the Face, the darkness is cast by the shadow of His hand, shielding us by way of concealment, as one must make shade to protect against the blazing sun. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:86): The Blessed One teaches human beings to exert effort, which is why the Torah began for Israel as the Written Torah; He wishes a person to arrive at His mysteries — as in the Midrash, "He who holds My mysteries…" — and to understand what He indicates to him with the compass. This is the essential effort: to come to the Oral Torah, which is the recognition that everything is from the Blessed One, the "finding" that comes after toil. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 12): The novel insights of Torah belong to the Oral Torah, whereas in the Written Torah, which is written and set down [before all], there are no novel insights; therefore the nations claim on the strength of the Written Torah, "We are Israel," and the Holy One, blessed be He, answers, "He who holds My mysteries…," for the Oral Torah exists only in the hearts of the children of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 4): Edom claims that they are the good and the pure by birth; therefore Haman's decree was a preparation for the Oral Torah, as the Midrash says: because the nations are destined to say "We are Israel," the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "He who holds My mysteries…" — for it is the Oral Torah that clarifies this. The Oral Torah is what springs from the heart of Israel, the hearts of the children of Israel being its originators, so that it is theirs alone, and this is the testimony that they, and no others, are the masters of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Just as there is wisdom among the nations but no Torah among the nations, so it says in Tanchuma, "He who holds My mysteries…": the Oral Torah was given over only to Israel. The nations, even if they study Torah and innovate in it by their wisdom, speak vanity and not Torah at all, for they innovate from their own wisdom, whereas the Torah is the wisdom of the Blessed One; but the sages of Israel bless over the Torah first and know that the Blessed One is the Giver of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 3): The essence of the Torah is the Oral Torah, which reveals the hidden things of the Written Torah, as it says in Shemos Rabbah that the nations are destined to translate the Torah into Greek… "He who holds My mysteries…." This is an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob alone: the Torah is handed over to them according to what they clarify through their dialectic and their wisdom. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): They said in Tanchuma that the Oral Torah was given because the nations are destined to translate the Torah into Greek and say "We are Israel," and the Holy One, blessed be He, will say, "He who holds My mysteries…." That is, the nations too have a connection to the Written Torah, which is why it was revealed in writing to all who come into the world; but the Oral Torah is the mysteries of the Holy One, blessed be He, which cannot be revealed in writing at all, only "the secret of the Lord is with those who fear Him" — the Congregation of Israel, who look to the Blessed One from the depths of their hearts. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 6): All the innovation of the Oral Torah comes through the unions and complete cleaving to the Holy One, blessed be He, and this is His mysteries, as they said in Tanchuma at the end of Ki Sisa: because the nations of the world are destined to translate the Torah and say "We are Israel," the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "He who holds My mysteries…." This is the telling of secrets, which is for Jacob alone — and "telling" does not mean in writing — so "He tells [His words to Jacob]" means the Oral Torah, the handing over of the words of Torah of which it is said "He has not done so for any nation"; whereas the Written Torah alone was written on the stones in seventy languages.
Our Sages of blessed memory said (Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tissa 34)
שֶׁנִּיתַּן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה לְפִי שֶׁעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת אוֹמְרִים אָנוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל כּוּלֵּי,
that the Oral Torah was given because idolaters would say, 'We are Israel,' and so forth.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי עִיקַּר הַהִתְאַחֲדוּת שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה הוּא מִצַּד הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה,
This means that the essential union attained through Torah comes through the Oral Torah:
הַיְינוּ מִצַּד הַעֲמָקַת הַשֵּׂכֶל בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה לְהַשִּׂיג חֶלְקוֹ בָּהּ.
through deepening one's understanding of Torah in order to attain one's portion in it.
שֶׁתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הוּא הַכֹּל שֶׁבָּהּ כָּל אֶחָד מַשִּׂיג כְּפִי חֶלְקוֹ.
For the Written Torah is the whole, in which each person attains understanding according to his portion.
אֲבָל הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא שָׁוֶה לַכֹּל,
But the Oral Torah is common to all,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ כְּלָלוּת עִנְיַן הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁקָּבַע הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּעוֹלָם,
this being the general institution of Torah that Hashem, blessed be He, established in the world:
שֶׁבָּזֶה יִהְיֶה עֵסֶק הַנִּבְרָאִים וְהַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
that created beings should occupy themselves with it and labor in words of Torah.
וּמִצַּד כְּלָלוּת הַתּוֹרָה יוּכְלוּ הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת לוֹמַר אָנוּ כּוּלֵּי,
Regarding Torah in this general sense, idolaters could say, 'We are,' and so forth,
כִּי עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה הוּא גַּם כֵּן אֶחָד מִמִּצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה,
for Torah study is itself one of the Torah's commandments,
וְהוּא מִכְּלָל שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת וּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה,
and is included among its six hundred and thirteen commandments;
וְיוּכְלוּ לוֹמַר שֶׁגַּם הֵם עוֹשִׂים זֶה כִּבְשְׁאָר מִצְוֹת.
they could claim that they, too, do this, just as with the other commandments.
רַק עִיקַּר מַעֲלַת הַתּוֹרָה נֶגֶד הַמִּצְוֹת
Yet the essential superiority of Torah over the commandments
הוּא מִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת הָאוֹר שֶׁבָּהּ הַמֵּאִיר לָאָדָם,
lies in attaining the light within it that illuminates a person;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת חֶלְקוֹ בָּהּ מִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
this comes through attaining one's portion in it, through understanding the Oral Torah.
וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת כְּלָל לְהַשִּׂיג אוֹר מֵהַתּוֹרָה
This is altogether impossible for idolaters—to attain light from Torah—
מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק בָּהּ.
since they have no portion in it.
וְעִיקַּר מַה שֶּׁהַתּוֹרָה אוֹר לֹא כְּנֵר מִצְוָה
The essential sense in which Torah is light, unlike the lamp of a commandment,
הוּא מִצַּד הַהַשָּׂגָה בָּהּ שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
is the understanding attained within it, which is called Oral Torah.
כִּי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הוּא דּוּגְמַת שֶׁמֶשׁ הַמֵּאִיר,
For Written Torah resembles the sun that shines,
וְקַבָּלַת הָאוֹר הוּא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
and receiving its light is the Oral Torah,
שֶׁחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל אֶחָד מְקַבְּלִים חֶלְקוֹ.
in which each of the sages of Israel receives his portion.

וְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת מוֹנִין לַחַמָּה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה טו)758 Shemot Rabbah 15:27 — Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, handed the secret of the moon to Israel, that they should reckon by it, while the idolaters reckon by the sun — that is to say: as the sun rules only by day, so they rule only in this world; and as the sun is of fire, so they are destined to be judged in it, as it is said, "For behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven." And as the moon is seen by day and by night, so Israel rule in this world and in the World to Come; and as the moon is of light, so Israel inherit the light, as it is said, "Light is sown for the righteous.",
Idolaters reckon by the sun (Shemot Rabbah, end of section 15),
שֶׁהֵם אֵין לָהֶם תְּפִיסָה רַק בַּדָּבָר הַגָּלוּי וּבָרוּר לָעַיִן,
for they grasp only what is openly visible and clear to the eye,
שֶׁזֶּה נִמְשָׁל לַחַמָּה,
which is likened to the sun,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין עב.)759 Sanhedrin 72a — The Sages taught: "There shall be no blood-guilt for him. If the sun has risen upon him" — and did the sun rise upon him alone? Rather, if the matter is as clear to you as the sun that he has no peaceful intent toward you, kill him; and if not, do not kill him. Rashi: "There shall be no blood-guilt for him" is juxtaposed with "if the sun has risen upon him," and we expound juxtapositions: when is it permitted to kill him? When the sun has risen upon him — that is, when it is clear to you that he has come to kill you if you stand against him; but where there is doubt, do not kill him. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos): The Re'em, like Tosafot, takes this baraita to speak of a father breaking in upon his son: since a father ordinarily has compassion on his son, one may kill him only when one knows with certainty that he has come to kill. But according to Rashi the clarity meant here is not actual certainty but a clarity of reasoning: "if it is clear to you" by reasoning "that he has no peace with you" — as with a son toward his father, and all the more so any other person — "kill him"; "and if not" — where the case departs from that presumption — "do not kill him." עַל פָּסוּק אִם זָרְחָה הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ,
as our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 72a) concerning the verse, 'If the sun has risen':
אִם בָּרוּר לְךָ הַדָּבָר כַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ.
if the matter is as clear to you as the sun.
וְהֵם אוֹמְרִים אָנוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִצַּד הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב
They say, 'We are Israel,' on the basis of the Written Torah,
דִּכְתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא וּגְלוּיָה לַכֹּל.
which is written down, set before us, and revealed to all.
אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹנִין לַלְּבָנָה שֶׁהִיא הַמְקַבֶּלֶת אוֹר הַחַמָּה,
Israel, however, reckon by the moon, which receives the light of the sun;
כִּי זֶהוּ הָעִיקָּר שֶׁל הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא מוֹרָה דֶּרֶךְ,
for Torah's essential purpose is to show the way,
דְּזֶהוּ שֵׁם תּוֹרָה,
which is the meaning of the name Torah:
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּקַבְּלוּ מִמֶּנָּה.
that people should receive from it.
וְזֶהוּ הָעִיקָּר אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל לְקַבֵּל אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה
For Israel, the essential aim is to receive the light of Torah,
וְאֵין מִסְתַּפְּקִים בַּתּוֹרָה עַצְמָהּ.
and they are not satisfied with Torah itself alone.
וְזֶהוּ מֶמְשֶׁלֶת הַיָּרֵחַ בַּלַּיְלָה שֶׁהוּא זְמַן הַהֶעְלֵם,
This is the moon's dominion at night, the time of concealment,

וְכִלְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מוֹעֵד קָטָן יז.)760 Moed Katan 17a — For Resh Lakish said: A Torah scholar who has gone astray is not excommunicated in public, as it is said, "And you shall stumble in the day, and the prophet also shall stumble with you in the night" — cover him over as the night covers. Rashi: "Cover him" — do not shame him in public. "As the night" — which is dark, and no man sees. Maharsha: "As it is said, 'And you shall stumble in the day, and the prophet also shall stumble with you in the night'" — "the prophet" here is the Torah scholar who has gone astray, of whom he was speaking. כַּסֵּהוּ כַּלַּיְלָה,
in the expression of our Rabbis of blessed memory (Moed Katan 17a), 'Conceal it like the night.'
כִּי קַבָּלַת הָאוֹר נֶעְלָם,
For receiving the light is hidden:
שֶׁאֵין אֶחָד מַשִּׂיג הַשָּׂגַת חֲבֵירוֹ,
no person apprehends another's understanding.
וְגַם הַשָּׂגַת עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ דָּבָר בָּרוּר כְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב דִּכְתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא,
Even one's own understanding is not something manifestly certain, like Written Torah, which stands recorded before us;
אֲבָל הַשָּׂגַת אָדָם אֵין בּוֹ בֵּירוּר כְּלָל.
human understanding has no such absolute certainty.
וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹמֶה לַלַּיְלָה,
This is the essential labor of this world, which resembles night:
וְכִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחֹשֶׁךְ הַשֵּׁם אוֹר לִי.
'When I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light for me.'
וְיָדוּעַ דְּעִיקַּר חֵשֶׁק הָאָדָם בְּחָכְמָה וְהַשָּׂגָה הוּא לְהַשָּׂגַת הַנֶּעֱלָמוֹת,
It is known that a person's principal desire for wisdom and understanding is to apprehend what is hidden,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ גַּם כֵּן פִילוֹסוֹפֵי הָאוּמּוֹת הַקַּדְמוֹנִים,
as the ancient philosophers of the nations also wrote.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵם גִּילּוּ חֶשְׁקָם שֶׁהוּא רַק לְהַשָּׂגַת חָכְמַת הַמְדוּמּוֹת אֶצְלָם לְחָכְמוֹת,
They, however, disclosed a desire only to attain those disciplines that they imagine to be wisdom;
אֲבָל חֵשֶׁק יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא לְהַשָּׂגַת הַתּוֹרָה.
Israel's desire is to attain understanding of Torah.
וְכַיָּדוּעַ מִדִּבְרֵי דָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּתְמַנְיָא אַפֵּי,
This is familiar from the words of King David, peace be upon him, in the 'eightfold' psalm, Psalm 119.
וְזֶה וָזֶה מִתּוֹקֶף חֶשְׁקוֹ לְהַשָּׂגַת הַנֶּעֱלָמוֹת,
Both arise from the intensity of the desire to apprehend hidden things;
וּכְפִי גּוֹדֶל הַחֵשֶׁק כֵּן הוּא הַהַשָּׂגָה דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
and the degree of one's desire determines one's attainment in the Oral Torah.
וְלָכֵן הַתְחָלַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הַגְּלוּיָה לָנוּ
Therefore, the Oral Torah as revealed to us begins
הוּא מֵאַנְשֵׁי כְנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁפָּסְקוּ נְבִיאִים אַחֲרוֹנִים.
with the Men of the Great Assembly, when the last prophets ceased.
שֶׁהַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבוּאָה הוּא מֵעֵין הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב,
Prophetic apprehension resembles the Written Torah,
שֶׁהוּא רַק גִּילּוּי מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
for it is revelation from Hashem, blessed be He.
וּבְהַגָּדַת כֹּה אָמַר הַשֵּׁם,
In the declaration, 'Thus said Hashem,'
שֶׁהֵם דְּבָרִים גְּלוּיִים אֵין סָפֵק בָּהֶם,
the words are revealed and admit of no doubt.
וְהֵם נִמְשָׁכִים הַכֹּל מִצַּד עִיקַּר קַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה
They all flow from the original reception of Torah,
שֶׁהָיָה תּוֹרָה מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
which was Torah from Heaven,
לִהְיוֹת הוּא יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמְלַמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְעַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל,
with Him, blessed be He, teaching Torah to His people Israel,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד וְלֹא יִכָּנֵף עוֹד מוֹרֶיךָ.
as it will be in the future: 'Your Teacher will no longer be concealed.'
וְכֵן הָיָה לְנָבִיא כָּל דּוֹר כְּפִי מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ הִתְגַּלּוּת מְפוֹרָשׁ,
So, too, each generation's prophet experienced explicit revelation according to his level.
וְזֶה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹמֶה לַלַּיְלָה
This does not derive from the aspect of this world that resembles night,
שֶׁהַתְחָלָתוֹ מִזְּמַן הַגָּלוּת בְּיִחוּד.
which begins especially with the period of exile.
וְכָל נְבִיאֵי הַגּוֹלָה אֵין סָפֵק לְדַעְתִּי
Concerning all the prophets of the exile, I have no doubt
שֶׁנּוֹלְדוּ מִכְּבָר מִזְּמַן הַבַּיִת,
that they had already been born in the time of the Temple.
וְכַמְפוֹרָשׁ בְּבִנְיַן בַּיִת שֵׁנִי
As is explicit concerning the building of the Second Temple,
שֶׁהָיוּ שָׁם חַגַּי זְכַרְיָה מַלְאָכִי נְבִיאִים הָאַחֲרוֹנִים,
when Chaggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the last prophets, were present,
שֶׁהָיוּ הַרְבֵּה מֵהֶם הַזּוֹכְרִים הַבַּיִת הָרִאשׁוֹן כִּי הֶאֱרִיכוּ יָמִים.
many of those present remembered the First Temple, for they had lived long lives.
אֲבָל מִזְּמַן חוּרְבַּן בַּיִת רִאשׁוֹן וָאֵילַךְ נִסְתַּם כָּל חָזוֹן
But from the destruction of the First Temple onward, all prophetic vision was closed off,
וְלֹא נוֹלַד עוֹד נָבִיא.
and no further prophet was born.
אֲבָל הָיָה הַתְחָלַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
Instead, there was the beginning of Oral Torah,
כְּשֶׁהֲדוּר קִבְּלוּהָ בִּימֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ מֵאַהֲבַת הַנֵּס,
when they accepted it anew in the days of Achashverosh out of love for the miracle,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת פח.)761 Shabbat 88a — "And they stood at the foot of the mountain" — Rav Avdimi bar Chama bar Chasa said: This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, held the mountain over them like a barrel and said to them: If you accept the Torah, well and good; and if not, there shall be your burial. Rav Acha bar Yaakov said: From here comes a great protest against the Torah [that it was accepted under duress]. Rava said: Even so, they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus, as it is written, "The Jews confirmed and accepted" — they confirmed what they had already accepted. Rashi: ["At the foot of the mountain":] actually beneath the mountain. ["A barrel":] a vat into which beer is put. ["A great protest":] for if He summons them to judgment [asking] why they did not fulfill what they took upon themselves, they have an answer: that they accepted it under duress. ["In the days of Ahasuerus":] out of love for the miracle that was done for them. Tosafos (s.v. "He held the mountain over them like a barrel"): And although they had already put "we will do" before "we will hear," [He held it over them] lest they retract when they saw the great fire at which their souls departed. As for Avodah Zarah (2b), where [the nations ask,] "Did You hold the mountain over us like a barrel?" — implying that had He held it over them they would have had no answer — while here it is called a great protest against the Torah: [that passage concerns] their not having accepted it, but for not having fulfilled it there is an answer. Tosafos (s.v. "Rava said: they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus"): The Ri found it puzzling: in Megillah (7a) Shmuel proves from "The Jews confirmed and accepted" — they confirmed above what they had accepted below — that Esther was said with the holy spirit, and Rava says that every other proof has a refutation except Shmuel's; yet Shmuel's too is refuted, since Rava himself uses this verse for another exposition, and in Chagigah (10a) a verse's being needed for another exposition counts as a refutation. If one reads "Rabbah" there, it is well; or else, in Megillah he means that the others are refuted in their reasoning, whereas Shmuel's is open only to the objection that the verse is needed for another exposition. Tosafos (s.v. "a great protest against the Torah"): As for what is said in Nedarim (25a), that Moses made a covenant with Israel over the Torah and the commandments and adjured them, and in Sotah (37b), that they accepted the whole Torah at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal — R. Tam says that this was at the Divine command, and so as though against their will; but in the days of Ahasuerus they accepted it of their own accord, out of love for the miracle. And the covenant Joshua made with them to serve the Lord was only [an undertaking] not to worship idols, as it is written, "Far be it from us to forsake the Lord" (Joshua 24:16). Maharsha: ["He held the mountain over them like a barrel":] Since it says not "beneath the mountain" but "in the nether part of the mountain," it implies within its lower part, like a barrel, which surrounds on the sides as well — and so "there shall be your burial," like a grave, which surrounds on the sides as well; [to Tosafot's question, why this was needed after "we will do and we will hear,"] one may further answer that their word in putting "we will do" before "we will hear" was not a complete acceptance until they afterwards took it upon themselves by covenant and oath. ["They confirmed what they had already accepted":] On its plain sense, referring to the Megillah, it should have said "accepted and confirmed," since acceptance certainly precedes confirmation; for this reason it is also expounded in Megillah (7a), "they confirmed above what they had accepted below," and in Shevuot (39a), of the Megillah reading as a later ordinance already included at Sinai — and these expositions are of equal weight, and all of them hold. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 32): He held the mountain over them not lest they retract — why should they, having already said "we will do and we will hear"? — but so that Israel should not say they accepted the Torah of themselves and might have refused: the whole world depends on the Torah, and without it would return to chaos, so it is not fitting that the completion of all existence hang on Israel's choice, something that might or might not be; therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, compelled them, and what is compelled admits no removal or annulment. "A great protest": in the end the acceptance was by compulsion, and that is not a complete acceptance, which must be by the recipient's will. In the days of Ahasuerus they accepted of their own will one commandment that the Blessed One had not decreed upon them, the reading of the Megillah — the last of all the commandments — and if they accepted that of themselves, all the more so the commandments that preceded it, so that it is as though the Torah had been accepted willingly from the beginning, the end proving the beginning. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3): On "until Your people pass over, O Lord": the first entry [into the Land] was only because they are "Your people," as a father pities his son even when he does not go in a good way, and their acceptance of the Torah too was under compulsion; but at the second entry, since "they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus" willingly and were righteous, they were "the people You acquired," acquired by exchange and not as a gift. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 4): Then too "they confirmed what they had already accepted" (Shabbat 88a), and there was surely an illumination in the heart of every Jew, an acceptance of the whole Torah like the illumination at Mount Sinai — yet without open miracles, thunder and lightning, but enclothed in the hearts of Israel themselves, who of their own accord fulfilled it all in their hearts. We suppose this a deficiency, but in truth it is an advantage, for accepting the words of Torah of their own accord is certainly greater, since otherwise there would be "a great protest against the Torah"; and accepting because of revealed miracles is not like accepting of their own accord without such revelation. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 9): As in the future, "with a mighty hand and with outpoured wrath will I reign over you," so too at the giving of the Torah the mountain was held over them like a barrel (Shabbat 88a), against their will, for this purpose: to establish that they are bound in servitude to the Blessed One against their will, and that it is impossible ever to leave His prior servitude. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Zachor 10): Amalek [in the generation of Mordechai and Esther] sought to abolish the Oral Torah from Israel, but it was overturned, and through this the Oral Torah was then established, as is said (Shabbat 88a), "they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus" — that is, the Oral Torah, for it was concerning it that the mountain was held over them like a barrel, whereas concerning the Written Torah they had said "we will do and we will hear." Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 93): At first the Blessed One illuminates a person who is not yet accustomed to it, so that it is hard for him to hold it fast and he loses it; afterward he yearns for it and seeks it, and the Blessed One does not open to him again except with great difficulty. This is the matter of the giving of the Torah, which came through holding the mountain over them like a barrel, and afterward "they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus" willingly; yet no miracle was done for them in the days of Ezra as in the days of Joshua son of Nun.,
as our Sages of blessed memory said (Shabbat 88a).
וְלֹא כְּקַבָּלָה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁהָיְתָה עַל יְדֵי כְּפִיַּית הַר כְּגִיגִית,
This differed from the first acceptance, which came through the mountain being held over them like a barrel,
דְּהַיְינוּ מִצַּד הַשְׁפָּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּלִי אִתְעֲרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא.
meaning through the bestowal of Hashem, blessed be He, without an awakening from below.
וְזֶה נִגְנַז בַּחוּרְבָּן,
This was concealed with the destruction,
דִּבְגָלוּת הַכֹּל רַק מֵאִתְעֲרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא
for in exile everything proceeds only from an awakening from below,
וּמִצַּד גּוֹדֶל אַהֲבָתָם וְחֶשְׁקָם לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה.
and from the greatness of their love and desire for words of Torah.
וְכַמְפוֹרָשׁ זֶה בְּסֵפֶר הֵיכָלוֹת,
As is explained in Sefer Heikhalot,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְגַּלָּה לָהֶם אָז רָזֵי הַתּוֹרָה
through this, secrets of Torah were then revealed to them
מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִתְגַּלָּה בְּבַיִת רִאשׁוֹן.
that had not been revealed in the First Temple period.
וְהַיְינוּ דִּבְבַיִת רִאשׁוֹן הָיָה רַק הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבוּאָה,
For in the First Temple period there was prophetic apprehension;

אֲבָל חָכָם עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יב.)762 Bava Batra 12a — Ameimar said: And a Sage is greater than a prophet, as it is stated: "And a prophet has a heart of wisdom" (Psalms 90:12). Who is compared to whom? You must say: the lesser is compared to the greater. Maharal (Gevurot Hashem, Introduction): Prophecy is like the sense of sight, which registers its object from outside: even though prophecy is not an apprehension of the bodily senses, still, just as the sense cleaves to what it perceives, so the prophet's prophetic faculty cleaves to the thing about which he prophesies. The Sage is therefore the greater, for he apprehends and knows hidden things and brings them out of his own intellect — which is why a prophet is called a "seer" and a "beholder," and a Sage is not. Accordingly the World-to-Come and the survival of the soul, which are wholly separate from man and so cannot be "seen," are set out by wisdom rather than by prophecy: "a Sage is greater than a prophet" in that he can reach what prophecy cannot reach. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 23): This is the lower Wisdom, the wisdom of King Solomon, which is the wisdom of the Oral Torah flowing from the hearts of the Sages of Israel, of which they said that a Sage is greater than a prophet, from the verse "and a prophet has a heart of wisdom": the wisdom in their hearts, the seat of feeling from which their wisdom flows, surpasses prophecy, which comes by sight, as it is written "for the prophet was formerly called a seer." Yet of the wisdom of the heart too it is said "my heart has seen much wisdom," for what one feels in the heart is as though he sees it with his eyes. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The essential delight in Torah and desire for words of Torah lie in the Oral Torah, in the renewal of Torah insights in the hearts of Israel; this is the drawing down of the supernal Wisdom itself, which is above the revelation of the Written Torah through Moses, of whom "there has not arisen a prophet [like Moses]." But "a Sage is greater than a prophet," and things not revealed to Moses were revealed to R. Akiva and his colleagues. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 12): The Written Torah is the prophetic apprehension of a great prophet such as Moses, but "a Sage is greater than a prophet," for he apprehends through the holy spirit from the supernal Holy, the higher Wisdom that is above the Written Torah, which is only "the unripe fruit of the supernal Wisdom." This does not mean that Moses did not attain what the Sage attains: through the holy spirit he certainly did, and everything a seasoned student would in future innovate was revealed to him, this being the apprehension of the Oral Torah, which comes from wisdom and the understanding of the heart. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sarah 5): This is the meaning of the Gemara's "and a Sage is greater than a prophet": it refers to one who attains the true intent of the Oral Torah, which comes through the holy spirit, as the Ramban writes; although they do not apprehend through prophecy, but it appears in the heart through the holy spirit, in this he is nevertheless greater than a prophet. For all the prophets prophesied through a lens that does not shine, whereas the Sage attains the level of "this," as one points with a finger, which belongs to the level of the shining lens. Thus a Sage is greater than a prophet in attaining the level of "this one has acquired wisdom" [zeh kanah, the Sages' reading of zaken], the wisdom being his as a possession, at the level of "this," which is explicit. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares, From Tanchuma 11): A Sage is greater than a prophet, just as "I am" precedes "You shall have no other" among the Commandments. For the prophet is the seer who attains lofty apprehensions, and to him comes the warning "You shall have no other," since that is where there is room for error, as Acher erred; while the Sage is the one occupied with Torah, and to him comes the warning of "I am," which he needs in order to remember it, for through immersion in Torah one can also come to forget the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 3): The level of prophecy is the culmination of recognizing the Presence, "You are with me," to the point that the spirit of the Lord speaks through him so that he says "Thus says the Lord," a recognition more revealed than that which comes through the wisdom of the Torah. For although "a Sage is greater than a prophet," that is in respect of depth; but revelation and sensory seeing are greater with the prophet.,
but a sage is greater than a prophet, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Bava Batra 12a).
וְהַיְינוּ דְּיוּכַל לְהַשִּׂיג יוֹתֵר,
This means that he can attain more,
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינָהּ הַשָּׂגָה גְּלוּיָה וּבְרוּרָה כְּהַשָּׂגַת נְבוּאָה,
although his attainment is not revealed and certain like prophetic apprehension.
שֶׁנִּקְרָא הָרוֹאֶה שֶׁהוּא כְּמוֹ רוֹאֶה דֶּרֶךְ זְכוּכִית וְאַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא.
The prophet is called 'the seer,' for he is like one who sees through glass, through a speculum.
אֲבָל אָז נִתְהַפֵּךְ מֵרוֹאֶה לְאוֹרָה,
But then ro'eh, 'seeing,' was transformed into orah, 'light,'

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְגִילָּה טז:)763 Megillah 16b — "The Jews had light and gladness, and joy and honor." Rav Yehuda said: "Light" — this is Torah, and so it says: "For the commandment is a lamp and the Torah is light." Rashi: "Light — this is Torah": Haman had decreed against them that they should not occupy themselves with Torah, and he had decreed against all of these as well; now they took the festivals upon themselves once more. "I rejoice over Your word" is circumcision, which was given with a "saying" and not with a "speaking" — "And God said to Abraham: And you shall keep My covenant"; and we find that David rejoiced over it, for when he was in the bathhouse and saw himself without Torah and without commandments, as soon as he looked at his circumcision he rejoiced. Maharsha: By the plain sense the verse should have read "there was light" [in the masculine], as in "there was light in their dwellings"; since it says "there was orah" in the feminine, they expounded it of the Torah, which is everywhere spoken of in the feminine. Certain commandments serve as a sign and a testimony for Israel — the Sabbath, the phylacteries [and circumcision] — and Haman decreed against these in particular because they are Israel's testimony, so that when his decree was annulled these testimonies returned to their former state. "Gladness" is the festival, which is a day of rest, and they turned from mourning to a festival; "joy" is circumcision, to which they returned, as "many of the peoples of the land became Jews"; and "honor" is the phylacteries, the glory of Israel, to which they returned, as "the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them." Maharal (Gevuros Hashem 39): R. Eliezer said specifically "the phylacteries of the head" because the phylacteries of the arm express the binding and cleaving of Israel to the Holy One, blessed be He, and where there is cleaving there is no fear. But in the phylacteries of the head there is no binding, only that His name is called upon them — and in being called "the God of Israel" He is set apart from them, and on that side there is fear, for it is fitting to fear the God of Israel, to whom belongs might. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Through the outpouring of wrath upon Haman — for "it is a joy to the righteous to do justice" — [Esther] drew down for the Jews "light and gladness": "light — this is Torah," the Oral Torah, which is a great light emerging from within the darkness; and "gladness" is the joy of the righteous in the Lord, their stronghold in a time of trouble, when the trouble, the dross of the judgments, is turned into strength and might. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 4): "The Jews had light" — this is the illumination of the yesod of Abba, which is called Torah; and "gladness — this is the festival," the sanctity of the times, which Israel sanctify: by virtue of Purim, the clothing of His wisdom in the Written Torah within the Congregation of Israel, the festival that Israel sanctify becomes holy like the Sabbath, which is fixed and established and sanctified by the Blessed One, for all is one; and from the sanctity of Purim comes an addition of joy to every festival. "And joy — this is circumcision": the sanctity of the yesod, in guarding the covenant. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Zachor 13): After they repented and wiped out Amalek, "the Jews had light," and the Sages expounded: "Light — this is Torah, as it says, 'and the Torah is light'" — that is, the Oral Torah, which is called orah, a feminine form, because it receives from the Written Torah, which is called "Torah or." So too "they accepted it anew in the days of Ahasuerus" refers to the Oral Torah, for which the mountain had been held over them like a cask, whereas of the Written Torah they had said, "We will do and we will hear." Sod Yesharim (Purim 13): "Light — this is Torah": just as at Creation the primordial will was revealed only after "the Lord God cast a deep sleep" upon Adam, so here — at that time the Blessed One began to build the revelation of the Oral Torah through the Men of the Great Assembly, and so precious a light could not emerge openly except through concealment, the "deep sleep" of the days of Ahasuerus. After that sleep it was openly revealed — "the Jews had light; light — this is Torah" — for the Oral Torah, previously contained and hidden within the Written Torah, was revealed through the Men of the Great Assembly, as the Sages hinted: "they fulfilled what they had already accepted" at Sinai. לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה זוֹ תּוֹרָה;
as our Sages of blessed memory said (Megillah 16b): 'The Jews had light'—this means Torah.
זֶה נִתְחַדֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַתּוֹרָה אוֹרָה מֵאִיר לְעֵינֵיהֶם בְּלֹא רְאִיָּה,
This was the new development: Torah would be a light illuminating their eyes without direct vision,
רַק כְּקַבָּלַת הַלְּבָנָה אוֹר הַחַמָּה,
like the moon's reception of sunlight.

דְּמַאן דְּאָכִיל דְּלָאו דִילֵיהּ בָּהִית לְאִסְתַּכּוּלֵי בְּאַפֵּיהּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי עָרְלָה פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ג)764 Jerusalem Talmud Orlah 1:3 — How does one know [from which vine the sunken shoot draws its life]? R. Bivai in the name of R. Ḥanina: If the leaves are turned toward the young vine, it is clear that it lives by the strength of the old one; and if the leaves are turned toward the old vine, it is clear that it lives by the strength of the young one. R. Yudan bar Ḥanin said: The sign is that one who eats from what belongs to another is ashamed to look at him. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "How does one know"): The leaves meant are those of the young vine: if they are turned toward the young vine itself, that is, away from the old one, it is certain that it lives by the strength of the old, and that is just why it turns its face away from it; and if they are turned toward the old vine, it is known that it lives by its own strength. This is what R. Yudan bar Ḥanin's sign means — one who eats from what belongs to his fellow is ashamed to look him in the face, and so turns his face the other way. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 12): In truth "all our deeds You have wrought for us," and everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, which is in the heart alone; only, the Blessed One wanted us to exert ourselves so that [our deeds] be called by our name and we come [to the good] by our own wages — for "one who eats what is not his…" — just as the Sages instituted for a wife that her handiwork is in exchange for her sustenance. Beis Yaakov (Vayigash 12): This is what the Sages intended in saying it is "more comfortable for a person" [not to have been created], rather than "better": for in truth it is better for him to have been created, since while the soul is in the world of souls the life in its hand is very constricted — "bread of shame," as stated in the Yerushalmi, "one who eats what is not his is ashamed to look at him." A person cannot reach the place of his root that befits him unless he passes through this world and is tested. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 16): On Pesach the salvation came without any service on man's part, as it is written, "and you were naked and bare" — naked of commandments. Yet in truth Israel is not at ease with this, as stated in the Yerushalmi, "one who eats what is not his is ashamed to look at him"; therefore the Blessed One afterwards set it that a person should clarify himself, so that the service be called the toil of his own hands — and this is "bring the Omer before Me on Pesach.",
For one who eats what is not his own is ashamed to look his benefactor in the face (Jerusalem Talmud, Orlah 1:3).

וְהִיא עוּלֵימְתָּא שַׁפִּירְתָּא דְּלֵית לָהּ עֵיינִין (זוֹהַר חֵלֶק ב צה עַמּוּד א)765 Zohar 2:95a — Who is the beautiful maiden who has no eyes, whose body is hidden and yet revealed? She comes forth in the morning and is concealed by day, and adorns herself with adornments that are not.,
She is 'a beautiful maiden who has no eyes' (Zohar, volume II, 95a);
וְאֵין שָׁם רְאִיָּה רַק קַבָּלַת אוֹרָה.
there is no direct vision there, only the reception of light.
וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִמְשָׁךְ מִמֵּילָא שִׂמְחָה וְשָׂשׂוֹן וִיקָר,
From this, joy, gladness, and honor follow of themselves;
הֵם שֶׁפַע בְּנֵי חַיֵּי וּמְזוֹנֵי,
these are the abundance of children, life, and sustenance.
כִּי עִיקַּר הַחַיִּים הוּא הַשִּׂמְחָה,
For the essence of life is joy,
שֶׁבְּעַצְבוּת קָץ בְּחַיָּיו וְאֵין קָרוּי חַיּוּת כְּלָל.
since in sadness a person loathes his life, and it cannot be called life at all.
וְשָׂשׂוֹן עִיקַּר הוֹרָאָתוֹ בִּלְשׁוֹן הַקּוֹדֶשׁ שְׂבִיעוּת הַשִּׂמְחָה שֶׁלֹּא תֵעָדֵר.
The essential meaning of sason in the holy tongue is fullness of joy, such that it will not be lacking.
וִיקָר הוּא כְּטַעַם תִּפְאֶרֶת זְקֵנִים בְּנֵי בָנִים,
Yekar, honor, is in the sense of 'Grandchildren are the glory of the aged.'

[וּמִן קֶרִי נַעֲשֶׂה יְקָר וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר766 Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses §16 (on the two Adars) — This is yakar [precious], the letters of keri [a seminal emission] … That is, yakar is made from keri: for, as is known, the souls that go out through drops of keri are the most precious, and when they are absorbed into holiness, yakar is made of them. … [R. Akiva's] colleagues are the ten martyrs of the kingdom … who were the ten sparks of keri that went out from Joseph the righteous, as is known; and when they were rectified and precious souls were made of them, they attained "every precious thing" (Job 28:10), all the preciousness of wisdom and apprehension that can be attained in the world.].
From keri, a seminal emission, comes yekar, honor, as I have written elsewhere.
וְנֶגֶד אַרְבָּעָה אֵלּוּ הֵם אַרְבַּע מִצְוֹת חֲכָמִים בְּיוֹם הַפּוּרִים,
Corresponding to these four are the four commandments instituted by the Sages for Purim,
שֶׁאָז יְכוֹלִים לִזְכּוֹת לָזֶה,
when it is possible to merit this,
כַּיָּדוּעַ מִקְּדוּשַׁת הַזְּמַנִּים,
as is known concerning the sanctity of appointed times.
שֶׁכָּךְ יִסַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
For Hashem, blessed be He, established it thus:
שֶׁהַיּוֹם הַהוּא נִזְכָּר וְנַעֲשֶׂה בְּכָל שָׁנָה וְשָׁנָה,
that this day is remembered and enacted in every year,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁהָיָה כְּבָר פַּעַם אַחַת הֶאָרָה לְטוֹבַת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
in the manner of the illumination that once occurred for Israel's benefit.
וַחֲכָמִים תִּקְּנוּ לְכָל דָּבָר מִצְוֹת מַעֲשִׂיּוֹת הַמַּשְׁפִּיעוֹת זֶה,
The Sages established practical commandments for each matter that draw forth this influence.
דּוּגְמַת כָּל מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
In the manner of all the Torah's commandments,
שֶׁהֵם הַשְׁפָּעַת אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה עַל יְדֵי מִצְוֹת מַעֲשִׂיּוֹת,
which draw forth the light of Torah through practical observances,
כָּךְ עָשׂוּ חֲכָמִים בְּשֶׁלָּהֶם.
the Sages likewise acted with their own enactments.
וְשֶׁפַע אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מִתְרַבֶּה
The abundance of the light of Oral Torah increases
עַל יְדֵי רִבּוּי גְּזֵירוֹת וְתַקָּנוֹת וּסְיָיגִים שֶׁתִּיקְּנוּ חֲכָמִים.
through the many decrees, enactments, and safeguards instituted by the Sages.
וְהַתְחָלָתָם פּוּרִים,
Their beginning is Purim,
דְּהַמְּגִילָּה הוּא מִצְוָה אַחַת שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוֹסִיפוּ עַל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב,
for the Megillah is one orally instituted commandment that they added to Written Torah,
וַעֲשָׂאוּהָ סְנִיף לַכְּתָב שֶׁהִיא מִכְּלָל הַכְּתוּבִים,
and they made it an adjunct to Scripture by including it among the Writings.
וּמִקְרָא מְגִילָּה הוּא הַגּוֹרֵם אוֹרָה זוֹ תּוֹרָה.
Reading the Megillah brings about 'light'—that is, Torah.
וְהַסְּעוּדָה וּמִשְׁלוֹחַ מָנוֹת וּמַתָּנוֹת לָאֶבְיוֹנִים הֵם נֶגֶד בְּנֵי חַיֵּי וּמְזוֹנֵי,
The feast, sending portions, and gifts to the poor correspond to children, life, and sustenance;
וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ עוֹד יוֹתֵר.
this is not the place to elaborate further.

sections.en: Israel's Enduring Inner Covenant

items.h: Even the most fallen Jew retains a hidden bond with Hashem that distinguishes Israel from the nations; Parashat Balak reveals this covenant at its most concealed edge.

Seif 1 — The Hidden Jewish Heart
Even profound sin cannot erase the innermost covenant that keeps Israel spiritually distinct from the nations.

p: הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק "וְלִבִּי עֵר", מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתוּב "צוּר לְבָבִי וְגוֹמֵר".
The Blessed One is the heart of Israel, as they taught in Shir HaShirim Rabbah on the verse “but my heart is awake,” from what is written, “the Rock of my heart, etc.”

וְזֶהוּ הַחִלּוּק בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים: דַּאֲפִלּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִרְבּוּ עֲבֵרוֹת עַד אֵין קֵץ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא — יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא, וְנִקְרָא "אַסָּא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי הוֹצֵי" (סַנְהֶדְרִין מד.)767 Sanhedrin 44a — "Israel has sinned" (Joshua 7:11). R. Abba bar Zavda said: Even though he has sinned, he is an Israelite. R. Abba said: This is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is still myrtle and people call it myrtle. Rashi: "Israel has sinned" — since it does not say "the people has sinned," [we learn that] the name of their holiness is still upon them. "Thorns" (chilfei) — in Old French, orties [nettles]. Maharsha: Even though he sinned and transgressed the entire Torah, as [the Gemara states] below, he is not like a gentile; and so it has been written that even one who is an apostate with regard to the entire Torah is an Israelite in all his laws. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 25): The Sages said in Song of Songs Rabbah that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the heart of Israel; therefore they said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, for the root in the depths of the heart is never severed from the Blessed One, and he is called "a myrtle standing among thorns." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The Blessed One rules over the depths of Israel's hearts, and they cannot turn from Him in the depths of their hearts at all, for their root cleaves to the living God and they are not separate from Him, with a choice to separate and become like the nations of the lands. Of this it says, "What comes into your mind shall not be," for "even though he has sinned, he is Israel"; and this is the meaning of the mountain overturned upon them like a barrel at the giving of the Torah: that they would accept it perforce. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:50): Because the world cannot exist without Israel, the Sages said that even though he has sinned he is Israel, "a myrtle standing among thorns": the very human form of the Israelite is nothing but the recognition of the Blessed One, and his sins are only a matter of "standing among thorns," like a rose among the thorns that prick it, the thorns to which the Sages likened the idolaters, as it is written, "and the peoples shall be ... thorns cut down." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): [The nations' wish that Israel become one people with them] is utterly impossible, for even an Israelite who has converted out, that is, who has piled one sin upon another, is Israel even though he has sinned, and the Sages likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns. For the body of an Israelite is distinct from birth from the body of an idolater, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to discern, as holy flesh. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): The root of the evil inclination lies in the nations, who are so in their essence, their root being from evil; not so Israel, whom the Sages likened to a myrtle standing among thorns, for their sins issue only from the thorns surrounding the rose. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 12): Why did the Gemara expound so much to Achan's discredit, attributing to him sins not explicit in Scripture, when even of those who have no share in the World to Come the Sages said not to expound to their discredit, since they are of Jacob's seed, save Balaam? Rather, since "Israel has sinned" is written of him, to teach that "even though he has sinned, he is Israel," the Sages came to show that whoever is of Israel, even if he has multiplied transgressions until his sins reach the heavens, is still Israel and is called "myrtle," only that he stands among thorns. That is, in truth "our will is to do Your will, and who prevents us? The leaven in the dough": by standing among the thorns, which hold the root of evil, the leaven in the dough spreads into the heart of Israel too. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): "Even though he has sinned, he is Israel": the holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from him even if he multiplies sins to the heights, and as is said there of Achan, who transgressed all five books of the Torah, sin can never reach so far as to uproot the very essence of Jewishness, the holiness at the root of every Jew inherited from the forefathers and Jacob our father; however he multiplies sins, it is all from the "leaven in the dough" and the subjugation to the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness. Therefore they likened him to a myrtle standing among thorns: the sins are only in the thorns surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 52): In truth none of the sins of Israel are of their essence; the Sages likened them to a myrtle standing among thorns. Hence the sufferings that come through sin are the thorn pricking it, but when the thorns around it are burned the rose remains whole, and indeed a rose among thorns is the more precious..

This is the distinction between Israel and the nations: even sinners of Israel who have multiplied transgressions without end—though a Jew has sinned, he remains a Jew, and is called “a myrtle standing among thorns” (Sanhedrin 44a).
דַּאֲפִלּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת, וּמַעֲמַקֵּי לְבָבָם דָּבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ נְקֻדַּת לִבָּם.
For even the sinners of Israel are filled with mitzvot, and the deepest recesses of their heart are attached to the Blessed One, Who is the root-point of their heart.

כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ768 Berakhot 17a — After he had prayed, R. Alexandri would say: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will — and what prevents us? The yeast in the dough and subjection to the kingdoms. May it be Your will to deliver us from their hand, that we may return to perform the statutes of Your will with a whole heart. Rashi: "And what prevents us" — from doing Your will. "The yeast in the dough" — the evil inclination in our heart, which leavens us. Maharsha: He explains it after what Maimonides wrote in the Eight Chapters, that a man must keep to the middle path in his traits and his deeds. The evil inclination drives him to one extreme within what is permitted him — to be arrogant and to indulge in permitted desire — and is therefore likened to the leaven in the dough, which raises the dough and makes it more than its true measure; while subjection to the gentile kingdoms forces him to the opposite extreme, for they do not allow Israel to hold themselves up but abase them utterly and withhold from them every good, even what they need for the service of God. Thus "our will is to do Your will" — to walk the middle path — "and what prevents us?" These two, each pulling toward its own extreme; may it be Your will to subdue them before us and behind us, that is, both extremes, "that we may return" to walk in the middle. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 21): In Israel a thought that is not for its own sake comes only from the [evil] inclination, which accustoms one to seek his own pleasure in everything, but the depths of the hearts of the children of Israel are solely for the sake of Heaven, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will." Hence, when there is an actual deed, that suffices to join it to the will in the depths of the heart, and no account is taken of the thought of the "yeast in the dough" that confuses it. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 1): The sign of the covenant testifies that the holy flesh of Israel does not desire evil, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will … and who prevents us …": this depth of will stems from our father Abraham, while the Torah is the spice against the [evil] inclination and the Land of Israel is the opposite of subjugation to the kingdoms. "Our will," the depth of the will, is freedom from the evil inclination and from subjugation; hence no exile came from Abraham's side, and the sufferings come only from the side of the inclination and the subjugation. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Though Israel sank in exile into the forty-nine gates of impurity, this was a clarification before Him who examines hearts of the difference between the nations' immersion, which stems from the essence of their hearts, and Israel's, which comes only from their being mixed among the nations, whereas in the essence of their hearts "it is revealed and known that our will is to do [Your will]." The essence of Israel's hearts is not immersed in impurity at all, and from this side comes the redemption from the nations. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): Even the wicked of Israel are all righteous, just as all Israel are called circumcised, even one actually uncircumcised; so one who is wicked in deed is so only from the side of the [evil] inclination and not from his heart, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will …," and as the Rambam explains the reason for coercing [a husband] until he says "I want." Though he is called wicked for his actual sin, even the sinners of Israel are full of regret, and there is no wicked Jew who does not regret for some moment once the pleasure has passed and the inclination no longer incites him, because of the depth of good in the depths of his heart. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 24): On Atzeres, the time of accepting the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, there is a mitzvah to give pleasure to the body as well, for the yoke is felt mainly by the body, whereas as for the soul, "it is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will." By this we show that although for the body it is a yoke, it nevertheless rejoices in accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, of Torah and of mitzvos. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The holiness of the name Israel at the root of every Jew cannot be uprooted, and even if he multiplies sins it is all from the side of the "yeast in the dough" and the "subjugation to the kingdoms" that surround the root of Judaism, as it says, "It is revealed and known that our will …" Therefore he is compared to a myrtle standing among reeds: the sins are only in the reeds surrounding the myrtle, but the essence of the myrtle has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 263): The reason the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join an evil thought to the deed is that in truth "the hidden things belong to the Lord our God" and "the Lord's portion is His people," as it says, "It is revealed and known … and who prevents us …"; but in idolatry, where one denies [God], God forbid, even an evil thought is joined [to the deed]. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In the depths of the heart "it is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will — and who prevents us …": even the hindrances in a heart that inclines to evil lie only in the revealed part of the heart, from the "yeast in the dough" that sits at the openings of the heart and the "subjugation to the kingdoms" — the thorns that surround the rose and clothe it, one from without and the other from within. But it is all only a garment and not the essence, which is the depth of his heart, where his essential vitality cleaves to the Blessed One. (בְּרָכוֹת יז.): "גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ וְכוּלֵי, וּמִי מְעַכֵּב וְכוּלֵי", וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן מַיְמוֹן (סוֹף פֶּרֶק ב מֵהִלְכוֹת גֵּרוּשִׁין)769 Mishneh Torah, Divorce 2:20 — And why is this bill of divorce not void, seeing that he was coerced, whether by gentiles or by Jews? Because we call a man coerced only when he is pressed and forced to do a thing that the Torah does not obligate him to do — for instance, one who was beaten until he sold or until he gave. But one whose evil impulse has overpowered him to annul a commandment or to commit a transgression, and who was beaten until he did the thing he is obligated to do, or until he kept away from the thing forbidden to him — this man is not coerced by another; rather he coerced himself by his own evil intent. Therefore, as for this man who does not wish to divorce: since he wishes to be of Israel, and wishes to perform all the commandments and to keep far from the transgressions, and it is only his impulse that overpowered him — once he has been beaten until his impulse is weakened and he says "I consent," he has already divorced willingly. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 21): This follows the Rambam's reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing'": in the depths of the heart everyone wishes to heed the words of the Sages and only the leaven in the dough holds him back, so once he has been beaten and his inclination has weakened until he also says with his mouth, "I am willing," it suffices. So too, intention not for the sake of Heaven in a Jew comes only from the inclination, which accustoms him to seek his own benefit in everything, whereas the depths of the heart of the children of Israel are solely for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): That the name Israel can never be uprooted from a Jew seems to take away his free choice; this is the mountain held over them at Sinai, that he will be Israel against his will. But when they accepted [the Torah] again in the days of Ahasuerus it was clarified that this is not coercion, for at his root he truly chooses the Blessed One of his own will; as the Rambam wrote on the reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing,'" even if he is wicked and unwilling to accept the words of the Sages, his true will is not so. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): "All Israel have a share in the World to Come" includes even the wicked of Israel, for all are called righteous, just as all Israel are called circumcised even one who is in fact uncircumcised. One who is wicked in deed is so only because of the evil inclination and not from his heart, as it says, "It is revealed and known before You that our will [is to do Your will]," and as is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing.'" Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 3): There was a "great protest" against the Torah [since it was accepted under coercion] until they accepted it again in the days of Ahasuerus, when the Blessed One clarified that the point of the heart is truly good; consequently there is no "great protest," as is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing'": since in truth he wants it, it is not called duress, and so they were already acquired as a people and for eternal life. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Even the wicked and the sinners of Israel have this: although they sin through the incitement of the inclination, the leaven in the dough, in their true will there is this point, that they can abandon all the desires of this world for the will of the Blessed One. That is why "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing'" is effective, as is known from the Rambam's reason; and this is an inheritance from our father Isaac. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 7): Therefore, although he has sinned, he is still Israel in every respect, for all of it comes only from the leaven in the dough and not from the truth of the point of the heart, as is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing,'" which holds even for one who apostatizes from the whole Torah out of spite. This stems from the root of Jewish holiness that was fixed as a lasting acquisition in the heart of all Israel at the giving of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): The holiness of the name Israel cannot be uprooted from a Jew however many his sins: even when he multiplies sins, it all comes from the leaven in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms that surround the root of Jewishness, as it says, "It is revealed and known before You that our will...," and similarly in the Rambam on the reason for "they coerce until he says, 'I am willing.'" Therefore [the Sages] compared [the sinner of Israel] to a myrtle standing among reeds: the sins are only in the reeds surrounding the myrtle, while the myrtle itself has not changed. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): As is known from the Rambam's words on the reason for "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing,'" what in the heart is unwilling is so only because of the evil inclination. On this it says, "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable [ratzon]," and I received the interpretation that even when one sees that his heart's will is not yet in it, speaking good with the mouth, which is called "the lips of the righteous," helps to teach and to draw the will into the heart as well. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Mishlei 10): "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable [ratzon]": as the Sages said, "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing,'" that is, through his speech he brings the will into his heart as well. What he says with his lips while his heart is not yet clarified helps him to clarify his heart toward the will wholeheartedly: for instance, when anger at his fellow sprouts in his heart, his counsel is first to speak kindly to his fellow even if not wholeheartedly, and by this he gradually brings love into his heart in place of hatred. Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 57): When a person shortchanges himself in divine service, this is "the buyer was defrauded," and a buyer defrauded by less than a sixth is like what the Talmud says, "they coerce him until he says, 'I am willing'": in truth the depth of the heart of Israel is drawn after the will of the Blessed One, but on the outer garment there are impediments that keep him from serving God, and he is shortchanged by them. Yet this is only less than a sixth, which is wholly waived [and the sale stands]. בְּטַעַם "כּוֹפִין עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר רוֹצֶה אֲנִי".

As they said (Berakhot 17a), “It is revealed and known that our will is to do Your will… and what prevents us…,” and as Rabbeinu Moshe ben Maimon wrote (end of chapter 2 of the Laws of Divorce) in explaining the rule that “we compel him until he says: I desire to do so.”
וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲמֹד עָלָיו שׁוּם בְּרִיָּה; רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעִיד שֶׁהוּא כֵּן אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
No created being can fully apprehend this; only the Blessed One testifies that this is truly so within Israel.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵצֶל עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת: אֲפִלּוּ חֲסִידֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁכָּךְ טוֹב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עֶצֶם לְבָבוֹ אֵינוֹ כֵּן.

This is not so among the idolatrous nations: even one of the righteous among the nations who recognizes that this path is good does not necessarily possess that orientation in the very essence of his heart.

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "מַה בֵּין תַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לְתַלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע וְכוּלֵי" — עַיֵּן שָׁם בְּפֶרֶק ה דְּאָבוֹת770 Pirkei Avot 5:19 — Whoever possesses these three traits is among the disciples of Avraham our father, and whoever possesses three other traits is among the disciples of Bilam the wicked. A generous eye, a humble spirit and a modest soul — the disciples of Avraham our father. A grudging eye, an arrogant spirit and a greedy soul — the disciples of Bilam the wicked. What is the difference between them? The disciples of Avraham our father eat in this world and inherit the World to Come; but the disciples of Bilam the wicked inherit Gehinnom and descend to the pit of destruction. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:18): As is known on the Sages' saying, "What is [the difference] between the disciples of Abraham our father and the disciples of Bilam the wicked": the main recognition lies in the spreading-forth that issues from a person, for the branch testifies about the root that it is entirely so. And since the Yesod is the foundation of the whole building, and when the foundation is destroyed the building falls, the main distinction lies in the Yesod. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 20): This is like what is stated in Avot, "What is [the difference] between the disciples of Abraham our father and the disciples of Bilam the wicked": the recognition lies in the disciples, and likewise in the children. For in deed even Esau spreads out his hooves like a swine so as to appear good, though the depth of his beginning is wholly evil, while in Israel it is the reverse, for even one who has sinned, the depth of his beginning cleaves to the good; and the recognition is in the children and disciples, in whom the depth of the father's beginning is revealed..
This is the meaning of their teaching, “What is the difference between the disciples of our father Abraham, peace be upon him, and the disciples of the wicked Balaam, etc.?”—see Avot, chapter 5.

וְנָקַט אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, לֹא מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם; כִּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לִמֵּד תּוֹרָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאַף הָעֵרֶב רַב וְהַגֵּרִים מֵעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת, כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּתְגַּיְּרוּ — בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכֻנּוּ.

They specifically said our father Abraham, peace be upon him, rather than Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, because Moshe taught Torah to Israel; and even the mixed multitude and converts from the nations, once they converted, are designated by the name Israel.
אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לִמֵּד לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, כִּי מִכָּל הַגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּר וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁעָשׂוּ — לֹא נִשְׁאַר מֵהֶם זֵכֶר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
But our father Abraham, peace be upon him, taught the nations of the world; for of all the converts he brought near and “the souls that they made,” no identifiable continuity remained within Israel.

כִּי עֲדַיִן לֹא הָיָה אָז שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁיְּהֵא גֵּר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּר כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד בְּיַהֲדוּת; דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים, דְּהוּא עַצְמוֹ הָיָה גֵּר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּר כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד לִהְיוֹת אֶזְרָחִי (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טו.)771 Bava Batra 15a — David wrote the book of Psalms by means of ten elders. But let it count Ethan the Ezrahite as well! Rav said: Ethan the Ezrahite — this is Abraham. Here it is written "Ethan the Ezrahite," and there it is written, "Who roused up one from the east, whom righteousness meets at every step." Rashi: Rashi rejects the variant in which the Gemara answers that the Ethan the Ezrahite counted in the baraita is Jacob — "we do not have this reading." According to another version, the baraita above counts both Abraham and Ethan the Ezrahite among the ten elders and does not count Asaph, since it holds that Asaph was one of the three sons of Korah. Tosafos (s.v. "and by Solomon and by the sons of Korah"): Some texts count Abraham and Ethan the Ezrahite as two separate men among the ten, and accordingly read the Gemara here as answering that the Ethan the Ezrahite of the list is Jacob. Tosafot objects to that reading: if Ethan the Ezrahite is not Abraham, we have no source at all that David composed the book of Psalms by means of Abraham. Maharsha: The verse "Who roused up one from the east" is expounded of Abraham in chapter Ḥelek; but from that exposition alone one might equally say that Heman the Ezrahite is Abraham. Rav must therefore have relied on the word "Ethan" itself, which is expounded elsewhere of the patriarchs — "the month of Ethanim" being the month in which the mighty ones [eitanim] of the world were born. That it is Abraham in particular, and not Isaac or Jacob, follows from "Ezrahite," from the east [mizraḥ]. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeira 9): Abraham merited to be a citizen [ezrach] in Israel, for he is called "Ethan the Ezrahite," as stated in Bava Basra, and he is called Israel, as stated in Bereishis Rabbah; he was the root of Israel, the first father. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): Once Jacob was clarified as the Lord's portion, his "bed" complete, Abraham and Isaac too were called fathers only of the seed of Jacob, and even Abraham is called Israel, as the Sages said that he is called "Ezrahite" because he merited to be a citizen [ezrach] in Israel..

For at that time the name Israel did not yet exist in the covenantal sense whereby a convert is like a newborn within Judaism. Our father Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first of the converts; he himself was, as it were, a convert reborn into the status of a native (Bava Batra 15a).

וּמִמֶּנּוּ הַתְחָלַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תּוֹלְדוֹת)772 Bereshit Rabbah 63:3 — Abram was called Abraham. Isaac was called Abraham, as it is stated: “These are the generations of Isaac son of Abraham; Abraham.” Jacob’s name was called Israel, as it is written: “No longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel.” Isaac’s name was called Israel, as it is written: “These are the names of the children of Israel who came to Egypt, with Jacob.” Abraham was called Israel. R. Natan said: This is a deep matter — “And the dwelling of the children of Israel who dwelt in Egypt” and in the land of Canaan and in the land of Goshen “was four hundred and thirty years.”, אֲבָל כָּל תַּלְמִידָיו הֵם אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
From him began the identity called Israel (Bereishit Rabbah, beginning of Parashat Toldot), but his disciples themselves belonged to the nations of the world.
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֵם עַצְמָם, כֵּיוָן דְּתַלְמִידִים קְרוּיִים בָּנִים, וְהַכָּתוּב קוֹרְאָן "וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ" — הֵם נִמְשָׁכִים אַחֲרָיו.
Nevertheless, those disciples themselves—since disciples are called children, and Scripture calls them “the souls that they made”—were drawn after Abraham.
וְסִימָנָם "עַיִן וְכוּלֵי" — הֵם טָהֳרַת הַגּוּף מִקִּנְאָה וְתַאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, שֶׁהֵם כְּלַל שִׁקּוּעֵי הַגּוּף שֶׁבָּהֶם מְשֻׁקָּעוֹת כָּל הַלְּבָבוֹת.
Their identifying signs—“a good eye, etc.”—express purification of the body from jealousy, desire, and honor, the general forms of bodily immersion in which all hearts can become sunk.

וְאַף חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יד)773 Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 — “When a woman conceives” — this is what is written, “Behold, in iniquity was I formed.” R. Acha said: Even the most pious of the pious cannot be free of some measure of transgression in this matter. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:10): The meaning of "the counsel of the serpent" is learned from Jesse, who is counted among the four who died through it, and of whom the Sages said, on "in iniquity was I formed," "even the most pious of the pious…". In Elijah, who did not die, even the serpent's counsel was rectified, and he, the angel of the covenant, testifies concerning birth that it is not, Heaven forbid, in iniquity, but that all are holy from the womb. Rav Tzadok (Es HaOchel 12): Death still comes through the counsel of the serpent, that is, the filth the serpent cast [into Eve], and that filth is the desire for lewdness, about which the Sages said of Jesse, one of the four who died through the serpent's counsel, "even the most pious of the pious…". Only Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai, had their filth cease, and then they were truly free of the evil inclination. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 19): The seminal drop is drawn from the brain, but because it comes with the desire of this world, as the Sages said, "even the most pious of the pious…", it imparts impurity; yet the Holy One, blessed be He, brings forth the pure from the impure, for a child is formed from it. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 16): The beginning [of a fall] is in matters of desire, where everyone is in any case somewhat lax about complete holiness like that of Jacob our father, who intended only to raise offspring and was aroused only for the sake of the mitzvah and of Heaven; not every person merits this, as the Sages said on "in iniquity," "even the most pious of the pious…". This comes from laxity in the service of the Blessed One and in bringing the holiness of the words of Torah into one's heart, for one whose thought cleaves to the love of Torah will let no desire for anything else enter him. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 1): On "in iniquity was I formed," with "iniquity" written full, the Midrash says that even the most pious of the pious intends only his own pleasure; this is Jesse, the father of David, and this is the counsel of the serpent, a deficiency in the birth of everyone born of woman, of the offspring of Eve, against which no effort avails, even for the most pious of the pious. Only, as the Sages said, "Who purifies you? The Holy One, blessed be He": the purification from this is His, for He testifies that this desire of Israel is clean and pure. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tazria 5): The impurity of childbirth applies even when a woman bears a righteous one, even the Messiah, and its reason is the Midrash on "Behold, in iniquity was I formed": R. Acha says, "even the most pious of the pious… did my father Jesse intend to bring me into being? Surely he intended only his own pleasure." This was said of Jesse, who died through the counsel of the serpent, and the serpent's counsel is what the serpent instilled in man, that he should feel his own pleasure; from this sprang the impurity of the menstruant and the seven-day impurity of childbirth. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): Jesse, who died through the counsel of the serpent, was clarified through the birth of David, who applied to himself "Behold, in iniquity was I formed," which the Sages expounded from "iniquity" being written full: "even the most pious of the pious…". As is known from the Arizal, wherever letters of the Divine Name are added they indicate added holiness, and vav is the letter of truth; for desire is called falsehood, being a pleasure of the moment, whereas the desire of Israel, who cleave to the living God, endures as they do, for all their powers cleave to holiness. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 147): Only the Unique One of the world can bring forth the pure from the impure, for in this desire lies the source of the deficiencies that come from the serpent, as the Sages said on "in iniquity" [written full], and that is Jesse, who died through the counsel of the serpent. Man's root is in truth impure, as it is written, "in iniquity was I formed," yet there is holiness and purity in it as well; Balaam, being of an evil root, did not believe this, for he did not know that there could be holiness here too. "בְּעָוֹן מָלֵא" לְעִנְיַן תַּאֲוָה.
Even regarding the most pious of the pious, our Sages of blessed memory said (Vayikra Rabbah 14) that he is “full of iniquity” with respect to desire.

וְנֶאֱמַר (מִשְׁלֵי כז, ד774 Proverbs 27:4 — Wrath is cruel and anger overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy? Rashi: “But who can stand before jealousy” — who can stand before the jealousy of Him who is jealous and vengeful? Metzudas Dovid: Fury brings a man to cruelty, and anger incites him to sweep away and destroy; but before a jealous man, who can stand and endure? For jealousy is harsher still than fury and anger, since the jealous man will choose the evil that falls upon his fellow as well over the good that would come to himself and his fellow alike. Malbim: “Fury” is inward anger, in which a man nurses hatred in his heart, and “anger” is outward anger. There is anger without inward fury, and it has sweeping force, since in his anger he sweeps on and chastises, but not cruelty; and there is fury without anger, which has cruelty but no sweeping force, since he does not punish now. But jealousy, when a man is zealous for his honor that has been profaned, has both cruelty and sweeping force, for the jealous man avenges himself at once. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 233): There is hardly a person entirely free of these three, jealousy, desire, and honor: as it says, "who can stand before jealousy?"; of desire the Sages said, "even the most pious of the pious…"; and needless to say honor, which includes both. Jealousy is the worst of them all and the root of the serpent, and corresponding to it is the leper, who is sent outside the camp of Israel.): "מִי יַעֲמֹד לִפְנֵי קִנְאָה"; וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר בְּכָבוֹד, שֶׁמָּצִינוּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה הֵעִידָה עָלָיו שֶׁהוּא עָנָו מִכָּל הָאָדָם, וַחֲשָׁדוּהוּ לְמִשְׂתָּרֵר.

And it is said (Proverbs 27:4), “Who can stand before jealousy?” All the more so with regard to honor: we find that although the Torah testified that Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, was humbler than every person, people still suspected him of seeking authority.
וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִסָּה הַמְעַכֵּב, וְאַף חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים יוּכַל לְפָגְעוֹ לִפְעָמִים עִנְיַן קִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, שֶׁלֹּא יִנָּצֵל.
This is the root of the “leaven in the dough” that obstructs a person; even the most pious can at times be struck by jealousy, desire, or honor and not entirely escape them.

אֲבָל הָעִקָּר הוֹלֵךְ אַחַר שֹׁרֶשׁ הַלֵּב. וּמִסְּתָמָא בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע, שֶׁהָיָה מִנְּבִיאֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, וְאֵין הַנְּבוּאָה שׁוֹרָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא עַל חָכָם, גִּבּוֹר וְעָשִׁיר (שַׁבָּת צב775 Shabbat 92a — And let us derive it from Moses. Perhaps Moses was different, for the Master said: The Divine Presence rests only upon one who is wise, mighty, wealthy, and of tall stature. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 92a): This matter is self-evident: it is not fitting for the Divine Presence to rest upon anything deficient; therefore all of these [qualities] are required, so that the person be whole, and then it is possible for the Divine Presence to rest upon him. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): "Prophecy rests only upon one who is wise, mighty and wealthy" means completeness in the three faculties of man. Wise in the brain; mighty in the strength of the heart, as in "Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination," which comes through the fear of Heaven that restrains his spirit, the inclination dwelling in the heart; and wealthy in deeds, as in "Who is wealthy? One who is happy with his portion," for the completeness of deeds is in the hand of the Omnipresent, so one should not seek great things but be content with what the Lord has allotted him. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part I 8): The essence of man is the soul, the body is his possession, lesser possessions are his money and property, and lesser still his friends and companions, and all of them require completeness: this is "Who is wise … mighty … wealthy … honored," the completeness of the four parts of man. But of prophecy the Sages said "upon one who is wise, mighty and wealthy," the completeness of the three, for [completeness] between a man and his fellow does not apply to a prophet, who is set apart from them; the early authorities placed him as an intermediate between man and angel. Rav Tzadok (Sefer HaZichronos 16): Purification of the heart alone is the main condition of prophecy, while wisdom is an ancillary matter: from the Sages' words, "Prophecy rests only upon one who is wise etc.," it is evident that wisdom is not what brings about prophecy but only an ancillary condition for the prophet, like might and wealth. The essence of prophecy, seeing the truth as it is with the eye of the intellect, comes only through purity of the heart. Beis Yaakov (Chayei Sarah 38): A person must guard the vessels of the body so that they are healthy and strong, and then he will grow wise and succeed in words of Torah, as the Talmud says, "The Divine Presence rests only upon one who is wise, mighty and wealthy"; for the Blessed One so ordained that through these vessels a person can receive words of Torah. For if a human soul is reincarnated in a beast or an animal, the human soul too is considered like a beast and has no stature..), כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.

But the essential measure follows the root of the heart. Presumably, the wicked Balaam, who was one of the prophets of the nations—and prophecy does not rest even in Israel except upon one who is wise, mighty, and wealthy (Shabbat 92a)—would all the more require such qualities among the nations.
