וְעָשִׁיר הוּא הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וְאֵינוֹ רַע עַיִן; וְגִבּוֹר — הַכּוֹבֵשׁ יִצְרוֹ, שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל נֶפֶשׁ רְחָבָה בְּתַאֲוָה; וְחָכָם בַּתּוֹרָה — הֵפֶךְ גַּס הָרוּחַ, שֶׁהוּא סִימָן לַעֲנִיּוּת דְּתוֹרָה, דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה יוֹרְדִים לְמָקוֹם נָמוּךְ וְרוּחַ נְמוּכָה, וְיָדוּעַ דְּכָל גֵּאֶה שׁוֹטֶה.

“Wealthy” means one who rejoices in his portion and is not stingy-eyed; “mighty” means one who conquers his inclination and is not broad-souled in desire; and one who is wise in Torah is the opposite of the arrogant, for arrogance signals poverty in Torah, since words of Torah descend to a low place and to a lowly spirit, and it is known that every arrogant person is foolish.

וְאִם כֵּן וַדַּאי בִּלְעָם הָיָה גַּם כֵּן נָקִי מִכָּל אֵלֶּה, וְהָיָה גַּם כֵּן מְלַמֵּד דֶּרֶךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּעֵין אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהֲרֵי הָיָה נָבִיא לַהַשֵּׁם וְיוֹדֵעַ מֵאֲמִתּוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהֲרֵי נְבוּאָתוֹ הָיְתָה נְבוּאַת אֱמֶת שֶׁנִּכְתְּבָה בַּתּוֹרָה.

If so, Balaam too must outwardly have been free of all these defects and capable of teaching the way of the Blessed One, in a manner resembling our father Abraham, peace be upon him; for he was a prophet to God and knew the truth of the Blessed One, as his prophecy was true prophecy recorded in the Torah.

רַק כָּל זֶה הָיָה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ; אֲבָל מַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ הוּא גּוֹי, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם שַׁיָּכוּת בֶּאֱמֶת לְכָל שָׁלֹשׁ הַמַּעֲלוֹת הַנִּזְכָּרוֹת, וּכְשֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְנִסָּיוֹן נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁהוּא הַהֵפֶךְ מִכֻּלָּם.

Yet all of this existed only in the revealed layer of his heart. In its depths he remained a gentile with no genuine connection to those three qualities; when he was tested, it became clear that inwardly he was their opposite.

וְכֵן הוּא מִתְבָּרֵר בַּתַּלְמִידִים, שֶׁהֵם דֻּגְמַת בָּנִים; דְּשָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁהֵם מַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב דְּאָב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר776 Likutei Ma'amarim, p. 223 (on Samson) — This is in the way of what is taught (Avos, ch. 5): “What is the difference between the disciples of our father Abraham and the disciples of the wicked Balaam?” — for the recognition lies in the disciples, and likewise in the children. In deed, Esau too spreads out his hooves like the swine; and Amalek is called “the first of the nations” because only the depth of his beginning is evil: he can spread out his hooves through all nine levels by which the depth of the beginning of thought unfolds, so as to appear good as well, yet the depth of his beginning is wholly evil, and so he is wholly evil. With Israel it is the reverse: “though he has sinned, he is Israel” — learned from Achan, of whom the Sages said (Sanhedrin 44a) that he denied the entire Torah — and even so the depth of the beginning cleaves to the good, and so he is wholly good. And the recognition is in the children and the disciples, in whom the depth of the father’s beginning is revealed..
The same becomes clarified through his disciples, who are analogous to children; for I heard that children reveal the deepest recesses of the father’s heart, as I have written elsewhere.

וּלְכָךְ הַחִלּוּק דְּאֵלּוּ נוֹחֲלִין עוֹלָם הַבָּא; כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא רוֹמֵז לְבִינָה — לִבָּא — וְהוּא מִצַּד דְּבֵקוּת הַלֵּב, דְּלָכֵן כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.

Hence the distinction that these disciples inherit the World to Come. As is known, the World to Come alludes to Binah—the heart—and comes through the heart’s attachment; therefore all Israel have a share in the World to Come.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן תַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל בִּלְעָם, דְּבִלְעָם עַצְמוֹ נִמְנֶה בְּאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
This is unlike Balaam’s disciples, for Balaam himself is counted among those who have no share in the World to Come.

וּכְבָר כָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר דִּזְכִיָּה גְּדוֹלָה הִיא לְבִלְעָם בְּמַה שֶּׁנִּמְנָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה דְּ"אֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא" בַּהֲדֵי גְּדוֹלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל777 Yisrael Kedoshim §5, p. 22 — It may be said that of itself the cloud did not truly cast out anyone at all, for before Heaven the depths of their hearts are revealed, that they were not torn from the root of Israel’s holiness. Even one who has multiplied sins exceedingly is still “a people that dwells alone and is not reckoned among the nations” (Numbers 23:9), as Balaam testified of them — and I have written elsewhere that he grasped only the virtue of the sinners of Israel, those who have no share in the World to Come like himself; and even so they bear no resemblance to him at all. This was his prophecy written in the Torah, which is the root of the souls of Israel, for they come from the letters of the Torah: those sinners of Israel who multiplied sins until, by the judgment of the Sages of the Mishnah, they have no share in the World to Come — the root of their souls is in these letters of the portion of Balaam. Compare Likutei Ma’amarim (on the Book of Joshua): In truth Balaam is not fit to enter this number, being a gentile after the giving of the Torah, and it is a great merit for him to be included among the commoners there..
I have already written elsewhere that it was a great privilege for Balaam to be counted in the Mishnah’s list of those who “have no share in the World to Come” alongside prominent figures of Israel.

וְנִרְאֶה לִי בָּרוּר דְּזֶה שֶׁאָמַר "תָּמֹת נַפְשִׁי מוֹת יְשָׁרִים וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהִקְשָׁה בְּלִקּוּטֵי תוֹרָה מֵהָאֲרִ"י, כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא עָלְתָה לוֹ כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג, קצד עַמּוּד ב)778 Zohar 3:194b — When that wicked one came down before Phinehas, he said to him: Wicked one, how many evil turns you have wrought upon the holy people! He said to Tzalya: Come and kill him — but not by the Name, for it is not fitting that supernal holiness be invoked over him, lest his soul go forth and be joined to matters of the holy grades, and there be fulfilled in him what he said, "Let my soul die the death of the upright." At that hour he inflicted upon him many kinds of death and he did not die, until he took a sword upon which a serpent was engraved on this side and a serpent on that side. Phinehas said to him: By his own, kill him; and by his own let him die. Then he killed him., לָמָּה נִכְתְּבוּ דִּבְרֵי בַטָּלָה שֶׁלּוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה.

It seems clear to me that this explains Balaam’s words, “May my soul die the death of the upright, etc.” Likkutei Torah in the name of the Ari asks: since this did not in fact occur for him, as stated in the holy Zohar (III, 194b), why were his apparently futile words written in the Torah?
וּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת י עַמּוּד א: "מֵת אַתָּה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא תִחְיֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא".
According to what I have written, this can be understood in light of Berakhot 10a: “You are dead in this world, and you will not live in the World to Come.”
הָכָא נָמֵי, מַה שֶּׁאָמַר "תָּמֹת" — "מוֹת" רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר, מִיתַת נַפְשׁוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא יִהְיֶה תּוֹךְ מִיתַת "יְשָׁרִים", הֵם בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹתָם שֶׁאָבְדוּ עוֹלָם הַבָּא.

So too here: when he said “may my soul die,” “death” means that the death of his soul with respect to the World to Come should be included among the “death of the upright”—those Israelites who lost their share in the World to Come.

דִּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה כָּל עִקַּר נְבוּאַת בִּלְעָם הָיְתָה רַק עַל אוֹתָם פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאָבְדוּ עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהֲרֵי הוּא נִסְתַּכֵּל רַק לְהַזְכִּיר חֶטְאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְדִבֵּר רַק מֵהַחוֹטְאִים.

For it appears that the entire focus of Balaam’s prophecy was precisely those sinners of Israel who lost the World to Come, since he looked only to invoke Israel’s sins and spoke specifically of the sinners.

וְגַם אֵין שׁוּם בְּרִיָּה מַשִּׂיג מַה שֶּׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מִמֶּנּוּ. וְאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לד:)779 Berakhot 34b — R. Chiya bar Abba said in the name of R. Yochanan: All the prophets prophesied only with regard to penitents; but as for the perfectly righteous, "No eye has seen, O God, but You, what He will do for one who waits for Him." Rashi: "They did not prophesy" — the good things and the consolations. "No eye has seen" — it was never seen nor revealed to any prophet. Maharsha: The reward of which the prophets spoke is a bodily reward, such as a man of flesh has the power to attain; but the reward of the perfectly righteous in the World to Come is a purely spiritual reward, without limit, which no human intellect or eye can reach — only the eye of God, who is without limit, as in "what He will do for one who waits for Him." Penitents, in whom the bodily and material power once prevailed, will have only that bodily reward, whereas the perfectly righteous will merit the great spiritual reward of which "no eye has seen." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 4): The prophets are men in a body; how could they see in their prophecy the rank of the righteous man who is separate from matter, the rank that will be his in the time to come? That is impossible; they prophesied only of the rank of penitents, whose souls had been sunk in matter when they sinned, and who even after returning have no wholly separate rank. Therefore the rank of the perfectly righteous is "No eye has seen, O God, but You," for the rank of the righteous man is hidden away. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shelach 14): The Gemara's two statements of R. Chiya bar Abba in the name of R. Yochanan, that all the prophets prophesied only about the days of the Messiah, but of the World to Come "no eye has seen," and only about penitents, but of the wholly righteous "no eye has seen," are one. In the future Gehinnom will be sanctified with the holiness of the Garden of Eden through the tears of the penitents, who are many, and it is sixty times the size of Eden; but the wholly righteous, who never blemished at all, are few, and theirs is Eden itself, over which no creature's eye has ruled, and so "no eye has seen" is said both of the World to Come and of the wholly righteous, whose level the prophets did not attain. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 164): In people's minds the penitent is not like a wholly righteous man, still less are the sins he committed reckoned as merits, even though one believes the Sages' words that deliberate sins become merits and that "in the place where penitents stand [the wholly righteous do not stand]"; this is because repentance is called the "hidden world," and its preciousness and beauty are not revealed to people. [In a bracketed note he adds that] the dissenting view concerns the perception of the prophets: the one master derives his view from the verse "to the far and to the near," which is in the Prophets, while in the other's view it is not so from the standpoint of prophecy, since of the wholly righteous it is said "no eye has seen," which is from the standpoint of the Blessed One alone. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Sanhedrin): As explained in Likutei HaShas, they do not disagree, and these and those are the words of the living God; their dispute is alluded to in the Mishnah, "The blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering because it atones; the limbs of the burnt-offering precede the sacrificial parts of the sin-offering because it is wholly consumed." The sin-offering is the penitent and its blood is the cry from the depth of the heart: the penitent's cry is greater, for he cries out because it seems to him that, God forbid, he has no remedy without the salvation of the Blessed One, and so his cry rises to the place where the righteous do not stand; but in the limbs of the burnt-offering, that is, the performance of the commandments, the wholly righteous take precedence, for their body is greatly refined and cleaves to the Blessed One, never separated for a moment.: "צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים — עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה"; וְהַיְנוּ עֵין נְבִיאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְאִם כֵּן נְבִיאֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם — אַף בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה בִּכְלַל "עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה".

Moreover, no created being can perceive what stands above its own level. Our Sages of blessed memory said (Berakhot 34b), regarding the completely righteous, “no eye has seen”; this means even the eye of Israel’s prophets. All the more so, for prophets of the nations even the level of true penitents lies within “no eye has seen.”
וְהוּא, שֶׁהָיָה מֵאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וַדַּאי לֹא הִשִּׂיג מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כֵּן אֶלָּא מַדְרֵגַת אוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
Since Balaam himself belonged to those with no share in the World to Come, he could certainly perceive within Israel only the level of those who likewise had no share in the World to Come.

וְעַל זֶה הָיְתָה עִקַּר טַעֲנַת בָּלָק: "כִּסָּה אֶת עֵין הָאָרֶץ" — רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר הָאָרֶץ הַיְדוּעָה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא", שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְעַמֵּךְ וְגוֹמֵר, לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ"; הֲרֵי דְּ"אֶרֶץ" רוֹמֵז לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.

This was the core of Balak’s claim: “it has covered the eye of the land”—meaning the well-known “Land,” as in the teaching, “All Israel have a share in the World to Come,” based on the verse, “Your people… shall forever inherit the land.” Thus “land” alludes to the World to Come.

וְזֶה הָיָה רְאִיַּת בָּלָק, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר "וַיַּרְא וְגוֹמֵר780 Numbers 22:2 — “And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites.” Rashi: He said: These two kings, on whom we relied, could not stand before them — how much more so we! Therefore “Moab was sore afraid.”", מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא לְבַד רָאָה וְלֹא אֲחֵרִים.
This was Balak’s unique perception, as the verse says, “And Balak saw, etc.,” implying that he alone saw what others did not.

וְהַיְנוּ דְּעִנְיַן הָאֱמֹרִי, שֶׁהִפְלִיג הַכָּתוּב כַּמָּה פְעָמִים בְּשִׁבְחוֹ: "אֲשֶׁר כְּגֹבַהּ אֲרָזִים גָּבְהוֹ וְחָסֹן וְגוֹמֵר"; וְכֵן נִזְכָּר בְּהַלֵּל הַגָּדוֹל מִלְחֶמֶת סִיחוֹן וְעוֹג — "כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ" — שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה חֶסֶד עוֹלָמִי.

This also explains the matter of the Amorites, whom Scripture repeatedly describes in lofty terms—“whose height was like the height of cedars, and he was strong, etc.” Likewise, the Great Hallel mentions the wars with Sihon and Og under the refrain “for His kindness is everlasting,” indicating an eternal kindness embodied in their defeat.
וְגַם מַה דְּנִתְיָרֵא מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מֵעוֹג, וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל גְּבוּרָתָם לְבַד, דִּכְלַפֵּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵין חִלּוּק בֵּין גִּבּוֹרִים לַחַלָּשִׁים.
Moshe Rabbeinu’s fear of Og certainly was not merely because of physical might, for before the Blessed One there is no distinction between the strong and the weak.
גַּם מַה שֶּׁשָּׁלַח לְסִיחוֹן לְשָׁלוֹם, וַהֲרֵי הוּא מִשִּׁבְעָה עַמְּמִין שֶׁנִּתְּנוּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.
The same question applies to Moses’ sending Sihon an offer of peace, even though he belonged to the seven nations assigned to Israel.
רַק יָדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב עַל עוֹג דְּפָלַט מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, דְּוַדַּאי אֵינוֹ בְּחִנָּם, רַק שֶׁהוּא הָיָה נָקִי מֵחֶטְאֵי דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל — עַד כָּאן.

Rather, it is known what is written of Og, that he escaped the generation of the Flood. This surely was not without reason; rather, he was free of the sins of the generation of the Flood—end of that citation.

וְיָדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, רטז, רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב)781 Zohar 3:216b — And further the Rabbis established: the generation that goes is the generation that comes — a lame man went, a lame man came; a blind man went, a blind man came. And further the Rabbis established that Moses was destined to receive the Torah in the generation of the Flood, but [it was not given] because they were wicked. This is what is written, “for that he also is flesh” — “beshagam” is Moses [by numerical value]. And why is he called “beshagam”? Because Ecclesiastes dropped the letter bet from “beshagam” in order to conceal the matter, saying, “I said that this too is vanity.” Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): The generations of the Flood and of the Dispersion are the general categories of the "secrets of illicit relations," for they correspond to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah: in the generation of the Flood it was fitting for the Torah to be given, as the Zohar says and as the Sages said on the verse, "beshagam" — this is Moses. And correspondingly their sin was the emission of seed, in the Yesod, as is known from the Zohar that writing belongs to the Yesod. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Noach 1): The ten generations from Adam to Noah were meant to repair all the damage of Adam's sin and to be refined in all the attributes, and then, in the generation of the Flood, it was fitting for the Torah to be given; the soul of Moses was present then, as hinted in "beshagam," which equals Moses in numerical value. They would have merited the Written and the Oral Torah, hinted in "all the fountains of the great deep burst forth" [the springs of wisdom below] "and the windows of heaven were opened" [the gates of wisdom above], and would have repaired all the damage of the serpent, as will be in the future; but because they provoked Him, these turned into raging waters and they were all swept away in the waters of the Flood., דְּהָיָה רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, וְהָיָה אָז גַּם כֵּן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם — "בְּשַׁגַּם" בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא "מֹשֶׁה" — אִלְמָלֵי זָכוּ; רַק שֶׁבְּחֶטְאָם נִתְהַפֵּךְ שֶׁפַע מֵי הַתּוֹרָה לְמֵי הַמַּבּוּל.

It is also known from the Zohar (III, 216b, beginning of the page) that the Torah could have been given in the generation of the Flood, and that the root of Moshe Rabbeinu was present then as well—“beshagam” has the numerical value of “Moshe”—had they merited it. Through their sin, however, the flow of the waters of Torah was transformed into the waters of the Flood.

וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בִּזְבָחִים (קטז.)782 Zevachim 116a — R. Elazar of Modi'in says: He heard of the giving of the Torah and came. For when the Torah was given to Israel, its sound carried from one end of the world to the other, and trembling seized all the kings of the nations in their palaces, and they uttered song. They all gathered to Balaam the wicked and said to him: What is this sound of tumult that we have heard? Perhaps a flood is coming upon the world? He said to them: The Holy One, blessed be He, has already sworn that He will bring no flood upon the world. They said to him: A flood of water He will not bring, but a flood of fire He may bring. He said to them: He has already sworn that He will not destroy all flesh. And what, then, is this sound of tumult that we have heard? He said to them: He has a precious treasure in His storehouse, hidden with Him nine hundred and seventy-four generations before the world was created, and He has desired to give it to His children, as it is stated, "The Lord will give strength to His people." At once they all opened and said, "The Lord will bless His people with peace." Rashi: "And in his palace all say: Glory" [Psalms 29:9]: the beginning of the verse is "The voice of the Lord makes the hinds to calve," and it speaks of the giving of the Torah — in the palace of each and every king, all say "Glory" to the Holy One, blessed be He. "He said to them: The Lord sits as King forever": He has already sworn that He will be King over His creatures forever and will not destroy them. "Nine hundred and seventy-four generations before the world was created": together with the twenty-six from Adam to Moses our teacher, these make "the word He commanded to a thousand generations" (Psalms 105:8); "strength" is the Torah, which is the stronghold of Israel. Maharsha (s.v. "And Jethro heard … what tiding did he hear"): Since Scripture does not say which deed it was that Jethro heard of, R. Elazar of Modi'in explains it by the event that was itself a thing heard — the giving of the Torah, which was heard throughout the world, for its sound went from one end of the world to the other. Maharsha (s.v. "The Lord will give strength to His people"): Rashi explains "strength" as the Torah; one may add that Balaam answered them that there was no change of will before Him in giving it now to Israel and not earlier to one of the nations, but the people of Israel is fit to receive it because they are the boldest of the nations, and so the Torah, which is called "strength," was given to them to sap their strength, whereas the other nations could not keep it, as is said in chapter Ein Tzadin [Beitzah 25b]. Accordingly the nations responded, "The Lord will bless His people with peace": had the Torah not been given to Israel, no nation or tongue could stand before them, so that the Torah is a gift of peace to the nations along with Israel. Maharsha (s.v. "but a flood of fire He does bring"): This implies that the oath of the waters of Noah covers fire as well, whereas in the first chapter of Sotah [11a] the Egyptians reasoned that He had sworn only against a flood of water. Balaam means that He will not bring even a flood of fire upon the whole world, having sworn by the waters of Noah not to bring destruction upon the whole world; but upon a single nation He certainly brings it, as it is written, "For by fire will the Lord contend" — and so too a flood of water upon a single nation, in which the Egyptians erred. Maharsha (s.v. "which was hidden with Him nine hundred and seventy-four generations"): He told them all this because it was fitting that the Holy One, blessed be He, come with sounds so great that the whole world would hear, to make known to all the world that a precious treasure was hidden with Him, and that He had removed from before Him nine hundred and seventy-four generations because they were not fit to fulfil its commandments — whose fulfilment is the world's existence, and without which the world would be fit to return to chaos and void, as it is said, the Holy One, blessed be He, made a condition with the works of creation, if Israel accept [the Torah]. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Zevachim 116a): The one who says he heard of the giving of the Torah and came holds that it is not plausible he came on hearing of the war with Amalek: though the evil enemy had been removed, how would other nations thereby join Israel, since Israel are one nation and the proselyte is of another? But once Israel had received a supernal level, the level of the Torah, proselytes too are able to receive the Torah, and so Jethro came to convert, since proselytes can be included with Israel in receiving the Torah. Moreover, whereas the splitting of the Sea came from the side of the right and the war with Amalek from the side of the left, the giving of the Torah is from the Blessed Name Himself, belonging neither to the left nor to the right but to the middle, and there is no level above it. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 30): A great change draws a great change after it: the giving of the Torah from Heaven was a new thing — the Torah, which is the separate intellect, coming into actuality in the physical world — and so a great upheaval followed it; hence he said 'a precious treasure hidden in His storehouse,' and 'nine hundred and seventy-four generations before the world was created,' to say that the Torah is separate from the physical world, and He, blessed be He, desired to give it to the world. And because all the words of the Torah are binding and necessary, and whatever is necessary is strong, its coming into the lower world drew after it things that come with strength, like thunders and lightnings, for like draws like. So the Midrash shows in saying "The Lord will give strength to His people": the sounds came because He was giving His people the Torah, which is called "strength" because all its words are binding. דִּבְשָׁעַת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נִתְקַבְּצוּ אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לְבִלְעָם.
And they likewise said in Zevachim (116a) that at the time of the giving of the Torah the nations of the world gathered to Balaam. –

וּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:)783 Sanhedrin 106b — A certain heretic said to R. Chanina: Have you heard how old Balaam was? He said to him: It is not written. But since it is written, "Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days," he was thirty-three or thirty-four years old. He said to him: You have spoken well. I myself saw the chronicle of Balaam, and in it was written: Balaam the lame was thirty-three years old when Phinehas the brigand killed him. Rashi: "Thirty-three years old" — R. Chanina does not hold with R. Simai, who said above (106a) that three were party to Pharaoh's counsel, Balaam, Job and Jethro; for according to R. Simai, since Balaam took part in Pharaoh's counsel, "Every son that is born you shall cast into the river," he lived through all the two hundred and ten years that Israel were in exile in Egypt, until the war of Midian. "Phinehas the brigand" — [he was] the commander of the army, and even if another killed [Balaam], the whole war is called by his name. Maharsha: "Or thirty-four" — that is, close to half his years, so that it be evident that he died for this reason, not reaching half his years. The reason is that since he did not turn back from his evil deeds by half his years, he will no longer turn back and is not fit to live any longer; and the reverse holds for the measure of the righteous, as we say in Yoma: once one has reached the greater part of his years without sinning, he will no longer sin. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 106b): He asked specifically about Balaam because he was a great wicked man, and for such a man life is not fitting: in proportion to the greatness of his stature his sin is reckoned so great that life is not fitting for him at all. The verse names two things: "men of blood," who shed others' blood and are unfit for life — this applies to Doeg and Achitofel — and "deceit," a master of deceit and stratagems like Balaam, for a sorcerer does not walk wholeheartedly, and sorcery is nothing but stratagem and deceit (hence his counsel to Moab to abandon their daughters). The wholehearted man has true existence, but deceit has none; and it says "half their days" because half is the essence of life, so that whoever does not reach half [of seventy] has not had the essence of a man's days. דְּבִלְעָם בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים וְשָׁלֹשׁ נֶהֱרַג, וְהוּא בִּשְׁנַת אַרְבָּעִים לִיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם, אִם כֵּן נוֹלַד שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים אַחַר מַתַּן תּוֹרָה.

Yet according to what they said in Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 106b), Balaam was thirty-three years old when he was killed, which occurred in the fortieth year after the Exodus; if so, he was born seven years after the giving of the Torah.

וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר: כְּמוֹ דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ נֶפֶשׁ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא "מֹשֶׁה", כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, דְּהָיָה בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, וְכֵן בַּתַּלְמוּד (שַׁבָּת קא:)784 Shabbat 101b — The mishna teaches: Boats tied to one another — one may carry from this one to that one. Is that not obvious? Rava said: It was necessary only to permit the small skiff between them. Rav Safra said to him: Moses, is what you say correct? We learned in the mishna, "One may carry from this one to that one"! Rashi: ["Is that not obvious"] — that one may carry. The Mishnah's "one may carry" was needed only to permit carrying from one boat to the other by way of a small skiff lying between the two large ones: although it is not itself tied, it is permitted through the tying of the two outer boats, and we are not concerned that it may slip out from between them so that he carries through the airspace of a karmelit. "Moses" — that is, our master, who is in his generation as Moses was in his; "is what you say correct?" is said in astonishment, for "from this one to that one" implies that no other boat intervenes for the one carrying to pass into. Tosafos (s.v. "Is that not obvious"): At this stage the Gemara supposes that both boats belong to one person, and therefore asks "Is that not obvious?"; when they are not tied one may not carry between them, by a decree lest the object fall into the water and he carry from a private domain into a karmelit and come to bring it back. Although above (97a) no such decree was made concerning two houses, with boats, which are not fixed in place, there is more reason to decree lest the object fall. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos, on Tosafot s.v. "Is that not obvious"): Tosafot mean that he may be unable to reach the fallen object by hand from inside the boat, and would take a long reed and extend it out of the boat over the water to reach it; he would then have carried the reed from a private domain into a karmelit, and would come to bring the object and the reed back from the karmelit into the private domain. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:18): Just as Moses our teacher is the root of all the wisdom of all the sages of Israel in every generation, as is known regarding the Gemara's expression "Moses, is what you say correct?", so Balaam is the root of all the wisdom of all the sages of the nations in every generation. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on the Book of Joshua 3): Moses our teacher merited the fig tree, which is the source of wisdom, so that the Torah is called by his name; for, as is known from the Arizal's explanation of the Sages' expression "Moses, is what you say correct?", the power of Torah and wisdom in all the souls of Israel is the soul of Moses our teacher. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 15): "Judah is my lawgiver" — the root of the "lawgiver," as Moses our teacher is called, who is the root of the Torah scholars of Israel, as is known from the mystery of the expression found in several places in the Gemara, "Moses, is what you say correct?"; so too Judah is the root of the Torah scholars of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 6): It is known from the Arizal's explanation of the Sages' expression "Moses, is what you say correct?" that Moses is the root of the da'as [understanding] in all the Torah scholars of Israel in every generation, for the soul of Moses is the one that encompasses the Torah as a whole. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim 1): Moses our teacher is the inwardness of all the souls of Israel, the da'as [understanding] in the souls of Israel in every generation; therefore the Gemara says, regarding words of Torah, "Moses, is what you say correct?" — in astonishment: where is your da'as? And there are leaders of a generation whose souls include that entire generation, like Moses, with their root in Moses, as the Arizal wrote on this expression: the great one of the generation is called by that name because he is a spark of Moses himself, reincarnated in every generation. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 77): [On "Even were he like Joshua son of Nun, I would not give him my daughter":] the speaker deliberately said "like Joshua son of Nun" and not "like Moses," because Moses is the root of the Torah, and with the crown of Torah there is no concern for lineage; had he been "like Moses" — that is, a great Torah scholar of the generation, who is "like Moses," as the Sages said, "Moses, is what you say correct?" — he would have given her. "מֹשֶׁה, שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרַתְּ" עַל אֵיזֶה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם בַּדּוֹר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ מֵחָכְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.

The answer must be that just as the root of Moshe Rabbeinu’s soul is called “Moshe,” as noted above, and was already present in the generation of the Flood—and likewise the Talmud (Shabbat 101b) can address a Torah scholar of a later generation with the words “Moshe, you have spoken well,” because he possesses something of Moshe Rabbeinu’s wisdom—
כָּךְ בִּלְעָם הוּא כְּנֶגֶד הַדַּעַת דְּסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא; הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת דְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם בְּדַעְתָּן נִקְרָא שֶׁנִּתְקַבְּצוּ לְבִלְעָם.
so Balaam denotes the counter-root of da’at on the side of impurity; the nations’ intellectual apprehension through their own da’at is therefore described as their gathering to “Balaam.”

וְכַיּוֹצֵא בָזֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (סוֹטָה יא.)785 Sotah 11a — R. Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of R. Simai: Three were present at that counsel [of Pharaoh] — Balaam, Job, and Yitro. Balaam, who gave the counsel, was slain; Job, who kept silent, was sentenced to sufferings; Yitro, who fled, merited that his descendants sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone. Rashi (s.v. "in that counsel"): [The counsel of] "Come, let us deal wisely with him" (Exodus 1:10). Maharsha: This statement is placed here, amid the exposition of the verses of Exodus 1, because [the Gemara] had just mentioned the counsel of "Come, let us deal wisely with him," at which these three were present; and they were punished by the two means discussed in that counsel, fire and the sword. Job, who kept silent, was sentenced to sufferings of fire — as it is written, "The fire of God has fallen from heaven" (Job 1:16), and boils too are fiery in nature — while Balaam, who counseled evil, was punished by the sword, as hinted in the verse concerning him, "with his sword drawn in his hand" (Numbers 22:23). Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 106a): The greatest among the nations, above all the rest, are three: two of them have a connection to Israel and are not wholly opposed to them, and one is wholly opposed — just as Abraham and Isaac have a connection to the nations (for from Abraham came several nations, and from Isaac came Edom), while the seed of Jacob, the third, is entirely separate from the nations. Corresponding to this there was Yitro, who was a proselyte as Abraham was; Job, a man of sufferings, corresponding to Isaac, who was a man of sufferings, as the Midrash says, "Isaac initiated sufferings" (Genesis Rabbah 65); and Balaam, who was wholly opposed to Israel. דְּהָיָה מִיּוֹעֲצֵי פַרְעֹה, וּלְפִי זֶה הֶאֱרִיךְ יָמִים הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד; וַהֲרֵי אִיתָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו:)786 Sanhedrin 106b — A certain heretic said to R. Chanina: Have you heard how old Balaam was? He said to him: It is not written. But since it is written, "Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days," he was thirty-three or thirty-four years old. He said to him: You have spoken well. I myself saw the chronicle of Balaam, and in it was written: Balaam the lame was thirty-three years old when Phinehas the brigand killed him. Rashi: "Thirty-three years old" — R. Chanina does not hold with R. Simai, who said above (106a) that three were party to Pharaoh's counsel, Balaam, Job and Jethro; for according to R. Simai, since Balaam took part in Pharaoh's counsel, "Every son that is born you shall cast into the river," he lived through all the two hundred and ten years that Israel were in exile in Egypt, until the war of Midian. "Phinehas the brigand" — [he was] the commander of the army, and even if another killed [Balaam], the whole war is called by his name. Maharsha: "Or thirty-four" — that is, close to half his years, so that it be evident that he died for this reason, not reaching half his years. The reason is that since he did not turn back from his evil deeds by half his years, he will no longer turn back and is not fit to live any longer; and the reverse holds for the measure of the righteous, as we say in Yoma: once one has reached the greater part of his years without sinning, he will no longer sin. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 106b): He asked specifically about Balaam because he was a great wicked man, and for such a man life is not fitting: in proportion to the greatness of his stature his sin is reckoned so great that life is not fitting for him at all. The verse names two things: "men of blood," who shed others' blood and are unfit for life — this applies to Doeg and Achitofel — and "deceit," a master of deceit and stratagems like Balaam, for a sorcerer does not walk wholeheartedly, and sorcery is nothing but stratagem and deceit (hence his counsel to Moab to abandon their daughters). The wholehearted man has true existence, but deceit has none; and it says "half their days" because half is the essence of life, so that whoever does not reach half [of seventy] has not had the essence of a man's days. "אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים וּמִרְמָה לֹא יֶחֱצוּ יְמֵיהֶם".

The same principle applies to their teaching (Sotah 11a) that Balaam was among Pharaoh’s advisers. Taken literally, this would make him extraordinarily long-lived, whereas Sanhedrin 106b applies to him the verse, “men of bloodshed and deceit shall not live out half their days.”

וּבְסֵפֶר הַיָּשָׁר כָּתוּב דְּיוֹעֵץ פַּרְעֹה הָיָה בִּלְעָם אַחֵר, זְקֵנוֹ שֶׁל זֶה; אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה לֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן. וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.)787 Sanhedrin 106a — "And he looked upon the Kenite and took up his parable." Balaam said to Jethro: Kenite, were you not with us in that counsel [to drown the Israelite infants]? Who set you beside the mighty ones of the world? And this is what R. Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of R. Simai: Three were party to that counsel — Balaam, Job, and Jethro. Balaam, who gave the counsel, was killed; Job, who kept silent, was sentenced to afflictions; and Jethro, who fled, merited that his descendants sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone. Rashi: "Were you not with us in that counsel?" — the counsel in which Pharaoh decreed, "Every son that is born [you shall cast] into the river"; it is said in astonishment: surely you were, as [taught] below. "Who set you beside the mighty ones of the world?" — for your descendants are destined to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and this is what is written, "Mighty is your dwelling place" (Numbers 24:21): do you then sit among the mighty ones of the world — who brought you to this? Maharsha: The Sages understood Balaam's words as an expression of astonishment, not as a plain acknowledgment that Jethro had earned this seat by fleeing; for were that so, he ought to have mentioned his merit in fleeing, just as he mentioned the merit of Israel in the passage "For there is no enchantment in Jacob" (Numbers 23:23). Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 106a): The greatest among the nations, standing above all the rest, are three: two of them have a bond with Israel and are not wholly opposed to them, and one is wholly opposed. For Abraham and Isaac had a bond with the nations — several nations came forth from Abraham, and Edom from Isaac — while the seed of Jacob, the third, was wholly separate from them; so corresponding to Abraham was Jethro, a convert as Abraham was; corresponding to Isaac, who "initiated afflictions," was Job, a man of afflictions, who was no more opposed to Israel than Isaac was to the nations; and because Jacob was opposed to the nations, as it is written, "And the children struggled within her," there came forth from them Balaam, who was wholly opposed to Israel. עַל "וַיַּרְא אֶת הַקֵּינִי וְכוּלֵי" — "עִמִּי הָיִיתָ בָּעֵצָה וְכוּלֵי".

Sefer HaYashar states that Pharaoh’s adviser was another Balaam, the grandfather of this Balaam, but the wording of our Sages does not imply that. The same is true of their interpretation (Sanhedrin 106a) of “he saw the Kenite, etc.”—“you were with me in that counsel, etc.”

אֲבָל הַכַּוָּנָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ הַדַּעַת דְּסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא נִקְרָא "בִּלְעָם", בֵּין שֶׁהָיְתָה מְלֻבֶּשֶׁת בְּאֵיזֶה נֶפֶשׁ פְּרָטִית, בֵּין שֶׁהָיְתָה בְּדַעַת פַּרְעֹה בְּעַצְמוֹ.]
Rather, the intent is as I have written: the root of da’at on the side of impurity is called “Balaam,” whether it was clothed in a particular individual soul or expressed within Pharaoh’s own mind.
"שֶׁמָּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מֵבִיא מַבּוּל" — שֶׁכְּפִי עִנְיָנָם הָיוּ חוֹשְׁבִים שֶׁפַע מֵי תּוֹרָה הַבָּא לָעוֹלָם לְמֵי מַבּוּל.

Thus they asked, “Perhaps the Holy One, blessed be He, is bringing a flood,” because in accordance with their own orientation they mistook the influx of the waters of Torah entering the world for the waters of a flood.

וְאִם כֵּן, עוֹג שֶׁנִּצּוֹל מִמַּבּוּל הֲרֵי הָיָה לוֹ קְצָת שַׁיָּכוּת בְּהֶכְרֵחַ לַתּוֹרָה. וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק טז)788 Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 16 — The steward of Abraham's household was his servant Eliezer. And from where did he come to be his servant? When Abraham went out from Ur of the Chaldeans, all the great men of the generation came to give him gifts, and Nimrod took Eliezer his firstborn and gave him to him as a slave forever. And when he had dealt kindly with Isaac, Abraham set him free, and the Holy One, blessed be He, gave him his reward in this world, so that there be no reward for the wicked in the world to come; and He raised him up to kingship — and he is Og king of Bashan. דְּהוּא אֱלִיעֶזֶר עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁהָיָה דּוֹלֶה וּמַשְׁקֶה מִתּוֹרַת רַבּוֹ (יוֹמָא כח:)789 Yoma 28b — Eliezer, servant of Abraham, was an elder who sat in the academy, as it is stated: "And Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had" (Genesis 24:2). R. Elazar said: he had mastery of his master's Torah. "He is Damascus [Dammesek] Eliezer" (Genesis 15:2) — R. Elazar said: he drew [doleh] from his master's Torah and gave others to drink [mashkeh]. Rashi: "Draws and gives to drink": Dammesek is read as an abbreviation [notarikon] of doleh u-mashkeh. Maharsha: "Who ruled over all that he had" cannot mean in its plain sense that he ruled over Abraham's possessions to do with them as he wished, for a servant has no such authority even when his master entrusts him with everything; so they expounded that he had mastery of his master's Torah: whatever he had received from his master he was permitted to teach to others in an academy, though not other matters, which were forbidden to him in the presence of Abraham his master. So too they expounded "Dammesek" as drawing and giving others to drink of his master's Torah, since Eliezer was evidently not from Damascus, as the Targum renders it: Damascus lies in Aram while Eliezer was a Canaanite slave, and Scripture never sets the gentilic before the proper name (compare "Jephthah the Gileadite", "Nabal the Carmelite"). Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Savo 7): Abraham cried, "What will You give me, seeing I go childless," because his whole aim was to root the holiness of the Blessed One in the land for all generations; and as for "the steward of my house, Dammesek Eliezer," although he drew from his master's Torah and gave others to drink, Abraham had no contentment from him. Only when he was told, "This one shall not inherit you, but he that shall come forth from your own body," is it said, "And he believed in the Lord." Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 118): Eliezer's stature was nothing but Abraham's stature, which is why [the Midrash] calls them "servants of the fathers"; and so it says, "Dammesek — he drew from his master's Torah and gave others to drink," for what a servant acquires his master acquires, and all the words of Torah he had are called "his master's Torah." Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Lech Lecha): Abraham did not consider it fitting that this inheritance — that the kingship of the Blessed One be made known in the world — should come through his servant Eliezer: for although he appeared as one who "drew from his master's Torah and gave others to drink," Abraham was in doubt whether his intent was for the sake of Heaven, or whether it was only as written, "A fool has no desire for understanding, but only that his heart may reveal itself." Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Pesachim 5): The service of the Patriarchs was to establish the recognition of the Blessed One in the heart of all creatures; therefore Eliezer too is called "the steward of my house" and "Dammesek," and the Talmud says that he drew from his master's Torah and gave others to drink — that is, he too brought the recognition of the light of the Blessed One to all creatures..

If so, Og, who survived the Flood, necessarily possessed some connection to Torah. This is all the more so according to Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 16), which identifies him with Eliezer, Abraham’s servant, who “drew forth and gave others to drink” from his master’s Torah (Yoma 28b).

וְאָמְרוּ בְּנִדָּה (סא.)790 Niddah 61a — "And the Lord said to Moses: Do not fear him." Now Sihon and Og were brothers, for the Master said: Sihon and Og were the sons of Ahijah son of Shamhazai. What was different about Og, that he feared him, and what was different about Sihon, that he did not fear him? R. Yochanan said that R. Shimon ben Yochai said: From the answer given to that righteous one you know what was in his heart. He said: Perhaps the merit of Abraham our father will stand by him — as it is stated, "And there came one who had escaped and told Abram the Hebrew"; and R. Yochanan said: This is Og, who escaped from the generation of the Flood. Rashi: "Sons of Ahijah": he was descended from Shamhazai and Azael, the two angels who came down in the generation of Enosh. "From the answer given to that righteous one": [you know what was in his heart, since] the Holy One, blessed be He, had to answer him that he should not fear him. "Og escaped from the Flood": he fled to the Land of Israel, as we say in [the chapter] Chelek. Tosafos (s.v. "This is Og, who escaped from the generation of the Flood"): Then Sihon too escaped from the generation of the Flood, since they were brothers; but it is known that this "one who had escaped" was Og and not Sihon for that very reason, because Moses feared him. It is further said that Og found Abraham our father standing at the threshing floors preparing cakes for Passover, and it is from this that he is called Og; and [the Talmud] brings it here because it has the look of slander, for the Midrash says that Og said in his heart, "I will go and tell Abraham, and he will go out to war and die, and I shall take Sarah his wife." Even so, Moses feared that the merit of Abraham might stand by him. Maharsha: "Sons of Ahijah son of Shamhazai" — as Rashi explains, and it is set out in the verse "and the sons of God saw the daughters of men": sons of God literally, and that is why they were called Nefilim, because they fell from heaven, as is found in the Midrashim. As for Rashi's saying that Og escaped by fleeing to the Land of Israel, "as we say in Chelek" — I did not find it in the aggada of Chelek; but in Zevachim it is said that Og stood on the sides of the ark, and it may be that [Rashi's account] holds only according to the one who says the Flood did not come upon the Land of Israel. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Niddah 61a): It is puzzling that the merit of the righteous one should stand by [Og] and yet not stand by his own sons. But understand: Abraham is called "the greatest man among the Anakim," for his measure is greatness, and it is from there that the giants receive their strength — so that Og's power is joined to the power of Abraham. Moses did not fear that Abraham's merit would protect Og as such, but that Og had some joining and attachment to Abraham's holy rank; and it was not so, for although Abraham was a giant his strength was a holy strength, whereas Og's strength was a strength of impurity. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Balak 1): Sihon and Og were brothers, sons of Ahijah son of Shamhazai, so presumably Sihon too was born before the Flood. And since Sihon too escaped the Flood, he presumably fled to the Land of Israel, the place of the nine measures of wisdom that the Land of Israel took, so that his power too came from the Oral Torah, the wisdom of the Land of Israel.: "סִיחוֹן וְעוֹג אַחִים, בְּנֵי אֲחִיָּה בַּר שַׁמְחֲזַאי"; נִרְאֶה דְּגַם סִיחוֹן כָּמוֹהוּ פָּלַט מִמַּבּוּל.
And they said in Niddah (61a), “Sihon and Og were brothers, sons of Ahiyah bar Shamhazai”; it therefore appears that Sihon too, like Og, survived from the generation of the Flood.
וְזֶה כָּל שִׁבְחָם לִמְלָכִים גְּדוֹלִים וְאַדִּירִים בְּגֹבַהּ וְחֹסֶן — הַיְנוּ בְּמַעֲלוֹת רוּחָנִיּוֹת וּגְבוּרָה דִּכְבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר.
This is the meaning of their praise as great and mighty kings, lofty and powerful—namely, that they possessed spiritual attainments and strength in subduing the inclination.

וְזֶהוּ עִקַּר חֶסֶד הַשֵּׁם לָעוֹלָם: שֶׁמִּשֶּׁנִּתְּנָה תּוֹרָה וְנִבְחֲרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְאֻמָּה אַחֶרֶת לְהִתְקָרֵב לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ מְכִילְתָּא: "עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְחֲרוּ וְכוּלֵי791 Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael, Bo 1 — Before the Land of Israel was chosen, all lands were fit for divine speech; once the Land of Israel was chosen, all other lands were excluded.".

This, then, is the essential everlasting kindness of God: once the Torah was given and Israel was chosen, no other nation can enter that covenantal nearness before Him except through joining Israel, as stated at the beginning of the Mekhilta, “before they were chosen, etc.”

וַאֲפִלּוּ יִשְׁמֹר כָּל מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה, צָרִיךְ לְהִתְגַּיֵּר וְלִהְיוֹת מְכֻנֶּה בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל; וּבְלֹא זֶה, עוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת הָעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה חַיָּב וְכוּלֵי, דְּהִיא "מוֹרָשָׁה לִקְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב" דַּוְקָא.

Even if a person from the nations were to observe the Torah’s commandments, he would still need conversion and the name Israel in order to enter this covenantal identity; without that, the Talmud’s restriction concerning a gentile’s Torah study applies, for Torah is specifically “an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob.”
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁשָּׁלַח לְסִיחוֹן לְשָׁלוֹם — הַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּתְגַּיֵּר; וְהוּא הָלַךְ לַמִּלְחָמָה כִּי הוּא טָעַן שֶׁהוּא הַנִּבְחָר, וְכֵן עוֹג.
This is why Moses sent peace to Sihon—meaning, an opening to join the covenant through conversion. Sihon instead went to war because he claimed that he himself was the chosen one; so too Og.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִתְיָרֵא מֵהֶם וַדַּאי לֹא לְחִנָּם, כִּי יָדַע עֹצֶם כֹּחָם וּמַעֲלָתָם בְּסוּר מֵרָע דְּכָל חֶטְאֵי דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל.

Moshe Rabbeinu’s fear of them was therefore certainly not baseless: he recognized the magnitude of their strength and their attainment in turning away from the evils that characterized the generation of the Flood.
וּבְמִשְׁפַּט בְּנֵי נֹחַ הֵם הָיוּ צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים, שֶׁאֵין כְּמוֹתָם בַּדּוֹר בִּבְנֵי נֹחַ.
Measured by the law applicable to the descendants of Noah, they were completely righteous—without equal among the non-Israelite peoples of their generation.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר "כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ": דְּתוֹרַת חֶסֶד שֶׁנָּתַן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל הִיא לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד, שֶׁמִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מֵהֶם אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם.

Concerning this the Psalm says, “for His kindness is everlasting”: the Torah of kindness that the Blessed One gave specifically to Israel endures forever, so that one who remains wholly outside that covenant has no standing within this particular inheritance.

items.h:
Seif 2 — Balak, Balaam, and the Boundary of Israel
Balak and Balaam approach holiness from outside but cannot enter the inherited covenant rooted within Israel.

p: וְזֶה הָיָה רְאִיַּת בָּלָק גַּם כֵּן, שֶׁבּוֹ הָיָה אָז גָּנוּז עֲדַיִן נִיצוֹץ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁיָּצָא מֵחֲלָצָיו מֵרוּת (נָזִיר כג:)792 Nazir 23b — Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: A man should always occupy himself with Torah and the commandments even not for their own sake, for out of doing them not for their own sake he comes to do them for their own sake — for in reward for the forty-two offerings that Balak the wicked brought, he merited that Ruth came forth from him. And R. Yose son of R. Chanina said: Ruth was the daughter of the son of Eglon king of Moab. Rashi (s.v. "the forty-two offerings"): From the seven altars he set up in three places, upon each of which he offered a bull and a ram — fourteen at each station, and three times fourteen is forty-two; and Balak's offerings were not for the sake of a commandment. "And Ruth came forth from him" — for David came forth from her, who slaked [rivahu] the Holy One, blessed be He, with songs and praises. Tosafos (s.v. "the daughter of the son of Eglon"): "The daughter of his son" is not exact, and neither is the statement elsewhere that she was Eglon's daughter; rather she lived many generations after him. For it is implied that Ruth was young when she converted, and from Eglon to Ivtzan — who is Boaz — is more than two hundred years; had she been Eglon's own daughter she would not have been young. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nazir 23b): When a man performs the commandment not for its own sake, that is the beginning of the service of the Holy One, blessed be He, and every beginning comes in the end to its completion. That is why he says that out of doing it not for its own sake he comes to do it for its own sake., וְהִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הָרוֹמֶזֶת לָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה.

This too was Balak’s perception: the spark of King David, peace be upon him, who would descend from him through Ruth (Nazir 23b), was still hidden within him, and he sensed that he had some connection to the Land of Israel, which alludes to the supernal Land.
וְכֵן קָרְבְּנוֹתָיו הֲרֵי הָיוּ לְשֵׁם הַשֵּׁם, וְחָשַׁב שֶׁגַּם הוּא יַעֲבֹד עֲבוֹדָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלָמָּה נִבְחֲרוּ אֵלּוּ דַּוְקָא.
His offerings too were brought to God, and he thought: I too will serve the Blessed One—why were these people alone chosen?

בְּמַה שֶּׁרָאָה וְהֵבִין מִמַּה שֶּׁעָשָׂה לָאֱמֹרִי, דְּמִי שֶׁחָפֵץ בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צָרִיךְ לְהִתְגַּיֵּר וּלְהִתְכַּנּוֹת בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּוְקָא — שֶׁהוּא "כִּסָּה אֶת עֵין הָאָרֶץ".

From what he saw had been done to the Amorites, he understood that one who desires the service of the Blessed One must convert and be designated specifically by the name Israel—and this is what he meant by “it covered the eye of the land.”
פֵּרוּשׁ, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְשׁוּם אֻמָּה וְלָשׁוֹן לְהַבִּיט לָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה בְּגִלּוּי שְׁכִינָה וְהַשָּׂגַת עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהוּא מְכֻסֶּה כֻּלּוֹ עַל יְדֵי הָאֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית.

That is: no other nation or tongue can gaze directly upon the supernal Land—the revelation of the Divine Presence and attainment of the World to Come—because that entire access is, as it were, covered by the Israelite nation.
וְזֶה הָיָה כָּל עִקַּר חֵפֶץ בָּלָק לְגָרְשׁוֹ מֵאֶרֶץ זוֹ, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַדָּבָר הֶפְקֵר כְּקוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה: הָרוֹצֶה לִזְכּוֹת לָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה — יִזְכֶּה.

Balak’s essential desire was therefore to drive Israel from this “Land,” so that the matter would again be open to all as before the giving of the Torah: whoever wished to attain the supernal Land could do so.

וְעַל זֶה שָׁלַח אַחַר בִּלְעָם, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה לְעֻמַּת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כַּיָּדוּעַ. וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא הַדַּעַת הַמְחַבֵּר חָכְמָה וּבִינָה, שֶׁהֵם מוֹחָא וְלִבָּא.
For this purpose he sent for Balaam, who, as is known, stood opposite Moshe Rabbeinu. Moshe represents da’at, which joins Chochmah and Binah—the mind and the heart.

זֶהוּ עִנְיַן הַתּוֹרָה, לְשׁוֹן הוֹרָאָה, שֶׁמּוֹרָה הַלֵּב לִהְיוֹת נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר הַחָכְמָה שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; דְּזוּלַת זֶה, כְּשֶׁאֵין מוֹרֶה לַלֵּב, אֵינוֹ נִקְרָא "תּוֹרָה" אֶלָּא "חָכְמָה" לְבַד.

This is the meaning of Torah, from the language of instruction: it instructs the heart to follow the wisdom of the Blessed One. Without that guidance of the heart, wisdom is not yet called Torah; it remains wisdom alone.
וְזֶה כֹּחַ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁבָּא וְהוֹרִיד הַתּוֹרָה לָאָרֶץ וְהִנְחִילָהּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ כֹּחַ זֶה לִהְיוֹת הַלֵּב נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר חָכְמַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
This is Moshe Rabbeinu’s power: he brought the Torah down to earth and bequeathed it to Israel, endowing Israel with the capacity for the heart to be drawn after Divine wisdom.

אֲבָל אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּכוּת לָזֶה. וּבִלְעָם, שֶׁהָיָה נֶגֶד זֶה, הִתְפָּאֵר "וְיֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן": שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ וּמַשִּׂיג דַּרְגָא דְּדַעַת זוֹ, אֶלָּא שֶׁקְּרָאָהּ "דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן" — פֵּרוּשׁ, עֶלְיוֹן מַה שֶּׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מִמַּדְרֵגַת מוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ, דְּאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה זֶה לְמַעְלָה מִן הַטֶּבַע.

The nations, however, do not naturally possess this connection. Balaam, who stood opposite Moshe, therefore boasted that he “knows the knowledge of the Most High”: he could intellectually know and apprehend the level of da’at, yet called it “higher knowledge,” meaning something above the natural level of his own mind and heart.
וְהַיְנוּ, אַף שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן הָיָה יוֹדֵעַ רִבּוֹנוֹ וּמִתְנַהֵג גַּם כֵּן בְּדֶרֶךְ הַתּוֹרָה בִּשְׁמִירָה מִקִּנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, בֶּאֱמֶת הָיָה מְשֻׁקָּע בָּהֶם כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.

Thus, although he knew his Master and outwardly conducted himself in the way of Torah, guarding against jealousy, desire, and honor, inwardly he was in fact immersed in those very traits, as explained above.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר אָז בְּאוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁהָיוּ לוֹ כָּל שָׁלֹשׁ מִדּוֹת רָעוֹת בֶּאֱמֶת בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ. וְאַף שֶׁהִשִּׂיג שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּחַר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל — רָצָה הוּא לְהֵפֶךְ.
That episode revealed that all three negative traits truly existed in the depths of his heart. Even though he understood that the Blessed One had chosen Israel, he wanted the opposite.

וְעַל יָדוֹ הָיָה כָּל בֵּרוּר עִנְיָן זֶה: שֶׁאַף שֶׁהוּא רָצָה לְעוֹרֵר חֶטְאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁגַּם בָּהֶם נִמְצָא הַמַּגְדִּילִים הַחֵטְא עַד שֶׁאוֹבְדִים חֵלֶק עוֹלָם הַבָּא, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַעֲלָתָם גְּדוֹלָה בֶּאֱמֶת.

Through Balaam himself this entire point was clarified: although he sought to arouse Israel’s sins, and some Israelites magnify sin to the point of losing their share in the World to Come, their underlying spiritual stature nevertheless remains profound.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק (קד:)793 Sanhedrin 104b — The expounders of hidden meanings used to say: All of them [the kings and commoners who were counted as having no share in the World to Come] do come to the World to Come, as it is said: "Gilead is Mine and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim also is the stronghold of My head, Judah is My lawgiver." "Gilead is Mine" — this is Ahab, who fell at Ramoth-gilead. "Manasseh" — as its plain sense. "Ephraim is the stronghold of My head" — this is Jeroboam, who came from Ephraim. "Judah is My lawgiver" — this is Ahitophel. Rashi: "The expounders of hidden meanings" are expounders of verses, as it is written, "that which is inscribed [ha-rashum] in the writing of truth" (Daniel 10:21); they would say that all of them have a share, even Manasseh, Jeroboam and Ahab. "Gilead is Mine and Manasseh is Mine" — it is upon Me to bear their iniquity so that they may merit [the World to Come]; "Manasseh" in its plain sense is Manasseh son of Hezekiah. Ahithophel [is "Judah"] because he was of the tribe of Judah like David, who called him "my familiar friend," that is, my kinsman. Maharsha: Ahab's fall and death at Ramoth-gilead was itself his atonement, by which he merits the World to Come; and Manasseh alone is named "in its plain sense" because the others are designated by other names, their own names having been names of wickedness all their lives, whereas Manasseh repented in his lifetime and his own name, now in repentance, brings him to the World to Come. Jeroboam is "the stronghold of My head" because he was the first of all the kings of Israel and was made king at the word of the prophet, so he is not fit to be among those who go down to Gehinnom. "Judah is My lawgiver" is spoken by David: Ahithophel was David's teacher — "my lawgiver" — and through David his disciple he merited the World to Come, just as R. Meir, his disciple, brought Acher to the World to Come. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 2): The world was created with measure and limit, with room for choice between good and evil and for reward and punishment, whereas the World to Come has no choice; therefore the dorshei reshumos said that all of them come to the World to Come, for the World to Come is truly without limit, as it is written, "and I will feed you the heritage of Jacob your father," a heritage without boundaries. This world is not so: it is bounded, with time and with deeds good and evil. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): There are many levels of what is called "having no share": such a soul still has existence and is not wholly annihilated like the souls of the nations, enduring forever through its attachment to its root in the living God, only it has no share of its own; and this apart from the dorshei reshumos saying that all of them have a share in the World to Come. Though they said it of the particular souls listed in the Mishnah, from the particular one learns about the whole, for these seven marked individuals correspond to seven kinds of corruption through which one's share in the World to Come can be lost. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): This is the exposition of the dorshei reshumos ["expounders of hidden meanings"] that all of them have a share in the World to Come, all who are of the seed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, except Balaam: "reshumos" denotes the level of chochmah above binah, binah being the World to Come and the heart, where feeling lies; chochmah in the mind is not felt, only its impression (reshimu) is felt in the heart. From the standpoint of the attainment of chochmah there is no dross at all in the seed of Jacob, and even things that have no remedy through repentance, which alludes to the World to Come, are rectified by the opening of the gate of chochmah, which is above the level of repentance.: "דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת אָמְרוּ, כֻּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא". פֵּרוּשׁ "רְשׁוּמוֹת" הוּא מִצַּד הָרְשִׁימָה שֶׁלָּהֶם, דְּכָל אוֹר שֶׁהָיָה, אַף שֶׁנִּתְנַתֵּק, מַנִּיחַ רְשִׁימָה.

As they said in Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 104b), “The expounders of traces said: all of them have a share in the World to Come.” “Traces” means the spiritual imprint that remains: every light that once existed leaves a trace even after it is severed.

וְאֵלּוּ, אַף שֶׁלְּרֹב חֶטְאָם אָבְדוּ וְנִתְּקוּ אוֹר עוֹלָם הַבָּא — הַיְנוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ דְּבֵקוּתָם בַלֵּב בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ — מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּבָר הָיָה זֶה בְּשָׁרְשָׁם בְּתוֹלָדָה, וַעֲדַיִן נִשְׁאַר הָרְשִׁימָה, וּמִצַּד הָרְשִׁימָה דָּרְשׁוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא.

These individuals, although through the magnitude of their sins they lost and severed the light of the World to Come—the root of the heart’s attachment to the Blessed One—possessed that attachment innately at their root. Its imprint still remained, and from that imprint the Sages expounded that they do have a share in the World to Come.
וְהֵם דָּרְשׁוּ רַק עַל שִׁשָּׁה מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא עַל בִּלְעָם, דְּאֶצְלוֹ לֹא הָיְתָה רְשִׁימָה מֵעוֹלָם.
They applied this teaching only to the six Israelites in that list, not to Balaam, for Balaam had never possessed that inner imprint.

וְאַף שֶׁהוּא זָכָה לְמַה שֶּׁבִּקֵּשׁ — "תָּמֹת וְכוּלֵי" — דְּמִצַּד מִיתַת נַפְשׁוֹ וַאֲבֵדָתוֹ מֵעוֹלָם הַבָּא נִכְלַל בִּכְלַל אוֹתָן מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּמְנוּ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד חֲזָרָתָן עַל יְדֵי דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת לֹא נִכְלַל עִמָּהֶם כְּלָל.

Thus, although Balaam attained what he requested—“may my soul die, etc.”—in the sense that his soul’s loss of the World to Come placed him in the same Mishnah alongside those Israelites who were listed as having no share, he was not included with them when the “expounders of traces” restored their share through the enduring imprint within them.

items.h:
Seif 3 — Parashat Balak and the Souls at the Edge
Even deniers remain represented within Torah, revealing that Israel's deepest identity survives apparent separation from Moshe's da'at.

p: וְזֶהוּ כָּל עִנְיַן פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק: לְבָרֵר עִנְיָן זֶה, מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת, אַף אוֹתָם רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּלָל, שֶׁהֵם כּוֹפְרִים בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי.

This is the entire purpose of Parashat Balak: to clarify Israel’s distinctive spiritual stature relative to the idolatrous nations—even with respect to those wicked Israelites who are said to have no share in the World to Come at all, such as those who deny the Torah, etc.
וְאֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּכוּת לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הַדַּעַת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מִצַּד חִבּוּר לְבָבָם לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהֵם נִתְּקוּ מֵעַצְמָם זֶה.
They have severed themselves from the level represented by Moshe Rabbeinu—the da’at of Israel that joins their heart to the Blessed One.
וְלָכֵן לֹא נֶאֶמְרוּ דְּבָרִים אֵלּוּ עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, רַק עַל יְדֵי בִּלְעָם.
For that reason these matters were not originally spoken through Moshe Rabbeinu, but through Balaam.

וְאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא (יד:)794 Bava Batra 14b — And who wrote them? Moses wrote his own book, the portion of Balaam, and Job. Joshua wrote his own book and eight verses of the Torah. Samuel wrote his own book, Judges, and Ruth. David wrote the book of Psalms by the hand of ten elders. Rashi: "Samuel wrote his own book and the book of Judges" — since all of them preceded him, he arose and wrote their book and what befell Israel in their days; and so too Ruth, which took place in the days of the Judges. "By the hand of ten elders" — he set down in it words spoken by these elders, some of whom lived before him and some in his own day, such as Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, of the Levite singers. Maharsha: The baraita does not count David himself among the ten, even though he wrote the book together with them. Rashi at the beginning of Psalms took a different path and counts David and Solomon among them while dropping Heman and Jeduthun — perhaps because he takes the Heman here to be Moses, and holds that the Jeduthun of this book is named for the "ordinances" and is not a separate person. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:12): "Moses wrote his book and the portion of Bilam": "his book" is the engraving of the wisdom in his mind, for in the Zohar "book" denotes wisdom, while the portion of Bilam lies outside Moses' wisdom, for Moses was its opposite and could not attain that wisdom which comes by falling and concealment, casually and by chance. Only after Bilam attained it did Moses take up those drops, return them to their place and bring them into his book, turning the profane into holy: when Bilam spoke them they were profane words to Israel, but when Moses wrote them in the Torah they became holy, the words of the living God. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Yisro 4): The Gemara says, "Moses wrote his book and the portion of Bilam and Job" — but why count the portion of Bilam separately, when it is part of the Torah and included in "his book"? The Torah is called "the Torah of Moses" because he wrote the words of commoners — of Laban, of Esau, of Hagar and the like — and through him they became words of Torah; but the portion of Bilam was itself the very word of God, as the Zohar says on "and thus shall you speak," so there Moses did not need to make words of Torah out of a commoner's words, and therefore it is not included in "Moses wrote his book.": "מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כָּתַב סִפְרוֹ וּפָרָשַׁת בִּלְעָם וְכוּלֵי" — נִרְאֶה מִזֶּה כְּאִלּוּ פָּרָשַׁת בִּלְעָם הִיא חוּץ מֵהַתּוֹרָה.

Thus Bava Batra (14b) says, “Moshe Rabbeinu wrote his book and the section of Balaam, etc.,” language that makes the section of Balaam sound as though it were somehow outside the ordinary body of Torah.

וְהַיְנוּ דְּהַתּוֹרָה נִקְרֵאת "תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה", וְ"סִפְרוֹ" הוּא הַשָּׂגַת חָכְמָתוֹ; אֲבָל פָּרָשַׁת בִּלְעָם אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְחָכְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא מְדַבֵּר מֵאֲנָשִׁים שֶׁכָּפְרוּ בַּתּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי.

The Torah is called “the Torah of Moses,” and “his book” corresponds to the reach of Moshe’s wisdom. The Balaam section, however, speaks about people whose condition lies outside the ordinary reach of that wisdom—people who denied Torah, etc.

אֲבָל הֵם בְּדַרְגָא דְּבִלְעָם "יֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן": שֶׁהַדַּעַת, דַּרְגָא דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַתָּקוּעַ בִּכְלָלוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל, הוּא אֶצְלָם "עֶלְיוֹן" וּלְמַעְלָה מֵהַשָּׂגָתָם בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לִבָּם בְּהַרְגָּשַׁת הַלֵּב, רַק בִּידִיעָה בְּעָלְמָא.

They are instead at Balaam’s level of “knowing the knowledge of the Most High”: the da’at represented by Moshe, embedded in Israel as a whole, is for them “higher”—above what they can inwardly feel in the depths of the heart, remaining only abstract knowledge.

וּבִלְעָם הוּא הַמַּבְחִין מַעֲלָתָם בְּשָׁלֹשׁ נְבוּאוֹת שֶׁאָמַר כְּנֶגֶד שְׁלֹשָׁה כֹּחוֹת הַלֵּב דְּקִנְאָה, תַּאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד, שֶׁהִבְחִין אָז שֶׁהוּא הַהֵפֶךְ מִכֻּלָּם עַל יְדֵי שָׁלֹשׁ הַכָּאוֹת דְּאָתוֹן.

Balaam himself becomes the instrument for discerning their stature through the three prophecies he uttered corresponding to the three powers of the heart—jealousy, desire, and honor—when the three blows involving his she-donkey revealed him to be the opposite of all three virtues.
דִּרְכִיבַת הַחֲמוֹר רוֹמֵז עַל מַה שֶּׁהוּא רוֹכֵב עַל הַחֹמֶר הַגּוּפָנִי וּמַנְהִיגוֹ כִּרְצוֹנוֹ; וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא לֹא הָיָה מַנְהִיגוֹ כִּרְצוֹנוֹ, רַק נִמְשָׁךְ אַחֲרָיו.
Riding the donkey symbolizes riding upon and governing one’s physical materiality. In truth, however, Balaam did not govern his material nature; he was drawn after it.

וּנְבוּאָה רְבִיעִית דְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים הוּא בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר הָרְשִׁימָה. אָז אָמַר "הִנְנִי הוֹלֵךְ לְעַמִּי", שֶׁאָז הִרְגִּישׁ דְּאַף דְּ"תָּמֹת נַפְשִׁי וְכוּלֵי", עִם כָּל זֶה הוּא אָמַר "הִנְנִי הוֹלֵךְ לְעַמִּי", שֶׁאֵין לוֹ אוֹר הָרְשִׁימָה בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים.

The fourth prophecy, concerning the end of days, relates to the revelation of the residual imprint. Then Balaam said, “Behold, I am going to my people”: even after saying “may my soul die the death of the upright,” he sensed that at the end of days he still goes to his own people, for he lacks Israel’s inner imprint.

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר "לְכָה אִיעָצְךָ וְגוֹמֵר" — דְּזֶה עֵצָה לְבָלָק בְּהַפְקָרַת בְּנוֹתָיו, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין קו.)795 Sanhedrin 106a — He said to them: The God of these people hates lewdness, and they crave linen garments. Come, I will give you counsel: make them enclosures of hangings and seat harlots in them, an old woman outside and a young woman within, and let them sell them linen garments. He made them enclosures of hangings from the Mountain of Snow as far as Beth-jeshimoth, and seated harlots in them, an old woman outside and a young woman within. Rashi: "Enclosures of hangings" — tents of hangings, such as are set up in marketplaces. "From the Mountain of Snow" — that is, Senir. Maharsha: They craved linen garments because flax was already plentiful in Egypt, as it is written, "those who work in combed flax" (Isaiah 19:9), and Israel had grown accustomed to them; during the forty years in the wilderness they went without them, and so they longed to buy them wherever they could find them..
This is the meaning of “Come, I will advise you, etc.”: he advised Balak to make the daughters of Moab sexually available, as our Sages of blessed memory explained (Sanhedrin 106a).
הַיְנוּ דְּכָל חֵשֶׁק בָּלָק לִהְיוֹת כְּיִשְׂרָאֵל — יְעָצוֹ לִקְלֹט זֶה עַל יְדֵי הַפְקָרַת בְּנוֹתָיו, דְּיִקְלְטוּ אוֹר מֵהֶם.
Since Balak’s whole desire was to become like Israel, Balaam advised him to absorb something of Israel’s light through such unions with the daughters of Moab.

אַף דְּיָדַע דְּהַבּוֹעֲלֵי אֲרַמִּית הֵם מִפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, עַד שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּעֵרוּבִין (יט.)796 Eruvin 19a — As for what is written, "Those who pass through the valley of weeping" (Psalms 84:7) — that refers to those who at that hour are liable to Gehenna; and our father Abraham comes and brings them up and receives them — except for a Jew who had intercourse with a gentile woman, whose foreskin has been drawn forward, so that Abraham does not recognize him. Rashi: "Does not recognize him" — Abraham does not know him for a Jew, since his foreskin has been drawn forward and he appears to him like one who was never circumcised. Tosafos (s.v. "except for a Jew who had intercourse with a gentile woman"): He is not to be reckoned among the three enumerated in the chapter "The Gold" (Bava Metzia 58b) who go down to Gehinnom and do not come up, since this one does come up once he has received his judgment. Maharsha: He understands that verse to be speaking of those who weep at that hour and justify the judgment against themselves — and these do ascend, as the Gemara concludes, that Abraham our father brings them up and receives them. Maharal (Derech Chaim, end of ch. 6): [Citing this passage:] The completely wicked, even if they go down to Gehenna, nonetheless come up after they have received their punishment. This is said of one whose sins are the majority — for the passage shows that he possesses a number of commandments — so that one with a majority of transgressions and a minority of commandments goes down to Gehenna, but Abraham brings him up. They do not go down merely to be refined and then come up at once; rather, they have a time in Gehenna according to the sin, and then Abraham brings them up. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): In Eruvin they said that all go down [to Gehinnom] "for the sake of worthless things," and there, that our father Abraham saves the children of Israel who are circumcised: that is, circumcision testifies that one's desire is for the Blessed One, and this is the root implanted from our father Abraham — therefore he saves them. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): Our father Abraham, head of the circumcised, brings all Israel up from Gehinnom, for all go down there "for the sake of worthless things," and whoever is enticed by his impulse falls there — that is, through lust — and the seal of the covenant testifies to save them, [showing] that their lust came only from the thorns surrounding the myrtle, while at their root they are circumcised and fenced off from lust. The exception is one who has relations with a gentile woman: through his desire to cleave to the nations she becomes for him a foreskin enveloping the circumcision; yet since one whose foreskin is drawn forward is still circumcised by Torah law, "Abraham does not recognize him" means that to the human eye he looks uncircumcised, and only the Blessed One Himself, who sees into the heart, saves him, for in the depths of his heart he too is circumcised. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): In all sins our father Abraham saves them: since [the sinner] is still recognizable as Abraham's seed, having a complete root of Judaism, the sin has no essential hold on him, only like the thorns surrounding the myrtle. But one who has relations with a gentile woman, who is bound to him like a dog, appears from the revealed sin to have departed from the root of Judaism, since such a thing is not fitting to befall one of Israel's root; therefore "Abraham does not recognize him" as his seed at all, as if he had no hidden root of Judaism — and so his hidden root is not revealed in this world in his son either. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 5): Through circumcision Israel are saved from Gehinnom, and our father Abraham, who by his own effort attained circumcision and left the ranks of the uncircumcised, is the one who saves them; for all of Gehinnom is over evil lusts, as they said that all go down "for the sake of worthless things" and forbidden relations, and circumcision testifies that the organ of lust of the children of Israel is holy to God. Even one who has relations with a gentile woman, whose foreskin is drawn forward, is truly circumcised by Torah law and needs re-circumcision only for appearance's sake; so "Abraham does not recognize him" refers to outward appearance, for man — even the greatest of giants, like our father Abraham — "sees what is before the eyes," while "the Lord sees into the heart" and will save them too. דְּלָא מְבַשְׁקַר לְהוּ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְאֵין עוֹלִין מִגֵּיהִנָּם.

He knew that those who cohabit with an Aramean woman are among the grave sinners of Israel, to the point that Eruvin (19a) says that our father Abraham does not recognize them and they do not ascend from Gehinnom.

אֲבָל אַחַר שֶׁגִּלָּה לוֹ "אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה הָעָם הַזֶּה" כְּמַרְאֶה בְּאֶצְבַּע — הֵם אוֹתָם רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהָיְתָה לוֹ הַשָּׂגָה בָּהֶם לִהְיוֹת כְּמַרְאֶה בְּאֶצְבַּע — דְּגַם הֵם קְדֻשָּׁתָם רַבָּה בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים.

But after revealing to Balak “what this people will do” as though pointing with a finger—referring to those very wicked Israelites who have no share in the World to Come, the level Balaam was capable of perceiving—he showed that even their holiness will be great at the end of days.

עַד שֶׁאַף הוּא, שֶׁהָיָה נָבִיא הַגָּדוֹל מִנְּבִיאֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לָהֶם וְהוֹלֵךְ לְעַמּוֹ נֶגְדָּם. אִם כֵּן מִמֵּילָא נִצְמַח מִזֶּה עֵצָה לְבָלָק בְּהַפְקָרַת בְּנוֹת מוֹאָב.

So great is that residual holiness that even Balaam, foremost among the prophets of the nations, has no share in their destiny and instead returns to his own people. From this, however, Balaam derived his scheme involving the daughters of Moab.

אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא לֹא יָדַע הַהֲלָכָה דְּ"בִּנְךָ הַבָּא מִן הַגּוֹיָה אֵינוֹ קָרוּי בִּנְךָ אֶלָּא בְּנָהּ" (יְבָמוֹת יז.)797 Yevamot 17a — When I said this before Shmuel, he said to me: Your son from an Israelite woman is called your son, but your son from a gentile woman is not called your son but her son. Rashi: "When I said this before Shmuel": Rav Yehuda says that when he afterwards repeated Rav Asi's ruling — that we are concerned for the betrothal — before Shmuel, [Shmuel replied]. "Your son from an Israelite woman is called your son…": this is derived from "For he will turn away your son from following Me" (Deut. 7:4) — not "she will turn away" — so the verse does not refer back to "nor shall you take his daughter for your son," for then it should have said "for the gentile woman will turn away"; learn from this that even a son she bears [to be raised] to idolatry is not called "your son," and therefore [the offspring of the ten tribes from gentile women] are complete gentiles. Tosafos (s.v. "but your son from a gentile woman is not called your son but her son"): Rabbenu Tam objects to Rashi's reading [that "he will turn away" refers to "your daughter you shall not give to his son"], for then Shmuel would already be saying what Ravina goes on to infer about a daughter's son. In Rabbenu Tam's second explanation, Shmuel and R. Yochanan infer from "for he will turn away your son" that the verse is concerned only with your son's being led astray and not his offspring's — for it does not say "he will turn them away" or "your son and his seed" — since [a child] from a gentile woman is not called your son but her son; whereas with a daughter even her offspring must be guarded from being turned away, whence Ravina's inference that a daughter's son from a gentile is called your son. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos, 16b, on Tosafot s.v. "a gentile who betrothed nowadays"): Rashi was precise to refer "When I said this before Shmuel" to Rav Asi's statement and not also to R. Yochanan's: Shmuel's reply, "Your son from an Israelite woman…," addresses only the ground on which Rav Asi disqualified them — [descent from] an Israelite man and a gentile woman — which is why the Gemara goes on to object, "But there are the daughters!"; whereas to R. Yochanan, who disqualified them on account of the daughters, Shmuel should have answered only that the daughters of that generation became barren. On Tosafot's view, that Rav Asi too disqualified them on account of the daughters, it requires study what Shmuel was answering him with "your son from an Israelite woman."
