Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 20): Edom was distanced from the congregation because its root is from Isaac and Rebecca, which is why [Esau] is called an apostate Israelite — unlike Ishmael, who left the family, since [such a son] "is not called your son but her son." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): This is the reason that "your son from a maidservant or a gentile woman is not called your son": betrothal does not take effect with them in their own right — unlike those forbidden on pain of karet, with whom betrothal can at least take effect for others — so they are wholly deficient, with nothing to complete the lack, and they bear wholly deficient offspring; therefore he is not called your son. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 21): In relations with a gentile woman there is no element of perpetuating the species, since [the child] "is not called your son but her son"; it is nothing but an attachment, like a dog's, to one's own desire alone., וְצָרִיךְ לְהַבְדִּיל גַּם הַנּוֹלָד מֵהֶם, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.

He did not know the halakhic principle that “your child born from a gentile woman is not called your child but hers” (Yevamot 17a); even the offspring must therefore be distinguished as not halakhically belonging to Israel through the father.

וּלְפִי שֶׁאוֹתוֹ שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא נִרְאֶה שֶׁהוּא הָיָה בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְיָצָא מֵהֶם לִהְיוֹת כִּבְנֵי נֵכָר — מִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ מְצִיאוּת יְצִיאַת טִפָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית לְהִתְהַוּוֹת מִמֶּנָּה בֶּן נֵכָר.

Because an Israelite who loses the World to Come appears to have begun within Israel and then gone out to become like a foreigner, this creates the conceptual possibility of an Israelite seed giving rise to offspring who are legally foreign to Israel.

וּכְשֶׁהִשִּׂיג בִּלְעָם דַּרְגָא דְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים, שֶׁאַף אוֹתָן דְּאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכֻנּוּ, חָשַׁב דְּגַם אוֹתָן טִפּוֹת הֵם כֵּן, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵין מְצִיאוּת לְטִפָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית לְהִשְׁתַּנּוֹת כְּלָל.

When Balaam perceived that at the end of days even those with no share in the World to Come are still called by the name Israel, he mistakenly thought the same would apply to such seed, reasoning that an Israelite point could never truly change.

וּבֶאֱמֶת וַדַּאי אוֹתָן טִפּוֹת בָּאִים גַּם כֵּן בַּחֲזָרָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק לֹא כְּמַחֲשֶׁבֶת אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע שֶׁבָּזֶה יִהְיֶה עֵצָה וְתִקּוּן לְאֻמַּת מוֹאָב, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לַקְּדֻשָּׁה שַׁיָּכוּת גַּם אֶצְלָם; דְּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר, כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי".

In the deeper providential process those sparks can indeed ultimately return to Israel, but not as Balaam imagined—that this would provide a rectification for Moab by making holiness belong within Moab itself. That cannot be, for “He did not do so for any nation.”
וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁהַטִּפּוֹת בְּלוּעוֹת בַּגּוֹיִם הֵם מִכְּלַל הַגּוֹיִם וְאֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּכוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק כְּשֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ לְהִקָּלֵט בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
As long as those sparks are absorbed among the nations, they are counted there and have no active connection to Israel; their return occurs only when they are reabsorbed into Israel.
וּבֶאֱמֶת עֵצָה זוֹ דַּיְקָא הָיְתָה הֲכָנָה לְ"מַה יַּעֲשֶׂה הָעָם הַזֶּה וְגוֹמֵר" וּ"מָחַץ פַּאֲתֵי מוֹאָב" — קוֹדֵם לַכֹּל לְהוֹצִיא בִּלְעָם מִפִּיהֶם.

In truth, that very scheme became the preparation for “what this people will do, etc.” and “he shall crush the corners of Moab”—first of all, by extracting from Moab the holiness that Balaam sought to capture.
וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע בְּעַצְמוֹ מַה שֶּׁהָיָה אוֹמֵר: דְּ"לְכָה אִיעָצְךָ, אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה וְגוֹמֵר" — דְּבָרִים כִּכְתָבָן, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה נוֹתֵן לוֹ עֵצָה כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה הָעָם וְגוֹמֵר.

Balaam himself did not grasp the prophetic irony of his own words: “Come, I will advise you—what this people will do…” literally meant that the advice he was giving would itself bring about what Israel would ultimately do to Moab.

וּלְפִי שֶׁבְּעִילַת אֲרַמִּית הִיא הִתְעָרְבוּת בָּאֻמּוֹת גַּם כֵּן הֵפֶךְ דַּרְגָא דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא בָּא מִצַּד חֶסְרוֹן הַדַּעַת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ה הֲלָכָה ב)798 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 5:2 — This accords with Rabbi, for Rabbi said: I am astonished at how they abolished "Who graciously grants knowledge" on the Sabbath. If there is no knowledge, whence prayer? And here likewise: if there is no knowledge, whence the distinction [between sacred and profane]? Pnei Moshe (s.v. "and this accords with Rabbi"): Rabbi said in the preceding chapter, halakha 4, "I am astonished…" with regard to prayer; and here likewise, if there is no knowledge, whence the distinction [between sacred and profane]? Hence the havdalah properly belongs to the blessing "You graciously grant man knowledge." Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:17): Knowledge is that which distinguishes one thing from another, for one knows the truth of things by the distinctions between them — as the Sages said in the Jerusalem Talmud [Berakhot 5:2] that they fixed the havdalah in the blessing "Who graciously grants knowledge," since it is by means of knowledge that one distinguishes between one thing and another. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 12): "And God separated between the light and the darkness" — the darkness being sadness — and this separation comes about through the fencing of the Torah, for every separation is made by a fence and partition, and that is the Torah, as it says, "If there is no knowledge, whence separation?" Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi 17): Distinguishing the holiness of the Sabbath from the six weekdays and distinguishing between Israel and the nations both require discernment through the insight of the intellect, as it says, "If there is no knowledge, whence separation?" For to the eye of flesh there is no difference between Jacob and Esau, and likewise nothing on the surface shows the holiness of the Sabbath as distinct from the weekdays, except to one whom the Blessed One has granted understanding. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 240): There are certainly divisions among the powers of the animal soul, and their Creator knows them, but man cannot grasp what distinguishes them, since animals have no knowledge, which is what makes distinction, as the Sages said, "If there is no knowledge, whence distinction?" Yet in truth there is some small difference, as is sometimes discernible even in the taste of the meat. Sod Yesharim (Hoshana Rabba 18): As the Jerusalem Talmud says, "If there is no knowledge, whence separation?" — that is, all separations exist only in the knowledge of Israel: according to the service within the grasp of their knowledge, so they can separate from the Tree of Life and can also bring into the Tree of Life. To the extent that Israel constrict themselves in the service of their knowledge, the garments are included through them in the Tree of Life, and the separation is diminished on their side.: "אִם אֵין דֵּעָה — הַבְדָּלָה מִנַּיִן".

Since cohabitation with an Aramean woman is itself a form of intermingling with the nations, it stands opposite the level of Moshe and arises from a deficiency of da’at, as the Yerushalmi teaches (Berakhot 5:2): “If there is no understanding, from where can there be separation?”
וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ הַהֶבְדֵּל בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ דֵּעָה, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהִדָּבֵק עִם גּוֹיָה כְּלָל.
Such a person fails to apprehend the distinction between Israel and the nations; one who possesses true da’at cannot attach himself in that way.
וְלָכֵן נֶעְלַם מִמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הֲלָכָה זוֹ דְּבּוֹעֵל אֲרַמִּית מַה דִּינוֹ, שֶׁהוּא אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לָזֶה כְּלָל.
For this reason the law governing one who cohabits with an Aramean woman was hidden from Moshe Rabbeinu: his own spiritual level had no experiential connection to such confusion.

עַד שֶׁבָּא פִּינְחָס, שֶׁאָמְרוּ עָלָיו שְׁבָטִים "בֶּן פּוּטִי וְכוּלֵי799 Midrash Tanchuma, Pinchas 1 — At the hour that Zimri was slain, the tribes stood against Pinchas and said: Have you seen this son of Puti, whose mother’s father fattened calves for idolatry — and he has slain a prince of a tribe in Israel! Therefore Scripture comes and traces the lineage of Pinchas to Elazar son of Aharon the priest.", שֶׁמִּצַּד הַזֶּה שֶׁבָּא מִיִּתְרוֹ הָיָה לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לַהֲלָכָה זוֹ, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (לט:)800 Sanhedrin 39b — R. Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said — let Obadiah come, who dwelt between two wicked ones and did not learn from their deeds, and let him prophesy concerning Esau the wicked, who dwelt between two righteous ones and did not learn from their deeds. Efrayim Miksha'a, the disciple of R. Meir, said in the name of R. Meir: Obadiah was an Edomite convert. And this is what people say: From the forest itself comes the handle for the ax. Rashi: "Two wicked ones" — Ahab and Jezebel; "two righteous ones" — Isaac and Rebecca. "From the forest itself comes the handle for the ax": from the forest's own wood [a piece] goes into the ax to become its handle, and with it the forest is cut down; so too Obadiah against Edom, and David against Moab, for he descended from Ruth the Moabite. Maharsha (s.v. "Obadiah was an Edomite convert"): That is, the prophecy is all the more confirmed because Obadiah was one of their own, testifying against them — just as David dealt with Moab as he did with no other nation he conquered because he himself came from Moab, so that it would be all the more established that they deserved it. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 39b): A person is more readily able to act upon himself than upon another, for a thing is close to itself; therefore it was Obadiah [the Edomite] who prophesied concerning Edom, to bring the punishment upon Edom. That is the meaning of "from the forest itself comes the handle for the ax": punishment commonly comes upon a person from his own side, since he is close to acting upon himself, whereas through others it is not so readily brought about. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 5): R. Akiva, the foundation of the Oral Torah, was a son of converts and came from Esau, in the manner of what the Sages said in Sanhedrin about Obadiah, an Edomite convert who prophesied against Edom, because "from the forest itself [comes the handle for the axe]." That is, because Esau came from Isaac, on which account the Sages call Esau "an apostate Israelite"; and since there was in some respect a connection to Isaac, the beginning of the Israelite lineage, Esau too had some share in it.: "מִינֵּיהּ וּבֵיהּ אַבָּא וְכוּלֵי".

It was Pinchas who acted, and the tribes disparaged him as “the son of Puti, etc.” Precisely because one side of his ancestry came through Yitro, he had a point of contact with this law, in the spirit of the saying in Sanhedrin (39b), “from within it and by means of it…”
וְלָכֵן נִכְתַּב גַּם זֶה בְּסִיּוּם פָּרָשַׁת בִּלְעָם, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְחָכְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
Therefore this episode too appears at the conclusion of the Balaam section, a realm that is not naturally related to Moshe Rabbeinu’s own mode of wisdom and attainment, as explained above.
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם, אַחַר שֶׁגִּלָּה בִּלְעָם דְּבָרִים הַלָּלוּ, הוֹצִיא מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו וְנִכְתְּבוּ בַּתּוֹרָה עַל יָדוֹ.
Nevertheless, once Balaam had revealed these matters, Moshe Rabbeinu extracted what Balaam had “swallowed” and incorporated it into Torah through his own writing.
אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְגַּלָּה דִּבְאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים מִצַּד הָרְשִׁימוּ גַּם הֵם בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, מִמֵּילָא יֵשׁ לָהֶם שַׁיָּכוּת לַתּוֹרָה גַּם כֵּן.
Once it was revealed that at the end of days, by virtue of the residual imprint, even those estranged sinners remain included within Israel, it follows that they too possess a connection to Torah.
וְכָל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה כַּנּוֹדָע; וְנַפְשׁוֹת הַכּוֹפְרִים וְהַמְשֻׁמָּדִים הֵם מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁבְּפָרָשָׁה זוֹ.
All Jewish souls are rooted in the letters of the Torah, as is known; the souls of deniers and apostates correspond to the letters contained in this very section.
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּרְאֶה שֶׁהוּא חוּץ לְתוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הוּא מִכְּלַל הַתּוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ, וְאֵין שׁוּם הֶבְדֵּל בֵּין פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ לְפָרָשַׁת "שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל".

Although this section appears to stand outside “the Torah of Moses,” it is in truth fully part of Torah itself; in sanctity there is no difference between this section and the section beginning “Hear, O Israel.”

items.h:
Seif 4 — Why Balak Could Have Entered the Shema
Parashat Balak teaches that even extreme sinners remain within Israel's unity, though this truth need not be rehearsed daily.

p: וְאָמְרוּ801 Berakhot 12b — R. Abbahu ben Zutrati said in the name of R. Yehuda bar Zevida: They sought to fix the portion of Balak within the reading of Shema, and why did they not fix it? Because of the burden upon the congregation. What is the reason? … Rather, R. Yose bar Avin said: Because there is written in it this verse — “He crouched, he lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who shall rouse him?” And let them say this verse alone and no more? — It is an accepted tradition: every portion which Moshe our teacher divided, we divide; and any which Moshe our teacher did not divide, we do not divide. Rashi: "He crouched, he lay down" was chosen because it resembles "when you lie down and when you rise": the Holy One, blessed be He, guards us in our lying down and our rising, so that we lie down tranquil and at ease like a lion and a lioness. On "And let them say this verse alone": for then there would be no burden on the congregation. Tosafos (s.v. "They sought to fix the portion of Balak within the recitation of the Shema"): It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 1:5) that the three portions were fixed in the recitation of the Shema because the Ten Commandments are contained in them; look there and you will find it all. Maharsha: "He crouched, he lay down" corresponds to the evening Shema, of which "when you lie down" is written, as Rashi explained, and "like a lioness, who shall rouse him" corresponds to the morning Shema, of which "when you rise" is written — for surely no one rouses him: he rises of himself with alacrity, and so a man should rise of himself with alacrity at the time of the morning Shema, that its time not pass. Maharsha adds that he afterwards found in Tanchuma that the preceding verse is cited — "Behold, a people that rises up like a lioness ... he shall not lie down until he devours the prey" — which suits this exposition of the morning and evening Shema better. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:12): When Bilam spoke them, his words were surely counted as profane among Israel, and so they truly were; only when Moses wrote them in the Torah scroll did they become holy and words of the living God — so much so that the Sages sought to fix the portion of Balak in the recitation of the Shema, for it holds great holiness, like the verse "Hear, O Israel." And it is good to bear these words on one's lips evening and morning, every day, constantly. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Balak 3): On the Gemara's statement that they sought to fix the portion of Balak in the Shema because of the verse "He crouched, he lay down like a lion," he asks what this verse — which, as Rashi explains, resembles "when you lie down and when you rise," for the Holy One, blessed be He, guards us when we lie down and rise — has to do with the Shema, which is the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and of the commandments. But the Midrash says that Bilam flattered Israel in his prophecies and made their hearts proud, so that they fell at Shittim — and this was through his saying "He crouched, he lay down"; and the Gemara there says that one who recites the Shema on his bed is as though holding a two-edged sword, whose main purpose is to slay the evil inclination. Sod Yesharim (Purim 3): My grandfather explained the verse "He crouched, he lay down like a lion": what might is evident in a lion once it has lain down, when a lion's might is praised only when it rises? But one who is not truly mighty cannot restrain himself from avenging himself at once upon his enemies, whereas one truly mighty and confident in his strength does not hasten, and can hold back until their measure is full and then repay them; so from his very crouching and lying down and refraining from vengeance, the greatness of his might is evident. (בְּרָכוֹת יב:) דְּבִקְּשׁוּ לִקְבֹּעַ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק בִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, הַיְנוּ לְכַוָּנָה זוֹ: שֶׁאַף פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּכְלַל אַחְדוּת הָאֻמָּה, וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק בַּ"הַשֵּׁם אֶחָד", וְנִבְדָּלִים מֵעַמִּים כָּאָמוּר.

They said (Berakhot 12b) that the Sages wished to establish Parashat Balak as part of the daily Shema. The intention was precisely this: even the sinners of Israel remain within the unity of the nation, have a share in “God is One,” and remain distinct from the nations as described above.

וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה טָמְנוּ דִּבְרֵיהֶם בְּרֶמֶז כְּדַרְכָּם, מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם)802 Berakhot 12b — What is the reason [they sought to fix the portion of Balak within the recitation of the Shema]? If you say because it is written in it, "God who brought them out of Egypt" — then let us say the portion of usury and the portion of weights, in which the exodus from Egypt is written. Rashi: "The portion of usury" is "Take no interest or increase from him" (Leviticus 25:36), which has the exodus from Egypt written next to it; "the portion of weights" is "Just balances, just weights" (Leviticus 19:36), the end of whose verse reads, "who brought you out of the land of Egypt." Maharsha: Maharsha remarks only that the reason the exodus from Egypt is stated in these two portions is set out in the chapter Eizehu Neshekh, and refers the reader to his own novellae there. דִּכְתִיב בָּהּ יְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם — רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁאָז הַתְחָלַת הֶבְדֵּל הָאֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, "גּוֹי מִקֶּרֶב גּוֹי", אַף שֶׁהַלָּלוּ עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְכוּלֵי (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כג)803 Vayikra Rabbah 23:2 — R. Elazar expounded the verse concerning the redemption from Egypt. Just as a lily set among thorns is hard for its owner to pluck, so was the redemption of Israel hard for the Holy One, blessed be He, to accomplish. That is what is written: "Or has any god ventured to come and take him a nation from the midst of a nation." These worshipped idols and those worshipped idols; these grew locks of hair and those grew locks of hair; these wore forbidden mixtures and those wore forbidden mixtures. If so, the attribute of justice would never have allowed Israel to be redeemed from Egypt. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 3): On "until Your people pass over, O Lord" [Berakhos 4a]: at the first entry [into the Land], "these worshipped idols…", and it was only because they are "Your people, O Lord," as a father has compassion on his son even though he does not walk in a good way; their acceptance of the Torah, too, was under compulsion. Not so the second entry, when they accepted it again willingly in the days of Ahasuerus. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 5): The exile of Egypt was an entry into their gates of impurity, as is known, and as the Sages said on the verse "a nation from the midst of a nation": "these worshipped idols…". Yet they "acted only for appearance's sake": they were idol worshippers only in their outer garment, not inwardly. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 7): The redemption of Nisan is what the Blessed One Himself arouses, which is why it is called Nisan, from nes [miracle]: when Israel repent, the salvation comes by right, and only a complete miracle in all the worlds is called a miracle — like the Exodus, when He brought out "a nation from the midst of a nation," as the Sages said, "these [worshipped idols]…," and as it is written, "and you were naked and bare." Only the Blessed One, in His abundant mercy and kindness, sent them a sudden flow of light. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 1): The Egyptian exile was a preparation for the giving of the Torah, which is a gift — and a gift is what does not come by way of obligation and reward, that is, not through any arousal from below at all, as the Sages said on the verse "a nation from the midst of a nation": "these worshipped idols…". Therefore the Torah is everywhere called a gift, [given] without any effort. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Yisro 1): Unlike a convert, who must first draw himself near, Israel the Blessed One draws near from His own side — as it was at the Exodus, when He took them "a nation from the midst of a nation" although they were enveloped in the shell of Egypt like a fetus in its mother's womb, as stated in the Pesikta and the Midrash, "these and those…". So too in the future, "as in the days of your going out of the land of Egypt I will show him wonders": the awakening will come from the side of the Blessed One..

Our Sages of blessed memory concealed this idea in allusion, as was their way, when they explained there that the section contains the Exodus from Egypt: that event marked the beginning of Israel’s separation as a nation, “a nation from the midst of a nation,” even though “these worshipped idols and those worshipped idols, etc.” (Vayikra Rabbah 23).
וְ"כָרַע שָׁכַב כַּאֲרִי" — הַיְנוּ אַף דְּהֵם בְּדִיּוֹטָא הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה, שְׁכִיבָא לְעַפְרָא, הֵם כַּאֲרִי.
And “he crouched, he lay down like a lion” means that even when Israel is on the lowest rung, lying in the dust, they still retain the inner identity of a lion.

וְזֶה כָּל עִנְיַן קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע "בְּשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ" — רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר, בֵּין שֶׁהֵם בְּמַעֲלָה עֶלְיוֹנָה, בֵּין בְּמַדְרֵגָה תַּחְתּוֹנָה, אֵינוֹ נִתָּק מִקַּבָּלַת עֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁעָלָיו וְהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּ"הַשֵּׁם אֶחָד".

This is the meaning of the Shema’s phrase “when you lie down and when you rise”: whether Israel stands on a lofty level or a low one, the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven upon them and their bond to the One God is not severed.

וְלֹא קְבָעוּהָ מִפְּנֵי טֹרַח צִבּוּר, דְּ"כָל פָּרָשָׁה דְּלָא פַסְקֵיהּ מֹשֶׁה וְכוּלֵי" — רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר, דְּסִדּוּר הַפָּרָשִׁיּוֹת וַדַּאי הַמְכֻוָּן דְּאוֹתוֹ עִנְיָן אֵינוֹ נִשְׁלָם אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי כָּל הַפָּרָשָׁה כֻּלָּהּ דַּוְקָא, דְּלָכֵן לֹא פַסְקֵיהּ מֹשֶׁה.

They did not institute it because of the burden it would place on the congregation, since “any passage that Moses did not divide…” This means that the Torah’s paragraph structure is deliberate: this theme is completed only through the entire section, which is why Moses did not break it into a shorter liturgical unit.

וּפָרָשַׁת בָּלָק, שֶׁהוּא גִּלּוּי קֶשֶׁר יִשְׂרָאֵל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַף הַמּוֹרְדִים וּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּתַכְלִית הַתֹּקֶף, בֵּרוּר זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּפִי סֵדֶר הַפָּרָשָׁה, עַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְהִתְבּוֹנְנוּתָם בְּדַעַת שֶׁלָּהֶם הֵם מְבָרְרִים לָעַיִן מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּזֶה.

Parashat Balak reveals the bond between Israel and the Blessed One even at the extreme point of rebellion and sin. This clarification emerges only through the full order of the parashah: the nations’ attempt to become like Israel, and their own intellectual reflection, ultimately make Israel’s unique inner stature visible.

וְכֵן בְּכָל דּוֹר כֵּן הוּא סֵדֶר הַבֵּרוּר, עַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁטּוֹעֲנִים "אָנוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא, כִּי תִשָּׂא לד)804 Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 34 — R. Yehudah bar Shalom said: When the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, "Write these words," Moses asked that the Mishnah too be put in writing. But the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that the nations of the world were destined to translate the Torah and read it in Greek, and to say, "We are Israel." Until now the scales are balanced. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the nations: You say that you are My children — I do not know; only those who hold My mysteries are My children. And which are they? This is the Mishnah, which was given orally, and from which everything is to be expounded. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): After prophecy departed, the sages of the Oral Torah began, and the Sages said, "He has set me in dark places — this is the Talmud of Babylonia"; but this is the mysteries of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it says in Tanchuma, "Those who hold My mysteries are Israel." For it is written, "He made darkness His hiding place" — there are His hidden things; and though it is darkness and the hiding of the Face, the darkness is cast by the shadow of His hand, shielding us by way of concealment, as one must make shade to protect against the blazing sun. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:86): The Blessed One teaches human beings to exert effort, which is why the Torah began for Israel as the Written Torah; He wishes a person to arrive at His mysteries — as in the Midrash, "He who holds My mysteries…" — and to understand what He indicates to him with the compass. This is the essential effort: to come to the Oral Torah, which is the recognition that everything is from the Blessed One, the "finding" that comes after toil. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 12): The novel insights of Torah belong to the Oral Torah, whereas in the Written Torah, which is written and set down [before all], there are no novel insights; therefore the nations claim on the strength of the Written Torah, "We are Israel," and the Holy One, blessed be He, answers, "He who holds My mysteries…," for the Oral Torah exists only in the hearts of the children of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 4): Edom claims that they are the good and the pure by birth; therefore Haman's decree was a preparation for the Oral Torah, as the Midrash says: because the nations are destined to say "We are Israel," the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "He who holds My mysteries…" — for it is the Oral Torah that clarifies this. The Oral Torah is what springs from the heart of Israel, the hearts of the children of Israel being its originators, so that it is theirs alone, and this is the testimony that they, and no others, are the masters of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Just as there is wisdom among the nations but no Torah among the nations, so it says in Tanchuma, "He who holds My mysteries…": the Oral Torah was given over only to Israel. The nations, even if they study Torah and innovate in it by their wisdom, speak vanity and not Torah at all, for they innovate from their own wisdom, whereas the Torah is the wisdom of the Blessed One; but the sages of Israel bless over the Torah first and know that the Blessed One is the Giver of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 3): The essence of the Torah is the Oral Torah, which reveals the hidden things of the Written Torah, as it says in Shemos Rabbah that the nations are destined to translate the Torah into Greek… "He who holds My mysteries…." This is an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob alone: the Torah is handed over to them according to what they clarify through their dialectic and their wisdom. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): They said in Tanchuma that the Oral Torah was given because the nations are destined to translate the Torah into Greek and say "We are Israel," and the Holy One, blessed be He, will say, "He who holds My mysteries…." That is, the nations too have a connection to the Written Torah, which is why it was revealed in writing to all who come into the world; but the Oral Torah is the mysteries of the Holy One, blessed be He, which cannot be revealed in writing at all, only "the secret of the Lord is with those who fear Him" — the Congregation of Israel, who look to the Blessed One from the depths of their hearts. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 6): All the innovation of the Oral Torah comes through the unions and complete cleaving to the Holy One, blessed be He, and this is His mysteries, as they said in Tanchuma at the end of Ki Sisa: because the nations of the world are destined to translate the Torah and say "We are Israel," the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "He who holds My mysteries…." This is the telling of secrets, which is for Jacob alone — and "telling" does not mean in writing — so "He tells [His words to Jacob]" means the Oral Torah, the handing over of the words of Torah of which it is said "He has not done so for any nation"; whereas the Written Torah alone was written on the stones in seventy languages..

The same pattern of clarification recurs in every generation, through movements among the nations that claim, in effect, “we are Israel,” as our Sages of blessed memory described (Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 34).
וְלָכֵן נִקְרֵאת הַפָּרָשָׁה עַל שֵׁם בָּלָק, לֹא עַל שֵׁם בִּלְעָם, כִּי בָּלָק הוּא הָיָה הַמִּתְעוֹרֵר בָּזֶה.
Therefore the parashah is called after Balak, not Balaam, because Balak was the one who initiated this challenge. –
וְסִיּוּמָהּ דְּ"בִלְעָם שָׁב לִמְקוֹמוֹ" — הַיְנוּ לְעַמּוֹ, שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק לִמְקוֹמוֹ בַּאֲרָם, שֶׁהוּא בַּאֲחוֹרַיִם דִּקְדֻשָּׁה כַּנּוֹדָע.

The ending, “Balaam returned to his place,” means that he returned to his own people, for he has no connection to Israel, but only to his place in Aram, associated in Kabbalistic language with the “back side” of holiness.

אֲבָל "בָּלָק הָלַךְ לְדַרְכּוֹ" — הוּא הַדֶּרֶךְ הַנִּזְכָּר בַּכָּתוּב לִרְדֹּף אַחַר קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל; דְּעַל כֵּן הִזְנָה בְּנוֹת מוֹאָב, כִּי נִיצוֹץ קָדוֹשׁ דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה מְכַשְׁכֵּשׁ בְּמֵעָיו וְלֹא הָיָה מַנִּיחוֹ לִשְׁקֹט מִזֶּה.]

But “Balak went on his way”: he continued on the path described in the verse, pursuing a connection to Israel’s holiness. Hence his involvement with the daughters of Moab, for the holy spark of King David, peace be upon him, was stirring within him and would not allow him to rest from this pursuit.

וְשֵׁם שֶׁל כָּל סִדְרָה שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁנָּהֲגוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לִקְרוֹתָהּ, הוּא הַמְכֻוָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַסִּדְרָה, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם וְכָל הַשֵּׁמוֹת דִּלְשׁוֹן הַקֹּדֶשׁ, שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַחַיּוּת דְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר.

The name by which Israel customarily calls each Torah portion expresses the inner intent of the entire portion, just as our Sages teach regarding human names and, more broadly, all names in the Holy Tongue: the name is the root of a thing’s life-force.
מִסְּתָמָא כֵּן גַּם בִּשְׁמוֹת סִפְרֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ כֻּלָּם, וְכֵן בִּשְׁמוֹת פָּרָשׁוֹת הַתּוֹרָה.
Presumably the same is true of the names of all sacred books and of the names of the Torah portions.

וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר זֶה הַטָּמוּן בְּרִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, עַל יְדֵי כֹּחַ בָּלָק — שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הָרְדִיפָה דְּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לִהְיוֹת כְּיִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְגָרֵשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִכִּסּוּי עֵין הָאָרֶץ.

This is the root by which the hidden light within Israel’s sinners becomes revealed: through the force represented by Balak—the drive of the nations to become like Israel and to dislodge Israel from its unique relation to the “eye of the Land.”

וְהִתְגַּלּוּת כֹּחַ זֶה בָּאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁחוֹטְאִים כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁנִּרְאֶה שֶׁאָבְדוּ חֵלֶק עוֹלָם הַבָּא וְנִתְגָּרְשׁוּ מֵהָאָרֶץ הָעֶלְיוֹנָה; עַל יְדֵי זֶה צוֹמֵחַ כֹּחַ אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לִטְעֹן שֶׁגַּם הֵם כֵּן.

This claim gains force among the nations only when some Israelites sin so severely that they seem to have lost the World to Come and been expelled from the supernal Land; this creates room for the nations to argue that they too can occupy the same spiritual place.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה עַצְמוֹ מִתְבָּרֵר וּמִתְגַּלֶּה מַעֲלַת אוֹתָן רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאוֹר הָרְשִׁימָה שֶׁלָּהֶם.
Yet that very challenge becomes the means by which the deeper stature of those Jewish sinners and the light of their residual imprint are clarified and revealed.

וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יד:)805 Bava Batra 14b — And who wrote them? Moses wrote his own book, and the portion of Balaam, and Job. Joshua wrote his own book and eight verses of the Torah. Rashi: "And the portion of Balaam" — his prophecy and his parables, even though they are not part of Moses' own affairs, his Torah, or the record of his deeds. "And eight verses" — from "And Moses died there" to the end of the book. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:12): "Moses wrote his book and the portion of Bilam": "his book" is the engraving of the wisdom in his mind, for in the Zohar "book" denotes wisdom, while the portion of Bilam lies outside Moses' wisdom, for Moses was its opposite and could not attain that wisdom which comes by falling and concealment, casually and by chance. Only after Bilam attained it did Moses take up those drops, return them to their place and bring them into his book, turning the profane into holy: when Bilam spoke them they were profane words to Israel, but when Moses wrote them in the Torah they became holy, the words of the living God. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Yisro 4): The Gemara says, "Moses wrote his book and the portion of Bilam and Job" — but why count the portion of Bilam separately, when it is part of the Torah and included in "his book"? The Torah is called "the Torah of Moses" because he wrote the words of commoners — of Laban, of Esau, of Hagar and the like — and through him they became words of Torah; but the portion of Bilam was itself the very word of God, as the Zohar says on "and thus shall you speak," so there Moses did not need to make words of Torah out of a commoner's words, and therefore it is not included in "Moses wrote his book." קְרָאוּהָ "פָּרָשַׁת בִּלְעָם"; דְּמִצַּד מַה שֶּׁנִּכְתְּבָה הַפָּרָשָׁה בַּתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוּא דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מַמָּשׁ, הוּא הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבַּסּוֹף, וְ"סוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה" — שֹׁרֶשׁ הַהִתְגַּלּוּת נִצְמַח מִבָּלָק.

Our Sages of blessed memory (Bava Batra 14b) called it “the section of Balaam.” From the perspective of its having been written into the Torah as actual words of Torah, the section represents the final revelation; and since “the end of the deed is first in thought,” the root of that revelation began with Balak’s challenge.

אֲבָל רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁדִּבְּרוּ מִמֶּנָּה כְּאִלּוּ הִיא חוּץ מִתּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה, קְרָאוּהָ עַל שֵׁם בִּלְעָם "הַיֹּדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן", כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַדַּעַת שֶׁלֹּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַשָּׂגַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּלָל.

But when the Sages speak of it as though it stands outside the ordinary “Torah of Moses,” they name it for Balaam, “the one who knows the knowledge of the Most High,” because it concerns a mode of da’at wholly unlike Moshe Rabbeinu’s inward attainment.

וּמִצַּד מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל הַכְּשֵׁרִים שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעוּ לְמַדְרֵגַת "אֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא", חַס וְשָׁלוֹם — אֵין שַׁיָּכוּת לָהֶם לָזֶה כְּלָל, וְכַנִּכְתָּב לְעֵיל.

Moshe Rabbeinu and upright Israelites who, God forbid, have never descended to the level described as “having no share in the World to Come” have no direct experiential relation to this theme, as explained above.
וְלָכֵן זֶה נֶחְשָׁב לְטֹרַח צִבּוּר, דִּכְלַל הַצִּבּוּר אֵינָם פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְזִכְרוֹן כָּל פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ הוּא טֹרַח לָהֶם, וְכָאָמוּר.

For this reason including the whole section in the daily Shema would count as an undue burden on the congregation: the community as a whole is not composed of such extreme sinners, and rehearsing this entire process each day would be burdensome for them, as stated.

sections.en: Affliction, Consolation, and the End of the Year

items.h: The year closes through darkness followed by consolation, teaching that suffering itself is ultimately reread as part of the divine movement toward light.

Seif 1 — Affliction before Consolation
The year's closing haftarot mirror creation's movement from darkness to light, revealing suffering itself within divine consolation.

p: עִנְיַן סִיּוּם הַשָּׁנָה בִּתְלָת דְּפוּרְעָנוּתָא וְשֶׁבַע דְּנֶחֶמְתָּא, שֶׁמַּפְטִירִין בְּעֶשֶׂר שַׁבָּתוֹת אַחֲרוֹנִים דְּכָל שָׁנָה,
The significance of concluding the year with the Three Haftarot of Affliction and the Seven of Consolation, which are read during the final ten Shabbatot of every year,
שֶׁהִיא סִיּוּם הַקּוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה וּזְמַן שֶׁל כְּלַל הַבְּרִיאָה,
is that the year represents the completion of an entire structure and the full cycle of creation as a whole.

שֶׁהִיא (שַׁבָּת עז:)806 Shabbat 77b — R. Zeira found Rav Yehuda standing at the door of his father-in-law's house, and saw that he was in a cheerful mood, such that had he asked him about all the hollows of the world he would have told him. He said to him: Why do the goats walk at the front and the sheep after them? He said to him: It is as in the creation of the world — first darkness and afterward light. Rashi: "All the hollows of the world": that is, the things that happen throughout the space of the world. "First darkness": goats are generally black, and ewes generally white. Maharsha: Although the natural philosophers gave reasons for how each thing is formed, and the Talmud too has a few such ("why is the whole ear hard and the lobe soft"), these reasons are forced in their plain sense, so they must be meant as a parable on matters of Torah: Greece is likened to a goat ("and the he-goat grew exceedingly great", Daniel 8:8) and Israel to a sheep ("Israel is a scattered sheep", Jeremiah 50:17), and he asked why in the Second Temple the goats — the kings of Greece, Alexander of Macedon and those after him — reigned first, and only afterward the sheep, the kings of Israel. He answered that this was already alluded to in the creation of the world: first darkness — "and darkness was upon the face of the deep", which Bereshit Rabbah expounds of Greece, who darkened Israel's eyes — and afterward light, the Hasmonean kingdom, who came to reign through the miracle of the Chanukah lights. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 77b): The goats derive from the power of the attribute of judgment, which is the attribute of night; and night came before day because the attribute of judgment, by the very strength of that attribute, hastens to go forth into actuality. So too the goats walk at the head of the flock because of the swiftness of action they receive from the attribute of judgment — and this is what he answered him: as at the creation of the world. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 1): With respect to night, which is darkness, cessation and darkness come before day, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness...": for one who stands in darkness, darkness comes first and afterward light, and so there were two thousand years of chaos and afterward two thousand of Torah. But for one who stands in the day, day comes first and afterward night, to rest from his toil; and so once the Torah was given there was light for the world, and light comes before darkness. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 61): Esau was the firstborn in birth, which is the emergence into actuality, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness": on the side of the refuse the left is the right and comes first, and the this-world of Esau, in which darkness prevails, comes first. But in formation [yetzirah], which is the hidden world, the thought of creation and the conception of the world, the right comes first. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): The creation of the world was "first darkness and afterward light": first comes the portion of Bereishis, in the knowledge of the vessels, and afterward the attainment of the light of Abraham our father through knowledge, in the manner of "the advantage of light over darkness." Such too is the order of man's attainment of the light of the Blessed One, like the creation of the world: first the six days of work and afterward Shabbos; but for man's own action the light must come first and afterward the making of the vessel. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): This light [of the soul's root] can be attained in this world only through repentance, for such is the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light." Thus for certain righteous men, such as King David in the trial of Bathsheba, the Blessed One arranged a deed of the wicked in order to establish the yoke of repentance, for this cannot come about except through a preceding darkness. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): [In the Oral Torah and the innovation of laws not yet clarified] it is impossible to stand at all without a prior stumbling, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light," for so is the light attained by created beings: specifically out of darkness and concealment. Therefore Esau was formed before Jacob, being the preceding darkness that leads to the attainment of the light of Torah afterward. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 21): On "Why do the goats go first... as at the creation of the world, first darkness and afterward light," Rashi explains that goats are ordinarily black. So Teves, whose sign is the kid, is the aspect of darkness, and specifically then [the Hasmoneans] brought about their miracle through their self-sacrifice, to shine out of the darkness with greater excellence, as the Zohar says, "there is no light except that which comes out of darkness"; and this is like the creation of the world. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Sheidim 1): Since it is of the working of the Blessed One that it be so, "first darkness and afterward light," for the advantage of light is recognized only from darkness, [the forces of evil] therefore begin to act first, and from this the light shines forth, as in "He made darkness His hiding place," for there He is hidden. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): Such is the way of the Blessed One in the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light"; and so [the Sages] said that He would create worlds and destroy them, these being the worlds of chaos, until the world of rectification emerged. So it is in everything: all the incarnations of the Messiah that have already been in the world are akin to "creating worlds and destroying them," and specifically through those destructions the world of rectification is built, by raising up the lights of the broken vessels. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 174): Since in natural things the Blessed One established this order, "first darkness and afterward light," it is certainly the essence of His will, as [the Sages said], "In the place where penitents stand...". Although, Heaven forbid, one may not say "I will sin and repent" and do so by choice, it nonetheless happens of itself, for "there is no righteous man on earth..."; and such is the order: "the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light," far beyond one who did not walk in darkness. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): From the standpoint of this world's imagination it seemed at first that everything belonged to Esau, for such is the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light," as [the Sages] said at the beginning of Berakhos, which is why the evening Shema was placed first. For the Shema, the recognition of [God's] unity, was the essence of the creation of the world, and first one must recognize it out of darkness and concealment, for that was the whole matter of creation. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Shabbos): This is as it is written, "The Lord my God illuminates my darkness": after a person recognizes his sin and is pained over it, he merits that the Blessed One shines for him a rectification for it. Through the darkness, the remorse and pain he felt over the deed, he merits the light that reveals its rectification; and this is "first darkness and afterward light." Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 71): The Blessed One set the light in this world surrounded and encompassed by darkness, to leave man room to distinguish himself, that he remove the darkness and shine even within it. Therefore, when the Blessed One shines His bright light, He will shine it only for one who on his part walked in the light and did His will; He created the darkness only for the sake of one who desires the light, that for his sake He will illuminate the darkness too. Tiferes Yosef (Shavuos 7): It is written, "who forms light and creates darkness," yet at the creation of the world "there was evening and there was morning," first darkness and afterward light, so here too it should have said "creates darkness" first. The explanation: the first light was not yet within creation's capacity to receive, and light that creation cannot receive is called darkness from creation's standpoint; therefore it says "forms light and creates darkness," for from creation's standpoint it begins with day, since in the first evening creation had no grasp at all. Sod Yesharim (Shabbos HaGadol 6): As my father and teacher explained, the whole purpose of the darkness that the Blessed One set first is only that the light afterward be the more explicit; therefore "it was evening" is said first and then "it was morning." So too with Abraham our father: all the concealment he had at first, until he said, "Shall you say the palace has no master?", was the darkness that came first, only so that the Blessed One would afterward shine to him with greater clarity, "I am the master of the palace." כִּבְרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם: בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא,
It follows the pattern of the world's creation (Shabbat 77b): first darkness, and afterward light.

עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סו)807 Bereshit Rabbah 66:4 — R. Yitzchak bar R. Chiya said: The wicked, because they begin in tranquility and end in suffering, open with blessing and close with curse — "Blessed be those who bless you and cursed be those who curse you." The righteous, because they begin in suffering and end in tranquility, open with curse and close with blessing — "Cursed be those who curse you and blessed be those who bless you." Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 170): This is the meaning of "The righteous — their beginning is suffering and their end is tranquility": in every matter, every good trait and good undertaking, the first entry into it comes with pain, as "all beginnings are hard." For this world is mostly evil, so whatever a person is aroused to, he first sees the evil force within it and is pained, and through the pain he sweetens it, and at once its end is tranquility. Beis Yaakov (Miketz 18): Joseph understood that Pharaoh had first seen good and then bad, for Pharaoh was of the wicked, whose order is "their beginning is tranquility and their end is suffering": the wicked spread themselves out in this world like the primordial worlds that were destroyed, upon which the Blessed One bestowed such abundant kindness that they imagined they had power of their own and did not accept His kingship, and so they perished entirely. But with Israel the good shines forth little by little, for His conduct with them is like the creation of the world, "first darkness and then light," and thereby they have the power to gather the wayward and wild forces in man into holiness.: צַדִּיקִים תְּחִלָּתָן יִסּוּרִין וְסוֹפָן שַׁלְוָה.
This accords with what they taught (Bereishit Rabbah 66): the righteous begin with suffering, but their end is tranquility.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהַהַתְחָלָה מְחוּלָק לְשָׁלֹשׁ, וְהַסּוֹף בְּהוֹצָאַת הַדָּבָר לַפּוֹעַל מְחוּלָק לְשֶׁבַע,
It is known that the beginning is divided into three, while the end—the stage in which the matter is brought into actuality—is divided into seven.
כַּנּוֹדָע מִסֵּדֶר הָעֶשֶׂר סְפִירוֹת, שֶׁשָּׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת הֵם כֹּחוֹת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, וְשֶׁבַע תַּחְתּוֹנוֹת הֵם כֹּחוֹת הַהַמְשָׁכָה לַפּוֹעַל.
This is known from the order of the Ten Sefirot: the first three are the powers of thought, and the lower seven are the powers through which thought is extended into action.
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: בַּתְּחִלָּה עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה לִבְרוֹא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין, וְאַחַר כָּךְ שִׁיתֵּף מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים.
This follows the teaching that at first it arose in the Divine thought to create the world through the Attribute of Judgment, and afterward He joined to it the Attribute of Mercy.

וּמִזֶּה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ808 Menachot 29b — R. Yehuda said in the name of Rav: When Moshe ascended on high he found the Holy One, blessed be He, sitting and affixing crowns to the letters. He said before Him: Master of the Universe, who stays Your hand? He said to him: There is a man who is destined to arise at the end of many generations, Akiva ben Yosef by name, who will expound heaps upon heaps of laws from every point of every letter. He said before Him: Master of the Universe, show him to me. He said: Turn around. He went and sat at the end of the eighth row, and did not understand what they were saying, and his strength failed him. When they came to a certain matter, the students said to him: Rabbi, from where do you know this? He said to them: It is a law given to Moshe at Sinai — and Moshe’s mind was set at ease. Rashi: "Crowns" are like the tagin of a Torah scroll. "Who stays Your hand?" — what is there in what You have written that requires You still to add these crowns to the letters? And "his mind was set at ease" — Moshe's, since R. Akiva said the thing in his name, even though he had not yet received it. Maharsha: A knot is tied in order to remember something by it, as is said of tzitzit, "that you may remember"; so these knots upon the letters allude to inner, supernal matters, to be remembered through them. Moshe thought that human understanding could not reach their intent, and so he asked: who stays Your hand — for You Yourself need no knot in order to remember, and a man's intellect is too short to stand upon them. He was answered that it is precisely for the sake of human understanding that He ties them, for R. Akiva is destined to expound heaps upon heaps of laws from them. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Menachos 29b): The tagin upon the letters indicate apprehensions as fine as a hair that issue from the Torah itself, and therefore the tag, which is thin as a hair, stands for them. "Who stays Your hand?" means: these fine apprehensions are remote from man, who belongs to this perceptible world, in which there is no such fineness of intellect — whom, then, do they serve? Moshe sat at the end of the rows and did not know what they were saying because he had no joining or conjunction with R. Akiva, and no relation to the crowns upon the letters, though he had relation to the body of the Torah; and his mind was set at ease when he heard "a law given to Moshe at Sinai," for apprehensions of that kind come to a man only through prophecy, and he was the prophet through whom they were given. (מְנָחוֹת כט:) בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: כָּךְ עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה לְפָנַי,
This is also the meaning of what was said concerning Rabbi Akiva (Menachot 29b): 'Thus it arose in thought before Me.'
רָצָה לוֹמַר, כְּפִי הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין.
That is to say, this was in accordance with the level of thought, where creation was conceived through the Attribute of Judgment.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, לֹא חָשִׁיד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא דְּעָבֵיד דִּינָא בְּלָא דִּינָא, אַף בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין;
Nevertheless, the Holy One, blessed be He, is not suspected of administering judgment without justice, even when acting through the Attribute of Judgment.
וְהוּא טָעַן: זוֹ תּוֹרָה וְזוֹ שְׂכָרָהּ, שֶׁאֵין מַגִּיעַ לוֹ בְּדִין זֶה.
Moshe's protest—'This is Torah and this is its reward?'—was precisely that such a judgment did not appear to be deserved.
וְאָמְנָם בֶּאֱמֶת יָדוּעַ דְּכֹחוֹת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, שָׁם הַדִּין בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם,
Yet in truth it is known that within the powers of thought, judgment exists in the most concealed form.
וְאֵין גִּילּוּי דִּין כְּלָל אֶלָּא בַּיְצִיאָה לַפּוֹעַל, וְזֶה לִכְאוֹרָה הֵיפֶךְ הַנִּזְכָּר.
Judgment becomes manifest only when it emerges into actuality, which at first glance seems the reverse of what was just explained.
אֲבָל עִנְיַן חִילּוּק בֵּין מַחֲשָׁבָה לַסּוֹף הַיְנוּ לִהְיוֹת: "עָשָׂה הָאֱלֹהִים הָאָדָם יָשָׁר, וְהֵמָּה בִקְשׁוּ וְגוֹמֵר", בְּמַה שֶּׁמָּסַר הַבְּחִירָה.
The distinction between thought and the final outcome is rooted in the verse, 'God made man upright, but they sought, etc.,' for God entrusted man with free choice.
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצָה שֶׁיִּבְחוֹר רַק בַּטּוֹב, וְזֶהוּ תַכְלִית מְכֻוָּן שֶׁל מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה;
The Blessed One desired that man choose only the good, and this was the ultimate intention of His thought in creation.
אַךְ כֵּיוָן שֶׁמָּסַר הַבְּחִירָה לָאָדָם, הֲרֵי סִילֵּק רְצוֹן מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ בָּזֶה.
Yet once He gave free choice to man, He seemingly withdrew the compelling force of that original intention.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, עַל הָאֱמֶת גַּם אַחַר שֶׁמָּסַר הַבְּחִירָה, עֲדַיִן הַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ,
Nevertheless, in ultimate truth, even after free choice was entrusted to man, everything still comes from Him.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כִּי מִמְּךָ הַכֹּל וְגוֹמֵר809 I Chronicles 29:14 — “For who am I and who are my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly like this? For everything is from You, and from Your own hand have we given to You.” Rashi: "Who am I and who is my people, that we should have the strength to offer so willingly" — that we pressed ourselves to give so much in this offering; and yet it is not of our own, for "all is from You," and You apportioned us but a little. "And of Your own have we given You": what You gave us from Your hand, of that we have given You a part. Metzudas Dovid: "Who am I" — that is to say, is the strength of our hand so great that we should have the power to amass wealth and make so large an offering as this? "For all is from You": all this wealth came from You, and what came from Your hand we have turned about and given back to You. Malbim: He explains that it is impossible that we should by our own strength have grown so exceedingly rich as to be able to give such a gift; it is neither by my strength nor by my people's, but "all is from You" — all this wealth we received from You. And even now it is not ours, that we should say we gave it to You out of our own hand; rather "of Your own have we given You," for it is still in Your hand and in Your possession and is Yours, so that what we have given You is Your own, and what was already in Your hand." לְעִנְיַן הַטּוֹבָה, וְכֵן לְעִנְיַן הַהֵפֶךְ: "לָמָּה תַתְעֵנוּ וְגוֹמֵר".
Thus Scripture says, 'For everything is from You, etc.,' regarding good, and likewise regarding its opposite, 'Why do You cause us to stray, etc.'
וְזֶהוּ תַכְלִית הַבְּחִירָה: לְהַגִּיעַ עַל יָדָהּ לִידִיעָה בְרוּרָה שֶׁאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ גַּם מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא הָעוֹלָם.
This is the ultimate purpose of free choice: through it one must arrive at the clear knowledge that there is nothing besides Him, even within the created world.
וְזוֹ הִיא צוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁחֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד,
This is the form of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, which is engraved upon the Throne of Glory.
שֶׁצּוּרָתוֹ הִיא כּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל הַצּוּרוֹת וְהַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
His form encompasses all the forms and souls of Israel.
וְזֶהוּ קַו הָאֶמְצָעִי הַמְחַבֵּר שֶׁבַע תַּחְתּוֹנוֹת עִם שָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת, לִהְיוֹת כּוּלָּא חַד מַמָּשׁ.
This is the middle line that joins the seven lower Sefirot with the first three, so that all is literally one.
וְהִנֵּה כְּפִי הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַכֹּל עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַטּוֹב, הִנֵּה זֶה נִקְרָא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין,
According to the original thought that everything should proceed in the way of good, this itself is termed the Attribute of Judgment.
דְּתַכְלִית הַבְּרִיאָה לְהֵטִיב, וּכְשֶׁהַטּוֹב מַגִּיעַ בְּמִשְׁפָּט, וַדַּאי שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא "טוֹב מְאוֹד".
For the purpose of creation is to bestow good, and when that good is attained by right and judgment, it is certainly called 'very good.'

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט)810 Bereshit Rabbah 9:5-7 — In R. Meir's Torah scroll they found written: "And behold, it was very good [me'od]" — and behold, death [mot] is good. R. Shimon ben Elazar said: "And behold, it was very good" — and behold, sleep is good. Is sleep very good? Rather, because a man sleeps a little he rises and labors much in Torah. R. Nachman bar Shmuel bar Nachman said in the name of R. Shmuel bar Nachman: "Behold, it was very good" — this is the good inclination; "and behold, it was very good" — this is the evil inclination. Is the evil inclination very good? Rather, were it not for the evil inclination a man would never build a house, nor marry a wife, nor beget children, nor engage in trade., דְּזֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע וּמָוֶת וְשֵׁינָה,
This is what our Sages of blessed memory taught (Bereishit Rabbah 9), that 'very good' includes the evil inclination, death, and sleep.
שֶׁכָּל זֶה בִּיטּוּל לְהַטּוֹב, רַק דְּכָל זֶה נִמְשָׁךְ מִן הַ"טּוֹב מְאוֹד";
All of these appear to negate the good, yet they themselves flow from the level of 'very good.'
דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצָה לִהְיוֹת טוֹב מְאוֹד, וְזֶה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֹּחַ בְּחִירָה וְיֵצֶר הָרָע, וְהֵם יִבְחֲרוּ בַּטּוֹב.
That is, the Blessed One desired that the good be 'very good,' which is possible when there is free choice and an evil inclination, and human beings nevertheless choose the good.
וּמִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר כָּךְ מַה שֶּׁנִּמְשָׁךְ, וְלִהְיוֹת גַּם אַחַר כָּךְ כּוּלָּא חַד, מִמֵּילָא גַּם אַחַר כָּךְ זֶה נִקְרָא "טוֹב מְאוֹד".
From this came all that subsequently unfolded; and because even afterward everything is ultimately one, the later course of events too is included within 'very good.'
וְהַיְינוּ לֶעָתִיד, כְּשֶׁיְּבוּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח וְיִתְבַּעֵר יֵצֶר הָרָע, יְבוֹרַר אֵיךְ זֶה מִכְּלַל "טוֹב מְאוֹד", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה הִגִּיעַ הַטּוֹב בְּמִשְׁפָּט.

In the future, when death is swallowed up forever and the evil inclination is eradicated, it will become clear how all of this belonged to 'very good,' for through it the good was attained through judgment.
וְהִנֵּה וַדַּאי הָיָה בִּתְחִלַּת מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חִלּוּקֵי מַדְרֵיגוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת,
Certainly, from the beginning of the Divine thought there were to be differing levels between Israel and the nations.
דְּאִם לֹא כֵן, מֵאַיִן נִתְהַוָּה זֶה אַחַר כָּךְ? וְכָךְ בְּרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם: חֲשׁוֹכָא וּנְהוֹרָא.
For if not, from where could this distinction later have arisen? This too is the pattern of creation: darkness and light.
אַךְ כֵּיוָן שֶׁהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה הָיָה הַכֹּל טוֹב, וַדַּאי גַּם הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת לֹא הָיָה הַמְכֻוָּן שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהֵם.
Yet since the original Divine thought was entirely good, the intention for the nations was certainly not that they remain as they later became.
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּמִּיתִי לַעֲשׂוֹת לָהֶם, אֶעֱשֶׂה לָכֶם", וְלֹא אָמַר "כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי";
Regarding this it is said, 'And it shall be, as I intended to do to them, so I shall do to you'—it does not say, 'as I did.'
שֶׁכְּבָר עָשָׂה רַע לְעַמְמִין בְּפוֹעַל, שֶׁלֹּא לְהַחֲיוֹת כָּל נְשָׁמָה, אוֹ עוֹנְשֵׁי שְׁאָר אוּמּוֹת; חָלִילָה לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל,
For He had already brought actual destruction upon nations, such as the command not to leave alive any soul, and the punishments of other peoples; Heaven forbid that such a thing be done to Israel.
כִּי אֲבַדּוֹן הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת הוּא אֲבַדָּן נִצְחִי.
For the destruction of the nations, in that sense, is a lasting destruction.
וְרַק "כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּמִּיתִי" — וְרָצָה לוֹמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁעָלוּ בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה,
Rather, the verse says only 'as I intended'—meaning, as they existed in the original Divine thought.
דְּמִצַּד מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּבוּקִים בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמָּשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ לֶעָתִיד,
For according to His thought, Israel were to be actually bound to Him, as they will be in the future.
הָיָה שֶׁהָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת יִהְיוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהֵם יִשְׂרָאֵל עַכְשָׁיו: שֶׁלֹּא יוּכְלוּ לְקַבֵּל רוֹב טוֹבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְסוֹף סוֹף גַּם הֵם יִזֻכְּכוּ.
The nations, in that design, would have been on the level Israel occupies now: unable to receive an abundance of good in this world, yet ultimately destined for refinement.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא הֵם נִכְרְתוּ לְגַמְרֵי, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁבוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה עַל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
Through sin, however, the nations became entirely cut off, while Israel came to occupy the position that the original thought had assigned to the nations.
שֶׁאֵין הַכֹּחוֹת וְהָרְצוֹנוֹת וְהַפְּעוּלוֹת נִמְשָׁכִים כָּל כָּךְ אַחַר רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אַךְ עִם כָּל זֶה שׁוֹרְשָׁם דָּבוּק בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים.
Their powers, desires, and actions do not always follow the Blessed One's will completely, yet their root remains attached to the living God.
וְנִמְצָא, מַה שֶּׁאֵין יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכוֹלִים לְקַבֵּל רוֹב טוֹבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא רַק מִצַּד שֶׁהֵרֵעוּ אֶת מַעֲשָׂם וְקִיפְּחוּ אֶת פַּרְנָסָתָם, רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן.
It follows that Israel's inability to receive an abundance of good in this world results only from having impaired their deeds and thereby diminished their sustenance—may the Merciful One save us.
אֲבָל בְּעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ: שׁוֹרְשָׁם, אִם הָיוּ כִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן;
With the nations, however, the matter is the reverse: at their root, had they remained according to the Divine will, this limited worldly condition would have been appropriate to them.
וּמִצַּד שֶׁהֵרֵעוּ מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם יֵשׁ לָהֶם מִשַּׁלְוַת הָרְשָׁעִים לְקַפְּחָם מֵעוֹלָם הַבָּא.
Because they corrupted their deeds, they are granted the tranquility of the wicked in this world in a manner that deprives them of the World to Come.
וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן גֵּרִים, עַל זֶה אָמַר: "כָּךְ עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה",
Regarding Rabbi Akiva, who descended from converts, this is the meaning of the response, 'Thus it arose in thought.'
שֶׁעוֹנְשָׁיו אֵינוֹ מִצַּד בְּחִירָה דְּרַע בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק מִצַּד שׁוֹרְשׁוֹ בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה.
His suffering was not rooted in an evil choice in this world, but in the dimension of his root within the primordial thought.
וְזֶהוּ "שְׁתוֹק", דְּבַמַּחֲשָׁבָה אֵין שָׁם דִּבּוּר, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג דָּבָר אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן מַגִּיעַ לְאוֹתָהּ מַדְרֵיגָה שֶׁהוּא הִסְתַּלְּקוּת הַדִּבּוּר.
This is the meaning of 'Be silent': at the level of thought there is no speech, and it cannot be grasped unless one reaches that level where speech falls away.
וּבֵיאוּר זֶה, כִּי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא הוּא יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, כַּיָּדוּעַ, שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת לַיְלָה;
The explanation is that Rabbi Akiva is the foundation of the Oral Torah, as is known, and the Oral Torah corresponds to the quality of night.

דְּהַיְינוּ הַשָּׂגַת יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת דְּחוֹמֶר וּלְבֵינִים, לִבּוּן הִלְכְתָא הָאָמוּר בַּזּוֹהַר (חֵלֶק א כז עַמּוּד א)811 Zohar 1:27a — "And they embittered their lives with hard labor" — that is a difficulty [raised in study]; "with mortar [chomer]" — that is an inference from minor to major [kal vachomer]; "and with bricks [levenim]" — that is the clarifying [libbun] of a law; "and with every labor in the field" — that is a baraita; "all their labor" and so forth — that is the Mishnah.,
That is, it is Israel's mode of attainment in this world through exertion—the 'mortar and bricks' of clarifying halakhah, as stated in the Zohar (I, 27a).
כִּי אוֹר יוֹם, שֶׁכֵּן יִהְיֶה אוֹר הַלְּבָנָה דְּלֶעָתִיד, הַכֹּל אוֹר עַצְמִי, הוּא אוֹרוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמֵּאִיר לְכָל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם.
The light of day—like the light of the moon in the future—is intrinsic light: the Blessed One's own light illuminating all who enter the world.
וְזֶהוּ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, וְהִיא כְּתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא לְכָל מִי שֶׁיִּרְצֶה,
This corresponds to the Written Torah, which is written and laid openly before anyone who wishes to approach it.

עַד שֶׁאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אוֹמְרִים: אָנוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא תִּשָּׂא לד)812 Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 34 — R. Yehudah bar Shalom said: When the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, "Write these words," Moses asked that the Mishnah too be put in writing. But the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that the nations of the world were destined to translate the Torah and read it in Greek, and to say, "We are Israel." Until now the scales are balanced. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the nations: You say that you are My children — I do not know; only those who hold My mysteries are My children. And which are they? This is the Mishnah, which was given orally, and from which everything is to be expounded. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): After prophecy departed, the sages of the Oral Torah began, and the Sages said, "He has set me in dark places — this is the Talmud of Babylonia"; but this is the mysteries of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it says in Tanchuma, "Those who hold My mysteries are Israel." For it is written, "He made darkness His hiding place" — there are His hidden things; and though it is darkness and the hiding of the Face, the darkness is cast by the shadow of His hand, shielding us by way of concealment, as one must make shade to protect against the blazing sun. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:86): The Blessed One teaches human beings to exert effort, which is why the Torah began for Israel as the Written Torah; He wishes a person to arrive at His mysteries — as in the Midrash, "He who holds My mysteries…" — and to understand what He indicates to him with the compass. This is the essential effort: to come to the Oral Torah, which is the recognition that everything is from the Blessed One, the "finding" that comes after toil. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 12): The novel insights of Torah belong to the Oral Torah, whereas in the Written Torah, which is written and set down [before all], there are no novel insights; therefore the nations claim on the strength of the Written Torah, "We are Israel," and the Holy One, blessed be He, answers, "He who holds My mysteries…," for the Oral Torah exists only in the hearts of the children of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 4): Edom claims that they are the good and the pure by birth; therefore Haman's decree was a preparation for the Oral Torah, as the Midrash says: because the nations are destined to say "We are Israel," the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "He who holds My mysteries…" — for it is the Oral Torah that clarifies this. The Oral Torah is what springs from the heart of Israel, the hearts of the children of Israel being its originators, so that it is theirs alone, and this is the testimony that they, and no others, are the masters of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Just as there is wisdom among the nations but no Torah among the nations, so it says in Tanchuma, "He who holds My mysteries…": the Oral Torah was given over only to Israel. The nations, even if they study Torah and innovate in it by their wisdom, speak vanity and not Torah at all, for they innovate from their own wisdom, whereas the Torah is the wisdom of the Blessed One; but the sages of Israel bless over the Torah first and know that the Blessed One is the Giver of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 3): The essence of the Torah is the Oral Torah, which reveals the hidden things of the Written Torah, as it says in Shemos Rabbah that the nations are destined to translate the Torah into Greek… "He who holds My mysteries…." This is an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob alone: the Torah is handed over to them according to what they clarify through their dialectic and their wisdom. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): They said in Tanchuma that the Oral Torah was given because the nations are destined to translate the Torah into Greek and say "We are Israel," and the Holy One, blessed be He, will say, "He who holds My mysteries…." That is, the nations too have a connection to the Written Torah, which is why it was revealed in writing to all who come into the world; but the Oral Torah is the mysteries of the Holy One, blessed be He, which cannot be revealed in writing at all, only "the secret of the Lord is with those who fear Him" — the Congregation of Israel, who look to the Blessed One from the depths of their hearts. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 6): All the innovation of the Oral Torah comes through the unions and complete cleaving to the Holy One, blessed be He, and this is His mysteries, as they said in Tanchuma at the end of Ki Sisa: because the nations of the world are destined to translate the Torah and say "We are Israel," the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "He who holds My mysteries…." This is the telling of secrets, which is for Jacob alone — and "telling" does not mean in writing — so "He tells [His words to Jacob]" means the Oral Torah, the handing over of the words of Torah of which it is said "He has not done so for any nation"; whereas the Written Torah alone was written on the stones in seventy languages., דְּמִי שֶׁיְּגַלֶּה מִסְטוֹרִין וְכוּלֵי.
Indeed, the nations can claim, 'We are Israel,' as our Sages of blessed memory taught (Midrash Tanchuma, Tisa 34), regarding one who reveals the hidden mysteries, etc.
תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא הַמְבָרֵר הַחִילּוּק, רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁאַף בְּהֶעְלֵם: "וְכִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחוֹשֶׁךְ, הַשֵּׁם אוֹר לִי",
The Oral Torah is what clarifies the distinction: even within concealment, 'Though I sit in darkness, the Lord is a light for me.'
בְּאוֹר הַלְּבָנָה הַמְקַבֵּל מֵאוֹר הַחַמָּה, וְיִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹנִין לָהּ, כִּי "לֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי".
It is the moonlight that receives from the sun, and Israel reckons its calendar by the moon, for 'He has not done so for any nation.'
וְהוּא מִצַּד הַדִּבּוּר, שֶׁהוּא הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה לַפּוֹעַל;
This belongs to the level of speech, which is the revelation of thought as it emerges into actuality.
וּמִצַּד הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, הֲרֵי הָיָה אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם רְאוּיִם לִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹ עַכְשָׁיו יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק שֶׁבַּהִתְגַּלּוּת נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁאֵין כֵּן.
From the perspective of the original thought, the nations could have occupied the level Israel occupies now; only in the stage of revelation was it clarified that this is not so.
וְהַבִּירוּר עַל יְדֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא בְּיִחוּד, שֶׁהָיָה רֹאשׁ חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּדוֹרוֹ,
This clarification came particularly through Rabbi Akiva, who was the foremost Sage of Israel in his generation.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יְבָמוֹת טז.)813 Yevamot 16a — He took hold of him and seated him upon a couch of gold. [R. Dosa] said to him: Rabbi, tell your other disciple to sit as well. He said to him: And who is he? Akiva ben Yosef. He said to him: Are you Akiva ben Yosef, whose name goes from one end of the world to the other? Sit, my son, sit; may such as you multiply in Israel. Maharsha: R. Dosa seated R. Yehoshua and R. Elazar ben Azaria with honor on a couch of gold because the one was Av Beit Din and the other Nasi, but not R. Akiva: although he spoke in his praise, R. Akiva was regarded in his eyes as a disciple, being also the disciple of R. Yehoshua; and he asked “who is he?” of R. Elazar ben Azaria and R. Akiva because he had not known them, whereas R. Yehoshua he knew already from the time of the Temple. And to R. Akiva, who descended from righteous converts of the line of Sisera, he said, “May such as you multiply in Israel” — and not from the converts: that the children of Israel should merit this, and not converts who come from the gentiles. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on the Book of Joshua 7): R. Akiva was the essence and foundation of the study of the Oral Torah — the anonymous teachings of the Sifra and Sifrei all follow R. Akiva, and the world was desolate until R. Akiva came — and therefore his name went "from one end of the world to the other." שֶׁשְּׁמוֹ הוֹלֵךְ מִסּוֹף הָעוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ; וַדַּאי הִילּוּךְ הַשֵּׁם הַיְינוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כֹּחוֹתָיו, הָיָה בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ,
As they said (Yevamot 16a), his name went from one end of the world to the other. The spread of his name signifies the extension of his spiritual powers throughout the world.
כִּי הוּא כּוֹלֵל הַדּוֹר, שֶׁכֵּן אוֹתִיּוֹת שְׁמוֹ יַעֲקֹב-א, כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ נֶפֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִיא כּוֹלֶלֶת נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל דּוֹר וָדוֹר מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל.
For he encompassed his generation; the letters of his name allude to Yaakov plus alef, since the root-soul of Jacob our father, peace be upon him, encompasses the souls of every generation of Israel.
וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא בֶּן גֵּרִים, וַדַּאי הָיָה בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן אֵיזֶה שׁוֹרֶשׁ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו,
In truth, the root of his soul was a soul of Israel; nevertheless, because he descended from converts, some root from his ancestors was certainly present within him as well.
וְהוּא אֵיזֶה שׁוֹרֶשׁ טוֹב שֶׁהָיָה גָּנוּז בָּהֶם מִצַּד שֶׁעָלוּ בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה.
That was the hidden root of good within them, deriving from the way they had existed in the original Divine thought.
וְכָל מַעֲלַת רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא הֵם מִצַּד הַדִּבּוּר בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהוּא הַיְּסוֹד,
All of Rabbi Akiva's distinctive greatness belongs to the level of speech in the Oral Torah, of which he is the foundation.
וּבוֹ נִתְבָּרֵר תַּכְלִית הַבִּירוּר בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים, שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם חֵלֶק מֵהֶם כְּלָל.
Through him the ultimate distinction between Israel and the nations was clarified: in this revealed level he contains no portion of them at all.
רַק מִצַּד הַהִתְעַלּוּת מֵעוֹלַם הַדִּבּוּר לַמַּחֲשָׁבָה, דְּשָׁם יֵשׁ אֵיזֶה דָּבָר טוֹב הַנִּמְצָא בָהֶם שֶׁקְּלָטָהּ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא.
Only when rising from the world of speech to the level of thought is there a certain good found among them, which Rabbi Akiva absorbed.
מִצַּד אוֹתוֹ קְלִיטַת טוֹב דְּמַחֲשָׁבָה מֵאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הִגִּיעַ לוֹ הָעוֹנֶשׁ.
It was from that absorption of the good rooted in the primordial thought concerning the nations that his suffering came.
אַף דְּזוֹ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּדִבּוּר, שֶׁהָיָה הוֹגֶה יוֹם וָלַיְלָה, וּמִצַּד הַדִּבּוּר לֹא שַׁיֵּיךְ לָזֶה,
Although his Oral Torah was expressed through speech, which he studied day and night, and from the standpoint of speech there was no connection to this ancestral root,
וּבַמַּחֲשָׁבָה זָכָה לְ"טוֹב מְאוֹד", וְהוּא הַנְּהוֹרָא דְּעִמֵּיהּ שַׁרְיָא;
at the level of thought he attained the 'very good'—the hidden light that rested with him.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, "יָשֶׁת חֹשֶׁךְ סִתְרוֹ": דְּכַלְפֵּי דִידֵיהּ הוּא נְהוֹרָא וְ"טוֹב מְאוֹד", אֲבָל כְּלַפֵּי דִידַן הוּא בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא.
Nevertheless, 'He makes darkness His concealment': from His perspective it is light and 'very good,' while from our perspective it first appears as darkness.
רַק עַל יְדֵי הַהֶעְלֵם בָּאִים לַגִּילּוּי, וְ"וְכִי אֵשֵׁב בַּחוֹשֶׁךְ" דַּיְיקָא, אָז "הַשֵּׁם אוֹר לִי".
Only by passing through concealment does one come to revelation; specifically when 'I sit in darkness,' then 'the Lord is a light for me.'

עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (גִּיטִּין מג.)814 Gittin 43a — Rabba bar Rav Huna then set an interpreter before him and expounded: "And let this stumbling block be under your hand" — a man does not stand upon words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them. Although they said that one who betroths half a woman, she is not betrothed, still a woman who is half maidservant and half free who was betrothed, her betrothal is a valid betrothal. Rashi (s.v. "and let this stumbling block be under your hand"): He set up an interpreter before him in order to expound a second time, and he opened from the verse, which was said of the men of Jerusalem when Torah had ceased among them, so that they would say to one another, "You have a cloak, be our chief" — that is, matters covered over like your cloak, in which you are expert, tell them to us and be our chief. "And let this stumbling block be under your hand" means words of Torah, upon whose truth a man does not stand until he has stumbled in them by ruling in error and is put to shame, and then he sets his heart to it and understands. So I too stumbled in my ruling, and therefore I retract. Maharsha: When he first taught this ruling it is not said that he set an interpreter before him. Perhaps an interpreter was set up only for the exposition of a verse that was published to the many, as here with "and let this stumbling block be under your hand," whereas earlier he had published to the many only the ruling itself.: אֵין אָדָם עוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְשַׁל,
This is as they said (Gittin 43a): a person does not fully comprehend words of Torah unless he has first stumbled in them.
עַד שֶׁדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה נִקְרָא "הַמִּכְשֵׁלָה הַזֹּאת", וְזֶה פֶּלֶא, כְּאִלּוּ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה מַכְשִׁילִין, חַס וְשָׁלוֹם.
Indeed, words of Torah are even called 'this stumbling block.' This is astonishing, as though Torah itself causes a person to stumble—Heaven forbid.
רַק הוֹאִיל וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲמוֹד בָּעִנְיָן אַחֵר, הֲרֵי הַמִּכְשׁוֹל הֲכָנָה אֶל הָעֲמִידָה עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה.
Rather, because there is no other way to arrive at full understanding, the stumbling itself becomes a preparation for grasping the words of Torah.
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה "בְּרֹאשׁ הוֹמִיּוֹת תִּקְרָא" לִרְדּוֹף אַחֲרֶיהָ, וְכֹחָהּ יָפֶה לְהַזְמִין כָּל מִינֵי סִיַּיעְתּוֹת לָאָדָם לַעֲמוֹד עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה,
Since the Torah 'calls at the head of the noisy streets,' summoning a person to pursue it, it has the power to arrange every form of assistance that will enable him to attain its words.
גַּם זֶה מִכְּלַל הַסִּיַּיעְתּוֹת: לְהַזְמִין לְפָנָיו בַּהַתְחָלָה מִכְשָׁלוֹת, כְּדֵי לַעֲמוֹד עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה.
Even this is included among those forms of assistance: that stumbling blocks are placed before him at the beginning so that he can ultimately stand firmly in the words of Torah.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהוּא בְּרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, כָּךְ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבָּהּ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וְהוּא הַדְּפוּס שֶׁל מַעֲשֵׂה בְּרֵאשִׁית,
Just as this is the pattern of the world's creation, so it is with the Torah through which the world was created, for Torah is the blueprint of the work of Creation.
מִסְּתָמָא גַּם הִיא כְּעִנְיַן בְּרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם מַמָּשׁ.
It follows that Torah itself must reflect precisely the same pattern as the creation of the world.

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת פט:)815 Shabbat 89b — "If your sins be like scarlet [ka-shanim]" — it should have said ka-shani, in the singular. R. Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel — even if your sins are as many as those years that have come in order from the six days of Creation until now, "they shall become white as snow." Rashi: "It should have said ka-shani" [in the singular] — parallel to "as snow," for it does not say "as snows." Maharsha: "Like these years that are ordered" refers to the multitude of sin — as many as the years, presumably the years that have run in order since the six days of creation. One cannot read ka-shanim as "like two years," the minimal plural, for what novelty would there be in two sins? We say in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah that He removes the first [sin] first, so for two sins "they shall be white as snow" would not be needed.
