Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 89b): Sin is open to atonement because it is committed by accident, and the accidental does not annul what a person is in essence; but sins committed in great number and constantly are no longer accidental, and so the Holy One, blessed be He, says that even if your sins are ordered and fixed like these years, they shall be white as snow. Nothing is more fixed and ordered than the years, which have run so since the six days of creation, yet even they will cease, since the world is physical and will end in destruction; so too Israel's sins, though fixed on the side of the physical, can be removed, because Israel's essential level is not physical. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 19): The holiness of Tisha B'Av in the future, when it becomes a festival, will not come from Israel's sanctifying it, for on the contrary they sinned and made it a day of calamity, but only because in the future "your sins will be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation," as stated in Shabbos 89b: then "they shall be white as snow" and be turned into merits, through this, that such was the will of the Blessed One from the six days of creation. Thus the essence of its holiness is only that this was the Blessed One's will at the beginning of creation, a holiness fixed and abiding like the holiness of Shabbos, except that it is revealed only in the future, after the rectification. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): "The scarlet [shanim] shall be white as snow" means that the scarlet of holiness, too, will be whitened, after they lift their eyes to the Blessed One, as stated in Shabbos there; and the sins will be "like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation," that is, like merits; and afterwards they will rise still further, to the supernal whiteness, which is Wisdom, above Understanding. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 17): The deed itself is ordered and set so, as "Bathsheba was destined for David from the six days of creation," and in truth this will be clarified in the future regarding all the sins of Israel, when they are refined and whitened, as the Sages said, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation, they shall be white as snow." That is, since the true will of the Blessed One was so, it is like a transgression for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): In the future this will be clarified regarding all the sins of Israel, as the Sages said in Shabbos 89b on the verse "If your sins be": "like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation" — it will be clarified that it was ordered from the true will of the Blessed One that it be so, and if so, in this too they did the will of the Blessed One, and it was all like a transgression for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Naso 2): Such was the intent in the creation of the world, "first darkness and then light," as the Zohar says, there is no light but that which comes out of darkness; and then "the Lord will not count iniquity to him," since it will be clarified that this was created only so that it be "very good." As they said, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation, they shall be white as snow," that is, they will be as merits. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 3): From the side of the hidden things that will be revealed in the future there was no sin at all, and of this they said, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation," that is, from the side of the "hidden things of the Merciful One," then "they shall be white as snow" entirely, for there is no sin at all. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Mishlei 31): Snow alludes to fear, and so the Gemara says, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation until now, they shall be white as snow": "years" alludes to cycles and order, that is, if there is an accusation, Heaven forbid, and it seems that a person sinned deliberately and in [recurring] cycles, the Blessed One will illuminate that this deed came only out of fear of the Blessed One, and this is "white as snow.": "חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית",
This is what they said (Shabbat 89b): 'Your sins are like these years, ordered and coming from the six days of Creation.'
הַיְנוּ שֶׁכָּךְ הוּא סֵדֶר יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית.
That is, this itself belongs to the ordered pattern of the days of Creation.
וְנִמְצָא, כָּל הָעֲוֹנוֹת וְעוֹנְשֵׁיהֶם, הַכֹּל "כָּךְ עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה" בַּהֲכָנַת הַיְצִיאָה לַפּוֹעַל,
It follows that all sins and their punishments were included in the sense of 'thus it arose in thought,' as part of the preparation for the eventual emergence into actuality.
שֶׁמִּתְבָּרֵר אַחַר שֶׁיּוֹצֵא לַפּוֹעַל: כְּשֶׁעוֹמֵד עַל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה אַחַר שֶׁנִּכְשַׁל, אָז מֵבִין אֵיךְ הַמִּכְשׁוֹל הָיָה בּוֹ צוֹרֶךְ וְסִיבָּה לָזֶה.

Only afterward, once the process has unfolded and he attains the Torah after first stumbling, does he understand how the stumbling itself was necessary and served as the cause that enabled this attainment.
וְזֶהוּ הַנֶּחָמָה לַפּוּרְעָנֻיּוֹת, שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ לְשׁוֹן נֶחָמָה, כְּמוֹ "וַיִּנָּחֶם" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן חֲרָטָה;
This is the consolation for the calamities. The root of the word nechamah, as in 'and He reconsidered, etc.,' can denote regret or a changed perspective.
וְכָךְ הַמִּתְנַחֵם מִפּוּרְעָנֻיּוֹת הוּא שֶׁמִּתְחָרֵט עַל צַעֲרוֹ אָז.
So too, one who is consoled after affliction comes to reconsider the anguish he experienced at the time.
וְזֶה כְּשֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה כְּלָל פּוּרְעָנֻיּוֹת מֵעוֹלָם, וּבְחִנָּם נִצְטַעֵר.
This occurs when it is later revealed to him that, in its ultimate purpose, it had never truly been a calamity at all, and his anguish had arisen from not yet seeing its end.
כִּי הַבִּירוּר שֶׁהוּא הָיָה הֲכָנָה לַטּוֹב, הֲרֵי כָּל דָּבָר נִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם תַּכְלִיתוֹ, נִמְצָא גַּם זֶה הָיָה טוֹב.
For once it becomes clear that the event was a preparation for good—and everything is defined by its ultimate purpose—it follows that this too was good.
וְזֶהוּ סְמִיכוּת שֶׁבַע דְּנֶחֶמְתָּא לְשַׁבַּת תְּשׁוּבָה, כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ הִתְהַפְּכוּת זֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה,
This explains why the Seven Haftarot of Consolation are followed closely by Shabbat Teshuvah, for the root of this transformation is teshuvah.
שֶׁהִיא גַּם כֵּן חֲרָטָה עַל הָרַע שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם.
Teshuvah too is a reconsideration and regret concerning the evil that came from man's side.
וְזֶהוּ בְּרֵאשִׁית שָׁנָה, שֶׁהוּא תְּחִלַּת הַזְּמַן: הַהַתְחָלָה הוּא אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא, וְסוֹפוֹ הוּא אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא — "וְאָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם".

At the beginning of the year, which is the beginning of the cycle of time, the beginning comes through an awakening from below, while its culmination is an awakening from Above—'and I will return to you.'
זֶהוּ הַנֶּחָמָתוֹת: לְהִתְחָרֵט אַפּוּרְעָנֻיּוֹת דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנִּצְטַעֲרוּ, שֶׁזֶּה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
This is the meaning of the consolations: to come to a changed understanding of the afflictions sent by the Blessed One over which they had grieved, recognizing that these too came from Him.
וְכֵן הַנֶּחָמָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "נַחֲמוּ" וְגוֹמֵר, "יֹאמַר" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהוּא הַמּוֹלִיד זֶה בַּלֵּב.
Likewise, the consolation comes from the Blessed One Himself—'Comfort, etc.,' 'shall say, etc.'—for He is the One Who brings this new realization into the heart.
וְהַדְּבָרִים עֲמוּקִים; לֹא אוּכַל לְהַאֲרִיךְ כָּעֵת יוֹתֵר.
These matters are profound, and I cannot elaborate further at present.

sections.en: The Shofar: Voice, Prayer, and Expansive Understanding

items.h: The shofar expands a narrow inner voice into broad revelation; its cries, numbers, and forms connect Torah, prayer, and the transformation of constriction into understanding.

Seif 1 — The Shofar as an Expanding Voice
The shofar broadens a narrow inner sound, joining Torah's plain voice with prayer's cry between them.

p: עִנְיַן הַשּׁוֹפָר בַּטֶּבַע הוּא מַרְחִיב הַקּוֹל וּמַגְבִּיהוֹ, שֶׁהַמַּשְׁמִיעַ לְתוֹכוֹ קוֹל נָמוּךְ בְּצִדּוֹ הַקָּצָר.
The nature of the shofar is to broaden and amplify a sound: one sounds a low voice into its narrow end.
עַל יְדֵי הַרְעָדַת חֶלְקֵי הָאֲוִיר בַּחֲלַל הַשּׁוֹפָר, הוּא נִשְׁמָע קוֹל גָּבוֹהַּ לַחוּץ דֶּרֶךְ צִדּוֹ הָרָחָב, כַּנּוֹדָע לַטִּבְעִיִּים.
By vibrating the particles of air in the hollow of the shofar, the sound emerges outward as a louder voice through its broad end, as is known to students of nature.
וְהוּא כְּלִי אֶמְצָעִי בֵּין הַמַּשְׁמִיעַ לַשּׁוֹמֵעַ, שֶׁיּוּכַל הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ לְקַבֵּל בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת רְחָבָה מַה שֶּׁהַמַּשְׁמִיעַ מַשְׁמִיעַ מִן הַמֵּצַר.
It is therefore an intermediary instrument between the one who sounds and the one who hears, enabling the listener to receive in broad expansion what the sounder produces from a constricted place.
וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתוּב: "כַּשּׁוֹפָר הָרֵם קוֹלֶךָ", שֶׁהַנָּבִיא אֶמְצָעִי בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לַאֲבִיהֶם שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם בְּהַשְׁמָעַת הַקּוֹל,
This is the meaning of the verse, “Raise your voice like a shofar”: the prophet stands as an intermediary in transmitting the voice between Israel and their Father in Heaven,
דֻּגְמַת הַשּׁוֹפָר, שֶׁהוּא מְקַבְּלוֹ בִּלְחִישָׁה מִלְמַעְלָה.
like the shofar, receiving the message above in a whisper and giving it expanded expression.
"וַהַשֵּׁם יִתֵּן אֹמֶר, הַמְבַשְּׂרוֹת צָבָא רָב" — שֶׁדִּבּוּר אֶחָד שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא מִתְפַּשֵּׁט בְּפִי הַנָּבִיא לְפָרָשָׁה שְׁלֵמָה.
Thus, “The Lord gives the word; the women who proclaim it are a great host”: a single Divine utterance expands in the mouth of the prophet into an entire passage.
וְזֶהוּ שׁוֹפָרוֹת דְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִשְׁמִיעָנוּ אֶת קוֹלוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם, "וְהָיָה קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר הוֹלֵךְ וְחָזֵק מְאֹד" — הַיְנוּ כֹּחַ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתוֹ.
This is the shofar of the Giving of the Torah: the Blessed One caused us to hear His voice from heaven, and “the sound of the shofar grew continually stronger”—meaning the power of its expansion.

כִּי מִקְרָא אֶחָד יוֹצֵא לְכַמָּה טְעָמִים (סַנְהֶדְרִין לד.)816 Sanhedrin 34a — Abaye said: The verse states, "God has spoken once, twice have I heard this" (Psalms 62:12) — one verse yields several meanings, but one meaning does not issue from several verses. The school of R. Yishmael taught: "And like a hammer that shatters the rock" (Jeremiah 23:29) — just as this hammer breaks into many sparks, so one verse yields several meanings. Rashi: "God has spoken once, twice have I heard this" — but God did not speak twice for a single thing to be heard. Tosafos (s.v. "just as the hammer"): Rabbeinu Shmuel reads "just as the hammer splits [the rock]", since it is not the hammer that is split but the rock; yet then the Gemara should have said "just as the rock is split", here and in Shabbos (88b). Rabbeinu Tam explains that the verse means the hammer is split against the rock, as in the Midrash of one who tested a sapphire by laying it on an anvil and striking it with a hammer: the anvil cracked and the hammer split, while the sapphire stayed whole. Maharsha: "One verse yields several meanings" — the verse gives the reason, "for strength belongs to God": it is the strength and power of God's wisdom that two things are heard from His single utterance, which is not so of human speech. From this too it infers that one meaning does not issue from several verses, for redundant speech is not divine wisdom — even in a man, superfluous and repetitive speech is not wisdom. Maharal (Be'er HaGolah, Be'er 3): The plain meaning is the root of the verse, and from it many things branch out on every side, like a tree whose single root puts forth branches, fruit and leaves; that is why one verse divides into several meanings, and it is no difficulty that a single verse is expounded in several ways. Even a natural thing spreads from one root into many, all the more so the words of the living God: His speech, the Torah, is not arbitrary will but follows wisdom, and from what wisdom necessitates further wisdom follows, so that one verse divides and spreads into many meanings, some far from its plain sense and some near it, yet all drawn from the one root.,
For a single verse can yield many meanings (Sanhedrin 34a),

וְלֵיכָּא מִידִי בִּנְבִיאִים וּבְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, וְכֵן בְּכָל חַכְמֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, דְּלָא רְמִיזִי בְּאוֹרַיְתָא (תַּעֲנִית ט.)817 Taanit 9a — Again R. Yochanan met the young son of Reish Lakish, who was sitting and saying: “The folly of a man perverts his way, and his heart frets against the Lord.” R. Yochanan sat and wondered, saying: Is there anything written in the Writings that is not hinted at in the Torah? He said to him: And is this itself not hinted at? Is it not written, “And their heart failed them, and they turned trembling one to another, saying: What is this that God has done to us?” Rashi: "The folly of a man perverts his way, and his heart frets against the Lord": when a person sins he perverts his way, so that misfortunes come upon him; and his heart frets against the Lord — he is angry and says, "Why has this misfortune befallen me?" "That is not hinted at": [that] Moses did not hint at in the Torah — for the Pentateuch is the foundation of the Prophets and the Writings, and for all of them support is to be found in the Torah. Maharsha: R. Yochanan surely knew this verse of Proverbs before he heard it from the child, but in its context he took it to mean that through folly a person corrupts his ways and deeds and also harbors thoughts against the Lord in matters of faith — which is certainly hinted at in the Torah, for "a person commits no transgression unless a spirit of folly has entered him" — and to read "his way" as a person's misfortunes seemed to him forced; only when the child recited it as "his verse" did he understand that it speaks of a person's misfortunes and of grumbling against the Lord and His attribute of justice, and at that he wondered. As for "What is this that God has done to us?": although the brothers confessed, "We are verily guilty concerning our brother," seeing that they were being repaid measure for measure for the sale of Joseph, these words sound as though they complained against His ways, as if it had come upon them crookedly — and in this they prophesied without knowing what they prophesied: that God had done all this to bring about their descent to Egypt, as it is said, "and he sent him from the valley of Hebron." Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): In the Written Torah, which is the "fallen fruit" of [supernal] wisdom, everything is also contained, for "there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Torah" (Taanit 9a); but once it has become fallen fruit, like a leaf or fruit fallen from the tree, the power of the tree is not revealed in it and it is utterly concealed, revealed only in the hearts of the Sages of Israel, who can draw down understanding from its first revelation. Thus the entire Oral Torah is alluded to in the Written Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 4): The entire Oral Torah is taken from the Written Torah, as is said (Taanit 9a) even of what is written in the Writings, that "there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Torah"; and on this they said (Eruvin 21b), on "His locks are curled," that on every tittle one may expound heaps upon heaps of laws.,
and there is nothing in the Prophets, in the teachings of our Sages of blessed memory, or in the words of the sages of the Oral Torah that is not alluded to in the Torah (Ta’anit 9a).
וְכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לוֹ הַשָּׂגָה אַחֶרֶת בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה.
Every Jew therefore has a distinct apprehension within the words of Torah.
שֶׁקּוֹלוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה הוּא בְּקוֹל שׁוֹפָר גָּדוֹל, שֶׁקּוֹל נָמוּךְ שֶׁלּוֹ נִתְרַחֵב לַשּׁוֹמְעִים בְּהַרְחָבָה גְּדוֹלָה לְאֵין שִׁעוּר.
His voice within Torah is thus the voice of a great shofar: His concentrated voice expands for its hearers without limit.
וּבְרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, שֶׁאָנוּ בָּאִים בְּקוֹל תְּפִלָּה, קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא יָהֵיב עֵיטִין בְּכֹלָּא לְקַבֵּל בְּרַחֲמִים וּבְרָצוֹן אֶת תְּפִלָּתֵנוּ,
On Rosh Hashanah, when we approach with the voice of prayer, the Holy One, blessed be He, provides counsel in every matter so as to receive our prayer with mercy and favor,

הַבָּאָה בְּקוֹל נָמוּךְ מְאֹד בְּתַכְלִית הַשִּׁפְלוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּתִּקּוּנִים (תִּקּוּן ו)818 Tikkunei Zohar 22a — "He turned this way and that and saw that there was no man" — rather, "each has turned to his own way," to their own affairs, "each to his gain from every quarter," to the profit of this world, to inherit this world. They are not of the side of those of whom it is said, "men of valor, God-fearing, men of truth who hate unjust gain." Rather they all cry out in their prayers on the Day of Atonement like dogs: Give, give us food, and pardon and atonement and life — write us down for life! And they are brazen of soul like dogs, like the nations of the world who howl to Him and have no shame. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 15): Of this they said in the Tikkunim, "They cry out like a dog: give us…": that is, they do not call upon Him in truth and by the power of the Torah, for which the Blessed One stands ready to give, but come with the plea "Sustain me like a dog," though unworthy. And although the Blessed One gives even to such a one by the power of the prayer of the poor, nevertheless He desires and longs that we be in complete perfection, as He wills. Sod Yesharim (Rosh Hashanah 64): As in the Tikkunei Zohar, "They cry out like a dog: give us food, forgiveness and atonement…" — that is, asking for food, life and forgiveness without the intent for the glory of Heaven found in them is like brazenness toward Heaven, and of this it says "they cry out in prayer like a dog." But if one prays for the glory of Heaven — for livelihood so that he may engage in Torah amply, or for children to increase the souls of Israel and magnify the glory of Heaven — then even bodily needs, which are only temporary, are rightly counted as for the glory of Heaven, and he may pray for them.: "צָוְחִין כְּכַלְבָּא: הַב לָן" וְכוּלֵי.
even though it comes in an exceedingly low voice, from the utmost lowliness, as the Tikkunim (Tikkun 6) describes people crying “like a dog: Give us…” and so forth.
וְאַף הַמַּאֲרִיךְ בִּתְפִלָּה וּמְעַיֵּן בָּהּ בְּכַוָּנָה שְׁלֵמָה — מִי יִצְדַּק לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּדִּין?
Even one who prays at length and concentrates with complete intention—who could be justified before Him in strict judgment?
וּלְעוֹלָם: "מִן הַמֵּצַר קָרָאתִי יָהּ", שֶׁהַקְּרִיאָה הִיא בַּמֵּצַר מְאֹד — הֵיכָן תּוֹרָה וְהֵיכָן מִצְווֹת דְּמַגְּנֵי עֲלָן?
Thus it is always, “From the narrow place I called to God”: our calling is from profound constriction—where is our Torah, and where are the mitzvot that can protect us?
רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹנֶה בַמֶּרְחָב.
Only the Blessed One answers us with expansiveness.
וְהָעֵצָה לָזֶה לָבוֹא בְּקוֹל שׁוֹפָר שֶׁלָּנוּ שֶׁאָנוּ תּוֹקְעִין, לְהַרְחִיב הַשְׁמָעַת קוֹלֵנוּ לְמַעְלָה יוֹתֵר מִכְּפִי דִּבּוּרֵנוּ.
The counsel for this is to come with our shofar blast, so that the sounding of our voice Above is broadened beyond the measure of our actual words.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּל מִינֵי הַשָּׂגוֹת וְשִׂכְלִיּוֹת דִּבְנֵי אָדָם וְכָל הַנִּבְרָאִים בְּהַשָּׂגָתָם כְּלוּלִים בְּקוֹל תּוֹרָה דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
Just as every kind of human understanding and intellect, and the apprehension of every created being, is included within the Divine voice of Torah,

כָּךְ הַכֹּל כָּלוּל בְּקוֹל תְּפִלָּה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי הַכֹּל אֶחָד, כַּנּוֹדָע מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים קיח.; בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כא)819 Pesachim 118a; Bereshit Rabbah 21:5 — When the wicked Nimrod cast our father Abraham into the fiery furnace, Gabriel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the Universe, let me go down and cool it and save the righteous man from the fiery furnace. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: I am unique in My world and he is unique in his world; it is fitting for the Unique One to save the unique one. And in Bereshit Rabbah on "Behold, the man has become as one of us" — R. Yehuda bar Simon said: like the Unique One of the world, as it is stated, "Hear, Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One." Rashbam: ["When Nimrod cast":] for on this account he was called Amraphel — because he said (amar) and cast (hipil) Abraham into the furnace. Maharsha: ["Gabriel said":] In this episode of Abraham it does not say that Yurkemo, the prince of hail, stood up to save him; perhaps Yurkemo knew that Abraham's rescue would come only through the Holy One, blessed be He, for the reason He gave — "I am unique... and he is unique..." — as it is written, "Abraham was one" (Ezekiel 33:24). Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:15): [On R. Yehuda bar Simon's "like the Unique One of the world" in Bereishis Rabbah:] Man's knowing good and evil derives from his uniqueness in this lower world, after the pattern of the Blessed Name among the upper beings; on this account man is fitted to know good and evil, which he did not have before he sinned. Maharal (Gevuros Hashem, ch. 64): When the Holy One, blessed be He, brings about something new in His world through kindness, He squares it all with the attribute of truth, so that there is no departure from truth. At the fiery furnace His conduct departed from the attribute of truth, for it would have been proper for Gabriel, the angel appointed over fire, to be the rescuer; but when the Holy One, blessed be He, rescued [Abraham] for the reason stated, He squared the matter with the attribute of truth by [letting Gabriel] rescue his descendants — and so, when he rescued them, Gabriel said, "and the truth of the Lord endures forever." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): Only Abraham, who recognized the unity of the Blessed One and was called "My beloved," merited through love of the Blessed One the love of creatures as well, the whole world having been created only to accompany him; for as the Blessed One is unique among the upper beings, so is he unique among the lower, like Adam before the sin, as they said on the verse "Behold, the man has become as one of us" — the whole world being the limbs of his stature — and he merited to beget "one nation." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 6): The Sages said on "Behold, the man has become as one of us": as I am unique among the upper beings, so is he unique among the lower. For the part is a replica of the whole, so that all may be complete unity: man comprises all of creation, and through him all creation is unified, so that below as well "there is none beside Him"; and Israel, "one nation in the land," are the portion and inheritance of the Blessed One.: "אֲנִי יָחִיד בָּעֶלְיוֹנִים וְהוּא יָחִיד בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים".

so too everything is included within the voice of Israel’s prayer, for all is one, as in the teaching (Pesachim 118a; Bereishit Rabbah 21), “I am unique in the upper worlds, and he is unique in the lower worlds.”
כִּי סוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה.
For the final act was first in thought.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁרֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא כּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ חִיּוּתָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב "וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם",
Just as the primordial Divine thought includes all things and is the source of their life—“You give life to them all”—
כָּךְ הָאָדָם נִקְרָא עוֹלָם קָטָן שֶׁכּוֹלֵל הַכֹּל, וְכָל הַכֹּחוֹת שֶׁל כָּל הַנִּבְרָאִים כְּלוּלִים בּוֹ, וְהוּא כָּלוּל בָּהֶם,
so man is called a microcosm that includes everything: all the powers of created beings are included within him, and he is included within them.
וּמַשְׁפִּיעַ לָהֶם מִצַּד סוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה, הַיְנוּ מִצַּד הַהַשְׁקָפָה אֶל הַתַּכְלִית.
He in turn influences them from the standpoint of the final act—that is, from the perspective of creation’s ultimate purpose. –
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר: כְּמוֹ דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כּוֹלֵל כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִצַּד הַהַתְחָלָה שֶׁהוּא שָׁרְשָׁם, כָּךְ מָשִׁיחַ כּוֹלְלָם מִצַּד הַתַּכְלִית.

As explained elsewhere: just as our father Jacob, peace be upon him, includes all the souls of Israel from the standpoint of their beginning and root, so Mashiach includes them from the standpoint of their ultimate purpose.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֹׁרֶשׁ נֶפֶשׁ מֵהָאָבוֹת, כָּךְ יֵשׁ בּוֹ שֹׁרֶשׁ מִנֶּפֶשׁ מָשִׁיחַ גַּם כֵּן].
And just as every Jew contains a root of soul from the Patriarchs, so too he contains a root from the soul of Mashiach.

וּמִצַּד הַזֶּה אָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא עה:)820 Bava Batra 75b — Rabba said in the name of R. Yochanan: In time to come the righteous will be called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, "Every one that is called by My name, whom I have created for My glory, I have formed him, yea, I have made him." And R. Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of R. Yochanan: Three are called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and these are they: the righteous, the Messiah, and Jerusalem. Rashbam: "They are called by His name" — that their own name shall be "the Lord." Maharsha (s.v. "in time to come the righteous will be called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He"): A man is not of himself fit for the attribute of glory, which belongs to the Holy One, blessed be He — "My glory I will not give to another," and all that He created He created only for His glory. Glory comes to a man only by way of his Torah, which is itself God's glory, as "there is no glory but Torah." Hence "every one that is called by My name" means the righteous, all of whose deeds are for His glory; "whom I have created for My glory" speaks of this world, and "yea, I have made him" adds that in the World to Come too he will bear His name, on account of the deeds he did here for God's glory. Maharsha (s.v. "three are called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He"): It says "called upon His name" and not "called by His name," which shows that the divine Name is joined to theirs as a qualifier: "righteous to the Lord," "the Lord our righteousness," "the city of the Lord." Each bears the Name because all his deeds are for the sake of Heaven — so the righteous, so the Messiah, and so Jerusalem in time to come, to which none will be admitted but those whose every deed is for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): This is the ultimate cleaving, until one is called wholly by the name of the Lord, as they said, "In the future the righteous will be called by the name of the Holy One, blessed be He." This will be when the ultimate perfection of the future is reached through the Messiah son of David, of the seed of Judah, by means of repentance, through which Israel is redeemed; for "in the place where penitents stand, the perfectly righteous cannot stand," a higher place.: עָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִקְרוֹא לַצַּדִּיקִים בִּשְׁמוֹ,
From this standpoint they taught (Bava Batra 75b) that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will call the righteous by His Name,
הַיְנוּ שֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה, שֶׁהוּא הָרוֹמֵז שֶׁמְּהַוֶּה אֶת הַכֹּל וְכוֹלֵל הַכֹּל.
namely the Name Havayah, which signifies that He brings everything into being and encompasses everything.

וְכָךְ הַצַּדִּיקִים, אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ח)821 Bereshit Rabbah 8:7 — R. Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in the name of R. Shmuel: He took counsel with the souls of the righteous. That is what is written, "These were the potters, and those that dwelt among plantings and hedges; there they dwelt with the king in his work." "These were the potters" — for "And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground." "Those that dwelt among plantings" — for "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden to the east." "And hedges" — for "I placed the sand as a boundary for the sea." "There they dwelt with the king in his work" — with the King, the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, dwelt the souls of the righteous, with whom the Holy One, blessed be He, took counsel and created the world. עַל פָּסוּק "הֵמָּה הַיּוֹצְרִים", שֶׁהָיוּ שֻׁתָּפִים כִּבְיָכוֹל בִּבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם.
So too regarding the righteous, our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereishit Rabbah 8), on the verse “These were the potters,” that they were, as it were, partners in the creation of the world.
הַכַּוָּנָה מִצַּד הַתַּכְלִית, שֶׁאֲלֵיהֶם הָיְתָה מְכֻוֶּנֶת כָּל הַבְּרִיאָה לְצַוּוֹת לָזֶה, וְנִמְצָא כֹּחָם הוּא הַמַּשְׁפִּיעַ כְּלַל הַבְּרִיאָה.
The meaning is from the standpoint of purpose: all creation was directed toward serving such a person, and therefore their power becomes a source of influence for creation as a whole.
וְהַדִּבּוּר הוּא חִיּוּת הָאָדָם, כַּנּוֹדָע: "לְנֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה" — לְרוּחַ מְמַלְּלָא.
Speech is the life-force of man, as is known from the rendering of “a living soul” as “a speaking spirit.”
וְדִבּוּר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית הוּא הַמְחַיֶּה כָּל הַבְּרִיאָה, כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי חִיּוּת הַכֹּל נִמְשָׁךְ מֵחִיּוּת חֵי הָעוֹלָמִים, וְחִיּוּתוֹ הוּא דִּבּוּרוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
The Divine speech of Creation gives life to the entire universe, for the life of all things is drawn from the Life of the worlds, and His life, as it were, is His Divine speech.

וְזֶהוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַדִּבּוּר דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי קוֹל שׁוֹפָר דְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, דְּבְאוֹרַיְתָא בָּרָא הָעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה וּבַזֹּהַר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים.

This is the expansion of Divine speech through the shofar-sound of the Giving of the Torah, for the world was created through Torah, as stated at the beginning of Bereishit Rabbah and many times in the Zohar.
וּבִשְׁעַת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נִתְבַּסֵּס הָעוֹלָם, הַיְנוּ יָשַׁב עַל כַּנּוֹ.
At the Giving of the Torah the world became established—set firmly upon its foundation.
שֶׁהַדִּבּוּר הוּא רוּחָנִי וְהוּא דָּבָר הָרוֹפֵף, וּכְשֶׁבָּא לְפֹעַל בִּכְתָב הוּא דָּבָר הַקַּיָּם שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹפֵף.
Speech is spiritual and fluid; when it becomes actualized in writing it takes on a fixed and enduring form.

וּבִשְׁעַת בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה רַק דִּבּוּר וּמַאֲמָר, וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ (גִּיטִּין ס:)822 Gittin 60b — R. Yehuda bar Naḥmani, the interpreter of R. Shimon ben Lakish, expounded: It is written, "Write down these words," and it is written, "For on the basis of these words I have made a covenant with you." How can both stand? Words that are written you may not recite orally, and words that are oral you may not recite in writing. The school of R. Yishmael taught: "These" — these you may write, but you may not write down the laws. Rashi: "It is written: Write you these words" — evidently they were written; "and it is written: on the basis of [by the mouth of] these words" — evidently they were not written. "Words" that I told you in writing you may not transmit to Israel by mouth. "And words that are oral you may not express in writing" — from here you learn that the Talmud was not given to be written, and it was written only because the Torah was being forgotten. Maharsha: At first glance these verses prove only that there are matters in writing and matters that are oral, but not that one may not express the one in the manner of the other. The inference is drawn from the word "these" written in each of them, as is shown by the teaching of the school of R. Yishmael — and the school of R. Yishmael stated only one of the two halves. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Gittin 60b): The Oral Torah is not fit to be put in writing, because it consists of the particulars of the commandments and their explanations, and to this there is no end or limit, since the particulars have no end; nor would it be anything whole were he to write only part of it and not all, and writing requires that the whole be there in its completeness — all the more so the Torah, of which it is written, "The Torah of the Lord is perfect." And the reverse likewise: since the Written Torah is whole and complete, it must be in writing and not by mouth, for one who says words by mouth says one part after another, and even were he to say the whole Torah, at the moment he says the later part the earlier part is already not there, and the Torah of the Lord is not perfect as it ought to be. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 27): The curses of Mount Eval are spelled out in the Torah but not the blessings of Mount Gerizim, for what the Torah sets down in writing, open to all, are matters revealed and graspable by all, visible to the eye, while what is not revealed to the eye was said orally: "words that are oral, which you may not recite in writing," since such matters cannot be revealed to all, only to one who attains them. The curses were only in this world, whereas those blessings were of the World to Come, and therefore they were not given in writing. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 7): The Torah was written out clearly in the seventy languages, for from the side of writing, which is the revelation of wisdom, it was revealed to all who come into the world, and the ancient philosophers too attained knowledge of God through their wisdom; yet their hearts were not changed one iota, and the Holy One, blessed be He, dwelt only in the hearts of Israel, to whom the Oral Torah was given over, that is, the revelation through speech of the understanding in the heart. Therefore "words that are oral you may not recite in writing," for the essence of oral words is in speech, through which what is in the heart is revealed. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 4): The Mishnah begins and ends with mem, to say that its whole scope is to refine deeds to their proper completeness, which is the matter of the Oral Torah that "you may not recite in writing." For the conduct of the supernal wisdom is the reverse of what appears to the eye of flesh, to which deeds seem the revealed part and mind and heart the hidden, writing the revealed and the oral the concealed; in the wisdom of the Blessed One the hidden is revealed and the revealed hidden, for the deed is in truth an image and the hidden is beyond image. Therefore the study that pertains to mind and heart is in writing, and that which pertains to deeds is oral.: "דְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה אִי אַתָּה רַשַּׁאי לְאָמְרָם בִּכְתָב".
At creation there was only speech and utterance, corresponding to the rule (Gittin 60b), “Matters of the Oral Torah you are not permitted to recite in written form.”
כִּי הַכָּתוּב הוּא דָּבָר קָצוּב וּמֻגְבָּל שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְשַׁנּוֹת, אֲבָל בְּמַה שֶּׁבְּעַל פֶּה יִפֹּל הַשִּׁנּוּי.
Writing is defined and bounded, not subject to alteration, whereas oral teaching admits variation.
וּלְפִי שֶׁבְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה יֵשׁ מַחֲלֹקֶת, "וְאֵלּוּ וְאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים",
Because the Oral Torah contains disagreement—“these and those are the words of the living God”—
הַיְנוּ שֶׁכָּךְ נִתַּן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַדָּבָר רוֹפֵף בְּיָדָם וְיוּכְלוּ לְהַטּוֹת לְכָאן וּלְכָאן; וּלְפִיכָךְ אִי אַתָּה רַשַּׁאי לְאָמְרָם בִּכְתָב, שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר מְבֹרָר.
it was entrusted to Israel in a flexible form that can be inclined in one direction or another; for that reason it was not to be fixed in writing, which conveys settled determination.
וּבִתְחִלַּת הַבְּרִיאָה גַּם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הָיְתָה מִכְּלַל דְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה.
At the beginning of creation, even the Written Torah was still in the category of oral matters, for Torah had not yet been given.

וְהַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב עַצְמָהּ הֲרֵי הִשִּׂיגָהּ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּהַשָּׂגָתוֹ, וְהוּא מִכְּלַל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַשָּׂגַת נְבִיאִים, שֶׁהִיא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
The Written Torah itself was apprehended by Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, through prophetic apprehension, which in that sense belongs to the mode of Oral Torah.
רַק מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַשָּׂגָתוֹ גְּדוֹלָה, וְהִגִּיד לָנוּ בְּשֵׁם הַשֵּׁם שֶׁזֶּה תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
Only Moses’ apprehension was uniquely exalted, and he told us in God’s Name that this was to be the Written Torah.
אֲבָל קֹדֶם שֶׁהוֹרִידָהּ לָאָרֶץ, הֲרֵי גַּם זֶה כְּמוֹ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁמָּסוּר לְהַשָּׂגַת בְּנֵי אָדָם,
Before he brought it down to earth, however, it still functioned like Oral Torah, entrusted to human apprehension,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ הָאָבוֹת שֶׁקִּיְּמוּ כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כֻּלָּהּ עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִתְּנָה בְּהַשָּׂגַת חָכְמָתָם, וְהַבְּחִירָה בְּיָדָם.
as with the Patriarchs, who fulfilled the entire Torah before it was given through the attainment of their own wisdom, while choice remained in their hands.

כְּמוֹ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁהָיָה אָז רָאוּי לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג רטז עַמּוּד ב)823 Zohar 3:216b — And the Sages further explained that Moses was destined to receive the Torah in the generation of the flood; but because they were wicked [he did not] — this is what is written, "for that he also [beshagam] is flesh": beshagam is Moses. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): The generations of the Flood and of the Dispersion are the general categories of the "secrets of illicit relations," for they correspond to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah: in the generation of the Flood it was fitting for the Torah to be given, as the Zohar says and as the Sages said on the verse, "beshagam" — this is Moses. And correspondingly their sin was the emission of seed, in the Yesod, as is known from the Zohar that writing belongs to the Yesod. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Noach 1): The ten generations from Adam to Noah were meant to repair all the damage of Adam's sin and to be refined in all the attributes, and then, in the generation of the Flood, it was fitting for the Torah to be given; the soul of Moses was present then, as hinted in "beshagam," which equals Moses in numerical value. They would have merited the Written and the Oral Torah, hinted in "all the fountains of the great deep burst forth" [the springs of wisdom below] "and the windows of heaven were opened" [the gates of wisdom above], and would have repaired all the damage of the serpent, as will be in the future; but because they provoked Him, these turned into raging waters and they were all swept away in the waters of the Flood., וְהֵם בָּחֲרוּ בַּהֵפֶךְ וְגָרְמוּ חֻרְבַּן הָעוֹלָם, רַחֲמָנָא לִצְלַן.

So too the generation of the Flood was then fit for the Giving of the Torah, as stated in the Zohar (III, 216b), but they chose the opposite and brought destruction upon the world—may the Merciful One save us.
וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא, הָיָה הָעוֹלָם רוֹפֵף.
As long as Torah had not been given to Israel in a fixed, written form, the world remained unstable.
וְזֶה עִנְיַן צִוּוּי מֵאֲכִילַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת, שֶׁהוּא הַיְדִיעָה וְהַחֲקִירָה בְּחָכְמָה.
This is the meaning of the command concerning eating from the Tree of Knowledge, which represents knowledge and intellectual investigation.
וְהַיְנוּ כִּי זֶה כָּל יִתְרוֹן הָאָדָם מִן הַבְּהֵמָה — בַּחָכְמָה וְשֵׂכֶל שֶׁבּוֹ.
For man’s entire advantage over the animal lies in the wisdom and intellect within him.
אַךְ הַחֲקִירָה בְּשֵׂכֶל אֱנוֹשִׁי יֵשׁ בָּהּ טוֹב וָרָע, כַּנּוֹדָע: דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּחֲקִירָתוֹ הִשִּׂיג אֱמוּנָה אֱלֹהִית וְזָכָה לְמַה שֶּׁזָּכָה.
Yet human intellectual inquiry contains both good and evil. Abraham our father, peace be upon him, through his investigation attained faith in God and reached his great spiritual achievements.
וּפִילוֹסוֹפֵי יְוָנִים וְדוֹמֵיהֶם בַּחֲקִירָתָם הִשִּׂיגוּ שֶׁהָעוֹלָם קַדְמוֹן וּשְׁאָר כְּפִירוֹת, כַּנּוֹדָע.
The Greek philosophers and those like them, through their inquiry, arrived instead at the eternity of the universe and other heresies.
רַק הָאָדָם צָרִיךְ לֵידַע תְּחִלָּה: "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹהֶיךָ" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת הַתּוֹרָה דֶּרֶךְ יְדִיעָה, לֹא דֶּרֶךְ צִוּוּי לָאָדָם שֶׁיַּאֲמִין,
A person must first know “I am the Lord your God, etc.” This opening of the Torah is presented as knowledge, not merely as a command that one should believe.
דְּזֶהוּ בְּהַשָּׂגַת אָדָם; רַק צִוּוּי סְתָמִי — הַיְנוּ לֵידַע זֶה דֶּרֶךְ יְדִיעַת מֻשְׂכָּלוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת.
A commanded belief would still rest upon human apprehension; rather, this is an unqualified imperative to know it with the certainty of first principles.
וּבִידִיעָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא בַּעַל כֹּחוֹת הָאָדָם כֻּלָּם, וְכָל שִׂכְלוֹ הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, זֶהוּ הַלְּקִיחָה מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים.
Knowing that the Blessed One is the Master of all human powers, and that all of one’s intellect comes from Him, is the proper taking from the Tree of Life.

שֶׁהִתְבּוֹנְנוּתוֹ בְּשִׂכְלוֹ הוּא מִצַּד הַשֵּׂכֶל הַנָּתוּן לוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ חִיּוּתוֹ גַּם כֵּן, וְאֶצְלוֹ אֵין חִלּוּק חִיּוּת, כַּנּוֹדָע, וְכֹחַ הַחִיּוּת הוּא עַצְמוֹ כֹּחַ הַמַּדָּע.

His contemplation through intellect then proceeds from the intellect bestowed by God, from Whom his very life derives; with Him there is no division in life-force, and the power of life is itself the power of knowledge.
וְעִקַּר בְּרִיאַת הָאָדָם הָיָה לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּשִׂכְלוֹ, כְּטַעַם: "מַלְכוּת פֶּה — תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה קָרֵינָן לָהּ".
The essential purpose of man’s creation was to use his intellect, in the sense of “Kingship is the mouth—we call it the Oral Torah.”
וְעִקַּר בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת כֹּחַ מַלְכוּתוֹ, כַּנּוֹדָע; דְּלָכֵן אוֹמְרִים בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה מַלְכֻיּוֹת: "שֶׁתַּמְלִיכוּנִי".
The essential purpose of the world’s creation is the revelation of His kingship; therefore on Rosh Hashanah we recite the verses of Kingship so that “you should make Me King.”
וְהַהַמְלָכָה הַיְנוּ שֶׁיַּשִּׂיג הָאָדָם שֶׁכָּל שִׂכְלוֹ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
Enthroning Him means that a person recognizes that his entire intellect comes from the Blessed One.
דְּזֶה כָּל חָכְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁאֵינָהּ כְּחָכְמָה אֱנוֹשִׁית שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג בְּשִׂכְלוֹ עַצְמוֹ; אֲבָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הִיא נוֹבַעַת מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
This is the essence of the wisdom of the Oral Torah: it is not human wisdom attained by autonomous reason, but wisdom that flows from the Written Torah.
דְּזֶהוּ עִקַּר מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּשֶׁמּוֹשֵׁל עַל שֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִקַּר צוּרַת הָאָדָם, שֶׁכָּל הַנְהָגַת הָאָדָם הִיא בְּשִׂכְלוֹ.
His kingship is realized most essentially when it rules over man’s intellect, for intellect is man’s defining form and directs all of his conduct.

וּבַזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א כז עַמּוּד א, וּשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת)824 Zohar 1:27a — Another interpretation of "And a river goes out of Eden": Above, in the Tree of Life, there are certainly no alien shells, as it is written, "evil shall not sojourn with You." But in the tree below there are alien shells, and it is planted in the garden of Eden of the Lesser Countenance. Its shells are, from this side, good, and from that side, evil — and this is forbidden and permitted, fit and unfit, impure and pure. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 15): Had Adam not sinned, the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, which stands right beside the Tree of Life — for in truth it is all one — would also have been turned into the Tree of Life and the evil wholly consumed from the world; but through his sin even the Tree of Life of the Torah was turned to be "from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, fit and unfit, impure and pure," as stated in the Tikkunim. It seems to me that these correspond to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah: had Adam not sinned, everything would have been in writing, with no need for an Oral Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 2): "Haman — where is he alluded to in the Torah? 'Is it from the tree [ha-min ha-etz]'" [Chullin 139b] means that through Haman they merited the light of the Oral Torah; this is alluded to in "the tree," following what the holy Zohar says, that there is Torah from the side of the Tree of Life, namely the Written Torah, and Torah from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil, which is forbidden and permitted, impurity and purity. The tree Haman made fifty cubits high corresponded to the fifty gates of understanding in the Oral Torah, which is from the side of the Tree of Knowledge. אָמְרוּ דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הִיא מִסִּטְרָא דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע — כָּשֵׁר וּפָסוּל וְכוּלֵי.
The Zohar (I, 27a, and elsewhere) teaches that the Oral Torah is from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil—kosher and unfit, and so forth.

הַיְנוּ דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת הוּא שֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שִׁנּוּיִים לְכָאן וּלְכָאן; אֲבָל עֵץ הַחַיִּים הוּא בְּתוֹךְ הַגָּן בִּנְקֻדַּת הַמֶּרְכָּז, שֶׁאֵינוֹ נוֹטֶה לַקְּצָווֹת וְאֵין בּוֹ נְטִיָּה לְכָאן וּלְכָאן, וְהוּא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
The Tree of Knowledge is human intellect, which can shift in either direction. The Tree of Life stands at the center of the garden, inclining to neither extreme; this is the Written Torah.
וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הָיָה שֶׁהָאָדָם יִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּשִׂכְלוֹ לְהַשָּׂגַת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, שֶׁהִיא הַשָּׂגַת דְּבָרִים קְצוּבִים וּבְרוּרִים,
God’s will was that man use his intellect to attain the Written Torah—the apprehension of matters that are fixed and clear—
וְהַיְנוּ עַל יְדֵי הַהַכָּרָה הַבְּרוּרָה שֶׁאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ, וְיִהְיֶה שִׂכְלוֹ מִשְׁכָּן לְשֵׂכֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמָּשׁ,
through the clear recognition that there is nothing besides Him, so that one’s mind becomes a dwelling place for Divine intellect itself,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: שְׁכִינָה מְדַבֶּרֶת מִתּוֹךְ גְּרוֹנוֹ, דְּעִמֵּיהּ שַׁרְיָא נְהוֹרָא, וְאֵין סָפֵק כְּלָל.
as it is said of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, that the Divine Presence spoke through his throat; with him the light rested, leaving no room for doubt.
שֶׁהַסָּפֵק הוּא רַק מִתּוֹךְ הַחֹשֶׁךְ וְהַהֶעְלֵם בְּמִדַּת לַיְלָה, וְכָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הָיָה מַשִּׂיג בְּדֻגְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד.
Doubt arises only from darkness and concealment, the quality of night; Moses attained the Oral Torah in a mode resembling the Written Torah, as will be the case in the future.
רַק שֶׁגָּרְמָה הֲסָתַת הַנָּחָשׁ: "וִהְיִיתֶם כֵּאלֹהִים" וְגוֹמֵר, הַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּשִׂכְלוֹ מֵעַצְמוֹ, וְזֶהוּ עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע.
The serpent’s enticement—“you will be like gods, etc.”—introduced the idea that man should use intellect as though it were self-derived; this is the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil.
וְנִתְרַפֵּף הָעוֹלָם עַד שֶׁנִּתְּנָה תּוֹרָה בִּכְתָב,
The world therefore remained unstable until the Torah was given in written form,

דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁנִּתְפַּשֵּׁט שֹׁרֶשׁ הַחָכְמָה דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמִּתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת בְּלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם — שֶׁהוּא הַהַשָּׂגָה דְּ"אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ" — שָׁרְשָׁהּ קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּם בְּלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יְדֵי קוֹל שׁוֹפָר דְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה.

when the root of Divine wisdom that extends into human hearts—the apprehension that “there is nothing besides Him”—was fixed and established in the hearts of Israel through the shofar-sound of the Giving of the Torah.

וַאֲנַחְנוּ בָּאִים בְּקוֹל שׁוֹפָר שֶׁלָּנוּ, לִהְיוֹת גַּם הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בְּחָכְמָה שֶׁלָּנוּ יְסוֹדָהּ מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, וּמִתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת וּמִתְרַחֶבֶת גַּם הִיא בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת עַד אֵין קֵץ.
With our own shofar-sound we seek that our wisdom of the Oral Torah likewise be founded upon the Written Torah, and that it too expand throughout all the worlds without end.

וְכַנּוֹדָע מִקְּדֻשַּׁת דִּבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בַּתַּלְמוּד מַמָּשׁ כְּעֵין קְדֻשַּׁת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁתַּלְמִיד וָתִיק עָתִיד לְחַדֵּשׁ הַכֹּל רָמְזוּ בְּדִבְרֵיהֶם, וְכֵן כָּל חָכְמַת חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָאֲמִתִּיִּים.

Thus the words of our Sages in the Talmud possess a sanctity akin to that of the Written Torah: everything a seasoned disciple will ever innovate is already hinted in their words, and so too with the authentic wisdom of Israel’s sages.
וְקוֹל דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה פָּסוּק וְקוֹל דִּתְפִלָּה — כּוּלָּא חַד, כַּנּוֹדָע בְּשָׁרְשָׁם.
At their root, the voice of Oral Torah and the voice of prayer are all one.

וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת ח.)825 Berakhot 8a — R. Chiyya bar Ami said in the name of Ulla: Since the day the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His world but the four cubits of halakhah alone. And Abaye said: At first I would study in my house and pray in the synagogue; but once I heard this teaching of R. Chiyya bar Ami in the name of Ulla, I would pray only where I study. R. Ami and R. Asi, although they had thirteen synagogues in Tiberias, would pray only between the pillars, where they studied. Rashi: "Between the pillars" — for the study house was built upon them, above. Maharsha: While the Temple stood there was the Chamber of Hewn Stone, from which decided halakhah went forth by the Sanhedrin, and with them the Divine Presence surely dwelt. Now that the Temple is destroyed, those four cubits of halakhah which every Torah scholar fixes as the place of his study in the Talmud stand in its stead, so that the Divine Presence is with him there. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael 70): The Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in the corporeal world, for the corporeal is removed from Him; what is His is the four cubits of halakhah. It is called halakhah because, as one who walks a road does not swerve to right or left, so a ruling of halakhah does not swerve from the point of truth. Just as He chose the Temple, which is fit for holiness because it stands at the centre — and the centre has no distance about it, distance belonging to the corporeal — so halakhah is wholly simple intellect, with no relation to the corporeal, and therefore the place where halakhah is belongs to Him. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 11): Torah is "voice", the male, and prayer, said in a whisper, is "speech", the female; and just as "a woman who seeds first bears a male" and the females are made dependent on the males, so it says "they would pray only where they studied", and in Megillah the reverse, "they would study only where they prayed": for through the voice of Torah one merits prayer, and through prayer one begets the voice of Torah. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): The word "voice" is joined to Jacob because the voice of the Oral Torah is the essential root of Jacob, and the voice of prayer is drawn from it, as with R. Ami and R. Asi, who would pray only between the pillars where they studied. For [the Sages] instituted that one first say "O Lord, open my lips", since one can pray only when the Blessed One opens his lips, and this opening comes through the Oral Torah.: "לָא מְצַלֵּי אֶלָּא בֵּינֵי עַמּוּדֵי דְּגָרְסִי" — רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ הַחָכְמָה וְקוֹל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ קוֹל הַתְּפִלָּה.
Thus they said (Berakhot 8a), “He would pray only among the pillars where they studied”—meaning that the voice of prayer is drawn from the wisdom and voice of Oral Torah.
וּכְפִי חָכְמַת הָאָדָם בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, כָּךְ כֹּחוֹ יָפֶה בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ.
The measure of a person’s wisdom in Oral Torah determines the power of his prayer.
וְקוֹלוֹת הַלָּלוּ הֵם תִּקּוּן לַאֲכִילַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת: תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִמְשֶׁכֶת מִסִּטְרֵיהּ, וּמִמֶּנָּה נִמְשָׁךְ קוֹל תְּפִלָּה.
These two voices repair the eating from the Tree of Knowledge: Oral Torah is drawn from that side, and from it comes the voice of prayer.
כִּי תְּפִלָּה דְּרַבָּנָן; הַיְנוּ דְּמִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת "אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ" מַמָּשׁ, דְּכוּלָּא חַד — מַה מָּקוֹם לִתְפִלָּה?
Prayer is rabbinic in institution; for from the absolute apprehension that “there is nothing besides Him,” where all is one, what place is there for prayer?
וְהַתְּפִלָּה הִיא רַק מִצַּד מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא וְנִבְרָא, וְהַנִּבְרָא מְבַקֵּשׁ מִבּוֹרֵא.
Prayer exists from the standpoint of His kingship, where there is Creator and creature and the creature petitions the Creator.
וְכָל חָכְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הִיא חָכְמַת נִבְרָא לְהַכִּיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא, וִיצִיאַת הַשָּׂגָה זוֹ לַפֹּעַל הִיא בִּתְפִלָּה.
All the wisdom of Oral Torah is the wisdom of a created being recognizing that there is a Creator, and the actualization of that recognition is prayer.
שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא, לֹא בְּהֶאָרָה גְּמוּרָה בְּמִדַּת יוֹם שֶׁאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ לְגַמְרֵי, רַק בְּדֶרֶךְ הֶעְלֵם — אָז מְעוֹרֵר לִבּוֹ לִתְפִלָּה.
When one recognizes a Creator, but not in the full illumination of day in which His absolute unity is manifest—rather through concealment—the heart is stirred to prayer.
וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית חָכְמָה דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, הַנִּמְשָׁךְ עַל יְדֵי אֲכִילַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת שֶׁהֶחְשִׁיךְ אַנְפֵּי בְנֵי נָשָׁא.
This is the culmination of the wisdom of Oral Torah that emerged through eating from the Tree of Knowledge, which darkened the faces of humanity.
וּלְכָךְ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה מַרְבִּין בִּתְפִלָּה לְתַקֵּן חֶטְאוֹ דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן אָז, וּמַעֲלִין אוֹתָהּ לְמַעְלָה בְּקוֹלוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹפָר הַמַּרְחִיב קוֹל הָאָדָם עַד אֵין קֵץ.
Therefore on Rosh Hashanah we increase prayer in order to repair Adam’s sin committed on that day, and we raise prayer Above through the shofar’s voice, which expands the human voice without limit.
וְהַיְנוּ עַל יְדֵי הִתְדַּבְּקוּתוֹ בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהוּא הָעֲנִיָּה דְּבַמֶּרְחָב.
This occurs through man’s cleaving to the Blessed One; this is the Divine answer “with expansiveness.”
וְנֶאֱמַר: "עָלָה אֱלֹהִים בִּתְרוּעָה" וְגוֹמֵר, דְּשֵׁם זֶה מוֹרֶה עַל שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל הַכֹּחוֹת כֻּלָּם; הַיְנוּ, בְּהִשְׁתַּמְּשׁוּת אָדָם בְּשִׂכְלוֹ — הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
Thus it says, “God ascends with the teruah, etc.” The Divine Name Elohim signifies that He is Master of all powers: even man’s use of his own intellect is from Him.
וְשֵׁם הֲוָיָ"ה מוֹרֶה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְהַוֶּה הַכֹּל, הַיְנוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הַשֵּׂכֶל הַנָּתוּן לוֹ מִצַּד מְקוֹר חִיּוּתוֹ.
The Name Havayah signifies that the Blessed One brings all into being; it points to the root of the intellect granted to man from the very source of his life.
הַכֹּל יֵשׁ עֲלִיָּה בְּקוֹל שׁוֹפָר, שֶׁהוּא הַמַּרְחִיב קוֹל מוּעָט כְּמוֹת שֶׁהוּא, לִהְיוֹת לוֹ עֲלִיָּה מַעְלָה מַעְלָה עַל יְדֵי הַהִתְרַחֲבוּת בַּשּׁוֹפָר.
Everything can be elevated through the shofar, which takes a small voice as it is and expands it so that it can rise higher and higher.
וְשֵׂכֶל אֱנוֹשִׁי עֲלִיָּתוֹ בִּתְרוּעָה, דִּמְתַרְגְּמִינַן "יְבָבָא", הָרוֹמֵז לְקוֹל תְּפִלָּה הַבָּא מִצַּד הַרְגָּשַׁת הַחִסָּרוֹן,
Human intellect rises through the teruah, translated as yevava, a sobbing cry. This signifies the voice of prayer that arises from the awareness of lack,
כִּי הַנִּצְרָךְ לְאֵיזֶה דָּבָר הוּא צוֹעֵק וּמִתְפַּלֵּל עַל זֶה.
for one who needs something cries out and prays for it.
אֲבָל קוֹל תּוֹרָה הוּא בְּשִׂמְחָה, דְּהֵם מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב, וְעִקַּר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
The voice of Torah, by contrast, is a voice of joy, for Torah gladdens the heart, and the root of Oral Torah is in the Written Torah, which comes from the Blessed One.
וְהָעֲלִיָּה שֶׁלּוֹ הִיא בְּקוֹל שׁוֹפָר פָּשׁוּט, שֶׁהוּא תְּקִיעָה הַמּוֹרָה שִׂמְחָה; וּבֶאֱמֶת הַכֹּל אֶחָד, כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
Its elevation is through the plain shofar sound, the tekiah, which expresses joy; in truth, however, the two are one, as explained above.
לָכֵן אַף דְּעִקַּר רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה נִקְרָא "יוֹם תְּרוּעָה", וְעִקַּר הָעֵסֶק בּוֹ בִּתְפִלָּה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ פְּשׁוּטָה לְפָנֶיהָ וּלְאַחֲרֶיהָ.
Therefore, although Rosh Hashanah is principally called a “day of teruah” and its central service is prayer, a plain tekiah is required before and after it.
כִּי הַתְּפִלָּה הִיא "בֵּינֵי עַמּוּדֵי דְּגִרְסָא" — הַיְנוּ בֵּינֵיהֶם, דְּפָשׁוּטָה מִכָּל צַד מַקִּיפָהּ, שֶׁהִיא הַעֲלָאַת קוֹל תּוֹרָה.
Prayer stands “between the pillars of study”: it is surrounded on both sides by the plain sound, representing the elevation of the voice of Torah.

items.h:
Seif 2 — The Cry of Sisera's Mother
The broken shofar cry reflects Oral Torah and prayer emerging from a power once enclosed within foreign domination.

p: וְעִנְיַן יְבָבָא מַהוּ, לָמְדוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לג:)826 Rosh Hashanah 33b — The length of a terua is like three yevavot [whimpers]. But it was taught: The length of a terua is like three shevarim [broken sighs]! Abaye said: In this they certainly disagree, for it is written "It shall be a day of blasting [terua] for you," and we render it in Aramaic: "It shall be a day of wailing [yevava] for you"; and it is written of the mother of Sisera, "Through the window she looked out and wailed [vateyabev], the mother of Sisera." One master holds that it is a groaning, and the other master holds that it is a whimpering. Rashi: Three yevavot are three mere sounds of any length, whereas shevarim are longer than yevavot. Although the first contradiction was resolved, here they must disagree, for there is no reconciling it: "terua" is rendered "yevava", the same expression that is written of Sisera's mother, "and she wailed." The one who says shevarim holds that it is a groaning — like a man groaning from his heart, as the sick draw out their groans; the other holds that it is a whimpering — like one who weeps and laments in short sounds close to one another. Tosafos (s.v. "The length of a terua is like three yevavot"): Rashi takes three yevavot as three mere sounds of any length; hence, since R. Abbahu instituted in Caesarea the sequences with shevarim, with terua, and with both (34a) — out of doubt whether the Torah's terua is a groaning, a whimpering, or both — one must take care not to draw out each shever to the length of three yevavot, for it would then be a tekia and not a shever. The Riva and R. Yitzchak ben R. Meir explain instead that each yevava is three minimal sounds, so that a terua is nine. The Aruch records that the stringent blew thirty sounds seated, thirty during the silent prayer and thirty in the order of the blessings, and ten more at the end of the prayer — a hundred, corresponding to the hundred cries of Sisera's mother. Maharsha (Chidushei Halachot): Against Tosafot's caution that no single shever be drawn out to the length of three yevavot lest it become a tekia, he objects: since shevarim represent groaning, the tekia that goes with shevarim is as long as three groans, which are longer than three minimal sounds — as Tosafot themselves require the tekiot of the shevarim sequence to be as long as three shevarim — so there is no concern if a single shever lasts as long as three minimal sounds. Sod Yesharim (Rosh Hashanah 95): We learned regarding the shofar blasts that the terua is a yevava, since "a day of terua" is rendered "a day of yevava" and of the mother of Sisera it is written "vateyabev"; the terua is a broken, interrupted sound, from "you shall break them [tero'em] with a rod of iron." So too the Targum's "umedayka," for dikduk is examining a matter minutely in one's mind and dividing it into its details, and the body's agitation follows the stirring of the mind: in sudden pain and fright, as one examines the matter with wondrous speed, he is moved to let out a sound of yevava. Therefore the term yevava applies to both together, and this is why "a day of terua" is rendered "a day of yevava." מֵאִימֵיהּ דְּסִיסְרָא.
As for the meaning of yevava, the Sages of blessed memory (Rosh Hashanah 33b) learned it from the mother of Sisera.

הַיְנוּ כַּנּוֹדָע דְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, שֶׁהוּא יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה כַּיָּדוּעַ, הוּא מִבְּנֵי בָנָיו שֶׁל סִיסְרָא (סַנְהֶדְרִין צו:, לְגִרְסַת עֵין יַעֲקֹב)827 Sanhedrin 96b — The Sages taught: Naaman was a resident alien; Nebuzaradan was a fully righteous convert. Of the descendants of Sisera, some taught Torah in Jerusalem [the Ein Yaakov text reads: and who was he? R. Akiva]; of the descendants of Sennacherib, some taught Torah in public — and who were they? Shemaya and Avtalyon; of the descendants of Haman, some taught Torah in Bnei Brak. Rashi: A resident alien: one who did not accept upon himself the other commandments, but accepted upon himself not to worship idols. Maharsha: Just as Nebuzaradan contemplated repentance in his heart and merited to enter under the wings of the Shechinah, so of these wicked men — Sisera, Sennacherib who blasphemed against Heaven, and Haman the wicked — who persisted in their wickedness and were killed for it, the descendants contemplated repentance and merited to enter under the wings of the Shechinah. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sanhedrin 96b): The power that Sennacherib had was a supernal power, only it inclined toward the side of impurity; and as a physician removes the bad until the good remains, so the Holy One, blessed be He, removed the bad from Sennacherib's power until the good remained. So too with Nebuzaradan: although he destroyed the Temple, a supernal power was mixed into his power, and when that bad was removed he was healed of his wickedness and became a righteous convert, and likewise Naaman, who was a resident alien; and so with Haman — it cannot be that there was no supernal power within his power, and when the dross was removed, refined silver remained. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 7): What is recounted here of the wicked whose seed converted into Israel and taught Torah in public is a wondrous matter: when the wicked are extreme in wickedness and have very great power, as these had, their power cannot but be joined to a supernal power, the power of God, blessed be He, except that with them it was in impurity. But in the children, once they converted, that power was refined, purified and made white, and therefore their descendants were great men who taught Torah in public. Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Ta'anis 2): With the Blessed One all is complete mercy, and He gives place to everything in the world, for from His side everything was created only for a good end, and the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing in vain, to the extent that the Sages said, "of the descendants of Haman some studied Torah in Bnei Brak; of the descendants of Sisera some studied Torah in Jerusalem." So too the Blessed One gave a place to Ammon and Moab, though Israel suffered from them, for the sake of the two good doves destined to come from them. Sod Yesharim (Shabbos Chol HaMoed Sukkos 40): On this the verse concludes, "On that day I will give Gog a place there, a grave in Israel": since the Blessed One created them there is surely glory of Heaven in them, for the Holy One, blessed be He, created nothing in vain, and it will remain within Israel, like the glory of Heaven left over from all who oppressed Israel, such as Haman and Sennacherib in their time, of whom the Gemara says, "of the descendants of Haman some studied Torah in Bnei Brak," and likewise "of the descendants of Sisera some studied Torah," and of the descendants of Sennacherib. But they themselves, in their own grasp, were lost and utterly nullified..
This is connected to the well-known tradition that Rabbi Akiva, the foundational figure of the Oral Torah, descended from Sisera (Sanhedrin 96b, according to the version of Ein Yaakov).
וּמִסְּתָמָא הָיָה כֹּחַ זֶה בְּסִיסְרָא, שֶׁאָז הָיְתָה כָּל הַחָכְמָה דְּחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לַחוּץ אֵצֶל אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע.
It follows that some root of this power was present in Sisera, for at that time the wisdom destined for Israel’s sages was still outside, enclosed within that wicked man.

דְּלָכֵן אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה828 Judges 4:3, 4:7 — “And the Children of Israel cried out to the Lord, for he had nine hundred iron chariots, and he oppressed the Children of Israel mightily for twenty years.” And in verse seven: “And I shall draw to you, to the brook of Kishon, Sisera the captain of Yavin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude, and I shall deliver him into your hand.” (מְגִלָּה יד., לְגִרְסַת יַלְקוּט שׁוֹפְטִים רֶמֶז מב, וְכֵן הוּא בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ט): "מַה תָּמָר" וְכוּלֵי, "כָּךְ חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר מוּעָטִים, וְאִשָּׁה הָיְתָה שׁוֹפֶטֶת".

Accordingly our Sages said (Megillah 14a, according to the version in Yalkut Shimoni, Judges 42, and Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah 9), “Just as a date palm…” and so on: “the sages of that generation were few, and a woman was judging.”

רֶמֶז לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, דְּהִיא מִדָּה הַמְקַבֶּלֶת; דְּאָז הָיְתָה הַתְחָלַת הִתְגַּלּוּת יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, בִּלְבוּשׁ עָב דִּקְלִפָּה גְּרוּעָה דְּסִיסְרָא הַמַּקִּיפָתוֹ.

This alludes to Oral Torah, the receptive quality. At that time the foundation of Oral Torah was beginning to reveal itself in this world, but it was wrapped in the coarse, degraded husk of Sisera that surrounded it.

וְאָמְרוּ (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר כב)829 Midrash Tehillim 22:16 — R. Berekhiah said: There are four sayings, three concerning a man and one concerning a woman. Dark is the living one who has need of the dead; dark is the strong man who has need of the weak; dark is the light that has need of the blind. And one concerning a woman, such as Deborah: dark is the generation that a woman leads — "and Deborah, a woman, a prophetess" (Judges 4:4).: "חָשׁוּךְ דָּרָא דְּאִתְּתָא דַּבְרִיתָא" — הַיְנוּ שֶׁהוּא הַחֹשֶׁךְ וּמִדַּת לַיְלָה, כַּנִּזְכָּר.
Thus they said (Shocher Tov, Psalm 22), “Dark is a generation led by a woman”—alluding here to darkness and the quality of night discussed above.

וְזֶה טַעַם תְּשַׁע מֵאוֹת רֶכֶב שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסָחִים קיח:)830 Pesachim 118b — The Holy One, blessed be He, said to the ministering angel of the sea: Spew them out onto the dry land. It said before Him: Master of the Universe, is there a servant whose master gives him a gift and then takes it back from him? He said to it: I will give you one and a half times their number. It said to Him: Master of the Universe, is there a servant who lodges a claim against his master? He said to it: The Kishon River shall be My guarantor. Immediately it spewed them out onto the dry land... What is "one and a half times their number"? Of Pharaoh it is written "six hundred chosen chariots," while of Sisera it is written "nine hundred chariots of iron." Rashi (Rashbam): "Whose master gives him a gift" — the sustenance of the fish. Maharsha: "Whose master gives him a gift": granted that what a slave acquires his master acquires, and that a master may say to him, "Work for me and I shall not feed you" — still, once he has already given him his food it is not the way [of a master] to go back and take it from him. "The Kishon River shall be My guarantor": although with an ordinary guarantor one first sues the borrower, here, since a slave does not sue his master, the guarantor became in effect an unconditional guarantor [who may be claimed from directly]. שֶׁהֶחֱזִיר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַיָּם אֶחָד וּמֶחֱצָה דְּמִצְרַיִם.
This is the meaning of Sisera’s nine hundred chariots, concerning which the Sages taught (Pesachim 118b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, returned to the sea one and a half times the force of Egypt.
הַיְנוּ דִּבְמִצְרַיִם הָיָה בְּגָלוּת הַדַּעַת דַּרְגָּא דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
In Egypt, the faculty of da’at—the level of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and the foundation of the Written Torah—was in exile.
וְלָכֵן הֵם גָּזְרוּ לְהַשְׁלִיךְ הַיְלָדִים לַיְאוֹר, וְכֵן הָיָה מִשְׁפָּטָם, כִּי הֵם רָצוּ לְהַעֲלִים אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
Therefore they decreed that the children be cast into the Nile, and this became their own judgment, for they sought to conceal the light of the Written Torah.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל הָיוּ רְאוּיִים לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה וְלֹא זָכוּ, וְהֵבִיאוּ מַבּוּל לָעוֹלָם, דְּתוֹרָה נִמְשְׁלָה לְמַיִם.
It is known that the generation of the Flood was fit to receive Torah but did not merit it, and instead brought a flood upon the world; Torah is compared to water.
וְכֵן רָצוּ הֵם לַהֲפֹךְ הַדָּבָר לְהַשְׁלִיכָם לַמַּיִם, וּ"בַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר זָדוּ" בָּא עֲלֵיהֶם.
The Egyptians likewise tried to invert this symbolism by casting Israel’s children into the water, and “in the very matter in which they acted presumptuously” punishment came upon them.

כִּי לִהְיוֹת הֵם הַלּוֹחֲצִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, מִסְּתָמָא הָיָה בָּהֶם אֵיזֶה לְבוּשׁ חִיצוֹנִי לְעִנְיַן הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב שֶׁהָיָה בְּנַפְשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהָיוּ תַּחְתֵּיהֶם, וּמְלֻבָּשִׁים בְּקִרְבָּם מַמָּשׁ,

Because they were the oppressors enclosing Israel, they necessarily bore an outer garment corresponding to the Written Torah present in the souls of Israel who were subjected to them and, as it were, enclothed within them.

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה831 Midrash Tehillim 107:4 — R. Abba bar Kahana said in the name of our Rabbis: Like a foetus lying within the womb of an animal, which the shepherd reaches in and draws out — so did the Holy One, blessed be He, do for Israel in bringing them out, as it is said, “to come to take Him a nation from the midst of a nation.” R. Aibu said in the name of R. Yose ben Zimra: Just as a goldsmith puts in his hand and takes the gold out of the furnace, so did the Holy One, blessed be He, bring Israel out of Egypt at once, as it is said, “And He brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt.” Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 20): Egypt, to whom Israel were slaves in complete servitude (and what a slave acquires, his master acquires), had all the holiness of Israel swallowed up within it, as the Sages said on the verse "a nation from the midst of a nation" that they were like a fetus in its mother's womb; and a fetus is reckoned as its mother's thigh, so great was the power of Egypt's connection to the holiness of Israel. Therefore the Torah did not write the prohibition of the Egyptian and the Edomite, only the permission of the third generation, and in the words "you shall not abhor." Rav Tzadok (Es HaOchel 14): The Exodus is called a birth in Ezekiel, "and as for your birth, on the day you were born," and so it is said of "a nation from the midst of a nation," like a fetus in its mother's womb. And the Sages said that the song of Egypt is in the feminine, unlike that of the future, when there will be the birth of a male, for then they will be redeemed through repentance; whereas the Exodus was the birth of a female, which has nothing of its own. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Because some root of Israel was hidden in Haman, his downfall came in Nisan, on Pesach, the time prepared for Israel's going out from the straits of the husks, when the root of Jewishness goes out from every place in which it is sunk. For on Pesach, as it were, He took out "a nation from the midst of a nation," which the Sages expounded "like a fetus in its mother's womb" — that even purity that has been swallowed up is expelled and comes out; and then Mordechai was given the house of Haman and absorbed all the good, and the evil perished of itself. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 3): Remembering the Exodus is a segulah for being remembered with children, for by recalling that miracle one arouses the power of remembrance and brings about the remembrance of the barren as well; for the Exodus too was in the mystery of birth, as the Sages said on "a nation from the midst of a nation," like a fetus slipping out of its mother's womb, and as is known from the Arizal that the Egyptian exile was in the mystery of gestation. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 7): The seed of Jacob, the root of truth in the world, was swallowed up within [Egypt], as it is said on "a nation from the midst of a nation," like a fetus in its mother's womb: that filth so surrounded them that they had no revealed existence of their own. And "he swallowed wealth and shall vomit it up" at the Exodus, when they were chosen as a unique people through the removal of the darkness of Egypt's filth that surrounded them. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares, from the Tanchuma 15): On the side of nature it is said "for My name is within him [bekirbo]," "within" meaning hidden and not perceptible to the eye, as the Sages said on "a nation from the midst [mikerev] of a nation," like a fetus in its mother's womb: it is hidden, yet the fetus is nonetheless recognized, for through understanding one knows there is a fetus in her womb, though it is not actually visible to the eye. This is from the side of wisdom, whereas prophecy is the complete seeing of the name of the Blessed One. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): As long as Israel were still in the Egyptian exile (and the Sages said on "a nation from the midst of a nation" that they were truly within them, wholly surrounded by them, like a fetus, which is its mother's thigh and has no life of its own), [Moses] had to be in Midian. Only after they left Egypt and were chosen as a distinct people was this clarified; but while they were in Egypt like a fetus in its mother's womb, the name "seed of Abraham" still applied to all who were of his seed. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Va'eschanan): "Or has God ventured to come and take Him a nation from the midst of a nation": Israel are so beloved before the Blessed One that even when they do deeds like those of the idolaters, the deeds of Israel are nonetheless good — just as Moses our teacher would not accept the mirrors of the women until the Blessed One answered him that in Israel there is great holiness in this. This is what is called "a nation from the midst of a nation," that the deeds of Israel are good, as the Midrash says: Israel were placed within Egypt like a fetus placed within the womb of an animal, and just as the shepherd puts his hand into her womb and draws it out, so did the Holy One, blessed be He. Sod Yesharim (Parashas Zachor 11): In Egypt Israel were in the aspect of a fetus, as the Midrash says, "like a fetus placed within the womb of an animal ... so did the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said, 'to come and take Him a nation from the midst of a nation'": that is, the Blessed One so surrounded them in Egypt that they were raised above the bounds of this world and returned there to the level of a fetus, as it is written, "when His lamp shone over my head." And "just as the shepherd puts his hand within her womb" means that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave them the one commandment of circumcision, which is two: the cutting, signifying the abiding recognition that they stem from the root of the Blessed One's will, and the uncovering, alluding to all the fences by which Israel restrain themselves. (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב מִזְמוֹר קז) עַל פָּסוּק "גּוֹי מִקֶּרֶב גּוֹי".
This is as our Sages taught (Shocher Tov, Psalm 107) on the phrase “a nation from within a nation.”
וּלְכָךְ נִשְׁלְכוּ לַמַּיִם, אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּפְלְטוּ, כִּי כְּבָר נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה וְנִתְגַּלָּה אוֹרָהּ, וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר לָהֶם שַׁיָּכוּת עִם הַמַּיִם עוֹד.
They were therefore cast into the waters; yet once Torah had been given and its light revealed, they were expelled from those waters, for no further connection to them remained.
וְנִתַּן לַיָּם תְּמוּרָתָם חֵיל סִיסְרָא, שֶׁכְּנֶגֶד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, דְּעֲדַיִן לֹא נִתְבָּרְרָה לְגַמְרֵי עַד עֵת קֵץ.
In their place the sea received Sisera’s army, corresponding to the Oral Torah, whose clarification is not yet complete until the time of the End.
וְהֵם בָּאוּ לַנַּחַל, שֶׁהוּא מִמֵּי גְשָׁמִים הַמִּתְקַבְּצִים אוֹ מַיִם נוֹבְעִים וּבָאִים מֵחָדָשׁ בְּכָל יוֹם.
They came to a stream, whose waters are gathered from rain or spring forth anew each day.
וְכָל הַנְּחָלִים הוֹלְכִים אֶל הַיָּם, שֶׁהוּא מַיָּא דִּקְבִיעִי וְקַיְּמִי, וְהוּא דֻּגְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
All streams flow to the sea, whose waters are fixed and enduring. The stream and sea thus parallel Oral and Written Torah.

וְאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרַשׁ חַנְחוּמָא, חֻקַּת ח)832 Midrash Tanchuma, Chukat 8 — Matters that are concealed from you in this world are destined to be revealed to you in the world to come, like a blind man who regains his sight, as it is written, "I will lead the blind by a way they did not know"; and it is written, "these things I have done" — it is not written "I will do" but "I have done," for I have already done them for R. Akiva and his colleagues. Another interpretation: matters that were not revealed to Moses were revealed to R. Akiva and his colleagues — "his eye has seen every precious thing" (Job 28:10): this is R. Akiva and his colleagues. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): When Moses our teacher passed away, his power and life remained in the world, spreading words of Torah in the hearts of Israel without end; this is the beginning of the Oral Torah, the multiplication of words of Torah without limit, to the point that they said, "the eye of R. Akiva saw what the eye of Moses our teacher did not see." Yet all of it is through Moses' drawing forth and the life he left in the world in the Written Torah, which is called by his name; thus his passing is the open spreading of his power into all the hearts of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 19): Converts are like a surplus and addition to Israel, and "the advantage of the land is in all" — even what is like a surplus has an advantage: "every precious thing" the eye of R. Akiva saw that Moses our teacher did not see, and he was of converts' stock. Moses was comforted when they reached one law and [R. Akiva] said, "it is a law given to Moses at Sinai," for he saw that had he not been the one who began, received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Israel, R. Akiva would have known nothing; all is contained in the Torah, but in the Written Torah it is concealed and in the Oral Torah revealed. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Lag BaOmer 8): The prophets attain through Netzach and Hod, which correspond to Moses and Aaron; but through the Oral Torah one is greater than a prophet, attaining through Da'as and meriting the fiftieth gate, as it is said, "his eye saw every precious thing," the eye of R. Akiva. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): Every new revelation of the Oral Torah comes only through forgetting and concealment, which increase from generation to generation; so after the destruction of the Second Temple it spread further still in the generations of the Tannaim and Amoraim, until the Sages said that "the eye of R. Akiva and his colleagues saw what the eye of Moses did not see." R. Akiva founded the general rules and particulars of the Oral Torah, and he was the arms-bearer of Bar Koziva, for he was fit to bear the arms of the Messiah, the Oral Torah he attained being a model of the vessels of the Messiah's Torah.: "כָּל יְקָר" וְגוֹמֵר — רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, דְּנִתְגַּלָּה לוֹ יוֹתֵר מִלְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.

Our Sages taught (Midrash Hanchuma, Chukkat 8), concerning “every precious thing,” that Rabbi Akiva’s eye saw what was revealed to him beyond what was revealed to Moses our teacher, peace be upon him.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּהַשָּׂגַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מְרֻבָּה יוֹתֵר, עַל דֶּרֶךְ נַנָּס הָרוֹכֵב עַל גַּבֵּי הָעֲנָק, שֶׁהוּא מַשִּׂיג גַּם כֵּן הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב.
The attainment of Oral Torah can extend farther, like a dwarf riding upon the shoulders of a giant: it includes the Written Torah as its foundation and reaches beyond it.

וְזֶה טַעַם (מְנָחוֹת כט:)833 Menachot 29b — Moses said before Him: Master of the Universe, show him to me. He said to him: Turn around.
