He went and sat at the end of the eighth row, and he did not know what they were saying, and his strength failed him. When they reached a certain matter, [R. Akiva's] students said to him: My teacher, from where do you know this? He said to them: It is a law given to Moses at Sinai. And Moses' mind was set at ease. Rashi: "When they reached a certain matter" — one that required a reason. "Moses' mind was set at ease" — since [R. Akiva] said it in his name, even though he had not yet received it [from him]. Maharsha (s.v. "He found the Holy One, blessed be He, sitting and tying crowns"): The "eight rows" are the eight differing arrangements of the alphabet that correspond to the eight vowel points, each carrying its own allusions; Moses did not grasp what they were saying in expounding the letters in reverse order, and his strength failed because it grieved him not to know their intent. When they reached "a certain matter" — the alef that stands at the end of the reverse order and signifies the One — his students asked how he knew that the alef should head the letters to signify unity rather than some other letter, and he answered that this is a law given to Moses at Sinai. At that his mind was set at ease, for he saw that such a matter rests upon human understanding, each man according to his intellect, and that it is impossible to attain all the secrets of the Torah. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Menachos 29b): His strength failed because in this matter R. Akiva's rank was greater than Moses' own. But when Moses perceived that all the laws that are "a law given to Moses at Sinai" were not attained by R. Akiva — since such perceptions are reached through no man, but only from the Holy One, blessed be He, by prophecy, and Moses was His prophet and his attainment was prophetic — he saw that this attainment was his alone; therefore his mind was set at ease, for he grasped by prophecy things that a man cannot grasp. "נִתְקָרְרָה דַעְתּוֹ" דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: "זוֹ מְנָא לָן? הֲלָכָה לְמֹשֶׁה מִסִּינַי".
This explains why Moses’ mind was calmed (Menachot 29b) when Rabbi Akiva’s students said, “From where do we know this? It is a law given to Moses at Sinai.”
דְּהַשֹּׁרֶשׁ הוּא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, רַק זֶה מַשִּׂיג תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב וְגַם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
The root remains the Written Torah; Rabbi Akiva’s attainment embraces both Written and Oral Torah.

וְהִנֵּה מָצִינוּ בַכָּתוּב: "וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵךְ עַד חֲצִי הַמַּלְכוּת" וְגוֹמֵר, דְּבְכָל תֹּקֶף מַעֲלַת הָאִשָּׁה אֵינָהּ מַגַּעַת אֶלָּא לַחֲצִי מַעֲלַת הָאִישׁ, דְּהוּא מוֹשֵׁל בְּכָל הַמַּלְכוּת.

We find in Scripture, “What is your request?—up to half the kingdom, etc.” In this symbolic scheme, even the fullest feminine/receptive level reaches half the masculine level that rules the whole kingdom.
וְזֶהוּ הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן אֶחָד וָחֵצִי דְּסִיסְרָא, שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׂגָה הַמְּעֻלָּה דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב גַּם כֵּן, וַהֲרֵי מַשִּׂיג אֶחָד וָחֵצִי.
This is the ratio of one and a half in Sisera: the heightened attainment of Oral Torah also encompasses Written Torah, and therefore amounts symbolically to one and a half.
וְכָךְ הָיָה בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַמָּסָךְ דִּקְלִפָּה הַחוֹפֵף עַל הַקְּדֻשָּׁה; עָשׂוּ מִזֶּה רֶכֶב בַּרְזֶל לִלְחֹץ אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלִמְנוֹעַ הַשָּׂגַת הַחָכְמָה הָאֲמִתִּית.
When this concealing husk spread over holiness, it became the iron chariot with which Sisera oppressed Israel and prevented access to true wisdom.

דְּזֶה כָּל עִנְיָנָם, שֶׁהוּא שִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכוּת, לְשַׁעְבֵּד מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּבְיָכוֹל, כְּטַעַם גָּלוּת הַשְּׁכִינָה — הַיְנוּ קוֹל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה דְּלָא כְּתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא, וְקוֹל תְּפִלָּה.

This is the essence of subjugation by a foreign kingdom: as it were, to subjugate the Divine attribute of Kingship itself—the exile of the Shechinah—manifest in the unfixed voice of Oral Torah and in the voice of prayer.

items.h:
Seif 3 — Nine Sounds and the Structure of the Worlds
The shofar's numerical patterns map created structure and strip away the shells surrounding the good within the lower worlds.

p: וְטַעַם חֶשְׁבּוֹן שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת וּתְשַׁע מֵאוֹת, כִּי מִסְפַּר תִּשְׁעָה קוֹלוֹת דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה — שְׁלֹשָׁה שֶׁל שְׁלֹשָׁה שְׁלֹשָׁה.
The meaning of the numbers six hundred and nine hundred is connected to the nine shofar sounds of Rosh Hashanah—three groups of three.

הַיְנוּ כִּי כָּל דָּבָר כָּלוּל מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה: שְׁנֵי קְצָווֹת וְאֶמְצַע; בְּאֹרֶךְ וּבְרֹחַב הֲרֵי תִּשְׁעָה, וְהַמָּקוֹם הַכּוֹלֵל הוּא הָעֲשִׂירִי, שֶׁהוּא כְּלַל הַמִּסְפָּרִים בְּכָל קוֹמוֹת הַנִּבְרָאִים, כַּנּוֹדָע.

Every structure contains three aspects—two extremes and a middle. Extended through length and breadth this yields nine points, while the encompassing space is the tenth, the inclusive number throughout the structures of creation.
וְכֵן לְמַעְלָה מַעְלָה בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ הַבְּרִיאָה: עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת, וּ"בְּרֵאשִׁית" נַמֵּי מַאֲמָר הוּא — מַאֲמָר כּוֹלֵל הַבְּרִיאָה.
So too, at the highest root of creation there are ten utterances, with “Bereishit” itself counted as an utterance—the utterance that includes creation as a whole.
וְהוּא דֻּגְמַת מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַמְּכֻוָּן בַּבְּרִיאָה; וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַמִּדּוֹת לְהַגִּיעַ לַתַּכְלִית הֵם תֵּשַׁע.
This corresponds to the attribute of Kingship, the intended culmination of creation; the nine other attributes extend toward that culmination.

וּבְרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה אוֹמְרִים מַלְכֻיּוֹת לְהַמְלִיכוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאַחַר כָּךְ זִכְרוֹנוֹת, דְּבָזֶה מִמֵּילָא "יַעֲלֶה זִכְרוֹנֵיכֶם" וְכוּלֵי (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה טז.)834 Rosh Hashanah 16a — The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Recite before Me on Rosh HaShana Kingships, Remembrances, and Shofarot — Kingships, so that you crown Me as king over you; Remembrances, so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good; and with what? With the shofar. Tosafos (s.v. "with a ram's shofar"): In chapter Ra'uhu Beit Din (26a) the Mishnah records that R. Yosei validates even a cow's horn; but we hold in accordance with R. Yehuda that one sounds with bent rams' horns, as the Gemara rules there (26b). Maharsha (s.v. "recite before Me Kingships"): The Sifrei derives them from the verse "And you shall sound… and they shall be to you for a remembrance… I am the Lord your God" (Numbers 10:10): "you shall sound" — these are Shofarot; "for a remembrance" — these are Remembrances; "I am the Lord your God" — this is Kingships. The intent of Kingships, Remembrances and Shofarot is explained in the chapter "How is the order of fasts" [Taanit, ch. 2]. Maharsha (s.v. "why do we sound a ram's horn"): The Ran explains that [R. Abbahu] asks this about the mere custom of sounding with a ram's horn; but it seems to me that he asks it on the Mishnah in chapter Ra'uhu Beit Din, "R. Yehuda says: On Rosh Hashanah one sounds with [the horns] of males," which is the accepted halachah. This follows the Midrash that Rashi cites on the Torah, that the yovel is a ram's horn (for in Arabic a ram is called yovla), since we derive the shofar of Rosh Hashanah below [in chapter 2] from the shofar of the Jubilee. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 16a, s.v. "Kingships, Remembrances, Shofarot"): Kingships: the Blessed One is King, and as King He comes to judge; therefore Remembrances follow, for remembrance is not judgment — on the contrary, it recalls what was forgotten, and since He remembers everything, reaching what is deep and inward, He remembers Israel for good, and by this they are saved from the attribute of judgment. And this is "by the shofar," for the tekia signifies elevation, and all elevation is mercy, as the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 29): when Israel take up their shofars and sound them, the Holy One, blessed be He, rises from the throne of judgment and sits upon the throne of mercy. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 16a, s.v. "with a ram's shofar"): Rosh Hashanah is the day of judgment, and when they sound a ram's horn it is as though the judgment had already been carried out, for He remembers the binding of Yitzchak, who was bound before the Holy One, blessed be He, as though judgment had been executed upon him. "I shall account it to you" because the father is the root of the son: when the father, the root of the lineage, was bound, the branch resembles him, for Israel too give themselves over to the honor of the Blessed One. In sum, the ram signifies binding and submission to the attribute of judgment, and by giving over our souls to the Blessed One we are saved from the Accuser — which is also why [the shofars] must be bent. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 13): Rosh HaShanah is the Day of Remembrance, for when a person remembers the Blessed One, the Blessed One remembers the person; this too is the matter of the shofar, of which the Sages said, "so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good — with what? With the shofar." Rambam wrote that the shofar hints, "Awake, sleepers, from your slumber … remember your Creator," for it was their way to rouse the people by sounding the shofar; and it is all one — their remembering the Blessed One and their remembrance rising before Him. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeitzei 3): The holiness of Rosh HaShanah, the Day of Remembrance — "so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good, and with what? With the shofar" — is present on the Sabbath to a greater degree; therefore when Rosh HaShanah falls on the Sabbath there is no need to raise our remembrance before Him for good through the act of the shofar, for [the Sabbath] is in itself a day of remembrance. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Rosh HaShanah): In Remembrances the benefit is explicit, but what is the benefit in reciting Kingships? Though a person imagines that the yoke of Heaven's kingship is servitude, in truth it is the true freedom from every servitude in the world, for where the Blessed One dwells no evil draws near, and one who crowns the Blessed One over himself is entirely free; so the Blessed One counsels Israel that in the days of Rosh HaShanah the word "King" be habitual on their lips, a safeguard from all evil. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh HaShanah 15): "Recite before Me Kingships... so that you crown Me": since the Blessed One desires Israel's crowning of Him, a person is obligated to crown Him over himself in every detail. "Remembrances, so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good" — but what has remembrance to do with the Blessed One, when there is no forgetting before His Throne of Glory? Rather it is from the human side, for a person has many distractions and must fix in himself that none will divert him, and "with what? With the shofar" — only through the shofar can he fix this recognition, for the shofar indicates that a person stations himself in the inner voice. Sod Yesharim (Rosh HaShanah 17): "Recite before Me Remembrances" — that you always bring yourselves near before Me and do not stand far off, behind; as much as a person fixes in his heart the awareness that he always stands before the Blessed One and is watched over every moment, so does the Blessed One truly watch over him. "With what? With the shofar" — a person fixes such awareness by contracting his own desires so as to want only the simple will of the Blessed One, and this contraction is called shofar..
On Rosh Hashanah we first recite Kingship verses to enthrone Him, and then Remembrances, through which “your remembrance will rise before Me” (Rosh Hashanah 16a).
דְּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הִיא מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּאֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם, וְיַעֲלֶה זִכְרוֹן כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל.
The collective soul of Israel corresponds to His Kingship, for there is no king without a people; hence the remembrance of Knesset Yisrael rises.
וּבַמֶּה? בַּשּׁוֹפָר, שֶׁהוּא הַמַּעֲלֶה לְמַעְלָה, כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
And by what means does it rise? Through the shofar, which elevates upward, as explained above.
וְהַהַמְשָׁכָה לְמַעְלָה הִיא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת וְהִתְרַחֲבוּת הַמָּקוֹם לְכָל תֵּשַׁע נְקֻדּוֹתָיו, וְהֵם תִּשְׁעָה קוֹלוֹת.
The upward extension is an expansion of the space through all nine of its points; these are the nine sounds.
וּשְׁלֹשָׁה מֵהֶם יְבָבוֹת בַּקַּו הָאֶמְצָעִי, שֶׁבּוֹ הִיא הַמְשָׁכָה הַיְשָׁרָה מִתַּתָּא לְעֵילָא עַל יְדֵי קוֹל דִּתְפִלָּה.
Three of them are yevavot along the middle line, the direct ascent from below to above through the voice of prayer.
דְּתְפַל הוּא דָּבוּק, שֶׁבּוֹ הָאָדָם דָּבוּק לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
The root of tefillah conveys attachment: through prayer man cleaves to the Blessed One.

וְדָא קָלָא דְּעָנִי הַצּוֹעֵק מִן הַמֵּצַר, דְּבָקַע רְקִיעִין וַאֲוִירִין וְסָלֵיק לְמַעְלָה בְּיֹשֶׁר (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קסח, סוֹף עַמּוּד ב)835 Zohar 1:168b — Come and see: the prayer of all other men is prayer; but the prayer of the poor man is the prayer that stands before the Holy One, blessed be He, and breaks through gates and openings and enters to be received before Him. This is what is written, "And it shall be, when he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am gracious"; and it is written, "I will surely hear his cry." "And pours out his complaint before the Lord" — like one who protests against the judgments of the Holy One, blessed be He.,
This is the voice of the poor person crying from constriction, which pierces the heavens and atmospheres and rises straight upward (Zohar I, 168b).
וּמוֹשֶׁכֶת עִמָּהּ לְפָנֶיהָ וּלְאַחֲרֶיהָ קוֹל תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהֵם שְׁנֵי קְצָווֹת.
It draws with it, before and after, the voice of Torah, corresponding to the two sides.
דִּבְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה יֵשׁ נְטִיָּה לִשְׁנֵי קְצָווֹת, כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קוֹל תְּפִלָּה הוּא הוֹלֵךְ בְּיֹשֶׁר לְאִתְדַּבְּקָא בְּעֵץ הַחַיִּים הָעוֹמֵד בַּמֶּרְכָּז.
Oral Torah can incline toward either side, as explained above; prayer moves directly through the center to cleave to the Tree of Life.
וְזֶה כָּל בַּקָּשָׁה דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לְחַיִּים — לְהִתְדַּבֵּק בְּעֵץ הַחַיִּים.
This is the essence of Rosh Hashanah’s petition for life: to cleave to the Tree of Life.
וְזֶה כְּלַל חִלּוּק הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה: שֶׁהֵם בִּמְקַבֵּל הַשֶּׁפַע שָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁל קַבָּלַת הַשֶּׁפַע, וְשָׁלֹשׁ אַחֲרוֹנוֹת שֶׁל הַשְׁפָּעָתָהּ לְמַטָּה, וְאֶמְצָעִיּוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ.
This is the general division into three: the first three aspects receive the influx, the last three transmit it downward, and the middle group joins them.
וְכֵן הַחִלּוּק בְּכָל שְׁלֹשָׁה, וְגוּפָא אוֹ קַו אֶמְצָעִי הוּא תְּפִלָּה, שֶׁבּוֹ הַדִּבּוּק דְּאָדָם בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּכְטַעַם "וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה".
The same division exists within every triad. The body, or middle line, is prayer, through which man attaches to the Blessed One—“I am prayer.”
וּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְּיָמִין, אוֹ שָׁלֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת דְּקַבָּלַת הַשֶּׁפַע, בְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב;
The three on the right—or the first three that receive the influx—correspond to Written Torah;
וּשְׁלֹשָׁה דִּשְׂמֹאל, אוֹ אַחֲרוֹנוֹת, הוּא הַשְׁפָּעַת אָדָם לַזּוּלַת עַל יְדֵי חָכְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
the three on the left—or the latter three—correspond to man transmitting to another, through the wisdom of Oral Torah, what he has apprehended from the Blessed One.
וְלִהְיוֹת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב כָּלוּל בָּהּ גַּם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, לְכָךְ הִיא מִסְפַּר וָו.
Because Written Torah includes Oral Torah within it, together they form the number six.
וּכְשֶׁבָּאָה תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה לְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת בַּלֵּב, דְּנִמְשָׁךְ מִמֶּנָּה הַתְּפִלָּה, אָז הֵם תִּשְׁעָה.
When Oral Torah expands into the heart and prayer is drawn from it, the total becomes nine.
וּמִסְפַּר מֵאוֹת — הַיְנוּ כַּיָּדוּעַ הִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת הַמִּסְפָּרִים חָמֵשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת: יְחִידוֹת, עֲשָׂרוֹת, מֵאוֹת, אֲלָפִים, רְבָבוֹת.
The use of hundreds relates to the known fivefold progression of numbers: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, and ten-thousands.

שֶׁבַּמִּסְפָּרִים כָּךְ הֵם מִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלִים בְּהִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת הָעוֹלָמוֹת, וְכֵן בַּנְּפָשׁוֹת: נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה, חַיָּה, יְחִידָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר836 Yisrael Kedoshim §5, p. 28 — The numbers — units, tens, hundreds, thousands — correspond to the four worlds, Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah. For in Atzilus there is complete unity, and the worlds of separation begin from Beriah; and the completeness of each thing is in the number ten. Therefore from the unfolding of the units that are in Atzilus there come to be ten in Beriah, a hundred in Yetzirah, and a thousand in Asiyah. Hence the blessings of this world, the physical world of Asiyah, come in the number one thousand, and in Yetzirah in the number one hundred, which is the end of number there..
These numerical levels parallel the unfolding of the worlds and, within the soul, nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah, and yechidah, as I have written elsewhere.
וּשְׁלֹשָׁה כֹּחוֹת נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה הֵם מַה שֶּׁבַּגּוּף, וּבָזֶה הוּא הַלְבָּשַׁת הַקְּלִפָּה שֶׁמַּקֶּפֶת הַגּוּף לְבַד, וּלְכָךְ הֵם מִסְפַּר מֵאוֹת.
The first three powers—nefesh, ruach, and neshamah—are those clothed within the body; the husk surrounds only this embodied level, and therefore the symbolic number is in the hundreds.

וּדְבוֹרָה צִוְּתָה לָקַחַת עֲשֶׂרֶת אֲלָפִים לְנַצְּחוֹ, הַיְנוּ אַחְדוּת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא נֶגֶד הַמָּקוֹם הַמְאַחֵד כָּל הַתֵּשַׁע, שֶׁהִיא מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל: "מִי כְעַמְּךָ גּוֹי אֶחָד".

Deborah commanded Barak to take ten thousand men to defeat him. This represents the unity of Israel corresponding to the encompassing point that unites all nine—the quality of Knesset Yisrael: “Who is like Your people, one nation?”
וּבִשְׁלֵמוּת כָּל חָמֵשׁ מַדְרֵגוֹת הַנֶּפֶשׁ הֵם עֲשֶׂרֶת אֲלָפִים.
When all five levels of soul reach completion, the corresponding number is ten thousand. –

וּבְפַרְעֹה נֶאֱמַר: "הָבָה נִתְחַכְּמָה" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁבָּאוּ עֲלֵיהֶם בְּחָכְמָה, וּכְדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (סוֹטָה יא.)837 Sotah 11a — "Therefore they set over him taskmasters" (Exodus 1:11) — it should have said "over them." The school of R. Elazar son of R. Shimon taught: This teaches that they brought a brick mold and hung it upon Pharaoh's neck, and to every Jew who said to them, "I am a delicate man," they said: Are you any more delicate than Pharaoh? "In order to afflict him with their burdens" — it should have said "to afflict them"; rather, to afflict Pharaoh with the burdens of Israel. Rashi: A brick mold is a kind of frame in which bricks are made: it is filled with clay and smoothed, and that is the brick. [They hung it] on Pharaoh, for the passage concerns him and continues from him — "And he said to his people … Come, let us deal wisely with him … and they set over him taskmasters"; "delicate" means pampered and unable to do work. "To afflict Pharaoh" — for the sake of Israel's burdens, so that they would bend their shoulders to bear [them]. Maharsha: On the plain sense — that they set taskmasters over Israel — the verb "set" does not suit the appointment of taskmasters, and it should have written "and they appointed taskmasters over him"; therefore they expounded that the verb does not refer to the taskmasters, but that they literally set a brick mold upon Pharaoh. The objection "it should have said 'over them'" is made only by way of a supporting allusion, as the Re'em writes. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 11a): Here too [the Sages] were exact about the word "over him": wherever it is written it comes to exclude, unlike other singular forms, so it cannot be read as referring to the whole people, and therefore they expounded it of Pharaoh. Yet this does not mean that "over him" refers to Pharaoh himself; rather, a reigning king makes the people like one man, since all depend upon the king, and "they set over him" means that they set taskmasters over the entire people as one — for even the king, who unifies the people, assisted in the building, and because of this all were enslaved as one. The verse hints thereby that all Egypt did to Israel was collective, which shows that it was decreed upon them as a whole by a Divine decree: accidental things are particular, but the matter of Egypt was not accidental, and so it fell upon the whole and not upon the individual. עַל פָּסוּק "וַיָּשִׂימוּ עָלָיו" וְגוֹמֵר, דְּגָזְרוּ גַּם עַל מִצְרַיִם וְאַף עַל פַּרְעֹה, הַכֹּל בְּעָרְמָה.

Regarding Pharaoh it says, “Come, let us deal wisely with them,” for Egypt attacked Israel through cunning. As our Sages explain (Sotah 11a) on “they set over him, etc.,” the decrees were framed as applying even to Egypt and Pharaoh, all through stratagem.
אֲבָל בְּסִיסְרָא נֶאֱמַר "בְּחָזְקָה", הַיְנוּ כִּי לְחִיצַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא הַעֲלָמַת הַחָכְמָה הָאֱנוֹשִׁית גַּם כֵּן, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לְהִתְחַכֵּם נֶגְדּוֹ, רַק בְּחָזְקָה].
With Sisera, however, Scripture says “with force,” because suppressing Oral Torah also suppresses human wisdom itself; such oppression requires no cunning, only force.

וְאַחַר מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר "בֵּין רַגְלֶיהָ כָּרַע" וְגוֹמֵר838 Judges 5:27-28; Yevamot 103a — “At her feet he sank, he fell, he lay; at her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell, despoiled. Through the window she looked out and cried, the mother of Sisera, through the lattice: Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why do the hoofbeats of his chariots tarry?” And in Yevamot 103a, R. Yochanan expounded the repeated language of the verse as indicating the several acts of that wicked man., שֶׁהוּא קְלִיטַת יָעֵל הַטּוֹב דְּסִיסְרָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּעוֹד מָקוֹם839 Takanas HaShavin §10 — And surely it is so with a woman too, in a transgression for the sake of Heaven, like Yael and Esther. As is known, it is said of Yael that she then absorbed the soul of R. Akiva from him [Sisera], and that was the beginning of its emergence from the husk; and presumably it was so with Esther as well. And just as what they did was only outwardly, so the punishment too was only outward, for appearance's sake in this world alone., שֶׁמֵּאוֹתָן בִּיאוֹת יָצָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, וּכְבָר יָצָא כָּל כֹּחוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ.

After the verse “Between her feet he sank, etc.,” which represents Yael’s absorbing the good within Sisera—as I have written elsewhere, that from those unions Rabbi Akiva ultimately emerged—all of Sisera’s holy potential had already departed from him.

נֶאֱמַר: "וַתְּיַבֵּב אֵם סִיסְרָא", כִּי עִקַּר כֹּחַ הַצְּעָקָה וּתְפִלָּה בָּאִשָּׁה, כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּהִיא מִסִּטְרָא דְנוּקְבָא, כִּי הָאִשָּׁה חֲסֵרָה וּמְבַקֶּשֶׁת הַשְׁלָמָה מִמַּשְׁלִימָהּ לְעוֹלָם.

Then it says, “The mother of Sisera wailed.” The essential power of crying out and prayer is associated with the feminine/receptive side, for the woman is described here as lacking and continually seeking completion from the one who completes her.

וְסִיסְרָא הָיָה בְּכֹחוֹ מַלְבִּישׁ כָּל כֹּחַ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה דְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, וְאִמּוֹ שֶׁהֱבִיאַתּוּ לָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהָיָה גָּנוּז כָּל זֶה בְּכֹחָהּ, הִיא הָיְתָה הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כֹּחָהּ בְּקוֹל צְעָקָה מֵעֵין קוֹל דִּתְפִלָּה.

Sisera’s power had clothed the entire potential of Rabbi Akiva’s Oral Torah; his mother, who brought him into the world and in whose power this potential had been hidden, expressed her own power in a cry resembling the voice of prayer.
אֲבָל לֹא בִּתְפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; שֶׁהִיא חֵלֶק רַע, רַק בִּיבָבָא דִילָהּ.
Yet it was not prayer to the Blessed One; its evil side remained only as her raw wailing.
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁכָּל שֹׁרֶשׁ קוֹל דִּיבָבָה הָיָה אָז מְעֻטָּף בִּלְבוּשׁ שַׂק דִּידָהּ, וַדַּאי הָיָה בָּהּ כָּל עֹצֶם כֹּחַ דִּיבָבָה.
Since the entire root-power of wailing was then wrapped in her sackcloth-like garment, the full intensity of yevava was concentrated within her.
כִּי וַדַּאי עִנְיַן הַנִּזְכָּר בַּכָּתוּב אֵינוֹ כְּסִפּוּר דְּבָרִים בְּעָלְמָא, וּכְשֶׁהַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר "וַתְּיַבֵּב", מִסְּתָמָא כָּל כֹּחַ דִּיבָבָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הָיָה בָּהּ אָז.

The Torah’s description is not mere storytelling. When Scripture says “she wailed,” it indicates that the total archetypal power of wailing present in the world was concentrated in her at that moment.

וְזֶה טַעַם מַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לג:)840 Tosafot on Rosh Hashanah 33b:5:1 — And the Arukh explained that this is what they used to do — he explained in the entry "erev": those who are stringent make thirty [blasts] while seated, thirty in the silent prayer, and thirty in the order [of the repetition], corresponding to the hundred cries that the mother of Sisera cried; and the remaining ten are those sounded when the whole prayer is completed, for the sound of the individual's blasts must be ten — tekia-shevarim-terua-tekia, tekia-shevarim-tekia, tekia-terua-tekia — and they are a hundred. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Hashanah 13): The hundred shofar blasts correspond to the hundred cries of Sisera's mother (Tosafot, citing the Arukh) because, as R. Menachem Azariah of Fano writes, R. Akiva, the root of the Oral Torah, issued from Sisera, who came upon Yael: that soul was in exile, surrounded by the husk, with Sisera, and Yael brought it out of him, which ended their life, for it had been the essence of their vitality. A hundred denotes utmost completeness, each of the ten attributes comprising all ten, and while the spark of the Oral Torah was with Sisera the husk too had a hundred powers; therefore his mother cried a hundred cries, and correspondingly we blow a hundred blasts, to merit thereby the aspect of the Oral Torah. Sod Yesharim (Rosh Hashanah 95): The accusers are called "windows," as in "through the window she looked out," and opposite them the Blessed One gives Israel counsel to arouse mercy, that He watch "from the windows" with salvation and mercy. Balaam cried out seventy times but the mother of Sisera a hundred, for Sisera came with greater power than Balak and Balaam, so that the stars had to fight him from their courses; and the hundred cries allude to a time of distress from the arousal of accusation, like the hundred cries of a woman in labor, ninety-nine toward death and one toward life. Therefore, to nullify the accusation of the hundred cries we blow a hundred blasts, to arouse providence "from the windows" opposite the windows of the accusers. בְּשֵׁם הֶעָרוּךְ, דְּמֵאָה קוֹלוֹת דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה נֶגֶד מֵאָה פְּעָיוֹת דְּפָעְיָא אִימֵיהּ דְּסִיסְרָא.
This is the meaning of Tosafot’s statement (Rosh Hashanah 33b), citing the Arukh, that the one hundred shofar sounds correspond to the one hundred cries uttered by Sisera’s mother.
וְהַיְנוּ כִּי כָּל כֹּחַ יְבָבָא הָיָה מְלֻבָּשׁ בָּהּ.
For the entire power of yevava was clothed within her.
וִיבָבָתָהּ עַל קְלִיטַת הַטּוֹב שֶׁבְּסִיסְרָא, שֶׁהוּא הֶעְדֵּר הַחִיּוּת דְּרַע לְגַמְרֵי, וַדַּאי הָיְתָה בְּכָל תֹּקֶף.
Her wailing over the removal of the good from Sisera—which meant the total loss of vitality from the evil—was therefore of the greatest intensity.

וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ מֵאָה פְּעָיוֹת לֹא נִזְכַּר מְנָא לְהוּ; אֲבָל נִמְצָא לָשׁוֹן זֶה בְּדִבְרֵי רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כז)841 Vayikra Rabbah 27:7 — R. Levi opened: "Behold, you are nothing, and your work is naught [me'afa]." "Nothing" — from nothing at all, from a putrid drop. "Me'afa" — from the hundred cries [me'ah pe'iyot] that a woman cries out while she sits upon the birthstool, ninety-nine of them toward death and one toward life. עַל פָּסוּק "מֵאַפֵּעַ" — מִמֵּאָה פְּעָיוֹת שֶׁהַיּוֹלֶדֶת פּוֹעָה בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁמּוֹלִידָה.

The source for the number one hundred cries is not stated there, but a similar expression appears in Vayikra Rabbah 27: the phrase me’afe’a is interpreted as the one hundred cries of a woman in labor.
וּלְפִי שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה דֻּגְמַת לֵידָה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי קְלִיטַת יָעֵל מִסִּיסְרָא הֻצְרַךְ לָצֵאת גַּם מִמֶּנָּה הַמְלֻבָּשׁ בָּהּ, וְיָצָא עַל יְדֵי יְבָבוֹת הַלָּלוּ.
Because Yael’s absorption of the good within Sisera was analogous to a birth, that same potential also had to emerge from Sisera’s mother, in whom it was clothed; it came forth through these cries.
וּכְבָר נִתְבָּאֵר דְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן מֵאָה הוּא כְּנֶגֶד כְּלַל שְׁלֹשָׁה כֹּחוֹת דְּנֶפֶשׁ הַמְלֻבָּשִׁים תּוֹךְ הַגּוּף,
It was explained above that the number one hundred corresponds collectively to the three powers of soul clothed within the body.
וְהוּא בִּכְלַל פְּעִיָּה אַחַת דְּ"יוֹם תְּרוּעָה", דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר צְעָקָה יְחִידִית, וּבְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּתָהּ הוּא מֵאָה, שֶׁמִּשָּׁם וָהָלְאָה תִּתְפַּשֵּׁט עַד אֵין קֵץ,
All of this is included in one primal cry of the “day of teruah,” a single cry which, when expanded, becomes one hundred and from there can extend without end.
אַחַר שֶׁיָּצָא מִכָּל מֵאָה פְּעָיוֹת דְּרַע הַמַּלְבִּישׁ וּמַקִּיף לַטּוֹב, הַמְכֻנֶּה בְּשֵׁם יְבָבוֹת דְּאִימֵיהּ דְּסִיסְרָא,
This occurs after it has emerged from all one hundred cries of evil that had clothed and surrounded the good—the cries identified with Sisera’s mother.
שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד תְּלָת עָלְמִין בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה, דְּשָׁם יֵשׁ מִשְׁכָּן לָרַע; מִשָּׁם וָהָלְאָה כֻּלּוֹ טוֹב וְאֵין מָקוֹם לָרַע כְּלָל.
These correspond to the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, in which evil has a foothold; beyond them all is good and there is no place for evil at all.
וּמִשָּׁם בָּאָה הָעֲנִיָּה דְּבַמֶּרְחָב, וְאֵין לְהַאֲרִיךְ כָּעֵת יוֹתֵר.
From there comes the answer of Divine expansiveness; I cannot elaborate further at present.

sections.en: Four Paths of Divine Apprehension

items.h: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David embody four modes of knowing Hashem: created faith, visionary recognition, holy unity, and the renewed closeness born through repentance.

Seif 1 — Abraham: Recognition of the Creator
The first path is simple recognition of a Creator, discovered through creation and inherited by Israel from birth.

p: אַרְבָּעָה מִינֵי הַשָּׂגוֹת וּדְרָכִים לָבוֹא לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יֵשׁ.
There are four kinds of apprehension and four paths by which one comes to serve the Blessed One.
הָרִאשׁוֹנָה — הַהַכָּרָה מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא נִבְרָא וְיֵשׁ בּוֹרֵא.
The first is recognition arising from the fact that one is a created being and that there is a Creator.

וְזֶהוּ הַשָּׂגַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (נְדָרִים לב. וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת)842 Nedarim 32a — R. Ami bar Abba said: Abraham recognized his Creator at the age of three years, as it is stated: "Because [ekev] Abraham hearkened to My voice" — the numerical value of ekev is one hundred and seventy-two [and Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years]. Rashi: "One hundred and seventy-two" — this is the sense of the verse: for the number of years equal to the numerical value of ekev, one hundred and seventy-two, Abraham hearkened to My voice; and since all his years were one hundred and seventy-five, it follows that he recognized his Creator at the age of three. Maharsha: It appears that the beginning of his knowledge, when he recognized his Creator, was at three years of age; but the "days of Torah" were not reckoned to him until his fifty-second year, when his knowledge was complete enough to be imparted to others, as is said in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah that the two thousand years of Torah are counted from Abraham's fifty-second year, as it is stated of him, "and the souls that they had made in Haran." Maimonides wrote in his Book of Knowledge that Abraham recognized his Creator at forty, and Rabad has already objected to him from this passage. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 32a): These three years correspond to the years of orlah, of which it is said, "When you plant any tree for food... three years it shall be as uncircumcised to you, and in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy for praise-giving" — as is explained in the Midrash on the portion of Kedoshim; when he reached three years the husk was removed from him and he was wholly sanctified. Understand further: man is in potential and comes forth into actuality, and is not actual from the beginning of his creation; and just as we find that a tree is in potential for three years — which is why its fruit is forbidden until three years — and only then comes forth into actuality, so too Abraham came forth into actuality when he was three years old, and then he recognized his Creator. שֶׁהִכִּיר אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁיֵּשׁ מִי שֶׁבְּרָאוֹ.

This was the attainment of our father Abraham, peace be upon him. Our Sages of blessed memory said (Nedarim 32a and elsewhere) that he recognized his Creator—that is, he recognized that there is One who created him.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה לט)843 Bereshit Rabbah 39:1 — R. Yitzchak said: This is like a man who was traveling from place to place and saw a certain palace alight. He said: Is it possible that this palace has no one in charge of it? The owner of the palace looked out at him and said to him: I am the owner of the palace. So too, because our father Abraham was saying, Is it possible that this world has no one in charge of it? — the Holy One, blessed be He, looked out at him and said to him: I am the Owner of the world. שֶׁאָמַר: אֶפְשָׁר לְבִירָה בְּלֹא מַנְהִיג?
Thus our Sages of blessed memory taught (Bereishit Rabbah, beginning of section 39) that he said: Can there be a palace without a master?
וְזֶהוּ כְּלָלוּת הַהַשָּׂגָה שֶׁל כָּל הַנִּבְרָאִים, שֶׁלְּתַכְלִית כֵּן נִבְרְאוּ — שֶׁיַּכִּירוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא.
This is the universal apprehension belonging to all created beings, for they were created for this purpose: to recognize that there is a Creator.
וְלָכֵן נִקְרָא "אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם", שֶׁהָיָה אָב לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, שֶׁהוּא הָאָב וְהַהַתְחָלָה לְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת זוֹ בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ.
Therefore he was called 'a father of a multitude of nations,' for he was a father to the entire world—the father and beginning of this awakening throughout the world.
כִּי כָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ כְּאִישׁ אֶחָד, וּכְשֶׁנִּבְרָא אֶחָד מִתְעוֹרֵר לְהַכָּרַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ — מְעוֹרֵר כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ עִמּוֹ.
For the entire world is like one person: when one created being awakens to recognition of the Blessed One, he awakens the whole world with him.
כְּמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל בְּאָדָם אֶחָד, כְּשֶׁאֵבֶר הַלֵּב מִתְעוֹרֵר לְאֵיזוֹ פְּעֻלָּה, כָּל הָאֵבָרִים מִתְעוֹרְרִים עִמּוֹ, וּבִלְבַד שֶׁהִיא פְּעֻלָּה הַשַּׁיֶּכֶת בָּהֶם.
By analogy, in a single person, when the organ of the heart is aroused toward an action, all the limbs are aroused with it, provided that the action is relevant to them.
וְהַשָּׂגָה זוֹ שֶׁל הַכָּרַת בּוֹרֵא הִיא הַשָּׂגָה הָרְאוּיָה לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ כְּשֶׁיִּהְיוּ בְּמַדְרֵגַת שְׁלֵמוּתָם, שֶׁזֶּה כָּל תַּכְלִיתָם בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא.
This recognition of a Creator is the apprehension appropriate to the whole world when its creatures attain their perfection, for this is their entire purpose in the created world.
וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא הָרִאשׁוֹן הַמְעוֹרֵר הַשָּׂגָה זוֹ בְּכָל כֹּחַ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ, עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אָב בָּזֶה לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ.
Our father Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first to awaken this apprehension through the full force of his own striving, until in this respect he became a father to the entire world.
וְלָאֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית בְּיִחוּד נֶאֱמַר: "בְּיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע".
With regard to the nation of Israel specifically, however, it is said: 'Through Isaac shall offspring be called yours.'

שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה אָב, אֵין הֵם קְרוּיִים זַרְעוֹ; כִּי זֶרַע נִקְרָא מַה שֶּׁלֵּדָתוֹ הוּא כְּמוֹ הָאָב, וְאֵין הַזֶּרַע צָרִיךְ לְשׁוּם פְּעֻלָּה לִהְיוֹת דּוֹמֶה לַדָּבָר הַמַּזְרִיעַ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִמֵּילָא טֶבַע הַתּוֹלָדָה.

Although Abraham was a father, they are not all called his seed. 'Seed' means that what is born resembles its father by nature; the offspring needs no act of its own to resemble the one who engendered it, for this likeness comes automatically through birth.

וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נִקְרָא (חֲגִיגָה ג.)844 Chagigah 3a — Rava expounded: What is meant by "How beautiful are your steps in sandals, O daughter of the noble"? How beautiful are the feet of Israel when they go up for the pilgrimage festival. "Daughter of the noble" — the daughter of Abraham our father, who is called noble, as it is said, "The nobles of the peoples are gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham." "The God of Abraham," and not the God of Isaac and Jacob? Rather, "the God of Abraham," for he was the first of the converts. Rashi: "Who is called noble" — because his heart moved him of its own accord to recognize his Creator. "The nobles of the peoples" — these are the converts, who volunteer from among the nations to take upon themselves the yoke of the commandments. Tosafos (s.v. "the first of the converts"): Because he was commanded concerning circumcision, unlike all those who came before him. Maharsha: "How beautiful are the feet of Israel" — for whoever's foot is not sound does not go up at all, as below, "excluding one who is lame." And their beauty is made to depend on their going in sandals, because one who goes barefoot goes in pain, as it is said, "Withhold your foot from being unshod" (Jeremiah 2:25), whereas these went up on foot in gladness, with their offerings of rejoicing; and so the Targum renders it, "How lovely are your steps, three times a year, in sandals." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 3): Tractate Avodah Zarah serves to clarify the distinctions between Israel and the idolaters, and Abraham's Avodah Zarah "was four hundred chapters," for Abraham is called "father of a multitude of nations" — as stated at the beginning of Chagigah, he is called "the first of the converts" — and, as it is said, he "recognized his Creator," implying that at first he did not. Hence [on Pesach night] one "begins with disgrace": "at first our fathers were idol worshippers." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): Abraham our father too is called "father of a multitude of nations," for he was not born from the womb of the seed of Israel, who are borne from the womb with the Blessed One as the rock of their heart by birth; for he is called "the first of the converts," since it was through his own effort that he merited the understanding of the heart and to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite" — like a native in Israel, who is an Israelite from the womb. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bechukosai 14): [If Israel cannot resemble Isaac, who was born in holiness, circumcised at eight days without his own knowledge, and so became Israel,] the deeds of Abraham suffice: for Abraham is called "the first of the converts" and sought to bring the whole world under the wings of the Shechinah, being "father of a multitude of nations" — the father of all converts — whereas Isaac is not found to have made converts. And although Abraham's converts were helped only in his lifetime, for after his passing they broke the covenant, his covenant helped at least his own seed, so that whoever is of the seed of Israel is in any case superior to a convert. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 9): Abraham our father, who is called "the first of the converts," is the beginning of the holiness that comes from below — fencing all his limbs and faculties within holiness — and he had to draw himself near, as is said of converts in Kiddushin; he was tested with ten trials so that every level would be clarified in him through his own holiness from below, in battle with the inclination. And although he afterwards merited to be called "Eitan the Ezrachite," reckoned as a native in Israel, that was after Jacob came forth from him. תְּחִלָּה לְגֵרִים, שֶׁהוּא בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ הִגִּיעַ לְהַכָּרַת בּוֹרֵא.
Our father Abraham, peace be upon him, is called (Chagigah 3a) the first of the converts, because through his own exertion he attained recognition of the Creator.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל — מַאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים בְּתוֹלָדָה.
The Children of Israel, by contrast, are believers, descendants of believers, by birth.
וּלְדָבָר זֶה אֵין צָרִיךְ שׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, כִּי מוֹרָשָׁה לָהֶם זֶה מִמַּה שֶּׁהֵם זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם.
For this they require no exertion, because it is their inheritance by virtue of being the seed of Abraham.

וְזֶהוּ הַחִלּוּק בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים: שֶׁכָּל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם לִהְיוֹת "בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכֻנֶּה" — דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (אָבוֹת דְּרַבִּי נָתָן פֶּרֶק לו; סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק יח)845 Avot DeRabbi Natan 36:1 — Others say: They do enter [the World to Come], and of them Scripture says, "One shall say, I am the Lord's; and another shall call himself by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe with his hand to the Lord, and surname himself by the name of Israel" (Isaiah 44:5). "One shall say, I am the Lord's" — these are the wholly righteous. "And another shall call himself by the name of Jacob" — these are the young children of the wicked. "And another shall subscribe with his hand to the Lord" — these are the wicked who turned from their ways and repented. "And surname himself by the name of Israel" — these are the righteous converts from among the nations of the world.: אֵלּוּ גֵּרֵי הַצֶּדֶק.

This is the distinction between Israel and the nations. Regarding all the striving of the nations to reach the state described as 'he shall be called by the name Israel,' our Sages of blessed memory interpreted it (Avot deRabbi Natan 36; Seder Eliyahu Rabbah 18) as referring to righteous converts.

שֶׁיַּגִּיעוּ לְהַכָּרָה זוֹ וְלֶאֱמוּנָה טִבְעִית שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁבַּעֲבוּרָהּ נִקְרְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהוּא אֶצְלָם בְּתוֹלָדָה — שֶׁתִּינוֹק בֶּן יוֹמוֹ נִקְרָא יִשְׂרָאֵל — וְאֶצְלָם הוּא בְּעֶצֶם וּמִשֹּׁרֶשׁ.

They attain this recognition and the natural faith found in Jewish hearts, on account of which they are called Israel. For Israel it is present from birth—a one-day-old infant is called an Israelite—and it belongs to them essentially and at the root.
וְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, בְּכָל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם, יוּכְלוּ לְהַגִּיעַ שֶׁ"בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכֻנֶּה" דֶּרֶךְ כִּנּוּי לְבַד, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּעֶצֶם אֶצְלָם.
The nations of the world, with all their striving, can reach a state in which they are 'called by the name Israel' only as a designation, since it is not intrinsic to them.
רַק בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת מַגִּיעִים לָאֱמוּנָה הַפְּשׁוּטָה שֶׁאֵצֶל כָּל זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּתוֹלָדָה.
Only through exertion do they attain the simple faith that exists by birth in every descendant of our father Abraham, peace be upon him.
וְזֶהוּ קְדֻשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת, דְּקְבִיעָא וְקַיְּמָא, זֵכֶר לְמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, וְהִיא אוֹת בֵּינִי וּבֵין בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
This is the sanctity of Shabbat, which is fixed and enduring, a remembrance of Creation, and 'a sign between Me and the Children of Israel.'
וְעוֹבֵד כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת שֶׁשָּׁבַת חַיָּב וְכוּלֵי, דְּהֵם צְרִיכִים לְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ לִזְכִירַת מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, דְּהַיְנוּ הַכָּרַת הַבּוֹרֵא.
A gentile who observes Shabbat is liable, and so forth, because the nations require exertion in order to come to remembrance of Creation—that is, recognition of the Creator.
דְּזֶה הָיָה אָז בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי הַבְּרִיאָה, שֶׁהוּא הוֹצָאַת הַנִּבְרָאִים לַפֹּעַל.
That recognition was manifest in the six days of Creation, the days in which the created beings were brought into actuality.
וְשַׁבָּת הוּא הַנַּיְחָא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אַחַר כָּךְ מִנִּבְרָאִים כְּשֶׁמַּכִּירִין בּוֹרְאָם.
Shabbat is the satisfaction, as it were, that the Blessed One has afterward from created beings when they recognize their Creator.
וְדָבָר זֶה, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַבְּרִיאָה, וַדַּאי צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מֻשְׁרָשׁ כֵּן אֵצֶל הַנִּבְרָאִים.
This, being the purpose of creation, must certainly be rooted within the created beings themselves.
רַק לְפִי שֶׁעִקַּר הַבְּרִיאָה הֵם יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֵין זֶה מֻשְׁרָשׁ בְּתוֹלָדָה רַק אֶצְלָם.
But because Israel is the primary purpose of creation, this is rooted by birth only within them.

וְזֶהוּ "בְּרֵאשִׁית" — בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי846 Vayikra Rabbah 36:4 — R. Berechiah said: Heaven and earth were created only in the merit of Israel, as it is written, “In the beginning God created” — and “beginning” means nothing but Israel, as it is said, “Israel is holy to the Lord, the first of His produce.”.
This is the teaching on 'Bereishit'—that the world was created for the sake of Israel, and so forth.

פֵּרוּשׁ, "רֵאשִׁית" הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה, כִּי הַכָּרַת נִבְרָא לַבּוֹרֵא הוּא בַּהַתְחָלָה; כִּי בַּהַתְחָלָה שָׁם הַהַכָּרָה מְפֹרֶשֶׁת לָעַיִן, שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם לְהִסְתַּפֵּק וְאֵין צָרִיךְ שׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת.

'Beginning' means precisely the beginning, because the created being's recognition of the Creator belongs to the beginning. At the beginning the recognition is plainly evident to the eye, leaving no room for doubt and requiring no exertion.

וְזֶהוּ (שַׁבָּת י847 Shabbat 10b — Rava bar Mechasya said in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav: One who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him, as it is stated, "to know that I, the Lord, sanctify you." This was likewise taught in a baraita: "To know that I, the Lord, sanctify you" — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses: I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name, and I wish to give it to Israel; go and inform them. Rashi: "Must inform him": [he should say,] "I will give you such-and-such a gift" — this is the respectful way, for otherwise he might be ashamed to accept it, whereas this way they come to terms in words beforehand and he is not ashamed of it; and likewise, if he left it in his house without his knowledge, he must let him know that it came from his hand, for through this he will love him. "To know that I, the Lord, sanctify you": I come to inform them that I wish to sanctify them. Tosafos (s.v. "one who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him"): This applies only to a gift given out of love, at which the recipient is not ashamed; but one who gives charity, at which the recipient is ashamed, [should give in secret, as it says,] "A gift in secret pacifies anger" (Proverbs 21:14). Maharsha (s.v. "in My treasure house"): According to the conclusion, which refers [the need to inform] to Shabbat's reward, which does not become known of itself, the "good gift" is the Shabbat of the World to Come, which is wholly good and wholly Shabbat, and "My treasure house" is the great good hidden away for the righteous, of which it is said, "No eye has seen, O God, besides You." On the initial supposition, that it speaks of the Shabbat of this world, which does become known, the good gift is the rest itself — for the labor of the six days belongs to Adam's curse, "by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread," which is why a Noahide who rests is liable — and "My treasure house" is the rest that Adam had on all days before he sinned. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 10b): Just as the one is a giver, the other must be a complete receiver of the gift — otherwise there is no giving here — and one who does not know from whom he receives is not called a receiver; therefore he must inform him, unless the recipient is poor and in need of sustenance, for then [the giver] intended only to sustain him. Shabbat in particular had to be made known because, unlike the other commandments, whose reward merely follows from them, its gift is itself the World to Come — for Shabbat is a semblance of the World to Come, "the day that is entirely Shabbat" — and so He said, "I have a good gift in My treasure house," that is, the good hidden away for the righteous, which is the World to Come. Maharal (Derech Chaim 3:14): When one makes his love known to another, he seeks that one's love in return, like one who says, "See, I have done you this kindness; it is fitting that you love me for it." For this reason they said, "One who gives a gift to his fellow must inform him": whoever receives a gift ought to love the one who gives it, and therefore one must let him know that one is giving him the gift, so that there may be peace between the giver and the receiver. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parashas Shekalim 15): Haman's offer "to bring into the king's treasuries" alludes to "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name": the horn exalted through the shekels and charity reaches without limit up to Atika [the Ancient One], and this is the holiness of Shabbat — the revelation of Atika that one merits on Shabbat — and this is "in My treasure house." Haman claimed that he too could "bring into the king's treasuries" by giving such lavish charity that his horn would be exalted. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): On "to know that I, the Lord, sanctify you," the Gemara says, "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name"; and of its reward, which He is not wont to reveal, He said "to know" — perforce, with "that I [the Lord sanctify you]" He informed them of its reward, for the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah, the holiness it brings into the heart. This is the good gift the Blessed One gave Israel: a root of holiness fixed and enduring in their hearts, from the light of His Presence that dwells with them even amid their impurity, without human effort. Beis Yaakov (Toldos 41): "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name; go and inform them" — that is, that Israel should know that the Blessed One sanctifies them, as it is written, "to know that I, the Lord, sanctify you"; this is a sign that Shabbat is exceedingly good and great, and the Blessed One said "go and inform them" because the main thing is recognition. When Israel wish to taste the holiness of Shabbat they must give over their recognition too to the Blessed One, and this is called "Ayin" [nothingness]. Sod Yesharim (Purim 10): My father explained that the supreme will, above human grasp, by which the Blessed One chose Israel even before their service, is the light called Atika, far above the grasp of creation; the Blessed One concealed this light in this world, and it is to this light that the Sages alluded: "I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbat is its name.":): "מַתָּנָה טוֹבָה יֵשׁ לִי בְּבֵית גְּנָזַי, וְשַׁבָּת שְׁמָהּ" וְכוּלֵי.
This is the meaning of the teaching (Shabbat 10b): 'I have a good gift in My treasure-house, and Shabbat is its name,' and so forth.

פֵּרוּשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לג:)848 Berakhot 33b — And R. Chanina said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, as it is stated: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear [Him]” (Deuteronomy 10:12). Is the fear of Heaven then a small matter? But R. Chanina said in the name of R. Shimon ben Yochai: The Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His treasury but a store of the fear of Heaven, as it is stated: “The fear of the Lord — that is his treasure” (Isaiah 33:6). Rashi: "Everything is in the hands of Heaven" — whatever comes upon a man is in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He: tall or short, poor or rich, wise or foolish, fair or dark, all is in the hands of Heaven. But righteous or wicked does not come by the hand of Heaven; this He delivered into man's own hand, and set two ways before him, and he will choose the fear of Heaven for himself. Maharsha: Fear is of two kinds: the natural fear, which is fear of punishment, and resembles a small vessel; and the fear of the intellect, awe before what is great and awesome, as in "and he was afraid and said, How awesome is this place" — and that is the complete fear, resembling a large vessel. The objection from "the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His treasury but a store of the fear of Heaven" concerns that complete, intellectual fear, which is indeed a treasured thing fit to be laid up in the Lord's treasury, and no small matter. The answer, that with Moses it is a small matter, is that Israel already feared Moses himself with that very fear of the intellect — "the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him" — and therefore he could say, "What does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear Him," as you fear me. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 1): The Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His treasury but fear, because fear alone reaches the very essence of His Godhood: the Aramaic rendering of "God" is "dachala," a word of fear, and in the language of the Sages, "He took His fear out of His bosom." And "with Moses it is a small matter": fear is not something added to a man, as wisdom is added when he acquires more of it, for the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world only that they should fear before Him. One who lacks fear lacks something great, but one who has it has acquired nothing beyond what is required of him — as with bread, upon which a man's life depends: having it is no surplus, while lacking it is a great lack. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 7): Shabbos, a semblance of the World to Come, is called a "good gift" "in My treasure-house," and the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing but a store of fear of Heaven: in the store of fear the Shabbos is hidden, for fear is the purity of the heart, and hence the Community of Israel is called "fear." In this world one uses the powers of action, while the World to Come is the heart alone. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Masei 9): One must understand: the Sages said the Holy One, blessed be He, has nothing in His treasure-house but a store of fear of Heaven, and that cannot be the "good gift" He gives Israel, since fear of Heaven is in man's hand alone. Rather, the treasure-house is the store of fear of Heaven, and within this store lies the good gift: the three gifts the Holy One created — wisdom, might and wealth — come "from the power of the Holy One's might," the attribute of Kingship, which is fear; all three are in His treasure-house, the store of fear of Heaven, and Shabbos, which includes all three, is therefore called a "good gift.": אֵין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא אוֹצָר שֶׁל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם — זֶהוּ בֵּית גְּנָזָיו.
That is, as they said (Berakhot 33b): the Holy One, blessed be He, has no treasure, as it were, except a treasury of fear of Heaven; this is His treasure-house.
כִּי גִּנְזֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ הֵם רְכוּשׁוֹ, שֶׁבַּעֲבוּר כֵּן נִקְרָא מֶלֶךְ.
For a king's treasures are his possessions, on account of which his kingship is expressed.
וְגִנְזֵי מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם הוּא הַיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֶׁיֵּשׁ עַל הַנִּבְרָאִים עַל יְדֵי הַכָּרָתָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא, שֶׁמִּזֶּה נוֹפֶלֶת יִרְאָה.
The treasures of the Kingdom of Heaven are the fear of Heaven that rests upon created beings through their recognition that there is a Creator, for from such recognition awe arises.
וְהַיִּרְאָה בָּאָה אַחַר הַהַכָּרָה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּרֵישׁ הַגָּהַת שֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ, אוֹרַח חַיִּים.
Awe follows recognition, as is written at the beginning of the glosses to the Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chaim.
וְהַיִּרְאָה הוּא מַה שֶּׁבִּידֵי אָדָם, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא "שׁוֹאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ" — רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר מֵעֶצֶם אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי, שֶׁהַהַכָּרָה אֶצְלוֹ בְּתוֹלָדָה.
Awe is the element placed in human hands, and the Holy One, blessed be He, 'asks it of you'—meaning from the very essence of the Jew, in whom recognition is present by birth.
וְזֶהוּ הַמַּתָּנָה טוֹבָה דְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁבָּאָה בְּמַתָּנָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הוּא הֵפֶךְ שְׁבִיתָה.
This is the good gift of Shabbat that is given as a gift to Israel, for exertion is the opposite of cessation.
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ לָזֶה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת; רַק הוּא אֱמוּנָה פְּשׁוּטָה בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, שֶׁכָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מַאֲמִינִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא וּמַנְהִיג וּמַשְׁגִּיחַ.
It cannot be reached through effort; rather, it is simple faith without exertion—the faith of every Jew that there is a Creator, a Guide, and a Providence.
וְאָמְנָם עֲדַיִן אֱמוּנָה זוֹ בְּהֶעְלֵם, שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ לְעִנְיָן שֶׁיַּעֲזוֹב בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִצַּד אֱמוּנָה זוֹ.
Yet this faith still remains concealed; it is not fully revealed in the heart to the extent that a person would truly relinquish all worldly concerns because of it.

וַאֲפִלּוּ מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מַה וְכוּלֵי — הֲרֵי זֶה מִקְּטַנֵּי אֲמָנָה849 Sotah 48b — It was taught: R. Eliezer the Great says — whoever has bread in his basket and says “What shall I eat tomorrow?” is nothing but one of those of little faith. Maharsha: Faith here means trusting the Holy One, blessed be He, to provide one's livelihood as well: a man ought to believe that the Holy One, blessed be He, feeds the whole world, from the horns of the wild oxen to the eggs of lice, and ought not to worry about his food from today to tomorrow, for he does not know what tomorrow will bring. One who worries over this worries over a world that is not his. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Sotah 48b): Since it is written, "Blessed be the Lord, day by day" (Psalms 68:20), and He, blessed be He, sustains His creatures each and every day, one who has bread in his basket and says "What shall I eat tomorrow?" is of those of little faith: he does not believe that He, blessed be He, sustains His world, for if he believed in Him he would have no doubt about what he will eat tomorrow. Sod Yesharim (Shemini Atzeres 32): The Gemara says that one who has what to eat today and says "What shall we eat tomorrow?" is of those of little faith [while Menachos and the Midrash count it a curse to buy grain from year to year, or to lack provision for three years]. This depends on the matter: one whose chief satisfaction and delight is only the outer garb of the good is of little faith if, having food for today, he asks what he will eat tomorrow; but one whose chief satisfaction is the [Divine] will hidden within the good may rightly wish to prepare good for himself even for three years. (סוֹטָה מח, סוֹף עַמּוּד ב), דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁהָאֱמוּנָה בְּקַטְנוּת.
Thus even one who 'has what...' and so forth is called one of little faith (Sotah 48b), meaning that his faith remains in a state of smallness.
וְהַגַּם דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל מַאֲמִינִים — הַיְנוּ בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל.
Although all Israel believes, this is so in a general and underlying sense.
וְהַיְנוּ כִּי אֱמוּנַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ הָיָה עַל יְדֵי עֹצֶם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ, שֶׁעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא תְּחִלָּה לְגֵרִים.
The faith of our father Abraham, peace be upon him, was revealed in his heart through the tremendous force of his own exertion; therefore he is called the first of the converts.

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תּוֹלְדוֹת)850 Bereshit Rabbah 63:3 — Abram was called Abraham. Isaac was called Abraham, as it is written: "These are the generations of Isaac son of Abraham; Abraham." Jacob was named Israel, as it is written: "Your name shall no longer be said to be Jacob, but Israel." Isaac was named Israel, as it is written: "These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt, with Jacob." Abraham was called Israel. R. Natan said: This is a deep matter — "The dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan and in the land of Goshen, was four hundred and thirty years.": אַבְרָהָם נִקְרָא יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁזָּכָה לִהְיוֹת כְּאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהוּא בְּתוֹלָדָה.

Nevertheless, our Sages of blessed memory taught (Bereishit Rabbah, beginning of Parashat Toldot) that Abraham is called Israel: he merited to become like a native-born Israelite, whose status is present by birth.
וְזֶה אַחַר לֵידַת יִצְחָק, שֶׁבּוֹ "יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע", שֶׁהוּא נִמּוֹל לִשְׁמוֹנָה.
This was clarified after the birth of Isaac, regarding whom it says 'shall offspring be called yours,' and who was circumcised at eight days.
דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁהוּא בְּתוֹלָדָה טוֹב וְנִמּוֹל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּטֶרֶם יֵשׁ לוֹ דַּעַת כְּלָל, וְזֶה מִצַּד כֹּחַ אַבְרָהָם בּוֹ.
That is, he is good by birth and circumcised unto the Blessed One before possessing any awareness at all; this comes from the power of Abraham within him.
וְנִמְצָא נִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נֶהְפַּךְ עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ לִהְיוֹת שָׁרְשׁוֹ כָּךְ, כְּאִלּוּ הוּא מִתּוֹלָדָה כָּךְ.
It therefore became clear that through his exertion our father Abraham, peace be upon him, transformed even his root, as though he had been born that way.
דְּהַהוֹלָדָה בְּדוֹמֶה הוּא בְּדוֹמֶה לְמַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּעֶצֶם וּבְשָׁרְשׁוֹ.
For reproduction in kind transmits what belongs to the essential nature and root of the parent.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאֵין סוּמָא מוֹלִיד סוּמָא, וְכֵן אֲפִלּוּ שׁוֹטֶה אֵין מוֹלִיד שׁוֹטֶה וְכַיּוֹצֵא; רַק מַה שֶּׁהוּא שִׁנּוּי בְּעֶצֶם, כְּמוֹ שׁוֹר מוֹלִיד שׁוֹר וַחֲמוֹר חֲמוֹר וְכַיּוֹצֵא.

A blind person does not necessarily beget a blind child, nor does a fool necessarily beget a fool, and the like. Only what belongs to essential kind is transmitted: an ox begets an ox, a donkey a donkey, and so on.

וְכָךְ שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא בְּתוֹלָדָה, דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹלִיד יִשְׂרָאֵל; אֲפִלּוּ יֶחֱטָא וְיָמִיר דָּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, לֹא פָּקַע שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמֶּנּוּ, כְּדְקַיְּמָא לָן (יְבָמוֹת מז:) לְעִנְיַן קִדּוּשִׁין וְגֵרוּשִׁין.

So too the designation Israel belongs by birth: an Israelite gives birth to an Israelite. Even if one sins and, Heaven forbid, changes religion, the status of Israel does not depart from him, as the law is established (Yevamot 47b) regarding marriage and divorce.
שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִשְׁתַּנּוֹת מִשָּׁרְשׁוֹ.
For this cannot be changed at its root.
וּמִשֶּׁנּוֹלַד יִצְחָק נִתְבָּרֵר דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שָׁרְשׁוֹ כָּךְ.
With Isaac's birth it became manifest that this was indeed the root of our father Abraham, peace be upon him.
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם, בֵּרוּר זֶה דְּתוֹלְדוֹת יִצְחָק שֶׁנִּמּוֹל לִשְׁמוֹנָה — הוּא שֶׁגַּם בְּקַטְנוּת הוּא כָּךְ.
Nevertheless, what Isaac's birth and his circumcision at eight days demonstrate is that this quality is present even in infancy.
זֶהוּ אֱמוּנָה בְּקַטְנוּת, וּלְכָךְ הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ לְקַטְנוּת הָאֱמוּנָה וְשֶׁבְּהֶעְלֵם.
This is faith in a state of smallness, and therefore it is the root of faith when it is still small and concealed.
וּכְלַל הַהַכָּרָה דְּמִצַּד הַבְּרִיאָה, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מוֹפְתֵי הַפִּילוֹסוֹפִים גַּם כֵּן עַל מְצִיאוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הוּא הַכָּרָה בְּקַטְנוּת.
In general, recognition derived from creation—including the philosophers' demonstrations of the existence of the Blessed One—is a form of recognition in smallness.
וְכַנִּכְתָּב לְעֵיל, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַכָּרַת הַגֵּרִים עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת בַּחֲקִירָה, וְאֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל מִקַּטְנוּת.
As explained above, this is the recognition attained by converts through the exertion of investigation, whereas among Israel it is present from childhood.

items.h:
Seif 2 — Isaac: Recognition through Vision
Miracle and prophetic sight reveal Hashem with the clarity of vision, a level reflected in Yom Tov and Isaac.

p: וְיֵשׁ עוֹד הַשָּׂגָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר, הַדּוֹמָה לִרְאִיָּה.
There is a further and greater apprehension, one that resembles actual sight.

כְּטַעַם (שַׁבָּת פט:)851 Shabbat 89b — They begin and say: "For You are our father." Isaac says to them: Before you praise me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He. And Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, with their own eyes. Immediately they lift their eyes on high and say: "You, Lord, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is Your name." Rashi: "For you are our father" — they said this facing Yitzchak, and he told them: Point toward the Holy One, blessed be He, for He is your father. Maharsha: Yitzchak divides the sins: those between Israel and the Omnipresent the Holy One, blessed be He, is to bear, and those between them and other people, which require appeasement, he will bear; "and if You say all are upon me" — that all are between them and other people — "I offered my life before You," and so can bear them all. Therefore they say to Yitzchak, "For you are our father," since he bears all their sins by the merit of having offered himself; but Yitzchak points them to the Holy One, blessed be He, for all their sins may be between them and Him, and at once they say, "You, O Lord, are our Father," that He atone for His Name's sake. Maharal (Netzach Yisrael, ch. 13): "If You say all are upon me, I offered my life before You": since Yitzchak gave himself over to the Blessed One, he belongs to Him entirely, and therefore he bears their iniquity entirely. Israel lift their eyes to Yitzchak as though he were their redeemer, but this is not so — through his attribute they are joined to the Blessed One, but the atonement itself is His; and Yitzchak, who is never separated from Him, shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, "in their eyes," that is, through the attribute of judgment, which is his. Then they lift their eyes on high and say "our Redeemer," for He Himself redeems them, and not through another. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): "And if You say it is all upon me," that is, that the existence of the dross comes only from my side, because there is dross in me, "I offered up my soul," and I am a perfect burnt-offering before You, with no dross in me from myself; it comes only from the spreading-forth that the Blessed One willed in creating the world. When it is revealed that everything comes from the root, from the Blessed One, the screen that the sins made between Israel and their Father in Heaven is removed, and through this "the Holy One, blessed be He, is shown to them before their eyes," even though "man shall not see Me and live": for the Sages said that at the time of death they see, since then the screen of this world is removed, and so too with this revelation of "half upon You" the screen of this world will be removed. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:83): The Torah was given specifically to the earth, the place of concealment, where face-to-face recognition is not known, and so one must judge only by the intellect of one in concealment; and face-to-face recognition comes from the side of strength [gevurah], in the sense of "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes." Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The recognition of "I am the Lord your God" is the recognition of "You are with me," and this is from the side of Isaac, as they said, "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes": complete seeing, face to face, comes through Isaac, for this apprehension, clear to the eye and in distinct levels, is from the attribute of contraction, which contracts apprehension into measures and levels. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 190): The root of Joseph is fear of sin, which is guarding the eye, and [fear, yirah,] has the letters of "seeing" [reiyah], in the sense of "Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes," for this comes from the power of Isaac and from his attribute. Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 17): [The blessing "Who revives the dead" is in the mystery of Isaac,] as the Gemara says: Isaac said to them, "Before you praise me, praise the Holy One, blessed be He," and Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes. This alludes to the resurrection of the dead: it is not in the power of any creature in the world to show a person his foundation and the root from which he was hewn, to heal the root of his deficiency and comfort him in his grief; this was entrusted to no intermediary but given into the hand of the Blessed One alone. Sod Yesharim (Sukkos 73): Isaac's attribute is always to hear from the depth of the supernal root, and the sight of the surface hue was a small thing to him; so the Gemara says that the Holy One says to Abraham and to Jacob, "Your children have sinned," but Isaac answered, "[They are] Your children, and not mine," for he always looked to the depth of the supernal root, where Israel are always called children of the Omnipresent, and therefore every kind of salvation for Israel is aroused from his side. Even the salvation that cannot be recognized in this world except by hearing, Isaac will show in the future to sight as well, so that it will be explicitly recognized upon all the hues of Israel's garments how His light dwells within them, as the Gemara says, "And Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, before their eyes.": "מַחְוֵי לְהוּ יִצְחָק הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעֵינֵיהוֹ".
This accords with the expression (Shabbat 89b): 'Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, with their own eyes.'
הוּא הַהַכָּרָה דְּמִצַּד הַנִּסִּים, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַנֵּס נִרְאֶה לָעַיִן פְּעֻלַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
This is the recognition that comes through miracles: by means of a miracle, the action of the Blessed One becomes visible to the eye.
וְזֶהוּ קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹם טוֹב, שֶׁנִּקְבְּעוּ עַל הַנִּסִּים, דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי.
This is the sanctity of Yom Tov, the festivals established upon miracles and sanctified by Israel.

דְּצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּקְדַּם לָזֶה קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּלָא עָבֵיד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא נִיסָּא לְשִׁקְרָא852 Berakhot 58a — R. Sheila flogged a man who had had relations with a gentile woman. The man went and slandered him in the king’s house. An officer was sent for him. When he came, they said to him: Why did you flog this man? He said to them: Because he had relations with a she-donkey. They said to him: Do you have witnesses? He said: Yes. Elijah came in the likeness of a man and testified. … As he was leaving, that man said to him: Does the Merciful One perform a miracle for liars like this? He said to him: Wicked one, are they not called donkeys? As it is written, “whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys.” Maharsha: The miracle the man speaks of cannot be their handing R. Sheila the strap to judge with — which is what is called a miracle further on — for in that he had said nothing false, and “are they not called donkeys?” would be no answer to it. Rather it is that Elijah came and testified that he had had relations with a she-donkey, which [the man held to be] a falsehood; and to this R. Sheila answered him well: Wicked one, are they not called donkeys?.
The prior sanctity of Israel must precede this, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not perform a miracle on behalf of falsehood.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִיא אֱמוּנָה הַפְּשׁוּטָה, עַל יְדֵי זֶה יָבוֹא לְהַשָּׂגָה גְּדוֹלָה הַדּוֹמָה לִרְאִיָּה.
Through Israel's antecedent sanctity—simple faith—one can then come to the greater apprehension that resembles sight.

שֶׁהוּא בְּיוֹם טוֹב, דִּ"יֵרָאֶה כָל זְכוּרְךָ"; וְדָרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (רֵישׁ חֲגִיגָה)853 Chagigah 2a — It is taught in a baraita: Yochanan ben Dehavai says in the name of R. Yehuda: One who is blind in one of his eyes is exempt from the mitzvah of appearance, as it is stated "will appear [yera'eh]" — read it "will see [yireh]": in the same manner that one comes to see, so he comes to be seen; just as one sees with both his eyes, so too one is seen with both his eyes. Rashi: The word is written "yera'eh" and read "yireh": read one way it means that a man sees the face of the Master, and written the other way it means that the Master comes to see you — so Scripture has likened your seeing to His seeing. Just as He comes to see you with both eyes, so He comes to be seen by a man with both of that man's eyes. Tosafos (s.v. "'will appear,' 'will see' — in the same manner that one comes to see"): Rabbeinu Tam rejects Rashi's reading — that just as the Holy One, blessed be He, comes to see you, namely with both eyes, so you come to see Him with both of yours — since "coming" is not applicable to the Divine Presence, which is in every place, and since it expounds the traditional spelling before the read text, whereas the read text should be expounded first. He therefore reads: just as a man comes to be seen before the Omnipresent with both of the Omnipresent's eyes, so a man comes to see the Omnipresent with both of his own. Maharsha (Chidushei Halachot, on Tosafos s.v. "'will appear,' 'will see'"): On Rashi's reading both the traditional spelling and the read text refer to the Holy One, blessed be He — the one that the Master comes to see you, the other that He comes to be seen by man. Tosafot object that "coming" does not apply to the Divine Presence, which is always in the Temple; and further, that here, where the read text does not differ from the traditional spelling, the read text is primary, so one should not expound the spelling first and hang the read text upon it. Rabbeinu Tam therefore reads both as referring to the man, hanging the traditional spelling upon the read text, which is primary.: "יֵרָאֶה — יִרְאֶה854 Chagigah 2a — All are obligated in the appearance offering, except a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor. Rashi: "All are obligated in the appearance" — in the mitzva of "all your males shall appear" (Exodus 23:17), that they must present themselves in the Temple courtyard on the pilgrimage festival. "Except a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor" — since they are not of sound mind, and are exempt from the commandments. Tosafos (s.v. "all are obligated in the appearance"): Rashi explained this of the mitzva of "all your males shall appear," i.e. presenting oneself in the courtyard; but R. Elchanan objected from what is taught immediately afterward, "Beit Shammai say: the appearance is two silver," which shows that an offering is meant, and from the baraita that an uncircumcised man and one who is ritually impure are exempt from the appearance. Rabbeinu Tam therefore holds that our mishna speaks of the offering as well as of appearing in the courtyard, and that Rashi mentioned appearing in the courtyard because it is the lesser case: if these are exempt even from presenting themselves, all the more so from the appearance offering. Tosafos (s.v. "except a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor"): One does not learn from generalizations, even where "except" is stated, as we say at the beginning of Eruvin (27a) — for the tanna taught this and yet omitted the scraper, the tanner and one who owns no land. Still, those are not really an omission, since the mishna is listing those disqualified in their own persons, to the exclusion of these, whose disqualification arises from something else, namely their trade. Maharsha (Chidushei Halachot): In the text of Rashi before us he explains nothing at "Who is a minor"; but what emerges from his comment on the opening clause, that "all are obligated in the appearance" means presenting oneself in person, is that he inferred it from the latter clause, "Who is a minor," which implies that the mishna is still speaking of the very minor it has just mentioned — and therefore it is speaking of presenting oneself, of a child who cannot walk there.".
This belongs to Yom Tov, of which it says, 'all your males shall appear'; our Sages of blessed memory expounded (beginning of Chagigah): 'he shall appear—he shall see.'
כְּטַעַם "אַבְרָהָם הוֹלִיד אֶת יִצְחָק", דְּזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּפַחַד יִצְחָק, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה בָּאָה הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ אוֹרַח חַיִּים.
This is the meaning of 'Abraham begot Isaac': it is the level of the 'fear of Isaac,' for awe arises through sight, as written in the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chaim.
וְזֶה טַעַם "בְּהַר הַשֵּׁם יֵרָאֶה", שֶׁנִּתְגַּלָּה בַּעֲקֵדַת יִצְחָק רְאִיָּה זוֹ.
This is the meaning of 'on the mountain of the Lord it shall be seen': at the Binding of Isaac this mode of vision was revealed.
שֶׁהַקְרָבַת נַפְשׁוֹ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְקָרְבָּן — זֶה בָּא מִצַּד הָרְאִיָּה.
His offering of his own life to the Blessed One as a sacrifice arose from this mode of vision.

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק ג, ה. וקי855 Zohar 3:5a — R. Chizkiyah was sitting before R. Shimon. He said to him: This that is called korban — it should have been called keiruv or kerivut; what is korban? He said to him: It is known among the companions. Korban means that those holy crowns all draw near together and are bound one to another until they all become one in perfect unity, to set the Holy Name in order as is fitting; this is what is written, "a korban to the Lord." And all this is in order to arouse mercy and not to arouse judgment — and therefore "to the Lord [YHVH]," and not "to Elohim": it is mercy we need, and not judgment..), דְּלָא שַׁיָּךְ קָרְבָּן רַק לְשֵׁם הֲוָיָה, לֹא לִשְׁאָר שֵׁמוֹת הַמּוֹרִים עַל מִדּוֹת.
As stated in the Zohar (III, 5a and 110a), sacrifice relates specifically to the Name Havayah, not to the other Divine Names that signify particular attributes.
דְּהַיְנוּ הַהַכָּרָה מִצַּד פְּעֻלּוֹתָיו וּמִדּוֹתָיו; אֲבָל הֲוָיָה הוּא שֵׁם הָעֶצֶם, וְהַכָּרַת הָעֶצֶם זֶה נִקְרָא רְאִיָּה.
Those other Names express recognition through His actions and attributes; Havayah, however, is the Essential Name, and recognition of the essence is called sight.
וּמִצַּד הַכָּרַת בּוֹרֵא בָּא מְסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ דְּאַבְרָהָם, כְּשֶׁכּוֹפִין לְהַכְחִישׁ בַּבּוֹרֵא, וְנִשְׁאַר כֵּן בְּטֶבַע לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל לִמְסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
From recognition of a Creator came Abraham's self-sacrifice when one is forced to deny the Creator; this capacity for self-sacrifice remained implanted in the nature of all Israel.
וּמִצַּד הַכָּרַת "שִׁוִּיתִי הַשֵּׁם לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" בָּא הַמְּסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ דֶּרֶךְ הַקְרָבָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּגוֹן מִי שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה מִצְווֹת בִּמְסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ וְכַיּוֹצֵא.
From the recognition of 'I have set the Lord before me always' comes another form of self-sacrifice: offering oneself to the Blessed One by performing mitzvot with self-sacrifice and the like.
וְגַם זֶה נִקְבַּע בְּטֶבַע תּוֹלְדוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִצַּד יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהִתְעוֹרֵר לַעֲשִׂיּוֹת מִצְווֹת רַבּוֹת.
This too became fixed in the inherited nature of Israel through our father Isaac, peace be upon him: they can be aroused to great acts of mitzvah-observance.
עַל דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל, אִם יִרְצוּ עַתָּה לִבְנוֹת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וְכַיּוֹצֵא, יְפַזֵּר כָּל אֶחָד יוֹתֵר מִכְּדֵי כֹחוֹ בְּמָמוֹנוֹ וְגוּפוֹ וּבִמְסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ מַמָּשׁ.
For example, if the people were now to undertake the rebuilding of the Temple, each person could expend beyond his normal capacity—in money, body, and even literal self-sacrifice.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁפְּרִיצֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעֵת הַחֻרְבָּן מָסְרוּ נַפְשָׁם עַל הַצָּלַת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, וְכַיּוֹצֵא בָזֶה.
So too, the fierce zealots of Israel at the time of the destruction gave their lives in the attempt to save the Temple, and similarly in other cases.
וּמְסִירוּת נֶפֶשׁ כָּזֶה לַעֲשֵׂה טוֹב, לֹא לְסוּר מֵרָע, זֶה נִמְשָׁךְ מֵהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכֵחַ.
Such self-sacrifice in actively doing good, rather than merely turning away from evil, flows from awareness of the Divine Presence standing before one.
וְגַם זֶה הוּא בְּתוֹלָדָה אֵצֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּהֶעְלֵם גָּדוֹל, כִּי מַה שֶּׁהוּא בְּתוֹלָדָה הוּא בְּקַטְנוּת, כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל.
This too is inherited by Israel in a deeply concealed form, for what is present by birth initially exists in a state of smallness, as explained above.

וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (פְּסָחִים סו.)856 Pesachim 66a — They said to him: Our teacher, if one forgot and did not bring a knife on the eve of Shabbat, what is the law? He said to them: I heard this ruling, but I have forgotten it. Leave it to Israel: if they are not prophets, they are the sons of prophets. The next day, one whose Paschal offering was a lamb stuck [the knife] in its wool, and one whose offering was a kid stuck it between its horns. He saw what they did and recalled the ruling, and said: This is the tradition I received from Shemaya and Avtalyon.
