Rashi: ["What is the law?"] Bringing the knife does not override Shabbat, since it could have been done the day before — so what is one to do? ["They are the sons of prophets"] — and you will see what they do. One whose offering was a kid, which has no wool but only hair, stuck it between its horns; this is not a load for which one transgresses the law of one's animal resting, since that is not the usual way of carrying, and in this manner they brought their knives — and "this is the tradition I received" means that the law is as these people did. Tosafos (s.v. "he sticks it in its wool"): And if you ask: [slaughter] requires a sacred vessel, as we derive (Zevachim 97b) from "and he took the knife" — one may answer that they consecrated [the knives]. Our sugya implies that the prohibition of a public domain applied in Jerusalem, which is difficult, since it is said (Eruvin 6b) that were Jerusalem's gates not locked at night one would be liable there for [carrying in] a public domain [— implying that, since they were locked, it was not one]; the Ri answered that here it was after breaches had been made in [its walls]. Maharsha: Certainly the fourteenth had fallen on Shabbat in earlier days, but it may have been long before, and how they had acted was forgotten — and Hillel too said, "I heard it once but have forgotten." To this he said: though they are not prophets, to know how they acted, they are nevertheless the sons of prophets, and perhaps there will be elders among Israel who remember how they acted before; and so it was made clear the next day. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAnavah 7): [The Gemara (66b) learns from Hillel, who "began to rebuke them" and then said "I heard this ruling, but I have forgotten it," that whoever is haughty, if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him.] Just as humility is a trait separate from the physical, so haughtiness is physical: one who singles himself out as a man of rank and not a simple person inclines toward the physical, above all when he regards himself as possessed of greatness. Therefore the separate, non-physical level — prophecy and wisdom — cannot be joined to one who is haughty, who in his own mind is great, for that is a physical trait. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tu BiShvat 2): "The custom of Israel is Torah," for "if they are not prophets, they are sons of prophets," so it is a custom of prophets [like the willow-beating, a custom of the prophets]; therefore through Israel's custom they can bring holiness into all kinds of fruit [on Tu BiShvat], so that they be only from the side of the Tree of Life and all eating be rectified in holiness. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 3): The generation of the wilderness all attained prophecy at the giving of the Torah — which is why the Sages said, "if they are not prophets, they are sons of prophets" — and from the grasp of "I am the Lord your God," which they all heard from the mouth of the Almighty, began the grasp of prophecy.: "אִם אֵינָן נְבִיאִים — בְּנֵי נְבִיאִים הֵם" וְכוּלֵי.
This is what they said (Pesachim 66a): 'If they are not prophets, they are the children of prophets,' and so forth.
וְהַנָּבִיא נִקְרָא רוֹאֶה, שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הָרְאִיָּה דִּנְבוּאָה; יֵשׁ אֵצֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק בְּהֶעְלֵם, שֶׁהֵם בְּנֵי נְבִיאִים.
A prophet is called a seer. The power of prophetic sight therefore exists within all Israel, but in concealment, for they are the children of prophets.

וְלֶעָתִיד יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת, דְּ"אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ רוּחִי" וְגוֹמֵר857 Joel 3:1-2 — “And it shall be afterward that I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your elders shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions. And also upon the servants and the handmaids in those days will I pour out My spirit.” Rashi: "And it shall come to pass afterwards" — in the time to come. "Upon all flesh" — upon whoever's heart has become soft as flesh, on the model of "and I will give you a heart of flesh." Radak: "Afterwards" is like "in the end of days": now you will know Me, but not with a complete knowledge, since you will still turn back and sin before Me; after that a time will come when you will know Me completely and sin no more, and that is the days of the Messiah. "I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh" means upon Israel, the great and the small alike, and "My spirit" is a spirit of knowledge and understanding; he does not say that all will prophesy, but only "your sons and your daughters." Metzudas Dovid: "Afterwards" means after many days, in the time of the Messiah. "I will pour out My spirit" — a spirit of wisdom and of recognition of the Godhead I will pour out upon all flesh, for even the nations will then recognize and know that the Lord is God; and "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" — not as in the days of the exile, when prophecy was withdrawn from Israel. Malbim: "The spirit of the Lord" takes in all the perfections of the soul — "a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and might, a spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord" — and He will pour it out upon all flesh in great abundance, as one pours out water that spreads everywhere and covers all alike. Yet there will still be a difference among them according to the readiness of those who receive it: the sons and daughters, born in the generation of the Messiah and so fitted for the Divine spirit, will prophesy outright; the elders, born in an earlier generation, will receive only true dreams, the lowest of the three degrees; and the young men, born nearer his time, "shall see visions," which stands midway between prophecy and dream..
In the future it will be revealed openly, as in the promise, 'I will pour out My spirit,' and so forth.

items.h:
Seif 3 — Jacob: Holiness as Union
Jacob represents a deeper holiness in which Israel cleaves to Hashem beyond investigation, intellect, or external distinction.

p: וּשְׁתֵּי הַשָּׂגוֹת אֵלּוּ הֵם רַק הֲכָנוֹת וְהַתְחָלוֹת לְהַשָּׂגָה שְׁלִישִׁית, שֶׁהוּא הַתַּכְלִית.
These two apprehensions are only preparations and beginnings for a third apprehension, which is the ultimate goal.
כְּטַעַם "וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים", דְּאַחַר הַהֲכָנוֹת דְּ"וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם" בָּא לְמַדְרֵגַת "וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים".
This is the meaning of 'sanctify yourselves and you shall be holy': after the preparations of 'sanctify yourselves,' one arrives at the level of 'you shall be holy.'

שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (חֻלִּין ז:)858 Chullin 7b — R. Pinchas ben Yair said to him: Do you suppose that I am under a vow not to derive benefit from Israel? Israel are holy. There is one who wishes [to give] and has not the means, and there is one who has the means and does not wish — and of him it is written, "Eat not the bread of one who has an evil eye, and do not desire his delicacies; for as one that reckons within himself, so is he: eat and drink, he says to you, but his heart is not with you." But you wish, and you have the means. Rashi: "Israel are holy" — and it is fitting to derive benefit from them. But there is one who would give others of his own and has not the means, and from him I do not wish to benefit, so as not to burden him; and there is one who has the means and does not wish to give others benefit, and though he says "Come and dine," his heart does not desire it, and from him I do not benefit, since it is written, "Eat not the bread of one who has an evil eye." Tosafos (s.v. "and there is one who has the means and does not wish"): Even such a one is still called holy, for he invites his fellow to eat with him out of shame. Maharsha (Chidushei Halachot): It seems to me that he means: I am under no vow of benefit; rather, Israel are holy, and one who derives benefit from them is as though he had derived benefit from a consecrated thing and committed misappropriation. For there is one who wishes and has not the means, from whom it is forbidden to benefit, as we say that it is forbidden to benefit from a meal that is not sufficient for its owner; and there is one who has the means and does not wish, from whom it is likewise forbidden to benefit, as it is written, "Eat not the bread of one who has an evil eye" — and in tractate Sotah (38b) we say that one who derives benefit from a stingy man transgresses a prohibition.: "יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשִׁים".
This level too belongs to all Israel, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Chullin 7b): 'Israel are holy.'
וּקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא הַהַבְדָּלָה לְגַמְרֵי מִכָּל תַּאֲוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, לִהְיוֹת דָּבוּק בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא דֶּרֶךְ הַכָּרָה רַק דֶּרֶךְ יִחוּד.
Holiness means complete separation from all desires of this world, cleaving to the Blessed One not merely through recognition but through unity.
וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּ"אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", שֶׁמִּטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה; דְּכַאֲשֶׁר כּוֹלָּא חַד לֹא שַׁיָּךְ פְּסֹלֶת.
This is the level of 'truth to Jacob,' whose bed was complete: when all is one, there can be no refuse or rejected element.
וְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כֻּלּוֹ עָלְמָא דְשִׁקְרָא, כִּי הָאֱמֶת הוּא: "אַתָּה הוּא עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וְאַתָּה הוּא" וְכוּלֵי, דְּהַכֹּל יִחוּד גָּמוּר.
This world is entirely an 'alma de-shikra,' a world of falsehood, for the truth is: 'You are He before the world was created, and You are He...'—everything is absolute unity.
וְהַשָּׂגָה זוֹ דִּדְבֵקוּת בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁ"יִשְׂרָאֵל קְדוֹשִׁים" גַּם כֵּן בְּתוֹלָדָה, זֶה בָּא מִצַּד יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁנִּקְרָא "אִישׁ תָּם".
This apprehension of cleaving to the Blessed One—the inherited holiness of Israel—comes from our father Jacob, peace be upon him, who is called 'a wholehearted man.'
שֶׁאֱמוּנָה כָּזוֹ לִהְיוֹת תָּקוּעַ בַּלֵּב דֶּרֶךְ אֱמוּנָה עַל כָּל פָּנִים, לֹא בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת הַלֵּב מַמָּשׁ, בָּא רַק עַל יְדֵי תְּמִימוּת.
For such faith to be fixed in the heart—even if only as faith and not as full inner revelation—comes only through wholehearted simplicity.
וְשֶׁלֹּא לַהֲרוֹס לַעֲלוֹת אֶל הַשֵּׁם בַּחֲקִירַת שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהַשָּׂגַת הַשֵּׂכֶל.
It requires not breaking through to ascend to God by investigating what lies beyond the capacity of the intellect.
כִּי בְּשֵׂכֶל אֱנוֹשִׁי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג אֲמִתּוּת דָּבָר זֶה עַל בֻּרְיוֹ, כַּיָּדוּעַ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ"ם עַל קֻשְׁיַת יְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה.
Human intellect cannot grasp this truth fully and precisely, as is known and as Maimonides wrote regarding the difficulty of Divine foreknowledge and human choice.
רַק בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֲשֶׁר נָגַהּ עֲלֵיהֶם אוֹר תּוֹרָה דִּכְתִיב בָּהּ "אֱמֶת", מַשִּׂיגִים זֶה.
Only the Children of Israel, upon whom the light of Torah—which is called truth—has shone, attain this.
הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים הַמְכֻנִּים בְּשֵׁם "יִשְׂרָאֵל" מַשִּׂיגִים זֶה בְּדֶרֶךְ הַחָכְמָה.
Torah scholars, who are designated by the name 'Israel,' attain it through wisdom.
וְעַל זֶה מוֹרֶה שֵׁם "יִשְׂרָאֵל", שֶׁהוּא מִן "כִּי שָׂרִיתָ" וְגוֹמֵר — שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה שַׂר עַל הַמַּלְאָכִים.
The name Israel points to this, deriving from 'for you have striven sarita...'—he became, as it were, a prince over the angels.
וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד הַדְּבֵקוּת הַגָּמוּר בֶּאֱמֶת לַאֲמִתּוֹ.
This comes from complete cleaving to the ultimate truth.

וְעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ הַמְכֻנִּים בְּשֵׁם "יַעֲקֹב" (בָּבָא מְצִיעָא לג:)859 Bava Metzia 33b — R. Yehuda son of R. Ilai expounded: What is meant by that which is written, "Declare to My people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sins"? "Declare to My people their transgression" — these are the Torah scholars, whose unwitting offenses are reckoned to them as deliberate ones. "And to the house of Jacob their sins" — these are the unlearned, whose deliberate offenses are reckoned to them as unwitting ones. Rashi: "To My people their transgression" — "My people," that is, the Torah scholars: their sin I call transgression, for they ought to have applied their minds to the reasons of their Mishnah and clarified which teaching is the authoritative one, and not ruled on the strength of a Mishnah that is not. "And to the house of Jacob" — the rest of the people; "their sins" — even what they do deliberately I call [mere] sin. Maharsha: The saying cannot mean that the unlearned man does better to throw off the yoke of study, nor that a deliberate sin should be lightly treated because he committed it knowingly; it is said in praise of learning. The scholar's "unwitting offenses" are of the kind into which any man may fall unawares — as one may know it is the Sabbath and not know which labors are forbidden — and since the scholar does know their prohibition and is on guard against them as all men are on guard against what is plainly forbidden, they are reckoned to him as deliberate. Conversely, because the unlearned man does not study, the plainly known prohibitions lie as near to him as unwitting slips lie to other men, and so even his deliberate offenses are reckoned as unwitting. Maharal (Derech Chaim on Avot 4:13): The Torah scholar has the shining lamp at his head — "the wise man's eyes are in his head" — and so he ought never to err in anything; he should be on guard even in matters of the body and not stumble at all, and therefore even his unwitting offenses are reckoned to him as deliberate. The unlearned man is the reverse: lacking intellect and being wholly of the body, he is like one who walks without a lamp, and therefore even his deliberate offenses are reckoned as unwitting. The scholar is punished the more for what he does unwittingly because intellect is his essence, and within the domain of intellect there is no error and no unwitting act. — עַל שֵׁם "יַעֲקֹב אִישׁ תָּם" — מַשִּׂיגִים זֶה עַל פִּי הַתְּמִימוּת.
The ordinary people, who are designated by the name 'Jacob' (Bava Metzia 33b), after 'Jacob was a wholehearted man,' attain it through simplicity.

וְדַרְגָּא זוֹ הִיא הָאוֹחֶזֶת בַּעֲקֵב עֵשָׂו, שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פְּסִיקְתָא דְּזָכוֹר, סִימָן ה)860 Pesikta Rabbati 12 — "And I will stand [nitzav] on the top of the hill, with the rod of God in my hand" (Exodus 17:9). It is not written "and I [ani]," but "and I myself [anokhi]": anokhi, by the merit of the Torah; nitzav, by the merit of the laws, as it is written, "The Lord stands up to plead" (Isaiah 3:13). "The top" — by the merit of the fathers, as it is said, "For from the top of the rocks I see him" (Numbers 23:9). "The hill" — these are the mothers, "and from the hills I behold him." "And the rod" — by the merit of the rod of God. Why all this? Because when we come by the merit of the fathers, they too come by the merit of the fathers. שֶׁבָּא בִּזְכוּת אָבוֹת.
This is the level that grips the heel of Esau, concerning whom our Sages of blessed memory said (Pesikta de-Zakhor 5) that he came with the merit of the Patriarchs.

רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּקִדּוּשִׁין (יח.)861 Kiddushin 18a — R. Chiyya bar Avin said in the name of R. Yochanan: A gentile inherits from his father by Torah law, as it is written, "For I have given Mount Seir to Esau as an inheritance." But perhaps an apostate Jew is different [and Esau was one]? Rather, from here: "For I have given Ar to the children of Lot as an inheritance." Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): Isaac taught Torah only to his sons, and even among them there was one who was unworthy, except that he is called an "apostate Israelite" in Kiddushin, for he had a root of Jewishness from birth — his head is buried in the Cave of Machpelah in Isaac's bosom — and therefore he too had some hold on words of Torah; yet in the end he too was waste. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 4): [Isaac, the first to be circumcised at eight days, was the one in whom holiness began to take root in all his offspring;] and his wish to draw Esau near was because Esau had free choice, being called an "apostate Israelite," so that the matter stood in the balance whether he could enter into the holiness of Israel. "יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר", כִּי גַּם הוּא נִמּוֹל לִשְׁמוֹנָה.
That is, in the first chapter of Kiddushin (18a) he is termed an 'apostate Israelite,' for he too was circumcised at eight days.
וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ כָּךְ הַהַכָּרָה וְהָרְאִיָּה מֵאַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, שֶׁהֵם הַהֲכָנוֹת לְדַרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב, כַּנִּזְכָּר.
Thus he possessed the recognition and sight inherited from Abraham and Isaac, which are the preparations for Jacob's level, as explained.
וְיַעֲקֹב הִשְׁתַּדֵּל לְהוֹצִיא מַדְרֵגָתוֹ לַפֹּעַל.
Jacob, however, exerted himself to bring his level into actuality.
וְזֶהוּ "יָדוֹ" — פֵּרוּשׁ, כֹּחַ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ — אוֹחֶזֶת בַּעֲקֵב עֵשָׂו.
This is the meaning of 'his hand'—the power of his exertion—grasping the heel of Esau.
שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן "עָשׂוּי", שֶׁנּוֹצַר וָלָד נִגְמָר בִּשְׂעָרוֹת, וְלֹא הָיָה צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת מִצַּד הַהֲכָנָה שֶׁלּוֹ מֵהָאָבוֹת.

Esau's name is associated with being already 'made': he emerged as a fully formed infant covered with hair, and from the standpoint of the preparation inherited from the Patriarchs he seemed to require no exertion.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא גָּרַם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ אַדְרַבָּה לְהֵפֶךְ, לִהְיוֹת "אִישׁ שָׂדֶה".
But through his own exertion he brought about precisely the opposite, becoming 'a man of the field.'
וְיַעֲקֹב הָיָה אוֹחֵז בַּעֲקֵבוֹ, בִּקְצֵה כֹּחַ הַהֲכָנָה הַתָּקוּעַ בּוֹ בְּפֹעַל גָּמוּר לִהְיוֹת עָשׂוּי כָּךְ.
Jacob grasped his heel—the very edge of the preparatory power that was already implanted within Esau as an actual, finished quality.
שֶׁהָיָה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁהוּא כְּבָר עָשׂוּי וְדַי לוֹ בְּכָךְ שֶׁהוּא מִלֵּדָה כֵּן, וְרַשַּׁאי עַתָּה לַעֲשׂוֹת כָּל שְׁרִירוּת לִבּוֹ.
Esau thought that he was already complete, that being born this way was sufficient, and that he could therefore follow every inclination of his heart.
אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָחַז בִּקְצֵה אוֹתָהּ הַהֲכָנָה הַגְּמוּרָה, וּבְכֹחַ יָדוֹ וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ נִגְמְרָה אֶצְלוֹ בְּפֹעַל גַּם כֹּחַ הֲכָנַת הָאָבוֹת.
Jacob seized the end of that complete preparation and, through the power of his hand and his exertion, brought the inherited preparation of the Patriarchs to actual completion within himself.

וְלָכֵן רַק "בְּיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא" וְגוֹמֵר, וְלֹא כָּל יִצְחָק (נְדָרִים לא.)862 Nedarim 31a — One who vows: I will not benefit from the seed of Abraham — is prohibited from deriving benefit from a Jew and permitted to benefit from the nations of the world. But is there not Ishmael [who is also of Abraham's seed]? It is written: "For in Isaac shall seed be called to you." But is there not Esau [who is of Isaac]? "In Isaac" — and not all of Isaac. Rashi: "But is there not Ishmael" — he too is of Abraham's seed, and he is among the nations of the world [so benefit from him should have been forbidden as well]. "For in Isaac shall seed be called to you" — and it is by that seed that the man vowed; and "in Isaac, and not all of Isaac" teaches that Esau is not called the seed of Isaac, and therefore the one who vowed is permitted to derive benefit from the nations of the world. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): The very essence of Abraham and Isaac was not yet wholly transformed until the birth of Jacob, when the promise "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac" was fulfilled, and Ishmael and Esau were pushed away from being called the seed of Abraham and Isaac. Then Abraham and Isaac too were perfected, their "bed" complete, for from then on only the seed of Jacob is called and traced to them. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): The titles "father" and "mother" refer only to their power that extends into the child; therefore they said in Nedarim, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you" — and not Esau and Ishmael, who are not called Abraham's seed: though he begot them, his power is not discernible in them after the begetting, unless one converts, for [a convert] is called a son of Abraham. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 13): The angels, who said "Sarah your wife shall have a son" [attributing him to the feminine side], saw that Esau's evil severities would also issue from him; but they did not know the depths revealed afterwards in the Torah in "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you," which the Sages expounded in Nedarim, "and not all of Isaac" — Esau is not called his seed at all, so that in truth [Isaac] was entirely holy. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Emor 6): Although Abraham and Isaac are also called by the name Israel, that is only after Jacob was born and named Israel, for then it was clarified that "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac," since Ishmael and Esau are not called their seed; then they too were called by the name Israel, but not before. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 78): Sometimes some good may come to a father even from wicked sons, as with Abraham, from whom Ishmael and the sons of Keturah issued, through whom the dross went out; but for this the father must merit that the status of "his seed" be stripped from them, as it says of Abraham, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you." Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): In truth the "bed" of Abraham and Isaac too was complete, for only "in Isaac shall seed be called to you — and not all of Isaac": Esau and Ishmael are not their seed at all, only Jacob, whose bed was complete. Once Jacob was clarified as having a complete bed without dross, they too were clarified, for the dross was pushed away from being called their seed at all. Beis Yaakov (Bereishis 28): Isaac thought to bless Esau because he reasoned that the Blessed One can shine even within darkness, and if the Holy One, blessed be He, consented to Esau's deeds they would be very exalted; but the Holy One, blessed be He, did not consent, for He had already sealed the name of Jacob, as it is written, "for in Isaac shall seed be called to you.".
Therefore the verse says only 'through Isaac shall offspring be called yours'—not all of Isaac's descendants (Nedarim 31a).
כִּי רַק בְּיַעֲקֹב וְזַרְעוֹ נִשְׁרַשׁ כֹּחַ הָאָבוֹת, שֶׁהוּא הִשְׁרִישָׁם בְּקִרְבּוֹ עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ גַּם כֵּן.
Only in Jacob and his descendants did the power of the Patriarchs become rooted, because Jacob himself rooted those powers within himself through exertion.
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רָאוּי לִקָּרֵא אָב לְבָנִים, דְּהַיְנוּ הַמִּתְהַפֵּךְ בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ.
He thereby became fit to be called a father to children—that is, one who transforms his very root.
שֶׁזֶּה כָּל כֹּחַ הָאָבוֹת: לַהֲפֹךְ כֹּחַ שָׁרְשָׁם עַד שֶׁיִּזְכּוּ לְכָל זַרְעָם אַחֲרֵיהֶם לִהְיוֹת נִמְשָׁכִים אַחַר הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ.
This is the entire power of the Patriarchs: to transform the power of their root so completely that all their descendants after them inherit a pull toward that root.
דְּמִטַּעַם זֶה נִקְרְאוּ "אָבוֹת", דְּלָזֶה צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עֲצוּמָה.
For this reason they are called 'fathers'; achieving such a transformation requires tremendous exertion.

וְהוּא נִקְרָא (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קנ. וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת)863 Zohar 1:150a — Another interpretation of "And behold, the Lord stood over him" — over Jacob, so that all should be a holy chariot: right and left, with Jacob in their midst, and the Assembly of Israel bound to them. This is what is written, "I am the Lord, God of Abraham your father and God of Isaac." How do we know that Jacob is in the middle? From the fact that it is written "God of Abraham your father and God of Isaac," and not "God of Isaac your father" — since he was bound to Abraham, he is found to be in the middle. And here he saw that he would be the completion of the fathers. "שְׁלִימוּ דַּאֲבָהָן", שֶׁבּוֹ נִשְׁלְמוּ כָּל הַשְּׁלֹשָׁה כֹּחוֹת לְהִשְׁתַּלֵּם לְגַמְרֵי.
Jacob is therefore called (Zohar I, 150a and elsewhere) the 'completion of the Patriarchs,' for in him all three powers reached complete perfection.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח)864 Bereshit Rabbah 68:12 — R. Salmoni said in the name of Resh Lakish: He showed him a stool of three legs. R. Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in the name of R. Levi: You are the third leg. This is R. Yehoshua of Sikhnin's own view in the name of R. Levi, who said: "For the Lord's portion is His people, Jacob the cord of His inheritance" — just as a cord is not twisted from fewer than three strands, so the patriarchs are not fewer than three. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Isaac was Israel from birth, so that even his dross is called "an apostate Israelite"; only, "the cord is not snapped with fewer than three," so it was still possible to apostatize and change — until Jacob, "the cord of His inheritance," in whom there is no dross at all. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 10): "Jacob the cord of His inheritance" — an inheritance that has no interruption — comes only from Jacob, as the Sages said, "the cord is not snapped with fewer than three," for three times make a presumption; so it says, "[My words] shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed ... from now and forever," for once established through three generations it holds in their seed forever. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 11): Joining the two mitzvos of the Chanukah lamp and the mezuzah to the thread of tzitzis [between them] strengthens that thread into a "threefold cord," and thereby it becomes the aspect of "Jacob the cord of His inheritance" — threefold from the holiness of all three patriarchs, like a cord that is not snapped with fewer than three; and this power was fixed and completed in the collective souls of Israel through the Chanukah lamp. שֶׁאֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע פָּחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
Thus they said (Bereishit Rabbah 68) that a cord of three strands does not readily break.
דְּבְאֶחָד וּשְׁנַיִם עֲדַיִן יוּכַל לִקָּרֵעַ וְלִפָּסֵק, אַף שֶׁהוּא בֶּאֱמֶת חֶבֶל הָאָרוֹךְ הַמּוֹשֵׁךְ.
With one or two strands the cord can still tear and be severed, though it is in truth a single extended cord.
וְנִמְצָא שֶׁגַּם חֶבֶל אֶחָד וּשְׁנַיִם מִתְחַזְּקִים שֶׁלֹּא יִפָּסְקוּ עַל יְדֵי הַשְּׁלִישִׁי; וְהָבֵן זֶה.
Thus the first and second strands themselves are strengthened against breaking by the addition of the third. Understand this well.
וּבַזְּמַן הוּא נֶגֶד זֶה קְדֻשַּׁת יְמֵי הַפּוּרִים דִּמְחִיַּת עֲמָלֵק, זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל עֵשָׂו.
In the dimension of time, this corresponds to the sanctity of Purim, the days of erasing Amalek, the descendant of Esau.
שֶׁאָז הָיָה הַהַשָּׂגָה הַגְּלוּיָה דְּגַם הַהַנְהָגָה הַטִּבְעִית הַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּהָיָה נֵס מִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּדֶרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
At Purim there was an open apprehension that even natural governance is entirely from the Blessed One, for the miracle was clothed in the course of nature.

דְּלָכֵן נִקְרָא (יוֹמָא כט.)865 Yoma 29a — R. Assi said: Why is Esther likened to the dawn? To tell you: just as the dawn is the end of all the night, so Esther is the end of all the miracles. Rashi: [Esther is likened to the "hind of the dawn" of Psalm 22 because] in Tractate Megillah (15b) it is said that Esther recited this psalm: when she reached the chamber of idols the Divine Presence departed from her, and she said, "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?" Maharsha: At first glance, since troubles are everywhere likened to night and redemption to day, it should rather have likened Esther to evening: just as evening is the end of the whole day, so Esther is the end of all the miracles, which are likened to day. But it refers to the fact that the celebrated miracles of this world began at midnight, as the liturgical poet composed, "Then You performed most miracles at night," concluding with "The Agagite nursed hatred and wrote decrees at night"; so Esther is the end of all the miracles of this world that were performed at night, even though miracles are likened to day. Maharal (Or Chadash, Introduction): Miracles belong to the night, for the day is set apart for the natural order; thus the plague of the firstborn was at night, while the going-out from Egypt, which was itself in the order of the world, was by day. The dawn, the end of the night that is set apart for miracles, is close to the day and reckoned neither as day nor as night; so too the miracle of Esther was a hidden miracle, not a revealed one, and is therefore not likened to the night, to which miracles belong, yet since it was a miracle after all, neither is it likened to the day, in which nature governs, but to the dawn, which is close both to the day and to the night. "סוֹף כָּל הַנִּסִּים", שֶׁהוּא הַמַּדְרֵגָה הָאַחֲרוֹנָה מִנֵּס.
Therefore Purim is called (Yoma 29a) the 'end of all miracles,' the final level in the progression of miracle.
שֶׁהוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁכָּל הַהַנְהָגָה הַטִּבְעִית הוּא מִנִּסִּים נִסְתָּרִים.
It reveals that all natural governance itself consists of hidden miracles.
שֶׁזֶּה תַּכְלִית כָּל הַנִּסִּים, לְהַגִּיעַ לְהַשָּׂגָה זוֹ שֶׁאֵין כָּאן נֵס, כִּי כָךְ לִי נֵס כְּמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע.
This is the purpose of all miracles: to reach the apprehension that ultimately there is no distinction—miracle and the way of nature are equally acts of God.

"מִי שֶׁאָמַר לַשֶּׁמֶן וְיַדְלִיק — יֹאמַר לַחֹמֶץ" וְכוּלֵי866 Taanit 25a — On one Sabbath eve R. Chanina ben Dosa saw his daughter downcast. He said to her: My daughter, why are you downcast? She said: I exchanged the vinegar vessel for the oil vessel, and I kindled the Sabbath lamp with vinegar. He said to her: My daughter, what does this matter to you? He who commanded oil that it should burn will command vinegar that it should burn. And it burned the whole day, until they took light from it for the Havdalah. Rashi: Wherever [the Gemara] teaches "bei shimshei" it means Sabbath eve; I have not heard the reason. "The vinegar vessel": the vessel with the vinegar in it; I put the vinegar in the lamp, and the lamp will go out. "Until they took light from it for Havdalah": he lit another lamp from it in order to have benefit from that one, and extinguished the lamp of the miracle. Maharsha: "Bei shimshei": Rashi explained it as Sabbath eve and wrote that he had not heard the reason; it seems that it is the hour of bringing in the Sabbath, while it is still day and the sun [shemesh] is still up, for one must add from the weekday onto the holy, and therefore that hour is called "bei shimshei." "It burned the whole day": she needed it to burn only on the Sabbath night, for the sake of peace in the home, but it burned the whole day to publicize the miracle to the many by day, and also so that they came to light a lamp from it for the mitzvah of Havdalah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Pesach 32): Why did R. Chanina ben Dosa mention "He who said to oil that it should burn"? Because one must recall that the Blessed One implanted burning in the nature of oil, and thereby one can draw down that He say to vinegar that it burn [as Elisha cast wood into the water, recalling that the Blessed One made wood float, so that the iron floated]. For him this was no miracle, since it was clear to him that there is no nature or habit except what the Blessed One gives, so oil burning and vinegar burning were alike to him; by saying aloud that oil burns only by the Blessed One's word, he drew that influence to the vinegar. Beis Yaakov (Vayechi 19): With one whose heart is in his own control, the Blessed One deals by the light of the Tetragrammaton, which brings everything into being by His simple will, and shows him things as they truly are — that nothing is subject to nature and time, for "He who said to oil that it should burn will say to vinegar that it should burn"; by the light of this Name all miracles are wrought. Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Ta'anis 23): A miracle exists only from man's side, who in his low grasp imagines a change in nature; when his grasp is refined he sees that there is no nature at all. So R. Chanina ben Dosa said, "He who said to oil that it should burn will say to vinegar that it should burn," for he understood well that just as oil needs His utterance every moment to burn, so His utterance can act on vinegar too. Sod Yesharim (Rosh Hashanah 1): R. Chanina ben Dosa said, "He who said to oil that it should burn will say to vinegar that it should burn": in this world oil and vinegar are two opposites, but since by the power of his service R. Chanina ben Dosa could draw from the root of the attributes their supernal light, from his side there were no opposites and no opposition between the attributes at all. Sha'ar HaEmunah (Entrance to the Gate 14): It was easy for R. Chanina ben Dosa to pray, "He who said to oil that it should burn will say to vinegar that it should burn," because he saw that oil too burns only by the utterance of the Blessed One; therefore his prayer took effect — for through faith a person can awaken the higher conduct to be revealed in this world as well. (תַּעֲנִית כה.), כִּי גַם דֶּרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע פְּעֻלַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
As they said (Ta'anit 25a), 'He who told the oil to burn can tell the vinegar to burn,' for the natural order too is the action of the Blessed One.
וְזֶהוּ הַשָּׂגַת הַיִּחוּד הַגָּמוּר דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
This is the apprehension of absolute Divine unity attained by our father Jacob, peace be upon him.
וְאָז הוּא מְחִיַּת עֵשָׂו וַעֲמָלֵק, שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע דְּעֵשָׂו הַבָּא מֵאֱלִיפַז, שֶׁהָיָה מִנְּבִיאֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְיָשַׁב בְּאָהֳלֵי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.

This brings about the erasure of Esau and Amalek. Amalek is the root of Esau's evil, descending from Eliphaz, who was among the prophets of the nations and dwelt in the tents of our father Jacob, peace be upon him.

כִּי הוּא קָלַט כָּל הַטּוֹב שֶׁבְּעֵשָׂו מֵהָאָבוֹת; וְתִמְנַע, שֶׁחָשְׁקָה לִדָּבֵק בְּזֶרַע הָאָבוֹת, רַק לְפִי שֶׁהִיא מִמְּקוֹר רַע דְּשֵׂעִיר, נִדְבְּקָה בּוֹ, שֶׁבּוֹ הָיָה הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁהָיָה בְּעֵשָׂו.

Eliphaz had absorbed the good inherited by Esau from the Patriarchs. Timna likewise desired to cleave to the seed of the Patriarchs, but because she came from the evil root of Seir she attached herself to him, in whom Esau's root was present.
וּלְפִי שֶׁבְּעֵשָׂו נִתְהַפֵּךְ הַכֹּל לְרַע וְנִפְסַק הַחֶבֶל, תֵּכֶף בַּעֲמָלֵק נִתְגַּלָּה שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע דְּעֵשָׂו.
Because in Esau everything was reversed toward evil and the cord was severed, in Amalek the evil root of Esau was immediately revealed.
שֶׁהוּא הֵפֶךְ הַיִּחוּד וְהַדְּבֵקוּת, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ בָּא הַהִתְלַהֲבוּת, כִּי "הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה".
It is the opposite of unity and cleaving, from which true spiritual ardor comes, for 'the Lord your God is a consuming fire.'
וַעֲמָלֵק הֵפֶךְ מִזֶּה — "אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ", שֶׁמְּקָרֵר וּמַפְסִיק הַדְּבֵקוּת.
Amalek is the opposite: 'who cooled you'—he cools and interrupts that cleaving.

כִּי הוּא מָלֵא הִתְלַהֲבוּת לְחֶמְדוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁנִּמְשָׁל לְתַנּוּר בּוֹעֵר מֵאֵשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (קִדּוּשִׁין פא.)867 Kiddushin 81a — When Rav Amram reached the middle of the ladder he braced himself, raised his voice and cried out: A fire in the house of Amram! The Sages came and said to him: You have shamed us. He said to them: Better that you be shamed in Amram's house in this world, and not be ashamed of him in the World to Come. He made it swear to come out of him, and something like a pillar of fire came out of him. He said to it: See, you are fire and I am flesh — and I am better than you. Rashi: "He braced himself" — he spread his legs apart and held himself fast in his place by force, in order to overcome his inclination. "He cried out: A fire in the house of Amram!" — he roused the neighbours to gather and come to put out the blaze, so that he should abandon his desire out of shame before them. "He made it swear" — Rav Amram adjured the evil inclination to go out of him. Maharsha: They, to be sure, understood that there was a fire in his house, as Rashi explains, but he himself certainly meant the fire of the evil inclination, as the conclusion shows — for R. Amram the Pious surely never let a falsehood out of his mouth. His adjuring it to leave him is like what they said of Boaz, that when he said "As the Lord lives" he was swearing to his inclination; and the inclination to transgress is called fire because, just as fire heats, so that inclination heats — as they also said, it is like fire in flax — and that is why he said, "See, you are fire and I am flesh, and I am better than you." Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 81a): He so nullified his inclination that the evil inclination went out of him entirely. Understand this oath: it is complete cleaving to Him, blessed be He, brought about by the oath, as it is written, "and by His name you shall swear" and "and to Him you shall cleave" (Deut. 10:20) — and through cleaving to Him, blessed be He, the evil inclination goes out; that is why it left him by his cleaving to Him, blessed be He, which is the oath in His name. And "See, you are fire": the evil inclination is a power that incites a man to evil, and because that power is spiritual it is called fire, for the separate [incorporeal] beings are likened to fire. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): The Torah is therefore likened to both fire and water: it is as water to extinguish the fire of the evil inclination, which is also fire, as the Sages say, "See, you are fire" — only it is a strange fire, and it is put out by the waters of the Torah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis 15): Gehinnom was created before the world; only the fire of Gehinnom was created on the second day. And Scripture says "and their fire shall not be quenched" — not "the fire of Gehinnom" but "their fire": that is, the fire of the evil inclination, which is fire, as the Sages say: "Something like a pillar of fire came out of him; he said to it: See, you are fire." Beis Yaakov (Miketz 18): In truth the body's powers and its longings for the things of this world are stronger than the power of the pure soul within man, as the Talmud says: "See, you are fire and I am flesh, and I am better than you." For the body's powers are drawn from the Ofanim and the holy Chayos of the Chariot, while man's soul is exceedingly fine — a subtle light which the Blessed One breathed into him from His innermost being in great contraction — so that it is beyond man's grasp whence he could find the strength to overcome the body's longings and powers. עַל יֵצֶר הָרַע: "חֲזִי דְּאַתְּ נוּרָא".

He may be filled with burning passion for worldly desires, likened to a furnace blazing with fire, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Kiddushin 81a) concerning the evil inclination: 'See that you are fire.'
וְאוּלָם עַל הָאֱמֶת הוּא קְרִירוּת וְהֵפֶךְ אֵשׁ הָאֲמִתִּי.
Yet in truth this is coldness, the very opposite of the genuine fire.
וְנֶאֱמַר: "וְהָיָה בֵית יַעֲקֹב אֵשׁ וּבֵית יוֹסֵף לֶהָבָה וּבֵית עֵשָׂו לְקַשׁ".
Thus it says: 'The house of Jacob shall be fire, the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau straw.'
אֲבָל עֲמָלֵק — אַף לְקַשׁ לֹא יִהְיֶה, כִּי אֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם מַמָּשׁוּת עַל הָאֱמֶת, כִּי הוּא מַמָּשׁ הֵפֶךְ דַּרְגָּא דְּ"אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַשֶּׁקֶר.
Amalek, however, will not remain even as straw, for in truth he has no substance at all. He is the absolute opposite of the level of 'truth to Jacob'—the ultimate expression of falsehood.

וְלָכֵן בָּחַר הָמָן בְּחֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר, שֶׁהוּא בְּאוֹת קוֹף כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה, שֶׁהוּא מֵאַתְוָון דְּשִׁקְרָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, ב868 Zohar 1:2b — The letter Shin entered before Him and said: Master of the worlds, may it please You to create the world by me, for by me Your name Shaddai is called, and it is fitting to create the world by a holy Name. He said to her: You are fitting, you are good, and you are true; but since the letters of forgery take you to be with them, I do not wish to create the world by you — for falsehood cannot stand unless Kuf and Resh take you. From here: whoever wishes to speak falsehood takes a foundation of truth first, and afterwards sets up his falsehood upon it, for the Shin is a letter of truth, the letter of truth of our forefathers. Kuf and Resh are letters that appear on the evil side, and in order to endure they take the letter Shin among them, and it becomes kesher [conspiracy]. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 17): This world is called "the world of falsehood," for sheker [Shin-Kuf-Resh] means joining "the foundation of truth" — a good thought and desire — to the desire for evil and its fulfillment, which is not truly so, since a Jew's foundation is in the good. At the giving of the Torah Israel had this "foundation of truth," the Shin, only by seeing and not as a possession, and so they joined again with the letters Kuf and Resh and became the common falsehood; therefore they were commanded the Mishkan, whose boards [kerashim] turn sheker into keresh, and when the Shin stands at the end, Kuf and Resh too are good, for in truth all twenty-two letters are holy. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 4): The Zohar's teaching that Shin is of the letters of truth, "the foundation of truth" that falsehood takes first, means that the Shin, the element of fire, is truth: so the soul too is punished, though it protests that only the body sinned, for the power of the body and the heart to sin comes through the wisdom within it, since one cannot speak falsehood unless he says something true at its beginning. That is, something that is wholly imagination is nothing — just as a beast, having no wisdom, has no sin — and only one who has "a foundation of truth first" can afterwards speak falsehood.:).
Therefore Haman chose the month of Adar, which according to Sefer Yetzirah corresponds to the letter qof, one of the letters associated with falsehood, as stated in the Zohar (I, 2b).
דְּאוֹת שִׁין הוּא יְסוֹדָא דִּקְשׁוֹט בְּקַדְמִיתָא, וְקוֹף הוּא הַתְחָלַת אַתְוָון דְּשִׁקְרָא.
The letter shin is the initial foundation of truth, whereas qof begins the letters of falsehood.
וְלָכֵן שָׂמַח שֶׁבּוֹ מֵת מֹשֶׁה, נוֹתֵן הַתּוֹרָה דִּכְתִיב בָּהּ "אֱמֶת", וְחָשַׁב דְּהוּא הֵפֶךְ הָאֱמֶת.
Haman therefore rejoiced that Moses, giver of the Torah in which 'truth' is written, died in that month; he thought the month represented the opposite of truth.
וְלֹא יָדַע דְּבוֹ נוֹלַד גַּם כֵּן.
He did not know that Moses was also born in that month.
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת "אֱמֶת מֵאֶרֶץ תִּצְמָח", וּמֵעָלְמָא דְשִׁקְרָא דַּיְקָא מִשָּׁם צְמִיחַת הָאֱמֶת, וּלְשָׁם נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה דַּוְקָא.
For in truth, 'truth will spring from the earth': specifically from the world of falsehood does truth grow, and it was precisely into such a world that Torah was given.
כִּי בְּרִיאַת עָלְמָא דְשִׁקְרָא הָיָה לְכַוָּנָה שֶׁיַּעַמְדוּ בּוֹ עַל הָאֱמֶת; נִמְצָא הוּא הֲכָנָה וּצְמִיחָה לָאֱמֶת.
The world of falsehood was created so that within it people would arrive at truth; it is therefore the preparation and seedbed for truth.

וְלִהְיוֹת שֶׁבִּשְׁלֹשָׁה דְבָרִים אָדָם נִכָּר — בְּכוֹסוֹ וְכוּלֵי (עֵירוּבִין סה:)869 Eruvin 65b — R. Ila'i said: In three things a man is known — in his cup, in his purse, and in his anger. And some say: also in his laughter. Rashi: "A man is known" — whether he is a worthy man. "In his cup" — whether his mind stays settled upon him with his wine. "In his purse" — whether he acts in good faith when he deals with people. "In his anger" — that he is not exacting beyond measure. Maharsha: The traits fall in general into three classes: good toward Heaven, good toward one's fellows, and good toward oneself. "In his purse" — whether he deals faithfully with men, that is, good or bad toward his fellows; "in his cup" — whether he remains settled with his wine, which is good toward himself, and not like those of whom it is said, "Who has woe, who has sorrow?"; "in his anger" — if he does not grow angry he is good toward Heaven, whereas of one who grows angry they said that it is as though he worshipped idols. And because these three words are close in sound, he took them as a mnemonic for those three divisions. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Purim 3): "In three things a person is known — in his cup...": that is, precisely through drunkenness, when understanding is taken from him, the difference between the holiness of Israel and the nations is recognized and made clear, for in Israel there is inner holiness even in this-worldly enjoyments. Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 12): The Sages give as the sign by which a person is known "his cup, his purse and his anger," and not the hour when he stands in the synagogue wrapped in a tallis and crowned with tefillin, implying that this is no proof. The main recognition comes when he enters the concealments of this-worldly affairs, dealing with people in the markets and streets; then one can recognize the preciousness in a person — what he is in the depths of his heart. — לָכֵן חַיָּב לְבַסּוּמֵי וְכוּלֵי.
Because a person is recognized in three things—among them 'his cup,' and so forth (Eruvin 65b)—one is therefore obligated on Purim to become intoxicated, and so forth.
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בְּפוּרִים, לִהְיוֹת אָדָם הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי נִכָּר בָּהֶם בְּהִבָּדְלוֹ מִן הָעַמִּים בְּתוֹלָדָה מֵהָאָבוֹת, בְּחֶבֶל שֶׁל שְׁלֹשָׁה שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִפְסָק.
This is what is revealed on Purim: the Jew is recognizable in these very states by his innate distinction from the nations, inherited from the Patriarchs as an unbreakable threefold cord.
וְדָבָר זֶה לֹא נִקְבַּע לוֹ זְמַן בַּתּוֹרָה, כִּי בֶאֱמֶת "יָד עַל כֵּס יָהּ, מִלְחָמָה לַהַשֵּׁם בַּעֲמָלֵק מִדּוֹר דּוֹר" בְּלֹא הֶפְסֵק.
This was not assigned a fixed time in the Torah, because in truth 'a hand is upon the throne of God; the Lord is at war with Amalek from generation to generation' without interruption.
וּקְדֻשַּׁת יַעֲקֹב חוֹפֵף עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּתָמִיד.
The holiness of Jacob continuously hovers over Israel.

רַק מִשֶּׁגָּלוּ לָעַמִּים, אָז הֻצְרְכוּ לְהַבְדָּלָה — "כָּל רֹאֵיהֶם יַכִּירוּם" וְגוֹמֵר870 Isaiah 61:9 — “And their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples; all who see them shall recognize them, that they are the seed the Lord has blessed.” Radak: When they travel in the lands of the nations, for pleasure or for trade, they will be recognized by their great honour even though they have no need to go. Walking in free and embroidered garments, people will say of them, "These are the children of Israel, these are the seed the Lord has blessed." Metzudas Dovid: The seed of Israel will be recognized by their distinction, and the children who come from them will be known among the peoples — the verse repeats the matter in different words. Whoever sees them will recognize in them that they are the seed blessed by the Lord. Malbim: Their seed will be known among the nations for renown and praise — not only the grown children but the little ones too, and not only among the lesser nations but among the important peoples as well. All who see them will say of them that these are the seed the Lord has blessed, for they will be marked out by a holy splendour. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): Even a Jew who apostatized is "Israel though he sinned," for the body of a Jew is set apart from birth from the body of a gentile, and even a day-old infant can be recognized, by one able to recognize, as holy flesh; and at the end of days this will be clarified, that "all who see them shall recognize them" — as some of the nations testified in times of forced conversion that they had toiled in vain even with those who converted, for on investigation it became clear to them that their heart was still toward Heaven. — לְבַל יִתְעָרְבוּ בַגּוֹיִם.
Only after Israel was exiled among the nations did an explicit distinction become necessary—'all who see them shall recognize them'—so that they would not be absorbed among the nations.
וְאָז נִתַּן לָהֶם קְדֻשַּׁת הַפּוּרִים, שֶׁהוּא הַכָּרָה שֶׁלֹּא מִצַּד יִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת.
Then the sanctity of Purim was given to them: a mode of recognition not dependent upon settled, conscious reasoning.
וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִחוּד הָאֲמִתִּי, שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִתְלֶה בְּחָכְמָה וְיִשּׁוּב דַּעַת אָדָם כְּלָל.
It comes through the true unity that does not depend at all upon human wisdom or settled understanding.

items.h:
Seif 4 — David: Renewal through Teshuvah
Rosh Chodesh expresses David's path, where return after distance produces a renewed closeness greater than unbroken innocence.

p: וּקְדֻשַּׁת רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ הוּא נֶגֶד דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, רֶגֶל רְבִיעִי שֶׁבַּמֶּרְכָּבָה, שֶׁהִיא מַדְרֵגָה הָרְבִיעִית מֵהַשָּׂגַת מֶרְכַּבְתּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים.

The sanctity of Rosh Chodesh corresponds to the level of King David, peace be upon him, the fourth leg of the Divine Chariot—the fourth level in apprehending the Blessed One's chariot in the lower world.

וְהוּא הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה (מוֹעֵד קָטָן טז:)871 Moed Katan 16b — R. Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of R. Yonatan: What is meant by the verse "The saying of David son of Jesse, and the saying of the man raised up on high [hukam al]"? The saying of David son of Jesse, who raised up the yoke [ulah] of repentance. Rashi: "Who raised up the yoke of repentance" — he repented first and so gave a way to penitents, as is said in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (4b): David was not fit for that deed, but it came about so that if an individual sins they may say to him, go to David, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, forgave that sin — you too return in repentance. Maharsha: "Who raised up the yoke of repentance" — this is explained in the first chapter of tractate Avodah Zarah. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael 48): He attained this supernal degree of repentance, so that through him it may be said that repentance is found in the world. Repentance is unlike the other virtues: one cannot say of Abraham that he established righteousness in the world, though he was the first righteous man, for righteousness is no new creation at all; but repentance is a new thing in the world, a degree above the world, and for this reason they said that repentance was created before the world was created. That degree was brought into act by the generation of the wilderness and by King David — Israel cleaving to the repentance of the many, and David to the repentance of the individual — for before them, though a man could repent, it was not common, and through them repentance became available and usual. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 36): David, ruddy, of the side of Isaac, is "the man who raised up the yoke of repentance," to repair all the sins that came before; and from his seed comes the Messiah, in whose days and through whom "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 18): David is "the man who raised up the yoke of repentance," for he afterwards came to understand that this is the essential repair of Adam's sin and the repair of the whole world through repentance: an individual who repents is forgiven together with the whole world, since by the power of his repentance he arouses thoughts of repentance in all the hearts of Israel, and through this they will merit that the Blessed One slaughter the evil inclination and the Angel of Death. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): [David] is "the man who raised up the yoke of repentance" for all Israel: since an individual who repents is forgiven together with the whole world, he arouses thoughts of repentance throughout the whole stature of the Congregation of Israel and in every soul of Israel. Even if this is not revealed in them in deed, one who has thought of repentance in his heart is a perfect tzaddik, and so the repair comes to the whole world., דְּשְׁלֹשֶׁת הָאָבוֹת הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּ לִהְיוֹת רַק טוֹב וְלֹא חָטְאוּ כְּלָל.
He is the man who established the yoke of repentance (Moed Katan 16b), whereas the three Patriarchs strove to be only good and not to sin at all.
וּמַה יַּעֲשֶׂה מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ כְּמוֹהֶם?
What, then, is one who is not like them to do?

וְזֶה חִדֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִים — אֵין" וְכוּלֵי872 Berakhot 34b — R. Abbahu said: In the place where penitents stand, the wholly righteous do not stand, as it is said, “Peace, peace, to him that is far off and to him that is near” — first to him that is far off, and then to him that is near. Maharsha: Though it seems far from reason that penitents should stand higher than the wholly righteous, the answer lies in the precision of R. Yochanan's language: "near" means one who was near to a transgression and distanced himself from it — not one who actually committed it, for then he would not be called merely "near to a transgression," but one who in his thought came near to transgressing and overcame his inclination and did not transgress. R. Abbahu holds that such a man, who mastered his inclination, stands higher than the wholly righteous, in whom the evil inclination never stirred at all; R. Yochanan holds that the wholly righteous are higher, since they did not sin even in thought. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 4): Repentance is possible only from a higher level, which is a stripping away from sin: one who has sinned and turned back has removed himself further from sin than one who never sinned, for the latter had no need to overcome his inclination, whereas the penitent must overcome his inclination and distance himself from sin altogether. Therefore Scripture writes "peace to the far," and only afterwards "to the near" — for the penitent is [now] the one near to the Holy One, blessed be He. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 7): This is the "very good" within the evil inclination, for "in the place where penitents stand the wholly righteous do not stand": through the sin, when one afterwards merits repentance, he reaches a greater level. The penitent is not helped to re-enter by the gate through which he went out, resolving henceforth to behave like a wholly righteous man as if he had never sinned and restraining himself because the thing is forbidden, for the inclination has already overpowered him there; he must raise himself to the upper gate, of doing nothing that is not for the satisfaction and fulfillment of the will of the Blessed One, and this is the gate through which penitents come, a higher place than the lower gate that is open to the righteous. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 8): R. Yochanan said that all the prophets prophesied only about penitents, but of the wholly righteous "no eye has seen," and R. Abbahu said that in the place where penitents stand the wholly righteous do not stand; one may say that these and those are the words of the living God and they do not disagree, but it depends on the quality of the repentance: through repentance out of fear of punishment deliberate sins become like unwitting ones, whereas through repentance out of love they become like merits. The one who repents out of love, the Blessed One shines upon him and repairs the deed itself so that it becomes a merit, and therefore he is superior to a wholly righteous man, for he has new merits that one righteous from the outset has no power to attain, as in "there is no light except that which comes out of darkness." Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 3): Repentance is above [human wisdom, the Torah and prophecy], and none of them can fathom its depth, as they said, "in the place where penitents stand the wholly righteous cannot stand": the place of the wholly righteous is what is due them according to their deeds, which follow the Torah, prophecy and wisdom without leaving their bounds, "this you shall do and this not," "thus far shall you come and no further." But the penitent has already breached the fence of the world as bounded by the Torah, the prophets and the sages, and sunk where he sank; and when he returns to God and repairs the past with the clear recognition that "You are with me" and that wherever he may be there is nothing besides Him, he merits the inheritance of Jacob, an inheritance without bounds. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 164): In people's minds the penitent is not like a wholly righteous man, still less are the sins he committed reckoned as merits, even though one believes the Sages' words that deliberate sins become merits and that "in the place where penitents stand [the wholly righteous do not stand]"; this is because repentance is called the "hidden world," and its preciousness and beauty are not revealed to people. [In a bracketed note he adds that] the dissenting view concerns the perception of the prophets: the one master derives his view from the verse "to the far and to the near," which is in the Prophets, while in the other's view it is not so from the standpoint of prophecy, since of the wholly righteous it is said "no eye has seen," which is from the standpoint of the Blessed One alone. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Sanhedrin): As explained in Likutei HaShas, they do not disagree, and these and those are the words of the living God; their dispute is alluded to in the Mishnah, "The blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering because it atones; the limbs of the burnt-offering precede the sacrificial parts of the sin-offering because it is wholly consumed." The sin-offering is the penitent and its blood is the cry from the depth of the heart: the penitent's cry is greater, for he cries out because it seems to him that, God forbid, he has no remedy without the salvation of the Blessed One, and so his cry rises to the place where the righteous do not stand; but in the limbs of the burnt-offering, that is, the performance of the commandments, the wholly righteous take precedence, for their body is greatly refined and cleaves to the Blessed One, never separated for a moment. (בְּרָכוֹת לד:).
This was King David's innovation: 'In the place where penitents stand, even the perfectly righteous cannot...' and so forth (Berakhot 34b).
שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׂגָה גְּבוֹהָה יוֹתֵר — מַה שֶּׁמַּשִּׂיג אַחַר שֶׁטָּעַם מֵהָרַע וְחָזַר לַטּוֹב.
It is a higher apprehension: what a person attains after having tasted evil and then returned to good.
כְּמָשָׁל בֶּן מֶלֶךְ שֶׁגָּלָה מֵעַל שֻׁלְחַן אָבִיו וְסָבַל עֹנִי וּדְחָקוּת, וְאַחַר כָּךְ חָזַר לְשֻׁלְחַן אָבִיו.
It is like a king's son who was exiled from his father's table, suffered poverty and hardship, and afterward returned to his father's table.
אֵין דִּמְיוֹן לְהַרְגָּשַׁת עִנּוּגוֹ שָׁם נֶגֶד הַרְגָּשַׁת עֹנֶג אוֹתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא גָלָה וְלֹא טָעַם עֹנִי כְּלָל.
The delight he then experiences cannot be compared to the delight of one who was never exiled and never tasted poverty at all.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ וּבַזֹּהַר כַּיּוֹצֵא בָזֶה, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
Similar teachings appear in the Midrash and the Zohar, as is known.
וְזֶהוּ קְדֻשַּׁת רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ, בְּהִתְחַדְּשׁוּת אוֹר הַיָּרֵחַ אַחַר שֶׁהֶאֱפִיל, וְנִתַּן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעֲתִידִים לְהִתְחַדֵּשׁ כְּמוֹתָהּ.
This is the sanctity of Rosh Chodesh: the renewal of the moon's light after it has darkened. It was given to Israel, who are destined to renew themselves like the moon.
כְּשֶׁיִּקָּבַע בַּלֵּב גַּם דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּנַפְשׁוֹת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל.
This will occur when the level of King David, peace be upon him, becomes fixed in the hearts and souls of all Israel.
וְזֶהוּ לֶעָתִיד שֶׁיְּבַקְשׁוּ אֶת דָּוִד מַלְכָּם, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹרוֹ בְּלֵב כֻּלָּם.
This is the future promise that they will 'seek David their king'—meaning the revelation of his light in every heart.

וְאָז "וְהָיָה מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ" וְגוֹמֵר873 Isaiah 66:23 — “And it shall come to pass, that from one New Moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, all flesh shall come to bow down before Me, says the Lord.” Radak: "From one new moon to another" is like "month by month," and the word "as often as" indicates that the thing continues without interruption. He mentions two intervals, the nearer for those who are near and the more distant for those who are far off, according to how far their lands are from Jerusalem. "All flesh" means all men, even the other nations. Metzudas Dovid: Whenever it is the new moon — and "in its month" means on the new moon itself, the set time not being allowed to pass — and likewise "from one Sabbath to another." "All flesh shall come" means all men, even the other nations, "to bow before Me" in the Temple. Malbim: In every month and on every Sabbath fresh men will come from among the nations to bow before Me, to receive the true faith and to cast away their idols., שֶׁיִּהְיֶה קְדֻשַּׁת הַחֹדֶשׁ כִּקְדֻשַּׁת הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה דִּקְבִיעָא וְקַיְּמָא.
Then 'from one new moon to another...'—the sanctity of the month will be like the sanctity of Shabbat, the first sanctity that is fixed and enduring.
וְהִיא עוֹד קוֹדֶמֶת לָהּ, כִּי "בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה" וְכוּלֵי, כַּנִּזְכָּר; וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ יוֹתֵר.
Indeed, it is even prior and higher, for 'in the place where penitents stand...' as explained. This is not the place to elaborate further.

sections.en: The Seven Days of Creation and the Songs of Shabbat

items.h: Each day of Creation reveals a distinct form of divine praise, culminating in Shabbat as the union, purpose, and completion of all created powers.

Seif 1 — The First Day: Creation and Divine Sovereignty
The first day reveals creation itself as the foundation of praise: all existence belongs to the Creator and remains under His rule.

p: עִנְיַן "וַיְבָרֶךְ... וַיְקַדֵּשׁ" דְּיוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי, שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה874 Genesis 2:3 — “And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, for on it He rested from all His work which God had created to do.” Rashi: He blessed it through the manna — on the other days of the week an omer fell for each person, and on the sixth day a double portion of that bread — and He sanctified it through the manna, in that none fell at all on the Sabbath; the verse is written with reference to the future. "Which God created to make": the work that would properly have been done on the Sabbath He doubled and did on the sixth day. Ramban: He cites Rashi, that God blessed and sanctified the day through the manna, and R. Abraham ibn Ezra, that the blessing is an added measure of well-being — a renewal of strength in the body and of understanding in the soul. But the truth, he says, is that the blessing of the Sabbath day is the wellspring of all blessings and the foundation of the world, and that He sanctified it in that it draws its sanctity from the holiness above. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Nasso 3): This is also the meaning of "He blessed" and "He sanctified" said of the Sabbath day: the Sabbath is in time what the Temple is in space, for on the Sabbath His holiness is revealed in the world — the revelation of the Shechinah, as in the Temple. Scripture says simply "He blessed" without stating with what, as it does for the blessing of man and of the fish, because this blessing comes through His coming to dwell among them, which is the Priestly Blessing; and "blessed" precedes "sanctified" as with the Mishkan. (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יא): "בֵּרְכוֹ בַּמָּן וְקִדְּשׁוֹ בַּמָּן".

The meaning of 'and He blessed... and He sanctified' regarding the seventh day is what our Sages of blessed memory taught (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 11): 'He blessed it with the manna and sanctified it with the manna.'
וְהַמִּקְרָא נֶאֱמַר בְּמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא הָיָה מָן.
Yet the verse was stated in the account of Creation, when the manna did not yet exist.
דְּעִקַּר הַבְּרָכָה וְהַקְּדֻשָּׁה נֶאֶמְרָה עַל עִצּוּמוֹ שֶׁל יוֹם, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּהַיְנוּ הַךְ.
The essential blessing and sanctity were therefore said of the very essence of the day; necessarily, these two ideas are one and the same.
וְזֶהוּ עֶצֶם קְדֻשַּׁת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת: "כִּי בוֹ שָׁבַת" וְגוֹמֵר.
This is the essential sanctity of the Sabbath day: 'for on it He ceased,' etc.
שֶׁהַשְּׁבִיתָה וְהַנַּיְחָא הַבָּאָה אַחַר גְּמַר הַמְּלָאכָה הִיא כְּשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג וּמַגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית הָרָצוֹן שֶׁכִּוֵּן בִּמְלַאכְתּוֹ.
The cessation and repose that come after a task is completed occur when one attains the purpose and intention that he sought through his work.

וְתַכְלִית בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם — לְמַעֲנֵהוּ, לְקִלּוּסוֹ (שׁוֹחֵר טוֹב, רֵישׁ מִזְמוֹר יט)875 Midrash Tehillim 19:1 — "For the leader. A psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God." This is what Scripture says: "The Lord has made everything for His own sake" (Proverbs 16:4) — for His praise, as it is said, "Sing to the Lord with thanksgiving" (Psalms 147:7). Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 2): The aim of the whole Torah is to come to a complete apprehension that there is a Creator, Ruler and Overseer, which was the purpose of the creation of the world: "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. All 613 commandments are counsels for reaching this, for the Torah is called truth, being counsels for reaching a clear apprehension in the heart, so manifest that it needs no faith. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 6): Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created for His glory, He created to reveal the glory of His kingship and His Presence among the lower beings, and "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise. The building of the Tabernacle and the Temple is man's work of building a place for His Presence after the sin, when the Presence is not revealed everywhere, in the pattern of the Blessed One's work in creation; had man not sinned, the whole world would have been a Tabernacle and a Sanctuary. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 2): The angels cry, "Where is the place of His glory?", but man grasps the Throne of Glory, for "the Lord made everything for His sake" — for His praise; the purpose of creation is the revelation of His glory, and its purpose is man. For the chief revelation of glory is when a person with free choice, whose body inclines toward impurity, nevertheless subdues his inclination and desires for the sake of Heaven's honor, which the angels, who have no evil inclination, cannot attain at all.,
The purpose of the world's creation is 'for His sake'—for His praise (Shocher Tov, beginning of Psalm 19),

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (לח.)876 Yoma 38a — When the Sages heard of the matter, they said: Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created for His glory, as it is stated: "Everyone who is called by My name, I have created him for My glory" (Isaiah 43:7) — and the House of Garmu returned to their place. And so again with the House of Avtinas: When the Sages heard of the matter, they said: Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created for His glory, as it is stated: "The Lord has made everything for His own purpose" (Proverbs 16:4). Maharsha: Since it is for the glory of Heaven that the bread not become moldy, the House of Garmu were restored to their place, as below: "they will seat you in your place." For the incense a different verse is cited: with the showbread, which the House of Garmu by their own skill knew how to remove [from the oven] so that it would not mold, the verse is "Everyone who is called by My name," that is, man, who is called by God's name, having been created in the image of God; but that verse does not fit the incense, for the House of Avtinas accomplished nothing by themselves, only through the herb that raises the smoke, so the fitting verse is "The Lord has made everything for His own purpose," since that herb was created for this very end, to raise the smoke of the incense heavenward. Maharal (Derech Chaim 1:2): The world was created only for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He, as the Sages explained with these verses: for if anything existed for itself, there would be, God forbid, something besides God, whereas in being for the glory of God, to serve Him, it is "for His own purpose." Hence when men do not serve the Holy One, blessed be He, and turn away from Him, destruction and loss from the world are their due, for they were created only for His glory, to serve Him. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chukas 5): The Sabbath is "the purpose of the making of heaven and earth," for then all Israel accept the yoke of His kingship; and this is "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only for His glory" — that is, on the Sabbath day, as it is said: "On the seventh day He ascended and sat on His throne of glory." Beis Yaakov (Noach 30): The saying "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only for His glory" was said only with respect to the creation: the Holy One, blessed be He, wishes to give His creatures a taste of His great kindness, that they may recognize His glory and know His might, and so He created the world in a pleasing order. But the Blessed One for His part needs not even this recognition of His glory, as is seen from the many worlds He created and destroyed, leaving nothing of them to tell of His glory.: כָּל מַה שֶּׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעוֹלָמוֹ לֹא בָּרָא אֶלָּא לִכְבוֹדוֹ.
as they taught in Yoma (38a): Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only for His glory.
וּבְכָל יוֹם מְיֻחָד הָיָה מִין בְּרִיאָה מְיֻחֶדֶת, הַיְנוּ הִתְגַּלּוּת מַדְרֵגַת כָּבוֹד מְיֻחֶדֶת כְּפִי בְּרִיאַת הַיּוֹם.
Each particular day contained a distinct type of creation—that is, the revelation of a distinct degree of Divine glory corresponding to that day's creation.
שֶׁכְּנֶגְדָּם קָבְעוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שִׁירֵי הַיּוֹם בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
Corresponding to these degrees, our Sages of blessed memory instituted the daily psalms in the Temple.

בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן: "לַהַשֵּׁם הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ", עַל שֵׁם שֶׁקָּנָה וְהִקְנָה וְשַׁלִּיט בְּעוֹלָמוֹ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לא.)877 Rosh Hashanah 31a — R. Yehuda said in the name of R. Akiva: On the first day, what would they recite? "The Lord's is the earth and its fullness" — because He acquired it and gave possession of it, and was sole ruler in His world. Rashi: They recited the whole psalm. He "acquired" heaven and earth and "gave possession" of the world to those who dwell in it — that is, He acquires in order to give possession; and He was "sole ruler" in His world, for the angels were not created until the second day. Maharsha: The three phrases follow the psalm itself: "The Lord's is the earth" is His acquiring it; "Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord… one of clean hands and a pure heart" is His giving possession of it; and "that the King of glory may come in — who is the King of glory?" is His ruling alone in His world. Beis Yaakov (Bereishis 50): On the first day they would say "The Lord's is the earth and its fullness," because He acquired and gave possession and was sole ruler in His world: for then [creation] was still in thought, and creation began from the utterance "In the beginning." The Blessed One raised it in His holy thought many times, until creation descended step by step to become a being and creature in its own right. Sod Yesharim (Seventh Day of Pesach 19): On the first day they would say "The Lord's is the earth and its fullness," because He acquired and gave possession and was sole ruler in His world, for no division among the attributes was yet discernible — as the Zohar Chadash says, the first day goes with all of them, to show that there is no separation among them and all are one. All division began on the second day, when they said "Great is the Lord and much praised," because He divided His works and reigned over them. Sha'ar HaEmunah (Entrance to the Gate 7): Through the division of His attributes His kingship came forth by way of [man's] choice, for before the division He is not called King: on the second day they said "Great is the Lord" because He divided His works and reigned over them, but on the first day "The Lord's is the earth and its fullness," because He acquired and gave possession and was sole ruler in His world — for "ruler" means one who rules perforce, without the kingship that comes from choice..
On the first day: 'The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord,' because He acquired, conveyed possession, and rules over His world (Rosh Hashanah 31a).
פֵּירוּשׁ, דִּבְיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן הוּא הַתְחָלַת הַבְּרִיאָה לַעֲשׂוֹת יְסוֹד לַנִּבְרָאִים.
That is: the first day is the beginning of Creation, establishing the foundations of created existence.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַבֵּנוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן נַחְמָן בְּפֵירוּשׁ "תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ", וְ"רוּחַ", וְ"חֹשֶׁךְ", וְ"אוֹר", וְ"מַיִם" — עַיֵּן שָׁם בִּפְנִים וּבִשְׁאָר הַמְפָרְשִׁים —
As Rabbeinu Moshe ben Nachman explained regarding 'formless and void,' 'spirit,' 'darkness,' 'light,' and 'water'—see his words there and the other commentators—
דְּהַכֹּל רוֹמֵז עַל יְסוֹדוֹת הַבְּרוּאִים וְהַתְחָלַת כָּל נִבְרָא.
all of these allude to the elemental foundations of created beings and to the beginning of every created thing.
וּמִצַּד הַזֶּה הוּא רֵאשִׁית הַהַכָּרָה דְּנִבְרָאִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא,
From this arises the first recognition available to created beings: that there is a Creator,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁהִכִּיר אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם עַל יְדֵי זֶה, דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְבִירָה בְּלֹא מַנְהִיג.
as Abraham our father, peace be upon him, recognized through the principle that a palace cannot exist without a master.
וְאִיתָא בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר יְצִירָה דְּכָל חָכְמָתוֹ הָיְתָה בְּצֵירוּף הָאוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁבָּהֶן נִבְרְאוּ שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ.
It is stated at the end of Sefer Yetzirah that all of his wisdom lay in the combinations of the letters through which heaven and earth were created.
רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, יְסוֹדֵי הַתְחָלַת הַבְּרִיאָה, דְּמִזֶּה הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא כַּאֲשֶׁר מַגִּיעַ לְרֵאשִׁית וְהַתְחָלַת הַכֹּל.
That is, the foundations at the beginning of Creation; from them comes the recognition that there is a Creator when one reaches the first source and beginning of everything.
דְּכָל הַנִּבְרָאִים מֻרְכָּבִים וַעֲלוּלִים, וְכָל עָלוּל יֵשׁ לוֹ עִלָּה,
For all created things are composites and effects, and every effect has a cause,
עַד שֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לַסִּבּוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁהֵן הַיְסוֹדוֹת הַפְּשׁוּטִים.
until one reaches the first causes, which are the simple elemental foundations.
וְגַם הֵם יֵשׁ לָהֶם הַתְחָלָה בְּהֶכְרֵחַ, כִּי לֹא עָשׂוּ אֶת עַצְמָם.
Yet even they must necessarily have a beginning, for they did not make themselves.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁיֵּשׁ אֶחָד שֶׁהוּא עִלַּת כָּל הָעִלּוֹת וְסִבַּת כָּל הַסִּבּוֹת.
Necessarily, there is One Who is the Cause of all causes and the Source of all sources.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ב)878 Bereshit Rabbah 2:3 — The Holy One, blessed be He, said: How long shall the world conduct itself in darkness? Let the light come. "God said: Let there be light" — this is Abraham. That is what is written: "Who roused righteousness from the east?" Do not read it "roused" but "illumined." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Noach 7): "Let there be light — this is Abraham," as it says, "Who roused righteousness from the east" — do not read "roused" but "illumined": the arousal came about because the Blessed One made the light shine upon Abraham, and through this came the awakening from his own side, which stirred his heart [to ask] "Who created these?" The "do not read" does not emend the text: "roused" stands as written, but since there must be an awakening from below, the Blessed One rouses by sending light into the heart, through which the awakening comes from the person's side — and this is called "lending" [the light].: "יְהִי אוֹר" — זֶה אַבְרָהָם.
Therefore our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 2): 'Let there be light'—this is Abraham.

וְאָמְרוּ (שָׁם פָּרָשָׁה יב)879 Bereshit Rabbah 12:9 — R. Yehoshua ben Korcha said: "when they were created [behibare'am]" — [read it] "for Abraham [be'Avraham]," for the merit of Abraham. R. Azarya said concerning this teaching of R. Yehoshua ben Korcha: "You alone are the Lord; You made the heavens... and all that is in them" — and for what was all this labor? For the sake of "You are the Lord God, who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and set his name Abraham.": "בְּהִבָּרְאָם" — בְּאַבְרָהָם,
And they said (there, parashah 12): 'When they were created'—through Abraham,
שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ הַתְחָלַת בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם וַאֲמִירַת "יְהִי אוֹר" וְכָל מַעֲשֵׂה יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן,
for on his account came the beginning of the world's creation, the command 'Let there be light,' and all the work of the first day,
שֶׁהָיָה לְמַעֲנֵהוּ לְקִלּוּסוֹ, שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה בָּזֶה עַל יְדֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
all of which existed for His sake and His praise, so that this recognition would be revealed through Abraham our father, peace be upon him.
שֶׁהַכָּרָתוֹ עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה יוֹם זֶה הַיְנוּ עַל יְדֵי הַעֲמָקָתוֹ בְּכָל דָּבָר עַד שָׁרְשׁוֹ וְהַתְחָלָתוֹ,
His recognition came through the work of this day: by penetrating into every thing until reaching its root and beginning,
וּמֵהַהַתְחָלָה הֵבִין שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא.
and from that beginning he understood that there is a Creator.
כְּמוֹ מִי שֶׁהָיָה עוֹמֵד, דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל, בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן לִבְרִיאַת עוֹלָם וְרָאָה בְּעֵינָיו הַתְחָלַת בְּרִיאַת יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן —
It was as though, by analogy, he stood on the first day of Creation and saw with his own eyes the beginning of creation ex nihilo—
כָּךְ הָיְתָה הַכָּרַת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם.
such was the recognition of Abraham our father, peace be upon him.
דְּעַל כֵּן חִבֵּר סֵפֶר יְצִירָה, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא הִשִּׂיג סוֹד הַיְצִירָה עַל בֻּרְיוֹ.
For this reason he composed Sefer Yetzirah—that is, he attained the secret of formation in its full clarity.

וְזֶה טַעַם "בָּרוּךְ אַבְרָם... קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ880 Genesis 14:19-20 — “And he blessed him and said: Blessed be Avram to God Most High, Maker of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your foes into your hand. And he gave him a tenth of everything.” Rashi: "Possessor (קונה) of heaven and earth" is like "Maker of heaven and earth" [in Psalms]: by making them He acquired them as His own. "Who has delivered (מגן) your foes into your hand" means who has handed them over, as in "How shall I surrender you, Israel"; and it was Abram who gave a tenth of all that he had, because Melchizedek was a priest. Ramban: "Possessor (קונה) of heaven and earth": Rashi rendered the word as "Maker," but these are in truth two distinct senses, although Scripture does use the language of acquisition for making, as in "For You acquired my innermost parts." Whatever belongs to a man is called his acquisition, and this is why Onkelos rendered the phrase "Whose possessions are heaven and earth." On "and he gave him a tenth of all": Abram would take nothing for himself, but the portion belonging to the Most High he set aside in order to give it to the priest.", שֶׁזֶּהוּ מַה שֶּׁפִּרְסֵם אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא "קֹנֵה" וְגוֹמֵר — דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁקָּנָה.
This is the meaning of 'Blessed be Abram... Possessor of heaven and earth': Abraham our father, peace be upon him, publicized that He is the 'Possessor'—meaning that He acquired them.
וּ"בָרוּךְ" וְגוֹמֵר, "אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן צָרֶיךָ" וְגוֹמֵר — הַיְנוּ שֶׁהִקְנָה.
And 'Blessed...'—'Who delivered your adversaries into your hand,' etc.—means that He conveyed possession.
כִּי בְּרִיאַת נִבְרָא הַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִמְצָא דָּבָר מַמָּשִׁי חוּץ מִבּוֹרֵא, כִּבְיָכוֹל, וְזֶה מַה שֶּׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר, דַּהֲרֵי "אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ" כְּתִיב.
For the creation of a creature seems to mean that something substantial exists outside the Creator, as it were; yet this is impossible, since Scripture states, 'There is nothing besides Him.'

אֲבָל אָמְרוּ בִּבְרָכוֹת (לה:)881 Berakhot 35b — R.
