Levi raised a contradiction: It is written, "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness" (Psalms 24:1), and it is written, "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, but the earth He has given to mankind" (Psalms 115:16)! It is not difficult: here — before a blessing; here — after a blessing. Rashi (s.v. "after a blessing"): After a blessing — then it belongs to human beings. Tosafos (s.v. "here — after a blessing"): So too in Shabbat 119a: when they would set down the table they would say "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness," and when they cleared the table away they would say "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, but the earth He has given to mankind." Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot, Berakhot 35a): He created everything for His glory, that a man should give Him glory by way of the blessings; but to derive benefit without a blessing gives Him no glory, and the thing is therefore still His. And so there is no need for Rashi's explanation that one "robs the Holy One of His blessings" — he robs the Holy One of the very thing he eats, since before the blessing it belongs to Him. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaAvodah 14): It is as though he had benefited from what is consecrated to Heaven, for "the earth is the Lord's and its fullness," and all belongs to Him; but one must ask how a blessing releases the fruit into unconsecrated use. Every consecrated thing is released by redemption, when its value is set in its place — and since all was created for His glory, the man who acknowledges his Creator by blessing over the fruit gives Him that glory, and this takes the place of that, so the fruit is released to him. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 35): The Rambam rules that all blessings can be fulfilled in the heart as well. For although "the earth He has given to mankind" after a blessing refers to the world of action, which calls for revelation in deed, it suffices that it be revealed in one's heart, which is the upper "earth," the attribute of His kingship and His Presence among the lower beings, in the hearts of Israel, which He "has given to mankind." Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot 1): The blessings over all bodily enjoyments were instituted to be said before the act, to recall that "the earth is the Lord's and its fullness"; then, after the blessing, "the earth He has given to mankind," and one may benefit, since he first recognized that all is from the Lord. As I heard on this, such are the ways of the Blessed One: when a person gives everything to the Lord, the Blessed One gives everything back to him and says it is all his, but when he does not recognize that all is the Blessed One's, the Blessed One gives nothing to human beings and says "It is all Mine." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on the Book of Joshua 18): The blessing is man's recognition that everything belongs to the Blessed One. "The earth is the Lord's" is said from the side of human beings, who recognize that all is the Blessed One's and they have nothing, while "the earth He has given to mankind" refers to the Blessed One, who from His side says that all belongs to human beings after a blessing, when they recognize that everything is in the hands of Heaven. Hence in the wilderness, where it was evident to all that the Blessed One is the Giver, they were said to eat of their own, but in the Land of Israel, where it appeared to be their own wealth and effort, they truly ate of what was not theirs. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): As I heard on "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness ... here before a blessing": the blessing is man's recognition that all is from the Blessed One. Before he recognizes this and thinks it is his, the Blessed One says "All is Mine"; but once he recognizes it and hands everything over to the Blessed One, the Blessed One hands everything over to him: "the earth He has given to mankind." Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Terumah): A blessing indicates that one recognizes he has a Master from whom the bounty comes to him; if you recognize this, you can say "Blessed are You," addressing the Blessed One directly, and of this it is said "and the earth He has given to mankind." Beis Yaakov (Lech Lecha 14): Before the blessing the good is not yet his, and were he to wish to benefit from it he would transgress "You shall not covet"; after the blessing, by which he proclaims the Blessed One King over the thing, he is permitted to benefit from it, for he receives it "from the table on High." Tiferes Yosef (Seventh Day of Pesach 1): After the blessing, when one says "Who brings forth bread from the earth," a person recognizes that every good is from the Blessed One, and then the Blessed One gives him the good as a fixed possession, "from the table on High"; this is not called "for free," for he has ownership of it. Before the blessing, when he does not yet recognize that the Blessed One is the Giver, he has no ownership of the good; then it is "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness," and he is called one who receives for free. Sod Yesharim (Second Day of Pesach 11): That is, to the degree that a person recognizes "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness," so the Blessed One gives it back to him: "and the earth He has given to mankind." And reaching that recognition in its completeness comes only through the jealousy that, as the Zohar says, comes out of love.: כָּאן לְאַחַר בְּרָכָה — "וְהָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִבְנֵי אָדָם".
But they taught in Berakhot (35b): here, after a blessing, 'the earth He gave to mankind.'
דִּלְאַחַר הַהַכָּרָה דְּ"קֹנֵה שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ", אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַקְנֶה הַכֹּל לוֹ, וְעוֹשֵׂהוּ נִבְרָא בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, כְּאִלּוּ הוּא כֹּחוֹ קָנוּי לוֹ.

After recognizing Him as 'Possessor of heaven and earth,' the Blessed One then grants everything to man and makes him, as it were, an independently existing creature whose power has been entrusted to him.
וּמִצַּד הַזֶּה כָּבַשׁ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אֶת הַמְּלָכִים.
From this standpoint Abraham our father, peace be upon him, conquered the kings.
כֵּיוָן שֶׁהַכֹּל פָּעַל לְמַעֲנֵהוּ לְקִלּוּסוֹ, וְאֵין בָּעוֹלָם אָז קִלּוּסוֹ עוֹלֶה אֶלָּא מֵאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם,
Since He made everything for His sake and His praise, and at that time His praise arose in the world only through Abraham our father, peace be upon him,
נִמְצָא אֵלָיו קָנוּי הַכֹּל, וְכָל הַבְּרִיאָה בִּשְׁבִילוֹ שֶׁהוּא יְקַלְּסוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל זֶה.
everything was, as it were, placed in Abraham's possession, and all creation existed for him to praise the Blessed One through it.
וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם חָזַר וְנָתַן מַעֲשֵׂר מִכֹּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
Abraham our father, peace be upon him, then gave a tithe of everything back to the Blessed One.
הוּא כְּטַעַם בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁאַחַר הָאֲכִילָה: דְּאַף דִּלְאַחַר בְּרָכָה "הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִבְנֵי אָדָם",
This parallels Grace after Meals following eating: although after the blessing 'the earth He gave to mankind,'
לֹא שֶׁהָאָדָם יַחְשֹׁב בְּדַעְתּוֹ, חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, כֵּן, "וַיִּשְׁמַן וַיִּבְעָט"; רַק הוּא לְעוֹלָם צָרִיךְ לְהַכִּיר דְּהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.

this does not mean that a person should imagine, Heaven forbid, that it is truly his and become one of whom it is said, 'Jeshurun grew fat and kicked.' Rather, he must always recognize that everything comes from the Blessed One.
וְזֶהוּ "וְשַׁלִּיט בְּעוֹלָמוֹ": דְּגַם אַחַר שֶׁהִקְנָה, יָדַע דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא הַשַּׁלִּיט.
This is the meaning of 'and He rules His world': even after granting possession, Abraham knew that He nevertheless remains the Ruler.
וְעַל זֶה מוֹרָה נְתִינַת הַמַּעֲשֵׂר, כְּדֶרֶךְ נוֹתְנֵי הַמֶּכֶס לַמְּלָכִים,
The giving of the tithe expresses this, like those who pay a royal tax to kings,
שֶׁאַף שֶׁהִקְנָה וְנָתַן לִבְנֵי אָדָם, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִפְרַד, חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, מִמֶּנּוּ, וְהוּא הַשַּׁלִּיט בְּעוֹלָמוֹ כְּמֶלֶךְ בְּעַמּוֹ.
for although He grants and gives to mankind, nothing is, Heaven forbid, severed from Him; He continues to rule His world as a king over his people.
וְזֶהוּ כְּלָלוּת הַהַשָּׂגָה דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא רֹאשׁ הָאֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, שֶׁהֵם מְכֻוַּן הַבְּרִיאָה לְפַרְסֵם הַכָּרָה זוֹ דְּ"לַהַשֵּׁם הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ".

This is the comprehensive apprehension of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, head of the Israelite nation—the nation that embodies the purpose of Creation by proclaiming the recognition that 'the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord.'
שֶׁהוּא הַכָּרָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא וְיֵשׁ נִבְרָא בַּעַל בְּחִירָה — הַיְנוּ בַּעַל כֹּחַ בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִקְנָה לוֹ אוֹתוֹ כֹּחַ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שַׁלִּיט בּוֹ.

It is the recognition that there is a Creator and a created being endowed with free choice—that is, a creature possessing a power of its own because the Blessed One granted it that power, while the Blessed One remains sovereign over it.
וְזֶה הָיָה תַּכְלִית כַּוָּנַת הַבְּרִיאָה בְּיוֹם רִאשׁוֹן, וְהַשִּׁיר וְהַקִּלּוּס הָעוֹלֶה מֵאוֹתוֹ יוֹם.
This was the ultimate intention of Creation on the first day, and the song and praise that arise from that day.

items.h:
Seif 2 — The Second and Third Days: Kingship within Multiplicity
Division, counsel, and varied growth reveal how many distinct forms remain unified in one originating source.

p: וּבְיוֹם שֵׁנִי: "גָּדוֹל הַשֵּׁם" וְגוֹמֵר, עַל שֵׁם שֶׁחִלֵּק מַעֲשָׂיו וּמָלַךְ עֲלֵיהֶן.
On the second day: 'Great is the Lord,' etc., because He divided His works and reigned over them.
פֵּירוּשׁ, דְּהַהֶבְדֵּל בֵּין שַׁלִּיט לְמֶלֶךְ — דְּגַם אָדָם בְּבֵיתוֹ נִקְרָא שַׁלִּיט, אֲבָל מֶלֶךְ אֵינוֹ בְּלֹא עָם.
The distinction between a ruler and a king is that a person may be called a ruler within his own house, whereas there is no king without a people.
וּ"בְּרָב עָם הַדְרַת מֶלֶךְ", דְּמְלוּכָה הוּא לְשׁוֹן עֵצָה, כְּטַעַם "לֵב מְלָכִים אֵין חֵקֶר".
And 'in the multitude of people is the king's glory,' for kingship is bound up with counsel, in the sense of 'the heart of kings is unsearchable.'
שֶׁמִּצַּד מֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ עַל רִבּוּי אֲנָשִׁים שׁוֹנִים שֶׁאֵין דַּעְתָּן שָׁוָה, צָרִיךְ לֵב רָחָב וְעֵצָה עַל זֶה אֵיךְ לְאַחֵד רִבּוּי דֵּעוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת הַהָפְכִיּוֹת.
Because a king governs many different people whose minds are not alike, he requires a broad heart and counsel for how to unite a multitude of differing and even opposing views.
וּלְכָךְ, כְּשֶׁרָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהַגְדִּיל וּלְהוֹסִיף הִלּוּלוֹ, בָּרָא גַּם הַבְּרִיאָה דְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, שֶׁהוּא הַהַבְדָּלָה בַּבְּרוּאִים — דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ בְּרוּאִים שׁוֹנִים.

Therefore, when the Blessed One wished to magnify and increase His praise, He created the work of the second day—the differentiation among created beings, so that there would be different kinds of creatures.
וְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְחָלַת הַבְדָּלַת הַנִּבְרָאִים הָיָה בַּעֲשִׂיַּת הָרָקִיעַ בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, לִהְיוֹת מַבְדִּיל בֵּין עֶלְיוֹן לְתַחְתּוֹן.
The root and beginning of differentiation among created beings was the making of the firmament on the second day, to separate what is above from what is below.
וְנִתְהַוָּה חִלּוּק בַּנִּבְרָאִים, וּמִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ כָּל מִינֵי הַבְדָּלוֹת.
A division among created beings thereby came into existence, and from it extend all forms of distinction.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר (חֵלֶק א, יז עַמּוּד א)882 Zohar 1:17a — "And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters." Here, in particular, is the mystery of separating the upper waters from the lower, in the mystery of the left. Here is dispute, in the mystery of the left; for until here it was the mystery of the right, and here it is the mystery of the left, and therefore disputes multiplied. The right is the completeness of all, and therefore of the right everything is written, for upon it all completeness depends. When the left was aroused, dispute was aroused; and in that dispute the fire of wrath grew strong, and out of that dispute Gehinnom went forth, and Gehinnom was aroused in the left and cleaved to it. The middle pillar, which is the third day, entered between them, removed the dispute and reconciled the two sides; Gehinnom went down below, the left was included in the right, and there was peace in all., דְּמַחֲלוֹקֶת נִמְשָׁךְ מִיּוֹם זֶה.
As stated in the Zohar (Part I, 17a), dispute extends from this day.
וְעַל כֵּן שִׁירוֹ אָמְרוּ בְּנֵי קֹרַח, שֶׁהֵם עָמְדוּ עַל סוֹד קִלּוּס זֶה דְּ"מְהֻלָּל מְאֹד בְּעִיר" וְגוֹמֵר.
Therefore the sons of Korah recited its song, for they grasped the secret of this praise: 'greatly praised in the city,' etc.

"כִּי הִנֵּה הַמְּלָכִים" וְגוֹמֵר883 Psalms 48:1-5 — “A song, a psalm of the sons of Korach. Great is the Lord and much praised, in the city of our God, His holy mountain. Fair of situation, joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, the far reaches of the north, the city of the great King. God in her palaces is known as a stronghold. For behold, the kings assembled, they passed on together. They saw — so they were astounded; they were terrified, they fled in alarm.” Rashi: “In the city of our God” — in the time to come, when He builds His city, He will be great and praised on her account; and “He is known as a stronghold” is what they will say when He dwells in her in the time to come. “Fair of situation” — a city that is a fair bough, from the boughs of a tree; and “the joy of all the earth” — what is her joy? The northern flank [of the altar], where sin offerings and guilt offerings are slaughtered, so that a man grieved over the transgressions in his hand brings a sin offering or a guilt offering, is forgiven, and goes out from there rejoicing. “The kings assembled” — to make war against her in the war of Gog and Magog. Radak: This psalm too speaks of the days of the Messiah and recounts the praise of Jerusalem: the Lord is great “in the city of our God,” for there all flesh will magnify Him. Mount Zion is “fair of region” — there is none in all the region so great as it; and its air was so well tempered and good that even the sick who came there were healed, so that it was the joy of all the earth. “God is in her palaces” — other cities have palaces strongly built and high, to take refuge in, but the strength of the palaces of Jerusalem is better than theirs, for God is known in them as a stronghold to all who seek refuge in Him; know this, for the kings assembled there with Gog and Magog to fight against Jerusalem and passed through her together. Metzudas Dovid: “In the city of our God” — that is, when His Presence rests in Jerusalem, His holy mountain, then He is great and much praised in the mouth of all. “Fair of region” — a fair region and the joy of all the earth is Mount Zion, which stands to the north of Jerusalem, and it is the city of a great king, namely David. “The kings assembled” — the kings who set an appointed day and then passed on to come against Jerusalem for war. Malbim: This psalm was composed upon a great storm of that time which shattered mountains and broke rocks, yet did no harm on Mount Zion, for the Lord who dwells on this mountain shielded her; and the storm was for Israel’s good, since the kings of the earth had then joined together and come down in ships of Tarshish to conquer the land of Israel, and the storm broke their ships and struck their army in the sea. Though Mount Zion has every excellence in itself — a fair climate, the joy of all the earth, the city of a great king — none of these is the stronghold and strength of the place, but only that “God is in her palaces,” and through this “He is known as a stronghold.” — רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר, בְּמִלְחָמָה וּמַחֲלוֹקֶת.
'For behold, the kings...'—that is, in war and dispute.
וְכָל מַחֲלוֹקֶת בְּנֵי אָדָם וּמִלְחָמָה הוּא מִצַּד שִׁנּוּי הַדֵּעוֹת, וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד הַשִּׁנּוּי שֶׁהָיָה בַּנִּבְרָאִים שֶׁאֵין דַּעְתָּן שָׁוָה.
Every human dispute and war arises from differences of opinion, and this stems from the differentiation embedded in creation, whereby people's minds are not alike.
וְהַנִּצּוּחַ הוּא בְּ"עִיר" וְגוֹמֵר, בַּמָּקוֹם שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן שָׁם, דַּעֲצַת הַשֵּׁם הִיא תָקוּם.
True victory belongs in the 'city,' etc.—the place where the Blessed One dwells, for 'the counsel of the Lord, it shall stand.'

וּמַחֲלוֹקֶת שֶׁהִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם — אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה884 Eruvin 13b — For three years Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disputed, these saying the law is like us and these saying the law is like us. A Heavenly voice went forth and said: These and these are the words of the living God — and the law is like Beit Hillel. Maharsha: The like of this was said in the first chapter of Chagigah [3b], and it is explained there. Maharal (Derech Chaim 5:16): One might ask why the Heavenly Voice said "these and those are the words of the living God" of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in particular, when every dispute of sages is likewise such that both sides are "from the mouth of the Master of all deeds." But there is a difference: in other disputes, although everything is from the Blessed One, one of the two opinions stands nearer to Him than the other; whereas with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel the two are the words of the living God in altogether equal measure, the reasons on the two sides being perfectly balanced, one to permit and one to forbid. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:83): The halakhah follows Beit Hillel because they taught both their own words and those of Beit Shammai: Beit Shammai taught only their own view, holding that the truth is with them alone, since truth is one, whereas Beit Hillel knew that "these and these are the words of the living God" and so taught Beit Shammai's words as well. Hence as soon as the Heavenly voice declared "these and these are the words of the living God," it immediately added that the halakhah follows Beit Hillel, for the one depends on the other — this was the essence of their wisdom and the point on which they differed from Beit Shammai. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 221): Words of Torah are called "words of the living God" in the language of the Sages: "these and these are the words of the living God." Because the Blessed One is called Elohim, Master of all the powers, what is with Him is called "words," speech in particulars: the angels proclaim only the general voice of His will for that day, while each person, through understanding and the heart's perception, grasps the particulars of the words of the living God according to his level — and "these and these are the words of the living God," even though they differ over particulars in the Oral Torah. (עֵירוּבִין יג:): "אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים".
Concerning a dispute for the sake of Heaven, our Sages of blessed memory taught (Eruvin 13b): 'These and those are the words of the living God.'
וּשְׁנֵיהֶם נִקְרְאוּ "עִיר אֱלֹהֵינוּ" וַעֲצַת הַשֵּׁם, כִּי הֲלֹא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא דֵּעוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת.
Both sides are thus called 'the city of our God' and the counsel of the Lord, for the Blessed One Himself created differing minds.
רַק דְּמִצַּד זֶה נִמְשָׁךְ גַּם כֵּן מַחֲלוֹקֶת קֹרַח וַעֲדָתוֹ.
Yet from this same root there also emerged the dispute of Korah and his assembly.

וְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר בְּרֵאשִׁית יז עַמּוּד ב: קֹרַח הֲוָה שֵׁירוּתָא דְּמַחֲלוֹקֶת כְּפוּם רוּגְזָא וְכוּלֵי; יְעֻיַּן שָׁם885 Zohar, Bereshit 17b — There were two kinds of dispute — one at the beginning and one at the end. And this is the way of the righteous, whose beginning is hard and whose end is peace. Korach was of the aspect of the left, in which the dispute begins — right and left, which is in anger and in the force of severities, for each wishes to nullify the illumination of his fellow; and from that there issues Gehinnom, and he cleaves to Gehinnom. Shammai was of the aspect of the left at the end of the dispute, right and left, when the anger and wrath have already subsided — for the righteous then arouse a dispute of love, that is, a dispute which by its way illumines them, and which receives assent and endurance from Heaven, for it is the deciding line, which clothes the one in the other..
The Zohar on Bereishit (17b) states: Korah was the beginning of dispute in the mode of anger, etc.; see there.
פֵּירוּשׁ, כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּ"עוֹלָם חֶסֶד יִבָּנֶה": הַתְחָלַת הַבְּרִיאָה הוּא מִצַּד מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם.
The meaning is as follows. It is known that 'the world is built through kindness': the beginning of Creation proceeds from the attribute of kindness associated with Abraham.
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדַּת חַסְדּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהַמְשִׁיךְ שֶׁפַע לִהְיוֹת נִבְרָא, וּמִצִּדָּהּ הוּא הַמְשָׁכָה לְכָל נִבְרָא בְּתַכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵמוּת הָאֶפְשָׁרִי.
This is His attribute of kindness: to extend an influx through which a creature can exist, and from this attribute each creature receives the fullest perfection possible to it.
וְאִם כֵּן אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חִלּוּק נִבְרָאִים שׁוֹנִים, שֶׁהוּא עַל כָּרְחֲךָ מִצַּד חֶסְרוֹן מַעֲלָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה מַה שֶּׁאֵין בָּזֶה.
Accordingly, differentiation into distinct creatures would seem impossible, since such differentiation necessarily means that one has a quality that another lacks.
וְעַל כֵּן נִבְרָא בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי מִדַּת הַצִּמְצוּם וּשְׂמֹאל הַדּוֹחָה נֶגֶד יָמִין הַמְקָרֶבֶת.
Therefore on the second day the attribute of constriction was created—the left hand that pushes away, corresponding to the right hand that draws near.
וּמִזֶּה נַעֲשֵׂית הַהַבְדָּלָה, לוֹמַר: עַד פֹּה יָבוֹא הַשָּׂגַת נִבְרָא זֶה, וְעַד פֹּה זֶה.
From this arises separation: the apprehension of this creature reaches this far, and that of another reaches only to its own boundary.
וּמִזֶּה בָּאָה הַשָּׂגַת יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁבָּא אַחַר אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהָיָה רֹאשׁ הַמַּשִּׂיגִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹרֵא עוֹלָם.
From this came the apprehension of Isaac our father, peace be upon him, who followed Abraham our father, peace be upon him, the first of those who attained recognition of a Creator of the world.
וְהוּא לֹא נִסְתַּפֵּק בְּהַשָּׂגַת אָבִיו, רַק רָצָה לְהַשִּׂיג עוֹד הַשָּׂגָה נִבְדֶּלֶת.
Isaac was not content merely with his father's apprehension; he sought to attain an additional, distinct apprehension.

כַּיָּדוּעַ, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא "אֱלֹהֵי" וְכוּלֵי886 Exodus 3:6 — “And He said: I am the God of your father, the God of Avraham, the God of Yitzchak and the God of Yaakov. And Moshe hid his face, for he was afraid to gaze upon God.” Ramban: On the plain level "the God of your father" is like "the God of your fathers," Scripture using the singular in place of the plural — the God of each one of your forefathers, since every one of them may be called a man's father. So too "the God of David your father," and "my father's God, and I will exalt Him." עַל כָּל אֶחָד, כִּי כָל אֶחָד הָיָה מַשִּׂיג הַשָּׂגָה מְיֻחֶדֶת וְנִבְדֶּלֶת.
Thus the Divine Name is associated separately with each Patriarch, because each attained a unique and distinct apprehension.
וְדָבָר זֶה חִדֵּשׁ יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: שֶׁיֵּשׁ הַשָּׂגוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת וּדְרָכִים שׁוֹנוֹת לְהַגִּיעַ לַאֲמִתּוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
This was Isaac's innovation: there are different apprehensions and different paths by which one can reach the truth of the Blessed One.
כִּי לוּלֵי זֶה הָיָה דַּי בְּנִבְרָא אֶחָד וּבִבְרִיאַת יוֹם אֶחָד בִּלְבַד.
Were this not so, a single creature and a single day of Creation would have sufficed.
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִבְדִּיל וְיָצַר נִבְרָאִים שׁוֹנִים, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּיֵשׁ הַשָּׂגוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת וְנִבְדָּלוֹת לְקִלּוּסוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְכָל אַחַת אֱמֶת לְעַצְמָהּ וּבִמְקוֹמָהּ.
Since the Blessed One differentiated and formed different creatures, there must be different and distinct apprehensions through which He is praised; each is true in itself and in its proper place.
וְזֶהוּ מִדָּתָן שֶׁל אָבוֹת, שֶׁאֵין כָּאן מַחֲלוֹקֶת בֶּאֱמֶת.
This is the character of the Patriarchs: in truth there is no dispute among them.
כִּי מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, שֶׁהֵן אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה כַּיָּדוּעַ, שְׁתֵּיהֶן אֱמֶת גַּם יַחַד, וְצָרִיךְ לְעָבְדוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּשְׁתֵּיהֶן.
The attributes of Abraham and Isaac—love and awe, as is known—are both simultaneously true, and one must serve the Blessed One through both.
וְכָל אַחַת אֱמֶת בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ וּכְפִי מַדְרֵגָתָהּ, כְּמוֹ מַיִם עֶלְיוֹנִים וְתַחְתּוֹנִים וְרָקִיעַ הַמַּבְדִּיל, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִשְׁנֵיהֶם מְצִיאוּת גָּמוּר, כָּל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹמוֹ.
Each is true independently according to its level, like the upper and lower waters and the firmament separating them: both possess complete reality, each in its own place.
אֲבָל בַּבָּנִים אַחַר כָּךְ — רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר בַּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת — כְּבָר הָיוּ כָּל אֶחָד כָּלוּל מִשְּׁתֵּי הַמִּדּוֹת, אֶלָּא שֶׁבְּאֶחָד גּוֹבֵר מִדָּה זוֹ וּבְאֶחָד גּוֹבֵר זוֹ.
Among the children afterward—that is, as these qualities spread outward—each person already contained both attributes, though one attribute predominated in one person and the other in another.
וּמִזֶּה נִתְהַוָּה הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת, דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁעַל דָּבָר אֶחָד עַצְמוֹ זֶה יֹאמַר כָּךְ וְזֶה יֹאמַר כָּךְ.
From this arose dispute: regarding the very same matter, one person says one thing and another says the opposite.
כִּי כְּבָר הֵם כֻּלָּם מְחֻבָּרִים וּמְיֻחָדִים יַחַד גַּם כֵּן בְּהִתְכַּלְלוּת, וּלְפִיכָךְ בָּא מִזֶּה שְׁפִיטָתָם עַל דָּבָר אֶחָד בְּחִלּוּף.
Because all of them are already interconnected and united through mutual inclusion, they can judge the same matter in opposing ways.
וּלְכָךְ הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת הִתְחִיל בַּבָּנִים, וּבִבְנֵי יַעֲקֹב הִתְחִיל בְּתֹקֶף הַשִּׂנְאָה עַד שֶׁ"לֹא יָכְלוּ דַּבְּרוֹ" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּגֶדֶר מַחֲלוֹקֶת כְּלָל רַק מִלְחָמָה.
Therefore dispute began among the children; among Jacob's sons it intensified into such hatred that 'they could not speak peaceably to him,' no longer merely a dispute but a state of war.

וְהַכָּתוּב אוֹמֵר: "כִּי תֵצֵא לַמִּלְחָמָה עַל אֹיְבֶיךָ" — לֹא עַל אָחִיךָ; "יְהוּדָה עַל אֶפְרַיִם" וְכוּלֵי (סוֹטָה מב.)887 Sotah 42a — "And he shall say to them: Hear, Israel, you draw near this day to battle against your enemies" (Deuteronomy 20:3) — against your enemies, and not against your brothers; not Judah against Simeon and not Simeon against Benjamin, for if you fall into their hands they will have mercy upon you, as it is stated: "And the men who were mentioned by name rose up and took the captives, and with the spoil clothed all that were naked among them... and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren" (II Chronicles 28:15). It is against your enemies that you march, for if you fall into their hands they will have no mercy upon you. Rashi: "And the men rose up": this is written in Chronicles concerning Pekah son of Remaliah, who fought against Ahaz and took many captives from the children of Judah. A prophet named Oded was there, who rebuked the children of Israel and said to them: "In the Lord's wrath against the children of Judah He delivered them into your hand, and you smote them beyond healing; and now you say you will subdue them as slaves — hear me and return the captives." Maharsha: "Against your enemies" would be superfluous, since one goes to war only against one's enemies; it is written to teach "and not against your brothers," for your brother is not included among your enemies, since it is forbidden to hate him, as it is written: "You shall not hate your brother" (Leviticus 19:17). It names Judah, Simeon and Benjamin rather than Judah and Ephraim, the war of the verse it cites, because this Mishna was taught in the Second Temple period, when only Judah and Benjamin, whom Nebuchadnezzar had exiled to Babylon, had returned, while the Ten Tribes exiled by the king of Assyria had not; and Simeon is named because his inheritance lay within Judah's, so that presumably they were exiled and returned together. "With the spoil clothed all that were naked among them, and arrayed them" is doubled: they clothed them from the spoil they had brought from the land of Judah and added garments of their own besides..
Yet Scripture says, 'When you go out to war against your enemies'—not against your brother; 'Judah against Ephraim,' etc. (Sotah 42a).
שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע קֹדֶשׁ וְגוֹי אֶחָד, וְכָל הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת בֵּינֵיהֶם הוּא רַק אֵיךְ לַעֲבוֹד אֶת הַשֵּׁם, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם מְכַוְּנִים לִכְבוֹדוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
In truth all Israel are holy seed and one nation, and their disputes concern how to serve the Lord; both sides ultimately intend the Blessed One's glory.

וַאֲפִלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ בִּזְמַן בַּיִת רִאשׁוֹן שֶׁבְּמַלְכוּת אֶפְרַיִם הָיוּ רֻבָּם רְשָׁעִים, דְּמִזֶּה נִצְמַח מַחֲלוֹקֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים שֶׁהֵרִיחוּ מַה שֶּׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד, כַּיָּדוּעַ —

This applies even to the wicked of Israel. In the First Temple period, most of the kingdom of Ephraim were wicked, and from this grew the tribal division, for the tribes sensed what would later unfold, as is known—

בֶּאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת פט:)888 Shabbat 89b — "If your sins be like scarlet [ka-shanim]" — it should have said ka-shani, in the singular. R. Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel — even if your sins are as many as those years that have come in order from the six days of Creation until now, "they shall become white as snow." Rashi: "It should have said ka-shani" [in the singular] — parallel to "as snow," for it does not say "as snows." Maharsha: "Like these years that are ordered" refers to the multitude of sin — as many as the years, presumably the years that have run in order since the six days of creation. One cannot read ka-shanim as "like two years," the minimal plural, for what novelty would there be in two sins? We say in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah that He removes the first [sin] first, so for two sins "they shall be white as snow" would not be needed. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 89b): Sin is open to atonement because it is committed by accident, and the accidental does not annul what a person is in essence; but sins committed in great number and constantly are no longer accidental, and so the Holy One, blessed be He, says that even if your sins are ordered and fixed like these years, they shall be white as snow. Nothing is more fixed and ordered than the years, which have run so since the six days of creation, yet even they will cease, since the world is physical and will end in destruction; so too Israel's sins, though fixed on the side of the physical, can be removed, because Israel's essential level is not physical. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Chalomos 19): The holiness of Tisha B'Av in the future, when it becomes a festival, will not come from Israel's sanctifying it, for on the contrary they sinned and made it a day of calamity, but only because in the future "your sins will be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation," as stated in Shabbos 89b: then "they shall be white as snow" and be turned into merits, through this, that such was the will of the Blessed One from the six days of creation. Thus the essence of its holiness is only that this was the Blessed One's will at the beginning of creation, a holiness fixed and abiding like the holiness of Shabbos, except that it is revealed only in the future, after the rectification. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): "The scarlet [shanim] shall be white as snow" means that the scarlet of holiness, too, will be whitened, after they lift their eyes to the Blessed One, as stated in Shabbos there; and the sins will be "like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation," that is, like merits; and afterwards they will rise still further, to the supernal whiteness, which is Wisdom, above Understanding. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on Samson 17): The deed itself is ordered and set so, as "Bathsheba was destined for David from the six days of creation," and in truth this will be clarified in the future regarding all the sins of Israel, when they are refined and whitened, as the Sages said, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation, they shall be white as snow." That is, since the true will of the Blessed One was so, it is like a transgression for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 4): In the future this will be clarified regarding all the sins of Israel, as the Sages said in Shabbos 89b on the verse "If your sins be": "like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation" — it will be clarified that it was ordered from the true will of the Blessed One that it be so, and if so, in this too they did the will of the Blessed One, and it was all like a transgression for the sake of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Naso 2): Such was the intent in the creation of the world, "first darkness and then light," as the Zohar says, there is no light but that which comes out of darkness; and then "the Lord will not count iniquity to him," since it will be clarified that this was created only so that it be "very good." As they said, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation, they shall be white as snow," that is, they will be as merits. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 3): From the side of the hidden things that will be revealed in the future there was no sin at all, and of this they said, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation," that is, from the side of the "hidden things of the Merciful One," then "they shall be white as snow" entirely, for there is no sin at all. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Mishlei 31): Snow alludes to fear, and so the Gemara says, "If your sins be like these years, which come in order from the six days of creation until now, they shall be white as snow": "years" alludes to cycles and order, that is, if there is an accusation, Heaven forbid, and it seems that a person sinned deliberately and in [recurring] cycles, the Blessed One will illuminate that this deed came only out of fear of the Blessed One, and this is "white as snow." דְּ"יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים" — הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית — "כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ".

yet our Sages of blessed memory taught (Shabbat 89b) that 'though your sins be as scarlet' refers to those arranged and coming from the six days of Creation, and nevertheless 'they shall become white as snow.'
וְאָז "אֶפְרַיִם לֹא יְקַנֵּא אֶת יְהוּדָה, וִיהוּדָה" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁעִקַּר מִלְחַמְתָּן בָּא מִצַּד הַחֶסְרוֹנוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד, וְכָל אֶחָד חוֹשֵׁב עַל חֲבֵרוֹ שֶׁהוּא רָשָׁע.
Then 'Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah...' etc.; for their war stems chiefly from the deficiencies each perceives in the other, each regarding his fellow as wicked.
וְכַיָּדוּעַ דִּבַּת יוֹסֵף עַל הַשְּׁבָטִים, וְכֵן הֵם שְׂנָאוּהוּ מִפְּנֵי הַלָּשׁוֹן הָרָע וְהַגַּאֲוָה בִּרְדִיפַת כָּבוֹד וּשְׂרָרָה שֶׁרָאוּ בוֹ.
Thus Joseph reported negatively about his brothers, while they hated him because they perceived in him evil speech and arrogance expressed in a pursuit of honor and authority.

וְהִיא שֶׁהוֹצִיאָתוֹ לְיָרָבְעָם מִן הָעוֹלָם (סַנְהֶדְרִין קא:)889 Sanhedrin 101b — Rav Nachman said: The arrogance that was in Jeroboam drove him from the world, as it is said, "And Jeroboam said in his heart: Now the kingdom will return to the house of David. If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the House of the Lord in Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn back to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah.", כִּמְפֹרָשׁ בַּמִּקְרָא.
That same pursuit of authority ultimately removed Jeroboam from the world (Sanhedrin 101b), as Scripture makes explicit.
וְדָבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד סֵדֶר הַבְּרִיאָה כְּלָל — לִהְיוֹת מִלְחָמָה וְשִׂנְאָה בָּעוֹלָם.
War and hatred in the world are not, in themselves, part of the intended order of Creation.
וְהַכָּתוּב מַזְהִיר: "וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ", "לֹא תִשְׂנָא אֶת אָחִיךָ" וְגוֹמֵר.
Scripture commands, 'You shall love your fellow as yourself' and 'You shall not hate your brother,' etc.

וַאֲפִלּוּ רָשָׁע גָּמוּר, כֵּיוָן שֶׁלָּקָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ (מַכּוֹת כג.)890 Makkot 23a — All those liable to excision who were flogged are exempted from their excision, as it is stated: "And your brother shall be degraded before your eyes" — once he has been flogged he is as your brother; these are the words of R. Chananya ben Gamliel..
Even one who is thoroughly wicked, once he has received his punishment, is again regarded as 'your brother' (Makkot 23a).

וְגַם כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים אַחִים וְרֵעִים בֶּאֱמֶת, וְכָל תַּעֲנִית שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מִפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי (כְּרִיתוֹת ו:)891 Keritot 6b — Rav Chana bar Bizna said in the name of R. Simeon the Pious: Any fast that does not include some of the transgressors of Israel is not a fast — for galbanum's odor is foul, and yet Scripture numbered it among the spices of the incense. Abaye said: [It is derived] from here — "and has founded His bundle upon the earth" (Amos 9:6). Rashi (s.v. "and His bundle"): "And His bundle" — the word implies that only when they are all together is it "founded upon the earth." Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot): He was precise to say "and Scripture numbered it among the spices" rather than "and it is burned with them": the point is that the transgressor is counted with them in their fast and does not separate himself from them. And from the hint one may learn further: as there were eleven kinds of spice, ten of good odor and one, galbanum, of foul odor, so the transgressor may be joined to them where there is a holy congregation of ten without him, but he is not to be counted as one of the ten. A remembrance of this is "I will not destroy for the sake of the ten" (Genesis 18:32) — for fewer than ten [Abraham] did not pray. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 7): The incense belongs to the attribute of judgment, as it is written, "they shall put incense before You" (Deuteronomy 33:10); and therefore it is made of spices, which have fragrance, for fragrance belongs to the attribute of judgment. A fast likewise belongs to the attribute of judgment, and therefore there must be among them transgressors who overcome the force of their evil inclination in joining them in the fast — and this too is called "fragrance." Galbanum was numbered by Scripture among the spices of the incense precisely because its power is greater than that of all the other spices., שֶׁאַף הֵם מִכְּלַל הָאֲגֻדָּה.
All Israel are truly called brothers and companions; a communal fast that does not include the sinners of Israel, etc. (Keritot 6b), is deficient, because they too belong to the collective bond.
וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּהָא דְּהָרוֹאֶה בַּחֲבֵרוֹ דְּבַר עֶרְוָה מֻתָּר לִשְׂנֹאתוֹ — הַיְנוּ מִצַּד הָרַע, אֲבָל מִצְוָה לְאָהֳבוֹ מִצַּד הַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ.
It is known that the permission to hate one in whom a sinful matter is witnessed applies only to the evil itself; one must still love him for the good that is within him.
וַהֲרֵי מְצֻוִּין לְהַפְרִישׁ מֵאִסּוּר אַף לִרְשָׁעִים, דְּלֹא אָמְרִינַן "הַלְעִיטֵהוּ לָרָשָׁע" וְגוֹמֵר אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁהוּא רָשָׁע בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר דַּוְקָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר.

We are commanded to separate even wicked people from transgression; the principle 'feed it to the wicked one,' etc., is said only when he is specifically wicked regarding that very matter, as I have written elsewhere.
וּצְרִיכִין לְזַכּוֹת לַחַיָּבִים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אֲלַמְּדָה פֹשְׁעִים דְּרָכֶיךָ" וְגוֹמֵר.
One must seek merit and restoration even for those who are guilty, as it is written, 'I will teach transgressors Your ways,' etc.

וְ"יִתַּמּוּ חוֹטְאִים" לֹא כְּתִיב, רַק "חַטָּאִים" (בְּרָכוֹת י.)892 Berakhot 10a — There were certain hooligans in R. Meir's neighborhood who caused him much distress, and R. Meir prayed for mercy concerning them, that they should die. Beruria his wife said to him: What is your reasoning? Because it is written, "Let sins cease"? Is "sinners" written? "Sins" is written. And further, look to the end of the verse: "and the wicked will be no more." Once sins cease, the wicked are no more. Rather, pray for mercy concerning them that they repent, and "the wicked will be no more." He prayed for mercy concerning them, and they repented. Rashi: Rashi glosses the "hooligans" as lawless men. On "'Sins' is written" he explains: read the word as "sins" — that the evil inclination itself should come to an end. And "look to the end of the verse" means literally: lower yourself to its end, for whatever stands last in a matter is called its lower part. Maharsha: Maharsha explains that had "sinners" been written — a word that can only be an adjective describing persons — R. Meir would have prayed rightly, since the death of the wicked is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world; but "sins" is a noun, and so one should rather pray that they live and that their sins cease. He then raises a difficulty: a man may pray for his own repentance, since "in the way a man wishes to go, they lead him" and "one who comes to purify himself is helped"; but how can prayer for another's repentance avail, given that "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven"? Maharal (Be'er HaGolah, Seventh Well, ch. 6): R. Meir thought to pray that the wicked should die, and his wife told him that such a prayer is not fitting: even of a wicked man one may not pray that he die, since it is still possible that he will turn from his sin — and why pray that a man be destroyed, when man is the handiwork of the Holy One, blessed be He? This is why the verse says "Let sins cease from the earth" and not "sinners," which is an adjective for the wicked man himself and would mean that the one who sins should die. "Let sins cease" means that the sin should no longer be found — that the Holy One, blessed be He, turn the sinner's mind so that he does evil no more; and that is how prayer ought to be., וְהַשִּׂנְאָה רַק לַחֲטָאִים.
And it is not written, 'Let sinners cease,' but 'sins' (Berakhot 10a); the hatred is directed only toward the sins.
וְגַם כִּי עִקַּר הַחֲטָאִים אֵינוֹ מִסֵּדֶר הַבְּרִיאָה כְּלָל, וְאִם כֵּן אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁתִּהְיֶה הַשִּׂנְאָה וְהַמִּלְחָמָה מִסֵּדֶר הַבְּרִיאָה.
Moreover, sins themselves are not part of the intrinsic order of Creation; therefore hatred and war cannot belong to that intrinsic order either.

רַק הוּא דָּבָר הַנִּמְשָׁךְ עַל יְדֵי בְּחִירַת אָדָם, וּכְמוֹ הַקְּלִפָּה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת לַפְּרִי וּ"בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא" וְכוּלֵי (שַׁבָּת עז:)893 Shabbat 77b — R. Zeira found Rav Yehuda standing at the door of his father-in-law's house, and saw that he was in a cheerful mood, such that had he asked him about all the hollows of the world he would have told him. He said to him: Why do the goats walk at the front and the sheep after them? He said to him: It is as in the creation of the world — first darkness and afterward light. Rashi: "All the hollows of the world": that is, the things that happen throughout the space of the world. "First darkness": goats are generally black, and ewes generally white. Maharsha: Although the natural philosophers gave reasons for how each thing is formed, and the Talmud too has a few such ("why is the whole ear hard and the lobe soft"), these reasons are forced in their plain sense, so they must be meant as a parable on matters of Torah: Greece is likened to a goat ("and the he-goat grew exceedingly great", Daniel 8:8) and Israel to a sheep ("Israel is a scattered sheep", Jeremiah 50:17), and he asked why in the Second Temple the goats — the kings of Greece, Alexander of Macedon and those after him — reigned first, and only afterward the sheep, the kings of Israel. He answered that this was already alluded to in the creation of the world: first darkness — "and darkness was upon the face of the deep", which Bereshit Rabbah expounds of Greece, who darkened Israel's eyes — and afterward light, the Hasmonean kingdom, who came to reign through the miracle of the Chanukah lights. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 77b): The goats derive from the power of the attribute of judgment, which is the attribute of night; and night came before day because the attribute of judgment, by the very strength of that attribute, hastens to go forth into actuality. So too the goats walk at the head of the flock because of the swiftness of action they receive from the attribute of judgment — and this is what he answered him: as at the creation of the world. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 1): With respect to night, which is darkness, cessation and darkness come before day, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness...": for one who stands in darkness, darkness comes first and afterward light, and so there were two thousand years of chaos and afterward two thousand of Torah. But for one who stands in the day, day comes first and afterward night, to rest from his toil; and so once the Torah was given there was light for the world, and light comes before darkness. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 61): Esau was the firstborn in birth, which is the emergence into actuality, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness": on the side of the refuse the left is the right and comes first, and the this-world of Esau, in which darkness prevails, comes first. But in formation [yetzirah], which is the hidden world, the thought of creation and the conception of the world, the right comes first. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 8): The creation of the world was "first darkness and afterward light": first comes the portion of Bereishis, in the knowledge of the vessels, and afterward the attainment of the light of Abraham our father through knowledge, in the manner of "the advantage of light over darkness." Such too is the order of man's attainment of the light of the Blessed One, like the creation of the world: first the six days of work and afterward Shabbos; but for man's own action the light must come first and afterward the making of the vessel. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): This light [of the soul's root] can be attained in this world only through repentance, for such is the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light." Thus for certain righteous men, such as King David in the trial of Bathsheba, the Blessed One arranged a deed of the wicked in order to establish the yoke of repentance, for this cannot come about except through a preceding darkness. Rav Tzadok (Poked Akarim 4): [In the Oral Torah and the innovation of laws not yet clarified] it is impossible to stand at all without a prior stumbling, as at the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light," for so is the light attained by created beings: specifically out of darkness and concealment. Therefore Esau was formed before Jacob, being the preceding darkness that leads to the attainment of the light of Torah afterward. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 21): On "Why do the goats go first... as at the creation of the world, first darkness and afterward light," Rashi explains that goats are ordinarily black. So Teves, whose sign is the kid, is the aspect of darkness, and specifically then [the Hasmoneans] brought about their miracle through their self-sacrifice, to shine out of the darkness with greater excellence, as the Zohar says, "there is no light except that which comes out of darkness"; and this is like the creation of the world. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Sheidim 1): Since it is of the working of the Blessed One that it be so, "first darkness and afterward light," for the advantage of light is recognized only from darkness, [the forces of evil] therefore begin to act first, and from this the light shines forth, as in "He made darkness His hiding place," for there He is hidden. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): Such is the way of the Blessed One in the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light"; and so [the Sages] said that He would create worlds and destroy them, these being the worlds of chaos, until the world of rectification emerged. So it is in everything: all the incarnations of the Messiah that have already been in the world are akin to "creating worlds and destroying them," and specifically through those destructions the world of rectification is built, by raising up the lights of the broken vessels. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 174): Since in natural things the Blessed One established this order, "first darkness and afterward light," it is certainly the essence of His will, as [the Sages said], "In the place where penitents stand...". Although, Heaven forbid, one may not say "I will sin and repent" and do so by choice, it nonetheless happens of itself, for "there is no righteous man on earth..."; and such is the order: "the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light," far beyond one who did not walk in darkness. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): From the standpoint of this world's imagination it seemed at first that everything belonged to Esau, for such is the creation of the world, "first darkness and afterward light," as [the Sages] said at the beginning of Berakhos, which is why the evening Shema was placed first. For the Shema, the recognition of [God's] unity, was the essence of the creation of the world, and first one must recognize it out of darkness and concealment, for that was the whole matter of creation. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Shabbos): This is as it is written, "The Lord my God illuminates my darkness": after a person recognizes his sin and is pained over it, he merits that the Blessed One shines for him a rectification for it. Through the darkness, the remorse and pain he felt over the deed, he merits the light that reveals its rectification; and this is "first darkness and afterward light." Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 71): The Blessed One set the light in this world surrounded and encompassed by darkness, to leave man room to distinguish himself, that he remove the darkness and shine even within it. Therefore, when the Blessed One shines His bright light, He will shine it only for one who on his part walked in the light and did His will; He created the darkness only for the sake of one who desires the light, that for his sake He will illuminate the darkness too. Tiferes Yosef (Shavuos 7): It is written, "who forms light and creates darkness," yet at the creation of the world "there was evening and there was morning," first darkness and afterward light, so here too it should have said "creates darkness" first. The explanation: the first light was not yet within creation's capacity to receive, and light that creation cannot receive is called darkness from creation's standpoint; therefore it says "forms light and creates darkness," for from creation's standpoint it begins with day, since in the first evening creation had no grasp at all. Sod Yesharim (Shabbos HaGadol 6): As my father and teacher explained, the whole purpose of the darkness that the Blessed One set first is only that the light afterward be the more explicit; therefore "it was evening" is said first and then "it was morning." So too with Abraham our father: all the concealment he had at first, until he said, "Shall you say the palace has no master?", was the darkness that came first, only so that the Blessed One would afterward shine to him with greater clarity, "I am the master of the palace.",
Rather, it is something that arises through human choice, like the shell that precedes the fruit and the principle that 'at first there is darkness,' etc. (Shabbat 77b).
כָּךְ בַּתְּחִלָּה נִתְגַּלָּה עִנְיַן הַשִּׂנְאָה בֵּין אָדָם לַחֲבֵרוֹ, הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵהַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר שֶׁמִּסֵּדֶר הַבְּרִיאָה לִהְיוֹת דְּבָרִים נִבְדָּלִים.
So too, hatred between people first appears as an outgrowth of disagreement, while disagreement itself does belong to the created order of distinct things.
וּמִמַּחֲלוֹקֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים עַד אַחַר מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, בְּמַחֲלוֹקֶת קֹרַח, הָיָה בֵּרוּר דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁאֵין בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שִׂנְאָה בֶּאֱמֶת כְּלָל.
From the dispute among the tribes until after the giving of the Torah, in Korah's dispute, this matter was clarified: in truth, there is no essential hatred within Israel.
דְּגַם שִׂנְאָתָם, גַּם קִנְאָתָם, הוּא בְּגֶדֶר מַחֲלוֹקֶת לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְפִי שָׁעָה — דְּנַעֲשׂוּ כְּאוֹיְבִים זֶה לָזֶה, "וְאֶת וָהֵב בְּסוּפָהּ".
Even their hatred and jealousy are, at root, a temporary dispute for the sake of Heaven: they may become like enemies to one another, but 'in the end, love.'
וְאָז הִתְחִיל שֵׁירוּתָא דְּמַחֲלוֹקֶת לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת, שֶׁעֲדַיִן הָיָה נָחָשׁ, הַקְּלִפָּה דְּשִׂנְאָה וְקִנְאָה, כָּרוּךְ עַל עֲקֵבוֹ.
Then the 'beginning of dispute' became revealed, while the serpent—the husk of hatred and jealousy—was still wound around its heel.
וְהַגַּם דְּעִקָּרוֹ מַחֲלוֹקֶת לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, שֶׁטָּעַן דְּ"כָל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים", שֶׁאֵין רָאוּי לְהִתְנַשֵּׂא,
Its essential claim was indeed a dispute for the sake of Heaven: Korah argued, 'the entire congregation are all holy,' and therefore no one should exalt himself over the others.
וְזֶה אֱמֶת גָּמוּר מִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת הֶעָתִיד לִהְיוֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְלֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ, כִּי כֻלָּם יֵדְעוּ" וְגוֹמֵר.
From the perspective of the future attainment, this is entirely true, as it is said: 'They shall no longer teach each man his fellow... for they shall all know Me,' etc.
וּלְכָךְ בְּנֵי קֹרַח, שֶׁהֵם לֹא בָּאוּ בָּזֶה מֵחֲמַת קִנְאָה וְשִׂנְאָה, לֹא מֵתוּ.
Therefore the sons of Korah, who did not enter the dispute out of jealousy and hatred, did not die.
וְלָכֵן הֵם אָמְרוּ קִלּוּס שֶׁל יוֹם זֶה: שֶׁעַל יְדֵי עִנְיַן הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת וְהַמִּלְחָמָה הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִזֶּה, מִזֶּה "גָּדוֹל הַשֵּׁם וּמְהֻלָּל מְאֹד בְּעִיר" וְגוֹמֵר.
Thus they recited the praise of this day: through dispute and the war that can emerge from it, 'Great is the Lord and greatly praised in the city,' etc.
בַּמָּקוֹם שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹכֵן, וּמִתְבָּרֵר הָאֱמֶת מִתּוֹךְ הַהֵפֶךְ, בָּזֶה נִכָּר יִתְרוֹן גָּדוֹל.
In the place where He dwells, truth becomes clarified specifically from within its opposite, and thereby a greater excellence is revealed.

וְזֶהוּ הִלּוּל "מְאֹד", עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה ט)894 Bereshit Rabbah 9:5-7 — In R. Meir's Torah scroll they found written: "And behold, it was very [me'od] good" — and behold, death [mot] is good. R. Shimon ben Elazar said: "And behold, it was very good" — and behold, sleep is good. And is sleep very good? Rather, because a man sleeps a little he rises and toils much in Torah. R. Nachman bar Shmuel bar Nachman said in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Nachman: "Behold, it was good" — this is the good inclination; "and behold, it was very good" — this is the evil inclination. And is the evil inclination very good? Rather, were it not for the evil inclination a man would never build a house, never marry a wife, never beget children, and never engage in commerce. עַל פָּסוּק "טוֹב מְאֹד": זֶה מָוֶת וְשֵׁנָה וְיֵצֶר הָרָע.
This is the praise of 'very,' as Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 9) expounds 'very good' to include death, sleep, and the evil inclination.
כָּל מַה שֶּׁנִּרְאֶה רַע — זֶה גּוֹרֵם לְ"טוֹב מְאֹד"; וְכֵן מִצַּד הַמַּחֲלוֹקֶת בָּא קִלּוּס "מְאֹד", וְהוּא הַמְּלוּכָה שֶׁהוּא יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁלִיטָה, כָּאָמוּר.
What appears evil becomes the cause of 'very good.' Likewise, dispute gives rise to a praise of 'very,' namely kingship, which is greater than mere rule, as explained.

וּשְׁנַיִם עֲדַיִן אֵינוֹ רִבּוּי, וְכַיָּדוּעַ (תּוֹסָפוֹת כְּתֻבּוֹת ח., סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל "שֶׁהַכֹּל895 Tosafot on Ketubot 8a:1:1 — And Rabbeinu Tam said that in the first chapter of Berakhot (11b), regarding the blessing over the Torah, our reading is: "R. Yochanan concluded with: And make pleasant" — for it is a single blessing; for if they were two blessings he would have had to open with "Blessed," even though it adjoins its fellow, since the one preceding it is short. And afterwards our reading is: "Therefore let us say both of them [tarvaihu]" — and we do not read "all of them [kulhu]," for if so it would imply that they are three blessings.") דְּלֹא שַׁיָּךְ לְשׁוֹן "כֹּל" עַל שְׁנַיִם, רַק עַל שְׁלֹשָׁה, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא כְּלָלוּת.
Two still do not constitute multiplicity in the full sense; as Tosafot notes (Ketubot 8a, s.v. 'shehakol'), the term 'all' does not properly apply to two but to three, which forms a collective.
וְשִׁיר יוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי הוּא: "נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת" וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁיִּסֵּד אֶרֶץ בְּחָכְמָתוֹ וְהֵכִין תֵּבֵל לַעֲדָתוֹ.
The song of the third day is therefore 'He stands in the congregation,' etc., for He founded the earth with His wisdom and prepared the inhabited world for His congregation.
וְעִקַּר לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב מוֹרֶה עַל מִלַּת "לַעֲדָתוֹ", דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ כְּלָלוּת עֵדָה שֶׁהַתֵּבֵל מוּכָן לָהֶם לְהַכִּיר עַל יָדָהּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִצָּב בְּתוֹכָם.

The central force of the verse lies in the word 'for His congregation': there is a collective assembly for whom the world is prepared, so that through it they may recognize that the Blessed One stands in their midst.
וְכֵן נִקְרֵאת "עֲדַת יַעֲקֹב", שֶׁעַל שֵׁם יַעֲקֹב נִקְרֵאת עֵדָה.
Thus Israel is called 'the congregation of Jacob'; the concept of congregation is associated specifically with Jacob.

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סח)896 Bereshit Rabbah 68:12 — R. Salmoni said in the name of Resh Lakish: He showed him a stool of three legs. R. Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in the name of R. Levi: You are the third leg. This is R. Yehoshua of Sikhnin's own view in the name of R. Levi, who said: "For the Lord's portion is His people, Jacob the cord of His inheritance" — just as a cord is not twisted from fewer than three strands, so the patriarchs are not fewer than three. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 38): Isaac was Israel from birth, so that even his dross is called "an apostate Israelite"; only, "the cord is not snapped with fewer than three," so it was still possible to apostatize and change — until Jacob, "the cord of His inheritance," in whom there is no dross at all. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 10): "Jacob the cord of His inheritance" — an inheritance that has no interruption — comes only from Jacob, as the Sages said, "the cord is not snapped with fewer than three," for three times make a presumption; so it says, "[My words] shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed ... from now and forever," for once established through three generations it holds in their seed forever. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 11): Joining the two mitzvos of the Chanukah lamp and the mezuzah to the thread of tzitzis [between them] strengthens that thread into a "threefold cord," and thereby it becomes the aspect of "Jacob the cord of His inheritance" — threefold from the holiness of all three patriarchs, like a cord that is not snapped with fewer than three; and this power was fixed and completed in the collective souls of Israel through the Chanukah lamp.: אֵין הַחֶבֶל נִפְקָע פָּחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה.
As they taught (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 68): a cord does not break when it is made of three strands.
דְּאָז נַעֲשָׂה יַעֲקֹב "חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ", לִהְיוֹת מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵמָה, שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כְּלָלִי וְלֹא פְרָטִי.
Then Jacob became 'the cord of His inheritance'; his household was complete, and he became a collective reality rather than merely an individual one.
וְהַיְנוּ כְּמוֹ חֶבֶל שֶׁהוּא מֵחוּטִין מְחֻבָּרִין וּשְׁזוּרִין יַחַד, כֵּן עֵדָה — חִבּוּר וְקִבּוּץ נִפְרָדִים יַחַד לִהְיוֹת גּוֹי אֶחָד.
Just as a cord consists of separate threads joined and twisted together, so a congregation is the joining and gathering of distinct individuals into one nation.

וְזֶה חִדֵּשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ עַל יְדֵי יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ הַשָּׂגוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת וְנִפְרָדוֹת זֶה מִזֶּה, בָּא הוּא וְחִדֵּשׁ דְּכָל הַהַשָּׂגוֹת הַשּׁוֹנוֹת וְהַנִּבְדָּלוֹת זֶה מִזֶּה הַכֹּל הוֹלֵךְ לְמָקוֹם אֶחָד, וְהַכֹּל אֶחָד מַמָּשׁ.

This was Jacob's innovation. After Isaac revealed that there are different, distinct apprehensions, Jacob revealed that all these differing apprehensions ultimately proceed to one place and are, in their root, truly one.

וְזֶה מִמַּה שֶּׁאָנוּ רוֹאִים בַּנִּבְרָאִים הַפְּרָטִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יב; וְזֹהַר חֵלֶק ג, לד עַמּוּד ב)897 Bereshit Rabbah 12:11 — Rav Huna said in the name of R. Yosef: Everything that is in the heavens and on the earth was created only from the earth. That is what is written: "For as the rain and the snow come down from the heavens." Just as the rain, though its descent is from the heavens, is created only from the earth, so everything that is in the heavens and on the earth is created only from the earth. R. Yudan derived it from here: "All go to one place; all came from the dust, and all return to the dust." Rav Nachman said: Even the orb of the sun, as it is said: "Who commands the sun and it does not shine." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 13): The "lip of truth" that "shall be established forever" springs "from the earth" specifically, the supernal earth, of which the Sages said "everything was from the dust, even the orb of the sun": it is the dust beneath the Throne of Glory, the source of the kav of chumton [the preservative earth] mixed into the wheat, which alludes to the twenty-two letters of the Written Torah. It would seem a flaw to mix earthiness into supernal Wisdom, but such is the will of the Blessed One, who brought the Torah down to the lower beings and cast truth to the ground, and all the nourishment of the heavenly household comes from the Torah among the lower beings.: הַכֹּל הָיָה מִן הֶעָפָר, וַאֲפִלּוּ גַּלְגַּל חַמָּה.
We can see this among individual creations, as our Sages of blessed memory taught (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 12; Zohar III, 34b): everything came from the earth—even the sphere of the sun.
וְכֵן כָּל מִינֵי צְמָחִים שֶׁנִּבְרְאוּ בְּיוֹם שְׁלִישִׁי, כֻּלָּם צוֹמְחִים מֵאֲדָמָה אַחַת, וְהֵם אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹרָן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבִּצְמִיחָתָן נִפְרָדִין.
Likewise, all the varieties of vegetation created on the third day grow from one earth; they are one at their source even though their growth branches into separate forms.
וְזֶהוּ "וְהֵכִין תֵּבֵל לַעֲדָתוֹ" — לְצוֹרֶךְ הַשָּׂגָה וְקִלּוּס זֶה.
This is the meaning of 'He prepared the world for His congregation': the world was prepared for this apprehension and this praise.

items.h:
Seif 3 — The Fourth Day: Torah's Light and Judgment
The luminaries parallel Torah's illumination, which separates Israel from idolatry and reveals divine praise even through judgment.

p: וְיוֹם הָרְבִיעִי, שֶׁבּוֹ בָּרָא חַמָּה וּלְבָנָה וְעָתִיד לִפָּרַע מֵעוֹבְדֵיהֶם.
On the fourth day He created the sun and the moon, and in the future He will exact punishment from those who worship them.
שֶׁבְּרִיאַת הַמְּאוֹרוֹת לְהָאִיר לָעוֹלָם הִיא דֻּגְמַת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהֵאִיר בְּאוֹר תּוֹרָה לְכָל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם.
The creation of the luminaries to illuminate the world parallels the giving of the Torah, which shone the light of Torah upon all who enter the world.

וְאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שַׁבָּת פט:)898 Shabbat 89a — Rav Chisda and Rabbah son of Rav Huna both said: What is "Mount Sinai"? A mountain upon which hatred [sinah] toward the nations of the world descended. And that is what R. Yosei son of R. Chanina said: it has five names — the wilderness of Zin, because Israel were commanded upon it; the wilderness of Kadesh, because Israel were sanctified upon it; the wilderness of Kedemot, because the ancient Torah was given upon it; the wilderness of Paran, because Israel were fruitful and multiplied upon it; the wilderness of Sinai, because hatred toward the nations of the world descended upon it. Rashi: "Hatred toward the nations" — because they did not accept the Torah on it. [On "the wilderness of Paran, because Israel were fruitful and multiplied upon it":] every man's wife conceived a male child through the command "Return to your tents"; but I do not know where this is alluded to. Tosafos (s.v. "the wilderness of Zin"): The Ri finds it difficult that Zin, Paran and Sinai should be one place: Zin lies at the southern edge of the Land of Israel, Paran is Kadesh-barnea, from which the spies were sent, several journeys separate Paran from Zin, and it is eleven days from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea. He answers that it was all one great wilderness — Sinai is Paran ("He shone forth from Mount Paran"), and Sinai is also Zin, since "the wilderness of Zin, that is Kadesh," and Sinai is called Kadesh ("The Lord shakes the wilderness of Kadesh," said of the Giving of the Torah). But it remains difficult for him that the wilderness of Kedemot lay east of the Land of Israel, whereas Zin and Paran lay to its south; how then could Kedemot be the wilderness of Sinai? Maharsha: The five names are descriptive names added to the mountain's proper name. Since, as Tosafot note, the wilderness of Kedemot lay east of the Land, it seems that the Torah was not all given in one place, and the names allude to this: "Zin, where Israel were commanded" denotes the commandments given at Sinai; "Kadesh, where they were sanctified," those given from the Tent of Meeting; and "Kedemot, where the primordial [Torah] was given," the plains of Moab, where the Torah already given at Sinai was given a second time as Deuteronomy. Maharal (Gevuros Hashem, ch. 23): The giving of the Torah is a supreme elevation for those who receive it, and once Israel merited it, the nations, who are unfit for it, necessarily received distance and hatred, for the Torah is the Divine order in the world and whoever lacks it is far from the Blessed One. Just as the Blessed One brings good to Israel out of love, so evil comes to the nations out of hatred; yet it is not called "the mountain of evil," God forbid, since no evil descends from above — rather He hates them, they are abandoned, and evil comes upon them. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 26): It is no difficulty that these names are not of one spot, for in the Sages' view the whole wilderness, from the time Israel reached the wilderness of Sinai, is one wilderness with no settled land in between. The wilderness, a place of the attribute of judgment where nothing natural and material is found, was fitting for the commandments decreed upon Israel, for their sanctification, and for the Torah that preceded the natural world. It is called "the wilderness of Sinai" because the Torah is near and beloved to the Blessed One, and when the nations distanced it they were utterly distanced from Him — and so hatred descended upon them. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Sivan 4): The essential time of the Giving of the Torah, when Israel merited that the statement "I am" should shine in their hearts and the evil inclination be uprooted from their hearts, is Shavuos. It is called Mount Sinai because at least hatred descended upon the nations of the world; yet it is also called Mount Horeb on account of the ultimate end in the future, when destruction will descend upon the nations, and this will come about through the power of the Giving of the Torah on Shavuos. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Vezos HaBerachah): On "The Lord came from Sinai and shone forth from Seir to them": the Gemara says "Sinai, for hatred toward the nations of the world descended upon it," and this is "came from Sinai," as in "and Esau I hated." From the moment He came to give the Torah, it was never in the Blessed One's mind to give it to them and draw them near; He asked them whether they would accept it only so that they would have no pretext, but in truth He asked them already in hatred, whereas of Israel it is said "I have loved you with an everlasting love." Tiferes Yosef (Shavuos 16): The Gemara answers that it is called Sinai "because hatred toward the nations of the world descended upon it": that is, the main thing is that Israel raises this point of holiness even onto the outermost garment, so that the more Israel is shown that he is bound to the light of His will, the more service he takes upon himself, and the more good the Blessed One bestows upon him, the more he accepts the kingdom of Heaven upon himself. The nations, by contrast, do not want service on their part, as the Midrash says that He went around to every nation and tongue and they did not accept it; therefore they were utterly nullified before Israel, and this is why it is called Sinai, because hatred toward the nations descended upon it. Sod Yesharim (Simchas Torah 2): [Moses] said to them "The Lord came from Sinai," as the Gemara says: why is it called Mount Sinai? Because from there hatred descended upon the nations of the world. That is, he told Israel that when they remove from themselves every self-interest on their own part, they will see His light, may He be blessed, explicitly within all the concealments. דְּנִקְרָא הַר סִינַי שֶׁיָּרְדָה שִׂנְאָה לְעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת עָלָיו,
Our Sages of blessed memory taught (Shabbat 89b) that Mount Sinai was so named because hatred descended there upon the idolatrous nations,

עַל יְדֵי מִדַּת הַנִּצּוּחַ, דַּרְגָּא דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁפָּנָיו כִּפְנֵי חַמָּה (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא עה.)899 Bava Batra 75a — "And you shall put of your honor upon him" — of your honor, but not all your honor. The elders of that generation said: The face of Moses was like the face of the sun, the face of Joshua like the face of the moon. Woe for that shame, woe for that disgrace. Rashbam: "The elders of that generation" — those who had seen both Moses and Joshua. "Woe for that shame" — that in so short a time the honor was so far diminished; for Joshua was prophet and ruler as Moses had been, and still could not reach his honor. Maharsha: Every righteous man has some distinction in some commandment that his fellow does not have, so that none of them is put to shame by another's canopy; the cry "woe for that shame, woe for that disgrace" is uttered over the man who has no distinction of his own at all. So too with Joshua: "of your honor, but not all your honor" means that he did not attain Moses's level in the wisdom of the Torah — which is what "the face of Moses was like the face of the sun" hints at — and yet he merited another great distinction, to enter the Land and to conquer its thirty-one kings..
through the attribute of victory, the level of Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, whose face was like the face of the sun (Bava Batra 75a).

וְאָמְרוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (נְדָרִים ח:)900 Nedarim 8b — R. Shimon ben Lakish said: There is no Gehenna in the World to Come; rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings the sun out from its sheath, and the righteous are healed by it and the wicked are punished by it. The righteous are healed by it, as it is stated: "But to you that fear My name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings"; and not only that, but they take delight in it, as it is stated: "And you shall go forth and gambol as calves of the stall." And the wicked are punished by it, as it is stated: "For behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace." Rashi: “The righteous are healed by it” — by that sun of the time to come; but in the sun of this world there is no healing. And “the day that comes shall set them ablaze” means the sun of that day. Tosafos (s.v. “and it differs from R. Shimon ben Lakish”): The exposition that applies “healing in its wings” to this world differs from R. Shimon ben Lakish, who applies the verse to a healing in the World to Come. Yet R. Shimon ben Lakish too concedes what people say, “when the sun rises the sick man rises”; he simply does not derive it from this verse. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Nedarim 8b): There is no Gehenna in the time to come because Gehenna is a deficiency of being, and in the time to come there is no deficiency of being, since everything will then be in its completeness. Rather the Holy One, blessed be He, brings the sun out of its sheath: the sheath is the obstructions and screens that in this world hinder the sun from performing its work, and in the time to come He will remove them. When the sun has no obstruction it burns the wicked, for the wicked cannot stand before a thing that is not material; but the righteous, who are separated [from matter], take delight in it, for the enjoyment of light belongs to the intellect, which is separate from the physical. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas HaChodesh 7): The nations count by the sun, which is fire, whereas Israel count by the moon, which is all light, for the moon only receives light from the sun and is not of fire. This is the meaning of "the Holy One, blessed be He, brings the sun out of its sheath; the righteous are healed by it": they attain only the light of the sun, like the moon that receives its light; "and the wicked are judged by it," for its fire burns them, as it is said, "the coming day shall set them ablaze." Sod Yesharim (Hoshana Rabbah 9): The very bestowal that is life to Israel, who receive it willingly, turns against the idolaters, who take it by compulsion and insolence, until they are utterly nullified by it. As the Gemara says, the Holy One, blessed be He, "brings the sun out of its sheath" and it heals Israel, while from it comes complete nullification to the idolaters.: אֵין גֵּיהִנֹּם לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, אֶלָּא שֶׁמֶשׁ מוֹצִיא מִנַּרְתִּיקָהּ — צַדִּיקִים וְכוּלֵי, וּרְשָׁעִים וְכוּלֵי.
Our Sages of blessed memory also taught (Nedarim 8b) that in the future there will be no Gehinnom; rather, the sun will be removed from its sheath—the righteous, etc., and the wicked, etc.
וְהוּא כְּטַעַם "צַדִּיקִים יֵלְכוּ בָם וּפֹשְׁעִים יִכָּשְׁלוּ בָם",
This follows the principle: 'The righteous shall walk in them, while sinners shall stumble in them.'

וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת פח:)901 Shabbat 88b — Rav Chananel bar Papa said: What is meant by "Hear, for I speak noble things"? Why are the words of Torah likened to a ruler? To tell you: just as a ruler has the power to put to death and to give life, so too the words of Torah have in them the power to put to death and to give life. This is what Rava said: For those who go to the right with it, it is an elixir of life; for those who go to the left with it, a deadly poison. Rashi: ["Those who go to the right with it":] those who occupy themselves with it with all their strength and are absorbed in knowing its secret, like a person who uses his right hand, which is the principal one. Maharsha: ["An elixir of life":] See Rashi; its meaning is that "those who go to the right with it" are those who engage in it for its own sake, and "those who go to the left with it," not for its own sake — as it is similarly expounded in Yoma (72b) on "And this is the Torah which Moses set": if he merits, it becomes for him an elixir of life; if he does not merit, it becomes for him an elixir of death. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 31): The Torah is from the Blessed One, and whoever has Torah in him has attachment to the Blessed One; and when he cleaves to the Blessed One, this surely brings life — "for those who go to the right with it, an elixir of life." But one who seeks to draw near to the Blessed One not as is fitting, cleaving to what is separate [and exalted] when such cleaving is not fitting for him, is killed by it: the Torah is nearness to the Blessed One, and where that nearness is alien and ought not to be, it kills him — so the Torah is a deadly poison for one for whom the nearness is not fitting. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:62): In this world the Written Torah is clothed in the garment of writing and letters, the "serpent's skin" that clothes its inner hidden light and confines it within the bounds of the letters. That is why "if he does not merit, it becomes for him a deadly poison," and why they said "to those who go to the left with it…"; the Oral Torah in itself has no such serpent's-skin garment. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 5): The cherubim are love and the flaming sword is fear, guarding the way to the Tree of Life, which is Torah; for Torah without fear and love does not fly upward, and "to those who go to the left with it, it is a deadly poison." It is guarded so that even one who goes to the left should not put forth his hand, eat of the Tree of Life and live forever; one must first pass through the gates of love and fear. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): When words of Torah enter, cunning enters the heart; therefore "transgressors stumble in them," in words of Torah, and "to those who go to the left with it, it is a deadly poison." Therefore it says "from His right hand, a fiery law for them": the fiery law, which is the attainment of wisdom, is only "from His right hand," for those who go to the right with it, from the side of Kindness. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 13): Words of Torah are likened to wine, which alludes to the Written Torah: some drink wine and it is good for them and some not, as with Adam and Noah, who brought lamentation into the world, and "to those who go to the left with it, it is a deadly poison." But for those who go to the right with it, "wine gladdens the heart of man" and "wine makes one wise," and this is only in the seed of Israel. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Miketz 1): When a person learns Torah without first repairing his deeds so as to turn from evil, his learning adds strength to the husk, as they said, "to those who go to the left with it, it is a deadly poison"; this is when he learns at the instigation of the serpent and the evil inclination. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 4): The power of the body and heart to sin comes through the wisdom within it, as it is said, "but transgressors stumble in them," and as the Sages said, "to those who go to the left with it, it is a deadly poison": through wisdom itself one stumbles and dies. Without it the body would not sin so, for one cannot speak a lie unless one first says something true, and a beast, which has no wisdom, has no sin. לַמַּשְׂמְאִילִים בָּהּ — סַם דְּמִיתָה, כִּי "חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה", וְהַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ הוּא הַמַּעֲנִישׁ.
Likewise, they taught (Shabbat 88b) that for those who turn to the left in Torah it becomes a potion of death; 'evil pursues sinners,' for the sin itself becomes the punishment.

כְּטַעַם (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז.)902 Bava Batra 16a — Reish Lakish said: Satan, the evil inclination, and the angel of death are one. He is Satan, as it is written, "And Satan went forth from the presence of the Lord." He is the evil inclination, for it is written there, "Only evil all the day," and it is written here, "Only against himself do not put forth your hand." He is the angel of death, as it is written, "Only spare his life" — evidently his life rests in his hand. Rashi: "Evidently his life rests in his hand" — it lies with Satan to take the soul, and God warned him not to take it. Maharsha: Our texts misquote the verse: it reads "only [akh] spare his life," not "only [rak]." The verbal analogy holds nonetheless, since "only [akh]" and "only [rak]" are alike terms of limitation. The hint in it is this: "only evil all the day" — let a man limit his evil inclination and master it, and then "only spare his life" — the Holy One, blessed be He, will limit the power of the angel of death, that he not rule over his soul. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Balak 14): [At Sinai,] when neither death nor the Satan ruled over [Israel], the whole original flaw from the serpent was repaired; and since death was annulled, the evil inclination was annulled entirely, as it says, "He is the evil inclination, he is the angel of death."
