Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 16a, s.v. "with a ram's shofar"): Rosh Hashanah is the day of judgment, and when they sound a ram's horn it is as though the judgment had already been carried out, for He remembers the binding of Yitzchak, who was bound before the Holy One, blessed be He, as though judgment had been executed upon him. "I shall account it to you" because the father is the root of the son: when the father, the root of the lineage, was bound, the branch resembles him, for Israel too give themselves over to the honor of the Blessed One. In sum, the ram signifies binding and submission to the attribute of judgment, and by giving over our souls to the Blessed One we are saved from the Accuser — which is also why [the shofars] must be bent. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 13): Rosh HaShanah is the Day of Remembrance, for when a person remembers the Blessed One, the Blessed One remembers the person; this too is the matter of the shofar, of which the Sages said, "so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good — with what? With the shofar." Rambam wrote that the shofar hints, "Awake, sleepers, from your slumber … remember your Creator," for it was their way to rouse the people by sounding the shofar; and it is all one — their remembering the Blessed One and their remembrance rising before Him. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeitzei 3): The holiness of Rosh HaShanah, the Day of Remembrance — "so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good, and with what? With the shofar" — is present on the Sabbath to a greater degree; therefore when Rosh HaShanah falls on the Sabbath there is no need to raise our remembrance before Him for good through the act of the shofar, for [the Sabbath] is in itself a day of remembrance. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Rosh HaShanah): In Remembrances the benefit is explicit, but what is the benefit in reciting Kingships? Though a person imagines that the yoke of Heaven's kingship is servitude, in truth it is the true freedom from every servitude in the world, for where the Blessed One dwells no evil draws near, and one who crowns the Blessed One over himself is entirely free; so the Blessed One counsels Israel that in the days of Rosh HaShanah the word "King" be habitual on their lips, a safeguard from all evil. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh HaShanah 15): "Recite before Me Kingships... so that you crown Me": since the Blessed One desires Israel's crowning of Him, a person is obligated to crown Him over himself in every detail. "Remembrances, so that your remembrance may rise before Me for good" — but what has remembrance to do with the Blessed One, when there is no forgetting before His Throne of Glory? Rather it is from the human side, for a person has many distractions and must fix in himself that none will divert him, and "with what? With the shofar" — only through the shofar can he fix this recognition, for the shofar indicates that a person stations himself in the inner voice. Sod Yesharim (Rosh HaShanah 17): "Recite before Me Remembrances" — that you always bring yourselves near before Me and do not stand far off, behind; as much as a person fixes in his heart the awareness that he always stands before the Blessed One and is watched over every moment, so does the Blessed One truly watch over him. "With what? With the shofar" — a person fixes such awareness by contracting his own desires so as to want only the simple will of the Blessed One, and this contraction is called shofar. עַמּוּד א: "שֶׁיַּעֲלֶה זִכְרוֹנֵיכֶם לְפָנַי לְטוֹבָה — בַּמֶּה? בְּשׁוֹפָר".
Concerning this they said in Rosh Hashanah 16a: "That your remembrance rise before Me for good - through what? Through the shofar."
וּכְשֶׁשּׁוֹאֵל "בַּמֶּה", מַשְׁמַע דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר עַל מִי שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם מַעֲשִׂים שֶׁיִּהְיוּ רְאוּיִים לְכָךְ כְּלָל.
The very question "through what?" implies that the teaching includes those who have no deeds that would otherwise make them worthy of such favorable remembrance.
רַק שֶׁעַל יְדֵי תְּקִיעַת שׁוֹפָר נֶאֱמַר שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ הָאוֹבְדִים וְהַנִּדָּחִים,
Rather, through the sounding of the shofar it is said that the lost and the banished will come,
וְהֵם אוֹתָם שֶׁכְּבָר נִטְמְעוּ בֵּין הָעַמִּים.
referring to those who have already become swallowed up among the nations.
כִּי "לֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח" — דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְהַפֵּךְ.
For "no one banished from Him shall remain banished"; the root of the seed of Israel cannot be transformed into something else.
וְעַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ קוֹל שׁוֹפָר גָּדוֹל,
And through that great shofar sound,
שֶׁהוּא רַק קוֹל הַצְּעָקוֹת שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
which is nothing other than the collected cry to the Blessed One of all Jewish souls throughout all generations,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי קִבּוּצָם נַעֲשֶׂה קוֹל שׁוֹפָר גָּדוֹל,
whose gathering together becomes the sound of a great shofar,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְעוֹרֶרֶת צְעָקָה גַּם בְּלֵב אוֹתָם הַנִּדָּחִים מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
thereby a cry is awakened even in the hearts of those banished from among the Children of Israel,
עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ לְהִשְׁתַּחֲווֹת וְכוּלֵי.
until they come to bow down, and so forth.

items.h:
Seif 2 — The Shofar and the Response from Above
Hearing the shofar below arouses a corresponding divine action above, culminating in Yom Kippur's fixed holiness.

p: וּתְקִיעַת שׁוֹפָר דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְעִנְיָן זֶה,
The sounding of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah likewise serves this same purpose,
וְהַמְקַיֵּם מִצְוַת הַשֵּׁם לִשְׁמֹעַ קוֹל זֶה — נַעֲשֶׂה דֻּגְמָתוֹ לְמַעְלָה.
and when a person fulfills God's commandment to hear this sound, a corresponding response is brought about above.

כְּטַעַם945 Berakhot 6a; Berakhot 7a — R. Avin bar Rav Ada said in the name of R. Yitzchak: From where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, wears tefillin? For it is said, “The Lord has sworn by His right hand and by the arm of His strength.” “By His right hand” — this is Torah; “by the arm of His strength” — these are tefillin. And what is written in them? “And who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the earth.” And on 7a: R. Yochanan said in the name of R. Yose — from where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays? For it is said, “And I shall bring them to My holy mountain and gladden them in My house of prayer” — it does not say “their prayer” but “My prayer”; from here that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays. And what does He pray? Rav Zutra bar Toviah said in the name of Rav: May it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger, and that My mercy prevail over My other attributes, and that I conduct Myself toward My children with the attribute of mercy, and that I deal with them beyond the line of strict justice. Rashi (s.v. "strength to His people"): And from where do we know that tefillin are strength for Israel? For it is written, "And all the peoples of the earth shall see [that the name of the Lord is called upon you], and they shall fear you." Rashi (s.v. "what is written in them"): Granted, in our tefillin are written "Hear, O Israel," "And it shall be, if you hearken," "Sanctify to Me every firstborn," and "And it shall be, when [the Lord] brings you" — passages in which [Israel] were commanded to set them as a remembrance of the commandments of the Holy One, blessed be He, a sign and a remembrance for Israel; but in His [tefillin], what is written? Tosafos (s.v. "who is like Your people Israel"): On this the liturgical poet based his line (for the first day of Passover): "The frontlet of His crown — my greatness." Maharsha (Berakhot 7a, s.v. "from where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays"): His "house of prayer" is the Temple above, which corresponds to the Temple below: just as below they pray that His mercy prevail over us, so above the Holy One, blessed be He, prays for this, as the Gemara concludes, "May it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger." This is the intent of the verse "and I shall gladden them in My house of prayer" — the Temple above, where [as the verse continues] "their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted," through the offering of Michael, who offers there the souls of the righteous, as the Midrashim say. Maharsha (s.v. "from where do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, wears tefillin"): Some have already written of a hidden mystery here, but I see in it something close to its plain sense: the mitzvah of tefillin is that we cleave to Him, blessed be He, and by putting them on we cause His Shechinah to rest upon us; correspondingly, the Holy One, blessed be He, has attachment to Israel and a singular bond with them, and that is His wearing tefillin — to cleave to and glory in His inheritance, Israel. He swore by two attributes: "His right hand" is the Torah, for the right is the attribute of lovingkindness, as it is said of the Torah, "and the Torah of lovingkindness is on her tongue"; "the arm of His strength" is the tefillin of the left arm, the attribute of might and strength, for by putting them on a person brings the Shechinah to rest upon himself before the peoples of the earth, so that they fear His might. And "what is written in them" asks for verses showing that He has attachment to Israel and a singular bond with them, just as the tefillin we wear show that we have attachment to Him and a singular bond with Him. Maharal (Be'er HaGolah, Be'er 4, on God's prayer): The Hebrew word for prayer derives from a root meaning thought and intention; the Holy One, blessed be He, "prays" in that He is the true Good, "who desires kindness", and seeks the good. It is called prayer because prayer is an intense request for something that would not come about of itself, and that His mercy should overcome His anger and that He should enter within the line of strict justice is not what strict justice yields, but He desires it exceedingly, and this is His prayer. By this the Sages rejected the view of the philosophers that all things issue from Him by necessity, without intention or will, for on their view there could be nothing in the world but strict justice. Maharal (Be'er HaGolah, Be'er 4, on God's tefillin): In this statement [the Sages] came to make known the difference between Israel and the other nations: all created things are the glory of the Holy One, blessed be He, but that glory is called His "garment", which is separate from the one who wears it, whereas the glory He has from Israel — who are called His children, being brought into existence by Him essentially and first — is attached to Him Himself, and it is therefore called "tefillin", an ornament of glory bound to the one who wears them. The head-tefillin are the glory He has from the very essence of the nation, which is praiseworthy in the highest degree in that they are "one nation", and which testifies to His wisdom; the arm-tefillin are the glory He has from having brought them into actual existence, for the arm is the power that brings into actuality, as it is written, "Your people and Your inheritance, whom You brought out with Your great power and with Your outstretched arm." שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבְרָכוֹת ו׳ עַמּוּד א: מִנַּיִן שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַנִּיחַ תְּפִלִּין,
This follows the teaching in Berakhot 6a that the Holy One, blessed be He, puts on tefillin,

וּמִתְפַּלֵּל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם ז946 Berakhot 7a — R. Yochanan said in the name of R. Yosei: Whence do we know that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays? For it is said, "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in the house of My prayer" — it does not say "their prayer" but "My prayer"; from here, that the Holy One, blessed be He, prays. What does He pray? Rav Zutra bar Toviya said that Rav said: May it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger, and that My mercy prevail over My other attributes, and that I conduct Myself toward My children with the attribute of mercy, and that I deal with them beyond the strict letter of the law. Maharsha: His "house of prayer" is the Temple above, set opposite the Temple below, as they said: in Zevul stand the heavenly Temple and altar, and Michael the great prince offers upon it. Just as below we pray that His mercy be rolled out over us, so above the Holy One, blessed be He, prays for that very thing, as the Gemara concludes. This is the sense of "and I will make them joyful in the house of My prayer" — the Temple above, where their offerings are accepted, Michael offering there the souls of the righteous. Maharal (Be'er HaGolah, Be'er 4): The word for prayer, tefillah, derives from a root denoting thought and intent, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is said to pray because He, the true Good, desires and seeks to do good. What strict justice yields needs no one to seek it, but that His mercy should overcome His anger and that He deal with His children beyond the strict letter of the law does not come from justice, and would not exist were He not seeking it with all His desire — and that is His prayer. The Sages thereby also rejected the philosophers' view that everything issues from Him by necessity, for what one asks for is not necessitated.׳ עַמּוּד א.
and that He prays, as they taught there on 7a.
הַיְנוּ שֶׁכָּל מִצְוָה שֶׁהָאָדָם עוֹשֶׂה — הֲרֵי "הַשֵּׁם צִלְּךָ",
The meaning is that with every mitzvah a person performs, "the Lord is your shadow":
כְּמַאֲמָרָם זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בַּמִּדְרָשׁ, שֶׁהוּבָא בְּסֵפֶר שְׁנֵי לֻחוֹת הַבְּרִית, רֵישׁ שַׁעַר הַגָּדוֹל וְסוֹף פָּרָשַׁת מִשְׁפָּטִים,
as the Sages of blessed memory taught in a Midrash, cited in Shnei Luchot HaBrit at the beginning of Shaar HaGadol and at the end of Parashat Mishpatim,
שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁהָאָדָם עוֹשֶׂה — הַצֵּל עוֹשֶׂה גַּם כֵּן.
that whatever a person does, the shadow does correspondingly.
וְעִנְיַן הַתְּפִלִּין הוּא הַהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת וְהַדְּבֵקוּת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
The meaning of tefillin is attachment and cleaving to the Blessed One;
כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְדַּבֵּק עִמּוֹ וְאוֹמֵר: "וּמִי כְעַמְּךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל", "אוֹ הֲנִסָּה" וְגוֹמֵר.
correspondingly, the Blessed One cleaves to Israel, as it were, and declares, "Who is like Your people Israel," and "Has any god ever attempted..." and so forth.
וְכֵן בִּתְפִלָּה — שֶׁהָעֵגֶל רוֹצֶה לִינֹק, הַפָּרָה רוֹצָה לְהֵינִיק כְּנֶגְדּוֹ,
So too with prayer: when the calf wants to nurse, the cow, correspondingly, wants to give milk,
וְכֵן בְּכָל דָּבָר.
and the same principle applies to every matter.
וּבְקוֹל שׁוֹפָר, שֶׁהוּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַצְּעָקָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
So too with the shofar sound, which is the awakening of the cry toward the Blessed One:
וּשְׁמִיעַת הַקּוֹל הַיְנוּ לְהַרְגִּישׁ זֶה בַּלֵּב,
hearing that sound means allowing this cry to be felt within the heart,
הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן שׁוֹמֵעַ קוֹל תְּרוּעַת עַמּוֹ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרַחֲמִים.
and correspondingly the Blessed One hears, in mercy, the sound of the shofar-blast of His people Israel.
וּמִמֵּילָא נִתְעַרְבְּבוּ וְנִתְבַּטְּלוּ כָּל הַמְעַכְּבִים.
As a result, all the obstructing forces are confounded and nullified.
כִּי כְּשֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹמֵעַ צַעֲקָתוֹ, הֲרֵי הוּא נִזְכָּר לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ,
For when the Blessed One hears a person's cry, that person is thereby remembered before Him,
וּמִמֵּילָא "וְנוֹשַׁעְתֶּם מֵאֹיְבֵיכֶם" — הוּא הַיֵּצֶר הָרַע שֶׁנִּקְרָא שׂוֹנֵא,
and then "you shall be saved from your enemies" - meaning the evil inclination, which is called an enemy,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה נ״ב947 Sukkah 52a — R. Avira, and some say R. Yehoshua ben Levi, expounded: The evil inclination has seven names. The Holy One, blessed be He, called it "evil"; Moses called it "uncircumcised"; David called it "impure"; Solomon called it "enemy," as it is said, "If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty give him water to drink, for you heap coals upon his head, and the Lord will repay you" — do not read "will repay you" but "will make him at peace with you"; Isaiah called it "stumbling block"; Ezekiel called it "stone"; Joel called it "the hidden one." Rashi (s.v. "if your enemy is hungry"): Your evil inclination is hungry and craves transgression. "Feed him bread": weary him in the battle of Torah, as it is written, "Come, eat of my bread" (Proverbs 9:5) [where "eat" is read as "do battle"]. "Give him water to drink": Torah, of which it is written, "Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water" (Isaiah 55:1). Rashi (s.v. "the hidden one"): As [the Gemara] goes on to explain: hidden in a man's heart. Rashi (s.v. "will make him at peace with you"): That your inclination may be at peace with you and love you, and not lead you to sin and to be lost from the world. Maharsha (s.v. "Ezekiel called it stone"): As was said above, the two hearts are the two inclinations: the heart of stone is the evil inclination, which is hard, as below, "if he is stone he dissolves," and the heart of flesh is the good inclination, which is soft like flesh. Maharsha (s.v. "Isaiah called it stumbling block"): "Stumbling block" denotes a sin that is not great, such as an inadvertent one: a small thing lying in the road may go unnoticed so that one stumbles over it, but a large, high thing in the road is noticed and one does not stumble. Hence "lift up the stumbling block": let it be raised high in the eyes of the righteous so that they do not stumble over it, as was said above that to the righteous it seems like a mountain, and they keep far from the very beginning of transgression. Maharsha (s.v. "Moses called it uncircumcised"): "The foreskin of your hearts" is written with a doubled letter [לבבכם], for when the heart of the evil inclination is repaired, the heart of the good inclination is repaired with it. Maharsha (s.v. "Solomon called it enemy"): According to Rashi, the word "bread" bears both its plain meaning and that of "battle." It may also be explained in light of "There is a small organ in a man: satisfy it and it hungers" and "as for the evil inclination, let the left hand push away and the right draw near": "if your enemy is hungry," give him a little of his desire in necessary things — "feed him bread and give him water to drink" — and by giving him a little of his desire he will be at peace with you. Maharsha (s.v. "the evil inclination has seven names"): A man's deeds, good or evil, are disposed according to the seven days of creation and the seven planets, and punishment comes according to the evil deed — "I will chastise you seven times for your sins" — so the inclination is called by these seven names after seven kinds of deeds. Since a man has two hearts, the good inclination and the evil, the Holy One, blessed be He, called the evil one "evil from his youth," for it is with him from the womb while the good inclination comes only at thirteen; and David, saying "Create in me a pure heart," speaks of creation because the good heart comes later, which implies that there is an impure one. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 1, on "Solomon called it enemy"): "If your enemy is hungry," enticing you to bodily desire because he is lacking, feed him the bread of Torah, giving the evil inclination something that satisfies so that he is no longer lacking; for only through the Torah is a man complete, and the evil inclination comes only on account of a deficiency in man. "And if he is thirsty" refers to the inclination to idolatry, for hunger belongs more to the body and thirst to the soul; and the Holy One, blessed be He, who desires no opposition, will make the evil inclination at peace [with you] in your hand. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 1, on the seven names): These names descend from the highest level to the lowest: the Holy One, blessed be He, the true good whose existence is necessary, called it "evil," for it is privation, the opposite of the good; Moses, to whose exalted level it bore no relation, called it "uncircumcised," as though it were a different creature; David called it "impure," which is separated yet not wholly, for the pure may become impure; Solomon, "enemy," which is separated but does not defile by contact; Isaiah, "stumbling block," which opposes a man only when he comes near it; Ezekiel, "stone," which is no stumbling block but only a hard burden upon a man; and Joel, "the hidden one," for it lies hidden in a man's heart and he does not know of it. Privation, which is the evil inclination, extends to seven levels and no more, and the levels of men correspond to them, from one who is not moved at all by a sin set before him to one in whose eyes whoever commits a sin is as though he were not a man and did not exist. עַמּוּד א.
as the Sages taught in Sukkah 52a.
כִּי זֶה כָּל כֹּחַ הֶקֵּף הַיֵּצֶר הָרַע לְמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב — עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁכְחָה.
For the entire power by which the evil inclination encloses the depths of the heart operates through forgetfulness.
דְּאַף שֶׁשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַלֵּב לְעוֹלָם דָּבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
Although the root of the heart is always attached to the Blessed One,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מַשְׁכִּיחַ זֶה לְגַמְרֵי,
the evil inclination can cause this truth to be completely forgotten,
עַד שֶׁכָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹת לִבּוֹ לָרַע לְגַמְרֵי, רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן,
until all the thoughts of the heart are turned entirely toward evil, may the Merciful One save us,
וְעַד שֶׁנִּכְתָּם עָוֹן מֵעֵבֶר לְעֵבֶר.
and the sin becomes stained through and through.
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁנִּזְכָּר לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם,
But when a person is remembered before the Lord,
הֲרֵי מִתְעוֹרֵר הַזִּכָּרוֹן בְּלִבּוֹ גַּם כֵּן, לִזְכֹּר בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
remembrance is correspondingly awakened within his own heart, causing him to remember the Blessed One.
וּמִמֵּילָא נִשְׁבְּרָה מְחִיצַת הַשִּׁכְחָה שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ,
The barrier of forgetfulness within his heart is thereby broken,
וְיוּכַל לְהוֹצִיא שֹׁרֶשׁ יַהֲדוּתוֹ הַנֶּעְלָם אֶל הַגִּלּוּי,
and he can bring the hidden root of his Jewish identity out into revelation,
עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא מְעַט מְעַט לְהַכָּרָה גְמוּרָה וְלִתְשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵמָה,
until, step by step, he reaches complete recognition and full repentance,
בְּכָל עֶשֶׂר מַדְרֵגוֹת שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְשׁוּבָה, שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה הַהֲכָנָה לָהֶם.
through all ten levels of repentance corresponding to the Ten Days of Repentance, for which this process prepares him.
וּתְחִלַּת הַכְּנִיסָה עַל יְדֵי הַשּׁוֹפָר דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, שֶׁהוּא "הַמְעוֹרֵר יְשֵׁנִים מִתַּרְדֵּמָתָם",
The entry into this process begins through the Rosh Hashanah shofar, which "awakens sleepers from their slumber,"
הַיְנוּ אוֹתוֹ שֶׁנִּשְׁקַע בָּעֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים הַמְעַכְּבִים אֶת הַתְּשׁוּבָה,
meaning the person who has sunk into one of the twenty-four things that obstruct repentance,
עַד שֶׁאֵין הִרְהוּרֵי תְשׁוּבָה עַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן פְּרָטִי הַיָּדוּעַ לוֹ לְכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא עוֹלִים בְּלִבּוֹ כְּלָל.
until no thoughts of repentance at all arise in his heart concerning that particular sin, known to each person according to his own condition.
וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד הָרִחוּק הַגָּמוּר שֶׁבּוֹ בְּאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר וְעִנְיָן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
This results from the complete distance from the Blessed One that he experiences in that particular matter,
כְּפִי עֹצֶם מַדְרֵגַת שִׁקּוּעוֹ בָּהּ.
in proportion to the depth of his immersion in it.
קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר מַחֲרִיד לִבּוֹ וּמְעוֹרְרוֹ,
The sound of the shofar causes his heart to tremble and awakens it,
עַד שֶׁרְחוֹקִים נַעֲשִׂים קְרוֹבִים,
until those who were distant become near,
וּמוֹעִיל אַחַר כָּךְ הַדְּרִישָׁה וְהַקְּרִיאָה.
after which seeking and calling can once again be effective.
כִּי טַעַם "בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ" וּ"בִּהְיוֹתוֹ קָרוֹב",
For the meaning of "when He may be found" and "when He is near"
הֲגַם דְּעַל יְדֵי הַדְּרִישָׁה וְהַקְּרִיאָה הוּא תָּמִיד כֵּן,
must be understood even though seeking Him and calling to Him are effective at all times,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "אִם תִּדְרְשֶׁנּוּ יִמָּצֵא לָךְ", "קָרוֹב הַשֵּׁם לְכָל קֹרְאָיו",
as Scripture says, "If you seek Him, He will be found by you," and "The Lord is near to all who call Him,"
וְלֹא קָבַע זְמַן.
without fixing any particular time.
זֶהוּ כְּשֶׁלֹּא נִכְתָּם הֶעָוֹן,
That is so when the sin has not become indelibly stained;
וְהֵם עֶשֶׂר מַדְרֵגוֹת דִּדְרִישָׁה וּקְרִיאָה,
then one can ascend through the ten levels of seeking and calling,
וְזֶהוּ "לְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָאֻהוּ בֶאֱמֶת".
which culminate in "all who call upon Him in truth."
דְּאַף שֶׁהוּא נִמְצָא לְכַפֵּר עָוֹן גַּם עַל יְדֵי פִּתּוּי פֶּה לְבַד,
Although He allows Himself to be found for the atonement of sin even through mere verbal entreaty,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הִתְקָרְבוּת — דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת —
true closeness - in which deliberate sins are transformed into merits -
הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי קְרִיאָה בֶאֱמֶת, דְּהַיְנוּ פִּיו וְלִבּוֹ שָׁוִין.
comes only through calling in truth, when one's mouth and heart are in accord.
אֲבָל דְּרִישָׁה הִיא בְּמַעֲשֶׂה וְדִבּוּר לְבַד, כְּשֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ עֲדַיִן לִנְקֻדַּת הַלֵּב.
Seeking, by contrast, can begin with action and speech alone, before the process has yet reached the innermost point of the heart.
וְאַחַר שֶׁנִּתְעַרְבֵּב הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִסָּה עַל יְדֵי הַשּׁוֹפָר,
Once the "leaven in the dough" has been confounded by the shofar,
יִתְאַמֵּץ לְגַלּוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ הַנֶּעְלָם, שֶׁהוּא לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
a person should exert himself to reveal his hidden will, which is to do the will of the Blessed One,
תְּחִלָּה בִּדְרִישָׁה עַל כָּל פָּנִים, בְּפֹעַל מַמָּשׁ, כַּאֲמִירַת תְּפִלּוֹת וְתַחֲנוּנִים.
beginning at least with active seeking, concretely, through the recitation of prayers and supplications.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יָבוֹא לְמַדְרֵגַת הַקְּרִיאָה בֶאֱמֶת מִלֵּב,
Through this he will come to the level of genuinely calling from the heart,
וְעַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא לְמַדְרֵגַת "יַעֲזֹב רָשָׁע דַּרְכּוֹ" וְגוֹמֵר,
until he reaches the level of "Let the wicked man forsake his way..."
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַשְּׁלֵמָה בַּעֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא לְגַמְרֵי.
This is complete repentance: totally abandoning the sin.

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ948 Yoma 86b — Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for through it deliberate sins are accounted to a man as merits, as it is said, “And when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does what is lawful and right, he shall live by them.” Rashi: "For you have stumbled in your iniquity": your iniquity will be reckoned as a stumbling, which is an unwitting sin. "He shall live by them": by all that he did — even by the transgressions. Maharsha: That intentional sins become like unwitting ones may be taken literally, as Rashi explained "Return, backsliding children" above: when one repents, He accounts it as though the sin began in youthful folly. That they become like merits is on its face astonishing, for the sinner would then profit; but one who repents out of love, of whom the Gemara concludes it speaks, surely repents fully and adds good deeds beyond what that sin required, and those added deeds become merits for him — as the verse shows: "and does what is lawful and right, he shall live by them," by the justice and righteousness he added to his repentance. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2): Since repentance reaches the Throne of Glory, by the exalted level the penitent now attains all he did before is reckoned unwitting — as one who was ignorant and later became wise calls his earlier deeds unwitting — for unwitting error stems from the material, and the penitent has raised himself from the material level at which he sinned to the level separate [from matter]. His intentional sins become merits because repentance is the very order of the world, all beings existing only by returning to God, from Whom they came; so the sinner's distance from God, which calls for his return, itself becomes merit for him when he returns. This holds only when the return is out of love, for there is no cleaving to Him except through love ("to love the Lord your God … and to cleave to Him"); one who returns out of fear has not come to cleave to Him, and so his intentional sins become only like unwitting ones. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeshev 11): Then "they shall be white as snow," for deliberate sins become like merits: the Blessed One will then make clear that the deed was not done by the person's choice at all — as the Arizal wrote, where there is [Divine] knowledge there is no choice; choice is given in the seven lower attributes, but in the upper three, in Atika, there truly is no choice — as will become clear once they merit repentance out of love, through which deliberate sins become like merits. בְּיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב: "הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה? בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה" וְכוּלֵי,
As they said in Yoma 86b: "What constitutes a true penitent? When the same woman..." and so forth,
הַיְנוּ דַּרְכּוֹ הַקּוֹדֵם — כְּשֶׁעוֹזְבוֹ, זֶהוּ בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר.
meaning that when he abandons his former path, he is a complete baal teshuvah.
וְעַד מַדְרֵגַת "וְיָשֹׁב אֶל הַשֵּׁם" בִּדְבֵקוּת,
Beyond this lies the level of "and let him return to the Lord," in cleaving,

וְהוּא הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין, שֶׁאֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִין לַעֲמֹד שָׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבְרָכוֹת ל״ד949 Berakhot 34b — R. Abbahu said: In the place where penitents stand, the perfectly righteous do not stand, as it is said, "Peace, peace, to him that is far off and to him that is near" — "to him that is far off" first, and only afterward "to him that is near." Maharsha: Though it seems far from reason that penitents should have a higher rank than the perfectly righteous, the wording of R. Yochanan's reply — "who was near to a transgression and has now distanced himself from it" — shows that the case is not one who actually committed a transgression, for then he would not have called him merely "near to a transgression," but one who in his thought was close to transgressing and overcame his inclination and did not transgress. R. Abbahu holds that such a man, who prevailed over his inclination, has a higher rank than the perfectly righteous, in whom the evil inclination never stirred at all and who never came near a transgression. R. Yochanan holds that even so the perfectly righteous are higher, for they did not sin even in thought, whereas this one who was near a transgression did at least transgress in thought. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 4): Repentance is possible only from a higher rank, for it is a stripping away from sin: one who sinned and then repented has removed himself from sin more than the righteous man who never sinned, since the one who never sinned had no need to overcome his inclination, while the penitent must overcome his and so separates himself from sin entirely. That is why Scripture says "peace to him that is far off" first, and only afterward "to him that is near." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 7): This is the "very good" within the evil inclination, for "in the place where penitents stand the wholly righteous do not stand": through the sin, when one afterwards merits repentance, he reaches a greater level. The penitent is not helped to re-enter by the gate through which he went out, resolving henceforth to behave like a wholly righteous man as if he had never sinned and restraining himself because the thing is forbidden, for the inclination has already overpowered him there; he must raise himself to the upper gate, of doing nothing that is not for the satisfaction and fulfillment of the will of the Blessed One, and this is the gate through which penitents come, a higher place than the lower gate that is open to the righteous. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash 8): R. Yochanan said that all the prophets prophesied only about penitents, but of the wholly righteous "no eye has seen," and R. Abbahu said that in the place where penitents stand the wholly righteous do not stand; one may say that these and those are the words of the living God and they do not disagree, but it depends on the quality of the repentance: through repentance out of fear of punishment deliberate sins become like unwitting ones, whereas through repentance out of love they become like merits. The one who repents out of love, the Blessed One shines upon him and repairs the deed itself so that it becomes a merit, and therefore he is superior to a wholly righteous man, for he has new merits that one righteous from the outset has no power to attain, as in "there is no light except that which comes out of darkness." Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 3): Repentance is above [human wisdom, the Torah and prophecy], and none of them can fathom its depth, as they said, "in the place where penitents stand the wholly righteous cannot stand": the place of the wholly righteous is what is due them according to their deeds, which follow the Torah, prophecy and wisdom without leaving their bounds, "this you shall do and this not," "thus far shall you come and no further." But the penitent has already breached the fence of the world as bounded by the Torah, the prophets and the sages, and sunk where he sank; and when he returns to God and repairs the past with the clear recognition that "You are with me" and that wherever he may be there is nothing besides Him, he merits the inheritance of Jacob, an inheritance without bounds. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 164): In people's minds the penitent is not like a wholly righteous man, still less are the sins he committed reckoned as merits, even though one believes the Sages' words that deliberate sins become merits and that "in the place where penitents stand [the wholly righteous do not stand]"; this is because repentance is called the "hidden world," and its preciousness and beauty are not revealed to people. [In a bracketed note he adds that] the dissenting view concerns the perception of the prophets: the one master derives his view from the verse "to the far and to the near," which is in the Prophets, while in the other's view it is not so from the standpoint of prophecy, since of the wholly righteous it is said "no eye has seen," which is from the standpoint of the Blessed One alone. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Sanhedrin): As explained in Likutei HaShas, they do not disagree, and these and those are the words of the living God; their dispute is alluded to in the Mishnah, "The blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering because it atones; the limbs of the burnt-offering precede the sacrificial parts of the sin-offering because it is wholly consumed." The sin-offering is the penitent and its blood is the cry from the depth of the heart: the penitent's cry is greater, for he cries out because it seems to him that, God forbid, he has no remedy without the salvation of the Blessed One, and so his cry rises to the place where the righteous do not stand; but in the limbs of the burnt-offering, that is, the performance of the commandments, the wholly righteous take precedence, for their body is greatly refined and cleaves to the Blessed One, never separated for a moment. עַמּוּד ב.
which is the place where penitents stand, a place that even perfectly righteous people cannot attain, as taught in Berakhot 34b.
וְהֵם אַרְבָּעָה פַּרְצוּפִים דְּאַבָּא וְאִמָּא, זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה,
These correspond to four configurations - Abba and Imma, male and female -
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל עֶשֶׂר מַדְרֵגוֹת, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
which are present within every complete set of ten levels, as is known.
שְׁנֵי יָמִים דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה הֵם כְּנֶגֶד חָכְמָה וּבִינָה,
The two days of Rosh Hashanah correspond to Chokhmah and Binah,
שֶׁהֵם אַבָּא וְאִמָּא הַמּוֹלִידוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּפֹעַל דִּימֵי תְשׁוּבָה.
which are Abba and Imma, the sources that give birth to the actual process of repentance during the Ten Days of Repentance.
וְעַל כֵּן הֵם יוֹמָא אֲרִיכְתָא, כַּיָּדוּעַ,
Therefore the two days are regarded as one "long day," as is known,
דְּהֵם תְּרֵין רֵעִין דְּלָא מִתְפָּרְשִׁין,
for they are "two companions who never separate,"
שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְמַחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ בְּלֹא רָצוֹן שֶׁבַּלֵּב,
just as thought in the mind cannot exist without some will in the heart,
וְלֹא רָצוֹן שֶׁבַּלֵּב בְּלֹא מַחֲשָׁבָה בַּמֹּחַ.
nor can a will in the heart exist without thought in the mind.
וְהַתּוֹרָה צִוְּתָה עַל יוֹם אֶחָד,
The Torah commanded the observance of one day of Rosh Hashanah,
כִּי דַּי לְעוֹרֵר רֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבַּמֹּחַ,
for from the divine perspective it is sufficient to awaken the first point of thought in the mind,
וְזֶהוּ הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָא.
and this is an arousal from above.
כִּי מִצְווֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הֵן אִתְעָרוּתָא לָאָדָם לַעֲשׂוֹת הַמִּצְוָה,
For the commandments of the Blessed One are themselves an awakening that moves a person to perform the mitzvah,
שֶׁלּוּלֵי צִוּוּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה.
which he would not have performed had God not commanded him.
וּמִצְווֹת דְּרַבָּנָן הֵן מַה שֶּׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל מִתְנַדְּבִים מֵעַצְמָם לְהִתְעוֹרֵר.
Rabbinic commandments, by contrast, express Israel's own voluntary initiative to awaken themselves.
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹרְרָם גַּם עַל זֶה בְּמַה שֶּׁמָּסַר רְשׁוּת לַחֲכָמִים בָּזֶה,
Yet the Blessed One also awakened them toward this by granting the Sages authority in such matters,
כְּאִלּוּ צִוָּה עֲלֵיהֶם שֶׁהֵם יְבַקְשׁוּ עוֹד תַּחְבּוּלוֹת לְעוֹרֵר הַלְּבָבוֹת.
as though He commanded them to devise additional means by which to awaken Jewish hearts.
וַהֲגַם דְּמִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁבָּרָא אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר,
From the divine side, insofar as God created man upright,
דַּי בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת דְּמוֹחַ לְבַד, וּמִתְעוֹרֵר בִּדְרִישָׁה לְבַד, שֶׁלֹּא בָּא עֲדַיִן לִנְקֻדַּת הַלֵּב,
an awakening of the mind alone would suffice, beginning with seeking that has not yet reached the heart,
אַחַר כָּךְ בָּא מִמֵּילָא לַלֵּב.
for it would then naturally reach the heart on its own.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם, מִצַּד קִלְקוּל הָאָדָם עַל יְדֵי שֶׁ"בִּקְשׁוּ חִשְּׁבוֹנוֹת רַבִּים",
But because humanity became corrupted by "seeking many calculations,"
נִקְבַּע גַּם יוֹם שֵׁנִי בִּתְקִיעַת שׁוֹפָר שֵׁנִית,
a second day was established, with a second sounding of the shofar,
לְעוֹרֵר גַּם הַלֵּב בִּקְרִיאָה בֶאֱמֶת עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשֶׂה קָרוֹב,
to awaken the heart itself into truthful calling, until the person becomes truly near,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַהַרְגָּשָׁה שֶׁבַּלֵּב.
which occurs through felt awareness in the heart.
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַקּוּרְבָא — כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא לִידֵי הֶרְגֵּשׁ גָּמוּר בַּלֵּב, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
This is true nearness: when the matter is fully felt in the heart, as is known.
וְאַחֲרָיו צוֹם גְּדַלְיָה הוּא הַדַּעַת הַמְחַבֵּר הַדְּרִישָׁה וְהַקְּרִיאָה,
Following them, the Fast of Gedaliah corresponds to da'at, which joins seeking and calling,
לִהְיוֹת נִקְבָּע בַּלֵּב עַד שֶׁיּוּכַל לָצֵאת לְפֹעַל עֲזִיבַת הָרָשָׁע,
causing them to become fixed in the heart until forsaking the wicked path can emerge into actual deed,
בְּשֶׁבַע תַּחְתּוֹנוֹת דַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְשׁוּבָה.
through the seven lower levels of the Ten Days of Repentance.
עַד גְּמַר מַעֲשֶׂה בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים,
The process reaches its completion in action on Yom Kippur,
דְּכֹהֵן גָּדוֹל נִכְנָס לְקָדְשֵׁי קֳדָשִׁים — אֶל הַשֵּׁם מַמָּשׁ,
when the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies - entering, as it were, directly "unto the Lord,"
מָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִין לַעֲמֹד בְּכָל הַשָּׁנָה כֻּלָּהּ,
a place in which even completely righteous people cannot stand throughout the rest of the year,
רַק בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, דְּהַכֹּל בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה.
but which is accessible on Yom Kippur, when all Israel stand as penitents.
וּמִצַּד אוֹתָהּ מַדְרֵגָה — "יַרְבֶּה לִסְלוֹחַ", בְּרִבּוּי,
From that level comes "He will abundantly pardon" - pardon in abundance.

הַיְנוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא פ״ו950 Yoma 86b — It was taught: R. Meir would say: Great is repentance, for on account of a single individual who repents, the whole world is forgiven, as it is stated, "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely, for My anger is turned away from him." It does not say "from them," but "from him." Rashi: "I will heal their backsliding": from the individual [who repented]. Maharsha: This may be explained by what they said at the end of the first chapter of Kiddushin: a person should always regard the world as half meritorious and half guilty, and the world is judged by its majority, so that if he performs one commandment, fortunate is he, for he has tipped the whole world to the side of merit. So too here: even where the world is guilty by a majority through him, if he repents completely out of love, his sins become like merits, and thereby he tips the whole world to the side of merit, and the whole world is forgiven. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 3): He and the whole world are forgiven because repentance stands above the world — as explained earlier, repentance was created before the world was created — and so the whole world is forgiven, for through repentance the world is joined to the level at which there is forgiveness for all. The penitent opens a supernal gate, the gate of repentance, and there is forgiveness for all; therefore the repentance that an individual performs is forgiveness for all. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:52): R. Elazar ben Durdaya worked so powerfully upon his own particular root that the root of evil in it was uprooted entirely, and as a result thoughts of repentance were aroused through him in the whole world, for whatever they had sinned in that same root of evil — in the sense of "an individual who repents is forgiven, together with the whole world." Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 18): [David,] "the man who raised up the yoke of repentance," came to understand that this is the essential rectification of Adam's sin — to rectify the whole world through repentance, since "an individual who repents is forgiven, together with the whole world": by the power of his repentance he arouses thoughts of repentance in all the hearts of the Children of Israel, and through this they will merit that the Blessed One slaughter the evil inclination and the Angel of Death. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 10): David is "the man who raised up the yoke of repentance" for all Israel, for "an individual who repents is forgiven, together with the whole world": he arouses thoughts of repentance in the entire stature of the Community of Israel and in all the souls of Israel. Even if it is not revealed in them in deed, once one has thought of repentance in his heart he is a complete tzaddik, and so the rectification extends to the whole world. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 159): "An individual who repents is forgiven, together with the whole world" — but how is such forgiveness possible? Only in that he arouses thoughts of repentance in their hearts as well. Not everyone who wishes can make himself that individual — there has not yet been one; only the Messiah son of David will be such, for his soul must include all souls, since otherwise his thoughts of repentance cannot beget thoughts of repentance in those who have no connection to his soul. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 10): When Joseph came out [of prison] to rule over Egypt, "the nakedness of the land," he thought he had already rectified everything completely, for "an individual who repents is forgiven, together with the whole world"; but it is the Messiah son of David who will be the individual who repents with such force of repentance that he brings forgiveness to the whole world, until even the peoples are turned to "a clear language" and the evil inclination is removed from the world. עַמּוּד ב: יָחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב — מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ.
As they said in Yoma 86b: when one individual repents, he and the entire world are granted forgiveness.
וְלֹא יִמָּלֵט הָעוֹלָם בְּשׁוּם דּוֹר מִיָּחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים,
No generation is entirely without at least one individual who truly repents on Yom Kippur,
שֶׁהוּא הָעוֹמֵד בְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר בִּמְקוֹם כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל הַנִּכְנָס לְקָדְשֵׁי קֳדָשִׁים,
and that person occupies, in his generation, the spiritual position of the High Priest entering the Holy of Holies,
הַיְנוּ שֶׁשָּׁב לְגַמְרֵי עַד "אֶל הַשֵּׁם" וְגוֹמֵר.
meaning that he has returned completely, all the way "unto the Lord."
"כִּי יַרְבֶּה לִסְלוֹחַ" — הַיְנוּ לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
"For He will abundantly pardon" therefore extends to all Israel,

וְעִצּוּמוֹ שֶׁל יוֹם מְכַפֵּר עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה אַף לְמִי שֶׁלֹּא שָׁב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּדּוֹן בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת י״ג951 Shevuot 13a — It is taught in a baraita: Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi] says: For all transgressions stated in the Torah, whether one repented or did not repent, Yom Kippur atones — except for one who casts off the yoke [of Heaven], one who expounds the Torah against its true meaning, and one who annuls the covenant of the flesh. For these, if he repented, Yom Kippur atones, and if not, Yom Kippur does not atone. Rashi: "One who casts off the yoke" — one who denies the fundamental [of faith]. "One who expounds the Torah against its true meaning" — one who approaches the words of the Torah with insolence and open brazenness, like Menasheh, who would sit and expound disparaging aggadot: "Had Moshe nothing to write but 'And Timna was a concubine' and 'Reuven went in the days of the wheat harvest'?" "The covenant of the flesh" — circumcision. Tosafos (s.v. "where he persists in his rebellion"): R. Shlomo of Dreux asked: in the last chapter of Yoma (85b) we say that death and Yom Kippur atone [only] together with repentance — whose view is that? Not Rabbi's, and not even the Rabbis', who hold that death without repentance atones for transgressions other than these three. One may answer that the Rabbis mean that death scours [sin] only together with the sufferings and judgments inflicted on him after death, through which he is not cut off from the World to Come, whereas together with repentance death scours completely; but for Rabbi, death and Yom Kippur scour completely even without repentance for the other transgressions. Maharsha (Chiddushei Halachos): [On Tosafot:] they did not wish to say that [the teaching in Yoma, that death and Yom Kippur atone only with repentance,] follows the Rabbis and concerns these three transgressions, since it is stated without qualification [and so refers to the other transgressions]; moreover, if it could be referred to the three transgressions according to the Rabbis, it could equally be referred to the three transgressions according to Rabbi [who also requires repentance for them]. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shevuos 13a): It has been explained in its place that on Yom Kippur all sinners who have become distant from the Blessed One return to Him, the root of all — as at the Jubilee all that was sold returns to its ancestral holding — so that one who was sold to "the old and foolish king," the evil inclination, returns to the Blessed One; but one who has nothing by which to return to the root, and does not return to Him, Yom Kippur does not atone for. Man is like the fruit of a tree, which hangs upon the root by means of the tree that mediates between them, and upon the tree by means of the stem attached to it: one who casts off the yoke denies the root itself; the Torah, "a tree of life," is the intermediary between the Blessed One and man, through which he cleaves to Him; and one who lacks circumcision, in the limb that is the stem, has no attachment to the tree. Through these three he returns to the root, and that is his atonement; if he lacks these three, Yom Kippur does not atone. עַמּוּד א,
and in this manner the essence of the day brings atonement even to one who did not personally repent, as discussed in Shevuot 13a,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר, דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים עֶצֶם לִבּוֹ קָשׁוּר בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
for, as explained, the very core of every Jewish heart is nevertheless bound to the Blessed One.
וְכָל נַפְשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל — קֶשֶׁר אֶחָד.
All Jewish souls form a single bond.
וְכַאֲשֶׁר נִקְשְׁרָה נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל לְגַמְרֵי בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ,
When one Jewish soul becomes completely bound to Him,
הֲרֵי מִמֵּילָא נִמְשָׁךְ הַכֹּל עִמּוֹ, כְּמוֹשֵׁךְ בִּקְצֵה חֶבֶל שֶׁנִּמְשָׁךְ כָּל הַחֶבֶל עִמּוֹ.
everything else is drawn along with it, like one who pulls the end of a rope and thereby moves the entire rope.
"יַעֲקֹב חֶבֶל נַחֲלָתוֹ":
This is the meaning of "Jacob is the rope of His inheritance":
רֹאשׁוֹ הָאֶחָד קָשׁוּר לְמַעְלָה בְּצוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב הַחֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד,
one end is tied above, in the image of Jacob engraved upon the Throne of Glory,
וְרֹאשׁוֹ הַתַּחְתּוֹן הוּא נַפְשׁוֹת פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַיּוֹתֵר גְּרוּעִים.
while its lower end consists even of the souls of the most degraded sinners of Israel.
וְכֵן הוּא הוֹלֵךְ מִמַּדְרֵגָה לְמַדְרֵגָה.
Between them the rope extends continuously from level to level.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְעוֹרֵר אֶת הַיָּחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב לִהְיוֹת נִכְנָס "אֶל הַשֵּׁם" לְבֵית קָדְשֵׁי קֳדָשִׁים,
Yom Kippur awakens the individual who has repented to enter "unto the Lord," into the Holy of Holies;
וּמִמֵּילָא נִמְשָׁךְ כָּל הַחֶבֶל עִמּוֹ בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָה וַעֲלִיָּה לְמַעְלָה,
thereby the entire rope is drawn with him in an awakening of repentance and ascent,
כָּל אֶחָד לְפִי עֶרְכּוֹ וּמַדְרֵגָתוֹ, וּמִמֵּילָא נִמְשֶׁכֶת כַּפָּרָה גַּם לָהֶם.
each person according to his own measure and level, and atonement is consequently extended to them as well.
וּפְלֻגְתַּת רַבִּי וַחֲכָמִים אִם מְכַפֵּר גַּם לְשֶׁאֵינָם שָׁבִים,
The dispute between Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi and the Sages as to whether Yom Kippur atones even for those who do not repent
הַיְנוּ בְּכַפָּרָה גְמוּרָה שֶׁלֹּא כְּפִי הָרָאוּי מִצַּד הַיָּחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב,
concerns complete atonement beyond the degree warranted by the repentance of the individual penitent;
שֶׁבָּזֶה הַכֹּל מוֹדִים דְּיֵשׁ מְחִילָה לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ.
all agree that through the penitent there is some forgiveness extended to the entire world.
אֲבָל זֶה תָּלוּי כְּפִי כֹּחַ תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ,
That extension, however, depends upon the strength of his repentance,
הַיְנוּ כְּפִי כֹּחַ מְשִׁיכוּתוֹ אֶת הַחֶבֶל לְמַעְלָה.
meaning the degree to which he is able to pull the rope upward.
וּמָשִׁיחַ, שֶׁהוּא יִהְיֶה תַּכְלִית מַדְרֵגַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַיּוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹנָה,
Mashiach will embody the ultimate and highest level of repentance;
תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ תִּפְעֹל מְחִילָה גְמוּרָה לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ,
his repentance will effect complete forgiveness for the entire world,
עַד שֶׁ"יְבֻקַּשׁ אֶת עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ" — לְגַמְרֵי בַּמְּצִיאוּת עוֹד עַד עוֹלָם.
until "the iniquity of Israel will be sought, but it will not be" - no longer existing in reality for all eternity.
אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין מַדְרֵגָתָם כָּל כָּךְ.
In this world, however, the level of repentance does not yet reach that degree.
וְהַכֹּל כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה,
Everything depends upon the individual's level of repentance,
וְכָךְ הוּא מְעוֹרֵר תְּשׁוּבָה גַּם כֵּן בְּלִבּוֹת הַשְּׁאָר,
and in corresponding measure he awakens repentance in the hearts of the others as well,
עַד שֶׁאֵין לִקְרוֹתָם עוֹד "אֵינָם שָׁבִים" לְגַמְרֵי, אַף שֶׁאֵין מוּרְגָּשׁ אֶצְלָם.
to the point that they can no longer be called wholly "non-repentant," even though the awakening may not be consciously felt by them.
אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא סָבַר דִּמְכַפֵּר לְשֶׁאֵינָם שָׁבִים לְגַמְרֵי,
Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, however, holds that Yom Kippur atones even for those who are completely non-repentant,
הַיְנוּ אַף שֶׁלֹּא עַל יְדֵי מַדְרֵגַת הַיָּחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב.
meaning even independently of the level attained by the individual penitent.
וְהַיְנוּ דְּיָדוּעַ דִּלְעוֹלָם גְּמַר מַעֲשֶׂה הוּא בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ,
The reason is that the completion of every process ultimately lies in the hand of the Blessed One,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבְרָכוֹת ל״ג עַמּוּד ב:952 Berakhot 33b — R. Chanina said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, as it is said, "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear Him." Rashi: "Everything is in the hands of Heaven" — whatever comes upon a man is in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He: tall or short, poor or rich, wise or foolish, fair or dark, all is in the hands of Heaven. But righteous or wicked does not come by the hand of Heaven; this He delivered into man's own hand, and set two ways before him, and he will choose the fear of Heaven for himself. Maharsha: R. Chanina's words, that everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, are to be understood of the fear of the intellect, which is not in the hands of Heaven because it depends upon a man's own choice. The natural fear, fear of punishment, is to some degree in the hands of Heaven, for He brings calamity upon others so that men may fear and return in repentance, as it is said, "Surely you will fear Me, you will accept correction." Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Yiras Hashem 1): The essence of fear is that a man is an effect standing before his Cause, and reckons himself as nothing before Him. What a thing is of itself — its nothingness — cannot come from the Cause, for the Cause brings it into being and gives it existence; and therefore the fear of Heaven cannot be in the hands of Heaven, but only on the side of man, who is the effect. This is why they said, everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 12): In truth "all our works You have wrought for us," and "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," which is only in the heart (as the Sages expound "and he has no heart"): that one recognizes his lack, that he has nothing of his own and everything is from the Blessed One. Only, the Blessed One wished us to exert ourselves so that [our deeds] be called by our name. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): "Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," for this is in man's hand; but the Torah is a gift of God to man — "from the wilderness, a gift" — for it is the Blessed One's, since wisdom is His, whereas fear has no place with respect to the Blessed One and is only in the hands of man. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, on the Book of Joshua 21): Of the king it says "[whom] you shall set up" — Israel are the ones who establish him — and this is what is said, "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven": this matter is in man's hand, and therefore in this rank they are the ones who make it, and the Blessed One does not of Himself raise up the soul of the king. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 18): The serpent misled Adam through the very power of choice the Blessed One wished to be in the world, making it appear that He does not govern everything — for if all is in His hand, why warn him? But in truth this is what the Blessed One wished: that everything be in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven; and when man removed the fear of Heaven from himself, the fears of this world came upon him. Rav Tzadok (Ohr Zarua LaTzaddik, The Egyptian Exile 4): The Sages said "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," for in fear of Heaven lie man's choice and effort; as is known, love can come into a man's heart of itself, but not fear. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Behar 3): The sanctity of Shemittah is chiefly from man's side — those who keep the Sabbatical year are "mighty in strength" — and this is from the side of fear, for "who is mighty? He who conquers his inclination"; this is from man's side, as it says "what does the Lord ask of you but to fear," and "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven." Yet it is also "from above," from the Blessed One's side, for were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, he could not overcome [his inclination]. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 6): [The word for] "seeing" has the letters of "fear," for this is from the side of the Blessed One's seeing, His gaze upon the revealed world, where "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven" — which is man's task in this world, the world of action. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 221): When a person arouses the powers of his heart toward the Blessed One — and this is through fear of Heaven, for "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," and in this lies man's power of arousal — then the Blessed One's will for that day is revealed to him in general, even without his own study, and afterward he clarifies it with his understanding in the chambers of his heart. Mei HaShiloach (vol. I, Vayeira): What the Gemara says, "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," holds only according to the bounds of human understanding; in truth everything is in the hands of Heaven, even the fear of Heaven, only in this world the Blessed One concealed His way. The trait of Isaac was to clarify and show that even fear of Heaven is in the hands of Heaven, and that even all the sins of Israel are under the Blessed One's providence. Beis Yaakov (Vayeira 21): The Blessed One set in man the perception that "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven," but this holds only within the bounds of man's grasp and understanding: within those bounds he has choice, while beyond them he has none, and there even fear of Heaven is in the hands of Heaven — only in this world did the Blessed One conceal His way. The trait of Isaac is to make known in the world that even fear of Heaven is not in man's hands but in the Blessed One's. Tiferes Yosef (Nitzavim 10): On "everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven": how can one say "except," when all is in the hand of the Blessed One? Rather, the Blessed One so ordered this world that the vessel is man's, and this is called fear of Heaven; and man's vessel is chiefly that he humble himself so that the majesty of the Holy One, blessed be He, may rest upon him — then, as he stands in prayer, the Blessed One bestows words of Torah upon him. "הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם".
as they said in Berakhot 33b: "Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven."

וְיִרְאָה הִיא תַּרְעָא לְאַעֲלָא לְגוֹ מְהֵימְנוּתָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר, חֵלֶק א, י״א עַמּוּד ב953 Zohar 1:11b — "In the beginning God created" — this is the first commandment of all. And this commandment is called the fear of the Lord, which is called "beginning," as it is written: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord," "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" — for this thing is called "beginning." And this is the gate through which one enters into faith, and upon this commandment the whole world stands. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh 7): [In the Zohar's words that Israel below stand] "to open paths," this is the aspect of fear, which is "the gate for entering into faith" — the arousal from Israel's side, as in "Open for Me one opening of repentance like the eye of a needle, and I will open for you openings through which wagons and carriages can enter"; this opening is fear, which comes from Israel's side. Sha'ar HaEmunah (Entrance to the Gate 1): The fear of the Lord is the receptacle for receiving the Torah. Faith is the root of fear, and fear is the vessel that holds faith: fear is rooted in a person's believing in the Blessed One, and through his faith in the vastness of His power and exaltedness [he comes to fear Him] — as in the Zohar's introduction, "In the beginning God created: this is the first commandment of all … and this is the gate for entering into faith.",
Fear is the gate through which one enters into faith, as stated in the Zohar, Part I, 11b;
הַיְנוּ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם בַּכְּנִיסָה לִקְדֻשָּׁה.
it represents man's own effort in entering holiness.
אֲבָל גְּמַר הַכְּנִיסָה — זֶהוּ בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם,
The completion of that entry, however, is in the hands of Heaven,

שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ — אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֻכָּה נ״ב954 Sukkah 52b — R. Shimon ben Lakish said: A man's evil inclination overpowers him every day and seeks to kill him, as it is said, "The wicked watches the righteous and seeks to slay him"; and were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, he could not withstand it, as it is said, "The Lord will not leave him in his hand, nor let him be condemned when he is judged." Rashi (s.v. "the Lord will not leave him in his hand"): It is written immediately after ["The wicked watches the righteous and seeks to slay him"]. Maharsha (s.v. "a man's inclination overcomes him"): In the first chapter of Kiddushin [30b] the reading [of R. Yitzchak's statement] is "renews itself upon him." Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 48): The evil inclination in man is the deficiency and privation that clings to existing things, and this privation seeks to deprive man of existence and diminish him entirely, were it not for the Holy One, blessed be He, who upholds existing things and sustains them, and therefore does not let the power of privation prevail. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): The neshamah is the soul in the brain, and it is entirely pure; it is the assistance of the Blessed One of which our Rabbis said, "were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him," and it is stated in Yoma that they assist him — and this is through God "who dwells with them in the midst of their impurity," which is the camp of the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Lech Lecha 10): "Their help and their shield is He" — these are the two ways by which a person is saved from the evil inclination; "help" is as stated, "A man's inclination overpowers him every day … and were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, he could not withstand it." For even when a person is in the study hall, the evil inclination can overpower him, harden his heart, darken the light of the Torah's vitality and holiness before him and confuse his mind, and for this he needs help from the Blessed One. עַמּוּד ב.
for were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him, he could not overcome the evil inclination, as taught in Sukkah 52b.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא גְּמַר הַכְּנִיסָה,
Yom Kippur represents the completion of that entry,
אֵין יַד הָאָדָם שׁוֹלֶטֶת שָׁם,
a point at which human effort no longer has control.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר: "וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה" בְּבֹאוֹ לְכַפֵּר בַּקֹּדֶשׁ,
Therefore the Torah says, "No man shall be" in the Tent when the High Priest enters to atone in the Sanctuary,
לְפִי שֶׁאֵין בָּזֶה שַׁיָּכוּת לְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם.
for this final point does not belong to human striving.
וְלָכֵן לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא, עִצּוּמוֹ שֶׁל יוֹם מְכַפֵּר בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם כְּלָל,
Therefore, according to Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, the very essence of Yom Kippur atones without any human effort at all,
כִּי הֶאָרַת אוֹתוֹ יוֹם הוּא דְּ"הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם".
for the illumination of that day belongs to the level of "everything is in the hands of Heaven."
וְזֶהוּ שְׁאֵלַת הַיְדִיעָה וְהַבְּחִירָה שֶׁנָּבוֹכוּ בָּהּ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים,
This touches upon the question of divine foreknowledge and human free choice over which the early authorities were perplexed.
וּבְתִקּוּנֵי זֹהַר חָדָשׁ, בְּסוֹפוֹ, תֵּרֵץ,
At the end of Tikkunei Zohar Chadash an answer is given,
וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹם בֵּאוּרוֹ; וְתַמְצִית דְּבָרָיו, דְּאֵינוֹ בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד,
whose full explanation does not belong here; in essence, the two principles do not operate on the same plane,
וּבִמְקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה — שָׁם אֵין בְּחִירָה, וּבִמְקוֹם הַבְּחִירָה וְכוּלֵי.
for in the plane of divine knowledge there is no free choice, while in the plane of free choice... and so forth.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא הִתְנוֹצְצוּת תַּרְעָא דְּחֵירוּ,
Yom Kippur is a glimmer of the "gate of freedom,"
שֶׁמִּמְּקוֹם הַבִּינָה שֶׁבִּידִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמְּקוֹם הַבְּחִירָה,
emanating from the level of Binah within divine knowledge, above the plane of free choice,
וּמִשָּׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לְחֵטְא כְּלָל, כֵּיוָן דְּהַכֹּל מְסֻדָּר בִּידִיעָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and from that perspective there is no place for sin at all, because everything is ordered within His knowledge.

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה, פֶּרֶק א955 Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 1 — Another interpretation: "Days were fashioned, and one of them is His" — this is the Day of Atonement for Israel, for there was great joy before the Holy One, blessed be He, that it was given to Israel in abundant love. They told a parable: to what may the matter be compared? To a king of flesh and blood whose servants and household would carry out the refuse and cast it before the door of the king's house; and when the king comes out and sees the refuse, he rejoices greatly. So the Day of Atonement is likened, which the Holy One, blessed be He, gave in abundant love and in joy. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 18): Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah expounds "Days were fashioned, and one of them is His" both of the Sabbath and of the Day of Atonement, and the two are one: the one before the sin, the other after one has sinned, when one needs the Day of Atonement that atones for everything, and through it the holiness of all the year's Sabbaths shines for him. Therefore the Day of Atonement is called "a Sabbath of Sabbaths" — the Sabbath gathered from the Sabbaths of the year, whose holiness Israel bring into the Day of Atonement, which, having no eating or drinking, is more a semblance of the World to Come. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 8): "Days were fashioned, and one of them is His" — this is the Day of Atonement: in the year, the counterpart of the world, the Blessed One fixed one day of a higher level than the other days, which are the seven days of building; and the Sabbath too is expounded there as likewise a semblance of the World to Come. The Day of Atonement is called "a Sabbath of Sabbaths" because the Sabbath is the mystery of the lower heh, which draws from the upper heh, while the Day of Atonement is the mystery of the upper heh itself; therefore it is a time of repentance for all.,
This is what the Sages of blessed memory taught in Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 1,
עַל פָּסוּק "יָמִים יֻצָּרוּ וְלוֹ אֶחָד בָּהֶם" — זֶה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל.
concerning the verse, "Days were formed, and one of them is His": this refers to Yom Kippur for Israel.
הַיְנוּ דִּכְלַל הַבְּרִיאָה הָיָה עַצְמוּת שֵׁם הֲוָיָה,
The totality of creation was embodied in the Divine Name Havayah,
כְּטַעַם "כִּי שֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים עָשָׂה הַשֵּׁם",
in the sense of the verse, "For six days the Lord made..."

דְּפֵרֵשׁ בַּזֹּהַר, חֵלֶק ג, צ״ד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב956 Zohar 3:94b — “Six days shall work be done” — these six days, what is their work? R. Yose said: It is written, “For six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth” — and it is not written “in six days” [but that He made the days themselves]. And this has been explained: each and every day performs its own work, and they are called the days of labor., עַל הַיָּמִים עַצְמָם,
which the Zohar, Part III, 94b, beginning of the page, explains as referring to the days themselves,
שֶׁהֵם כְּלַל הַבְּרִיאָה, כַּיָּדוּעַ.
for those six days encompass the structure of creation, as is known.
וּמֵהַיְצִירָה וָאֵילָךְ שָׁם מַתְחִיל כֹּחַ הַבְּחִירָה,
From the world or level of Yetzirah onward, the power of free choice begins,
דְּשָׁם הוּא עֵרוּב הַטּוֹב וָרָע, כַּנּוֹדָע בְּתִקּוּנֵי זֹהַר.
for there begins the mixture of good and evil, as is known from Tikkunei Zohar.
"וְלוֹ אֶחָד" הַיְנוּ שֶׁהוּא לְחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבִידֵי שָׁמַיִם,
The words "and one is His" mean that this one day belongs to the portion of the Blessed One and to the domain of Heaven,
וְאֵין הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת דְּאָדָם פּוֹעֶלֶת בּוֹ כְּלָל.
so that human striving is not the operative force within it at all.
וְזֶהוּ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים וְכֹחַ הַמְכַפֵּר לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכָאָמוּר.
This is Yom Kippur and the source of its power to atone for Israel, as explained.

sections.en: Rosh Hashanah, Divine Thought, and the Shofar

items.h: Rosh Hashanah reaches the primordial thought of Creation; the shofar awakens that inner root and distinguishes Israel's life-giving bond from the nations' judgment.

Seif 1 — Rosh Hashanah and Primordial Divine Thought
Rosh Hashanah returns to the first divine thought of Israel and uses the shofar to awaken that concealed inner source.

p: עִנְיַן רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה דְּנִקְרָא מֶלֶךְ יוֹשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא דִּין בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לְ"ב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב.
The matter of Rosh Hashanah, which is called “the King sitting upon the throne of judgment,” as stated in Rosh Hashanah 32b.

כִּי הוּא מִן מַחֲשֶׁבֶת הַבְּרִיאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת כ"ז א' דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל כְּמַאן בְּשֵׁם רַבֵּינוּ תָּם וּדְבָרָיו דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים957 Tosafot, Rosh Hashanah 27a — And as for what R. Eliezer HaKalir composed for the rain of Shemini Atzeret according to R. Eliezer, who says the world was created in Tishrei, and for Pesach he composed according to R. Yehoshua — Rabbeinu Tam says: These and these are the words of the living God, and it is possible to say that in Tishrei it arose in thought to create, but it was not created until Nisan. And Rashi on Genesis 1:1: “God created” — and it does not say “the Lord created,” for at first it arose in thought to create it with the attribute of strict justice; He saw that the world could not endure, so He gave precedence to the attribute of mercy and joined it to the attribute of justice — as it is written, “on the day the Lord God made earth and heaven.” וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (הוּבָא בְּפֵירוּשׁ רַבֵּינוּ שְׁלֵמָה יִצְחָקִי בְּרֵאשִׁית)958 Rashi on Genesis 1:1:3 — "God created" — and it does not say "the Lord created," because at first He thought to create it with the attribute of strict justice; He saw that the world could not endure, so He gave precedence to the attribute of mercy and joined it to the attribute of justice. And that is what is written: "On the day that the Lord God made earth and heaven." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 7): Just as at Sinai mercy was given first and afterwards the Torah from the side of strength, so it was at the beginning of creation: in all the utterances of the six days the name Elokim is written, and in the second chapter, "On the day that the Lord God made," for, as Rashi says, at first it arose in thought to create with the attribute of justice, He saw that the world could not endure, and He joined to it the attribute of mercy, the Name Havayah. So the world arose in thought in Tishrei, whose letters run in reverse and denote justice, but after He joined the attribute of mercy it was actually created in Nisan, called Aviv, whose letters run in order and denote mercy. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 101): In deed it is impossible for a person not to depart somewhat from the strict line of justice, but in thought and in the heart's will he can resolve to conduct himself so and not sin. This is the meaning of "At first it arose in thought to create [the world] with the attribute of justice": in deed there is departure from the strict line of justice, but in thought all is by the attribute of justice and there is no departure. דְּבַתְּחִלָּה עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה לִבְרוֹא בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין וְרָאָה וְכוּלֵי.

For it belongs to the primordial thought of Creation, as Tosafot wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Tam; his words are the words of the living God, corresponding to the teaching that at first it arose in thought to create the world through the attribute of strict justice, until He saw otherwise.

הָעִנְיָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה א)959 Bereshit Rabbah 1:4 — Six things preceded the creation of the world; some of them were created, and some of them arose in thought to be created. The Torah and the Throne of Glory were created. The patriarchs, Israel, the Temple, and the name of the Messiah arose in thought to be created. Israel, from where is it derived? As it is said: "Remember Your congregation, which You acquired of old." R. Huna and R. Yirmeya said in the name of R. Shmuel bar R. Yitzchak: The thought of Israel preceded everything. Mei HaShiloach (vol. II, Anthology, Ki Savo; from Tiferes Yosef, Ki Savo): After forty years Israel had clarified that their entire purpose is the glory of Heaven, and so "the Lord has affirmed you this day to be His treasured people": the Blessed One shows that His entire purpose is for Israel and that all the creation of the world was for the sake of Israel, as the Midrash says, "Israel arose first in thought." Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 2): The first intention of the Blessed One in creation, as it is written, "I said, the world shall be built with kindness," was all for the sake of Israel, and "Israel arose first in thought." Although afterwards the Blessed One set up many garments, down to the utterance "Let us make man," all is included in the beginning, so that a person who walks in [divine] service reaches this first will, that "Israel arose first in thought." יִשְׂרָאֵל עָלָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה כַּיָּדוּעַ דִּתְחִלַּת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה הוּא עַל סוֹף הַמַּעֲשֶׂה וְהַתַּכְלִית שֶׁבְּעִנְיָן זֶה.
The meaning is as the Sages taught: Israel arose first in the Divine thought; for the beginning of thought is directed toward the end of the act and toward its ultimate purpose.
וְתַכְלִית בְּרִיאַת עוֹלָם הוּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ כַּנּוֹדָע דְּרָצָה שֶׁיַּכִּירוּ כֹּחַ מַלְכוּתוֹ וְאֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עִם.

The ultimate purpose of the world’s creation is the awakening and revelation of His attribute of Kingship: that creatures recognize the power of His sovereignty, for there is no king without a people.

וְאִם כֵּן הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה הוּא כְּפִי הַתַּכְלִית שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַכָּרָה זוֹ בָּעוֹלָם וְבְּמַחֲשָׁבָה אֵין רַע כְּלָל כַּיָּדוּעַ כִּי שָׁם עֲדַיִן כּוּלּוֹ חַד אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְמַעֲשֵׂה שֶׁאָז בְּהֶכְרֵחַ נִרְאֶה כְּנִפְרָד מֵהַבּוֹרֵא וְיֵשׁ מָקוֹם לִטְעוֹת בָּרָע עַל כֵּן הוּצְרַךְ לְשַׁתֵּף מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים.

Accordingly, the primordial thought follows that ultimate purpose, in which this recognition fills the world. In the realm of thought there is no evil at all, for there everything is still entirely one; but when it reaches the realm of action, where the created being necessarily appears separate from the Creator and room exists to err through evil, the attribute of mercy had to be joined to justice.
וְזֶהוּ בְּנִיסָן שֶׁהוּא זְמַן גְּאֻלַּת יִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת רַק עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְגַּלָּה מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי יִתְרוֹן הָאוֹר מֵהַחֹשֶׁךְ.
This is expressed in Nisan, the time of Israel’s redemption, for precisely through this process the unique greatness of Israel becomes revealed: the advantage of light is known from darkness.

אֲבָל בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כָּל בָּאֵי עוֹלָם עוֹבְרִים כִּבְנֵי מָרוֹן וְנִסְקָרִים בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.)960 Rosh Hashanah 18a — "On Rosh HaShana all who come into the world pass before Him like benei maron." What is benei maron? Here they rendered it: like a flock of sheep. Reish Lakish said: Like the ascent of Beit Maron. R. Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: Like the troops of the house of David. Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of R. Yochanan: And they are all surveyed in a single glance. Rashi: "Like benei imrana" — like sheep counted for the tithe, which go out one after another through a small opening, unable to go out together; "like the ascent of Beit Maron" — the path is narrow and two cannot walk side by side, for the valley is deep on either side of the road. "Like the troops of the house of David" — maron being an expression of lordship and mastery, i.e., like the troops of the king, who were counted as they went out one after another to war. "And they are all surveyed [in a single glance]" — even though they pass one after another. Maharsha (s.v. "and they are all surveyed in a single glance"): Were it not for Rashi's explanation, it seems that Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of R. Yochanan comes to explain that [the Mishnah] does not literally mean that they pass before Him one after another; rather, it likens them to benei maron because when many walk together a man cannot see them all at once, but when they pass one behind another even a man standing to the side can see them all at once — so the Holy One, blessed be He, sees them all at once, in a single glance, attending to each in particular. Maharsha (s.v. "like the ascent of Beit Choron"): So reads the text before us in all editions of the Gemara. One may say they do not disagree, but all these explanations of benei maron hold, alluding to the three classes of men judged on Rosh Hashanah — the righteous, the wicked and the intermediate: whoever explains "like sheep" refers to the wicked, for as sheep are counted for slaughter, so the wicked are counted for death; whoever explains "like the ascent" refers to the intermediate, who like those on the ascent are counted on a middle path between two sides, whether to the left or to the right. And whoever explains "like the troops of the house of David," counted as they go out to war, refers to the righteous, as explained in chapter Asarah Yuchasin [Kiddushin 76b], that [they were reckoned by lineage] so that their merit and the merit of their fathers might assist them. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Rosh Hashanah 18a): "Like sheep" means, in its plain sense, that the Blessed One examines His creatures as a shepherd examines his flock; Reish Lakish adds how the examination is done — like the ascent of Beit Maron, where they go up one by one and the place holds only one — for He examines each one with particular knowledge, since every man is a world of his own, man having been created single. Shmuel holds "like the troops of the house of David," who march to war ordered each according to his own rank and yet bound together in one bond: for each man stands by himself and at the same time has order and connection with the rest of mankind, and so the Blessed One knows him — not like a shepherd who examines only the flock as a whole, nor wholly like the ascent of Beit Maron, where each passes alone with no connection to another. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): Since the beginning on Rosh HaShanah is in concealment, [corresponding to] Keser and Chochmah, which are above human grasp, it is then the Day of Judgment and three books are opened; for from the standpoint of contemplating the letters of thought, "all who come into the world pass like benei maron" in a single glance, since in thought there are no perceptible divisions as in the letters of speech and writing, and the end of the deed is embedded in it as well. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 1): In a full year every kind of change passes over a person, and if these do not move him from his standing, that is the victory [over the inclination]. Therefore every Rosh HaShanah is a day of judgment for all who come into the world, since each year is a complete cycle of the time fit for conquering the inclination, and all who come into the world pass "like benei maron" to see whether they have completed their allotment in this cycle. גַּם אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אֶלָּא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל קָדְמֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא ח' ב'961 Rosh Hashanah 8b — It was taught elsewhere: “For it is a statute for Israel” — I know only Israel; from where do we know the nations of the world? Scripture says: “a judgment for the God of Yaakov.” If so, what does “a statute for Israel” teach?
