וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מִשְׁלֵי ד, כג): "מִכָּל מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ וְגוֹמֵר".
as it is written (Proverbs 4:23): "Above all that you guard, keep your heart, etc."
כִּי בוֹ הוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה וּגְמָרָהּ לְהוֹצִיא לַפּוֹעַל,
For in the heart unfolds the manifestation of thought and its culmination in practical execution,
דְּ"עַיִן רוֹאָה וְלֵב חוֹמֵד, וּכְלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גּוֹמְרִים" (רַשִּׁ"י בַּמִּדְבָּר טו, לט).
for "the eye sees, the heart covets, and the instruments of action bring it to completion" (Rashi, Numbers 15:39).
"עַיִן" הוּא בָּרֹאשׁ נֶגֶד הַמּוֹחַ, וְרוֹמֵז לְעֵינֵי הַשֵּׂכֶל וְהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה;
"Eye" is situated in the head opposite the brain, symbolizing the eyes of intellect and thought;
וְחִלְּקָם פְּעָמִים לִשְׁנַיִם,
and Scripture divides them at times into two distinct faculties,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בַּמִּדְבָּר טו, לט): "לֹא תָתֻרוּ אַחֲרֵי לְבַבְכֶם וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם",
as it is written (Numbers 15:39): "And that you do not follow after your heart and after your eyes",
וְנֶאֱמַר (מִשְׁלֵי כג, כו): "תְּנָה בְנִי לִבְּךָ לִּי, וְעֵינֶיךָ וְגוֹמֵר".
and it is stated (Proverbs 23:26): "My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes, etc."

וְאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דִּבְרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ה)1154 Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 1:5 — "You shall not commit adultery" corresponds to "you shall not stray after your hearts and after your eyes." R. Levi said: The heart and the eye are the two brokers of sin. It is written, "My son, give Me your heart, and let your eyes keep My ways." The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you have given Me your heart and your eyes, I know that you are Mine. Pnei Moshe (s.v. "It is written, 'My son, give Me your heart'"): He expounds "and your eyes" as belonging to what precedes it: if you give Me your heart and your eyes, then "they will keep My ways" — as he concludes, "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you have given Me your heart and your eyes, I know that you are Mine." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 35): Because of the Yerushalmi's "if you give Me your eye and your heart, I know that you are Mine," they expounded "you shall guard yourself [from every evil thing]" as a warning against [impure] thoughts: even where such a thought incurs no punishment, the mitzvah of guarding one's heart rests upon him. For the essence of Jewishness is in the heart, and fear [of Heaven], the essence of what God asks of you, is only in the heart. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2): In the Yerushalmi's "if you give Me your eye and your heart," the eye is wisdom ("the wise man's eyes are in his head"; "who is wise? one who sees what will be born") and the heart is the understanding of the heart, the two powers by which a person overcomes his inclination and gives birth to a good deed; [the Yerushalmi] reverses the order of the verse "after your hearts and after your eyes." A person need give the Blessed One only these, while the completion comes from the Blessed One's help. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 10): Of the righteous man whose nature is not evil Ezekiel speaks in the future tense, yet "his eyes he did not lift" and "his neighbor's wife he did not defile" are in the past tense, for these are the two agents of which the Sages said, "if you give Me your eye and your heart, I know that you are Mine." Once he has handed these two over to the Blessed One in actual deed, through the effort of turning from evil when a transgression came his way and he was saved, he no longer needs effort in deed, only that his heart be ready to turn from evil and do good when the occasion comes. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 6): David, praised as "beautiful of eyes", was truly pure of all the filth of this world's desires, and this showed in the eyes, for the eye and the heart are the two agents of sin, and "if you give Me your eye and your heart, I know that you are Mine." The heart is hidden from all ("man sees with the eyes, but God sees into the heart"), whereas the eyes are in the open. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 190): The eye and the heart are the agents of sin, as the Yerushalmi says, and likewise agents for good, as it says there, "if you give Me your eye and your heart"; they are the two levels of seeing and knowing, of which it is said "Send Your light and Your truth," the essence of seeing being light. They are the levels of Jacob and Joseph: "truth to Jacob" and "light is sown for the righteous.":
And they taught in the Yerushalmi, Berakhot (1:5):
"אִי אַתְּ יָהֵיב עֵינָא וְלִבָּא לִי, אֲנָא יָדַע דְּאַתְּ דִּילִי".
"If you give your eye and your heart to Me, I know that you are Mine."
כִּי עִיקַּר הָאָדָם הוּא הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבְּמוֹחַ וָלֵב,
For the absolute core of man is the thought within the brain and the heart,

וּ"מַחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה" (קִדּוּשִׁין מ.)1155 Kiddushin 40a — A good thought the Holy One, blessed be He, joins to the deed, as it is stated: "Then those who feared the Lord spoke one with another, and the Lord listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the Lord and who think upon His name." What is meant by "and who think upon His name"? Rav Asi said: Even if a man intended to perform a commandment and was prevented by circumstances beyond his control and did not perform it, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it. But an evil thought the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join to the deed, as it is stated: "If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear." Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot, s.v. "Even if a man intended to perform a commandment and was prevented"): The word "even" attaches to "and did not perform it"; but "was prevented by circumstances beyond his control" is stated precisely, for had he failed to perform it when nothing prevented him he would have transgressed a positive commandment [and would be credited with nothing]. So too the verse brought for the evil thought, "If I had regarded iniquity in my heart," does not come to teach the obvious case of one who simply did not commit the sin, since no man escapes thoughts of transgression in a single day; it teaches rather of one who was prevented and would have sinned had he not been prevented — and even so the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join his thought to the deed. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 40a): A good thought the Holy One, blessed be He, joins to the deed, because a good thought is fit to be brought to a deed, and one who comes to purify himself is assisted; it is therefore reckoned as though he had performed the deed. An evil thought He does not join to the deed, because one who comes to defile himself is not assisted, and further because such a thing is not fit to come into being at all — and therefore it is not reckoned a deed until it has actually been done. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 4): The head of the soul is the neshamah in the brain, which is pure and inclines toward cleaving to the Blessed One, while at its end, in the powers of action, lies the sense of being separate from the Blessed One. Therefore evil is only in deed, as the Sages said, "an evil thought the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join to the deed"; the essence of evil is in the deed, where evil is revealed, and of that it is said, "There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin" — in deed specifically. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 145): In every human act the deed is like the body and the thought the soul. Since "the soul You placed within me is pure," "an evil thought the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join to the deed," for all evil thoughts in truth come from a spirit of folly — imagination that mimics wisdom like an ape before a man — and only when it goes out into deed, in [the world of] action, is the place where evil and the power of imagination rule; whereas in the performance of mitzvos a good thought is joined [to the deed], because it is real.,
and "a good thought the Holy One combines with deed" (Kiddushin 40a),
וּמִיָּד בִּנְתִינַת עֵינָא וְלִבָּא "אֲנָא יָדַע וְכוּלֵי".
and instantly upon surrendering the eye and the heart, "I know you are Mine."
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה דְּאֵין מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה,
In contrast, regarding an evil thought which He does not combine with deed,
נֶאֱמַר רַק: "לֹא תָתֻרוּ אַחֲרֵי וְגוֹמֵר",
it is merely stated: "Do not seek after, etc.",
שֶׁלֹּא יִמָּשְׁכוּ אַחֲרֵי הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה שֶׁבְּמוֹחַ וָלֵב לְהוֹצִיא לַפּוֹעַל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה,
that they should not be dragged after the sinister contemplation within brain and heart to actualize the deed,
אֲבָל כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא יָצָא לְמַעֲשֶׂה אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם.
yet as long as it has not emerged into practical execution, it is treated as nothing.
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן הַהֶבְדֵּל בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק א' דְּפֵאָה (הֲלָכָה ד),
And this is also the fundamental distinction between Israel and the nations as stated in Yerushalmi, Peah (1:4),

כִּי אֶצְלָם הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ1156 Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:1 — A good intention the Omnipresent joins to the deed; an evil intention the Omnipresent does not join to the deed. This is said of Israel; but with the nations it is the reverse — a good intention the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join, while an evil intention the Holy One, blessed be He, does join. Pnei Moshe: "Then those who fear the Lord spoke with one another" — the verse ends "and thought upon His name," from which it is expounded that even one who sat down to perform a commandment and was prevented by force and did not perform it, Scripture accounts it to him as though he had performed it. Of the nations it is written of Darius that he "strove to plead for" Daniel and not "to deliver him" — for though he meant to rescue him outright, the word Scripture uses implies only that he exerted himself to speak on his behalf. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 40a): A good thought is one that is fit to be brought to actual performance, and one who comes to purify himself is helped; therefore a good thought is reckoned as though he had already done the deed. An evil thought He does not join to the deed, because one who comes to defile himself is not helped, and further, because a thing that ought to be done is already counted as done, whereas an evil thing ought not to be done at all, and so it is not reckoned a deed until it is actually done.;
for with the nations it operates in reverse;
כִּי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
for the Holy One is the very heart of Israel,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ה, ב): "וְלִבִּי עֵר", מִקְרָא (תְּהִלִּים עג, כו): "צוּר לְבָבִי וְגוֹמֵר",
as they expounded in Shir HaShirim Rabbah on the verse (Song of Songs 5:2): "and my heart is awake," citing (Psalms 73:26): "the Rock of my heart, etc.",
הַיְינוּ שֶׁמַּעֲמַקֵּי לְבָבָם בֶּאֱמֶת דָּבוּק בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
meaning that the absolute depths of their heart are in truth cleaved unto Him, blessed be He.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק ב' דִּבְרָכוֹת (יז.):
And as they stated in the second chapter of Berakhot (17a):
"גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנֶךָ, וּמִי מְעַכֵּב? שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבַּעִיסָּה" –
"It is revealed and known that our true desire is to do Your will, and what hinders us? The leaven in the dough" –

הוּא יֵצֶר רָע הַשּׁוֹכֵן עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב (שָׁם סא.)1157 Berakhot 61a — Rav said: The evil inclination is like a fly, and it sits between the two entrances of the heart, as it is stated: "Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment fetid and putrid." And Shmuel said: It is like a kind of wheat, as it is stated: "Sin crouches at the door." Rashi: "Make putrid [yabia]" is an expression of blistering — every liquid that turns foul throws up a seething of bubbles. "Sin [chatat]" — he expounds it from the word for wheat [chitah]. Maharsha: The fly is a small and feeble creature, yet it makes a precious thing — the perfumer's ointment — putrid; so too the evil inclination, of which they said that at first it is like a [spider's] thread. It sits between the two entrances of the heart, in keeping with what follows, "a wise man's understanding is at his right hand, but a fool's understanding at his left." Shmuel likens it to a kind of wheat, which is likewise a small thing, and perhaps he holds like the one who says that the tree from which Adam the first man ate was wheat, and that through it the evil inclination came. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv Koach HaYetzer 2): The evil inclination is compared to a fly because the fly is a loathsome and perishable thing — nothing decays so quickly as a fly — and so too the evil inclination, which is the power of desire that craves base things, is likened to the most loathsome of creatures. Wheat and the fly are two opposites: no substance is as clean as wheat, and nothing is as low and contemptible as a fly; Rav holds that like is drawn to like, the loathsome loving what is loathsome, while Shmuel holds that it is from the clean and choice element in man that he is drawn after the inclination, for a perfection in which there is a defect longs for its opposite. All agree that it sits upon the two entrances of the heart, for the heart is the root of man, and the evil cleaves to man at his root.,
which is the evil inclination situated upon the two chambers/entrances of the heart (ibid., 61a),
רַק בִּמְקוֹם הַפְּתִיחָה וְהִתְגַּלּוּת הַלֵּב.
operating exclusively at the threshold of the heart's outward manifestation.
וּלְפִיכָךְ, אִם הוּא גַּם בַּלֵּב טוֹב – וַדַּאי לֵית טָב מִינַּהּ,
Therefore, if a person is also virtuous within the manifest chambers of the heart, surely there is nothing better,
שֶׁאֵין מַנִּיחוֹ בַּהַתְחָלָה לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט כְּלָל.
preventing the inclination at the outset from expanding at all.
וְגַם אִם שָׁם לֹא כֵן, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא יָצָא בְּפוֹעַל וְהִתְגַּלּוּת,
Yet even if it is not so there, as long as it has not emerged into active manifestation,
הֲרֵי שָׁם בְּעוֹדוֹ בַּלֵּב עֲדַיִן מְחוּבָּר לִמְקוֹרוֹ שֶׁבְּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב;
behold, while still resting within the interior of the heart, it remains attached to its source in the profound depths of the heart;
וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם עֲדַיִן דָּבוּק בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ טוֹב,
and as long as it remains concealed, it clings to the hidden Root which is absolute good,
עַל כֵּן לֹא נֶחְשָׁב רַע עֲדַיִן, אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁיָּצָא לַפּוֹעַל בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת וְנִפְרַד מֵהַהֶעְלֵם.
hence it is not yet reckoned as evil until it breaks forth into outward execution and is severed from concealment.
וְאֵצֶל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ,
Whereas with the idolatrous nations, it is the exact reverse,
כִּי הֵם שָׁרְשָׁם בְּרַע וְעֹמֶק לִבָּם כֻּלּוֹ רַע.
for their root is embedded in evil and the depth of their heart is entirely corrupted.
רַק כַּאֲשֶׁר הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת כְּשֶׁנִּפְרֶדֶת מֵהַהֶעְלֵם טוֹב – נֶחְשָׁב טוֹב;
Only when the outward manifest deed, having separated from the hidden root, is virtuous, is it accounted good;
אֲבָל מַה שֶּׁבְּהֶעְלֵם טוֹב, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא יָצָא לַפּוֹעַל,
however, a good thought hidden within them, as long as it has not materialized into deed,
הֲרֵי עֲדַיִן מְחוּבָּר בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ הָרַע וְלֹא נִתְבָּרֵר וְנִפְרַד עֲדַיִן שֶׁיָּחוּל עָלָיו שֵׁם טוֹב;
remains tied to its corrupt root, having not yet been refined or detached so that the title 'good' may rest upon it;
וּמַה שֶּׁבְּהֶעְלֵם רַע – וַדַּאי רַע גָּמוּר, שֶׁדָּבוּק גַּם בְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ הָרַע.
and that which is hiddenly evil within them is assuredly complete evil, being cleaved to its rotten root.
וְלָכֵן כָּל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָעַמִּים אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּמַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּגְלֵית לְבַד,
Therefore all striving of the nations resides strictly within the outward visible deed,
וְעַל כֵּן אוֹכְלִים שְׂכָרָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד שֶׁהוּא עוֹלַם הַנִּגְלֶה,
and consequently they receive their recompense solely in this world which is the manifest realm,
וְנִקְרָא "מִצְווֹת קַלּוֹת" בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא דַּף י' עַמּוּד ב',
and these are termed "minor, flimsy mitzvot" in Bava Batra 10b,
כִּי חִישׁ קַל יָעוּפוּ וְאֵינָם, מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ טוֹב.
because they swiftly vanish and disperse, possessing no sacred root.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל: "הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם וּמָחָר לְקַבֵּל שְׂכָרָם" (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ג.)1158 Avodah Zarah 3a — R. Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written, "which I command you this day, to do them" (Deuteronomy 7:11)? Today is the time to do them, and not tomorrow to do them; today is the time to do them, but today is not the time to receive their reward. Rashi: "This day to do them" — in this world; "and not tomorrow" — because one cannot perform them in the World to Come. Tosafos (s.v. "this day to do them, and not tomorrow to do them"): Tosafot asks why the Sages objected to the men of Jericho, who ran the words of the Shema together and did not pause at "this day, upon your heart," so that it sounded like "this day upon your heart and not tomorrow upon your heart" (Pesachim 57a) — what harm is there in that, seeing that it is true, as is implied here? He answers that there one might err and take "this day" and "tomorrow" quite literally, whereas here "this day to do them" stands in a verse that speaks of the payment of reward — "and repays them that hate Him" [Deuteronomy 7:10] — and the reward of the righteous is paid in the World to Come. Maharsha: The objection could have been raised from the Holy One's own words just above, "Fools of the world! One who took trouble on the eve of the Sabbath..." — except that even so He deals with them beyond the letter of the law and tells them to make a sukkah. It may therefore be that the objection is drawn not from "this day to do them and not tomorrow to do them" but from "this day to do them, but not this day to receive the reward": since the nations have already received the reward of their commandments in this world — "and repays them that hate Him to their face" — they receive nothing further in the World to Come, for otherwise justice would be impaired, Israel receiving only the reward of the World to Come. And by the commandment of sukkah He hinted to them that they should have kept the commandments in this world, which is like a sukkah, a temporary dwelling. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Avodah Zarah 3a): The Gemara’s objection from this teaching [to the nations’ being offered the sukkah in the time to come] is the very same difficulty as above — "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, from where will he eat on Shabbat?" — only that here it is written in the Torah, and since it is written in the Torah, it cannot possibly be otherwise at all. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 1): Tefillin, the recognition of God's name upon a person in actual deed, belong only to the weekdays and not to Shabbat and festivals, when the recognition in the heart must be clear without any deed, like the world to come, a day [of clear intellectual illumination] that is entirely Shabbat, a cessation from deeds, as it says, "today to do them and not tomorrow." Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part II 25): Shabbat is [the day on which God Himself is one's light, needing no fire of fear]; nevertheless one must toil to cook the food on the eve of Shabbat, for "one who did not toil on the eve of Shabbat, what will he eat on Shabbat?" and "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward": this light does not come to a person by itself. So too the Shabbat lamp must be lit from the eve of Shabbat, for on Shabbat there is no longer time to arouse fear, the day being entirely love and cleaving to God. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 17): This world is the world of toil, and "one who toiled on the eve of Shabbat will eat on Shabbat" refers to the world to come, the day that is entirely Shabbat, where there is no doing even of Torah and mitzvot, as they said, "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; and Shabbat is a semblance of the world to come, the time of the Blessed One's rest. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Savo 16): The verse ["all these blessings will come upon you"] certainly does not speak of the reward and punishment for the mitzvot, which are not in this world, for it is only "today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward"; it speaks of the blessings of this world, that God will give every assistance so that one can serve Him all the more. And if, Heaven forbid, they do not listen, the reverse too will serve as an assistance, through which they will take it to heart to return and mend their ways. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares, from the Yerushalmi 14): The world to come is likened to day because there will be no departure there from the [fixed] order, such departure coming about through changes in deeds, as they said, "today to do them and not tomorrow to do them." But in this world, the day of action, where choice is in man's hand, the order changes through deeds: toward evil, as troubles and exile, through evil deeds, and toward good through cleaving to the Blessed One.,
Unlike the children of Israel, regarding whom: "Today is for doing them, and tomorrow is for receiving their reward" (Avodah Zarah 3a),

וּשְׂכַר מִצְוָה בְּהַאי עָלְמָא לֵיכָּא (קִדּוּשִׁין לט:)1159 Kiddushin 39b — Rava said: Whose opinion is this? It is R. Yaakov's, who says: There is no reward for a commandment in this world. As it is taught: R. Yaakov says: There is not a single commandment written in the Torah whose reward is stated alongside it that is not dependent upon the resurrection of the dead. A man's father said to him, Climb the tower and fetch me fledglings; he climbed the tower, sent away the mother and took the young, and on his way back he fell and died. Where is the goodness of this one's days, and where is the length of this one's days? Rather, "that it may go well with you" — in the world that is wholly good; "that your days may be long" — in the world that is wholly long. Rashi (s.v. "that is not dependent upon the resurrection of the dead"): The reward stated alongside the commandment is not paid out here at all; it is stated in this way to make known to you that there is no giving of reward except in the world to come. Tosafos (s.v. "the mishna refers to a case where they make him a good day and a bad day"): Rashi's reading is difficult, for Rava's "Whose opinion is this? R. Yaakov's" implies that until now the mishna had not been established according to R. Yaakov, whereas on Rashi's explanation Abaye too had established both the mishna and the baraita according to him. Rabbeinu Tam therefore explains that both the good day and the bad day are in this world — sometimes a good day is made for the wicked man so that he may receive the reward of his commandments here, and a bad day for the righteous man so that his sins may be scoured away here — and this is not like R. Yaakov, who holds that there is no reward for a commandment in this world at all. Maharsha: Do not object from all the promises of the Torah, which can only be understood of this world. R. Yaakov concedes that the merit of the community and its good deeds bring upon it in this world too all the blessings and good things named in the Torah, and the reverse for the community's sin; he spoke only of the individual, whose reward, when his merits are many, is wholly in the world to come, since here evil is done to him in order to give him merit there — and conversely one whose sins are many is given good here in order to drive him from the world to come. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Kiddushin 39b): Because the reward that belongs to the commandments is so great, their reward is not in this world; and one cannot say that He pays part of the reward of a commandment in this world and part in the world to come, for there is no payment by halves — hence there is no reward for a commandment in this world. R. Yaakov concedes that a wicked man does receive payment for a commandment he performed, since his reward is not so great; and because it is not great it can be discharged here, for a great reward cannot be given in this world, as they said, "one hour of contentment in the world to come is better than all the life of this world." Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 25): Every commandment has its own reward, in the world to come and also in this world through its fruits: only the reward of the commandment itself "is not in this world," but a reward of fruits exists for every commandment, each in its own way — like "tithe so that you become rich," or children for sending away the mother bird. The Mishnah's "things whose fruits a person eats [in this world]" means only that for these one is assured of eating the fruits here, whereas for other commandments the fruits too may remain for the world to come. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 4): Sins have a limit, as this world has a limit, but the commandments have none; therefore "there is no reward for a commandment in this world," since this world is bounded and the reward of the commandments has no bound. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 7): The world to come is the cessation of activity, where the righteous enjoy the radiance of the Presence, and Shabbos is a taste of it; though "there is no reward for a commandment in this world," it is for this reason that Shabbos is called a "good gift." Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 13): Life does not depend on merit but on mazal because "there is no reward for commandments in this world"; but that is only the reward of a commandment done out of obligation, whereas what one does beyond the letter of the law the Holy One, blessed be He, repays in one's lifetime. That is why [the Gemara] lists acts of piety as the cause of long life. Rav Tzadok (Tzidkas HaTzaddik 171): "There is no reward for a commandment in this world" because the Holy One, blessed be He, gives a full load, and this world cannot receive that abundance of good at all; so here only sins are repaid, unless one merits tasting the fruit of his deeds or of commandments that bear fruit. Hence a time, place or soul "prepared for calamity" [pur'aniyos] is prepared for repayment [pera'on]: there the abundance of the repayment becomes calamity, as in the breaking of the vessels through excess of light. Beis Yaakov (Vayeitzei 6): Because "there is no reward for a commandment in this world," Israel holds only the markers [tziyunim] of the good, while the essence of the good is with the nations; in the future both will be joined together with Israel, as the Blessed One returns the essence to the place of the markers — hence the blessing "Who returns His Presence to Zion [Tziyon]." אַף עַל מַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּגְלֵית בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
and reward for a mitzvah does not exist in this world (Kiddushin 39b), even for manifest physical deeds enacted here.
כִּי עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת,
For with idolaters, all their deeds originate solely from outward display,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא שָׁם: שֶׁאֵין עוֹשִׂים אֶלָּא לְהִתְיַהֵר,
and as they stated in Bava Batra there: they act exclusively to glorify themselves,
וּבִפְשִׁיטוּת טְלָפַיִם דְּעֵשָׂו: "רְאוּ שֶׁאֲנִי טָהוֹר" (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה סה).
and by way of Esau extending his split hooves, boasting: "See that I am kosher" (Bereishit Rabbah 65).
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַפֵּחַ שְׂכַר כָּל בְּרִיָּה;
Nevertheless, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any creature;
וּלְפִי שֶׁרוֹצֶה לְהַרְאוֹת עַצְמוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת טוֹב,
and since such a person wishes to display himself in this world according to outward virtue,
עַל כֵּן שְׂכָרוֹ כֵּן רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת לְבַד.
his reward is tailored accordingly: strictly in this world, commensurate with outward appearance alone.
שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה: "עֹשֶׁר שָׁמוּר לִבְעָלָיו לְרָעָתוֹ" (קֹהֶלֶת ה, יב),
For in ultimate truth, even in this world: "riches are kept for their owner to his hurt" (Ecclesiastes 5:12),
וּ"מַרְבֶּה נְכָסִים מַרְבֶּה דְאָגָה" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ב, ז), וְלִבּוֹ מָלֵא יָגוֹן וַאֲנָחָה,
and "he who multiplies possessions multiplies anxiety" (Avot 2:7), his heart being full of sorrow and groaning,
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת הוּא קִיבּוּל שָׂכָר טוֹב.
except that from the perspective of superficial manifestation it appears as favorable reward.
אֲבָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עִיקַּר כַּוָּונָתָם עַל הַנֶּעְלָמוֹת וְלַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן קוֹנָם לְבַד,
However, regarding the children of Israel, their primary intent focuses upon the hidden realms to fulfill their Maker's will alone,
וּמַה שֶּׁעוֹשִׂים נִגְלוֹת גַּם כֵּן – הוּא רַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁכֵּן רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
and whatever overt actions they perform are enacted solely because such is the will of Hashem, blessed be He.
וַאֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אֵיזֶה כַּוָּונָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ,
And even one who harbors an impure, ulterior motive,
אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּמַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵין מִצְטָרְפוֹת לְמַעֲשֶׂה,
is regarded merely like an intrusive evil thought in Israel which is not joined to the deed;
כִּי עֹמֶק הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה הַנֶּעְלֶמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵן,
for the hidden depth of his soul's thought is not aligned with that distraction,
כִּי מַעֲמַקֵּי לִבָּם בֶּאֱמֶת דָּבוּק בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים,
since the innermost depths of their heart are truly cleaved unto the Living God,
וְזֶה כָּל מְגַמַּת מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם בֶּאֱמֶת.
and this is the true objective of all their deeds and striving.
וְלָכֵן אֵינוֹ בַּדִּין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה קִיבּוּל הַשָּׂכָר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
Therefore it is contrary to divine justice that their reward be paid in this world,
שֶׁהוּא שָׂכָר שֶׁמִּצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת לְבַד בְּלִי שׁוּם דִּיבּוּק בִּפְנִימִיּוּת,
which is an ephemeral reward of mere surface manifestation devoid of internal attachment,
כִּי מַה יִּתְרוֹן לָאָדָם בְּכָל רְכוּשׁוֹ דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא רַק כְּמוֹ רָגַע.
for what profit has a man in all worldly wealth which endures but a fleeting moment?
וְאַף דְּכָל הַתּוֹרָה מְלֵאָה מִבִּרְכוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה גַּם כֵּן בִּשְׂכַר הַמִּצְווֹת,
And even though the entire Torah is replete with material blessings of this world as recompense for the mitzvot,
אֵין זֶה שִׁילּוּם הַשָּׂכָר,
this does not constitute the ultimate payment of reward;
רַק הוּא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּא לְסַיֵּיעַ לְאָדָם שֶׁטּוֹב,
rather it represents Hashem coming to assist the person who chooses good,

כְּמִשְׁפַּט "הַבָּא לִטָּהֵר – מְסַיְּיעִין אוֹתוֹ" (שַׁבָּת קד.)1160 Shabbat 104a — This supports Resh Lakish, for Resh Lakish said: What is meant by that which is written, "If it concerns the scorners, He scorns them, but to the humble He gives grace"? One who comes to defile himself — they open the way for him; one who comes to purify himself — they assist him. Rashi: "He scorns" — he scorns of his own accord: they neither assist him nor prevent him; "but to the humble" — to one who is drawn toward the good trait — "He gives grace": they assist him from Heaven. "They assist him" — and prepare an opening for him. Tosafos (s.v. "one who comes to defile himself"): Some read [of one who comes to defile himself] "there are openings for him" — that is, he has openings through which to enter — whereas one who comes to purify himself is assisted, in that an opening is opened for him to enter, corresponding to the kuf above, which leaves him an opening to enter. For those who read "they open for him," one must say that "they assist him" is more than "they open." Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 104a): When a person comes to purify himself and to be wholly good in actuality, Heaven assists him to become so, for once he has begun to go out from potential to actuality, the Blessed One, who perfects all things, brings him to completion; but one who does not come to purify himself and remains in potential is not assisted from Heaven. One who comes to defile himself is left alone and not hindered at all; and it says "they open" because he is like one who stands at the door seeking to enter, to whom they open — since he supposes this to be his completion, what he imagines to be his completion is opened to him. But purification is true completion, and so one who comes to purify himself is assisted all the more. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas HaShabbos 2): Although the Blessed One assisted in the building of the First Temple, it hung on a condition, and once it was destroyed it became retroactively clear that it was the work of flesh and blood. What was built of itself in it was only in the manner of "one who comes to purify himself is assisted" — mere assistance, and "an assistant counts for nothing" where the one is able and the other is not; hence it was not built by the hand of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Takanas HaShavin 15): Were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, opens a gate to those who knock in repentance, one could not prevail against the inclination and truly return; but "one who comes to purify himself is assisted," at times by way of great gates and at times by way of doorways and windows, all according to the nature of his sins and the dullness of his heart. So long as there still remains a small opening, even like the point of a needle, through which he may enter to be roused to return, it keeps widening like the opening of a hall. Beis Yaakov (Vayishlach 6): A person cannot rely on the strength of his good deeds in this world to bring him good, for all the strength and assurance in this world lies only in words of Torah: "one who comes to purify himself is assisted," and whoever comes to draw near to the Blessed One, the Blessed One draws him near. Only at times, when the upper world is united with the lower, does the Blessed One let a person taste the fruit of his deeds in this world. Tiferes Yosef (Talmud Anthology, Pesachim 4): Like a nazir who became impure, worries stir in a person's heart that perhaps even his original intention was mistaken and not for the sake of Heaven: for had it been acceptable at its outset — surely "whoever comes to purify himself is assisted" — why did such an act come his way to spoil his intention? So it seems to him that he is utterly cut off from the Blessed One, and he has no recourse but to undo his first count and begin anew. Sod Yesharim (Seventh Night of Pesach 10): Abimelech wished to liken himself in all his deeds to Abraham, and one may ask why all his service did not avail him, since the Sages said, "One who comes to purify himself is assisted." But the Blessed One showed Abraham, "your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies": whoever does not, before his service, include himself in the gate of Abraham our father gains nothing from all the righteousness of his service, and even the most righteous convert, with all his mighty service, is not called a righteous convert so long as he does not include himself in Abraham's gate.,
in accordance with: "He who comes to purify himself is aided" (Shabbat 104a),
דְּעַל יְדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ פַּרְנָסָה בְּרִיוַּוח וּשְׁאָר טוֹבוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה יוּכַל לְהוֹסִיף בַּעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
so that by possessing ample sustenance and worldly ease he may expand his divine service.
וּמִצַּד הַזֶּה יֵשׁ חִיבּוּר לְטוֹבַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה עִם טוֹבָה הָאֲמִיתִּית הַמִּתְקַיֶּימֶת לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד,
And from this vantage point, worldly blessing connects to the authentic, everlasting good,
כַּאֲשֶׁר עַל יְדֵי זֶה עוֹבֵד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ;
when through it one actively serves Hashem;
וְנִמְצָא אֵין הַשָּׂכָר טוֹבַת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּלָל,
and consequently the reward is not material bounty at all,

רַק כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד1161 Pirkei Avot 4:2 — Ben Azzai said: Run to a light commandment as to a weighty one, and flee from transgression; for one commandment draws another commandment after it, and one transgression draws another transgression after it. For the reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression., ב): "שְׂכַר מִצְוָה – מִצְוָה",
but rather as they taught (Avot 4:2): "the reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah",
שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְסַיְּיעוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה אַחֶרֶת, וְנִמְצָא עֲדַיִן הוּא בִּכְלַל "הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם".
in that Hashem enables him to perform another mitzvah, remaining situated within "today for performing them."
וְזֶהוּ הַקִּיבּוּל שָׂכָר שֶׁמִּצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
And this is the nature of reward received in this world:
דְּ"יָפָה שָׁעָה אַחַת בִּתְשׁוּבָה וּמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִכָּל חַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא",
that "better is one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come",
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְסַיְּיעוֹ וּמְעוֹרְרוֹ עוֹד לִתְשׁוּבָה וּלְמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים, הֲרֵי שְׂכָרוֹ בַּשָּׁעוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
and since Hashem assists and stirs him further toward repentance and deeds, his reward is realized within those sanctified hours in this world.
אֲבָל אֵין זֶה עִיקַּר הַשָּׂכָר עֲדַיִן,
Yet this is not the ultimate core of reward,
שֶׁהֲרֵי גַּם עַל אוֹתָן שָׁעוֹת עוֹד עָתִיד לְהוֹסִיף לְקַבֵּל שָׂכָר;
for even upon those very hours he is destined to receive additional recompense;
וְעִיקַּר הַשָּׂכָר הוּא הַקּוֹרַת רוּחַ דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁבִּפְנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב,
and the primary reward is the serene contentment of the World to Come within the inner heart,
שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא עִיקַּר שְׁלֵימוּת הָעֲבוֹדָה דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
wherein resides the essence of Israel's completed service.
וּפֵירוּשׁ "קוֹרַת רוּחַ" – קְרִירוּת רוּחַ:
And the meaning of korat ruach is cooling of the spirit:
אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְחַמֵּם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
after becoming heated through the dynamic toil of this world,
שָׁם שֶׁ"נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ", הוּא מִתְנַפֵּשׁ וּמִתְקָרֵר מֵחֲמִימוּת הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת;
there, where "his soul rested," he catches his breath and cools down from the heat of holy exertion;
וְזֶהוּ הַנַּיָּיחָא כְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת שֶׁבּוֹ שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַשׁ מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ דְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה.
and this is tranquility like the Sabbath day, wherein He ceased and rested from His labor of the six working days.
וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית הָעֹנֶג:
And this is the pinnacle of delight:
כְּשֶׁמִּתְעַנֵּג אַחַר כָּךְ מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ וְרוֹאֶה דְּלֹא לָרִיק יָגַע,
when one subsequently relishes his accomplishments, beholding that he did not labor in vain,
וְכָל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה "הִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד",
and all that he wrought is "behold, very good",
וְשֶׁכְּבָר נִשְׁלַם כָּל מְלַאכְתּוֹ כֻּלָּהּ וְלֹא חָסַר כְּלוּם –
and that his entire labor is fully finished with nothing lacking—
זֶהוּ תַּכְלִית שְׁלֵימוּת הָעֹנֶג דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא;
this is the absolute perfection of delight of the World to Come;

שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נב)1162 Shemot Rabbah 52:3 — She said to him: Rabbi, does a man see his fellow in the World to Come? Does not each and every righteous man have a world to himself, as it is said, "For the man goes to his eternal home [beit olamo], and the mourners go about the streets"? It is not written olamim, in the plural, but olamo — his own world. Rav Tzadok (Sichas Malachei HaShares 3): [Against those who believe only in the creation before their eyes,] the Sages explained in several places that there exist different worlds, clear and recognizable to the eyes of the discerning though not to the fleshly eyes of fools — as on the verse "for man goes to his eternal home": "each righteous man has a world of his own." עַל פָּסוּק (קֹהֶלֶת יב, ה): "כִּי הֹלֵךְ הָאָדָם אֶל בֵּית עוֹלָמוֹ":
concerning which our Sages expounded (Shemot Rabbah 52) on the verse (Ecclesiastes 12:5): "For man goes to his eternal home":
שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ עוֹלָם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ,
that each individual possesses a distinct world unto himself,
הַיְינוּ מִדַּת נַפְשׁוֹ, דְּהָאָדָם נִקְרָא "עוֹלָם קָטָן";
meaning the spiritual measure of his soul, for man is titled a "microcosm";
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הִשְׁלִים כָּל בִּנְיַן קוֹמָתוֹ עַל תִּיקּוּנָהּ וּשְׁלֵימוּתָהּ,
and when he has brought the entire stature of his soul to its rectification and completion,
הֲרֵי הִתְקִין לוֹ כָּל מְלֶאכֶת עוֹלָמוֹ בִּשְׁלֵימוּת,
he has perfected the entire fabrication of his personal universe,
וְזוֹכֶה לִשְׁבִיתָה וְנַיָּיחָא הַשְּׁלֵימָה בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא,
meriting the complete rest and tranquility of the World to Come,

דְּ"אֵין בּוֹ וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא צַדִּיקִים יוֹשְׁבִים" (בְּרָכוֹת יז.)1163 Berakhot 17a — Rav was wont to say: The World to Come is not like this world. In the World to Come there is no eating and no drinking, no procreation and no commerce, no envy and no hatred and no rivalry. Rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads and take delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence, as it is stated: “And they beheld God, and they ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11). Rashi: "And they ate and drank" — they were sated by the radiance of the Divine Presence as though they had eaten and drunk. Maharsha: He derives the point from the redundancy and the change of wording in the verse: Scripture had already said "and they saw the God of Israel," and then says again "and they beheld God" — and "beholding" generally denotes an intellectual vision, a prophecy. They beheld and took delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence as though they had eaten and drunk; for at the giving of the Torah they were in the likeness of the World to Come, their crowns upon their heads, as it is said [in Shabbat 88a] that every Israelite received two crowns, and they were removed from bodily things, as it is said of Moses that he did not eat for forty days. Maharal (Derech Chaim on Avot 3:16): The meaning is that in the World to Come a man needs no completing, unlike this world, in which a man must receive his completion; there he will be complete on a higher level. He will therefore need no eating and drinking to complete himself, nor procreation — for offspring are a man's completion — nor commerce, by which a man supplies what he lacks; and there will be no envy or hatred, since these are themselves a defect. And "the righteous sit": the World to Come is not a thing of motion as this world is, and sitting signifies that a man is already complete in actuality and no longer moving toward his completion. Rav Tzadok (Divrei Soferim 4): Seeking to be a son of the World to Come purely for one's own sake is no different from seeking a reward in this world; but the essence of the World to Come, that "they delight in the radiance of the Shechinah," is not self-benefit. One can merit this even in this world — the "one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world" that is better than all the World to Come — when the reward of a mitzvah brings one to repentance, love and cleaving; for such a reward one may hope, and serving for it is wholly for its own sake, out of love. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 7): Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World to Come, and the World to Come is the absence of the action of "today to do them" — only "the righteous [sit] … and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah" — and Shabbat holds a semblance of this, which is why, though there is no reward for mitzvos in this world, Shabbat is called "a good gift." In this world one employs the powers of action, whereas the World to Come is the heart alone. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 11): From within this world, which is likened to night, they will merit the light of the World to Come, which is wholly day with no darkness or evil — the light of the world of Atzilus, the light of the seven days of creation hidden away for the righteous — when they sit "with their crowns on their heads," that is, their attachment to their root in the Blessed One, "and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah," that is, the upper Shechinah. This is the first heh of the Name, alluding to the understanding in the heart, the secret of the World to Come, where the attachment of the hearts of Israel to their source is revealed. Tiferes Yosef (Rosh Hashanah 1): With the creation of man "tohu and bohu" were set aside, for a person can raise his actions without limit and reach a lofty place, as stated: "In the World to Come there is no eating and no drinking … rather the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah." Through the act of the mitzvah of shofar one arouses the "great shofar," which shows that Israel raise all their actions up to the "upper sun," to the place where the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah, and through the shofar one can reach with one's actions and service to the light of the Infinite.,
wherein "there is no eating, etc., but the righteous sit" (Berakhot 17a),
הַיְינוּ לֹא מְהַלְּכִים כְּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
meaning they sit at rest, not walking dynamically as in this world.
כִּי עַל אָז נֶאֱמַר (קֹהֶלֶת ו, ט): "טוֹב מַרְאֵה עֵינַיִם מֵהֲלָךְ נָפֶשׁ",
For regarding that future state it is said (Ecclesiastes 6:9): "Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire",
שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא הִילוּךְ הַנֶּפֶשׁ, וּמֵאוֹתוֹ מַהֲלָךְ נִבְנֶה הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא;
for in this world unfolds the striving march of the soul, and from that spiritual journey the World to Come is constructed;
וְשָׁם אֵין בּוֹ עוֹד הִילוּךְ, אֶלָּא רְאוּת עֵינָיו,
whereas there, striving motion ceases, replaced by the direct perception of the eyes,
כְּעִנְיַן: "וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה" דְּמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית "וְהִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד" (בְּרֵאשִׁית א, לא).
akin to: "And God saw all that He had made" during Creation "and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31).
וְ"עַטְרוֹתֵיהֶם בְּרָאשֵׁיהֶם" (בְּרָכוֹת יז.) –
And "their crowns upon their heads" (Berakhot 17a) –
הֵם הָעֲטָרוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם שֶׁעָשׂוּ לְעַצְמָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
these are their very own crowns that they fashioned for themselves in this world;
וְהֵם שְׁתֵּי עֲטָרוֹת,
and they consist of two crowns,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (פח.)1164 Shabbat 88a — R. Simai expounded: When Israel gave precedence to “We will do” over “We will hear,” six hundred thousand ministering angels came and tied two crowns to each and every one of Israel, one corresponding to “We will do” and one corresponding to “We will hear.” And when Israel sinned, one million two hundred thousand angels of destruction came down and stripped them off, as it is stated: “And the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments from Mount Horeb.” Rashi: ["Two crowns":] of the radiance of the Divine Presence. ["One million two hundred thousand":] each one took one crown. Tosafos (s.v. "one million two hundred thousand came down"): He expounds the doubled number from "stripped themselves" (vayitnatzlu), read twice; some texts say explicitly: "It does not say vayinatzlu but vayitnatzlu." And though the measure of good exceeds the measure of retribution, here too [the good] is greater: a good angel would tie two crowns, while an angel of destruction had power to remove only one. Tosafos (s.v. "two crowns"): They were [crowns] of splendor; therefore, when Moses took them [as the Gemara goes on to say], the skin of his face shone. Maharsha: Through the crown of Torah they merited two further crowns, kingship and priesthood — "you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests" — because they took upon themselves both parts of the Torah, the positive commandments ("we will do") and the prohibitions ("we will hear"), putting the doing of the positive commandments before the hearing of the prohibitions; each angel bore one crown on the right, for priesthood and the attribute of lovingkindness, and one on the left, for kingship and the attribute of judgment. When they sinned with the calf, transgressing both the positive command "I am" and the prohibition "You shall have no [other gods]," which they heard from the mouth of the Almighty, the Angel of Death gained dominion over them and the angels of destruction stripped them of kingship and priesthood — which took effect when they went into exile for that sin, at the destruction, for "from Mount Horeb" alludes to the Temple mount laid waste (charev). The angels of destruction are doubled, 1,200,000, because at each of the two destructions 600,000 stripped Israel of kingship and priesthood. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 88a): Six hundred thousand tied the crowns but one million two hundred thousand took them away because when they were tied on their heads there was one angel [to each], for "we will do" and "we will hear" are one thing, neither existing without the other, and so it was not fitting that there be two angels, only one for "we will do and we will hear." But when they were taken from them, they had after all two diadems, and there was an angel of destruction for each crown, for in the taking away the two diadems were not joined. Maharal (Tiferes Yisrael, ch. 29): In every person there are two things, the being of the soul, which performs the deed, and the intellect; while the intellect is embedded in the body neither is free, for the intellect rules the soul and directs it by its understanding, and the intellect itself is sunk in the body. When they said "we will do" at once, before "we will hear," without the intellect's direction, the soul was in perfection and needed no guidance, and all the more so the intellect, which is higher, was no longer sunk in matter; so both became kings, neither needing the other, and the crowns tied on each one's head show that they were free and not embedded in matter. When they sinned they were no longer fit for these crowns, for the sinner is enslaved to his matter and his inclination and is no king — were he a king, he would rule over his inclination — and so the crowns departed from them.: דִּבְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה עִיטְּרוּ לְכָל אֶחָד שְׁתֵּי עֲטָרוֹת נֶגֶד "נַעֲשֶׂה" וְ"נִשְׁמָע".
as they stated in Shabbat (88a): at the Giving of the Torah they crowned each person with two crowns corresponding to "we will do" and "we will hear".
הַיְינוּ כְּלַל הָעֲבוֹדָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּנִגְלוֹת וּבְנִסְתָּרוֹת,
Meaning the entirety of divine service in this world: through manifest deeds and through concealed inner devotion;

דְּגַם הַדִּבּוּר כְּמַעֲשֶׂה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם (קיט:)1165 Shabbat 119b — Whoever prays on the eve of the Sabbath and recites "And the heavens and the earth were finished" — Scripture accounts it to him as though he had become a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the work of Creation. R. Elazar said: From where do we know that speech is like action? As it is stated, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made." Rashi: [Read not "were finished" but] "they finished": the Holy One, blessed be He, and this person, who recounts the praise of the Omnipresent and the praise of the Shabbat. Maharsha: One who says "And [the heavens and the earth] were finished" bears witness to the work of Creation, and so becomes a partner with the Holy One, blessed be He, for without his testimony His work would not be known. And just as the making was by utterance alone — hence the proof "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made" — so his testimony is by utterance, and it is as though he became a partner through utterance. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Shabbos 119b): Israel alone are the essential creation of the Holy One, blessed be He — the creation of the nations is secondary, following upon it — and an essential effect testifies to its cause; so when Israel say "And [the heavens and the earth] were finished," the effect bearing witness to the Cause who made all, it is as though they became partners with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the work of Creation. Alternatively, in its plain sense: unlike His other acts in the world, which are carried out through intermediaries, heaven and earth were made by His word alone — hence the proof that speech is called action, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made" — and so one who says "And they were finished" at its proper time, when sanctifying the day, joins his speech to the speech by which the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world.: "עֲקִימַת שְׂפָתָיו הָוֵי מַעֲשֶׂה",
for speech is also akin to action, as they stated there (119b): "the movement of the lips is deemed action",
וְהוּא מִכְּלַל הַנִּגְלוֹת לַזּוּלַת.
belonging to that which is manifest to others.
וְהֵם שְׁתֵּי מַדְרֵגוֹת בְּנִגְלוֹת, כִּשְׁתַּיִם שֶׁבְּנִסְתָּרוֹת בְּמוֹחַ וָלֵב,
And these are two rungs in the manifest realm, mirroring the two hidden rungs within the brain and the heart,
שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם כְּלוּלִים בְּ"נִשְׁמָע".
both of which are encompassed within "we will hear."
וְהָעֲטָרָה הוּא שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהָרֹאשׁ,
And the crown is positioned above the head,
הַיְינוּ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיוּ נִמְשָׁכִים אַחַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְמַעְלָה מִשִּׂכְלָם.
meaning because they followed after Hashem, blessed be He, above the bounds of their intellect.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁזֶּה בִּשְׁבִיל הַקְדָּמַת "נַעֲשֶׂה" לְ"נִשְׁמָע",
And even though this was merited by advancing "we will do" before "we will hear",
אִם כֵּן הָיָה רַק עַל יְדֵי הַ"נַעֲשֶׂה" לְבַד – הָאֱמֶת הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ;
which might imply that it was earned through "we will do" alone—the truth is the reverse;
דְּוַודַּאי אִלּוּ הָיוּ עוֹשִׂים זֶה בִּבְהִילוּת, בְּלִי הִתְבּוֹנְנוּת בַּלֵּב כְּלָל וְשׁוּם הִתְיַישְּׁבוּת הַדַּעַת,
for surely had they uttered this impulsively, without inward heartfelt contemplation and sober balance of mind,
לֹא הָיָה זֶה נֶחְשָׁב בִּשְׁבַח דְּ"נַעֲשֶׂה" גַּם כֵּן,
this would not have been accounted to the praise of "we will do",
כֵּיוָון שֶׁבָּא מִצַּד חֶסְרוֹן יִשּׁוּב הַדַּעַת שֶׁלָּהֶם.
since it would have stemmed merely from a lack of emotional equilibrium.
וְכָךְ קְרָאָם הַהוּא מִינָא: "עַמָּא פְּזִיזָא דְּקַדְמִיתוּ וְכוּלֵי",
And thus that heretic derided them: "Rash nation that advanced your mouths, etc.",
דְּחָשַׁב זֶה לְמַעֲשֶׂה מְבוֹהָל וְנִמְהָר שֶׁאֵין מִתְבּוֹנֵן עַל דְּרָכָיו.
presuming this was a panicked, reckless move by one who does not evaluate his steps.
אֲבָל רָבָא הֱשִׁיבוֹ: "אֲנַן דְּסַגִּינַן בִּתְמִימוּתָא, כְּתִיב בַּן (מִשְׁלֵי יא, ג): 'תֻּמַּת יְשָׁרִים תַּנְחֵם'",
Yet Rava retorted unto him: "We who walk in wholeness, regarding us it is written (Proverbs 11:3): 'The integrity of the upright shall guide them'",
שֶׁלֹּא מִצַּד הַמְּהִירוּת הָיָה, רַק מִצַּד הַתְּמִימוּת;
showing that this act was born not of recklessness, but of holy simplicity;
דְּהִתְבּוֹנְנוּ יָפֶה וְהֶעֱלוּ עַל לִבָּם דְּאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר כָּבֵד וְקָשֶׁה מְאֹד לְקַבֵּל,
for they contemplated deeply and realized that it might be extraordinarily demanding to accept,
אֲבָל דָּחוּ מַחְשְׁבוֹת לְבָבָם וְהָלְכוּ בִּתְמִימוּת עִם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הִקְדִּימוּ הַ"נַעֲשֶׂה".
yet they set aside human calculation and walked in complete faith with Hashem, thereby advancing "we will do".
וְזֶהוּ "תַּנְחֵם" כְּעִנְיַן "בְּהִתְהַלֶּכְךָ תַּנְחֶה",
And this is "shall guide them", echoing "when you walk it shall guide you",
הַיְינוּ הִילוּךְ הַ"נַעֲשֶׂה";
referring to the practical stride of "we will do";
וְ"תֻּמַּת יְשָׁרִים" הוּא הַתְּמִימוּת שֶׁבַּלֵּב,
while "the integrity of the upright" is the simplicity in the heart,
וְהַיַּשְׁרוּת הוּא בַּלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תְּהִלִּים צז, יא): "וּלְיִשְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה".
and uprightness resides in the heart, as it is written (Psalms 97:11): "and gladness for the upright in heart".

וְאָמְרוּ בְּתַעֲנִית (טו.)1166 Taanit 15a — R. Nachman bar Yitzchak said: I too say — not all are for light, and not all are for gladness. The righteous are for light, and the upright for gladness. The righteous for light, as it is written, "Light is sown for the righteous"; and gladness for the upright, as it is written, "and gladness for the upright in heart." Rashi: The correct reading is: "Not all is for light and not all is for gladness, as it is written, 'Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart'": the upright are for gladness, for the upright are superior to the righteous. Tosafos (s.v. "light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart"): One cannot say here, as above [of the kings and the princes], that the upright have both gladness and light: if "the upright in heart" referred back to light, "the righteous" would likewise refer forward to gladness, since the two stand side by side; and there is surely a difference between them, for otherwise Scripture would have joined them and written, "for the righteous and the upright in heart, light and gladness." Above, the kings and the princes were not side by side, but "shall see and arise" stood between them, and so applied to the princes written after it as well as to the kings before it; here, however, the verse can only mean light for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart. Maharsha: Rashi explains that the upright are superior to the righteous, whereas the Rashba writes that the upright are a level below the righteous, as appears from the order in Nishmat: "upright, righteous, pious, holy"; yet the Rashba's claim that the righteous merit light, the essence of delight, and all the more so gladness, does not fit the wording "not all is for gladness." Rather, "light" denotes spiritual delight in the World to Come and "gladness" bodily delight: the righteous merit light in the World to Come, and it is called "sown" because, as what is sown sprouts and grows, so the light of the righteous one's apprehension sprouts and grows continually, as it is said, "the righteous sit and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah." The upright do not merit this, but only gladness, a bodily delight that gladdens the heart of the upright. Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 16): The holiness of bodily matters — being able to do them in holiness without having to hold back from anything one's heart desires, since all is holy to God — brings gladness, as Ta'anis says, "the righteous are for light and the upright for gladness": the righteous man fences himself in and subdues his desires, and so dwells without much gladness, meriting only "light," which is Torah, an inner feeling; but the upright of heart, whose heart is straight and desires only what the Blessed One wishes him to desire, need not fence himself in, and he has gladness. And this is the essence of the gladness of Adar, through the revelation of the uprightness of Israel's heart. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Toldos 8): "The righteous are for light": the righteous man is one whose heart is not yet entirely straightened — the foolish heart is not yet purified and he still wrestles with it — and he needs light, that the Blessed One illuminate him with wisdom and understanding to subdue his inclination. Afterwards, when his heart is straightened and even the foolish heart is cleansed of foolish thoughts, "the light of the righteous rejoices," and this is "gladness for the upright in heart," for he has become entirely whole and cleaves to the Holy One, blessed be He, and from this comes gladness.: "לֹא הַכֹּל לְאוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי, צַדִּיקִים לְאוֹרָה וִישָׁרִים לְשִׂמְחָה",
And they taught in Ta'anit (15a): "Not all are for light, etc.; the righteous are for light, and the upright are for joy",
נִרְאֶה לִי כִּי "אוֹרָה" וְ"שִׂמְחָה" הוּא עִינּוּגִים הַנִּמְשָׁכִים מִכֹּחַ הָעֲטָרוֹת הַנִּזְכָּרוֹת;
it appears to me that "light" and "joy" are transcendent delights drawn from the power of these two crowns;
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָעֲטָרוֹת הֵם שְׁתַּיִם לְכָל אֶחָד, הָעִינּוּג הוּא מֵאוֹתָהּ הַמַּבְהֶקֶת בְּיוֹתֵר.
for even though the crowns are two for every individual, the primary delight is derived from whichever one shines most radiantly.
וּבָזֶה אֵין הַכֹּל שָׁוִים:
And in this not all are identical:
צַדִּיקִים הֵם עוֹבְדֵי ה' בַּפּוֹעַל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּגְלֵית, וַעֲטֶרֶת הַ"נַעֲשֶׂה" הָעִיקָּר אֶצְלָם,
the righteous are those who serve Hashem in practical execution through manifest action, the crown of "we will do" being primary for them,
זוֹכִים לְ"אוֹרָה", שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן עֹנֶג הַגָּלוּי, כִּי הָאוֹר הוּא גַּם כֵּן דָּבָר הַגָּלוּי וְנִרְאֶה.
and they merit "light," which is an overtly perceived delight, light being visible and manifest.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַשִּׂמְחָה הוּא בַּלֵּב וְאֵין נִגְלֶה לַזּוּלַת,
In contrast, joy resides within the heart and is hidden from outsiders,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מִשְׁלֵי יד, י): "וּבְשִׂמְחָתוֹ לֹא יִתְעָרַב זָר", וְזֶהוּ לְיִשְׁרֵי לֵב.
as it is written (Proverbs 14:10): "and with its joy no stranger can intermingle", and this belongs to the upright in heart.
וְאֵלּוּ הָעֲטָרוֹת הוּא מִשֶּׁלָּהֶם מֵהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
And these crowns belong to them from their spiritual toil in this world,
אֲבָל שְׂכָרָם בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא "וְנֶהֱנִין מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה" (בְּרָכוֹת יז.).
yet their ultimate reward in the World to Come is "delighting in the radiance of the Shechinah" (Berakhot 17a).
וְיָדוּעַ דִּשְׁכִינָה הוּא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹךְ לִבְבוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל,
And it is known that the Shechinah embodies Hashem dwelling within the hearts of Israel,
דְּעַל כֵּן הִיא נִקְרֵאת "כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל",
which is why she is designated the "Congregation of Israel",
דְּזֶהוּ מַה שֶּׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל;
for this represents the Holy One being the heart of Israel;
דִּכְלַל מַעֲמַקֵּי לִבְבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהוּא כְּלַל הַכְּנֵסִיָּה, הוּא כְּלַל שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מַה שֶּׁשּׁוֹכֵן בְּתוֹכָם גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
such that the sum of the inner recesses of Jewish hearts, which forms the collective body, constitutes His Shechinah dwelling amidst them even in this world.
אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם עָצוּם בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי לְבָבוֹ,
Except that in this world this Divine Presence is shrouded in profound concealment within the heart's depths,
וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא מַבְהִיק וְיוֹצֵא מִמַּעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב שֶׁל כָּל אֶחָד אֶל הַגִּילוּי לִהְיוֹת נֶהֱנֶה מִזִּיווֹ.
whereas in the World to Come it blazes forth from the heart of each individual into revelation to delight in His radiance.
וְהַנָאָה זוֹ הִיא עֶצֶם הַנָאַת עוֹלָם הַבָּא
And this bliss constitutes the very essence of the World to Come's delight,
שֶׁמִּצַּד הַשְּׁבִיתָה וְנַיָּיחָא שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ לְשׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
emanating from the rest and tranquility that requires no further striving,
וְאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם חִילּוּף וְהִשְׁתַּנּוּת מַדְרֵגוֹת.
admitting no differentiation or fluctuations of rungs.
אֲבָל הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת הֵם מִצַּד הָעֲטָרוֹת שֶׁהֵם בָּאִים מִצַּד הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת,
However, distinct levels emerge from the crowns which reflect specific human striving,
שֶׁבָּזֶה אֵין כָּל אֶחָד דּוֹמֶה לַחֲבֵירוֹ;
in which no two individuals are identical;
וְכֵן אֵצֶל כָּל אֶחָד אֵין זְמַן אֶחָד דּוֹמֶה לַחֲבֵירוֹ,
and likewise within each individual no single moment resembles another,
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר (יְשַׁעְיָה סו, כג): "וְהָיָה מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ [בְּחָדְשׁוֹ וּמִדֵּי שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ] יָבוֹא כָל בָּשָׂר וְגוֹמֵר" גַּם לֶעָתִיד.
and concerning this it is said (Isaiah 66:23): "And it shall come to pass that from one new moon to another, and from one Sabbath to another, shall all flesh come, etc." even in the future.
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ סוֹף בְּרָכוֹת (סד.):
And this corresponds to what they stated at the end of Berakhot (64a):

"צַדִּיקִים אֵין לָהֶם מְנוּחָה, לֹא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלֹא בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: 'יֵלְכוּ מֵחַיִל אֶל חָיִל1167 Berakhot 64a — R. Chiya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav: Torah scholars have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come, as it is said, “They go from strength to strength, each appears before God in Zion.” Rashi: "They have no rest" — [they go] from one academy to another and from one house of study to another. Maharsha: One may object that the World to Come, which Torah scholars attain, is entirely rest — "a day that is wholly Sabbath and rest for life everlasting." But "rest" means the ceasing and completion of labor, as at creation, where with the coming of the Sabbath the work was finished and completed. Of the Torah scholar, whose activity is intellectual contemplation, he says that neither in this world nor in the next does that activity ever cease; and that very contemplation is itself the rest of the World to Come, in which the righteous sit and delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence. Maharal (Nesivos Olam, Nesiv HaTorah 9): It does not mean, Heaven forbid, that they have no rest, for they certainly have rest; it means that the level of a Torah scholar admits of no completion, for the intellect never reaches completion, since apprehension has no end — whatever one has grasped, more can still be grasped — and a thing that has no completion has no rest, since rest lies in a thing's being complete. In the World to Come too the scholar has no rest, since there also no apprehension is complete; hence "they go from strength to strength," passing from one apprehension to the next until he apprehends of Him what it is possible to apprehend, and that is "each appears before God in Zion." Nor is this a hardship: like the heavens, which are forever in motion and yet are not called weary, the intellect knows no toil — only that it has no completion, since all rest is an end, and to the intellect no end applies. Rav Tzadok (Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 4): Sins have a limit, as this world is bounded, whereas mitzvos have none — which is why there is no reward for a mitzvah in this world — and there is a view (Niddah 61b) that the mitzvos are not annulled in the time to come. So the Sages said, "The righteous have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come, as it is said, 'They go from strength to strength'" — for there too there is room for mitzvos. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 1): The Ra'aya Mehemna's "men of valor, from the side of Abraham's right, where there is the seeing of the Torah" refers to the Oral Torah, which "valor" alludes to, as the Sages said, "Torah scholars have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come, as it is said, 'They go from strength to strength'" [the same word], which Rashi explains as from yeshivah to yeshivah and from midrash to midrash. This is the seeing of the Torah, of the Oral Torah. Rav Tzadok (Yisrael Kedoshim 7): Jacob's rest is a complete rest, "a rest in which You delight," as the Sages said, "The righteous have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come," for "they go from strength to strength": their whole rest is when they are able to pursue the Lord. That is why it is a mitzvah to run to a mitzvah and to words of Torah even on the Sabbath, and why the communal offerings override the Sabbath — for this is their rest, to merit serving the Blessed One in truth.'".
"Torah scholars have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come, as it is stated: 'They shall go from strength to strength'."
וְאַף שֶׁשָּׁם הֵם "יוֹשְׁבִים" – לֹא "מְהַלְּכִים",
And even though there they "sit" and are not "walking",
הַיְינוּ מִצַּד עַצְמִיּוּתָם;
this pertains to their fundamental essence;
אֲבָל מִצַּד הַלְּבוּשִׁים וַעֲטָרוֹת שֶׁסִּיגְּלוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַה דְּ"יִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי",
yet from the perspective of the spiritual garments and crowns they amassed in this world through what "Israel sanctifies",
הֵם אֵין חֲפֵצִים בִּקְדוּשָּׁה שֶׁל נַיָּיחָא גְּמוּרָה,
they do not desire a sanctity of stagnant, static rest,
רַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְעוֹלָם קְצָת הֲלִיכָה וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, וְזֶהוּ הַהֲלִיכָה "מֵחַיִל אֶל חָיִל".
seeking rather an eternal dynamic advancement and striving, which is going "from strength to strength."
וְדָרְשׁוּ שָׁם גַּם עַל בֵּית הַכְּנֶסֶת וּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ,
And they expounded there also concerning the synagogue and the study hall,
הָרְמוּזִים גַּם כֵּן לִשְׁתֵּי עֲטָרוֹת דְּ"אוֹרָה" וְ"שִׂמְחָה":
which likewise allude to the two crowns of "light" and "joy":
"אוֹרָה" – זוֹ תּוֹרָה, וְ"שִׂמְחָה" – זוֹ תְּפִלָּה וַעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב;
"Light"—this is Torah, and "joy"—this is prayer and service of the heart;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (יְשַׁעְיָה נו, ז): "וְשִׂמַּחְתִּים בְּבֵית תְּפִלָּתִי",
and as it is written (Isaiah 56:7): "And I will make them joyful in My house of prayer",
וְנֶאֱמַר (תְּהִלִּים ק, ב): "עִבְדוּ אֶת ה' בְּשִׂמְחָה".
and it is stated (Psalms 100:2): "Serve Hashem with joy."
כִּי הַהֲלִיכָה אָז יִהְיֶה רַק בִּשְׁתֵּי עֲטָרוֹת אֵלּוּ;
For dynamic progression then will unfold specifically through these two crowns;
בְּעִנְיַן הַבְהָקָתָם יִהְיֶה לָהֶם הֲלִיכָה מֵחַיִל אֶל חַיִל וּמִמַּדְרֵגָה לְמַדְרֵגָה,
in the intensity of their radiance they will advance from strength to strength and from rung to rung,
"מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ וְשַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ" כְּפִי שִׁינּוּי הַזְּמַנִּים.
"from one new moon to another and from one Sabbath to another" according to the shifting seasons.
דְּגַם הַשַּׁבָּת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא קְדוּשָּׁה דִּקְבוּעָה וְקַיָּימָא,
For even Shabbat, although it is an inherently fixed and eternal sanctity,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נָהַג בּוֹ מִדָּה טוֹבָה וּנְתָנוֹ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל,
nonetheless Hashem, blessed be He, acted graciously and bestowed it upon Israel,
שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם זֶה שַׁיָּיךְ לָהֶם וּבִכְלַל מַה דְּאִינְהוּ מְקַדְּשֵׁי;
so that this too belongs to them, included in what they actively sanctify;
שֶׁהֲרֵי קִידּוּשׁ הַיּוֹם דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא,
for the verbal sanctification of the day is a biblical obligation,
שֶׁהֵם צְרִיכִים לְקַדֵּשׁ הַשַּׁבָּת כְּאִלּוּ הֵם בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם זָכוּ לָזֶה.
demanding that they sanctify Shabbat as though through their own effort they merited it.
וְכֵן אָמַר (שְׁמוֹת לא, טז): "וְשָׁמְרוּ וְגוֹמֵר לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת" –
And so Scripture states (Exodus 31:16): "And they shall keep... to observe/make (la'asot) the Sabbath" –
קָרֵי "עֲשִׂיָּה" בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁאֵינָהּ אֶלָּא שְׁבִיתָה מֵעֲשִׂיָּה!
calling it "making/doing" on Shabbat, when it is actually complete cessation from action!
אֶלָּא שֶׁמְּסָרָהּ לָהֶם לִהְיוֹת הֵם עוֹשִׂים אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
Rather, He entrusted it to them so that they "make" the Sabbath day
עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה:
through their diligent striving during the six working days:
בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים דִּמְקַמֵּי שַׁבַּתָּא וּשְׁלֹשָׁה דִּלְבָתַר שַׁבַּתָּא,
in the three days preceding Shabbat and the three days following Shabbat,
בִּקְדוּשַּׁת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה –
through the sanctity of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah—
עַל יְדֵי זֶה הֵם עוֹשִׂים אֶת יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת וּנְשָׁמָה יְתֵירָה שֶׁבּוֹ.
and through this they actively fashion the Sabbath day and its additional soul.
וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי קְדוּשַּׁת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בַּפּוֹעַל וּבְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת
And this is attained through the sanctity of concrete action and holy effort
לִהְיוֹת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם;
to ensure all their deeds are performed for the sake of Heaven;
עַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכִים לִהְיוֹת גַּם מִצְוַת הַשְּׁבִיתָה קָרוּי עַל שְׁמָם.
through this they merit having the commandment of Sabbath rest credited to their name.
וּבֶאֱמֶת עִיקַּר הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם הוּא בַּעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב,
And in truth, man's primary spiritual effort resides in the service of the heart,
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת לג.): "מָה ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה",
and as they expounded (Berakhot 33a): "What does Hashem your God ask of you but to revere",
וְהַיִּרְאָה הִיא בַּלֵּב,
and awe is seated in the heart,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (עב:): עַל פָּסוּק (מִשְׁלֵי יז, טז): "וְלֶב אָיִן" – עַל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם.
as they expounded in Yoma (72b) on the verse (Proverbs 17:16): "seeing he has no heart"—concerning a Torah scholar who lacks fear of Heaven.
וְהַתּוֹרָה הִיא עֲבוֹדָה הַנִּגְלֵית,
While the Torah represents manifest service,
דָּבָר זֶה עִיקָּרוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם,
this matter being fundamentally granted from Heaven,
וּכְדִשְׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (ו:): "לְאוֹקְמֵי גִּירְסָא – סִיַּיעְתָּא דִּשְׁמַיָּא".
and as they stated in Megillah (6b): "to retain one's learning requires assistance from Heaven".

וְאָמְרוּ בְּנִדָּה (טז:)1168 Niddah 16b — R. Chanina bar Pappa expounded: The angel appointed over conception is named Night. He takes the drop and sets it before the Holy One, blessed be He, and says before Him: Master of the Universe, this drop — what is to become of it? Mighty or weak? Wise or foolish? Rich or poor? But wicked or righteous he does not ask — in accordance with R. Chanina, who said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, as it is stated: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear [Him]” (Deuteronomy 10:12). Rashi: “Everything is in the hands of Heaven” — all a man's qualities and all that befalls him come upon him by the decree of the King, except this one. “But to fear” — this alone He asks of you, because everything else is in His hand and this is in yours. Tosafos (s.v. “the angel appointed over conception”): But over birth no angel is appointed, as is said at the beginning of Ta'anit: three keys are in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He — of a woman in childbirth, of rain, and of the resurrection of the dead. Even those three keys are at times handed over to an agent for a time, for Elijah held the key of rain and revived the dead, and so did Elisha and many righteous men; and even Beri, who is the prince of rain, acts only by the permission of the Holy One, blessed be He. Tosafos (s.v. “everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven”): In “Elu Na'arot” it is said that everything is in the hands of Heaven except cold and heat. Here the statement concerns a man's nature and his traits, while there it concerns the things that befall him, such as illnesses and calamities, all of which are decreed upon him and against which he cannot guard himself — except cold and heat, against which he can guard himself. Maharsha (Chidushei Agadot, s.v. “this drop, what shall become of it — mighty or weak, wise [or foolish]”): This is the meaning of the verse “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom”: what is compelled is neither praised nor blamed, and therefore these three — wisdom, might and wealth — which are compelled by the decree from the hour of a man's formation, are no ground for glorying. “But let him that glories glory in this, that he understands and knows Me” — for that is the thing which depends upon his choice. Maharal (Chiddushei Aggados, Niddah 16b): He is called Night because the gestation takes place in the woman's belly, “like the bones in the womb of her that is with child,” and the child is there in darkness. Therefore the angel appointed over gestation is called Night, since in the belly it is always night and never day. Rav Tzadok (Kometz HaMinchah, part I 4): "If you have learned much Torah, do not claim credit for yourself" [as if] you were better than others, "for that is why you were created," as stated in Niddah: "wise or foolish." And so the early authorities explained "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom … but let him who glories glory in this," in keeping with what is said there: "righteous or wicked he does not say." Rav Tzadok (Likutei Ma'amarim, festival discourses 11): The Torah is called "a good lekach [lit. "taking"] I have given you," both a taking and a gift: in truth it is a good gift that the Blessed One gave in this world, a semblance of the World to Come, of which it is said "I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious," without any effort, for "wise or foolish" is from birth, and only "righteous or wicked he does not say," and "all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven." That fear of Heaven, which is a man's own effort, is "the beginning of wisdom," and so [the Torah] appears as something taken, because of his effort in fear of Heaven. Rav Tzadok (Machshavos Charutz 8): The Sages said "You created righteous, You created wicked," yet they said "righteous or wicked he does not say"; but in truth "a gourd is known by its shoot," and one can recognize even in children that some are formed from the outset with a good nature, to walk in innocence and uprightness, and some the opposite, and this falls under "wise or foolish," for the intent is not human wisdom but the wisdom of truth, to conduct oneself as is fitting. This has nothing to do with the choice between righteous and wicked: even one created righteous has an inclination that overpowers him every day, and the choice is his, and one created wicked likewise has the choice to subdue the inclination of heart he was born with and return to the Blessed One.: דְּנִכְרָז בַּתּוֹלָדָה: "חָכָם אוֹ טִפֵּשׁ", וְהַיְינוּ חָכָם בַּתּוֹרָה;
And they said in Niddah (16b): at conception it is proclaimed "wise or foolish," referring to wisdom in Torah;
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם לָזֶה צָרִיךְ יְגִיעָה וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת.
save that nevertheless, this too requires toil and personal exertion.
וְאַדְּרַבָּה, רוֹב מִצְווֹת הַתּוֹרָה הוּא בְּמַעֲשֶׂה בַּפּוֹעַל;
And on the contrary, most commandments of the Torah are rooted in practical action;
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם בְּכוּלָּם: אַחַר כַּוָּונַת הַלֵּב הֵן הַדְּבָרִים,
nevertheless, across all of them: matters are judged by the intention of the heart,
וְהוּא הָעִיקָּר בָּעֲבוֹדָה.
and that constitutes the essence of divine service.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא עִיקַּר קְדוּשַּׁת הַחֹדֶשׁ דְּ"יִשְׂרָאֵל מְקַדְּשֵׁי",
And through this manifests the core sanctity of the month which "Israel sanctifies",
לִהְיוֹת מִתְחַדֵּשׁ כָּל יוֹם תָּמִיד אַחַר הַהֶעְלֵם;
being continuously renewed every single day after concealment;
כִּי הַרְגָּשַׁת הַחִידּוּשׁ וְהַהֶעְלֵם הוּא בַּלֵּב.
for the dynamic sensation of renewal and concealment takes place within the heart.
וְגַם רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ בִּכְלַל שִׂמְחָה,
Moreover, Rosh Chodesh is included within joy,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בַּמִּדְבָּר י, י): "וּבְיוֹם שִׂמְחַתְכֶם וּבְמוֹעֲדֵיכֶם וּבְרָאשֵׁי חָדְשֵׁיכֶם",
as it is written (Numbers 10:10): "And in the day of your gladness, and in your set feasts, and in the beginnings of your months",
כִּי קְדוּשַּׁת הָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב מְבִיאָה שִׂמְחָה לַלֵּב.
for the sanctity of heart-centered service infuses joy into the heart.
אֲבָל בְּשַׁבָּת לֹא נִזְכַּר שִׂמְחָה, רַק אוֹרָה;
However, on Shabbat joy is not explicitly mentioned, only light;

אָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה יא)1169 Bereshit Rabbah 11:2 — "And God blessed the seventh day" — He blessed it with the light of a man's face, and He sanctified it with the light of a man's face: the light of a man's face on all the days of the week is not like the light of his face on the Sabbath. Rav Tzadok (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis 2): Adam's radiance, the first of the six things taken from him after the sin, which will all return in the time to come, is the light of the face of the Sabbath, as it says, "He blessed it with the light of a man's face"; for through the holiness of the Sabbath, a semblance of the World to Come, one surely merits these six things already. עַל פָּסוּק (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב, ג): "וַיְבָרֶךְ אֱלֹהִים אֶת יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי" – בֵּרְכוֹ בִּמְאוֹר פָּנָיו,
they taught in Bereishit Rabbah (11) on the verse (Genesis 2:3): "And God blessed the seventh day"—He blessed it with the light of His countenance,
וְכֵן לֹא נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ "וַיְהִי עֶרֶב" כִּי כֻּלּוֹ אוֹר.
and likewise "and there was evening" is not stated regarding it, because it is entirely luminous.
כִּי בִּקְדוּשַׁת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה זוֹכֶה לְאוֹר תּוֹרָה הַמְּאִירָה לָאָדָם,
For through the holiness of practical action one merits the light of Torah which illuminates man,
